- **CRYSTALS-Dilithium becomes ML-DSA (FIPS 204): the signature half of the NIST pair (new to the record).** Submitted as CRYSTALS-Dilithium in twenty eighteen by a seven-researcher team (Ducas, Kiltz, Lepoint, Lyubashevsky, Schwabe, Seiler, Stehlé); NIST picked it on July fifth, twenty twenty-two, as its primary digital-signature standard alongside Kyber for encryption and Falcon and SPHINCS-plus for signatures; the final standard, ML-DSA, was published as FIPS 204 on August thirteenth, twenty twenty-four. [CORROBORATED — selection and publication dates carried by multiple independent outlets; authorship from the submission's own citation] The construction is a lattice Schnorr built on Lyubashevsky's "Fiat-Shamir with aborts" paradigm: the signer proves knowledge of a short secret lattice vector by producing a signature that passes norm checks, with no trapdoor to steal and no Gaussian sampling to get wrong — the implementation pitfall that has kept the Falcon-based follow-on in draft. Security rests on the module short-integer-solution and module learning-with-errors problems. Three parameter sets (ML-DSA-forty-four, -sixty-five, -eighty-seven) at NIST security levels two, three, and five; NIST positions it as the main signature standard with hash-based SLH-DSA as the backup on different math, so one surprise cannot sink both. [CORROBORATED — multiple secondary summaries of the standard; the main/backup framing is NIST's own] Why the decoder keeps it: ML-DSA is the receipt-stamping primitive the migration ledger runs on — verifiable evidence, attested containers, and receipt chains that must survive a quantum adversary all need a quantum-resistant signature, and this is the one actually standardized. The Cosmos production entry above is ML-DSA signing a live consensus layer. [DOCTRINE]
- **Autonomous quantum error correction beyond break-even (Nature Physics, October twenty twenty-six; new to the record).** A logical qubit encoded across the internal spin states of a single trapped ion, with engineered interactions moving error entropy into motion that a helper ion then cools away — correction with no repeated measurements and no real-time classical feedback loop. Under deliberately injected low-frequency noise, the corrected qubit lasted about eleven point six milliseconds, against under one millisecond for the bare physical qubit and the uncorrected encoding. The honest caveats: one logical qubit, one error type, lab-injected noise — not a scalable machine, no universal protected gates, no useful calculation yet, and this week's event is peer-reviewed publication of an April twenty twenty-five preprint, not a new experiment. Decoder significance: a third attack on the fault-tolerance bottleneck — not faster classical decoding, not cheaper states, but correction that needs less machinery around it. The watch items are whether it extends to several error types at once, preserves entanglement across logical qubits, and supports fault-tolerant gates without losing its low-overhead advantage. [CORROBORATED — peer-reviewed journal paper plus an agreeing secondary brief; paper not read first-hand this pass]
- **Modular graph neural decoder for surface-code memory and lattice surgery (Gothenburg and Chalmers, preprint, reported October twenty twenty-six).** A renormalization-inspired graph neural network: a shared local network processes small three-by-three-by-two space-time clusters of syndrome detection events, coarse-grained through lightweight convolutional layers and integrated across time by a gated recurrent unit. The design sidesteps the dense recurrent-Transformer bloat of decoders like AlphaQubit — attention bottlenecks that grow with the fourth power of code distance, and training clusters to match. Total parameter count stays bounded at roughly two to three million across code distances three, five, seven, and nine, and training fits on a single commercial graphics card. Validated on superconducting hardware data from IBM Quantum's Nighthawk generation and Google Quantum AI's below-threshold Sycamore processor: it beats minimum-weight perfect matching on memory experiments and successfully decodes a real two-patch lattice-surgery operation, and the same architecture transfers across hardware, noise profiles, and multi-patch logical operations. Decoder significance: the classical-decode bottleneck race gains its first transferable, cheap-to-train neural decoder that handles logic operations, not just memory — if the preprint's numbers hold on independent hardware runs, real-time decoding stops being a per-machine bespoke build and becomes a portable module. Honest caveats: preprint, single-outlet coverage, memory and lattice-surgery scope only, no fault-tolerant computation demonstrated. [CLAIMED — preprint via a trade outlet, October twenty twenty-six; not read first-hand; no peer review]
- **Mamba state-space neural decoder for real-time quantum error correction (Yonsei University, peer-reviewed, npj Quantum Information; reported October twenty twenty-six).** A neural decoder built from a stabilizer embedder, a recurrent core, a syndrome mixer, and a readout network, on the Mamba state-space architecture. The advance is cost, not accuracy: decoding complexity falls from fourth-power to second-power scaling in code distance, matching Transformer-based models on experimental memory benchmarks while removing the attention bottlenecks that block real-time feedback on physical hardware. Why the decoder keeps it: a decoder has to keep up with the machine mid-computation, and attention's scaling is what blocks that — so this is the second cheap-to-run neural decoder this week attacking the same wall from a different architecture family, after the Gothenburg graph network. The honest caveats: memory-benchmark scope as reported, no fault-tolerant computation demonstrated, and the paper itself was not read first-hand this pass. [CORROBORATED — peer-reviewed journal paper plus an agreeing secondary brief; paper not read first-hand]
- **Selective-orthogonality quantum LDPC code (Kasai, Institute of Science Tokyo; TechXplore carrier, September 2026, reporting a paper in the journal Quantum; new to the record).** Classical LDPC design theory transfers to quantum codes only if the two error-check types are made orthogonal; Kasai applies orthogonality only to the selected rows used for error correction, using affine permutation matrices, preserving classical design freedom. The resulting (3,12)-regular, girth-8 code is written [[9216,4612,d]] with d at most 48: it protects 4,612 logical qubits with 9,216 physical qubits — roughly one logical qubit per two physical qubits — with weight-48 logical operators constructible explicitly and X- and Z-type distances both exactly 48 for the latent structure; searches and simulations found no lower-weight logical errors, though a global lower bound on distance remains open. Decoding is belief-propagation with low-complexity postprocessing: a clear decoding waterfall close to the classical density-evolution benchmark (about 0.057 — the classical benchmark, not a measured threshold of the quantum code), with frame error rate reaching one in one hundred million at 4% depolarizing noise. Why the catalogue keeps it: surface codes pay roughly an order of magnitude more physical qubits per logical qubit, so a near-one-to-two rate with distance evidence near 48, if it survives scrutiny, changes what a fault-tolerant machine costs and what its decoder must chew through. It joins the hyperbolic surface-code and IQM barbell code-geometry entries but with a journal publication and explicit distance evidence rather than a preprint or vendor claim. The honest caveats: simulation and code construction only, no hardware run; global distance bound unproven; threshold not measured; a September paper caught late by the loop, filed November second. [CLAIMED — single secondary carrier, paper not read first-hand; MATERIAL — quantum decoding advance]

- **Maximal-Matching-Mixture decoder for correlated atom loss in neutral-atom quantum low-density parity-check codes (Jacob W. Murri, University of California, Los Angeles, with University of California collaborators; arXiv 2610.38283, reported November second, twenty twenty-six; new to the record).** Neutral-atom loss is correlated, not random: when one atom fails during a gate, its entangled gate partner is often lost with it, and existing decoders either ignore losses or treat them as merely co-occurring. The new decoder prices the correlation: it builds weighted mixtures of decoding hypergraphs over likely loss scenarios and reads them with standard belief propagation, focused on syndrome-extraction circuits within the Gross-code framework. On [[144,12,12]] Gross codes the reported gain is up to twenty-five times lower logical error rate than decoders unaware of losses, and roughly twice as good as the previous loss-aware state of the art. Why the catalogue keeps it: the decoder buys fidelity by modeling the machine's actual failure shape rather than an idealized one, and for neutral atoms the failure shape is paired loss. If the gain generalizes past the Gross code, neutral-atom overhead falls without any hardware change. The honest caveats: preprint, single secondary carrier, paper not read first-hand; Gross-code scope only, with extension beyond that structure an open question; no hardware run stated in the carrier. [CLAIMED — preprint via a single secondary carrier, not read first-hand; MATERIAL — quantum decoding advance]
- **Triage neural decoder for ultra-high-rate quantum low-density parity-check codes (Hong-Ye Hu, Zhenlai Wang, Binzhao Luo, Tao Xiang, Chinese Academy of Sciences, with Chen Zhao, Eastern Institute of Technology; arXiv 2610.40490, reported November second, twenty twenty-six; new to the record).** The speed-versus-accuracy wall for high-rate codes — blocks encoding several hundred logical qubits in roughly one thousand physical data qubits, at encoding rates exceeding one half — is attacked by adaptive computation: a local graph-neural-network decoder rapidly predicts corrections by message-passing over qubits and checks, then computation is allocated where syndrome consistency demands it and refined iteratively. Reported results: decoding latency down one to two orders of magnitude versus belief propagation and belief propagation with ordered-statistics decoding, at accuracy comparable to near-optimal algorithmic decoders; on Kasai-code tests at an error rate of 0.015, total convergence above 99.97 percent with amortized latency around thirty milliseconds, and durability when initial error assumptions are wrong. Why the catalogue keeps it: Triage is the decoder half of the Kasai filing from the last quantum pass — the same high-rate codes that cut qubit overhead now have a decoder fast enough to keep up with them, and it is the third cheap-to-run neural decoder in the catalogue's recent run, attacking the real-time wall from the latency side rather than the scaling side. The honest caveats: preprint, single secondary carrier, paper not read first-hand; the carrier's institutional attribution is muddled, so the byline is adopted here; scaling to the thousands of qubits a useful computation needs is explicitly unproven; no hardware run stated in the carrier. [CLAIMED — preprint via a single secondary carrier, not read first-hand; MATERIAL — quantum decoding advance]

- **Recurrent Bipartite Graph Neural Network decoder for Quasi-Cyclic Moderate Density Parity-Check codes (Parth Rajeshkumar Tandel and Elisabeth Fink, Middlesex University; reported November second, twenty twenty-six; new to the record).** Quasi-Cyclic Moderate Density Parity-Check codes are the code family behind post-quantum code-based cryptography (BIKE and McEliece variants), and their classical decoding stalls on short cycles in the parity-check structure — a stall that is a security vulnerability, not just a slowdown, because decoding failures leak through the failure channel. The new decoder attacks the stall by retaining information from previous decoding steps across a recurrent bipartite graph, rather than restarting each attempt from scratch. Reported results: a sixty-three point seven percent reduction in decoding failures at moderate noise levels versus established Bit-Flipping and Min-Sum decoders, across twenty previously unseen matrix topologies, with faster convergence in fewer computational steps. Why the catalogue keeps it: this is the post-quantum-cryptography side of the week's neural-decoder run — the earlier entries attacked quantum-code decoding, this one attacks the classical decoding of the codes that post-quantum cryptography itself is built on, and it lands directly on the catalogue's BIKE entry, where the first grading rung is the failure oracle. The honest caveats: preprint via a single secondary carrier, not read first-hand, and the carrier's archive link is truncated so no archive identifier is adopted here; generalization beyond the twenty evaluated topologies is untested; performance without pre-training is explicitly open; a failure-rate cut is not a proof at the level-one failure-rate target. [CLAIMED — single secondary carrier, not read first-hand; MATERIAL — quantum decoding advance]
- **State-discrimination decoders from Petz recovery maps (National Taiwan University and Hon Hai Quantum Computing Centre; reported November second, twenty twenty-six; new to the record).** Secure quantum communication reframed as a discrimination problem: instead of decoupling techniques that need pre-shared keys or classical assistance, the team constructs explicit decoders from Petz recovery maps and demonstrates exponential error decay at rates below coherent information — below the threshold where previous methods could only achieve such decay at the threshold itself. The construction carries quantifiable guarantees for entanglement generation regardless of channel usage. Why the catalogue keeps it: decoding as identification rather than correction — the receiver does not repair a corrupted message so much as recognize which message was sent, and the below-threshold decay, if it survives scrutiny, moves the bound on what a noisy quantum channel can carry. The honest caveats: single secondary carrier, paper not read first-hand; the framework leans on simplified product sources, so realistic correlated channels are out of scope for now; no hardware run stated in the carrier. [CLAIMED — single secondary carrier, not read first-hand; MATERIAL — quantum decoding advance]

- **Rydberg-Parity code — the embedding is the error-correcting code (ParityQC, University of Innsbruck, QuEra Computing; preprint and first-party release, reported November sixth, twenty twenty-six; new to the record).** When an optimization problem is embedded onto a Rydberg atom array, the auxiliary atoms introduced by the embedding are not overhead but an intrinsic classical error-correcting code: counting local excitations extracts an error syndrome at no additional hardware cost, converting the bare embedding into the Rydberg-Parity code. Reported: an error-correction threshold of twenty-six percent bit-flip probability across layout geometries, and the Cluster decoder recovering exact optimization solutions with an average success rate of at least around eight percent on systems of up to one hundred seven atoms on the QuEra Aquila quantum processing unit — even when bare hardware and standard greedy post-processing find none. Why the catalogue keeps it: the decoder buys fidelity from the problem layout itself, not from added hardware — the embedding step and the decoding step collapse into one design decision, and it is the first entry in this catalogue where the code is the layout. The honest caveats: first-party release and preprint, paper not read first-hand; the eight percent success rate is a recovery floor on the largest layouts, not a general guarantee; no fault-tolerant computation demonstrated. [CORROBORATED — first-party release from the research group and preprint, not read first-hand; MATERIAL — quantum decoding advance]
- **Autonomous quantum error correction beats break-even (Jiangfeng Du team; Nature Physics; reported November first, twenty twenty-six; new to the record).** A fully autonomous error-correction system — no real-time feedback, no measurement-conditioned corrections — surpassed the break-even point: error correction actively improved qubit reliability, with a net improvement in the coherence time of the encoded quantum information, on a small trapped-ion system. Why the catalogue keeps it: the measurement-and-feedback loop is the classical bottleneck in every error-correction architecture; a system that corrects without it removes the decoder's latency wall by removing the decoder from the loop — the counterpoint to the whole neural-decoder run that attacks the same wall by making the decoder faster. The honest caveats: Nature Physics paper via a secondary carrier, paper not read first-hand; small system, single architecture; scaling unproven. [CORROBORATED — Nature Physics paper via a secondary carrier, not read first-hand; MATERIAL — quantum decoding advance]
- **Bistable qubit — one extra measurement cuts errors by more than half (Regensburg and MIT, Berritta and colleagues; Applied Physics Reviews; reported November third, twenty twenty-six; new to the record).** A single additional measurement before a series of quantum operations cut the average error rate from about zero point one four percent to about zero point zero six five percent (about fifty-four percent), up to seventy-seven percent against the largest observed error without feedback, on a superconducting circuit at the Israeli Quantum Computing Center. Why the catalogue keeps it: a calibration-side error cut — the cheapest error reduction is one you get before the computation starts, and a single pre-measurement is nearly free compared to a full error-correction cycle. The honest caveats: peer-reviewed journal via a secondary report, paper not read first-hand; works only when the possible frequencies are known in advance and sufficiently distinct. [CORROBORATED — peer-reviewed journal via a secondary report; paper not read first-hand]
- **IBM, AMD, and Oak Ridge joint quantum error-correction platform (reported November fifth, twenty twenty-six; new to the record).** IBM's quantum computers (including the one hundred twenty qubit Nighthawk chip) pair with Oak Ridge's Umbra supercomputer (AMD Instinct graphics processors and EPYC central processors) so researchers can test error-correction approaches with classical and quantum resources tightly integrated; supports the United States Department of Energy goal of a scientifically useful quantum computer by late twenty twenty-eight — IBM said ongoing experiments are roughly two hundred thirty times short of that target. Why the catalogue keeps it: the classical decode side of fault tolerance is now an institutional program with its own supercomputer attached — the decode bottleneck has a budget line, not just papers. The honest caveats: launch announcement, no results yet; the two hundred thirty times figure is IBM's own framing. [VERIFIED — Reuters report of the launch]
- **NIST Internal Report eighty-five forty-seven, final version — the strength split is gone (published October twenty-seventh, twenty twenty-six; analysis November second through sixth, twenty twenty-six; update to the filed entry).** The final report deprecates every quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithm after twenty thirty at every approved key strength (the twenty twenty-four draft deprecated only the one hundred twelve bit versions) and disallows them after twenty thirty-five; ML-KEM seven hundred sixty-eight named the default parameter set. Federal agency migration plans were due October twenty-second, twenty twenty-six; two FedRAMP requests for comment close November seventeenth and nineteenth; the Federal Acquisition Regulation Council contractor rule is due December nineteenth. Why the catalogue keeps it: the migration deadline is now unconditional on key size — the harvest-now-decrypt-later window has a hard edge, and the parser-plumbing failures the catalogue already tracks now have a fixed date to be fixed by. [CORROBORATED — two independent analyses of the final report; report not read first-hand this pass]
- **PriorTilt — sparse prior perturbations beat Relay-BP and beam search on quantum low-density parity-check codes (Min Ye and Nicolas Delfosse, IonQ; arXiv twenty-six eleven point one three three seven three, November ninth, twenty twenty-six; new to the record).** Belief propagation is the workhorse decoder for classical low-density parity-check codes but stalls on quantum low-density parity-check codes; PriorTilt keeps belief propagation's message-passing rules and perturbs only a small fraction of prior log-likelihood ratios in rounds, choosing offsets from recent posterior and outgoing-message statistics. On three benchmark codes under circuit-level noise it beats both Relay-BP and beam search at every tested data point: on the one hundred forty-four, twelve, twelve Gross code at a noise rate of one in a thousand, the logical error rate falls four point three times against Relay-BP and three point one times against beam search, and about six hundred ten times below standard min-sum belief propagation at the same iteration budget — while perturbing fewer than half a percent of priors per round on average. Mean decoding time is lower than Relay-BP on all three codes, about two point six to three times faster than beam search, and ninety-ninth percentile times beat beam search on all three codes. Why the catalogue keeps it: the cheapest accuracy gain in the catalogue's belief-propagation lane — no new message-passing machinery, no neural network, just a nudge to the priors where the decoder is already unsure — and the tail-latency win is the one that matters for real-time decoding, where a slow shot is a failed shot. The honest caveats: preprint, paper not read first-hand (abstract and secondary summary read); three benchmark codes only, Gross-code headline; no hardware run stated. [CLAIMED — preprint via arXiv abstract and secondary summary, not read first-hand; MATERIAL — quantum decoding advance]
- **FusionQ — a generic fusion-decoding framework for ultra-low-latency quantum error correction (arXiv twenty-six eleven point one three one one one, November ninth, twenty twenty-six; new to the record).** Quantum error-correction decoding has been organized around fixed instances — a monolithic space-time detector error model, or a predetermined temporal window, handed to a backend decoder after enough syndrome data arrives. FusionQ derives local decoding tasks from the observed syndrome instead: it builds open-boundary local detector error models around fired detector clusters, expanding footprints only when a local optimum uses virtual boundary errors, then fuses the local results into a single global correction. It is generic in the backend — exact solvers, matching-style decoders on graphlike models, and heuristic decoders can share the runtime, since the scheduler needs only a local solution and a boundary-use flag. The compositional optimality theorem: with an exact minimum-weight local backend and boundary-free publication, fusing the published local results yields a global most-likely-error solution of the original model — and with an exact backend FusionQ matches the monolithic most-likely-error result on every shot in evaluation. Latency falls because local decoding overlaps with hardware syndrome acquisition instead of waiting for the full window. Why the catalogue keeps it: the latency lane's structural answer — instead of making one decoder faster, it dissolves the monolith into local problems that start solving while the machine is still measuring, and the optimality theorem says nothing is lost when the backend is exact. The honest caveats: preprint, paper not read first-hand (abstract read via secondary summary); the optimality guarantee holds only with an exact backend; no hardware run or latency numbers in the abstract as read. [CLAIMED — preprint via arXiv abstract and secondary summary, not read first-hand; MATERIAL — quantum decoding advance]
- **PRISM — a transformer decoder for fusion-based quantum computing in real time (Barter and colleagues, PsiQuantum and AMD; arXiv twenty-six eleven point one three six three zero, submitted November tenth, twenty twenty-six; new to the record).** Photonic fusion-based computing is dominated by erasures — photon loss and probabilistic fusion measurements — and PRISM is built for exactly that regime: a code-aware transformer decoder that exploits the known locations of erasures under both Pauli and erasure errors. Benchmarked across surface codes, colour codes and quantum low-density parity-check codes up to distance twenty-four, it matches the logical error rates of integer-programming-based decoders while running significantly faster, including at error rates up to fifty percent of threshold. The hardware figure: an optimized implementation on an AMD VP1902 field-programmable gate array decodes distance-eight logical blocks with six point five nine microseconds latency and one point five six microseconds amortized decoding time per logical block. A secondary read of the full paper (Atlas of the Present dossier, November eleventh) adds the fully-mapped figure — ten point one microseconds at two hundred fifty megahertz, with six point five nine microseconds projected at four hundred megahertz — and notes zero logical errors in thirty billion trials at distance twenty-four on one hundred nodes of eight AMD MI355X each. Why the catalogue keeps it: the erasure lane's first transformer decoder with a measured field-programmable gate array latency — it joins PriorTilt (accuracy) and FusionQ (latency structure) as the third November decoding paper, and it is the one aimed at the photonic architecture the catalogue's photonic track already follows. The honest caveats: preprint, abstract read first-hand (full paper not read); simulation benchmarks, no photonic processor run; the thirty-billion-trial figure is the dossier's read of the paper, not verified here. [CLAIMED — preprint, abstract read first-hand; MATERIAL — quantum decoding advance]
- **GARI++ — a general-purpose decoder for quantum error correction (Maan and colleagues; arXiv twenty-six eleven point one two eight three three, submitted November ninth, twenty twenty-six; new to the record).** A two-stage pipeline that stays competitive with state-of-the-art accuracy across surface, bivariate-bicycle and colour codes without ensembles: stage one is GARI, a normalized min-sum decoder with random serial scheduling on the GARI-transformed matrix; stage two fires only where stage one fails to converge, and the pipelining is predictive — stage one hands forward the iteration outputs expected to deliver the best accuracy downstream, along with the residual syndrome and soft information. The hardware figures: the field-programmable gate array implementation of GARI averages two hundred one nanoseconds to eleven point eight microseconds latency per round for surface-code distances seven to twenty-five at a physical error rate of zero point zero zero one under uniform circuit-level depolarising noise, while the residual second stage stays near-constant and below one microsecond per round on a single Apple M two core for surface-code distances up to fifty-one using Union-Find, with accuracy on par with correlated minimum-weight perfect matching. The design motivates a hybrid field-programmable gate array and central processing unit architecture for real-time decoding. Why the catalogue keeps it: the fourth November decoding paper joins PRISM (transformer, erasure lane), PriorTilt (accuracy) and FusionQ (latency structure) — and it is the generalist of the four, one pipeline across three code families with measured latencies at both ends, which is exactly the shape a real fault-tolerant machine needs: fast first pass, cheap mop-up, no ensemble tax. The honest caveats: preprint, abstract read first-hand (full paper not read); simulation benchmarks, no hardware run; the sub-microsecond residual figure is on a single Apple M two core, a consumer chip, not a deployed decoder board. [CLAIMED — preprint, abstract read first-hand; MATERIAL — quantum decoding advance]
- **Nighthawk r3 — the link-timing conflict is resolved by IBM's own release (announced November eleventh, twenty twenty-six; update to the filed entry).** IBM's newsroom release says Nighthawk r3 (five hundred twenty programmable qubits, two thousand thirty-four total physical qubits, designed for ten thousand quantum operations) will be linked as two processors into a single system of more than one thousand qubits in twenty twenty-seven — the filed twenty twenty-seven timing stands confirmed, and the System Report claim of a link before the end of twenty twenty-six is retired as a conflict. New measured figures from the same release: Nighthawk r1 processors linked with four l-couplers at ninety-nine point three percent quantum state-transfer fidelity, toward a ninety-nine point nine percent target; two cryogenic modules connected into a single system for the first time, reaching operating temperature in under five days and cooling below fifteen millikelvin. Nighthawk r2 track record: in service since September, up to one hundred thousand samples per second, partners (E.ON, Algorithmiq, Q-CTRL) have run thirty-four billion circuits with reported performance improvements of up to nineteen times. No availability date given for r3 itself — a design target, not yet built. Why the catalogue keeps it: the modular link is the scale path the error-correction platform must decode across, so the l-coupler fidelity number is the one to watch. [CORROBORATED — first-party vendor release plus Ars Technica, SiliconANGLE, SiliconReport, Hardware Busters retells]

The universal quantum decoder stays [SPECULATION] until proven.

## Photonic comms & power

- **Chip-scale free-space beam steering (Opto-Electronic Advances, 2026).**
  MIT/SMART team: two-dimensional steering across a measured 161-degree field
  of view at near-diffraction-limited quality — a silicon photonic chip routing
  light through on-chip switches to a freeform micro-optical reflector,
  instead of a phased array of tuned shifters. A chip-scale steering front-end
  is what free-space optical comms needs to leave the lab bench.
  [CORROBORATED — peer-reviewed journal]
- **Self-stabilizing photonic lasers (Nature Photonics, Oct 2026).** Reichler
  et al: self-injection locking held across the full drive-current range cut
  frequency noise by more than 5,000x versus the free-running laser, with
  linewidth under 10 Hz and mode-hop-free 1.5 GHz chirps — all without active
  control. Ultralow-noise self-stabilizing lasers are the transmitter side of
  coherent optical comms, lidar, and quantum sensing.

Star Catcher Protostar will release a CubeSat, track it, and beam optical power at its off-the-shelf solar panels — claimed first wireless optical power transfer between two untethered spacecraft (Caltech's 2023 MAPLE test used microwaves). Until the tests fly, these are beaming tests, not beaming systems. Reason-1 is reportedly communicating daily since launch; early development of its laser and optical payloads was funded by the Department of Defense's Operational Energy Capability Improvement Fund. Pre-flight proton-beam testing at UC Davis's Crocker Nuclear Lab: chips survived a dose Google says exceeds a five-year mission dose without hard failure; memory irregularities appeared above a threshold dose. Honest scope: a four-chip survival test, not a data center — Google makes no economic claim, and launch-cost/radiator-mass/no-repair economics are contested on the record. The long-term concept is 81 satellites in kilometer-scale arrays linked by high-bandwidth short-distance laser communications. Decoder significance: the power race is pulling compute off the planet — an orbital laser-linked mesh is the natural endpoint, and the decoder's future interception surface is increasingly above the atmosphere. Update (ESA report, November 2, 2026): ESA itself has now reported the link as Greece's first optical link with a low Earth orbit satellite, with vendor-reported figures of one gigabit per second, two links a day after commissioning, and above eighty five percent availability for passes higher than fifteen degrees — the link is agency reported, the figures remain vendor reported. - **Photonic chip reads momentum-space topology (Physical Review Letters, Oct 2026).** KTH group: a programmable photonic chip measuring topological wave properties under realistic energy-losing conditions — the physics of light devices that keep working despite defects. Decoder significance: self-defending transport — signals that route around defects without scattering don't leak there either. [CORROBORATED — peer-reviewed PRL paper confirmed 2026-10-23 (publication listed, open-access version on arXiv)]

Decoder significance: daylight was the hard barrier on wireless quantum communication; the beam-tracking layer that beat it is the same tracking layer power beaming and laser comms depend on — free-space quantum channels are becoming a working comms surface. The system learns from real measurements, so hardware imperfections get trained around instead of engineered away. Decoder significance: the channel starts doing its own thinking before the data becomes digital — the model's inferences arrive embedded in the light itself. Decoder significance: the quantum-carrier lane is being hardened on the encoding side too — a quantum channel that degrades without failing outright gives the decoder no easy error signal. - **Self-aligning octave-spanning frequency comb on a foundry chip (Nature, published Sep 30, 2026).** A four-institution collaboration drove a microresonator with two pump lasers placed an octave apart, creating a cavity soliton that fills the spectrum between them — a self-aligned comb without the single-pump architecture's low-noise stabilization struggle across a full octave. Decoder significance: combs are the light-rulers underneath coherent optical communications and quantum links; the absolute frequency reference moves from tabletop to chip. Decoder significance: the seam between quantum memory and the fiber network is being built at chip level — the decoder's future quantum interception surface starts at this interface. - **Silicon-photonics reservoir computer equalizes at line rate (reported July 2026; NTT addendum September 2026).** A silicon-photonics chip integrating both the computing reservoir and the programmable read-out equalized a 28 Gbps signal across up to 50 km of fiber in real time, at the full line rate, with no buffering — the equalization happening in the optical domain. In September, programmable photonic processors at intermediate nodes along a 1,300 km three-mode fiber system manipulated the optical transmission in flight, reducing modal dispersion and the digital post-processing needed at the receiver. Decoder significance: the processing is moving into the optical path — the fiber plant becoming a programmable, self-optimizing machine. The deficit is in stability, not sensitivity: angle random walk of 0.88 degrees per square root of hour and bias instability of 302 degrees per hour remain far behind established inertial instruments. A laboratory rotation-measurement advance on a semiconductor-compatible platform, not a navigation-grade sensor yet. [CORROBORATED — peer-reviewed paper per a detailed secondary assessment; paper not read first-party.]

- **Chip-scale light source that shines straight up, in a new color (Opto-Electronic Technology, reported October twenty twenty-six).** A research team in China demonstrated an on-chip source emitting coherent light nearly straight up off the chip surface at about 817 nanometers — a wavelength conventional semiconductor emitters struggle to reach — using a thin-film lithium niobate microdisk resonator and a nonlinear optical process, so the emitted color is no longer dictated by the gain bandwidth of the underlying material. Vertically emitting sources are among the most practical building blocks of photonic chips: dense two-dimensional arrays, simple free-space collection, a bridge between on-chip platforms and external optics. [CORROBORATED — peer-reviewed journal via trade-press summary]

The chip replaces bulky free-space optics that demand precise alignment, and improves on earlier on-chip routes with limited beam diversity. Decoder significance: structured-light multiplexing gives free-space optical links a denser alphabet — more orthogonal channels per beam — and each new multiplexing axis is one more axis the decoder must learn to read. [CORROBORATED — peer-reviewed study via trade coverage; paper not read first-hand]

The orbital beaming tests (Protostar, Reason-1) are unaffected — this one is ground-based. Decoder significance: a beam-tracking stack that can aim power at several targets at once is a targeting layer worth modeling. Conventional Mach-Zehnder modulators are hitting physical limits; this is positioned as their more efficient replacement for data-center fiber links. The scaling claim is deposition, not assembly: molecular qubits laid down as thin films directly onto thin-film lithium niobate photonic chips, with first prototype integrated chips expected in the fourth quarter of 2026; the platform is said to tolerate up to seventy percent photon loss, so it runs on standard silicon photonics. The module was interfaced with a calcium forty trapped-ion system at extremely low excitation rates, delivering ultrahigh signal-to-noise and high-fidelity operations; the paper adds a model predicting how imperfections in the patterned polarization regions cut efficiency, and a noise-control mechanism using differential tuning of difference-frequency generation versus pump-induced nonlinear noise. Stated next targets: ytterbium one hundred seventy-one, strontium eighty-eight, and barium one hundred thirty-eight ions. Decoder significance: the ultraviolet-emitting ion lane gains a chip-scale on-ramp to the telecom fiber network, and the decoder's future quantum channel now has an ultraviolet-to-telecom seam with measured efficiency and noise, not a roadmap claim. Fast ultraviolet switching previously needed bulky crystals and high voltages. Ultraviolet is the native color of trapped-ion quantum machines, so a chip-scale ultraviolet modulator is the transmit side of a future ultraviolet quantum link. Funded under Horizon Europe's QU-PIC project; joining the material to low-loss alumina circuits remains hard. Decoder significance: the decoder's interception model gains an ultraviolet lane that no longer needs a bench. DOI 10.1038/s41467-026-78862-6. Blue light travels through water more easily than the infrared used in today's optical communications, so the stated lanes are underwater communication, coherent aerosol sensing, and quantum technologies. Decoder significance: the underwater optical lane — a channel that propagates where radio does not — gains a chip-scale, frequency-agile source, and the decoder's tap model must reckon with water as a medium, not just fiber and free space. - **Silicon chips that process light with light (Frontiers of Optoelectronics, reported October thirtieth, twenty twenty-six).** A Chinese research team reports a family of silicon photonic chips that filter, regenerate, and logically process optical signals entirely in the optical domain, without the round trips between light and electronics that dominate today's fiber networks: ultra-low-loss waveguides, microring resonators with quality factors above two million, a bandwidth-tunable filter sweeping continuously from zero point five five picometers to six hundred forty-eight point seven two picometers, a five-stage filter with thirty-one discrete free-spectral-range settings, monolithic logic arrays operating at one hundred gigabits per second, and an eight-channel chip integrating one hundred thirty-six optical and electrical devices on a standard eight-inch CMOS-compatible platform, with a total demonstrated processing capacity of eight hundred gigabits per second. In a live demonstration, three four-K video streams were routed through the packaged chip with reconfigurable filtering, real-time signal regeneration, and logic-based encryption all performed in the optical domain. The authors frame these as research demonstrations, not deployed technology — phase-sensitive amplification demands strict mutual coherence, and temperature and vibration drift remain practical challenges. Decoder significance: when the fiber plant filters and encrypts in light itself, interception above the optical layer reads the computation's output, not the wire, and the tap model must move down to the photon or not at all. - **Chip-scale beam-shaped optical wireless system — Cambridge VCSEL array (Advanced Photonics Nexus, twenty twenty-six).** A University of Cambridge team built a five by five VCSEL array with custom beam-shaping optics forming a structured grid: a two-metre free-space link, twenty-one of twenty-five lasers operational, about thirteen to nineteen gigabits per second per laser, three hundred sixty-two point seven gigabits per second aggregate, about one point four nanojoules per bit, roughly half the energy per bit reported for state-of-the-art Wi-Fi under comparable conditions. Throughput was limited by the commercial photodetector's bandwidth, not the array. A room-bounded, directional optical link at Wi-Fi-beating energy per bit is a comms surface no radio tap can hear, joining the VCSEL-interconnect lanes as a free-space sibling rather than a rack fabric. - **Quantum light chip guides single photons on chip (Nature Communications, October twenty-eighth, twenty twenty-six).** A Technical University of Denmark team built a quantum light chip from atom thin crystals, with tiny light emitters sitting directly on top of light carrying channels, so single photons flow straight into the chip with very high purity — the source and the waveguide on one chip, instead of a bench emitter coupled in from outside. The honest caveats are that it only works near four kelvin, about minus two hundred sixty-nine degrees Celsius, so it needs a bulky cryostat; the detectors sat off the chip; and indistinguishability, a key property for many quantum protocols, has not yet been measured. An early lab demonstration, not a deployable link. Decoder significance: the quantum comms source lane gains a chip integrated single photon emitter — the transmit side of chip based quantum light — and quantum light that starts on a chip needs no bench at either end, once the cryogenics and detectors catch up. - **Topological photonic crystal terahertz chip at one hundred gigabits per second (Advanced Materials, twenty twenty-six; reported November fourth, twenty twenty-six).** A team at the Jawaharlal Nehru Centre for Advanced Scientific Research built a silicon photonic crystal whose structure mimics the honeycomb lattice of graphene: triangular holes in a carefully designed pattern guide terahertz waves along the boundary between two regions, and an engineered barrier created by changing the hole sizes over a short section of the waveguide is crossed with little loss. The splitter supported one hundred gigabits per second using thirty-two-state quadrature amplitude modulation, which encodes information in the signal's amplitude and phase. Terahertz frequencies, between microwaves and infrared light, offer the wide bandwidth future sixth-generation wireless networks are expected to use. Decoder significance: this is the lane's first room-temperature silicon routing result with a measured data rate — the lithium tantalate terahertz core already in the catalogue runs at four kelvin, while this one is silicon at ambient conditions, which is the form a future network would actually ship in. Honest scope: a laboratory chip demonstration, not a deployed link — no range, power, or bit-error-rate figure is published in the release, so none is adopted. - **Isolator-free silicon photonic transmitter at one hundred eighty gigabits per second (Journal of Lightwave Technology, October seventh, twenty twenty-six).** A team at Waseda University in Japan built an integrated optical transmitter that runs stably without an optical isolator, the discrete component that normally shields a laser from destabilizing back-reflections, by coordinating the optical responses of silicon nitride ring resonators, which provide wavelength-selective filtering, with a thin-film lithium niobate modulator in a cross-platform spectral co-design. The external-cavity wavelength-tunable laser held stable output without active temperature control and demonstrated data transmission at one hundred eighty gigabits per second, the highest rate investigated, across approximately sixty-seven nanometers, with signals still distinguishable at that rate. Decoder significance: the isolator is a discrete, alignment-sensitive part in every laser transmitter, so deleting it without losing stability is a packaging and cost step toward compact high-capacity photonic integrated circuits, joining the catalogue's transmitter lane as a component advance, not a deployed link. Honest scope: a laboratory transmitter demonstration — no bit-error-rate, power-consumption, or production figure is published in the carrier, so none is adopted. Decoder significance: the lane's first single-platform all-distance coherent result at this rate — one platform spans the unamplified short-reach and trans-oceanic-scale long-haul ends that previously needed different solutions — joining the catalogue's transmitter lane as a measured platform result, not a component demo. - **Silicon photonics grating coupler array for light collection in optical wireless communication (Journal of Lightwave Technology, volume forty-four, issue one, pages two hundred twenty-nine to two hundred thirty-five, January first, twenty twenty-six).** A team at Eindhoven University of Technology built a silicon-on-insulator surface grating coupler array — four focusing grating couplers — as the light-collection device for a beam-steered optical wireless receiver: a measured vertical field of view above six degrees, a three hundred sixty degree horizontal field of view, and error-free eight gigabit per second transmission over fifteen centimetres at one thousand five hundred fifty nanometres. The combining penalty is six point five decibels; the penalty versus coupling from single-mode fiber is one point two decibels. Decoder significance: the receive side of beam-steered optical wireless — a chip-scale light-collection aperture with a wide field of view, joining the Cambridge VCSEL array, the transmit side, as the receiver sibling; a room-scale optical link whose receiver is a photonic integrated circuit, not a bench telescope, and a comms surface no radio tap can hear.
