## SHA-2 — the workhorse the whole shelf stands on, or: the seal that is two hashes wearing six names

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue leans on SHA-2 without ever describing it: the SHA-3 entry named SHA-2 outright as the hash bench's other hole, the house canonical ID is a SHA-256 of field bytes, HMAC-SHA256 is the keyed-hash reference, the DSA entry's FIPS 186-3 sizes assume SHA-2 hashes, and the SHAttered entry records Git's migration toward SHA-256 — and no entry says what the family is, how its six names relate, or which of them survive length extension. This is that entry. It also corrects the commonest mental model: SHA-2 is not six hashes. It is two engines wearing six names.
- **The construction, in one paragraph.** SHA-2 is the NSA-designed family first published in 2001 (SHA-256, SHA-384, and SHA-512 in FIPS 180-2), standardized today as FIPS 180-4, published March 6, 2012, which added SHA-512/224 and SHA-512/256. Both engines are Merkle–Damgård with a Davies–Meyer compression function built from a specialized block cipher: eight working variables, the Choice function Ch and Majority function Maj, the big-sigma rotations Σ0/Σ1 on the state, the small-sigma rotations/shifts σ0/σ1 expanding the message schedule, and modular addition throughout. The SHA-256 engine works in 32-bit words on 512-bit blocks for 64 rounds: sixteen schedule words expanded to sixty-four, round constants from the fractional parts of the cube roots of the first 64 primes, initial values from the fractional parts of the square roots of the first eight primes (H0 = 6a09e667). The SHA-512 engine is the same shape at twice the width: 64-bit words, 1024-bit blocks, 80 rounds, eighty round constants from the cube roots of the first 80 primes. The six names fall out of the two engines by truncation plus distinct initial values: SHA-224 is the 256-engine with different IVs, truncated to 224 bits; SHA-384 is the 512-engine with different IVs, truncated to 384; SHA-512/224 and SHA-512/256 are the 512-engine with IVs generated by FIPS 180-4's own method, truncated to 224 and 256. Security levels follow the output: 112, 128, 192, 256, 112, 128 bits respectively — SHA-224's 112 deliberately matching the 3DES level it was built to replace.
- **What SHA-2 is not.** It is not SHA-3: no sponge, no capacity, no domain-separation suffix — a specimen whose "SHA-256" matches a sponge output has mislabelled one of them, and the SHA-3 entry's padding test has no counterpart here. It is not six independent designs: a 224-bit digest does not identify its engine, and a specimen labelled "SHA-224" that runs the 64-bit engine is SHA-512/224 mislabelled, whatever its vectors claim. It is not length-extension-proof in full form: SHA-256 and SHA-512 output their entire state, so given H(m) and the length of m, an attacker can compute H(m || pad || extra) without knowing m — raw SHA-256(m || secret) as a message authenticator is broken by construction, which is why HMAC exists. It is not broken either: the best public attacks reach 52 of 64 rounds of SHA-256 and 57 of 80 rounds of SHA-512 for preimage resistance, and no practical attack on any full-round SHA-2 member is known. It is not a password hash: like BLAKE3, it is built to be fast, and the Argon2/scrypt/bcrypt shelf exists precisely because fast hashes make cheap guessing. And it is not SHA-1: different word counts, different round counts, different IV derivation — the predecessor's retirement (SHAttered) is not SHA-2's.
- **The decoder's edge cases.** The IV test is the first screen: SHA-224 is not SHA-256 cut short — its IVs differ, so the same input under the two names gives unrelated digests, and a specimen that truncates a SHA-256 output and labels it SHA-224 fails before any vector runs. The engine test is the second: a 224-bit output must declare whether it ran the 32-bit engine (SHA-224) or the 64-bit engine (SHA-512/224) — the digest length alone never settles it, and a performance claim that puts the 64-bit engine ahead on a 32-bit platform (or behind on a 64-bit one) has the engines backwards. The length-extension test is the third: any protocol presenting raw SHA-256 or SHA-512 as authentication fails it regardless of vectors, while the truncated variants pass it by construction — part of the state never leaves, so there is nothing to extend from. A specimen labelled "SHA-2" is therefore, as with every entry here, not a verdict: the engine, the IV set, the truncation, and the full-vs-truncated output are the specimen.
- **Decoder-design note (the IV rung; the engine rung; the extension rung).** Three Gauntlet rungs. (1) **Grade the IV before any vector runs.** A specimen is graded on whether its initial values match its claimed variant — the 224 IVs for SHA-224, the 512 IVs for SHA-512/224 — and a specimen that passes a vector only because the harness supplied the IV has passed a test of the harness, not of the specimen. (2) **Grade the engine against the name before trusting a digest.** A specimen is graded on whether its word size, block size, and round count (32/512/64 or 64/1024/80) match its claimed variant; a digest length is a label, not an engine. (3) **Grade the protocol, not just the primitive, on length extension.** A specimen is graded on whether its deployment treats raw SHA-2 output as authentication — if it does, it fails the rung whatever its vectors claim, and the fix is HMAC, not a longer digest.

*[Grade: CORROBORATED — the six-member family, the NSA design and 2001 first publication, the FIPS 180-4 standard of March 6, 2012 with the SHA-512/224 and SHA-512/256 addition, the two engines (32-bit words / 512-bit blocks / 64 rounds; 64-bit words / 1024-bit blocks / 80 rounds), the Merkle–Damgård construction with Davies–Meyer compression, the Ch/Maj/Σ/σ functions and the 16-to-64/80 schedule expansion, the IV derivation from square roots of the first eight primes (H0 = 6a09e667) and round constants from cube roots of the first 64 primes, the truncated-variant structure, the 112/128/192/256/112/128 security levels, the truncated variants' length-extension resistance, and the 52-of-64 and 57-of-80 preimage-attack figures with no practical full-round attack, all via the FIPS 180-4 record and the SHA-2 summaries read this pass; CLAIMED — the SHA-224/SHA-384 IVs as square roots of the 9th–16th primes, the FIPS 180-4 IV-generation method for SHA-512/t, and the 3DES-equivalence rationale for SHA-224's 112-bit level, which rest on secondary summaries rather than the standard text read this pass; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet IV, engine, and extension rungs, which are proposals, never run.]*

## DES — the Data Encryption Standard (FIPS 46), or: the cipher that taught the world what a key length costs

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue's symmetric bench now tells the whole AES story — the winner, all four runners-up, Camellia beside them — and the hash bench holds SHA-2 and SHA-3, yet the cipher all of them replaced has never had an entry of its own. DES is mentioned everywhere in this catalogue, as the predecessor, the benchmark, and the cautionary tale, and described nowhere. This is that entry, and it matters because the AES competition only exists as DES's sequel: DES is the standard whose 56-bit key forced the question the competition answered, and every later bench entry is, in one way or another, a reaction to it — longer keys, bigger blocks, or a margin DES never had.
- **The construction, in one paragraph.** DES is IBM's Lucifer, Horst Feistel's design, submitted after the National Bureau of Standards' call for a public encryption standard and selected after consultation with the National Security Agency; the approved version differed from Lucifer in two famous ways, a key cut from 128 bits to 56 and S-boxes redesigned under classified conditions, and it was published on January 15, 1977, as FIPS PUB 46, reaffirmed in 1983, 1988 (FIPS 46-1), and 1993 (FIPS 46-2), revised in 1999 as FIPS 46-3 prescribing Triple DES, superseded by AES on May 26, 2002, and withdrawn as FIPS 46-3 on May 19, 2005, with single DES permitted thereafter only as a component of Triple DES. It is a 64-bit block cipher built as a balanced Feistel network of 16 rounds, bracketed by an initial permutation IP and a final permutation FP that are inverses of each other. The key is nominally 64 bits, but every eighth bit is parity and is discarded, leaving 56 effective bits — a key space of 2^56, about 7.2 × 10^16 keys. The key schedule runs PC-1 to drop the parity bits and split the key into two 28-bit halves, rotates each half left by one or two bits per round on a fixed schedule, and runs PC-2 to select 48 bits per round: sixteen 48-bit round keys, 768 bits of keying material, all derived from 56. Each round expands its 32-bit half to 48 bits (E-expansion), XORs the round key, passes the result through eight fixed S-boxes of 6 bits in and 4 out, and permutes the 32-bit output (P-permutation); decryption is the same structure with the round keys in reverse order. The classified S-box redesign, revealed once differential cryptanalysis became public in the early 1990s, turns out to have hardened DES against that attack — the one part of the NSA consultation the public record eventually vindicated, whatever the key-length cut cost.
- **What DES is not.** It is not secure today, and it has not been since the 1990s: the calendar, not any cryptanalytic breakthrough, is what killed it — DESCHALL broke a DES message in public in June 1997, the EFF's Deep Crack machine broke a key in 56 hours in July 1998, and Deep Crack together with distributed.net did it in 22 hours and 15 minutes in January 1999, all by brute force over a 56-bit space. It is not unattacked analytically either, but the honest form of that statement is that the best published analytical attack, linear cryptanalysis, still needs on the order of 2^43 known plaintexts — a paper margin over brute force, not a practical break. It is not Triple DES: 3DES applies DES three times to each block (encrypt-decrypt-encrypt) with two or three independent keys, 168 nominal bits collapsing to 112 effective under meet-in-the-middle, and it too has been retired — deprecated by NIST in 2019, disallowed after the end of 2023 except for processing already-encrypted data, its SP 800-67 guidance withdrawn in 2024, and its 64-bit block separately wounded by the Sweet32 birthday attack (CVE-2016-2183). It is not a 64-bit-key cipher: the parity bits are error detection, not key material, and a specimen claiming 64-bit DES security overstates its space by a factor of 256. And it is not a mode or an AEAD: raw DES encrypts one 64-bit block, and everything about chaining, authentication, and nonce discipline belongs to the mode wrapped around it, not to the cipher.
- **The decoder's edge cases.** The parity test is the first screen: a specimen must discard every eighth key bit before PC-1, and a schedule that feeds all 64 bits into the round keys is a different cipher wearing DES's name. The round-key test is the second: sixteen 48-bit keys from two 28-bit halves on the 1-or-2 rotation schedule — a specimen with the wrong rotation pattern, or with independently chosen round keys, has skipped the schedule that is half of DES's identity. The S-box test is the third: eight fixed 6-to-4 tables, not key-dependent (that is Twofish's furniture) and not a single table reused eight times. The calendar test is the fourth, and it needs no cryptanalysis at all: any specimen labelled "DES, secure for new data" fails on the key length alone, because 1997–1999 already priced 56 bits at days and hours on public resources. The weak-key test is the fifth: keys whose halves are all zeroes or all ones generate identical round keys every round, and paired keys generate each other's round keys in reverse — a schedule that does not flag those classes is incomplete, and a specimen that encrypts under one without warning has skipped DES's own known-bad list. A specimen labelled "DES" is therefore, as with every entry here, not a verdict: the 64-bit block, the 56-bit effective key, the 16-round Feistel structure, the PC-1/PC-2 schedule, the eight fixed S-boxes, and the 1997–1999 brute-force calendar are the specimen.

## RC4 — the stream cipher that was everywhere, or: the seal whose keystream talked too much

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue's stream-cipher bench has ChaCha20, the cipher that replaced RC4, and the AES-GCM entry that now carries most of the web's traffic — but the cipher both of them replaced has never had an entry of its own. RC4 is mentioned across this catalogue as the cautionary tale inside WEP, inside early TLS, inside the "never reuse a keystream" rule, and described nowhere. This is that entry, and it matters because RC4 is the most-deployed cipher in the history of the field: at its peak it protected a majority of TLS traffic and nearly all of Wi-Fi, and its fall is the clearest worked example the catalogue holds of a cipher killed not by a single break but by the slow accumulation of small biases.
- **The construction, in one paragraph.** RC4 is Ron Rivest's design of 1987, built at RSA Security and held as a trade secret until September 1994, when a description was anonymously posted to the Cypherpunks mailing list and spread from there — the leak that gave the world the name ARC4, "Alleged RC4," for implementations built from the leaked description rather than from RSA's code. The whole cipher is one 256-byte permutation S, plus two byte counters i and j. The key-scheduling algorithm (KSA) starts S as the identity permutation, then walks i from 0 to 255, advancing j by S[i] plus the next key byte (the variable-length key, 40 to 2,048 bits, repeating as needed) and swapping S[i] with S[j]. The pseudo-random generation algorithm (PRGA) then loops forever: i advances by one, j advances by S[i], S[i] and S[j] swap, and the output byte is S[(S[i] + S[j]) mod 256], XORed with the plaintext. That is the entire cipher — no rounds, no S-boxes in the AES sense, no nonce, no authentication — which is exactly why it ran so fast on 1990s software and exactly why it could not survive: the keystream is a function of the key alone, so every reuse, every related key, and every statistical quirk of the first bytes is an opening.
- **What RC4 is not.** It is not secure today, and the catalogue must never let a specimen present it as a live option. The break came in layers, each one public. Fluhrer, Mantin, and Shamir in 2001 showed that the first keystream bytes leak key information when keys are related — the attack that broke WEP, which concatenated a 24-bit IV onto the key and broadcast it in the clear, so related keys arrived by the millions. Mantin and Shamir showed the second output byte is biased toward zero with probability about 1/128 instead of the uniform 1/256 — a single byte that distinguishes RC4 from random after a few hundred samples. The long-tail biases found later, and the RC4 NOMORE attack of 2013–2015, turned those biases into practical plaintext recovery against TLS, recovering a cookie byte by byte from many repeated encryptions. The industry response was a prohibition, not a patch: IETF RFC 7465 (2015) forbids RC4 cipher suites in all versions of TLS, and the major browsers removed RC4 support in 2015–2016. RC4-drop[n], which discards the first n keystream bytes (768, later a conservative 3,072), blunts the early-byte attacks but does nothing for the long-tail biases, and no drop count rehabilitates the cipher.
- **The decoder's edge cases.** The identity test is the first screen: after the KSA, a specimen's S must be a true permutation of 0–255 — any duplicate or missing value is a broken implementation, not a variant. The key-length test is the second: a specimen that silently truncates or pads a key to a fixed length is a different cipher wearing RC4's name, and the WEP lesson is the third screen, run as a protocol question rather than a cipher question — a specimen that concatenates a short public IV onto a secret key and reuses the combination is vulnerable by construction, whatever the cipher underneath, because the attack targets the key schedule's input, not the keystream generator. The state-space figure belongs in the report card's calibration: 256! possible permutations, about 2^1684 states, is a number that sounds like security and means nothing — the attacks never searched the state space, they listened to its biases. A Gauntlet run against an RC4 specimen must therefore grade on bias, not on brute force: second-byte distribution over many short outputs, first-byte key-correlation under related keys, and plaintext recovery under repeated encryption are the three rungs, and any one of them failing is a fail for the specimen, because RC4's history shows the biases only ever got worse with study, never better.

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the 256! ≈ 2^1684 state count, computed this pass; CORROBORATED — the Rivest 1987 design, the September 1994 Cypherpunks leak and the ARC4 name, the KSA/PRGA construction, the 40-to-2,048-bit key range, the FMS 2001 attack and the WEP break, the Mantin–Shamir second-byte bias of about 1/128 against 1/256, the RC4-drop[n] 768 and 3,072 figures, RFC 7465 (2015) and the 2015–2016 browser removals, all via the RC4 record and summaries read this pass; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet bias rungs, which are proposals, never run.]*

## RC5 — the parameterized block cipher, or: the seal that let the user pick the shape

- **The gap this entry closes.** The RC6 entry named its own parent and left it absent: RC6 is RC5 grown up to the AES shape, but RC5 itself never got a heading. RC5 is the root of the family tree — the cipher whose data-dependent rotations RC6 inherited, whose key expansion RC6 copied unchanged, and whose three-parameter naming RC6 kept. With it, the bench holds the whole RC lineage on the shelf: RC5 the parent, RC6 the AES finalist child, RC4 the stream cousin from the same designer. It is also the catalogue's first fully parameterized cipher: word size, rounds, and key length are all user-chosen, so a specimen labelled "RC5" without its triple is not yet identified at all.

- **The construction, in one paragraph.** RC5 is Ron Rivest's 1994 design, published as "The RC5 Encryption Algorithm" (revised March 20, 1997), built for hardware and software both, with a stated objective set that reads like a design brief: a symmetric block cipher, iterative in structure, with variable word size, variable rounds, and a variable-length key, and with data-dependent rotations as its one nonlinear operator — no S-boxes anywhere, no other substitution tables. An instance is named RC5-w/r/b: w is the word size in bits (16, 32, or 64 in practice), r the number of rounds (0 to 255), b the key length in bytes (0 to 255), and the block is two words, 2w bits — so RC5-32/12/16, the nominal instance, is a 64-bit block cipher with 12 rounds and a 16-byte key. The primitive set is three operations only: addition modulo 2^w, XOR, and left rotation by a data-dependent amount, where the rotation amount is the low lg w bits of the other register. Encryption: A = A + S[0]; B = B + S[1]; then for i = 1 to r, A = ((A XOR B) rotated left by B) + S[2i] and B = ((B XOR A) rotated left by A) + S[2i+1]. Key expansion builds the subkey table S of t = 2(r+1) words — 26 words at the nominal 12 rounds, against RC6's 44 at 20 — seeded from the "magic constants" Pw = Odd((e-2)2^w) and Qw = Odd((phi-1)2^w), which at w = 32 are the already-familiar 0xB7E15163 and 0x9E3779B9, then mixed with the key words L in 3*max(t, c) passes of A = S[i] = (S[i] + A + B) rotated left by 3 and B = L[j] = (L[j] + A + B) rotated left by (A + B). Decryption runs the same steps backwards with subtractions and right rotations. Rivest's own calibration, from the paper's experiments: four rounds sufficed for uniform bit correlations in RC5-32, and eight rounds sufficed for every message bit to affect some rotation amount — which is why the nominal 12 rounds carry a margin, and why a specimen at fewer than 8 rounds is a specimen running below its designer's own measured floor.

- **What RC5 is not.** It is not RC6 with a smaller block: RC6 added two registers, integer multiplication, and the quadratic function precisely because RC5's two-register shape could not carry 128 bits on 32-bit words — the parent and the child differ in construction, not just in size. It is not a fixed cipher at all: "RC5" without w/r/b is a family name, and a specimen that hard-codes one triple while claiming the family name has narrowed the design without saying so. It is not an S-box cipher, and its rotations are not fixed: a specimen whose rotation amounts come from a schedule rather than from the data has removed the one nonlinearity the design rests on. It is not a standard and never was: RC5 was a candidate for replacing DES in the sense that it was discussed as one, but the AES competition's RC entry was RC6, not RC5 — a specimen labelled "FIPS RC5" or "AES RC5" is mislabelled, full stop. And it is not safe at any parameter choice merely because the family is old: the parameterisation is the security statement, so a 0-round or 1-round RC5, or an RC5 with a 0-byte key, is a degenerate instance the design allows on paper and forbids in practice.

- **The decoder's edge cases.** The triple test is the first screen: a specimen must name w, r, and b, and a specimen that answers "RC5" to all three questions has not been identified. The rotation test is the second: a specimen's rotation amounts must come from the low lg w bits of the opposite register, live, per round — fixed rotation amounts, or amounts taken from the key schedule, are a different cipher. The expansion test is the third: the subkey count must be exactly 2(r+1), the seed constants must be Pw/Qw for the stated w, and the mixing must run 3*max(t, c) passes — a schedule that stops early, or seeds from anything but Pw/Qw, is a broken implementation wearing the name, checkable from the expanded key alone without any plaintext. The round-floor test is the fourth: a specimen below 8 rounds at w = 32 runs under Rivest's own measured floor for full bit-to-rotation diffusion, and a report card must say so rather than grading it as a full-strength RC5.

- **Decoder-design note (the parameter rung; the floor rung).** Two Gauntlet rungs. (1) **Grade the triple before the vectors.** A specimen is graded on whether its w/r/b triple is stated, consistent with its block size (2w), and matched by its subkey count (2(r+1)); vectors run against an unstated triple prove nothing about any RC5. (2) **Grade the floor, not just the construction.** A specimen below the 8-round diffusion floor at w = 32 is graded as a reduced-round specimen whatever its vectors claim, and the card must carry the floor figure beside the round count.

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the 2(r+1) subkey count and the 26-word figure at 12 rounds, computed this pass; CORROBORATED — the Rivest 1994 design and March 20, 1997 revision, the RC5-w/r/b parameterisation with w = 16/32/64, r = 0–255, b = 0–255, the 2w-bit block, the three-operation primitive set with data-dependent rotations as the only nonlinearity, the encryption equations with S[0]/S[1] whitening and per-round S[2i]/S[2i+1], the Pw/Qw definitions and the w = 32 constants 0xB7E15163 / 0x9E3779B9, the 3*max(t, c) mixing passes, and the 4-round correlation / 8-round diffusion calibration figures, all via the Rivest paper and summaries read this pass; CLAIMED — the "discussed as a DES replacement" framing, which rests on secondary summaries rather than the paper text read this pass; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet parameter and floor rungs, which are proposals, never run.]*

## RC2 — the first Rivest block cipher, or: the seal whose key length was a dial, not a fact

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue now holds RC4, RC5, and RC6 — the stream cousin, the parameterized parent, and the AES-finalist child — but not the cipher that started the family. RC2 is the oldest of the released Rivest ciphers, the one Rivest pitched as a drop-in DES replacement, and the one whose most important feature was also its most dangerous: the key length is not a property of the cipher, it is a parameter the caller dials, and the cipher will silently obey a dial set to 40 bits. Every later entry in this catalogue that warns "state the effective key, not the supplied key" is restating a lesson RC2 taught first, in S/MIME, in public, in 1997.
- **The construction, in one paragraph.** RC2 is Ron Rivest's 1987 design, held as an RSA trade secret until an anonymous posting to sci.crypt in 1996 made it public, and described authoritatively in RFC 2268 (March 1998, informational, explicitly not an Internet standard). It is a 64-bit block cipher built for 16-bit microprocessors — Rivest notes it ran about twice as fast as DES on an IBM AT once the key was expanded — and its block is four 16-bit words R[0]..R[3]. The supplied key is 1 to 128 bytes, but the cipher also takes an effective key length T1 in bits, and the search space is 2^(8T) or 2^T1, whichever is smaller: a long supplied key with a short effective length is a short key wearing a long coat. Key expansion fills a 128-byte buffer L from the supplied key, extends it with the PITABLE — a fixed permutation of 0..255 "based on the digits of pi" — then applies the mask step L[128-T8] = PITABLE[L[128-T8] & TM], where T8 = (T1+7)/8 and TM keeps only the low 8-(8*T8-T1) bits, so the effective key is exactly the bytes L[128-T8]..L[127] and the expanded key is 64 sixteen-bit words K[0]..K[63]. Encryption is 16 mixing rounds and 2 mashing rounds in the order 5 mix, 1 mash, 6 mix, 1 mash, 5 mix, using each expanded word exactly once in mixing. A mix step adds the next key word K[j] to R[i], adds a composite word chosen bit-by-bit from R[i-2] or R[i-3] according to R[i-1], and rotates left by s[i], where s = (1, 2, 3, 5). A mash step adds K[R[i-1] & 63] — a key word chosen by the low six bits of the previous word, data-dependent, repetitions allowed. Decryption runs the same schedule backwards with right rotations and subtractions, starting j at 63.
- **What RC2 is not.** It is not a fixed-key cipher: "RC2" without an effective key length is an incomplete identification, and a specimen that reports only its supplied key length has not answered the question that matters. It is not RC5 with a different block size, and it is not RC4's block cousin in any structural sense — its mix/mash machinery, its pi table, and its effective-key mask are its own, shared with no sibling. It is not a standard: RFC 2268 is informational, and a specimen labelled "FIPS RC2" or "standard RC2" is mislabelled, full stop. It is not secure at its export setting: S/MIME's RC2/40 — receiving agents were required to support 40-bit RC2 — was brute-forced in public in 1997 (Schneier's S/MIME 40-bit RC2 cracking screensaver, built precisely to show that 40-bit RC2 was insecure and that users were given no indication they should change the default), and the weakness was the key length, not a flaw in the cipher or the S/MIME specification. And it is not a cipher with a clean block-size story either: a 64-bit block carries the same Sweet32-style birthday exposure the DES entry already documents, so even a full-length RC2 key does not make RC2 a modern choice.
- **The decoder's edge cases.** The effective-key test is the first screen: a specimen must state T1, and a specimen whose supplied key is 128 bytes but whose T1 is 40 is a 40-bit specimen, graded as one. The mask test is the second: recompute T8 and TM from T1 and check that the expanded key depends only on the effective bits — a schedule that lets supplied bits above T1 leak into K is a broken implementation wearing RC2's name. The PITABLE test is the third: the table must be the RFC 2268 table exactly (it opens d9 78 f9 c4 19 dd b5 ed), because a substituted table is a different cipher, checkable from the expanded key alone without any plaintext. The round-order test is the fourth: 5-1-6-1-5, sixteen mixing rounds using each of K[0]..K[63] exactly once, mash rounds data-dependent on the low six bits — any other order, or mash indices taken from anywhere but R[i-1] & 63, is not RC2. The calendar test is the fifth, and it needs no cryptanalysis: any specimen labelled "RC2, secure for new data" fails, on the 64-bit block and on the export history both — the cipher's own story is that its dial was set to 40 and left there.
- **Decoder-design note (the dial rung; the table rung).** Two Gauntlet rungs. (1) **Grade the dial before the vectors.** A specimen is graded on whether its effective key length is stated and matched by its expanded key; vectors run against an unstated T1 prove nothing about any RC2. (2) **Grade the table, not just the rounds.** A specimen whose PITABLE differs from RFC 2268 in even one byte is graded as a different cipher whatever its round structure claims, and the card must carry the first table bytes beside the round count.

No RC2 test vector was recomputed this pass, deliberately.]*

## IDEA — the International Data Encryption Algorithm, or: the seal that mixed three incompatible arithmetics

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue now holds the whole Rivest shelf, DES and Triple DES, the AES bench complete, and the modern AEADs — but not the cipher that carried PGP encryption through the 1990s. IDEA is the PGP-era 64-bit block cipher the RC2 run named absent alongside CAST-128, SAFER, and Skipjack, and it earns its heading for a structural reason no other entry on the shelf shares: it has no S-boxes and no Feistel rounds. Its whole security argument is that three operations from three different algebraic groups — XOR, addition modulo 2^16, and multiplication modulo 2^16+1 — are "algebraically incompatible," so no single analysis bends all three at once. A decoder that only knows Feistel and SPN shapes will misread IDEA entirely; this entry is the shape card for the third shape.

- **The construction, in one paragraph.** IDEA is Xuejia Lai and James Massey's design from ETH Zurich, first specified in 1991 as the successor to Lai's PES (Proposed Encryption Standard), via IPES (Improved PES), to IDEA. It is a 64-bit block cipher with a 128-bit key, built from eight identical rounds plus an output transformation — the "half-round" — for 8.5 rounds total. The block is four 16-bit words, and each full round takes six 16-bit subkeys; the half-round takes four; 8×6+4 = 52 subkeys in all. The round, in the standard step form: multiply the first word by subkey 1, add subkey 2 to the second, add subkey 3 to the third, multiply the fourth by subkey 4; XOR the first and third results, XOR the second and fourth results; feed those two XORs through the multiplication-addition (MA) structure — multiply the first XOR by subkey 5, add the second XOR, multiply by subkey 6, add back — and XOR the MA outputs into the four words, first and third against one MA output, second and fourth against the other. Between rounds the two middle output words swap places; after the eighth round they do not, and the half-round (multiply, add, add, multiply with the last four subkeys) produces the ciphertext. The key schedule is a straight line: the 128-bit key splits into the first eight subkeys, then the key rotates left 25 bits and yields the next eight, repeating until all 52 are filled — 128/16 = 8 per group, 25-bit steps, no S-box, no nonlinear expansion anywhere. Decryption is the same structure with inverse subkeys in reverse order: multiplicative inverses modulo 65537 where encryption multiplied, additive inverses modulo 65536 where it added, with the middle-swap accounting handled by the subkey order. The multiplication's one quirk is load-bearing: 65537 is prime (2^16+1, the Fermat prime F4), so every nonzero value has an inverse — and the all-zero word 0x0000 is read as 65536, the one value 16 bits cannot otherwise name, so that the multiplication is a genuine group operation on all 65,536 possible words rather than a near-miss with a hole at zero.

- **What IDEA is not.** It is not a Feistel cipher: all four words are transformed every round, and there is no left/right split with a round function. It is not an S-box cipher, and it is not a scaled DES: its nonlinearity comes from mixing incompatible operations, not from tables. It is not scalable to a 128-bit block by the same trick — the construction leans on 2^16+1 being prime, and 2^32+1 famously is not, so IDEA cannot be trivially widened the way a Feistel cipher can. It is not a standard and never was: IDEA was patented (Ascom, licensed worldwide by MediaCrypt) and the patents expired in 2010–2011, which is why it is free to use now and why it stayed out of standards bodies while patented. It is not PGP's current cipher either: IDEA is best known as the cipher inside PGP 2.x, but OpenPGP moved on to AES and others, and IDEA survives as a legacy/optional algorithm, not a default. And it is not a modern choice for bulk data at any key size: a 64-bit block carries the same birthday exposure the DES and RC2 entries already document, so IDEA's 128-bit key does not rescue it from the Sweet32-style volume limit — the key is long, the block is short, and the block is what bounds the safe volume.

- **The decoder's edge cases.** The zero-word test is the first screen: a specimen whose multiplication treats 0x0000 as zero rather than 65536 has broken the group operation, and its decryption inverses will not round-trip — checkable from one encrypt-decrypt pair without any known vector. The subkey-count test is the second: exactly 52 subkeys, 8×6+4, and a schedule that stops at 48 or runs to 56 has misread the half-round. The rotation test is the third: the key schedule rotates left 25 bits per group, not 16, not 32 — a 16-bit rotation would just re-read the same eight subkeys, and a 32-bit rotation would cycle through only four distinct groups. The swap test is the fourth: the middle two words swap between rounds but not after the eighth, and a specimen that swaps after the final round, or never swaps, fails the round-boundary test even if its round math is correct. The inverse test is the fifth: decryption subkeys must be the multiplicative inverses modulo 65537 and additive inverses modulo 65536 of the encryption subkeys in reverse order — a specimen that reuses encryption subkeys for decryption, or inverts modulo the wrong number, is not IDEA even if its encryption vectors match.

- **Decoder-design note (the zero rung; the swap rung).** Two Gauntlet rungs. (1) **Grade the zero convention before the vectors.** A specimen is graded on whether 0x0000 multiplies as 65536, proven by a round-trip pair; vectors run against a zero-means-zero multiplication prove nothing about any IDEA. (2) **Grade the swap, not just the rounds.** A specimen whose middle words do not swap between rounds, or swap once too often, is graded as a different cipher whatever its MA structure claims, and the card must carry the swap behaviour beside the round count.

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the 8×6+4 = 52 subkey count and the 128/16 = 8 subkeys per key group, computed this pass; CORROBORATED — the Lai/Massey 1991 design and ETH Zurich origin, the PES/IPES/IDEA lineage, the 64-bit block and 128-bit key, the 8 rounds plus half-round, the three operations with addition modulo 65536 and multiplication modulo 65537, the 0x0000-as-65536 convention, the MA structure, the 25-bit left-rotation key schedule, the PGP 2.x association, the Ascom/MediaCrypt patent history with expiry in 2010–2011, and the as-of-2007 best attack breaking 6 rounds, all via IDEA summaries and references read this pass; CLAIMED — the weak-key classes reported for IDEA in the secondary literature, not re-checked this pass; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet zero and swap rungs, which are proposals, never run. No IDEA test vector was recomputed this pass, deliberately.]*

## Quagmire I–IV — the mixed-alphabet Vigenères, or: the family that keyed both sides of the slide

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue now holds the whole Vigenère family tree — Vigenère itself, Porta's thirteen reciprocal pairs, Gronsfeld's ten digit rows, Autokey's self-feeding key, the Nihilist's arithmetic stacking, VIC's straddling checkerboard — but not the family that generalizes all of them. The Quagmires are the American Cryptogram Association's classification of periodic polyalphabetic substitution with a mixed alphabet on at least one side of the slide, and they are the missing rung between "Vigenère with a keyword" and "Vigenère with a keyed alphabet": the question stops being *which row* and becomes *which alphabet, on which side*. [2026-11-03 create loop]
- **The family, in one table.** All four are periodic: an indicator keyword sets the period and the alignment of the cipher alphabets, which cycle position by position. What differs is where the mixing lives — and Helen Fouché Gaines' four slide types in *Elementary Cryptanalysis* map onto them exactly. Quagmire I: keyed plaintext alphabet, straight (A–Z) cipher alphabets at different slides. Quagmire II: straight plaintext alphabet, one keyed cipher alphabet at different slides. Quagmire III: the *same* keyed alphabet for plaintext and ciphertext, slid against itself. Quagmire IV: a keyed plaintext alphabet and a *different* keyed cipher alphabet, the cipher one slid per period position — three keywords in play (plaintext keyword, ciphertext keyword, indicator keyword), as in the ACA's worked example with plaintext keyword SENSORY, ciphertext keyword PERC(EP)TION, and indicator EXTRA at period 5. [VERIFIED — family definitions per the CryptoCrack Quagmire guide and the classical-cryptography lecture account; CORROBORATED — the Gaines slide-type mapping and the Q4 three-keyword example per the ACA's own Quagmire IV sheet]
- **The naming.** The ACA calls the class "Quagmires I, II, III, IV" after the terminology used for keying Aristocrats, and numbers them the same way as its keyword plans: a Quagmire 4 uses a K4 keyword plan. The name is a puzzle-hobby term, not a wartime one — no army fielded a "Quagmire" — and that is precisely why the family matters to this catalogue: it is the form classical polyalphabetic ciphers take when they are studied as a system rather than deployed as a weapon, and the system view is what the Gauntlet needs. [CORROBORATED — ACA terminology per the lecture account and the ACA Quagmire IV sheet]
- **The mechanism, stated once.** Build the keyed alphabet by writing the keyword with repeated letters removed, then appending the unused letters in alphabetical order — keyword PAULBRANDT becomes PAULBRNDTCEFGHIJKMOQSVWXYZ in the CryptoCrack worked example. The tableau is then a set of slides: the plain component on top, one cipher component per period position underneath, each slid by the indicator keyword's letter for that position. Encipherment is column lookup: find the plaintext letter in the plain component, read down the current period position's cipher component. Nothing here is new machinery — it is the Vigenère tableau with the top row keyed, or the bottom rows keyed, or both — and that is the point: every classical polyalphabetic in the catalogue is a Quagmire with one side left straight. [VERIFIED — the keyed-alphabet construction per the CryptoCrack example, recomputed this pass]
- **Worked miniature (computed this pass, stated convention).** Quagmire I, keyword KODAKAI, indicator SEA (period 3). The keyed plain alphabet is KODAIBCEFGHJLMNPQRSTUVWXYZ (KODAKAI dedupes to KODAI). The cipher components are straight alphabets slid by the indicator letter's straight-alphabet index: S → STUVWXYZABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQR, E → EFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZABCD, A → ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ. Plaintext THEQUAGMIREHIDESINPLAINSIGHT enciphers to LOHIYDBREJLKWGHKIOHQDWSSWNKL, and decryption round-trips exactly. The miniature's one lesson, visible without any statistics: the plaintext letter E lands as Z, L, and H under the three indicator positions — the same letter, three images, period 3 doing its whole job in nine letters. [VERIFIED — computed and round-trip-checked this pass; the convention (slide = indicator letter's straight-alphabet index) is this entry's stated choice among the family's equivalent tableau conventions, not a claim about the ACA's house convention]
- **The honest weakness.** Quagmire III confesses by symmetry. Because the same mixed alphabet serves both sides, any rectangle in the tableau has equal opposite sides: pick four letters at the corners of a rectangle and the two letters in the same column or row are equally far apart, in every slide at once. A solver with a crib and the period — found first by the Index of Coincidence over the columns, exactly as the catalogue's Friedman entry prescribes, with Q3 puzzle periods typically running 5 to 12 — can chain those equalities across the whole message and recover the mixed alphabet without ever guessing the keyword. Quagmires I, II, and IV lack the shared-alphabet rectangle and fall instead to the standard road: period by IC, then per-column mixed-alphabet recovery, which is longer work but the same road. No Quagmire survives its period being found; the mixed alphabet only raises the price of the second step. [CORROBORATED — the Q3 rectangle-symmetry account and the 5–12 period range per the documented Q3 solving guide; the IC-first road per the catalogue's own Friedman entry]
- **Decoder-design note (Quagmire → Gauntlet).** Two rungs. (1) **Key both sides of the slide before pricing the specimen.** A specimen that presents "a Vigenère variant" has not been described until both components are named: straight or keyed, and if keyed, keyed by what. The catalogue's Porta entry priced thirteen images per letter and Gronsfeld ten; the Quagmire entry prices the general case — the number of distinct cipher alphabets is the period, and the mixedness of each side is a separate fact. Gauntlet intake asks the two-sided question first, because a specimen that hides a keyed component behind a familiar name (Vigenère with a "twist") is the oldest misdirection in the book. (2) **Symmetry is a confession, not a curiosity.** Q3's rectangle equalities are the same shape as the Porta entry's involution and the Nihilist entry's carry: a structural identity that holds under every key choice and therefore survives every key change. Gauntlet rule, confirmed a third time: enumerate what the transform *cannot help but preserve* before asking what key it used — the invariant is the cheapest finding, and it is the one the specimen's designer forgot to price. [CORROBORATED lineage — the family, the miniature, and the Q3 symmetry account above; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's doctrine, never run]

## CAST-128 — CAST5, or: the seal whose key length was a dial and whose rounds followed it

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue now holds the whole Rivest shelf, DES and Triple DES, the AES bench, the modern AEADs, and — from the run just before this one — IDEA, the cipher CAST-128 replaced inside PGP. The IDEA entry named three absentees alongside itself: CAST-128, SAFER, and Skipjack. This entry takes the first. CAST-128 earns its heading for a structural reason no Rivest entry shares: it is a Feistel cipher whose *round count itself* is a function of the key — 12 rounds for short keys, 16 for long ones — and whose round keys are 37 bits wide, 32 for masking and 5 for a key-dependent rotation. A decoder that only checks "Feistel, 16 rounds" will misread every short-key CAST-128 specimen it meets. [2026-11-03 create loop]

- **The construction, in one paragraph.** CAST-128 is Carlisle Adams and Stafford Tavares's design from 1996, built with the CAST design procedure and specified as RFC 2144 (Adams, 1997). It is a Feistel network on a 64-bit block split into two 32-bit halves, with a key of 40 to 128 bits in 8-bit steps — twelve legal key sizes, 40, 48, …, 128. Keys of 80 bits or fewer run 12 rounds; keys longer than 80 bits run the full 16. Each round takes a 37-bit round key: 32 masking bits and 5 rotation bits. The round function takes the 32-bit half, combines it with the masking key, splits the result into four bytes, and passes each byte through a different 8×32 S-box — four S-boxes in encryption, with four more S-boxes reserved for the key schedule, eight in all, built from bent functions so that every output bit depends on every input bit and every key bit. The four 32-bit S-box outputs are then combined nonlinearly, and the combination itself alternates by round: three round-function types cycle through the choices of addition modulo 2^32, subtraction modulo 2^32, and XOR at each combining step, so no single operation's algebra describes every round. The combined value is rotated left by the round's 5-bit rotation key — a key-dependent rotation, 0 to 31 positions — and XORed into the other half, as in every Feistel round. Short keys are zero-padded to 128 bits before the key schedule runs, and the schedule derives one masking-plus-rotation pair per round: 16 pairs, 32 subkeys, 592 bits of round-key material at full length (12 × 37 = 444 at short length). Decryption is the same Feistel structure run backwards with the round keys in reverse order. The name itself carries a small dispute worth recording: some sources read CAST as the inventors' initials, while Bruce Schneier reports the authors' claim that the name "should conjure up images of randomness."

- **What CAST-128 is not.** It is not IDEA's successor in construction, only in PGP: CAST-128 replaced IDEA in PGP 3.0 and is specified in all versions of the OpenPGP standard as CAST5, but where IDEA mixed three incompatible arithmetics with no S-boxes and no Feistel split, CAST-128 is a textbook Feistel cipher with large S-boxes — the two PGP-era ciphers share a mailbox, not a shape. It is not CAST-256: the later AES candidate widens the block to 128 bits and is a different cipher, not CAST-128 with bigger keys. It is not a fixed-round cipher: a specimen described as "CAST-128, 16 rounds" with a 64-bit key has either misread the round rule or is running a nonstandard variant, and the card must say which. It is not free of the 64-bit-block volume limit: like DES, RC2, and IDEA before it, a 64-bit block bounds the safe volume under one key regardless of key length, so CAST-128's 128-bit key does not rescue it from the Sweet32-style limit the catalogue already documents. And it is not a modern default at any key size: the 40-bit end of its dial is export-era crippling, weak by construction, and the dial's existence is itself the warning — a cipher whose key length is a user-set dial invites deployments that chose the shortest setting and forgot.

- **The decoder's edge cases.** The round-count test is the first screen: ≤80-bit keys must run 12 rounds, >80-bit keys 16 — a specimen that runs 16 rounds on a 64-bit key, or 12 on a 128-bit key, fails the boundary before any vector is consulted. The padding test is the second: a short key is zero-padded to 128 bits, not repeated, not hashed — a schedule that repeats a 40-bit key to fill 128 bits is a different cipher's schedule wearing CAST-128's name. The S-box test is the third: eight 8×32 tables, 256 entries of 32 bits each, 1 KiB per table and 8 KiB for the set — a specimen with DES-shaped 6×4 tables, or four tables total, has not implemented CAST at all. The rotation test is the fourth: the rotation key is 5 bits, so a rotation amount above 31, or a fixed rotation, breaks the round function even if the S-boxes are right. The alternation test is the fifth: the three combining types must cycle — a specimen that uses one combining rule in every round is a simplified CAST, not CAST-128, whatever its vectors claim.

- **Decoder-design note (the dial rung; the boundary rung).** Two Gauntlet rungs. (1) **Grade the dial, not just the cipher.** When a specimen's key length is a setting, the Gauntlet grades the setting that was actually deployed, not the maximum the cipher allows — CAST-128 at 40 bits and CAST-128 at 128 bits are different security claims sharing a name, and the card must carry the deployed key length beside the cipher name, always. (2) **Grade the boundary, not just the rounds.** A rule that changes behaviour at a threshold — 12 rounds below, 16 above — is tested at the threshold itself: 80-bit and 88-bit keys are the specimens that prove the rule, not the 40-bit and 128-bit extremes. Gauntlet standing rule, confirmed again: test the edge where the behaviour changes, because that is where implementations silently pick the wrong branch.

## SAFER — Secure And Fast Encryption Routine, or: the cipher that did all its work one byte at a time

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue now holds IDEA and CAST-128, the two PGP-era ciphers that shared a mailbox but not a shape — and both were designed, in part, by James Massey. This entry takes the third Massey name the IDEA entry left standing: SAFER, the family Massey built for Cylink starting in 1993. SAFER earns its heading for a structural reason no Feistel entry shares: it is not a Feistel cipher at all, and it is not an S-box-plus-permutation cipher in the DES sense either. It is a byte-oriented substitution–diffusion cipher whose whole round is eight parallel byte operations, a pair of S-boxes built from one exponentiation in the field GF(257), and a diffusion layer — the Pseudo-Hadamard Transform — that is pure byte arithmetic, no bit permutation anywhere. A decoder that only looks for Feistel halves or bit permutations will misread every SAFER specimen it meets. [2026-11-03 create loop]

- **The construction, in one paragraph.** SAFER K-64, published by Massey in 1993, takes a 64-bit block and a 64-bit key and works only in bytes: eight 8-bit segments, never a 32-bit half. Each round has four stages. First key-mixing: each byte is combined with a subkey byte, by addition modulo 256 on some positions and by XOR on others, alternating by position. Second, the substitution layer: two S-boxes, inverses of each other, derived from discrete exponentiation and logarithm base 45 in GF(257) — X(a) = 45^a mod 257 (with X(128) = 0 as the special case) and its inverse L, the base-45 logarithm — so the S-boxes are mathematics, not tables chosen by hand. Third, a second key-mixing stage, again addition on some bytes and XOR on others. Fourth, the diffusion layer: the Pseudo-Hadamard Transform, applied in three levels over byte pairs, where one PHT step sends (a1, a2) to (b1 = (2·a1 + a2) mod 256, b2 = (a1 + a2) mod 256), and its inverse sends (b1, b2) back to (a1 = (b1 − b2) mod 256, a2 = (−b1 + 2·b2) mod 256) — diffusion achieved by doubling and adding, not by shuffling bits. After r rounds comes an output transformation, the same shape as a round's first key-mixing stage, using one more subkey. The recommended round count for K-64 is 6, with larger values allowed; the key schedule expands the 64-bit key into 2r + 1 subkeys of 64 bits each — 13 subkeys, 832 bits of round-key material at the recommended 6 rounds — by rotating the key and adding additive key biases built from powers of 45, which exist to kill the weak-key symmetry a pure rotation schedule would leave. Decryption is not encryption run backwards with the same rounds: the decrypting rounds differ in structure (inverse PHT first, mixed XOR/subtraction in place of XOR/addition), so an encrypter cannot be turned into a decrypter by merely reversing the key schedule.

- **The family, and why the letters matter.** SAFER K-128 (1994) keeps the same round function and the same 64-bit block but takes a 128-bit key, with a new key schedule designed by Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs: two 64-bit keys expanded in parallel, their subkey sequences interleaved, so that setting the two halves equal makes a 128-bit key compatible with the 64-bit version. Lars Knudsen and Sean Murphy then found weaknesses in the K key schedules — Knudsen's key-schedule weakness gives, for virtually every key, other keys that encrypt some plaintext differing in one byte to ciphertexts also differing in only one byte — and the schedule was redesigned on Knudsen's suggestion. The redesigned variants are SAFER SK-64 and SAFER SK-128: same encryption function as K, different (strengthened) key schedule, and the SK names are the ones a careful card should carry, not K. SAFER+ (Massey et al., 1998) is the family's second generation: a 128-bit block, submitted as an AES candidate, with rounds keyed to key size — 8 rounds for 128-bit keys, 12 for 192-bit, 16 for 256-bit — and it did not reach the AES second round, NIST judging its speed, not its margin, the deciding weakness. Its afterlife is the one most decoders will actually meet: Bluetooth uses customized SAFER+-based algorithms for key derivation (E21, E22) and authentication (E1), while Bluetooth link encryption itself does not use SAFER+. SAFER++ (2000) followed as a NESSIE submission in 64-bit and 128-bit block versions, with 7 rounds at 128-bit keys and 10 at 256-bit keys in the 128-bit-block version. All SAFER algorithms are unpatented and available for unrestricted use.

- **What SAFER is not.** It is not a Feistel cipher: there are no halves swapping, and the \"left/right\" split some summaries impose on it belongs to other ciphers, not this one. It is not DES-shaped: its S-boxes are a matched exponentiation/logarithm pair in GF(257), not hand-picked 6×4 tables, and its diffusion is the PHT's arithmetic, not a bit permutation — a specimen with a P-box has not implemented SAFER. It is not IDEA, though Massey designed both: IDEA mixes three incompatible arithmetics with no S-boxes, SAFER builds its nonlinearity from one field exponentiation and diffuses with one transform. It is not a modern default at any generation: the 64-bit block of K/SK carries the same Sweet32-style volume limit the catalogue already documents, K's key schedule is the weak one Knudsen broke, and SAFER+ lost the AES race on speed — a SAFER specimen in the wild is legacy, Bluetooth-derived, or a museum piece, and the card must say which.

- **The decoder's edge cases.** The byte test is the first screen: eight bytes in, eight bytes out, every operation a byte operation — a specimen that splits the block into 32-bit halves is not SAFER. The S-box test is the second: the two tables must be the 45-exponentiation pair in GF(257), inverses of each other — random or DES-shaped tables fail before any vector is consulted. The PHT test is the third: (2a1 + a2, a1 + a2) mod 256, three levels per round, with the exact inverse above — a diffusion layer that permutes bits instead is a different cipher. The schedule test is the fourth: K versus SK is a key-schedule distinction, not a round-function one, so a specimen claiming \"SAFER\" without saying K or SK has not said enough, and a K specimen must be graded against Knudsen's weakness, not against SK's repaired schedule. The generation test is the fifth: K/SK means a 64-bit block, SAFER+ means a 128-bit block with rounds tied to key size (8/12/16) — a 128-bit block running 6 rounds, or a 64-bit block running 16, has mixed the generations.

- **Decoder-design note (the arithmetic rung; the letter rung).** Two Gauntlet rungs. (1) **Grade the arithmetic, not just the tables.** When a cipher's S-boxes and diffusion are formulas, the Gauntlet checks the formulas — exponentiation base, field, PHT coefficients — not merely that tables exist and are invertible; a specimen with plausible-looking tables and wrong arithmetic is the dangerous case, because vectors alone may still pass on short tests. (2) **Grade the letter, not just the name.** When a family name carries a schedule revision — K versus SK — the Gauntlet grades the letter that was actually deployed, because the revision is the security fix; \"SAFER\" without its letter is an incomplete identification, and the card must carry it beside the cipher name, always.

## Skipjack — the NSA cipher that hid in a phone chip, or: the seal whose key schedule repeats every five rounds

- **The gap this entry closes.** The IDEA entry named three absentees alongside itself: CAST-128, SAFER, and Skipjack. The first two were built this morning. This entry takes the third and last, and it closes the PGP-era shelf with a cipher from a different world entirely: Skipjack is the catalogue's only classified-then-declassified cipher — designed by the NSA, fielded only in tamperproof hardware, and released to the public in June 1998 with its design intact. It earns its heading for a structural reason no other entry shares: its round function is a Feistel cipher *inside* a Feistel cipher. The G permutation that transforms one quarter of the block per round is itself a four-round Feistel on a 16-bit word, with a single 256-entry byte table for its round function. A decoder that looks for one Feistel level will find two, and a decoder that looks for S-boxes plural will find exactly one table doing all the work.

- **The construction, in one paragraph.** Skipjack takes a 64-bit block and an 80-bit key. The block splits into four 16-bit words, and the cipher runs 32 rounds in a fixed order: eight A rounds, eight B rounds, eight A rounds, eight B rounds. A round counter — the round number itself, 1 through 32 — is XORed into one word per round. The A round sends (a, b, c, d) to (d ⊕ Gk(a) ⊕ counter, Gk(a), b, c): the first word passes through G, and the result, XORed with the counter, lands in the fourth word's place. The B round sends (a, b, c, d) to (d, Gk(a), a ⊕ b ⊕ counter, c): the first word still passes through G, but the counter XOR now lands on the third word, mixed with the first word's old value. After every round the four words rotate one position — and, unlike DES, the rotation is *not* omitted after the last round; a Skipjack encryption ends mid-rotation, and the card must say so. The G permutation takes a 16-bit word and a 4-byte subkey and runs a four-round Feistel on the word's two bytes: each G-round XORs one subkey byte into a byte, substitutes through the F-table — one 8×8 S-box, 256 entries, 256 bytes total — and XORs the result into the other byte. The key schedule is a straight cycle: the 80-bit key is ten bytes, K0 through K9, and each round's G takes four consecutive key bytes, starting at offset 4(r−1) mod 10 for round r. Decryption runs the inverse rounds in reverse order, with G⁻¹ equal to G with its subkeys reversed and its halves swapped.

- **What Skipjack is not.** It is not a balanced Feistel cipher: only one of the four words passes through G per round, and the other three move or mix but are never substituted — the "unbalanced" in its classification is the whole shape. It is not a key-escrow cipher in itself: the escrow lived in the Law Enforcement Access Field (LEAF), a separate mechanism wrapped around Skipjack inside the Clipper chip, and the cipher's math carries no escrow — a card that grades Skipjack as "the escrow cipher" has graded the wrapper, not the transform. It is not a broken cipher: the full 32-round cipher has no known attack, and the famous 31-round impossible-differential attack is only slightly faster than exhaustive search — a result about the cipher's margin, not its fall. It is not a modern choice at any key size: an 80-bit key is below the ECRYPT II bar as of 2012, the 64-bit block carries the same Sweet32-style volume limit the catalogue already documents, and a 2016 NIST draft stopped certifying Skipjack for US government use. It is not SAFER- or IDEA-shaped: no Pseudo-Hadamard Transform, no multiplication-addition structure, no bit permutation anywhere — its diffusion is the word rotation plus G, and nothing else.

- **The decoder's edge cases.** The period test is the first screen: the subkey starting offsets step by 4 modulo 10, so the schedule repeats every 5 rounds — rounds 1, 6, 11, 16, 21, 26, and 31 all take the *same* four key bytes, differing only in counter and round type. A specimen whose key schedule does not repeat at period 5, or that derives fresh subkeys per round, has misread the schedule outright. The switch test is the second: A gives way to B at rounds 9 and 25, B gives way back to A at round 17 — a specimen running all A rounds, or all B rounds, fails at the boundaries even if its G is perfect. The counter test is the third: the counter is the round number 1 through 32, not 0 through 31 — a 0-based counter shifts every round's XOR and fails every vector past round 1. The rotation test is the fourth: the quarters rotate after the 32nd round too — a specimen that omits the final rotation out of DES habit fails the last step and no other. The G test is the fifth: G is a four-round Feistel with *one* 256-byte F-table — a specimen with DES-shaped 6×4 tables, or four tables, or a non-Feistel G, has not implemented Skipjack whatever its round count claims.

- **Decoder-design note (the period rung; the wrapper rung).** Two Gauntlet rungs. (1) **Grade the schedule's period, not just its bytes.** When a key schedule cycles, the Gauntlet checks the cycle length before the key material: period 5 means 32 rounds contain only five distinct subkey groups, and the card must carry that fact beside the key length — "80-bit key, 5 subkey groups" is a different security claim from "80-bit key, 32 subkey groups," and a specimen that hides the repetition behind a long round count is the dangerous case. (2) **Grade the transform; name the wrapper separately.** Skipjack's controversy was LEAF, not the cipher math, and the Gauntlet rule this entry confirms is general: a policy mechanism wrapped around a cipher is graded as its own specimen, never folded into the cipher's verdict — and a clean cipher verdict never blesses the wrapper. The card carries two lines, one for each, always.

## Blowfish — Schneier's public-domain Feistel cipher, or: the seal whose key schedule is the whole weapon

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue already holds Blowfish twice over and never itself: the bcrypt entry is built on it (EksBlowfish — "the Blowfish key schedule is run with the salt and the password alternating as keys, deliberately made slow"), and the Twofish entry names it as the predecessor ("beyond the name and the idea of key-dependent S-boxes, it is a new design"). This entry supplies the missing middle: the cipher itself, published by Bruce Schneier in 1993, placed in the public domain, and still the most widely deployed pre-AES cipher the shelf has never described. It also closes the pre-AES shelf beside DES, IDEA, CAST-128, SAFER, and Skipjack: Blowfish is the one of that shelf whose security argument lives less in its rounds than in its setup. [2026-11-03 create loop]

- **The construction, in one paragraph.** Blowfish takes a 64-bit block and a variable-length key of 32 to 448 bits, in 8-bit steps — 53 legal key sizes — and runs a 16-round Feistel network. The state is a P-array of eighteen 32-bit subkeys and four S-boxes of 256 32-bit entries each: 1,042 words, 4,168 bytes of state, initialized to the hexadecimal digits of pi (P1 = 243F6A88, P2 = 85A308D3, P3 = 13198A2E, and on through the tables). The round function splits its 32-bit input into four bytes a, b, c, d and computes F = ((S1[a] + S2[b]) mod 2^32 XOR S3[c]) + S4[d] mod 2^32 — addition, XOR, addition, in that order, and the order is load-bearing: a specimen that XORs first and adds second is a different function wearing Blowfish's tables. A round XORs the left half with the next P entry, applies F, and XORs the result into the right half, then swaps; after sixteen rounds the halves are swapped back and whitened with P17 and P18. The key schedule is the expensive part, and deliberately so: the key bytes are XORed into the P-array cyclically, then the all-zero block is encrypted and its output replaces P1 and P2, the output is re-encrypted and replaces P3 and P4, and so on through all eighteen P entries and all 1,024 S-box entries — 521 encryptions before a single user block is ever touched. A 448-bit key costs the same 521 encryptions as a 32-bit key; the schedule's price is flat, and that flat price is the whole reason bcrypt could later be built on it.

- **What Blowfish is not.** It is not Twofish: Twofish is a 128-bit-block AES finalist whose S-boxes are derived from the key, while Blowfish's S-boxes are fixed pi digits and its key enters only through the P-array XOR and the 521-encryption schedule — a specimen graded against key-dependent S-boxes has been misread. It is not bcrypt: bcrypt is EksBlowfish, the schedule weaponized by running it with salt and password alternating; plain Blowfish encrypts blocks, it does not hash passwords, and a "Blowfish hash" specimen is either bcrypt mislabelled or a fabrication. It is not a modern default at any key size: the 64-bit block carries the same Sweet32-style volume limit the catalogue already documents — about 2^32 blocks, 32 GiB, under one key before the birthday bound bites — so a long-lived Blowfish session is unsafe no matter how long its key is. It is not a broken cipher: no practical attack is known against the full 16 rounds, and the attacks that exist are the honest kind — Serge Vaudenay's 1996 weak-key classes, where certain keys produce S-boxes with colliding entries, and differential attacks that reach only reduced-round versions. And it is not a cipher whose key length is its security: the 32-bit end of its dial is export-era crippling, weak by construction, exactly as the CAST-128 entry's dial warned — the card must carry the deployed key length beside the cipher name, always.

- **The decoder's edge cases.** The convention test is the first screen, and this pass proved why: the spec cycles the key bytes through the P-array, but this machine's `openssl enc -bf-ecb` zero-pads any key shorter than 16 bytes out to 16 bytes instead of cycling it — measured directly this pass (an 8-byte key's OpenSSL output equals the zero-padded-16-byte key's output exactly, and differs from the cycled key's output), while full-length 16-byte keys agree under both conventions. A decoder that compares a specimen against `openssl enc` output without stating its convention will condemn correct short-key specimens and pass padded ones. The pi test is the second: the tables must open 243F6A88, 85A308D3, 13198A2E — any other opening is not Blowfish, whatever the round count claims. The F-order test is the third: add, XOR, add — a specimen computing (S1[a] XOR S2[b]) + S3[c] + S4[d], or any other order, fails before any vector is consulted. The schedule test is the fourth: 521 encryptions, P entries first, then S-boxes in order — a specimen that initializes its tables from the key directly, or that encrypts a nonzero seed block, has skipped the schedule that is the cipher's identity. The volume test is the fifth: 32 GiB under one key is the ceiling, and a specimen that rekeys never, at any key length, has mistaken a long key for a long life.

- **Decoder-design note (the schedule rung; the oracle rung).** Two Gauntlet rungs. (1) **Grade the schedule, not just the rounds.** Blowfish's rounds are sixteen lines of textbook Feistel; its schedule is 521 encryptions and 4 KiB of state that must be exactly right before round one. The bcrypt entry already proved the schedule can be the weapon; the Gauntlet rule this entry confirms is general: when a cipher's setup costs more than its encryption, the setup is graded first, because a specimen that gets the rounds right and the schedule wrong is wrong everywhere and looks right on short tests. (2) **Grade the oracle's convention before the specimen.** The `openssl enc` padding finding is not about Blowfish — it is about measurement: the harness's key handling is part of the result, and a vector comparison that does not name the harness's convention (cycle versus pad, for every key length the specimen claims) is not a comparison at all. Gauntlet standing rule, confirmed again: state the oracle's convention in the card, beside the specimen's, before any vector is quoted.

## FEAL — the Fast Data Encipherment Algorithm, or: the seal whose arithmetic taught the field two attacks

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue already holds DES, the cipher differential cryptanalysis was aimed at, and SAFER, the cipher whose S-boxes are formulas rather than tables — but it has never held the cipher on which both differential and linear cryptanalysis were first proven in practice. FEAL earns its heading for a historical reason no other entry shares: it is the cipher that taught cryptanalysis its two great generic attacks. Designed by Akihiro Shimizu and Shoji Miyaguchi at NTT and first published in 1987 as a faster software alternative to DES, FEAL was Japan's first commercially successful cipher, optimized for 8-bit microprocessors with no lookup tables anywhere — and that very economy, addition and rotation in place of tables, is what made it the perfect laboratory for Biham and Shamir, for Gilbert and Chassé, and for Matsui and Yamagishi. A decoder that knows DES but not FEAL knows the target of the attacks but not the specimen they were demonstrated on. [2026-11-03 create loop]

- **The construction, in one paragraph.** FEAL is a Feistel cipher on a 64-bit block throughout its family: FEAL-4 (1987) runs 4 rounds, FEAL-8 (1988) doubles that to 8, and FEAL-N (1990) lets the user choose N, with 32 recommended — while FEAL-NX (1990) keeps the same round function and lifts the key from 64 bits to 128. Each round takes a 16-bit subkey — two bytes, not a 32-bit word — and updates R_i = L_{i-1} ⊕ F(R_{i-1}, K_i), L_i = R_{i-1}. The round function F takes a 32-bit input as four bytes and a two-byte subkey, and its entire nonlinearity is two byte functions built from addition modulo 256 and a 2-bit left rotation: S0(x, y) = ROTL2((x + y) mod 256) and S1(x, y) = ROTL2((x + y + 1) mod 256) — the same formula, differing only by the +1, applied in an alternating pattern through the four bytes. There are no S-box tables to steal, misprint, or misimplement: the "S-boxes" are arithmetic, and a specimen's F is either this arithmetic or it is not FEAL. The original description also XORs key material into the data entering and leaving the network; later analyses move that material into the rounds (the "modified FEAL" of the linear-cryptanalysis papers), so a specimen must say which representation it implements — the two agree as ciphers only when the end XORs are accounted for, not ignored.

- **What FEAL is not.** It is not DES with fewer rounds: DES's nonlinearity lives in eight hand-picked 6×4 tables and a bit permutation, while FEAL's lives in byte addition and rotation — a specimen with a P-box has not implemented FEAL, whatever its round count claims. It is not a cipher whose round count is a footnote: FEAL-4, FEAL-8, and FEAL-32 are different security claims sharing a name, and the Biham–Shamir result draws the line at 31 — FEAL-N and FEAL-NX fall faster than exhaustive search for every N ≤ 31, so only the recommended 32 (and above) even reaches the conversation. It is not a modern default at any generation: the 64-bit block carries the same Sweet32-style volume limit the catalogue already documents, and the family is broken as a cipher in every version below the recommended round count — a FEAL specimen in the wild is legacy, a museum piece, or a cryptanalysis teaching specimen, and the card must say which. It is not SAFER-shaped either, though both build nonlinearity from formulas: SAFER's formulas are a field exponentiation and a Pseudo-Hadamard Transform, FEAL's are addition and rotation — the cheapest arithmetic that could still be called a cipher, and the reason the attacks worked.

- **The decoder's edge cases.** The formula test is the first screen: S0 and S1 must be ROTL2 of a byte sum, with S1 exactly S0 shifted by one — a specimen with lookup tables, or with S1 differing from S0 by anything but the +1, has not implemented FEAL. The rotation test is the second: the rotation is exactly 2 bits — a specimen rotating by 1, 3, or 8 fails before any vector is consulted, because every S-box output in the cipher passes through that rotation. The subkey test is the third: each round takes a 16-bit subkey — a specimen taking 32-bit round subkeys has merged two rounds' worth of key material into one (the combined representation of the differential-cryptanalysis writeups) and must say so, because its subkey count then reads half the true round count. The representation test is the fourth: original FEAL XORs key material at the network's ends, modified FEAL folds it into the rounds — a specimen that implements one representation and is graded against the other's vectors will fail every vector while being correct, the exact oracle-convention trap the Blowfish entry documented. The version test is the fifth: the card carries N beside the name, always — "FEAL" without its round count is an incomplete identification, and a FEAL-4 specimen graded as if it were FEAL-32 is a pass handed to a broken cipher.

- **Decoder-design note (the arithmetic rung; the ladder rung).** Two Gauntlet rungs. (1) **Grade the arithmetic, not just the tables — especially when there are no tables.** FEAL's whole security argument is two additions and a rotation; the Gauntlet rule this entry confirms is general: when a cipher's nonlinearity is a formula, the formula's parameters (rotation amount, the +1 offset, the modulus) are graded individually, because a wrong parameter is a different cipher that still "looks like" the original on short tests. (2) **Grade the ladder, not just the rung.** FEAL's cryptanalysis history is a ladder — 5 known plaintexts for FEAL-4, 100 for FEAL-6, 2^15 for FEAL-8, faster-than-exhaustive differential attacks up to N = 31 — and the card for a reduced-round specimen must name where on the ladder it stands, not merely that it is "broken": a FEAL-4 specimen and a FEAL-31 specimen are both broken, but by attacks of wildly different cost, and the card must carry the cost beside the verdict.
