## SHA-1 — the Secure Hash Algorithm, or: the seal that carried the world's trust until its collision

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue tells SHA-1's fall without ever describing SHA-1: the SHAttered note records the 2017 collision, the SHA-2 entry names SHA-1 as the retired predecessor, the SHA-3 entry contrasts its sponge with SHA-1's Merkle–Damgård shape, the DSA entry assumes SHA-1 as its original hash, the PBKDF2 entry recomputes HMAC-SHA1 vectors, and the DEX and WIM entries cite SHA-1 signatures inside file formats — and no entry says what the function is, how its eighty rounds work, or which of its properties actually died in 2017. This is that entry, and it matters because SHA-1 is the hash that carried the world's trust infrastructure for two decades — TLS certificates, PGP signatures, Git object IDs, software checksums — so a decoder that cannot state its construction cannot grade any specimen that still speaks it, and there are still many: Git addresses every object by SHA-1 today.

- **The construction, in one paragraph.** SHA-1 is the NSA-designed hash standardized as FIPS 180-1 in 1995, successor to SHA-0 (FIPS 180, 1993). It takes a message of fewer than 2^64 bits and returns a 160-bit digest: five 32-bit state words, processed in 512-bit blocks through a Merkle–Damgård chain. Each block expands sixteen 32-bit words into eighty by W[t] = ROTL1(W[t-3] ⊕ W[t-8] ⊕ W[t-14] ⊕ W[t-16]) for t = 16..79 — that single 1-bit rotation is the entire difference from SHA-0, and the rotation test below proves it load-bearing. The eighty rounds run four functions in order: Choice (rounds 0–19, K = 5A827999), Parity (20–39, K = 6ED9EBA1), Majority (40–59, K = 8F1BBCDC), Parity again (60–79, K = CA62C1D6), each round rotating the first state word left by 5, the second by 30, and adding the round constant, the function output, and the schedule word. The initial state is 67452301 EFCDAB89 98BADCFE 10325476 C3D2E1F0 — the first four words shared with MD5's initial state, SHA-1's MD4 lineage showing in its opening values. Padding is the Merkle–Damgård classic: a 1 bit, zeros to 448 mod 512, then the original length as a 64-bit big-endian integer — and that padding is the whole of the length-extension story below.

- **What SHA-1 is not.** It is not SHA-0: the two agree everywhere except the schedule rotation, and that one rotation is the difference between a cipher broken in 1998 (Chabaud–Joux) and one that stood until 2017 — a specimen omitting the rotation is SHA-0 wearing SHA-1's name, and it fails every SHA-1 vector while being internally consistent. It is not MD5: same IV family, but 160 bits against 128, eighty rounds against sixty-four, and different round functions — a specimen whose "SHA-1" matches an MD5 vector has mislabelled one of them. It is not SHA-2: different state width (160 vs 256 bits), different round count (80 vs 64), different round functions and constants, and a different IV derivation — the predecessor's retirement is not SHA-2's, and the SHA-2 entry's truncated-variant length-extension resistance has no SHA-1 counterpart, because SHA-1 outputs its entire state. It is not a password hash: like SHA-2 and BLAKE3, it is built to be fast, and the Argon2/scrypt/bcrypt shelf exists precisely because fast hashes make cheap guessing. It is not safe for signatures, and has not been since February 23, 2017 — but it is not dead for every use either: a collision attack forges a digest, it does not by itself forge an HMAC, so HMAC-SHA1's standing is a different question from SHA-1's, and the card must say which question it is answering.

- **The decoder's edge cases.** The IV test is the first screen: five words, 67452301 EFCDAB89 98BADCFE 10325476 C3D2E1F0 — a specimen with any other opening state is not SHA-1, whatever its vectors claim, and a specimen whose first four words match MD5's IV but whose fifth differs has the lineage right and the function wrong. The rotation test is the second, and this pass measured it: the same from-scratch implementation with the ROTL1 removed digests "abc" to 0164b8a914cd2a5e74c4f7ff082c4d97f1edf880, while SHA-1 gives a9993e364706816aba3e25717850c26c9cd0d89d — the rotation is not an optimization, it is the identity. The padding test is the third: "abc" pads to the block 61626380 followed by zeros and the length word 0000000000000018 (24 bits) — a specimen whose padded block ends anywhere else has the length encoding wrong, and every multi-block message after it is wrong too. The length-extension test is the fourth, and this pass ran it: given only the digest of an unknown 31-byte message and its length, the extension construction produced abd6e7a26c62c35a493d5ec3728a0f517fec8496 for the message plus "&role=admin" — exactly hashlib's digest of the full forged message — so any protocol presenting raw SHA-1(secret || message) as authentication fails this rung regardless of vectors, and the fix is HMAC, not a longer secret. The collision-budget test is the fifth: a SHA-1 digest offered as authenticity evidence carries a forgery budget priced in 2017 at ~$110,000 and cheaper since for chosen-prefix collisions — Git objects must therefore be verified with collision-detected SHA-1, never naive SHA-1, and a specimen presenting a SHA-1 digest as signature-era attestation fails the calendar rung, not the vector rung.

- **Decoder-design note (the rotation rung; the extension rung; the budget rung).** Three Gauntlet rungs. (1) **Grade the schedule rotation before any vector runs.** A specimen is graded on whether its message expansion rotates by one bit — the SHA-0 trap is the cheapest misidentification in the catalogue, because a rotationless implementation is self-consistent, passes its own tests, and fails every SHA-1 vector. (2) **Grade the protocol, not just the primitive, on length extension.** A specimen is graded on whether its deployment treats raw SHA-1 output as authentication — if it does, it fails the rung whatever its vectors claim, the same rung the SHA-2 entry confirmed for SHA-256/512, and here with no truncated-variant escape, because SHA-1 has no truncated variant. (3) **Grade the collision budget, not the name.** A specimen is graded against the adversary's collision budget at today's price, not the algorithm's 1995 reputation — SHAttered is the catalogue's standing proof that a name can stay standard while its security leaves, and every "SHA-1, never broken" claim in a specimen is priced at the 2017 figure and the cheaper chosen-prefix figure beside it.

## Enigma — the rotor machine, or: the cipher whose strength was its wiring and whose fall was its operators

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue's stated scope opens "Enigma to post-quantum," and the timeline carries Enigma's breaks in detail — the Polish break of 1932, the Bombe, the Naval 4-rotor re-break of December 1942, the 2026 agentic-AI breaks of MVUEH and the second message — but no entry has ever described the machine itself: what its signal path is, what its daily key consists of, or which of its properties the breaks actually exploited. A decoder that cannot state Enigma's construction cannot grade any specimen that claims to implement it, and Enigma simulators are the commonest historical-cipher specimens in the wild. This is that entry, built the way the FEAL and SHA-1 entries were built: construction first, then the traps, then the Gauntlet rungs — with every computable claim recomputed this pass.

- **The construction, in one paragraph.** Enigma is an electromechanical rotor cipher patented by Arthur Scherbius in 1918, sold commercially from 1923, and adopted by the German military through the 1920s–30s. A keypress sends current from the keyboard through the plugboard (Steckerbrett, up to 13 swapped letter pairs; the Army typically used 10), through the fixed entry wheel, through the rotors right-to-left, around the reflector (Umkehrwalze, UKW), back through the rotors left-to-right, back through the entry wheel and plugboard, to the lampboard. Each rotor is a disk carrying a fixed 26-letter permutation — Enigma I's five: I EKMFLGDQVZNTOWYHXUSPAIBRCJ (notch Q), II AJDKSIRUXBLHWTMCQGZNPYFVOE (notch E), III BDFHJLCPRTXVZNYEIWGAKMUSQO (notch V), IV ESOVPZJAYQUIRHXLNFTGKDCMWB (notch J), V VZBRGITYUPSDNHLXAWMJQOFECK (notch Z) — plus a movable alphabet ring whose setting (Ringstellung) rotates the wiring against the window letter, and a notch that drives stepping: the rightmost rotor advances every keypress, the middle advances when the right rotor sits at its notch, and the famous double-stepping anomaly advances the middle rotor twice in succession when the middle itself sits at its notch. The reflector is a fixed-point-free involution — B: YRUHQSLDPXNGOKMIEBFZCWVJAT, C: FVPJIAOYEDRZXWGCTKUQSBNMHL — and because the return path reuses the same wires, the whole machine is an involution: encryption and decryption are the same operation at the same settings, and no letter ever enciphers to itself. The daily key is four things: which rotors in which order (60 orders from five, 336 from eight for the Navy), the ring settings, the starting window positions, and the plugboard pairs.

- **What Enigma is not.** It is not a polyalphabetic cipher in the Vigenère sense: its alphabet changes every keypress, but by a mechanical stepping rule, not by a key stream — a specimen with a repeating key period has implemented a Vigenère, not an Enigma. It is not unbreakable-by-mathematics: its keyspace is enormous (computed this pass: 60 rotor orders × 26³ ring settings × 26³ start positions × 150,738,274,937,250 ten-pair plugboard combinations = 2,793,925,870,508,516,103,360,000, about 2.79×10²⁴), and it still fell — because the Bombe never searched the keyspace, it searched the crib space, and the no-self property pruned that search by contradiction. It is not the Naval M4: the 1942 four-rotor Kriegsmarine machine used thin B/C reflectors plus a Beta or Gamma fourth rotor, and a specimen with a wide reflector and four rotors has built a machine that never existed. It is not broken by brute force in any telling of the story: every real break — Rejewski's 1932 mathematics, the Bombe's crib runs, the 2026 Astra break of MVUEH — came through procedure (cribs, depths, indicator reuse, operator error), never through enumerating keys. And it is not SIGABA: the American machine that never fell answered Enigma's predictable stepping with irregular stepping driven by control rotors, and the catalogue already carries that negative control.

- **The decoder's edge cases.** The no-fixed-point test is the first screen, and this pass measured it: at two different settings, 26 successive keypresses produced zero letters mapping to themselves — a specimen that ever maps a letter to itself is not Enigma, whatever its rotors claim, because the reflector's fixed-point-free involution forbids it at every position. The reciprocity test is the second: this pass enciphered HELLOENIGMA to ILBDANRBYVK and re-enciphered the ciphertext at the same start back to HELLOENIGMA — a specimen that needs a separate decrypt mode has not implemented Enigma's involution. The vector test is the third: rotors I, II, III left-to-right, reflector B, rings AAA, start AAA, no plugs, AAAAA → BDZGO, reproduced exactly this pass by the from-scratch implementation in hidden_files/enigma-mini.py — a specimen failing this vector has a wiring, a stepping, or a signal-path error, and the vector alone does not say which. The double-stepping test is the fourth, and this pass measured it precisely: with the middle rotor at its notch (II at E) and the right rotor at its notch (III at V), one keypress moved the positions L/M/R from 0/4/21 to 1/6/22 — the middle rotor stepped twice, the left once — so a specimen whose middle rotor never double-steps has implemented odometer stepping, not Enigma stepping, and will diverge from every true Enigma after the first turnover. The reflector test is the fifth: reflector B is a permutation with zero fixed points and is its own inverse, both checked this pass — a reflector with a fixed point, or one that is not an involution, breaks reciprocity and the no-self property together. The plugboard test is the sixth: plug pairs must be disjoint and involutive — a letter appearing in two pairs, or a pair that does not swap both ways, is a wiring error, not a key choice.

- **Decoder-design note (the invariant rung; the operator rung; the keyspace rung).** Three Gauntlet rungs. (1) **Grade the invariant before the keyspace.** Enigma's no-self property is a structural invariant, not a setting — and it is exactly what made the Bombe possible, because a crib placement that would force a letter to encipher to itself is a contradiction the machine rules out. The Gauntlet rule this entry confirms is general: a specimen's invariants are its attack surface, and the interrogation names them before it counts anything. (2) **Grade the operator before the mechanism.** Every Enigma break in the catalogue's timeline came through procedure — cribs from stereotyped messages, depths from reused settings, indicator discipline failures, the MVUEH outlier wheel order plus transcription errors plus a typo — never through the machine's mathematics failing. The Gauntlet's interrogation order (provenance → operator → usage → mechanism) is Enigma's lesson stated as procedure: a specimen that is honest at every mechanical rung can still fall at the operator rung, and the card must say which rung failed. (3) **Grade the keyspace honestly, then ignore it.** 2.79×10²⁴ keys is the catalogue's standing proof that keyspace is not security when the search is structured: the Bombe searched crib-consistent settings, not keys, and the keyspace figure never entered the attack's cost. Any specimen whose security argument is its key count alone fails this rung whatever its vectors claim — the same rung the SHA-1 entry confirmed for collision budgets, here for enumeration budgets.

No wartime traffic was decrypted this pass; the vectors are simulator checks, not breaks.]*

## Playfair — the digraph square, or: the cipher that encrypted pairs before pairs were fashionable

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue carries monoalphabetic ciphers (Atbash), polyalphabetic ciphers (Vigenère, the Quagmire family), and the rotor machine (Enigma) — but no entry has ever described the cipher that sits between them: the first literal digraph substitution cipher, the one that taught cryptanalysis to count pairs instead of letters. Playfair is also the commonest pen-and-paper specimen in the wild, and a decoder that tests it letter by letter will miss everything it does. This is that entry, built the way the Enigma entry was built: construction first, then the traps, then the Gauntlet rungs — with every computable claim recomputed this pass.

- **The construction, in one paragraph.** Playfair was devised by Charles Wheatstone in 1854 — the first recorded description is a document signed by Wheatstone on 26 March 1854 — and bears the name of his friend Lord Playfair (Lyon Playfair), who promoted it to British officials. It uses a 5 × 5 square holding 25 letters: the keyword's letters first, duplicates dropped, then the rest of the alphabet in order, with I and J merged into one cell (some variants omit Q instead). The key PLAYFAIREXAMPLE gives the square P L A Y F / I R E X M / B C D G H / K N O Q S / T U V W Z. The message is prepared into digraphs: a doubled letter inside a pair is split with an X (Q in some variants, and Q when the doubled letter is X itself), and an odd-length tail is padded with X. Then four rules, in order: same row → each letter shifts one place right, wrapping; same column → each letter shifts one place down, wrapping; otherwise the rectangle rule → each letter takes the column of its partner, staying in its own row. Decryption reverses the two shifts (left, up) and keeps the rectangle rule unchanged. The canonical vector, reproduced exactly this pass: HIDETHEGOLDINTHETREESTUMP prepares to HI DE TH EG OL DI NT HE TR EX ES TU MP and enciphers under PLAYFAIREXAMPLE to BMODZBXDNABEKUDMUIXMMOUVIF.

- **What Playfair is not.** It is not a substitution cipher on letters: single-letter frequency analysis fails against it, because its unit is the digraph — a specimen graded by letter frequencies has been graded against a cipher it is not. It is not secure because of its keyspace: 25! possible squares (computed this pass: 15,511,210,043,330,985,984,000,000, about 1.55 × 10²⁵) looks unassailable, and it falls anyway — digraph-frequency analysis plus hill-climbing against quadgram statistics recovers the square routinely, and keyword-derived squares are far weaker than random ones, since the keyword's letters sit in the square's first cells in order. It is not length-hiding: ciphertext length equals prepared-plaintext length, and the filler leaks — decrypting the canonical vector gives HIDETHEGOLDINTHETREXESTUMP, where the X after TRE is filler, not message, and no rule inside the cipher distinguishes the two. It is not I/J-faithful: merging I and J is lossy, so a specimen that claims exact round-trips on J-containing messages without stating its J convention (merge, omit Q, or another rule) has not specified its cipher. And it is not a modern cipher wearing old clothes: any specimen that adds a keystream, a stepping rule, or a changing square has built something else and borrowed Playfair's name.

- **The decoder's edge cases.** The vector test is the first screen: PLAYFAIREXAMPLE on HIDETHEGOLDINTHETREESTUMP must give BMODZBXDNABEKUDMUIXMMOUVIF — reproduced exactly this pass by the from-scratch implementation in hidden_files/playfair-mini.py, and a specimen failing it has a square, preparation, or rule error. The rule spot-checks are the second: same row PL → LA, same column PI → IB, rectangle HI → BM, all verified this pass against the canonical square — a specimen failing one rule while passing the vector has a rule implementation that happens to agree on the vector's digraphs, not a correct cipher. The reversal test is the third, and this pass measured it over all 600 possible digraphs (25 × 25 ordered pairs minus the 25 same-letter pairs preparation forbids): enciphering BA always gives the reverse of enciphering AB — a specimen breaking the reversal property has broken the rectangle rule's symmetry. The no-fixed-digraph test is the fourth, also measured over all 600: no digraph ever enciphers to itself — the row and column shifts move every letter, and the rectangle rule moves both — so a specimen producing a fixed digraph has a rule error, not a key choice. The filler test is the fifth: decryption of the canonical vector must show the filler X (HIDETHEGOLDINTHETREXESTUMP), and a specimen that silently strips it has smuggled a post-processing rule into its decryptor. The J test is the sixth: the specimen must state its 25-letter convention up front — I/J merged, Q omitted, or other — because the same keyword builds different squares under different conventions, and a specimen that never says which has an unspecified key.

- **Decoder-design note (the unit rung; the preparation rung; the keyspace rung).** Three Gauntlet rungs. (1) **Grade the unit before the alphabet.** Playfair's unit is the digraph, and every test that treats letters as the unit — letter frequencies, letter fixed points, letter keyspaces — misses the cipher entirely. The Gauntlet rule this entry confirms is general: name the specimen's unit before testing it, and test at that unit's granularity. (2) **Grade the preparation before the square.** The X-insertion rule is where specimens diverge: X versus Q fillers, doubling of X itself, odd-tail padding, J handling. Two specimens with the same square and different preparation disagree on every doubled-letter message — preparation is part of the key, not a formatting detail, and the card must record it as such. (3) **Grade the keyspace honestly, then ignore it.** 1.55 × 10²⁵ squares is the catalogue's second standing proof, after Enigma's 2.79 × 10²⁴ keys, that keyspace is not security when the search is structured: the attack is on digraph statistics, not enumeration, and the keyspace figure never enters the attack's cost. Any specimen whose security argument is its square count alone fails this rung whatever its vectors claim.

## ASN.1 / DER — the grammar every certificate speaks, or: the decoder that reads the world's locks

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue carries the ciphers that live inside certificates — RSA, EdDSA, ML-KEM, ML-DSA — and the PQC migration note states the standing lesson plainly: migration fails in the parser plumbing, not the math. But no entry has ever described the plumbing itself: the encoding every X.509 certificate, every TLS handshake, every CMS/S/MIME message, and every PKCS#1 signature is written in. A decoder that can grade a cipher but cannot walk a Tag-Length-Value stream cannot grade a single real certificate, because the certificate *is* a DER byte string before it is anything else. This is that entry, built the way the Enigma and Playfair entries were built: construction first, then the traps, then the Gauntlet rungs — with every computable claim recomputed this pass.

- **The construction, in one paragraph.** ASN.1 (Abstract Syntax Notation One) is the notation for describing data structures; BER (Basic Encoding Rules) is the original rule for writing them as bytes; DER (Distinguished Encoding Rules) is the canonical subset of BER that gives every value exactly one encoding. The lineage: ASN.1 began inside CCITT X.409 (1984, part of the X.400 mail series), moved to its own standard X.208 in 1988 with BER as X.209, and was substantially revised in 1995 into the X.680–X.683 series, with the encoding rules consolidated in X.690 (BER, CER, DER); DER itself was first defined in X.509 §8.7, because certificates are signed and a signature needs stable bytes. Every BER value is TLV: a Tag byte (class bits — universal, application, context-specific, private — plus a constructed bit and a tag number), a Length (short form, one byte, for lengths under 128; long form, a leading byte 0x81–0xFE saying how many length bytes follow, for longer values), and the Value bytes. The universal tags a certificate decoder meets daily: SEQUENCE 0x30 (constructed, the container everything nests in), INTEGER 0x02 (two's complement, signed), BIT STRING 0x03 (a leading byte counts unused bits), OCTET STRING 0x04, NULL 0x05, OID 0x06 (first byte packs the first two arcs as 40x+y, the rest base-128), UTF8String 0x0C, PrintableString 0x13, UTCTime 0x17, GeneralizedTime 0x18. DER's canonical restrictions, the whole point of the subset: shortest length form always, minimal INTEGER encoding (a leading 0x00 only when the next byte's high bit would flip the sign, a leading 0xFF only for the mirror case), BOOLEAN exactly 0x00 or 0xFF, SET children sorted by their encoded bytes, and no indefinite length (BER's 0x80, closed by 00 00, is forbidden).

- **What ASN.1/DER is not.** It is not a cipher and not a signature scheme: it carries keys, signatures, and certificates the way an envelope carries a letter, and a specimen that "breaks DER" has broken a parser, not a cryptosystem. It is not BER: BER tolerates long-form lengths for short values, non-minimal INTEGERs, any-nonzero BOOLEANs, unsorted SETs, and indefinite lengths — every one of those is a valid BER encoding and a DER violation, so a decoder that accepts them is BER-tolerant, not DER-strict, and the card must say which. It is not PEM: PEM is base64 armor with BEGIN/END lines wrapped around DER bytes, and a specimen that claims to parse PEM but never decodes the armor has parsed a text file, not a certificate. It is not self-describing like JSON or XML: the bytes carry types and lengths but no field names, so the schema (the ASN.1 module: what a Certificate SEQUENCE contains, in what order) lives outside the bytes — a decoder without the module can walk the structure perfectly and still not know what any field means. And it is not length-hiding or order-free: the length prefix announces every field's size before its content, and DER's sorted-SET rule makes field order part of the encoding, which is exactly why re-encoding a parsed value is only safe when the parser preserved the original bytes.

- **The decoder's edge cases.** The walk test is the first screen: the SHA-256 DigestInfo prefix `30 31 30 0d 06 09 60 86 48 01 65 03 04 02 01 05 00 04 20` plus 32 hash bytes walks this pass as SEQUENCE(49) → SEQUENCE(13) → OID 2.16.840.1.101.3.4.2.1, NULL, OCTET STRING(32) — a specimen that cannot reproduce that walk cannot verify a PKCS#1 v1.5 signature at all. The INTEGER sign test is the second: `02 01 80` is −128, not 128, and `02 02 00 80` is +128 — the leading zero is the sign's bodyguard, and a decoder reading the first as 128 has a sign bug that corrupts every RSA modulus whose top bit is set. The minimal-length test is the third: `02 02 00 7f` decodes to 127 but is DER-invalid (the leading zero is unnecessary, since 0x7F's high bit is clear) — a strict decoder flags it, a tolerant one swallows a non-canonical encoding that would break a signature computed over canonical bytes. The OID test is the fourth: `06 03 2a 03 04` decodes to 1.2.3.4 (0x2A = 42 = 40×1 + 2) — a specimen that reads the first byte as two arcs any other way has the arc packing wrong. The length-form test is the fifth: length 5 must be the single byte 0x05, and `81 05` for the same 5 bytes is BER-valid but DER-invalid — the exact tolerance BERserk exploited (below). The indefinite-length test is the sixth: a SEQUENCE opened with length 0x80 must be rejected outright by a DER decoder, not walked until 00 00 — accepting it means the decoder's length accounting is BER-shaped, and length accounting is where the forgery lived. The trailing-data test is the seventh: one DER value must consume exactly its declared length, and bytes after it are a second value or garbage, never "part of" the first — a decoder that ignores trailing bytes will happily verify a signature over a prefix while the attacker reads the suffix. The BOOLEAN test is the eighth: only 0x00 and 0xFF are TRUE/FALSE in DER, so `01 01 01` is invalid, not "truthy."

- **The BERserk receipt.** In September 2014, Mozilla's NSS shipped a signature-forgery flaw (CVE-2014-1568, fixed in Firefox 32.0.3 and Chrome 37.0.2062.124) whose root cause was exactly the length-form tolerance above: signature verification parsed the DigestInfo as BER, and a BER length field can be stretched across many bytes that a vulnerable parser then skipped, letting a forged PKCS#1 v1.5 signature verify — a variant of Bleichenbacher's 2006 forgery. A sibling NSS flaw the same month (CVE-2014-1569, in the definite-length decoder) accepted an arbitrary-length encoding of 0x00. The lesson is the entry's thesis in one incident: the cipher (RSA) was fine, the signature scheme (PKCS#1 v1.5) was fine, and the decoder's length handling forged certificates for any domain. Parser plumbing is the attack surface; the math inside it is the bystander.

- **Decoder-design note (the canonical-form rung; the schema-outside rung; the length-accounting rung).** Three Gauntlet rungs. (1) **Canonical form is the security property, not a tidiness preference.** DER exists so that a signature computed over bytes verifies over the same bytes everywhere; any specimen that parses and re-encodes before verifying has inserted a transformation between the signature and its input, and the card must record whether re-encoding is byte-identical or merely value-equal — value-equal is not signature-safe. (2) **Interrogate the schema separately from the bytes.** DER walks structure without meaning, so a specimen's claim to "understand" a certificate decomposes into two graded claims — the TLV walk (testable with vectors like the DigestInfo above) and the module it walks against (the X.509 definition, whose version the specimen must name). A specimen that conflates them will pass structure tests while misreading fields. (3) **Length accounting is a first-class probe, not a parser detail.** Every historical ASN.1 forgery ran through length handling — stretched lengths, indefinite lengths, trailing bytes — so the Gauntlet's DER fixture leads with hostile lengths (over-long forms, 0x80, lengths past the buffer, trailing garbage) before it ever tests a real certificate. A specimen that survives hostile lengths and fails a real certificate has a schema problem; a specimen that fails hostile lengths has a forgery problem, and the card grades the second far more severely.

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the DigestInfo walk (SEQUENCE 49 → SEQUENCE 13 → OID 2.16.840.1.101.3.4.2.1, NULL, OCTET STRING 32), the INTEGER sign vectors (−128 for 02 01 80, +128 for 02 02 00 80, 127 for 02 01 7f), the non-minimal-INTEGER flag (02 02 00 7f), the OID vector (06 03 2a 03 04 → 1.2.3.4), the short-form vs long-form length flag (05 vs 81 05), the indefinite-length rejection (0x80), the trailing-byte rejection, and the BOOLEAN rule (0x00/0xFF only), all computed this pass by hidden_files/asn1-mini.py; CORROBORATED — the X.409 (1984) → X.208/X.209 (1988) → X.680–X.683 (1995) / X.690 lineage, DER's X.509 §8.7 origin and one-encoding-per-value purpose, the universal tag numbers, the OID first-byte 40x+y packing, and the BERserk account (CVE-2014-1568, September 2014, Firefox 32.0.3 / Chrome 37.0.2062.124 fixes, Bleichenbacher-2006 variant) plus the sibling CVE-2014-1569 definite-length-decoder flaw, via the references read this pass; SPECULATION — the three Gauntlet rungs, which are proposals, never run. No real certificate was parsed or verified this pass; the vectors are constructed byte strings, not breaks.]*

## Hill — the matrix cipher, or: the cipher that turned a message into arithmetic

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue carries monoalphabetic ciphers (Atbash), polyalphabetic ciphers (Vigenère, the Quagmire family), a digraph cipher (Playfair), and the rotor machine (Enigma) — but no entry has ever described the cipher that stopped substituting letters and started multiplying them: the first polygraphic cipher built on linear algebra, the one that made a block of letters a vector and a key a matrix. A decoder that tests Hill letter by letter, or even pair by pair, will miss everything it does, because its unit is the block and its operation is a matrix product. This is that entry, built the way the Enigma, Playfair, and ASN.1 entries were built: construction first, then the traps, then the Gauntlet rungs — with every computable claim recomputed this pass.

- **The construction, in one paragraph.** Lester S. Hill published the cipher in 1929, in "Cryptography in an Algebraic Alphabet" in the American Mathematical Monthly — the first cipher to use matrix algebra, and the first polygraphic cipher in the modern sense: it enciphers blocks of m letters at once, not letters or pairs. The key is an m × m matrix K over Z₂₆ (A = 0 … Z = 25), and encryption is a matrix product: split the plaintext into blocks of m letters, treat each block as a column vector p, and output c = K·p mod 26. The textbook 3 × 3 key is K = [[6, 24, 1], [13, 16, 10], [20, 17, 15]] — its determinant is 441, which is 25 mod 26, i.e. −1, and therefore coprime to 26, so the key is invertible and decryption is c ↦ K⁻¹·c mod 26, with K⁻¹ = [[8, 5, 10], [21, 8, 21], [21, 12, 8]]. The canonical vectors, reproduced exactly this pass: ACT → POH and CAT → FIN under that key. A message whose length is not a multiple of m is padded — conventionally with X — and Hill's own paper proposed the cipher for telegraphic and mechanical use, including a machine that was never practically built; the cipher's real career was as a teaching cipher and as the ancestor of every linear diffusion layer since.

- **What Hill is not.** It is not a substitution cipher at any granularity: the same plaintext letter enciphers differently depending on its block-mates, and the same block always enciphers the same way — a specimen graded by letter frequencies has been graded against a cipher it is not, and a specimen graded by digraph frequencies has been graded against a cipher one unit too small. It is not secure because of its keyspace: a random 3 × 3 matrix over Z₂₆ has 26⁹ ≈ 5.4 × 10¹² possible keys, and it falls anyway — not by enumeration, but by algebra, in three known blocks (below). It is not a modern block cipher wearing old clothes: it has no rounds, no S-box, no nonlinearity — it is one linear map applied once, and any specimen that adds rounds or a nonlinear step has built something else and borrowed Hill's name. It is not length-hiding: ciphertext length equals padded-plaintext length, and the padding is visible at the tail. And it is not key-agile in the way modern ciphers are: changing the key means changing the whole matrix, and a matrix that fails the invertibility condition is not a weak key — it is not a key at all, because decryption does not exist.

- **The decoder's edge cases.** The vector test is the first screen: the textbook key must take ACT to POH and CAT to FIN — reproduced exactly this pass by the from-scratch implementation in hidden_files/hill-mini.py, and a specimen failing either has a matrix, an ordering, or a modulus error. The invertibility test is the second: a key is valid if and only if det(K) is coprime to 26 — odd and not divisible by 13 — and this pass confirmed both failure modes: a diagonal key with determinant 8 (gcd 2 with 26) and a diagonal key with determinant 13 (gcd 13) are both correctly rejected, because neither has a modular inverse and neither can decrypt. The inverse test is the third: K·K⁻¹ mod 26 must be the identity, verified this pass for the textbook key, and a specimen whose inverse does not satisfy it has an adjugate or determinant error, not a key disagreement. The round-trip test is the fourth: POH decrypts to ACT, and HELLOX round-trips exactly — a specimen that fails the round-trip while passing the vectors has a decrypt path that is not the inverse of its encrypt path. The linearity test is the fifth, and it is the cipher's tell: because encryption is linear, enciphering the sum of two plaintext blocks gives the sum of their ciphertexts (mod 26) — a specimen that breaks linearity has smuggled in a nonlinearity, and a specimen that preserves it is Hill-shaped whatever it calls itself. The known-plaintext test is the sixth, and it is the break: given three known plaintext/ciphertext block pairs whose plaintext matrix is invertible mod 26, the key is recovered exactly as K = C·P⁻¹ — this pass recovered the textbook key from ACT/DOG/THE → POH/WLY/AJN, so a specimen whose security argument survives three known blocks has not understood its own cipher.

- **Decoder-design note (the unit rung; the invertibility rung; the linearity rung).** Three Gauntlet rungs. (1) **Grade the unit before the alphabet.** Hill's unit is the m-letter block, and every test at a smaller unit — letter frequencies, digraph frequencies, letter fixed points — misses the cipher entirely. The Gauntlet rule this entry confirms is general: name the specimen's unit before testing it, and test at that unit's granularity — the same rung Playfair confirmed for digraphs, here for blocks. (2) **Grade the key's existence before its strength.** A Hill key that is not invertible mod 26 is not weak, it is absent: decryption does not exist, and no amount of keyspace arithmetic rescues it. The Gauntlet's key screen therefore checks det(K) coprimality before it checks anything else — the same "grade the premise before the performance" order the Enigma entry confirmed for invariants. (3) **Grade linearity as the vulnerability, not as a property.** Hill's linearity is what makes it teachable and what makes it fall: three known blocks recover the key, and block sums commute through encryption. Any specimen whose security argument is its key count alone, while its map is linear, fails this rung whatever its vectors claim — and the rung generalizes: every modern cipher's nonlinear layer exists precisely because Hill's linear one did not survive, which is why AES's MixColumns is a linear diffusion layer *inside* a nonlinear round, never the whole cipher.

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the textbook key's determinant (441, i.e. 25 mod 26), its inverse [[8, 5, 10], [21, 8, 21], [21, 12, 8]], K·K⁻¹ = I mod 26, the canonical vectors (ACT → POH, CAT → FIN), the round-trip (POH → ACT, HELLOX intact), the known-plaintext key recovery from ACT/DOG/THE → POH/WLY/AJN, and the rejection of determinant-8 and determinant-13 keys, all computed this pass by hidden_files/hill-mini.py; CORROBORATED — Lester S. Hill's 1929 "Cryptography in an Algebraic Alphabet" in the American Mathematical Monthly as the first matrix-algebra cipher and first modern polygraphic cipher, the textbook 3 × 3 key and its POH/FIN vectors, and the known-plaintext attack via matrix inversion, all via the standard references read this pass; CLAIMED — the 26⁹ ≈ 5.4 × 10¹² keyspace figure for 3 × 3 keys, stated as arithmetic, not enumerated; SPECULATION — the three Gauntlet rungs, which are proposals, never run. No historical Hill traffic was decrypted this pass; the vectors are textbook checks, not breaks.]*

## MD5 — the message digest that taught the field the collision lesson, or: the seal that still checksums the world after its death

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue carries SHA-1 (the seal that carried the world's trust until its collision), SHA-2, SHA-3, and BLAKE3 — the whole post-MD5 hash shelf — but never the hash they all learned from: MD5, the 128-bit digest that was the world's default fingerprint for a decade and still turns up in checksums, ETags, and legacy verifiers. A decoder that cannot spot MD5 cannot grade half the digests it meets in the wild, and cannot tell a harmless checksum from a dead seal.

- **The construction, in one paragraph.** Ronald Rivest, RFC 1321 (April 1992), MD4's successor: a 128-bit digest over the Merkle–Damgård construction, 512-bit blocks, 64 steps in four rounds of sixteen. The state is four 32-bit words (67452301, efcdab89, 98badcfe, 10325476); each round mixes them with one nonlinear function — F (choose), G, H (xor), I — a per-round shift table (7/12/17/22, 5/9/14/20, 4/11/16/23, 6/10/15/21), and a sine-table constant per step. Padding is a 0x80 byte, zeros to 56 mod 64, then the 64-bit little-endian bit length; the digest is the four state words in little-endian order. Nothing about the design is exotic — that ordinariness is why it spread everywhere, and why its fall mattered everywhere.

- **What MD5 is not.** It is not a MAC: Merkle–Damgård length extension means MD5(secret || message) lets anyone append data without the secret, so a specimen using bare MD5 as a MAC fails by construction, not by attack. It is not a password hash: fast and unsalted by design, the opposite of the bcrypt/scrypt/Argon2 entries' slow side. It is not collision-resistant: dead for signatures and certificates since Xiaoyun Wang's first practical collision in 2004, with the Stevens et al. rogue-CA chosen-prefix demonstration in 2008 and the Flame malware's forged Microsoft code-signing certificate in 2012 as the receipts. It is not a random oracle: chosen-prefix collisions let the attacker fix both documents' beginnings and still collide. And it is not wholly "broken": preimage resistance stands — no one can invert a given digest, or forge a second document matching an already-fixed one. "MD5 is broken" without the property qualifier is a grading error, not a verdict.

- **The decoder's edge cases.** The vector test is the first screen: the seven RFC 1321 vectors — empty, "a", "abc", "message digest", the lowercase alphabet, the 62-character alphanumeric set, "1234567890" eight times — reproduced exactly this pass by the from-scratch implementation in hidden_files/md5-mini.py (no hashlib in the implementation), cross-checked against hashlib and the system md5sum. The shift-table trap is the second: round-4 shifts are 6/10/15/21, and this pass's first implementation used 19 and failed every vector, all seven, not some — a specimen with the same slip fails totally, not partially, and partial failure points elsewhere. The padding-boundary test is the third: lengths 55 (fits one block), 56 (spills to two), 63, 64, 65, 119, 120, all verified this pass against hashlib — a specimen failing exactly at 56 or 120 has a padding bug, not a compression bug. The property screen is the fourth: a specimen "breaking MD5" by exhibiting a collision has broken collision resistance only — demand the property named: collision, second-preimage, or preimage. The chosen-prefix screen is the fifth, and it is the Flame pattern: two documents with attacker-chosen beginnings and one digest — a verifier that accepts an MD5 digest as document identity accepts both documents. The length-extension screen is the sixth: any secret-prefix MAC construction over MD5 is forgeable on sight.

- **Decoder-design note (MD5 → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Grade the property, not the primitive.** MD5 is the catalogue's standing proof that "broken" is not a verdict: collision-broken, preimage-intact, and the two grades travel separately — the same lesson as the SHA-1 entry, with MD5 as the earlier, cheaper receipt. Every interrogation states which property the specimen relies on before grading it. (2) **The chosen-prefix canary.** If a specimen binds identity to a digest, the Gauntlet must produce two distinct canary documents with the same digest before trusting the binding — because the attacker, not the verifier, chooses the documents. Flame is why this rung exists: the forged certificate was not a lucky collision, it was a chosen-prefix construction aimed at a live CA path. (3) **The checksum trap.** MD5 survives as a fast non-adversarial checksum long after its death as a seal — speed and ubiquity are not security claims. The Gauntlet checks what the digest is USED for before grading the primitive: checksum use is legitimate and uninteresting; identity, signature, and certificate use is where the verdict bites. (Usage rung, cf. the SIGABA note: mechanism and handling on separate ledgers.)

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the seven RFC 1321 vectors and the seven padding-boundary lengths, all recomputed this pass by hidden_files/md5-mini.py and cross-checked against hashlib and md5sum; the round-4 shift table (6/10/15/21) as the failure that caught the first implementation; CORROBORATED — RFC 1321 authorship and date, the Wang 2004 first practical collision, the Stevens et al. 2008 rogue-CA chosen-prefix demonstration, and the Flame 2012 forged-Microsoft-certificate case, via standard references read this pass; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]*

## RIPEMD-160 — the European 160-bit digest that outlived its predecessor, or: the hash that Bitcoin shrank its addresses with

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue carries MD5, SHA-1, SHA-2, SHA-3, and BLAKE3 — the hash shelf from Rivest through the SHA-3 competition — but never the European digest that sits between MD4 and SHA-1 in the lineage and still does live work inside every legacy Bitcoin address: RIPEMD-160. A decoder that cannot spot a 20-byte digest cannot tell a HASH160 address payload from a truncated SHA-256, and cannot grade a specimen that chains two hashes instead of one.

- **The lineage, in one paragraph.** RIPEMD stands for RACE Integrity Primitives Evaluation Message Digest, built in the European Union's RIPE project (RACE Integrity Primitives Evaluation, 1988–1992). The original RIPEMD was a 128-bit MD4-family digest; Hans Dobbertin found collisions for a two-round-reduced version in the first half of 1995, and the original RIPEMD was later found to have collision issues (reported 2004). RIPEMD-160 is the strengthened successor, designed by Hans Dobbertin, Antoon Bosselaers, and Bart Preneel at KU Leuven's COSIC group, published in *Fast Software Encryption* (LNCS 1039, Springer, 1996, pp. 71–82) and described again in *Dr. Dobb's Journal* (January 1997). It was adopted in ISO/IEC 10118-3:2004 alongside RIPEMD-128 and SHA-1, and it is not patented. [CORROBORATED — the RIPEMD-160 project page, VeraCrypt documentation, and standard references read this pass]

- **The construction, in one paragraph.** A 160-bit (20-byte, 40-hex-character) digest over the Merkle–Damgård construction, tuned for 32-bit processors: 512-bit blocks, MD-style padding (a 1 bit, zeros, then the 64-bit little-endian bit length), and a compression function that runs two parallel lines — left and right — each of five rounds of sixteen steps (80 steps per line), with different Boolean functions and message-word orders per line, combined at the end. The twin-line design is the point: where MD5 runs one line and SHA-1 runs one line, RIPEMD-160 makes a differential attack satisfy two differently-ordered lines at once. The family also includes RIPEMD-128 (128-bit), RIPEMD-256, and RIPEMD-320; this entry covers the 160-bit member only. [CORROBORATED — standard descriptions read this pass]

- **What RIPEMD-160 is not.** It is not the original RIPEMD: the 2004 collision findings attach to the 128-bit predecessor, and citing them against RIPEMD-160 is a version error — the same grading error as citing MD4 breaks against MD5, only with the names closer together. It is not collision-proof: a 160-bit digest carries an 80-bit birthday bound, so its collision margin is thinner than SHA-256's 128-bit bound whatever the cryptanalysis record says, and secondary guidance steers new security-sensitive uses to SHA-256 or SHA-3. It is not a password hash or a MAC: fast and unsalted by design, like every digest in this shelf, and a bare hash is not authentication. And it is not broken in the practical sense: no practical collision against the full RIPEMD-160 has been reported, and published attacks reach only reduced-round variants — an absence-of-break that is filed as a standing record, never as a proof of security. [CORROBORATED — secondary security summaries read this pass; the no-practical-collision claim is absence-of-evidence, filed as such]

- **The decoder's edge cases.** The vector test is the first screen: empty string → 9c1185a5c5e9fc54612808977ee8f548b2258d31; "a" → 0bdc9d2d256b3ee9daae347be6f4dc835a467ffe; "abc" → 8eb208f7e05d987a9b044a8e98c6b087f15a0bfc; "message digest" → 5d0689ef49d2fae572b881b123a85ffa21595f36; the lowercase alphabet → f71c27109c692c1b56bbdceb5b9d2865b3708dbc — all reproduced this pass via the system hashlib implementation (not a from-scratch implementation, so a specimen is graded against the same vectors, not against this entry's code). The length test is the second: a 20-byte digest is RIPEMD-160-shaped, a 32-byte digest is not — a specimen handing over 20 bytes and calling it SHA-256 has truncated, mislabeled, or chained. The chain test is the third, and it is the live one: Bitcoin's HASH160 is RIPEMD-160(SHA-256(public key)), so a Bitcoin address payload is a second hash, not a first — a specimen that tests the payload against SHA-256 alone, or against RIPEMD-160 of the raw key, fails both, and only the ordered pair passes. The version test is the fourth: RIPEMD, RIPEMD-128, and RIPEMD-160 are three different digests sharing a name stem, and any report that says "RIPEMD" without the number is ungraded until the number is pinned.

- **Decoder-design note (RIPEMD-160 → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Grade the bound, not just the break record.** RIPEMD-160's honest grade is two numbers side by side: no practical full collision reported, and an 80-bit birthday bound. The MD5 entry's "grade the property, not the primitive" rung, sharpened: a primitive can be unbroken and still be the wrong margin for a long-lived seal, and the report card must carry both facts or it misleads by omission. (2) **Interrogate the chain, not just the link.** HASH160 proves a specimen's digest may be the second hash in a chain, and the chain order is itself evidence — SHA-256-then-RIPEMD-160 is a different specimen from RIPEMD-160-then-SHA-256, and from either hash alone. The Gauntlet's digest screen therefore tests ordered pairs before it tests single algorithms, because a chained digest defeats every single-algorithm test by construction. (3) **A strengthened successor does not heal its predecessor, and a broken predecessor does not condemn its successor.** RIPEMD fell and RIPEMD-160 stands; MD4 fell and MD5 stood for a decade before falling in its turn. Versions earn separate verdicts, and the report card never lets a family name carry a grade — the number after the name is part of the verdict.

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the five test vectors above, recomputed this pass via hashlib and matching the published RIPEMD-160 vector set; CORROBORATED — the RIPE project origin and 1988–1992 dates, the Dobbertin/Bosselaers/Preneel authorship, the 1996 FSE publication and 1997 Dr. Dobb's description, the ISO/IEC 10118-3:2004 adoption, the twin-line 5×16 construction, the Bitcoin HASH160 chain (RIPEMD-160 after SHA-256), and the 2004 collision findings against the original RIPEMD; CLAIMED — the "no practical full collision" record, which is absence-of-evidence from secondary summaries, not a proof; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]*

## RIPEMD-128 — the 128-bit twin that shares a name with a broken predecessor, or: the digest that length alone cannot identify

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue carries RIPEMD-160, but a decoder that knows only the 160-bit member will misread the family's 128-bit member twice over: once by length, because a 32-hex-character digest is also exactly MD5-shaped and exactly original-RIPEMD-shaped, and once by name, because "RIPEMD" unqualified usually means the broken 1992 original, not this 1996 redesign. A specimen handing over 16 bytes needs a test that names which 128-bit digest it is, not a guess from its size.
- **The lineage, in one paragraph.** RIPEMD-128 is the 128-bit member of the strengthened RIPEMD family designed by Hans Dobbertin, Antoon Bosselaers, and Bart Preneel at KU Leuven's COSIC group, published alongside RIPEMD-160 in *Fast Software Encryption* (LNCS 1039, Springer, 1996) and adopted in ISO/IEC 10118-3:2004. It is not the original RIPEMD: that 1992 RIPE-project digest was also 128-bit, and the 2004 Wang-group collision findings attach to it — the same name stem, a different function. RIPEMD-128 shares RIPEMD-160's twin-line design at a smaller size: two parallel lines, four rounds of sixteen steps each (64 steps per line), MD-style padding, 512-bit blocks. [CORROBORATED — the RIPEMD-160 entry's lineage sources, and the Peyrin ChinaCrypt 2013 slides read this pass, which state RIPEMD-128's parameters as 128-bit digest, 64 steps, 4 rounds of 16]
- **What RIPEMD-128 is not.** It is not the original RIPEMD, and citing the 2004 collisions against it is a version error — the mirror image of the error the RIPEMD-160 entry warns about, except here the digest sizes match, so the error survives even a length check. It is not MD5: same 128-bit length, same 32 hex characters, different function, different vectors — a report that says "128-bit digest" and stops has identified nothing. It is not unbroken in the strong sense, and it is not broken in the practical sense: published cryptanalysis reaches reduced-round compression functions — a 48-step collision at complexity 2^40 [MNS12] and 52-step nonrandomness at 2^107 [SW12] — while the full 64-step function has no practical collision on record. And it is not a safe margin for anything long-lived regardless of that record: a 128-bit digest carries a 64-bit birthday bound, the same thin margin that retired MD5's size class from security work, and no clean break record repairs a bound. [CORROBORATED — the reduced-round figures from the Peyrin slides read this pass, which cite the papers rather than reproducing them; the no-practical-full-collision claim is absence-of-evidence, filed as such]
- **The decoder's edge cases.** The vector test is the first screen: empty string → cdf26213a150dc3ecb610f18f6b38b46; "a" → 86be7afa339d0fc7cfc785e72f578d33; "abc" → c14a12199c66e4ba84636b0f69144c77; "message digest" → 9e327b3d6e523062afc1132d7df9d1b8; the lowercase alphabet → fd2aa607f71dc8f510714922b371834e — all computed this pass by a from-specification implementation (hidden_files/ripemd128-mini.py) that reproduced six independently published RIPEMD-128 digests exactly (the digit strings 9481063, 8398103, 103156052, 41380232, 46078913, 16413120) before any catalogue vector was trusted. The name test is the second: any report saying "RIPEMD" without a number is ungraded until the number is pinned, and "RIPEMD-128" must never inherit either the original RIPEMD's break or RIPEMD-160's cleaner record — the number after the name is part of the verdict, as the RIPEMD-160 entry already rules. The length test is the third, and it fails by design: 16 bytes cannot separate RIPEMD-128 from MD5 from original RIPEMD, so a specimen identified by length alone is unidentified, and the vector test, not the ruler, is the identifier. The library test is the fourth: RIPEMD-128 still ships in older crypto libraries (BeeCrypt carries ripemd128 headers), so a specimen built on a legacy stack may legitimately emit it — presence in a library is not evidence of current fitness, and a legacy digest in a new seal is a finding, not a pass.
- **Decoder-design note (RIPEMD-128 → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Test the function, never the length.** The digest-length screen is a filter, not an identification: every 128-bit digest passes it, so the Gauntlet's digest screen must run the vector test before it names any algorithm, and must report "128-bit, unidentified" rather than a guessed name when the vectors fail. (2) **A shared name is a shared trap.** RIPEMD, RIPEMD-128, and RIPEMD-160 are three functions under two name stems, and the catalogue's version rule — the number is part of the verdict — exists precisely because the trap survives length checks, literature searches, and library headers alike. The report card names the exact function or names nothing. (3) **Grade the bound alongside the break record, again.** RIPEMD-128's honest grade is two numbers side by side, as RIPEMD-160's was: no practical full collision reported, and a 64-bit birthday bound. A specimen sealed with RIPEMD-128 today is not condemned by a break it does not have, and it is not cleared by a record that cannot outrun its own bound — both facts ride on the card, or the card misleads by omission.

## ADFGVX — the fractionating field cipher of 1918, or: the cipher that split every letter in two before scrambling it

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue carries Enigma, Playfair, and the Vigenère family, but never the First World War field cipher that invented fractionation — the two-stage construction that made a hand cipher resist the best cryptanalyst of its day for weeks, and that still teaches the Gauntlet its central lesson about layered specimens: attack the layers in reverse order, or attack nothing at all.
- **The lineage, in one paragraph.** Invented by German signal corps Lieutenant Fritz Nebel and introduced in March 1918 as the "Secret Cipher of the Radio Operators 1918" (*Geheimschrift der Funker 1918*, GedeFu 18), the five-letter ADFGX version ran on the Western Front through the Spring Offensive; the six-letter ADFGVX version followed in June 1918, expanding the square from 5×5 (25 cells) to 6×6 (36 cells) so digits could be enciphered alongside letters. French Army Lieutenant Georges Painvin of the Bureau du Chiffre broke ADFGX in April 1918, then broke ADFGVX on 2 June 1918 after roughly 26 hours of continuous work on the first ADFGVX intercept — a 1 June transmission from German outposts near Remaugies, north of Compiègne, the so-called Radiogramme de la Victoire, whose plaintext revealed a munitions buildup and let the Allies meet the German offensive of 9 June prepared. Nebel, who had originally proposed a double columnar transposition for the second stage and been overruled in favour of a single one, did not learn his cipher had been broken until 1966, and met Painvin in 1968. [CORROBORATED — the ADFGVX and Georges Painvin articles and the NKU cryptology notes read this pass; the March first-use day differs across sources (1 vs 5 March), so this entry dates it to March 1918 only]
- **The construction, in one paragraph.** Two stages, and the order matters. (1) **Fractionation:** a keyed mixed alphabet fills a 6×6 Polybius square whose rows and columns are labelled A, D, F, G, V, X — letters chosen because their Morse forms are maximally dissimilar (A ·−, D −··, F ··−·, G −−·, V ···−, X −··−), so a wireless operator mishearing a dot or a dash would not silently substitute one label for another. Each plaintext character becomes two ciphertext letters: its row label, then its column label. (2) **Keyed columnar transposition:** the fractionated stream is written in rows under a keyword, and the columns are read out in the keyword's alphabetical order. Worked illustration, alphabet-order square (A–Z then 0–9, computed this pass): "attack" → AAGDGDAAAFDV; under keyword KAISER the transposition then reads AAGDGAAADVDF. The ADFGX predecessor is the same machine with a 5×5 square and no V label.
- **What ADFGVX is not.** It is not a substitution cipher: frequency analysis run on the raw ciphertext fails, because the transposition scatters the two halves of each digraph into different columns, so no ciphertext letter-pair corresponds to a plaintext letter. It is not unbroken: Painvin broke each version within days to weeks of its debut, and modern hill-climbing breaks it routinely — its reputation as "the most famous field cipher" is about its design, not its survival. It is not the same cipher as ADFGX: the 5×5 and 6×6 squares differ in alphabet size, and a break of one is not a break of the other. And its six-letter alphabet is not a keyspace: six letters is a transmission feature (Morse-robust labels), while the real secret is the keyed square plus the keyword.
- **The decoder's edge cases.** The alphabet test is the first screen: any ciphertext character outside A, D, F, G, V, X is not ADFGVX, or is corrupted in transit — and a V anywhere proves the 6×6 version, never the 5×5. The length test is the second: fractionation doubles length, so a genuine ADFGVX ciphertext is even-length before and after transposition. The digit test is the third: digits in the recovered plaintext prove the 6×6 square, since ADFGX had no room for them. The ragged-column test is the fourth, and it is Painvin's lever: when the message length is not a multiple of the keyword length, the final row is incomplete, so columns come out uneven — and that unevenness leaks the keyword length to anyone counting. The repeated-beginning test is the fifth: messages sharing a plaintext beginning or ending under the same day key ("messages en tête") let the analyst line the columns up against each other, which is exactly how Painvin entered the 1 June intercept.
- **Decoder-design note (ADFGVX → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Strip the layers in reverse order.** A layered specimen must be interrogated layer by layer, last-applied first: recover the transposition, then solve the substitution. Any Gauntlet screen that attacks the composite ciphertext with a single method — frequency counts on fractionated text, say — is testing its own method, not the specimen. (2) **Usage flaws beat mathematics, again.** Painvin's break came from repeated beginnings and ragged columns, the same family as Enigma's operator errors and JN-25's additive reuse: the Gauntlet hunts usage flaws before it hunts mathematical ones, because history keeps breaking ciphers at the operator, not the algorithm. (3) **A rejected stronger design is a finding, not a footnote.** Nebel's double transposition would have cost Painvin far more than 26 hours; the single transposition that shipped was an organisational decision, not a design limit. A report card that grades only the shipped specimen without noting the stronger design that was refused understates what the specimen's authors knew — and what the next specimen from the same shop might ship.

*[Grade: CORROBORATED — the Nebel invention, March 1918 ADFGX debut, June 1918 ADFGVX expansion, Painvin's April 1918 ADFGX break and 2 June 1918 ADFGVX break, the Remaugies/Compiègne intercept, the Radiogramme de la Victoire, the Morse-dissimilarity rationale for the six labels, and the refused double transposition, all from the sources read this pass; VERIFIED — the worked "attack" fractionation and KAISER transposition above, computed this pass from an alphabet-order square; CLAIMED — nothing in this entry rests on a single-party claim; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]*

## RIPEMD-256 — the 256-bit digest that is only 128 bits strong, or: the length that lies twice

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue carries RIPEMD-128 and RIPEMD-160, but a decoder that knows only those two will misread the family's 256-bit member twice over: once by length, because a 64-hex-character digest is exactly SHA-256-shaped and exactly SHA3-256-shaped, and once by name, because "256" sounds like double the RIPEMD-128 strength. Both readings are wrong. RIPEMD-256 is RIPEMD-128's construction stretched to twice the output, not a 256-bit design — and a specimen handing over 32 bytes needs a test that names which 256-bit digest it is, not a guess from its size.
- **The lineage, in one paragraph.** RIPEMD-256 is the double-length extension proposed by Hans Dobbertin, Antoon Bosselaers, and Bart Preneel in the same 1996 paper as RIPEMD-128/160 (*Fast Software Encryption*, LNCS 1039, section 3.3, "Optional Extensions to 256 and 320 bit Hash-Results"). The construction needs no second instance: RIPEMD-128 already has two parallel lines, so the extension omits the combination of the two lines at the end of every compression-function application, and introduces interaction between the lines by swapping registers across them — after round 1 the contents of A and A', after round 2 B and B', after round 3 C and C', after round 4 D and D'. The chaining variable grows to eight words (67452301, EFCDAB89, 98BADCFE, 10325476, 76543210, FEDCBA98, 89ABCDEF, 01234567); each line's final state is added back to its own half of the chaining variable (feed-forward), since the RIPEMD-128 combination step is the thing omitted. Padding is MD-style, blocks are 512 bits. [CORROBORATED — the 1996 paper, section 3.3, read this pass; the swap schedule, eight-word state, and feed-forward form are also the exact form of the implementation validated 4/4 below]
- **What RIPEMD-256 is not.** It is not SHA-256 and it is not SHA3-256: same 32-byte length, different function, different vectors — a report that says "256-bit digest" and stops has identified nothing, and a report that credits SHA-256-class strength on length alone has graded nothing. It is not twice RIPEMD-128's strength: secondary summaries state plainly that it carries only RIPEMD-128-class collision resistance, because it is built from RIPEMD-128's rounds, not from a 256-bit design — the longer digest does not deliver 256-bit security. It is not two RIPEMD-128 digests concatenated: the cross-line swaps mix the halves, so neither half of a RIPEMD-256 digest equals the RIPEMD-128 digest of the same input (checked this pass: RIPEMD-128("abc") is c14a12199c66e4ba84636b0f69144c77, while RIPEMD-256("abc") begins afbd6e228b9d8cbbcef5ca2d03e6dba1 and ends 0ac0bc7dcbe4680e1e42d2e975459b65 — neither half matches). And it is not a drop-in modern seal: no local implementation existed this pass (Python hashlib, OpenSSL, and Node crypto all lack RIPEMD-256, offering only RIPEMD-160), so a specimen emitting it is running a legacy or dedicated stack, and must name its library.
- **The decoder's edge cases.** The vector test is the first screen: empty string → 02ba4c4e5f8ecd1877fc52d64d30e37a2d9774fb1e5d026380ae0168e3c5522d; "a" → f9333e45d857f5d90a91bab70a1eba0cfb1be4b0783c9acfcd883a9134692925; "abc" → afbd6e228b9d8cbbcef5ca2d03e6dba10ac0bc7dcbe4680e1e42d2e975459b65; "message digest" → 87e971759a1ce47a514d5c914c392c9018c7c46bc14465554afcdf54a5070c0e; the lowercase alphabet → 649d3034751ea216776bf9a18acc81bc7896118a5197968782dd1fd97d8d5133 — all computed this pass by a from-specification implementation (hidden_files/ripemd256-mini.py) that reproduced four independently published RIPEMD-256 digests exactly (the digit strings 103156052, 8042576, 9481063, 8398103) before any catalogue vector was trusted. The length test is the second, and it fails by design: 32 bytes cannot separate RIPEMD-256 from SHA-256 from SHA3-256, so a specimen identified by length alone is unidentified, and the vector test, not the ruler, is the identifier. The halves test is the third: neither half of a claimed RIPEMD-256 digest may be graded as RIPEMD-128 — the swaps forbid it, and a report that splits the digest and grades the halves has invented two specimens. The library test is the fourth: RIPEMD-256's absence from the standard libraries above means a specimen claiming native support without naming its implementation is ungraded until the implementation is pinned.
- **Decoder-design note (RIPEMD-256 → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Length is not a security grade.** A 64-hex-character digest earns no SHA-256-class credit: the Gauntlet grades the construction, not the size, and a 256-bit output built from 128-bit rounds carries its parent's margin on the card, not its own length's. (2) **Test the function, never the length — now in the 256-bit class.** The RIPEMD-128 entry's rung extends upward: every 256-bit digest passes the length screen, so the digest screen must run the vector test before it names any algorithm, and must report "256-bit, unidentified" rather than a guessed name when the vectors fail. (3) **A doubled digest is not a doubled margin.** Extensions inherit their parent's margin: RIPEMD-256 inherits RIPEMD-128's, as RIPEMD-320 will inherit RIPEMD-160's. The report card names the construction lineage alongside the digest size, or a longer digest quietly launders a shorter design's weakness into a stronger-looking grade.

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the five test vectors above, computed this pass by a from-specification implementation validated 4/4 against independently published RIPEMD-256 digests (103156052, 8042576, 9481063, 8398103), which also verifies the swap schedule, eight-word chaining variable, and feed-forward form as implemented; CORROBORATED — the Dobbertin/Bosselaers/Preneel authorship, the 1996 FSE publication, and the section 3.3 double-length extension with its A/B/C/D swap schedule, from the paper read this pass, and RIPEMD-256's absence from Python hashlib, OpenSSL, and Node crypto, checked this pass; CLAIMED — the "RIPEMD-128-class collision resistance, not 256-bit security" assessment, from a secondary summary, not from a cryptanalysis record graded in this entry; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]*

## RIPEMD-320 — the 320-bit digest that is only 160 bits strong, or: the widest member of the family

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue carries RIPEMD-128, RIPEMD-160, and RIPEMD-256, but not the family's widest member — and a decoder that knows only those three will misread a 40-byte digest twice over: once by width, because an 80-hex-character digest looks like a stronger grade than any 160-bit design, and once by name, because "320" sounds like double the RIPEMD-160 strength. Both readings are wrong. RIPEMD-320 is RIPEMD-160's construction stretched to twice the output, not a 320-bit design — and with this entry the 1996 family's shelf is complete: 128, 160, 256, 320, each with its own vectors, its own construction, and its own margin.
- **The lineage, in one paragraph.** RIPEMD-320 is the double-length extension proposed by Hans Dobbertin, Antoon Bosselaers, and Bart Preneel in the same 1996 paper as RIPEMD-128/160 (*Fast Software Encryption*, LNCS 1039, section 3.3, "Optional Extensions to 256 and 320 bit Hash-Results"). The construction needs no second instance: RIPEMD-160 already has two parallel lines, so the extension omits the combination of the two lines at the end of every compression-function application, and introduces interaction between the lines by swapping registers across them — but NOT in the order a reader of the RIPEMD-256 entry would predict. The RIPEMD-320 swap schedule is permuted: after round 1 swap B and B', after round 2 swap D and D', after round 3 swap A and A', after round 4 swap C and C', after round 5 swap E and E'. The chaining variable grows to ten words (67452301, EFCDAB89, 98BADCFE, 10325476, C3D2E1F0, 76543210, FEDCBA98, 89ABCDEF, 01234567, 3C2D1E0F); each line's final state is added back to its own half of the chaining variable (feed-forward), since the RIPEMD-160 combination step is the thing omitted. Padding is MD-style, blocks are 512 bits. [CORROBORATED — the 1996 paper, section 3.3, for the extension itself; the permuted B/D/A/C/E swap schedule was NOT read from the paper this pass — it was found by brute-force search over all 6^5 per-round swap choices x 4 candidate second-half IVs x 3 final combinations (93,312 constructions), of which exactly one matched the independently published empty-string digest, and that construction then matched the full 8-vector set below]
- **What RIPEMD-320 is not.** It is not twice RIPEMD-160's strength: secondary summaries state plainly that it carries only RIPEMD-160-class collision resistance, because it is built from RIPEMD-160's rounds, not from a 320-bit design — the longer digest buys a wider fingerprint, not a deeper margin, and its birthday bound is still its parent's 80-bit bound. It is not two RIPEMD-160 digests concatenated: the cross-line swaps mix the halves, so neither half of a RIPEMD-320 digest equals the RIPEMD-160 digest of the same input (checked this pass: RIPEMD-160("abc") is 8eb208f7e05d987a9b044a8e98c6b087f15a0bfc, while RIPEMD-320("abc") begins de4c01b3054f8930a79d09ae738e92301e5a17 and ends 085beffdc1b8d116713e74f82fa942d64cdbc4682d — neither half matches). It is not a truncated SHA-512 or a SHA-384 variant: 40 bytes matches no SHA-2 output length, and a report that calls an 80-hex digest "SHA-family" on length alone has identified nothing. And it is not a drop-in modern seal: no local implementation existed this pass (Python hashlib, OpenSSL, and Node crypto all lack RIPEMD-320, offering only RIPEMD-160), so a specimen emitting it is running a legacy or dedicated stack, and must name its library.
- **The decoder's edge cases.** The vector test is the first screen: empty string → 22d65d5661536cdc75c1fdf5c6de7b41b9f27325ebc61e8557177d705a0ec880151c3a32a00899b8; "a" → ce78850638f92658a5a585097579926dda667a5716562cfcf6fbe77f63542f99b04705d6970dff5d; "abc" → de4c01b3054f8930a79d09ae738e92301e5a17085beffdc1b8d116713e74f82fa942d64cdbc4682d; "message digest" → 3a8e28502ed45d422f68844f9dd316e7b98533fa3f2a91d29f84d425c88d6b4eff727df66a7c0197; the lowercase alphabet → cabdb1810b92470a2093aa6bce05952c28348cf43ff60841975166bb40ed234004b8824463e6b009 — all computed this pass by a from-specification implementation (hidden_files/ripemd320-mini.py) that matched the Linux kernel tcrypt RIPEMD-320 vector set 8/8, including the 62-character, 80-digit, and 56-character multi-block vectors, before any catalogue vector was trusted. The halves test is the second: neither half of a claimed RIPEMD-320 digest may be graded as RIPEMD-160 — the swaps forbid it, and a report that splits the digest and grades the halves has invented two specimens. The schedule test is the third, and it is the live one: a from-specification reimplementation that assumes the RIPEMD-256 sequential swap order (A, B, C, D, E) fails every vector — an earlier draft of this entry's own implementation did exactly that, and matched nothing until its round-5 tables were corrected against the KU Leuven pseudo-code and its swap schedule was search-derived. Any implementation claiming RIPEMD-320 must be run against the vectors, not trusted on its construction story. The library test is the fourth: RIPEMD-320's absence from the standard libraries above means a specimen claiming native support without naming its implementation is ungraded until the implementation is pinned.
- **Decoder-design note (RIPEMD-320 → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Never extrapolate a construction across family members.** The sequential swap order that RIPEMD-256 validated does not extend to RIPEMD-320 — the permuted B/D/A/C/E schedule was found only because 93,311 other constructions were tried and rejected. A decoder that reasons "the 256 pattern, plus one round" builds a function that matches no published vector and then blames the specimen. Constructions are verified per member, never inherited by analogy. (2) **A repaired implementation is evidence, not embarrassment.** This entry's implementation failed twice in public ways — wrong round-5 tables, wrong swap order — and each failure named its own fix: the tables against the KU Leuven pseudo-code, the schedule against the vector set. The Gauntlet keeps the failed drafts on record (hidden_files/ripemd320-mini.py carries the repair history in its docstring) because a repair trail is what lets the next reader trust the passing vectors. (3) **The shelf is now complete, and the shelf is the lesson.** Four members, one lineage, four different margins — 128-class, 160-class, 128-class again, 160-class again — and the digest length in every case is the wrong number to grade. The report card names the construction lineage alongside the digest size, or a longer digest quietly launders a shorter design's weakness into a stronger-looking grade. RIPEMD-320 closes the family; the next gap is a family the catalogue does not carry at all.
