## Trivium — the eSTREAM stream cipher that fits in 3,488 gates, or: the cipher whose whole state is three shift registers and one AND per register

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue carries Grain and SNOW, but not the eSTREAM hardware portfolio's simplest member — and a decoder that knows only block ciphers and hashes will misread a Trivium specimen twice over: once by size, because an 80-bit key looks like a toy next to AES-256, and once by shape, because a stream cipher has no rounds, no S-box, and no block to test. Trivium's whole design is three shift registers, three taps, and one AND gate per register. With this entry the catalogue's stream-cipher shelf gains the design that proves how little machinery a serious cipher needs — and how thin the margin gets when the machinery is that small.
- **The lineage, in one paragraph.** Trivium was designed by Christophe De Cannière and Bart Preneel, submitted to Profile II (hardware) of the eSTREAM competition, and selected for the eSTREAM portfolio for low-area hardware ciphers. It is not patented and is specified as an International Standard under ISO/IEC 29192-3. It takes an 80-bit key and an 80-bit IV and generates up to 2^64 bits of keystream from a 288-bit internal state: three shift registers of 93, 84, and 111 bits. To initialize, the key is written into the first register, the IV into the second, and the third register's last three bits are set to 1,1,1 with the rest zero; the cipher is then clocked 1,152 times (4 × 288) with no output, so that every state bit depends on every key and IV bit in a complex nonlinear way, before keystream begins. Each round computes three intermediate values — t1 from the first register's taps at bits 66 and 93, t2 from the second's at 162 and 177, t3 from the third's at 243 and 288 — outputs their XOR, then feeds each register a new bit that XORs its intermediate value with one AND of two neighbouring bits and one tap from another register (s91·s92 with s171; s175·s176 with s264; s286·s287 with s69). No tap falls on the first 65 bits of any register, so a newly generated bit is not used for at least 65 rounds — the property that lets 64 bits be generated in parallel in hardware (5,504 gates) and that gives software implementations around 4 cycles per byte. A straightforward hardware implementation needs 3,488 gates and produces one bit per clock cycle. [VERIFIED — the multi-source consensus: the register sizes, tap positions, 1,152-round warm-up, gate counts, and 4 cycles/byte figure agree across the sources read this pass]
- **What Trivium is not.** It is not a 128-bit cipher wearing an 80-bit key: the key is 80 bits, the brute-force bound is 2^80, and a report that grades it alongside AES-256 has graded the wrong number. It is not broken — as of 2025 no published attack beats brute force on the full cipher — but it is not comfortable either: the best published practical cube attacks recover the key of reduced-round Trivium with up to 832 of its 1,152 initialization rounds, at a reported time complexity not exceeding 2^50, which is why secondary summaries call the security margin "rather slim." It is not Bivium: Bivium is Trivium's weakened two-register cousin, and Bivium falls to algebraic IV-differential attack outright — a specimen calling itself "Trivium-like" with two registers is a different, broken cipher, not a variant. And it is not safe under IV reuse: Trivium is a synchronous stream cipher, so the same key with the same IV produces the same keystream, and two plaintexts under one keystream XOR to each other — the break that needs no cryptanalysis at all.
- **The decoder's edge cases.** The vector test is the first screen, and it must name its bit order before it names any result: key and IV hex are read LSb-first within each byte, and keystream bits are packed back into bytes the same way (byte = Σ 2^j · bit_j), the mapping the specification itself states for stream-to-byte conversion. Under that mapping, first 16 keystream bytes: key 00000000000000000000, IV 00000000000000000000 → fbe0bf265859051b517a2e4e239fc97f; key 00000000000000000001, IV 00000000000000000000 → 38eb86ff730d7a9caf8df13a4420540d; key FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF, IV 00000000000000000000 → dda5be0d7acf12398c4c0823c793a06b; key 00000000000000000000, IV FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF → 14cec428681646ee598fda312e8bcb36; key 80000000000000000000, IV 80000000000000000000 → 02aaeb59c5a4109d38d70125f7613457 — all computed this pass by a from-specification implementation in two independent formulations (shift-register pseudocode and recursive-equation form) agreeing 5/5 over 128 bits each, with an encrypt/decrypt roundtrip on "attack at dawn" (ciphertext 599ff29e10665afddbad955b334e under key 00000000000000000001, IV zero) returning the plaintext exactly. The ordering test is the second, and it is the live one: the two published formulations agree ONLY when the recursive form's pre-history segments carry the key/IV bits reversed relative to the shift form's loading — the formulations differ in the direction key bits are read into the pre-history, not in the cipher — so an implementation that reads key bits the other way produces a different stream from the same hex and fails every vector above. Any implementation claiming Trivium must be run against the vectors under a stated mapping, not trusted on its construction story. The warm-up test is the third: output taken before 1,152 rounds is not Trivium keystream, and a specimen streaming from round zero is ungraded, not broken. The IV test is the fourth: a specimen reusing an IV under one key is graded on the reuse, not on the cipher — two ciphertexts under one keystream are one finding, whatever the cipher's margin.
- **Decoder-design note (Trivium → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Name the bit order before grading any stream.** A stream cipher's vectors are meaningless without their byte mapping: the Gauntlet's stream screen states key, IV, mapping, and warm-up count on the card, and a vector that fails under one mapping is re-tested under the other before any verdict, because this entry's own two formulations disagreed until the mapping was pinned. (2) **Test IV discipline before mathematics.** Reuse breaks a synchronous stream cipher with no attack at all, the same family as Enigma's operator errors and the ADFGVX repeated beginnings: the Gauntlet hunts usage flaws before it hunts mathematical ones, and a reused IV is a finding about the operator, graded before the cipher. (3) **A thin margin is graded as thin.** A cipher with published attacks at 832 of 1,152 rounds does not earn a clean bill because the full cipher still stands: the report card carries the round count of the best attack beside the full round count, so a reader can see how much margin is left instead of reading "unbroken" as "comfortable."

## SM3 — the Chinese national hash that wears SHA-256's shape, or: the 256-bit digest that is not SHA-256

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue's 256-bit class runs SHA-256, SHA3-256, RIPEMD-256, and BLAKE2s, but not the member a Chinese commercial-cryptography stack actually emits — and a specimen arriving with an SM2 signature or a GM/TLS handshake that hands over a 64-hex-character digest will be misread as SHA-256 by any decoder that grades the 256-bit class by length. SM3 is the first catalogue member from a national standards family outside the NIST/ISO Western lineage, and its presence in OpenSSL and Python's hashlib means a specimen emitting it may be mainstream, not legacy.
- **The lineage, in one paragraph.** SM3 (ShangMi 3) is China's commercial-cryptography hash, published by the State Cryptography Administration on December 17, 2010 as GM/T 0004-2012, standardized nationally as GB/T 32905-2016, and admitted to ISO/IEC 10118-3:2018 — the same ISO part that carries RIPEMD-160 and SHA-256. It was designed by Wang Xiaoyun's group, and the design is a deliberate SHA-256 cousin, not a copy: Merkle–Damgård over 512-bit blocks, 64 rounds, 256-bit output, MD-style padding with a 64-bit big-endian length. The differences are where the decoder must look: the initial value is 7380166f 4914b2b9 172442d7 da8a0600 a96f30bc 163138aa e38dee4d b0fb0e4e; the Boolean functions switch at round 16 (FF is XOR below 16, majority at and above; GG is XOR below 16, the (X AND Y) OR (X AND Z) OR (Y AND Z) form at and above); the permutations are P0(x) = x XOR rotl(x,9) XOR rotl(x,17) and P1(x) = x XOR rotl(x,15) XOR rotl(x,23); the round constants are 79cc4519 below round 16 and 7a879d8a at and above, each rotated left by (j mod 32); and the message expansion is the widest in the catalogue — 68 words W plus 64 derived words W'[j] = W[j] XOR W[j+4], 132 words against SHA-256's 64. [CORROBORATED — multi-source consensus read this pass: publication date and GM/T number, GB/T 32905-2016, ISO/IEC 10118-3:2018, Wang et al. design, 512-bit blocks, 64 rounds, 256-bit output]
- **What SM3 is not.** It is not SHA-256: same output length, same block size, same round count, unrelated digests — a report that says "256-bit digest" and stops has identified nothing, and a report that credits SHA-256's analysis record to an SM3 digest has graded the wrong function. It is not a SHA-256 variant in the compatible sense: the "improved on the basis of SHA-256" phrasing in IETF drafts describes design lineage, not shared vectors — no SHA-256 vector validates an SM3 implementation, and this entry's implementation was validated against SM3 vectors only. It is not broken in the practical sense, and it is not unattacked: published cryptanalysis reaches step-reduced versions — preimage attacks on 29- and 30-step SM3 and pseudo-preimage attacks on 31- and 32-step SM3 out of 64 (Wang/Shen, 2012) — while the full 64-round function has no practical attack on record, filed as absence-of-evidence. And it is not an obscure national curiosity a decoder may skip: it is the hash of the SM2 signature suite and of GM TLS cipher suites, so any specimen speaking Chinese commercial cryptography speaks SM3 by default.
- **The decoder's edge cases.** The vector test is the first screen: empty string → 1ab21d8355cfa17f8e61194831e81a8f22bec8c728fefb747ed035eb5082aa2b; "abc" → 66c7f0f462eeedd9d1f2d46bdc10e4e24167c4875cf2f7a2297da02b8f4ba8e0; "message digest" → c522a942e89bd80d97dd666e7a5531b36188c9817149e9b258dfe51ece98ed77; the lowercase alphabet → b80fe97a4da24afc277564f66a359ef440462ad28dcc6d63adb24d5c20a61595; "abcd" repeated 16 times (exactly one block before padding) → debe9ff92275b8a138604889c18e5a4d6fdb70e5387e5765293dcba39c0c5732 — all computed this pass by a from-specification implementation matching OpenSSL's sm3 7/7, including two multi-block inputs ("a" × 200 and bytes 0–255), and the empty and "abc" vectors matching the standard's published example vectors. The suite test is the second: SM3 travels with SM2 signatures and the SM4 cipher — a specimen naming SM2 but hashing with SHA-256 has mixed suites, and a specimen naming SHA-256 inside a GM/TLS handshake has done the same in reverse; the hash is graded against the suite it arrived with, not the suite the reader expected. The library test is the third: SM3 ships in OpenSSL 3 and Python's hashlib, but standard OpenJDK has no SM3 MessageDigest (Bouncy Castle's SM3Digest is the route) — a Java specimen claiming native SM3 without naming Bouncy Castle is ungraded until the implementation is pinned. The shape test is the fourth, and it fails by design: 32 bytes cannot separate SM3 from SHA-256 from SHA3-256 from RIPEMD-256 from BLAKE2s, so a specimen identified by length alone is unidentified, and the vector test, not the ruler, is the identifier.
- **Decoder-design note (SM3 → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Same shape, different standards family.** The RIPEMD-256 rung extends beyond one family: the 256-bit class now has a national-standard member, so a report card must name the standard body (NIST, ISO, GB/T) alongside the digest size, or a Chinese-stack specimen gets graded against an American record. (2) **Suite coherence before mathematics.** Check the hash against the signature and cipher it arrived with before attacking any of them — a mixed suite is a finding about the operator, graded before the functions, in the same family as the Trivium IV-reuse rung. (3) **Grade step-reduced attacks by rounds remaining, not by the headline.** "Attacked" without a round count is ungraded: 32 of 64 steps attacked leaves half the rounds standing, which is margin, not a break — the report card carries the attacked step count beside the full round count, as the Trivium entry carries 832 of 1,152.

## CBOR — Concise Binary Object Representation (RFC 8949), or: the grammar that fits a whole JSON in a handful of bytes

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue carries ASN.1/DER — the grammar every certificate speaks — but no CBOR, the grammar every COSE signature, CWT token, and WebAuthn attestation speaks. A specimen arriving as a COSE_Sign1 object or a CTAP2 attestation would be misread as opaque binary by any decoder that only knows DER, JSON, and the catalogue's ciphers. CBOR is the first catalogue member whose whole design is a serialization format for structured data rather than a cipher or a hash, and its presence closes the gap between "we can decode the message" and "we can decode the envelope the message arrived in."
- **The lineage, in one paragraph.** CBOR was designed by Carsten Bormann and Paul Hoffman, published as RFC 7049 in 2013 and obsoleted — without any wire-format change — by RFC 8949 in December 2020 (STD 94). Its data model is JSON extended with byte strings: eight major types carried in the top three bits of the first byte (0 unsigned, 1 negative, 2 byte string, 3 text string, 4 array, 5 map, 6 tag, 7 float/simple), an additional-information field that holds values 0–23 inline and lengths of 1, 2, 4, or 8 bytes for larger ones (additional-information values 24–27), indefinite lengths for byte strings, text strings, arrays, and maps closed by the break byte 0xff, and tags (major type 6) that extend the model — tag 0 a standard date/time string, tag 1 an epoch-based date/time, tags 2 and 3 bignums, tags 4 and 5 decimal fractions and bigfloats, and tag 55799 self-described CBOR (encoded 0xd9d9f7), a deliberate magic number so a sniffer can name the format from three bytes. Deterministic encoding (RFC 8949 §4.2) is preferred serialization — the shortest form of every value — plus length-first map key ordering, the rule that makes a CBOR byte string a signable object. The media type is application/cbor, and the format carries COSE (RFC 9052), CWT (RFC 8392), and the WebAuthn/CTAP2 attestation objects. [VERIFIED — the format facts above, from RFC 8949 read first-party this pass: authors, RFC 7049 → 8949 lineage with no wire change, STD 94, the eight major types, the additional-information scheme, indefinite lengths with break 0xff, the tag numbers named, tag 55799, the §4.2 deterministic rules, and the application/cbor media type]
- **What CBOR is not.** It is not JSON: binary, byte strings native, no schema required but self-describing, and a CBOR text string is UTF-8 by definition where JSON is text by definition. It is not ASN.1 DER: DER needs a schema to mean anything and encodes tag-length-value with explicit lengths throughout, while CBOR's major type rides in the first byte and a generic decoder can walk any CBOR item blind. It is not MessagePack: the two share a JSON-plus-binary shape, but CBOR's tag extension model and indefinite lengths are its own, and MessagePack's type families do not map one-to-one onto CBOR's major types — a decoder that reads CBOR as MessagePack misreads every tag and every indefinite-length item. It is not canonical by default: the same value has many well-formed encodings (0 as 0x00, 0x1800, 0x190000, 0x1a00000000, or 0x1b0000000000000000), so byte equality is not value equality unless deterministic encoding was used. And it is not self-validating: RFC 8949's own hierarchy is well-formed (processable at all), valid (checked by a validity-checking generic decoder), and expected (checked by the application) — three different bars, and a report that calls a well-formed item "valid" has graded one rung up from what it checked.
- **The decoder's edge cases.** The vector test is the first screen: 47 RFC 8949 Appendix A examples matched this pass by a from-specification implementation (hidden_files/cbor-mini.py), encode and decode both ways — 0 → 00, 24 → 1818, 1000 → 1903e8, 2^64−1 → 1bffffffffffffffff, 2^64 → c249010000000000000000 (tag 2 bignum), −1 → 20, −1000 → 3903e7, 1.5 → f93e00, h'01020304' → 4401020304, "IETF" → 6449455446, [1,2,3] → 83010203, {"a":1,"b":[2,3]} → a26161016162820203, tag 0 date → c074323031332d30332d32315432303a30343a30305a, tag 24 content → d818456449455446. The non-preferred test is the second: 0x1800 and 0x190000 both decode to 0 and are both well-formed, but neither is preferred serialization — a decoder that compares bytes will call two encodings of the same value different, so the Gauntlet compares decoded values, never raw bytes. The indefinite-length test is the third: (_ h'0102', h'030405') → 5f42010243030405ff decodes to h'0102030405' and (_ "strea", "ming") → 7f657374726561646d696e67ff decodes to "streaming" — a decoder that stops at the first chunk, or treats 0xff as data, fails both. The bignum test is the fourth: a decoder without tag 2/3 support reads c249010000000000000000 as a 9-byte string, not the number 18446744073709551616. The self-description test is the fifth: d9d9f700 is tag 55799 wrapping 0, and any specimen whose first three bytes are d9d9f7 announces itself as CBOR before a single item is parsed. The deterministic test is the sixth: {"bb":2,"a":1} encodes deterministically as a261610162626202 — "a" first, because its encoded key is shorter — and {"b":2,"a":1} as a2616101616202, "a" before "b" by encoded bytes; a specimen whose map keys arrive in any other order is not deterministically encoded, whatever else it claims.
- **Decoder-design note (CBOR → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Decode to value, compare values, never bytes.** Non-preferred encodings are well-formed, so byte comparison is a false difference: the Gauntlet's CBOR screen decodes first and compares the decoded structure, in the same family as the Trivium bit-order rung — the mapping is pinned before any verdict. (2) **Deterministic encoding is the seal.** A specimen claiming a signature over CBOR must be checked against the deterministic form — re-encode with preferred serialization and length-first key order and compare — because a signature over non-deterministic bytes verifies against bytes the signer never canonicalized, and a report that verifies the signature without checking the encoding has verified the wrong object. (3) **Tags are the extension surface, not an error.** An unknown tag must not fail the decode — the format is designed for decades of extension, and a generic decoder carries the tag through — so the Gauntlet grades tag handling as CARRY vs REJECT, and a specimen that rejects an unknown tag has failed the format's own evolution rule, in the same family as the ASN.1/DER screen that grades unknown OIDs.

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the 47 Appendix A vectors above, matched this pass by a from-specification implementation in both directions, plus the non-preferred, indefinite-length, bignum, self-described-tag, and deterministic-ordering checks, all run this pass; the RFC 8949 facts (authors, RFC 7049 → 8949 lineage with no wire change, STD 94, eight major types, additional-information scheme, indefinite lengths with break 0xff, the tag numbers named, tag 55799, §4.2 deterministic rules, application/cbor media type, the well-formed/valid/expected hierarchy) from RFC 8949 read first-party this pass; CORROBORATED — COSE (RFC 9052), CWT (RFC 8392), and WebAuthn/CTAP2 attestation usage, from the standards record, not from a fresh read this pass; CLAIMED — the MessagePack non-mapping, from the RFC's own Appendix E comparison, not graded in this entry; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]*

## MessagePack — the JSON-shaped binary wire format, or: the grammar that fits a whole JSON in one byte per value

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue carries CBOR — the grammar every COSE signature speaks — but not its older, leaner sibling, and a specimen arriving as a Fluentd event stream or an RPC payload in MessagePack would be misread as opaque binary by any decoder that only knows CBOR, JSON, and DER. MessagePack is the first catalogue member whose whole design is "JSON, but binary and smaller" — no tags, no indefinite lengths, no schema — and its presence closes the gap between "we can decode the envelope" (CBOR) and "we can decode the wire format the log pipeline actually speaks."
- **The lineage, in one paragraph.** MessagePack was designed by Sadayuki Furuhashi; the specification (msgpack/msgpack spec.md, last modified 2017-08-09) defines two concepts — a type system (Integer, Nil, Boolean, Float as IEEE 754 double, Raw split into String and Binary, Array, Map, Extension, Timestamp) and formats, one byte at a time. Integers run −(2^63) to (2^64)−1; binary, string, array, and map sizes cap at (2^32)−1. The format table is a single byte: positive fixint 0x00–0x7f, fixmap 0x80–0x8f, fixarray 0x90–0x9f, fixstr 0xa0–0xbf, nil 0xc0, 0xc1 never used, false 0xc2, true 0xc3, bin 8/16/32 0xc4–0xc6, ext 8/16/32 0xc7–0xc9, float 32/64 0xca–0xcb, uint 8/16/32/64 0xcc–0xcf, int 8/16/32/64 0xd0–0xd3, fixext 1/2/4/8/16 0xd4–0xd8, str 8/16/32 0xd9–0xdb, array 16/32 0xdc–0xdd, map 16/32 0xde–0xdf, negative fixint 0xe0–0xff. All multi-byte integers are big-endian. Extension types run 0–127 for applications and −128 to −1 reserved; the only predefined extension is Timestamp, type −1, in three forms: 32-bit (fixext 4, seconds as uint32, [1970-01-01, 2106-02-07 06:28:16)), 64-bit (fixext 8, 30-bit nanoseconds packed above 34-bit seconds, to 2514-05-30 01:53:04), and 96-bit (ext 8, 12 bytes: nanoseconds uint32 then seconds int64, −292277022657-01-27 to 292277026596-12-04), with nanoseconds never above 999,999,999. The spec's one normative encoder rule is a SHOULD: when several formats fit, use the smallest number of bytes. The old raw 16/32 formats became str 16/32 when the bin family split strings from bytes, and the spec's own "Profile" idea — restrict semantics, sort map keys — is how applications make the bytes deterministic enough to hash. [VERIFIED — the format facts above, from the specification read first-party this pass]
- **What MessagePack is not.** It is not JSON: binary, byte strings native, extension types, no schema — and a JSON parser handed MessagePack sees control bytes, not text. It is not CBOR: the two share a JSON-plus-binary shape, but MessagePack has no tags, no indefinite lengths, and no deterministic-encoding rule — only a SHOULD for the smallest form — so a decoder that reads MessagePack as CBOR misreads every ext and every fixext, and one that reads CBOR as MessagePack chokes on every tag. It is not protobuf: protobuf needs a schema to mean anything and can canonicalize away wire anomalies; MessagePack is self-describing, so a blob with no schema is still a complete document. It is not canonical by default: the same value has many well-formed encodings (0 as 0x00, 0xcc00, 0xcd0000, 0xce00000000, or 0xcf0000000000000000), so byte equality is not value equality unless the producer followed the smallest-form SHOULD and sorted its map keys — and the spec leaves key order unspecified, so two encoders of the same map may legitimately disagree on bytes.
- **The decoder's edge cases.** The vector test is the first screen: 28 smallest-form vectors matched this pass by a from-specification implementation (hidden_files/msgpack-mini.py), encode and decode both ways — 0 → 00, 127 → 7f, 128 → cc80, 255 → ccff, 256 → cd0100, 65535 → cdffff, 65536 → ce00010000, 2^32−1 → ceffffffff, 2^64−1 → cfffffffffffffffff, −1 → ff, −32 → e0, −33 → d0df, −128 → d080, −129 → d1ff7f, −32768 → d18000, −2^63 → d38000000000000000, nil → c0, false → c2, true → c3, "" → a0, "a" → a161, "hello" → a568656c6c6f, b"\x01\x02\x03" → c403010203, [] → 90, [1,2,3] → 93010203, {} → 80, {"a":1} → 81a16101, {"compact":true,"schema":0} → 82a7636f6d70616374c3a6736368656d6100. The float test is the second: 1.5 as float 32 is ca3fc00000 and as float 64 is cb3ff8000000000000 — same value, different bytes, and a decoder that compares bytes calls them different numbers. The non-canonical test is the third: cc00 and d1007f both decode — to 0 and 127 — and both are well-formed, but neither is the smallest form, so a decoder that rejects them has rejected legal MessagePack, and a decoder that hashes bytes has hashed two encodings of one value. The never-used test is the fourth: 0xc1 is the spec's one reserved byte, and a decoder that accepts it has accepted a format the spec says does not exist — the single hard rejection in the whole format table, and the tripwire a fuzzer aims at. The timestamp test is the fifth: 2026-11-05 00:00:00 UTC (1,793,836,800 s) encodes as d6ff6aebc700 in the 32-bit form, as d7ff773594006aebc700 with 500,000,000 ns in the 64-bit form (30-bit nanoseconds packed above 34-bit seconds), and (−1 s, 999,999,999 ns) as c70cff3b9ac9ffffffffffffffffff in the 96-bit form — and a decoder that reads the 64-bit form's packed word as plain seconds is off by a factor of 2^34. The str/bin test is the sixth: "a" is a161 (fixstr) while b"a" is c40161 (bin 8) — same payload byte, different family — and a decoder that conflates str and bin has merged the type system's one deliberate split, the split the whole raw-to-bin migration was made for.
- **Decoder-design note (MessagePack → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Decode to value, compare values, never bytes.** Non-canonical encodings are well-formed, so byte comparison is a false difference: the Gauntlet's MessagePack screen decodes first and compares the decoded structure, in the same family as the CBOR screen — the mapping is pinned before any verdict. (2) **The smallest-form SHOULD is a producer fingerprint, not a validity rule.** A specimen that encodes 0 as cc00 is legal, but it is not the encoder the spec recommends — and a stream full of padded integers betrays a non-standard producer, in the same family as the protobuf anomaly taxonomy: the padding is evidence, not noise. (3) **0xc1 is the tripwire, and the ext family is the extension surface.** A decoder that accepts 0xc1 has accepted a non-format, and an unknown ext type must be carried as opaque data, never rejected — the spec says so explicitly — so the Gauntlet grades ext handling as CARRY vs REJECT, and a specimen that rejects an unknown ext has failed the format's own evolution rule, in the same family as the CBOR tag rung.

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the 28 smallest-form vectors above, the float 32/64 pair, the non-canonical cc00/d1007f decodes, the 0xc1 rejection, the ext roundtrip, and the three timestamp forms, all matched this pass by a from-specification implementation (hidden_files/msgpack-mini.py) run twice; the spec facts (author, type system, limits, the full format table, big-endian integers, the ext-type ranges, the three timestamp forms and ranges, the 999,999,999 ns cap, the smallest-form SHOULD, the raw→str/bin split, the Profile idea) from the specification read first-party this pass; CORROBORATED — Fluentd's MessagePack-native event stream, from the ecosystem record, not from a fresh read this pass; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]*

## BSON — Binary JSON, or: the grammar that length-prefixes everything and reads little-endian

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue carries CBOR and MessagePack — the two self-describing binary JSONs — but not the third member of the family, the one the database actually speaks. A specimen arriving as a MongoDB wire-protocol payload, a dump file, or an oplog entry is BSON, and a decoder that only knows CBOR and MessagePack misreads it twice over: BSON is little-endian where both siblings are big-endian, and every document carries its total length up front, so a CBOR reader sees a length where it expects a type byte. BSON is the first catalogue member whose design is "JSON, but traversable without parsing" — the length prefix lets a reader skip any element wholesale — and its presence closes the gap between "we can decode the envelope" (CBOR) and "we can decode the database's own wire format."

- **The lineage, in one paragraph.** BSON was designed at 10gen (now MongoDB) for the MongoDB wire protocol, first released 2009; the specification (bsonspec.org) defines one rule that governs everything: all integers are little-endian. A document is int32 total length + element list + 0x00 terminator. An element is a type byte + cstring key + value. The type table: 0x01 double (IEEE 754), 0x02 string, 0x03 embedded document, 0x04 array, 0x05 binary, 0x06 undefined (deprecated), 0x07 ObjectId (12 bytes), 0x08 boolean (0x00/0x01), 0x09 UTC datetime (int64 milliseconds since the Unix epoch), 0x0A null, 0x0B regular expression (pattern cstring + options cstring), 0x0C DBPointer (deprecated), 0x0D JavaScript code, 0x0E symbol (deprecated), 0x0F code with scope (deprecated), 0x10 int32, 0x11 timestamp (uint64: increment in the low 4 bytes, seconds in the high 4), 0x12 int64, 0x13 decimal128, 0xFF min key, 0x7F max key. A string is int32 length (bytes plus one for the trailing null) + UTF-8 bytes + 0x00; a cstring is bytes + 0x00 and must not contain 0x00 — modified UTF-8, not full UTF-8. Binary is int32 length + subtype + bytes; subtypes run 0 generic, 1 function, 2 binary-old (deprecated), 3 UUID-old (deprecated), 4 UUID, 5 MD5, 6 encrypted, 7 compressed column, 8 sensitive, 9 vector, 128–255 user-defined. Arrays are documents whose keys are "0", "1", "2", ... — there is no separate array wire form. [VERIFIED — the format facts above, from the specification read first-party this pass]

- **What BSON is not.** It is not JSON: binary, length-prefixed, typed, no schema — and a JSON parser handed BSON sees a length prefix, not text. It is not CBOR: CBOR is big-endian and tag-driven with indefinite lengths; BSON is little-endian, has no tags and no indefinite lengths, and every document announces its total size — a decoder that reads BSON as CBOR misreads the length as a type byte and everything after it as garbage. It is not MessagePack: MessagePack packs a type into a single byte and carries no document length at all; BSON spends four bytes on the length so a reader can skip, and splits its integers into int32 and int64 where MessagePack has one integer family — and BSON has no unsigned integer type at all. It is not canonical by default: key order is significant (it is the document's order, and MongoDB compares documents in key order), and a decoder that sorts keys has reordered the document it was asked to preserve. And it is not self-validating: the length prefix is a claim, not a proof — a document whose stated length disagrees with its actual bytes is malformed, and the check is the first thing a decoder runs, before any element is trusted.

- **The decoder's edge cases.** The vector test is the first screen: 15 vectors matched this pass by a from-specification implementation (hidden_files/bson-mini.py), encode and decode both ways — {} → 0500000000, {"a":1} → 0c0000001061000100000000, {"a":"hello"} → 120000000261000600000068656c6c6f0000, {"a":true} → 090000000861000100, {"a":1.5} → 10000000016100000000000000f83f00, {"a":null} → 080000000a610000, {"a":[1,2]} → 1b0000000461001300000010300001000000103100020000000000, {"a":ObjectId(507f1f77bcf86cd799439011)} → 14000000076100507f1f77bcf86cd79943901100, {"a":b"\x01\x02\x03"} → 10000000056100030000000001020300, {"a":MinKey} → 08000000ff610000, {"a":MaxKey} → 080000007f610000, {"a":2^40} → 10000000126100000000000001000000, {"a":/ab*c/i} → 0f0000000b610061622a6300690000, {"a":Timestamp(1, 1793836800)} → 100000001161000100000000c7eb6a00, {"a":{"b":1}} → 140000000361000c000000106200010000000000. The datetime test is the second: 2026-11-05 00:00:00 UTC is 1,793,836,800,000 ms since the epoch, and a decoder that reads the int64 as seconds is off by a factor of a thousand — the same trap as the MessagePack timestamp test, one family over. The traversal test is the third: a document's length prefix lets a reader skip a 100-byte string element wholesale and land exactly on the next element — the property that makes BSON traversable without a full parse, and the property a decoder must verify by checking the stated length against the actual bytes before trusting the skip. The int32/int64 split is the fourth: 2^40 needs int64, and a decoder that reads it as int32 has read four bytes of an eight-byte value and silently truncated the specimen. The deprecated-types test is the fifth: undefined, DBPointer, symbol, code-with-scope, and the old binary/UUID subtypes are deprecated, not absent — a decoder that rejects them has rejected legal BSON from an old producer, and the Gauntlet grades them as CARRY vs REJECT. The cstring test is the sixth: a key containing 0x00 is not a long key, it is a malformed document, and a decoder that accepts it has accepted a document whose keys cannot be read back.

- **Decoder-design note (BSON → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Verify the length before trusting anything.** The int32 total length is the first check: a document whose stated length disagrees with its bytes is malformed, and every element read after a bad length is evidence built on sand — in the same family as the CBOR well-formed/valid/expected hierarchy, the length check is the well-formed rung. (2) **Little-endian is the tripwire, and the int32/int64 split is the truncation trap.** A decoder that reads BSON big-endian misreads every length and every number; a decoder that reads int64 as int32 truncates silently — the Gauntlet's BSON screen checks both by construction, in the same family as the MessagePack smallest-form screen. (3) **Key order is data, and deprecated types are carried, never rejected.** BSON documents compare in key order, so a decoder that sorts keys has altered the specimen; and the deprecated types are part of the format's history, so the Gauntlet grades their handling as CARRY vs REJECT, in the same family as the MessagePack ext rung.

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the 15 vectors above, the datetime check, the length-prefix traversal check, and the mixed-document roundtrip, all matched this pass by a from-specification implementation (hidden_files/bson-mini.py) run twice; the spec facts (little-endian rule, document grammar, the full type table, string/cstring/binary grammars, the subtype table, code_w_s, array-as-document) from the specification read first-party this pass; CORROBORATED — the MongoDB/10gen origin and 2009 first release, the ObjectId 12-byte layout (4-byte timestamp, 5-byte random, 3-byte counter), and Decimal128 as IEEE 754-2008 BID, from the ecosystem record, not from a fresh read this pass; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]*

## JWT — JSON Web Token (RFC 7519), or: the three-part token that signs its own claims

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue carries CBOR, MessagePack, and BSON — the binary JSONs — and ASN.1/DER, the grammar certificates speak, but not the token format every API on the wire actually hands a decoder: the JSON Web Token. A specimen arriving as an Authorization header, a cookie, or a query parameter is very likely a JWT, and a decoder that only knows the binary grammars reads it as opaque text. JWT is the first catalogue member whose payload is JSON text carried in base64url, and whose security is a signature over two strings, not over bytes — the header and the payload are each base64url, joined by dots, and the signature covers exactly those encoded strings. Its presence closes the gap between "we can decode the envelope" (CBOR) and "we can decode the credential the envelope carries."
- **The lineage, in one paragraph.** JWT is RFC 7519 (May 2015, Jones, Bradley, Sakimura), built on JSON Web Signature (RFC 7515), JSON Web Encryption (RFC 7516), and JSON Web Algorithms (RFC 7518). A JWT is a sequence of URL-safe parts separated by period ('.') characters, each part base64url-encoded with no padding: header.payload.signature for a signed JWT (JWS Compact Serialization), five parts for an encrypted one (JWE Compact Serialization). The JOSE header names the cryptographic operation — "alg" is the algorithm, "typ" is RECOMMENDED to be "JWT", "cty" MUST be "JWT" when a nested JWT is carried. The claims set is a JSON object: seven registered claim names — "iss" (issuer), "sub" (subject), "aud" (audience), "exp" (expiration time), "nbf" (not before), "iat" (issued at), "jti" (JWT ID) — plus public names (which MUST be collision-resistant, usually a URI) and private names (agreed between producer and consumer, collision-prone). Times are NumericDate: seconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z UTC, ignoring leap seconds — seconds, not milliseconds. Claim names MUST be unique; a parser MUST either reject duplicates or keep the lexically last. Section 8 makes only two algorithms mandatory for a conforming implementation: HMAC SHA-256 ("HS256") and "none"; RS256 and ES256 are RECOMMENDED. Section 6 defines the unsecured JWT: "alg":"none", an empty signature, and the token ends with a trailing period. [VERIFIED — the format facts above, from RFC 7519 and RFC 7515 read first-party this pass]
- **What JWT is not.** It is not JSON: it is three base64url parts joined by dots, and a JSON parser handed a JWT sees one long string, not an object. It is not JWS: JWS is the container and its signature machinery, JWT is the claims payload that rides inside it — the same token shape carries non-JWT payloads too. It is not encrypted by default: base64url is an encoding, not protection, and anyone can decode the header and payload of a signed JWT and read every claim — signing proves who wrote it, not who may read it. It is not canonical: whitespace is explicitly allowed in the header and claims set, and no canonicalization is performed before encoding — the same claims set written with different spacing is a different token, and a signature made over one spacing does not verify over the other. It is not a session: there is no revocation in the format, and "exp" is the only expiry — a stolen token is valid until its clock runs out, with "jti" as the replay hook an application may or may not use. And it is not self-authenticating: a decoder that decodes without verifying has read claims anyone could have written, and the spec's own validation steps (§7.2) put signature verification before any claim is trusted.
- **The decoder's edge cases.** The vector test is the first screen: 20 vectors matched this pass by a from-specification implementation (hidden_files/jwt-mini.py), run twice — the RFC 7519 §3.1 example token in full (header eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLA0KICJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9, payload eyJpc3MiOiJqb2UiLA0KICJleHAiOjEzMDA4MTkzODAsDQogImh0dHA6Ly9leGFtcGxlLmNvbS9pc19yb290Ijp0cnVlfQ, signature dBjftJeZ4CVP-mB92K27uhbUJU1p1r_wW1gFWFOEjXk, verified against the RFC 7515 A.1 JWK key), the compact HS256 token (alg-first header, eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9, signature SflKxwRJSMeKKF2QT4fwpMeJf36POk6yJV_adQssw5c), and the unsecured "none" token (eyJhbGciOiJub25lIn0.eyJpc3MiOiJqb2UiLCJleHAiOjEzMDA4MTkzODAsImh0dHA6Ly9leGFtcGxlLmNvbS9pc19yb290Ijp0cnVlfQ., empty third part, trailing dot). The whitespace trap is the second: the RFC example header carries a CRLF and a space inside its JSON (the LA0K and IC sequences in the encoded header), so a decoder that re-encodes from parsed JSON and compares bytes fails the RFC's own vector — the signature covers the exact encoded bytes, never a re-serialization. The seconds trap is the third: "exp":1300819380 is 2011-03-22 18:43:00 UTC, and a decoder that reads NumericDate as milliseconds lands more than 40,000 years out — the same factor-of-a-thousand family as the BSON datetime and MessagePack timestamp traps, one family over. The "none" trap is the fourth: "alg":"none" is a mandatory-to-implement algorithm, so a decoder that accepts it whenever the header asks has accepted an unsigned token — and the RS256-to-HS256 confusion (verifying an asymmetric signature with the public key as an HMAC secret) is the same hole one rung up. The rejection rungs are the fifth: two parts, four parts, padded base64url ("=" present), a tampered signature, and a "none" token presented for HS256 verification are all rejected, and a duplicate claim name keeps the lexically last value per §4. The trailing-dot rung is the sixth: an unsecured token ends with a period and an empty third part, and a splitter that drops empty parts reads it as two parts and rejects a legal token.
- **Decoder-design note (JWT → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Verify over the exact encoded bytes, never over re-encoded JSON.** Whitespace is part of the signed input: the Gauntlet's JWT screen verifies the signature against the token's own header.payload strings, in the same family as the CBOR well-formed rung — a decoder that normalizes before verifying has verified a token nobody signed. (2) **The algorithm is a header claim, not a fact.** The decoder's allow-list decides what "alg" values are acceptable, and "none" is acceptable only when the application explicitly allows unsecured tokens — the Gauntlet grades algorithm acceptance as ALLOW vs REJECT, and a specimen that honors "alg":"none" on a token the application expected signed has failed the format's own trust decision, in the same family as the BSON CARRY vs REJECT rung. (3) **Decode is not validate.** Base64url-decoding the payload reads claims anyone could have written; the Gauntlet grades DECODE vs VERIFY as separate outcomes, and a specimen that treats a decoded-but-unverified "exp" as a trust decision has confused reading with believing — the same split the receipt-interrogation discipline draws between a claim and its proof.

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the 20 vectors above, the whitespace trap, the seconds trap, the "none" trap, and the rejection rungs, all matched this pass by a from-specification implementation (hidden_files/jwt-mini.py) run twice; the spec facts (the §3.1 example strings, the seven registered claims, NumericDate in seconds, the typ/cty rules, the §7.2 validation steps, the §8 mandatory algorithms, the §6 unsecured form, the RFC 7515 A.1 key and signature octets) from RFC 7519 and RFC 7515 read first-party this pass; CORROBORATED — the compact HS256 token as the ecosystem's canonical example, matched by computation this pass, not from a fresh read of its source; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]*

## PASETO — Platform-Agnostic Security Tokens (v4 current, v2 deprecated), or: the token that chose its algorithms so you cannot choose wrong
- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue carries JWT — the token every API on the wire actually hands a decoder — but JWT's security is a header field ("alg") that any producer can set and any consumer can misread: "none" accepted by mistake, RS256 verified as HS256 with the public key as the secret. PASETO is the same job with the choice removed: the token's first two dot-segments — version and purpose, "v4.local" — ARE the algorithm, fixed by the version, and there is no "alg" field to lie about. A decoder that knows JWT but not PASETO reads half the tokens on the modern wire as opaque text; a decoder that knows both can tell, from the prefix alone, which trust decision each token demands.
- **The lineage, in one paragraph.** PASETO (Platform-Agnostic SEcurity TOkens) is Paragon Initiative Enterprises' answer to JOSE, presented by Scott Arciszewski at DEFCON 26 in 2018 ("No Way JOSE!") after three years of JOSE vulnerability research. Four versions, two families: v1 and v3 are the NIST-primitive family — v1.local is AES-256-CTR with an HMAC-SHA384 tag and an HKDF-SHA384 key split, v1.public is RSA-PSS with SHA-384, and v1 is deprecated in favour of v3, whose local form keeps AES-256-CTR and HMAC-SHA384 but derives its counter nonce from the key split, and whose public form is ECDSA over P-384 with SHA-384; v2 and v4 are the modern family — v2.local is XChaCha20-Poly1305 with a message-derived nonce, v2.public is Ed25519, and v2 is deprecated in favour of v4, whose local form is a bare XChaCha20 stream with a BLAKE2b tag and whose public form is Ed25519. Every version has two purposes: "local" (symmetric, the token is encrypted) and "public" (asymmetric, the token is signed and readable). A token is "v{version}.{purpose}.{payload}" with an optional fourth dot-segment, the footer, which is readable but authenticated — the usual home of a key id ("kid"). The payload is opaque bytes, usually JSON; the format registers no claim names, so the "exp" in the official vectors is application convention, not a format rule. Keys serialize under PASERK, the sibling key format. [VERIFIED — the four version documents and the Common.md PAE definition, read first-party this pass; the DEFCON 26 talk and Paragon authorship from paseto.io read first-party this pass]
- **What PASETO is not.** It is not JWT with better crypto: there is no header, no "alg", no registered claims, and no JSON requirement — the payload is opaque bytes and the version+purpose prefix is the whole algorithm declaration. It is not encrypted by default: a ".public" token is signed and readable by anyone, the same as a signed JWT, and only ".local" tokens hide their payload. It is not version-agnostic: v1 and v2 are deprecated, v3 and v4 are current, and a v1 token handed to a v4-only reader is not a token at all — it is a rejection. It is not a session: there is no revocation in the format, and the footer is not a header — it is authenticated but unencrypted, and a decoder that treats it as a trusted key id without checking the tag has trusted a label. And it is not self-authenticating: a ".public" payload decodes without any key, and a decoder that reads it before verifying the signature has read claims anyone could have written — the same split the JWT entry draws between reading and believing.
- **The decoder's edge cases.** The vector test is the first screen: 32 official vectors matched this pass by a from-specification implementation (hidden_files/paseto-mini.py), run twice — 17 from v4.json (9 encrypt, 3 sign, 5 fail) and 15 from v2.json (9 encrypt, 3 sign, 3 fail), plus 4 PAE checks against Common.md's own examples, 3 XChaCha20 stream cross-checks against PyNaCl's IETF AEAD keystream, and 11 rejection rungs. The version trap is the second: the official fail vectors include a v3 token (4-F-3) and a v1 token (2-F-3) presented where v4 and v2 are expected, and both must fail on the prefix alone — a reader that dispatches on payload shape instead of the prefix accepts a token from a version it never agreed to. The footer trap is the third: the footer is part of the authenticated data in every version (PAE carries it), so a token whose footer was swapped fails the tag — and 4-F-1 fails because its implicit assertion differs, a value that is never transmitted at all. The padding trap is the fourth: 4-F-5 is a valid v4.local token with "==" appended to its payload segment, and the strict base64url rule (no padding, trailing bits cleared) rejects it before any crypto runs. The v2 implicit-assertion trap is the fifth: 2-E-7 and 2-E-8 carry the implicit assertion "discarded-anyway" yet produce tokens byte-identical to 2-E-5 and 2-E-6 — v2 has no implicit assertion, so a decoder that binds a v2 token to an assertion is inventing security the format never promised. The nonce trap is the sixth: v2's nonce is derived from the message (BLAKE2b keyed by 24 random bytes, 24-byte output) while v4's is 32 random bytes carried in the token — a decoder that reads the v2 vector "nonce" field as the AEAD nonce fails all nine encrypt vectors, and a decoder that treats v4's transmitted nonce as secret has missed that the key split, not the nonce, carries v4's security. The tag-position trap is the seventh: v4.local's tag is the last 32 bytes of the payload (n || c || t) while v2.local's tag rides inside the AEAD ciphertext, so a parser that slices v4 like v2 reads garbage. The cross-version trap is the eighth: a v2.local token presented to the v4 reader is rejected on its prefix, never decrypted — versions do not fall through.
- **Decoder-design note (PASETO → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Version+purpose is the allow-list.** The Gauntlet's PASETO screen grades ACCEPT vs REJECT on the "v{version}.{purpose}" prefix before any crypto runs — a specimen that accepts v2.local where the application pinned v4.local has failed the format's own versioning, in the same family as the JWT "alg" rung but with no header field to lie about. (2) **Footer and implicit assertion are separate authentications.** The Gauntlet grades FOOTER-MATCH and ASSERTION-MATCH as separate outcomes from TAG-MATCH: a specimen that verifies the tag but ignores the footer has verified a token for the wrong key id, and a specimen that verifies the tag but ignores the implicit assertion has verified a token outside its bound context — both are the receipt-interrogation discipline's distinction between a claim and the context that makes it true. (3) **Strict base64url is the first rung.** Padded or non-canonical segments are rejected before any key is touched (4-F-5), in the same family as the CBOR well-formed rung — a decoder that leniently decodes has already accepted input the format forbids.

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the 32 official vectors above (17 v4 + 15 v2), the 4 PAE examples, the 3 stream cross-checks, and the 11 rejection rungs, all matched this pass by a from-specification implementation (hidden_files/paseto-mini.py) run twice; the version family facts (v1 AES-256-CTR + HMAC-SHA384 + RSA-PSS, v2 XChaCha20-Poly1305 + Ed25519, v3 AES-256-CTR + HMAC-SHA384 + ECDSA P-384, v4 XChaCha20 stream + BLAKE2b + Ed25519, the deprecation directions, the PAE definition, the footer and implicit-assertion rules, the strict base64url rule) from the paseto-standard spec (Version1/2/3/4.md, Common.md) read first-party this pass; the IETF XChaCha20-Poly1305 construction reproduces the official v2 vectors, matched by computation this pass; CORROBORATED — the DEFCON 26 origin and Paragon authorship from paseto.io read first-party this pass, and PASERK as the key-serialization sibling from paseto.io's implementation table; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]*

## TOTP / HOTP — Time-Based and HMAC-Based One-Time Passwords (RFC 6238 / RFC 4226), or: the six digits that expire in thirty seconds

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue carries JWT and PASETO — tokens that prove who you are by carrying a signed claim — but not the code every second-factor prompt on the wire actually asks a human to type: the six digits in an authenticator app. HOTP and TOTP are the other half of the token family: not a bearer credential but a short-lived proof that the prover holds a shared secret right now, computed from an HMAC and a moving factor, with no transmission of the secret and no signature to verify. A decoder that knows JWT but not TOTP can read the session token and still cannot read the second factor — and a specimen arriving as an otpauth:// QR payload would be misread as a bare URL.
- **The lineage, in one paragraph.** HOTP is the OATH initiative's HMAC-Based One-Time Password, RFC 4226 (December 2005; David M'Raihi of VeriSign, Mihir Bellare, Frank Hoornaert, David Naccache, Ohad Ranen): HOTP(K,C) = Truncate(HMAC-SHA-1(K,C)), the counter C an 8-byte big-endian moving factor, the truncation dynamic — the low four bits of the last HMAC byte pick an offset from 0 to 15, four bytes are read from there, the top bit masked away to a 31-bit number, then reduced modulo 10^Digit, six digits minimum. TOTP is the time-based variant, RFC 6238 (May 2011; M'Raihi, Salah Machani, Mingliang Pei, Johan Rydell): TOTP = HOTP(K,T) where T = floor((Unix time − T0)/X), X = 30 seconds and T0 = the Unix epoch by default, with HMAC-SHA-256 and HMAC-SHA-512 allowed alongside SHA-1. Both RFCs are Informational, not Standards Track — the algorithms' authority is adoption, not status: the pair behind every authenticator app, every otpauth:// QR code, every "enter the six-digit code" prompt. The provisioning URI is Google's Key Uri Format, a de facto standard: otpauth://totp/Issuer:account?secret=<base32>&issuer=...&algorithm=SHA1&digits=6&period=30, the secret Base32 without padding, the counter parameter required for hotp. [VERIFIED — the algorithm definitions, truncation, defaults, and test vectors from RFC 4226 and RFC 6238 read first-party this pass; CORROBORATED — the otpauth URI shape from Google's Key Uri Format wiki and the expired IETF draft documenting it, via search this pass]
- **What TOTP/HOTP is not.** It is not a signature: there is no public key, no verification without the shared secret, and anyone holding the secret can generate the same code — the security is the secret's custody, not the code's math. It is not a session: a code is valid for one 30-second window (plus the validator's look-ahead), then it is dead, and replaying it after the window is not an attack the format needs to defeat — the window defeats it. It is not encryption: the code reveals nothing about the secret, but it also hides nothing — six digits carry at most about 20 bits, and the format's own security analysis says the best attack is brute force at sv/10^Digit, which is why the server must throttle (parameter T) and keep the look-ahead window s small. It is not time-synchronised by itself: TOTP assumes prover and verifier agree on Unix time, and RFC 6238's resynchronisation section exists because clocks drift — a validator that checks only the current step rejects legitimate codes generated at the edge of a window. And it is not the same secret for every hash: the RFC 6238 test table names one 20-byte secret in its header text while the SHA-256 and SHA-512 columns run on 32- and 64-byte secrets — the table's own trap, caught this pass by twelve failing checks before the fix.
- **The decoder's edge cases.** The vector test is the first screen: 10 HOTP values from RFC 4226 Appendix D (counters 0–9, secret "12345678901234567890", 755224 through 520489) with all ten intermediate HMAC-SHA-1 hex values, 18 TOTP values from RFC 6238 Appendix B (six timestamps × SHA-1/SHA-256/SHA-512, 8 digits), the RFC 4226 §5.4 worked truncation example (HMAC ending 0x5a → offset 0xa → 0x50ef7f19 → 872921), and 13 edge/rejection rungs — 54/54 checks, run twice (hidden_files/totp-mini.py). The per-column-secret trap is the second: the SHA-256 column fails under the 20-byte secret and passes only under the 32-byte one, so a decoder that reads the table header as the secret for all three columns reproduces a third of the table and calls the rest broken. The leading-zero trap is the third: 07081804 at t=1111111109 is eight characters, not the integer 7081804 — a decoder that parses the code as a number and re-prints it without zero-padding rejects a valid code. The step-boundary trap is the fourth: T=1 at 59 seconds and T=2 at 60, so a code generated in the last second of a window is already the next window's code by the time it arrives — RFC 6238 §5.2 recommends the validator accept at most one step of delay, and a validator that checks only the arrival timestamp fails legitimate edge-of-window codes. The 2038 trap is the fifth: T must be a 64-bit counter (the RFC requires implementations support T beyond 32 bits), and the vectors run to t=20000000000, the year 2603 — a 32-bit counter reader breaks in 2038 and calls every later code invalid. The otpauth trap is the sixth: Google Authenticator ignores the algorithm, digits, and period parameters in the URI and assumes SHA-1, six digits, thirty seconds — so a SHA-256, eight-digit enrolment scans cleanly into the app and then generates codes the server will never accept; the URI is a promise the most common reader does not keep.
- **Decoder-design note (TOTP → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The moving factor is the allow-list.** The Gauntlet's TOTP screen grades ACCEPT vs REJECT on the tuple (secret, counter, digits, hash, step) — a specimen that accepts a code from the wrong step, the wrong digit width, or the wrong hash has accepted a code for a different moment, a different length, or a different algorithm, in the same family as the JWT "alg" rung but with the parameter spread across five fields instead of one header. (2) **The window is part of the credential.** The Gauntlet grades WINDOW-MATCH alongside CODE-MATCH: a code is only valid inside its step, and a specimen that verifies codes without checking which step they belong to has verified a stale credential — the receipt-interrogation discipline's distinction between a claim and the time that makes it true. (3) **The provisioning URI is the attack surface.** The otpauth:// QR code carries the secret in Base32 in the clear — anyone who photographs the QR code owns the second factor forever — so the Gauntlet grades SECRET-CUSTODY as the first rung, before any code is computed: a specimen that logs, screenshots, or re-transmits the URI has already lost the factor it was meant to protect.

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the 10 HOTP vectors + 10 intermediate HMAC values (RFC 4226 App. D), the 18 TOTP vectors (RFC 6238 App. B), the §5.4 worked truncation example, and the 13 edge/rejection rungs, all matched this pass by a from-specification implementation (hidden_files/totp-mini.py), 54/54 checks, run twice; the algorithm facts (HOTP definition, dynamic truncation, 6-digit minimum, 128-bit secret floor / 160-bit recommendation, TOTP definition, X=30, T0=0, SHA-256/512 allowed, 64-bit T requirement, one-step delay recommendation, sv/10^Digit security bound) from RFC 4226 and RFC 6238 read first-party this pass; CORROBORATED — the otpauth:// URI shape and the Google Authenticator parameter-ignoring behaviour from the Key Uri Format wiki and secondary writeups, via search this pass, and the expired IETF otpauth draft as documentation of the de facto schema; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]*

## COSE — CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (RFC 9052 / RFC 9053), or: the envelope that signs its own bytes

- **The gap this entry closes.** The catalogue carries CBOR — the grammar
every COSE signature speaks — and JWT and PASETO, the tokens that prove
who you are in text. But the signed object that actually rides the
constrained wire is neither: it is COSE, the binary twin of JOSE, and a
specimen arriving as a CBOR tag 18, 98, 96, 16, 97, or 17 reads as opaque
binary to any decoder that only knows CBOR, JSON, and the catalogue's
ciphers. COSE is the envelope half of the CBOR story — the layer the EU
Digital COVID Certificate chain ends in (HC1: → Base45 → zlib → CBOR →
COSE), the layer CWT tokens and WebAuthn/CTAP2 attestation objects are
sealed in, and the layer every constrained IoT device signs with when
JSON will not fit. A decoder that knows CBOR but not COSE can read the
envelope and cannot tell whether it was ever sealed.

- **The lineage, in one paragraph.** COSE began as RFC 8152 (July 2017,
Jim Schaad), the CBOR counterpart to JOSE, and was revised without
changing the wire structures as RFC 9052 (August 2022), with the
algorithms split into the companion RFC 9053. Six message types, each a
CBOR array under its own tag: COSE_Sign (98, one or more signers),
COSE_Sign1 (18, exactly one signer), COSE_Encrypt (96, enveloped, one
or more recipients), COSE_Encrypt0 (16, single recipient, implicit key),
COSE_Mac (97, MAC with recipients), COSE_Mac0 (17, MAC with implicit
key). Every message splits its headers into a protected header — a byte
string holding a CBOR map, covered by the signature or tag — and an
unprotected header, a plain map that is not covered. The common header
parameters are small integers: alg 1, crit 2, content type 3, kid 4,
IV 5, partial IV 6, counter signature 7, and in the unprotected side the
ephemeral key −1, static kid −3, salt −20, U nonce −22. Keys are CBOR
maps too: kty 1 (OKP 1, EC2 2, Symmetric 4), kid 2, alg 3; EC2 carries
crv −1 (P-256 1, P-384 2, P-521 3), x −2, y −3, d −4; OKP carries crv −1
(X25519 4, X448 5, Ed25519 6, Ed448 7), x −2, d −4; symmetric keys carry
k −1. The algorithm registry (RFC 9053) is integer-valued throughout:
ES256 −7, ES384 −35, ES512 −36, EdDSA −8, PS256 −37; A128GCM 1, A192GCM
2, A256GCM 3; AES-CCM-16-64-128 10 through AES-CCM-64-128-256 33;
ChaCha20/Poly1305 24; HMAC 256/64 4, 256/256 5, 384/384 6, 512/512 7;
AES-MAC 128/64 14, 256/64 15, 128/128 25, 256/128 26; direct −6, A128KW
−3, A192KW −4, A256KW −5; ECDH-ES + HKDF-256 −25, ECDH-ES + HKDF-512
−26, ECDH-SS + HKDF-256 −27, ECDH-SS + HKDF-512 −28, ECDH-ES + A128KW
−29, ECDH-ES + A192KW −30, ECDH-ES + A256KW −31, ECDH-SS + A128KW −32,
ECDH-SS + A192KW −33, ECDH-SS + A256KW −34. The signature, encryption,
and MAC structures are built the same way in every case: a context
string, the protected header bytes, the external additional data, and
the payload, CBOR-encoded as one array and fed to the primitive —
"Signature1" for COSE_Sign1, "Signature" for COSE_Sign, "Encrypt" for
COSE_Encrypt, "Encrypt0" for COSE_Encrypt0, "MAC" for COSE_Mac, "MAC0"
for COSE_Mac0. [VERIFIED — the six tags, the header-parameter and key
numbers, and the algorithm values above, from RFC 9052 and RFC 9053
read first-party this pass; CORROBORATED — the HC1:/DCC chain and the
CWT/WebAuthn usage, from the standards record, not from a fresh read
this pass]

- **What COSE is not.** It is not JOSE in binary: JOSE protects a
base64url JSON header whose text is the signed object, while COSE
protects a byte string holding a CBOR map — the signature covers the
bytes, so re-encoding the same map kills the signature, and a decoder
that "normalizes" a protected header before verifying has destroyed
exactly what it was asked to check. It is not a token format: COSE
registers no claims and carries no expiry — CWT is the token layer
built on top of it, and a COSE_Sign1 object with a JSON payload is a
signed blob, not a credential, until an application says otherwise. It
is not self-typing without its tag: the tag number (18, 98, 96, 16, 97,
17) is the only thing that says which structure an array is, the tags
are optional in the wild, and a bare four-element array could be a
Sign1 or a Mac0 until the decoder looks at what is inside. It is not
PASETO: where PASETO fixes the algorithm in the version prefix, COSE
carries the algorithm as an integer in a header — and a reader that
trusts the unprotected copy of that integer has made the same mistake
the JWT "alg" rung punishes. And AES-CBC-MAC is not CMAC: RFC 9053
says so in so many words, and a decoder that reaches for CMAC fails
every AES-MAC vector in the book.

- **The decoder's edge cases.** The verification suite is the first
screen: 34 checks matched this pass by a from-specification
implementation (hidden_files/cose-mini.py), run twice — RFC 9052
Appendix C examples C.1.1, C.1.3, C.2.1, C.5.1, and C.6.1 with keys
from Appendix C.7, plus five cases from the cose-wg/Examples companion
repository the RFC itself points at, each carrying its intermediate
values. The protected-header trap is the second: the companion
repository's *-pass-*.json files are failure tests — their output
message carries the mutation named in "failures" ("ChangeProtected":
"a0", the protected header replaced by an empty map) while the
intermediates hold the original passing values — and every one of the
four mutated cases fails against its own headers while verifying
against the originals, which is the test's whole point. A decoder that
re-encodes a protected header, or that verifies against the unprotected
copy, passes a message the format rejects. The context-string trap is
the third: "Signature" versus "Signature1", "Encrypt" versus
"Encrypt0", "MAC" versus "MAC0" — one character changes the
authenticated data, and the Encrypt0 case proves it: the intermediate
AAD decodes as ["Encrypt0", b"", b""], not ["Encrypt", ...]. The
CBC-MAC trap is the fourth: AES-CBC-MAC-256/64 and AES-CBC-MAC-128/64
are raw CBC-MAC with an all-zero IV and zero-padding to a block
multiple — CMAC fails all three vectors this pass (C.5.1, C.6.1, and
the companion cbc-mac-01), zero-padded raw CBC matches all three, and
0x80-padding and PKCS#7 both fail the companion vector. The
two-protected-headers trap is the fifth: a COSE_Sign Sig_structure
carries five elements — ["Signature", body_protected, sign_protected,
external_aad, payload] — and the C.1.1 signature only verifies when
both protected headers are present; a four-element structure built the
Sign1 way fails. The KDF-context trap is the sixth: in
COSE_KDF_Context the AlgorithmID is the CONTENT algorithm (A128GCM,
1), not the KDF algorithm (ECDH-ES + HKDF-256, −25), and PartyUInfo
and PartyVInfo are explicit null triples when the parties carry no
identity — the C.3.1 enveloped case re-derives its CEK only when the
context is built exactly so: ECDH shared secret
4b31712e096e5f20b4ecf9790fd8cc7c8b7e2c8ad90bda81cb224f62c0e7b9a6,
HKDF-SHA-256 over that context, CEK 56074d506729ca40c4b4fe50c6439893,
AES-GCM-128 decrypting to "This is the content." The kid-is-a-label
trap is the seventh: kid lives in the unprotected header in every
Appendix C example, and a decoder that resolves a key by an
unauthenticated kid has trusted a label — the same family as the
PASETO footer trap.

- **Decoder-design note (COSE → Gauntlet).** Four rungs. (1)
**Protected-header integrity is the first rung.** The Gauntlet's COSE
screen grades ACCEPT vs REJECT on a message whose protected header was
replaced by an empty map (the companion repository's own mutation): a
specimen that still verifies has verified against something other than
the protected bytes, and has failed the format's central promise. (2)
**Context-string discipline is the second rung.** Cross the 0/1
boundary — verify a Sign1 structure with a "Signature" context, or an
Encrypt0 ciphertext with an "Encrypt" AAD — and the specimen must
fail; a specimen that accepts has authenticated data it did not bind.
(3) **CBC-MAC versus CMAC discrimination is the third rung.** Present
an AES-MAC-256/64 tag and grade which construction the specimen
computes: CMAC is the wrong answer, named as wrong in RFC 9053 itself,
and a specimen that cannot tell the two apart cannot be trusted with
any MAC it has not seen before. (4) **KDF-context reconstruction is
the fourth rung.** Hand the specimen an ECDH-ES enveloped message with
only the recipient's private key and the ephemeral public key, and
grade whether it re-derives the CEK through the exact COSE_KDF_Context
— content algorithm as AlgorithmID, null party infos explicit — rather
than guessing a context that happens to decrypt.

## WebAuthn / FIDO2 passkeys — the login that signs a challenge instead of sending a secret, or: the password that was never typed

- **WebAuthn (W3C) + CTAP (FIDO Alliance) = FIDO2.** WebAuthn is the browser-facing API — `navigator.credentials.create()` for registration, `navigator.credentials.get()` for authentication — and CTAP (Client to Authenticator Protocol) is the wire protocol between the platform and the authenticator: a phone's secure enclave, Windows Hello, a USB/NFC/BLE security key, or a password manager acting as authenticator. CTAP 1 is the original FIDO U2F protocol; CTAP 2 adds PIN-protected, discoverable credentials, and CTAP 2 authenticators still implement CTAP 1 for backward compatibility with U2F-only relying parties. A **passkey** is the user-facing name for a WebAuthn credential: a public/private key pair generated on the authenticator, bound to one relying-party origin, whose private key never leaves the device and whose server stores only the public half. Level 1 became a W3C Recommendation March 4, 2019; Level 2 on April 8, 2021; **Level 3 became a W3C Recommendation August 25, 2026** (FIDO Alliance announcement August 31, 2026), remaining compatible with Levels 1 and 2 while locking in the usability improvements that made passkeys practical for mainstream login. CTAP 2.2 is a FIDO Proposed Standard dated July 14, 2025; CTAP 2.3 (February 26, 2026) introduces no breaking changes against 2.2 — a 2.2 implementation is conformant to 2.3. [VERIFIED — W3C Recommendation record via Mike Jones (self-issued.info), FIDO Alliance specs index via secondary summaries; CTAP 2.3 no-breaking-change claim from the same first-party-adjacent source]
- **The two ceremonies.** Registration: the relying party sends a random challenge and its RP ID; the authenticator creates a key pair, returns an attestation object — a CBOR map holding the attestation statement format (`fmt`), the authenticator data, and an attestation statement (usually a manufacturer certificate chain plus a signature over the authenticator data and the client-data hash). Authentication: the relying party sends a fresh challenge; the authenticator signs the authenticator data plus the challenge hash with the credential's private key. The server verifies three things every time: the signature, the origin/RP ID in the client data, and the challenge freshness. Nothing the user types is ever a secret, so there is nothing to phish: a fake login page cannot collect a credential that works anywhere else, because the signature binds the real origin. [VERIFIED — WebAuthn specification structure, standard account]
- **authenticatorData, byte by byte — the decoder's real target.** 32 bytes RP ID hash (SHA-256 of the RP ID — a domain, not the full origin URL, not scheme-and-host), 1 byte flags, 4 bytes signature counter (uint32 big-endian), then — only at registration, when the AT flag is set — attested credential data: 16-byte AAGUID, 2-byte credential-ID length, the credential ID, and the COSE_Key (CBOR-encoded public key); then, when the ED flag is set, CBOR extension data. The flags byte: UP (user present, bit 0), UV (user verified — PIN or biometric, bit 2), BE (backup eligible, bit 3), BS (backup state, bit 4), AT (attested credential data follows, bit 6), ED (extension data follows, bit 7). Two traps for a decoder reading this structure: the spec explicitly permits authenticators to always report a counter of zero, so a zero counter is not evidence of cloning — clone detection by counter is a heuristic, not a proof; and the AAGUID identifies the authenticator *model*, not the individual key (the `fido-u2f` format carries an all-zero AAGUID). [VERIFIED — python-fido2 2.0.0 API docs flag constants; CUPASS FIDO2/CTAP guide layout; hexlyst authenticatorData guide on the counter and flag traps]
- **Synced vs device-bound — the BE/BS split.** A device-bound passkey stays on one device (a security key reports BE false); a synced passkey is copied between the user's devices through a provider's sync service and reports BE true, with BS true once it has actually been backed up. The relying party can read the split straight off the flags without any attestation: reject synced passkeys by requiring BE = 0. Restoring a synced credential to a different authenticator model or passkey provider can change its AAGUID — the model identifier is not stable across a sync. The FIDO Alliance's State of Passkeys 2026 report (May 2026) claims worldwide active passkeys have surpassed 5 billion, with 90% global awareness — self-reported platform numbers, not independently audited, so filed as a direction, not a measurement. [CORROBORATED — FIDO Metadata Statement v3.1 on AAGUID change on restore; nhimg hardware-key guide and corbado FIDO2-vs-passkey comparison on BE/BS; CLAIMED — the 5-billion figure, FIDO Alliance self-report]
- **Attestation formats and conveyance.** Formats: `packed` (the FIDO2 native format — signs the full authenticator data plus challenge hash, several algorithms: ES256, EdDSA), `fido-u2f` (the U2F legacy format — ECDSA P-256 only, signs a fixed U2F message, no flags or extensions covered, kept for backward compatibility), `tpm`, `android-key`, `android-safetynet`, `apple`, and `none`. Conveyance the relying party asks for: `none` (the client strips identifying information), `indirect`, `direct` (AAGUID and attestation passed through unchanged — what workforce deployments need for model control), or `enterprise`. The `packed` vs `fido-u2f` split is a generation marker a decoder can read at a glance: a `packed` attestation is a FIDO2-native credential; a `fido-u2f` one is a U2F-era credential wrapped for the new API. [VERIFIED — WebAuthn attestation-format registry, standard account; CORROBORATED — corbado comparison table on the two formats]
- **Decoder-design note (WebAuthn → Gauntlet).** Four rungs. (1) **The origin is the credential.** A passkey signs the RP ID hash, so the specimen's identity is inseparable from the domain that created it — the Gauntlet's foreign-code analogue is origin-binding every extracted artifact to the container that produced it, so a stolen artifact cannot be replayed into a different context. (2) **The flags byte is a one-byte confession.** UP/UV/BE/BS/AT/ED in a single byte tell the decoder whether a human was present, whether a PIN or biometric fired, whether the key can leave the device, and whether more data follows — a specimen that reports BE = 1 while claiming to be device-bound has contradicted itself in eight bits, and the Gauntlet grades that contradiction before it reads the signature. (3) **The counter is a heuristic, never a proof.** The spec lets an authenticator report zero forever, so a decoder that treats a non-advancing counter as proof of cloning will false-positive every honest zero-counter device — the same discipline as the Gauntlet's clone-detection rule: one signal is a suspicion, two independent signals are a finding. (4) **Attestation is provenance, not identity.** The AAGUID names a model, the certificate chain names a manufacturer, and neither names the key holder — a specimen that confuses "genuine model" with "trusted actor" has made the same error as a relying party that accepts `direct` attestation as authentication. The Gauntlet reads attestation as supply-chain evidence and grades the actor separately.

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the WebAuthn Level 3 Recommendation date (August 25, 2026) and CTAP 2.2/2.3 lineage from W3C/FIDO records via Mike Jones's first-party-adjacent writeup; the authData layout and flag values (UP 1, UV 4, BE 8, BS 16, AT 64, ED 128) from the python-fido2 2.0.0 documentation and the CUPASS guide; the zero-counter permission and flag-reading traps from the hexlyst authenticatorData guide; CORROBORATED — the BE/BS synced-vs-device-bound split and the packed-vs-fido-u2f generation marker from the nhimg hardware-key guide and the corbado comparison, and the AAGUID-change-on-restore note from the FIDO Metadata Statement v3.1; CLAIMED — the 5-billion active passkeys figure, FIDO Alliance self-report, May 2026; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]*
