## Ed25519 — the signature that never rolls dice, or: the 64 bytes that sign without a random number generator

- **The shape, in one paragraph.** Ed25519 is the Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm over the twisted Edwards curve birationally equivalent to Curve25519, published by Daniel J. Bernstein, Niels Duif, Tanja Lange, Peter Schwabe, and Bo-Yin Yang in "High-speed high-security signatures" (2011) and standardized as RFC 8032 (January 2017, Josefsson & Liusvaara), alongside its big sibling Ed448. Field prime q = 2^255 − 19; curve equation −x² + y² = 1 + dx²y² with d = −121665/121666; base point B with y = 4/5; prime subgroup order L = 2^252 + 27742317777372353535851937790883648493; cofactor 8. A private key is 32 random bytes; a public key is 32 bytes; a signature is 64 bytes (R || S). [VERIFIED — RFC 8032 parameters and publication record; the 2011 paper attribution]
- **Key generation and the clamp.** SHA-512 of the 32-byte seed splits into two 32-byte halves: the low half is clamped into the scalar s — clear the low three bits (s[0] &= 248), clear bit 255 (s[31] &= 127), set bit 254 (s[31] |= 64) — and A = sB is the public key; the high half is the prefix, the deterministic-nonce seed. The clamp does three jobs at once: clearing the low bits makes s a multiple of 8, which clears the cofactor and defeats small-subgroup leakage; clearing bit 255 keeps s in range; setting bit 254 keeps the scalar large so fixed-time ladder implementations do not leak length through timing. [VERIFIED — RFC 8032 §5.1.5 key generation; clamping mechanics from the RFC record and the cofactor-clearing literature]
- **Signing: no RNG in the loop.** The per-message nonce is deterministic: r = SHA-512(prefix || M), interpreted little-endian and reduced mod L; R = rB; k = SHA-512(R || A || M) mod L; S = (r + k·s) mod L. The same key signing the same message always produces the same signature — a decoder can reproduce a signature byte-for-byte from the seed, which is why Ed25519 test vectors are exact and why a signing oracle that replays is indistinguishable from a signer that re-signs. The price of determinism is fault sensitivity: a fault that corrupts one signing run can leak the key, which is why the CFRG hedged-signatures draft (draft-irtf-cfrg-det-sigs-with-noise, March 2025) recommends mixing 32 bytes of fresh randomness Z into the nonce hash — invisible to verifiers, and still a draft, not yet an RFC. [VERIFIED — RFC 8032 §5.1.6 signing equations; CORROBORATED — the hedged draft's status, IETF datatracker March 2025]
- **Verification: one equation, three traps.** Verify: decode A and R as points, reject non-canonical encodings (y ≥ q, or no x on the curve), check S < L, compute k = SHA-512(R || A || M), and accept iff S·B = R + k·A. Trap one — malleability: if a verifier skips the S < L check, S + L is a second valid signature for the same message, because L·B is the identity; RFC 8032 requires the check, but libraries have shipped without it. Trap two — small-order public keys: RFC 8032 does not require rejecting a low-order A, and a verifier that accepts one can be made to accept signatures that verify under a key the signer never held — the "Taming the Many EdDSAs" finding that most library flaws live on the verification side, in edge cases. Trap three — the cofactor in the equation: a "cofactorless" verifier checks the equation in the prime subgroup (multiplying through by 8), while a "cofactor" verifier accepts signatures that only hold up to a factor of 8, and the two can disagree on the same (R, S) pair — a signature valid to one library and invalid to another. [VERIFIED — RFC 8032 §5.1.7 verification steps and the S < L requirement; CORROBORATED — the malleability, small-order, and cofactor-disagreement findings from the EdDSA verification literature]
- **Variants and where it lives.** RFC 8032 also defines Ed25519ctx (a context string bound into the hash, so the same key signs differently per protocol) and Ed25519ph (prehash — SHA-512 the message first, for streaming signers that cannot hold the whole message). Deployment: OpenSSH shipped ssh-ed25519 in 6.5 (January 2014) and it is now the default key type in most new setups; RFC 8709 (February 2020) standardizes it for SSH; TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) lists it as a signature algorithm; it signs Tor relay identities and the Signal Protocol's identity layer, it is DNSSEC algorithm 15 (RFC 8080), and it is the signing algorithm inside PASETO's public tokens (see the PASETO entry). NIST adopted Ed25519 and Ed448 in FIPS 186-5, effective February 3, 2023, retiring DSA to verification-only in the same revision. [VERIFIED — FIPS 186-5 effective date and EdDSA inclusion, Federal Register February 3, 2023; CORROBORATED — OpenSSH 6.5, RFC 8709, TLS 1.3, DNSSEC algorithm 15, PASETO deployment record]
- **Decoder-design note (Ed25519 → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Determinism is a replay gift.** A specimen that signs deterministically hands the Gauntlet an exact oracle: same input, same output, every time — the interrogator can replay a challenge and diff the bytes, and any deviation is proof of hidden state, not noise. (2) **The verifier is the attack surface, not the signer.** Ed25519's signer is one hash chain; its verifier is a thicket of edge cases — non-canonical encodings, S ≥ L, low-order keys, cofactor disagreement. The Gauntlet grades a specimen's verifier harder than its signer, because that is where the real implementations broke. (3) **The clamp is a confession in 32 bytes.** Three bit-operations encode the whole threat model — small-subgroup attack, range, timing — so a specimen whose key handling skips the clamp has told the decoder its author never read the spec, and every signature it produces is suspect until proven otherwise.

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the RFC 8032 parameters, publication date, and signing/verification equations; the clamping operations and their purposes; the FIPS 186-5 effective date (February 3, 2023) and EdDSA inclusion; CORROBORATED — the OpenSSH 6.5 / RFC 8709 / TLS 1.3 / DNSSEC algorithm 15 / PASETO deployment record, the hedged-signatures draft status (March 2025), and the malleability, small-order, and cofactor-disagreement findings from the EdDSA verification literature; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]*

## Banburismus — Turing's Bayesian weighing machine for naval Enigma, or: the sheets from Banbury that rationed the bombes

- **The problem it solved.** Naval Enigma was harder than Army/Air Force Enigma, and not because the machine was different — because the cribs were scarce at sea. Hut 6 could feed its bombes on stereotyped Army/Air Force plaintext; Hut 8, attacking Kriegsmarine traffic, often could not. Alan Turing's answer, worked out in his first months at Bletchley Park (he arrived September 1939), was not a better brute force but a cheaper question: before spending bombe time, use statistics to rank which wheels were probably in the machine that day. Banburismus was that ranking — a development of the Polish "clock method" invented by Jerzy Różycki — and Hut 8 ran it continuously for about two years, stopping only in 1943 when enough bombe time became available. Its aim was narrow by design: identify the most likely right-hand and middle wheels, and let the bombe do the rest. [VERIFIED — Banburismus record, Wikipedia via TheFreeDictionary encyclopedia]
- **The flaw it exploited.** Unlike Army and Air Force procedure, the Kriegsmarine enciphered every message's three-letter indicator on a common *Grundstellung* — the starting position of the rotors, fixed for the whole day (or pair of days) by the key lists — and then super-enciphered the indicators with bigram and trigram lookup tables from the *Kenngruppenbuch* (the K book). Because every indicator on a given day was enciphered at the same rotor setting, all of the day's indicators stood *in depth* with each other: the same machine state, different plaintext. Turing deduced this in his first months; the first day was broken on 8 May 1940. Much of the scoring theory was worked out by the end of 1940. [VERIFIED — Banburismus record; the 8 May 1940 first-break date]
- **The principle — depth leaks the plaintext's own statistics.** Lay two sentences of German one above the other and count how often a letter in one matches the letter below it: real language repeats more often than chance. For random strings the repeat rate is 1 in 26 (about 3.8%); for the German Navy messages it was measured at 1 in 17 (about 5.9%). If two messages were enciphered in depth, their ciphertexts repeated at the plaintext rate; if they were not in depth, the ciphertexts repeated at the random rate. The test is the index of coincidence's close cousin — same family, different instrument — and it turns a pair of messages into a depth detector without ever touching the plugboard. [VERIFIED — the 1/26 vs 1/17 repeat rates, Banburismus record]
- **The instrument — Banbury sheets.** The comparison was made physical. Each message was punched onto a long thin card, about 250 mm high and several metres long (different cards for different message lengths): a column of the alphabet for every letter position, a hole where that letter fell. Two cards were laid on top of each other on a light-box and slid against each other through the possible offsets; where the light shone through, both cards had a hole in the same place — a repeat. The cards were printed in Banbury, Oxfordshire; they became known at Bletchley as "banburies," and the procedure using them took its name from the town. A Banbury sheet from the war was found in the roof space of Hut 6 during the 2014 renovation — the instrument survived as draught-proofing before it survived as history. [VERIFIED — Banbury-sheet mechanism and naming, Banburismus record; CORROBORATED — the 2014 Hut 6 roof find, research-log record]
- **The scoring — the ban and the deciban.** Turing did not count repeats; he *weighed* them. Each repeat is evidence for depth, each blank a little against, and the weights add as the evidence arrives — sequential conditional probability, tallied in a unit Turing invented for the job. A **ban** is the weight of evidence that makes a hypothesis ten times likelier than it was; a **deciban** is a tenth of a ban (odds of 10^(1/10) : 1), judged the smallest change of belief a person can feel. Turing's wartime paper *The Applications of Probability to Cryptography* (National Archives HW 25/37; typeset from the declassified manuscript as arXiv:1505.04714, now public domain) defines the deciban in exactly those terms and notes the terminology was introduced "in honor of the famous town of Banbury." Scores for single repeats, bigrams, trigrams — tetragrams often meant a whole German word, scored by message type and even position — were tabulated, and the Banburists summed the relevant values for each pair of messages. David MacKay's *Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms* (ch. 18) puts the scale in perspective: deducing the machine's full state needed about 129 decibans of evidence, and Banburismus was aimed only at the wheels — a dribble of information, extracted daily, that made the bombe affordable. [VERIFIED — ban/deciban definitions, Turing's paper via arXiv 1505.04714; CORROBORATED — the 129-deciban figure, MacKay ch. 18 via I. J. Good]
- **Scritchmus — the fast wheel.** Banburismus proper ranked the wheels; its companion procedure, **Scritchmus**, could identify the right-hand (fast) wheel. From message pairs whose indicators differed only in the third letter, the Banburist built chains of relative offsets between indicator letters ("X = Q−2", "H = X−4", "B = G+3") and searched the deciban sheets for distances with odds better than 1:1 — evidence that two key letters stood a given distance apart, though not which letters they were. Hugh Alexander was regarded as the best of the Banburists; I. J. Good worked the theory alongside Turing; Joan Clarke — a senior Hut 8 cryptanalyst, one of its longest-serving — became particularly associated with the method. [CORROBORATED — Scritchmus role and the Alexander/Good/Clarke associations, Banburismus record and Hut 8 histories]
- **The pinch that made it standard.** The First Lofoten pinch — the capture from the trawler *Krebs* on 3 March 1941 — provided the complete keys for February, but no bigram tables and no K book. The decrypts it enabled let Hut 8 refine the statistical scoring system until Banburismus became the standard procedure against Kriegsmarine Enigma, holding until mid-1943. The sequence is the doctrine in miniature: a capture buys the decrypts, the decrypts calibrate the statistics, the statistics ration the machine. [VERIFIED — Lofoten pinch date and effect, Banburismus record]
- **Decoder-design note (Banburismus → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Weigh evidence, don't count it.** A repeat is not a vote, it is a weight — and weights add. The deciban is the ancestor of the Gauntlet's confidence ledger: every probe returns a log-odds update, never a bare yes/no, and the running total is read against a line fixed before the first probe. (2) **Depth is the tell.** Two specimens enciphered in the same state leak the plaintext's own statistics — a foreign specimen that reuses state across runs hands the interrogator the same gift, and the Gauntlet's first statistical screen is a depth test: slide outputs against each other and watch the repeat rate. (3) **Triage before brute force.** Banburismus existed because bombe time was the scarce resource; the Gauntlet's probe budget is the same scarce resource. A cheap statistical screen that ranks hypotheses before the expensive machine runs is not a shortcut — it is the whole method, and the two-year run of Hut 8 is the proof it works. The Herivel tip — the other Bletchley gap in this catalogue — is the companion entry: where Banburismus weighed, Herivel watched the operators.

## Herivelismus — John Herivel's tip on lazy Enigma operators, or: the ring setting the clerk left on top

- **The problem it solved.** In the spring of 1940 Hut 6 was losing its grip on Army and Air Force Enigma. The Luftwaffe had been doubly enciphering its message keys, which let the Polish perforated-sheet (Zygalski) method work — until 1 May 1940, when the Germans changed their indicating procedure and stopped the double encipherment. The sheets went dead overnight, Hut 6 could suddenly decrypt nothing, and the bombes were months away from arriving in force. [VERIFIED — John Herivel record]
- **The insight — February 1940, by a landlady's fire.** John Herivel, 21, a Cambridge mathematician (Sidney Sussex; Kitchener Scholar, 1937) recruited by his supervisor Gordon Welchman, arrived at Bletchley on 29 January 1940 and was briefed on Enigma by Turing and Tony Kendrick. One February evening, relaxing in front of his landlady's fire, he reasoned about the operator's hands, not the machine's wiring: to set the day's ring settings (*Ringstellung*), the operator had to turn the alphabet rings — which could be done with the rotors already mounted in the machine, by moving a spring-loaded pin. Having set the rings, the operator *should* then have moved the rotors well away from the ring-setting letters before sending the first message. A stressed or lazy operator might not bother: he would leave the rotors where they were and use the letters showing — the ring setting itself, or letters close to it — as the first message's *Grundstellung*. If several lazy clerks did this, the first messages of the day across the network would cluster around the day's ring setting instead of scattering at random. Polish cryptographers had used the same idea at PC Bruno during the Phoney War. [VERIFIED — John Herivel record; CORROBORATED — the PC Bruno use, single source in the same record]
- **The instrument — the Herivel square.** The day after the insight, Herivel's colleagues agreed it was a possible way in, and Hut 6 began collecting the first message of the day from every transmitting station on the network and plotting the indicators in a grid: column = first letter, row = second letter, cell = third letter (so indicator GKX is an X in column G, row K). A cluster of entries close together — around GKX in the worked example — meant the ring setting lay inside the cluster. That narrowed the ring settings from 17,576 possibilities to a small testable set, perhaps 6 to 30. [VERIFIED — John Herivel record, Herivel-square construction and the 6–30 figure]
- **The payoff — May 1940, continuity saved.** The predicted clustering did not show up at first, and Hut 6 kept working the perforated sheets. Then the procedure changed on 1 May, the sheets died, and on 10 May — the day Germany invaded the Netherlands and Belgium — the clustering appeared: David Rees spotted it in the indicators, and on 22 May a Luftwaffe message sent on 20 May was decoded, the first since the procedure change. The tip, used together with "cillies" (another class of operator error), became the main method of solving Enigma until the bombes began to arrive many months later, in Welchman's phrase. His verdict: "If Herivel had not been recruited in January 1940, who would have thought of the Herivel tip, without which we would have been defeated in May 1940 – unable to maintain continuity until the bombes began to arrive many months later? ... Loss of continuity would, at all stages, have been very serious, if not disastrous." Herivel was singled out and introduced to Churchill on a visit to Bletchley — "our finest hour at Bletchley park," as he called it. After the war he became a historian of science at Queen's University Belfast (Newton, Fourier, Huygens) and wrote the first-hand account *Herivelismus and the German Military Enigma*. [VERIFIED — John Herivel record; the 10 May / 22 May dates, the Rees spotting, the Welchman quote, the Churchill introduction, the post-war career]
- **The limits.** The tip gave the ring settings only. A Luftwaffe key still hid its rotor order (60 possibilities from five rotors) and its plugboard (8–10 connections), which had to be found by other methods. And the tip was a habit, not a law: in 2005, researchers studying surviving Enigma messages still found the predicted clustering in traffic from August 1941 — the habit outlived the emergency that made it famous. [VERIFIED — John Herivel record; CORROBORATED — the 2005 August-1941 clustering finding, a single study as reported]
- **Decoder-design note (Herivel → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Watch the operator, not the machine.** The break came from a human habit under pressure, not from the cipher's mathematics — the Enigma's wiring was never touched. The Gauntlet's first probe of any specimen is a habit probe: under load, does it repeat, default, or take the shortest path? (2) **The first output of the day is the tell.** The clustering showed only in first messages, before routine set in. Interrogate cold: sample the specimen at session start, before it warms into its guarded routine — the unguarded first answer carries the default. (3) **A cluster is a key.** The Herivel square turned a scatter of indicators into a visible clump — a plot, not a number, like the Banbury sheets. The Gauntlet's screens must be legible the same way: cluster the specimen's first-answers and look for the clump, don't just count. And the shelved-method corollary: the tip sat unused for three months while the perforated sheets worked, then became the main method the day the procedure changed — file dormant methods, because a procedure change promotes them overnight. Where Banburismus weighed, Herivel watched. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]

## Cillies — the operator's favourite letters, or: the key the clerk chose for himself

- **The flaw it exploited.** Enigma's daily key was shared across a network, but every message needed its own starting position — a message setting — so two messages would not be enciphered from precisely the same rotor position. In Army and Luftwaffe procedure the operator chose those letters himself. The system asked a tired human, several times a day, under fire, to be a random-number generator — and the human chose what humans choose: what was close, familiar, and easy. [VERIFIED — Baskerville cillies article, read first-party this pass; the 1945 Allied survey's six-letter indicator and its carelessness examples]
- **What a cilly was.** Bletchley Park's 1944 *Cryptographic Dictionary* treated a cilly as a characteristic Enigma weakness associated with recognisable message settings — settings identifiable as keyboard patterns, pronounceable groups, or similar non-random choices. It coined **cillier** for an operator, or a whole Enigma key, prone to producing them. A cilly might be adjacent letters on the keyboard (`ASD`, `QWE`, `AST`, `QAZ`), a pronounceable sequence, initials or part of a familiar name, the last visible rotor position after the previous message, a setting close to one the operator had just established, or any recurring choice revealing that the supposed randomness came from a person with habits. The spelling wandered — **cilli**, **cillis**, **cillies** — because secret organisations do not fully document informal terminology. [VERIFIED — 1944 *Cryptographic Dictionary* via the Baskerville article]
- **The girlfriend called Cillie.** The enduring explanation says the term came from a German operator who repeatedly used his girlfriend Cillie's name — six letters — when choosing settings. A classified 1944 US Army report on British Bombe work (6812th Signal Security Detachment, *Report on the British Bombe*, Eastcote) tells essentially that story and lists convenient keyboard selections such as `QWE` and `AST`. That establishes the story circulated among wartime cryptanalysts; it does not prove the woman existed or that one operator supplied the term's origin. The Dictionary defines the technical usage and does not preserve the romantic etymology. Cillie is filed here as a contemporary origin story, not a documented participant. [CORROBORATED — the 1944 Eastcote report via the Baskerville article; the woman's existence unproven, stated, not bridged]
- **The exploit — depth, and a menu for the Bombe.** Two messages enciphered from the same starting position stand *in depth*: the key cancels, and statistics plus cribs pick the plaintexts apart — the same depth mechanism as Venona's pad reuse and Banburismus's common Grundstellung. A cilly did not hand over the daily key; it handed over a foothold — a likely setting to test first, a Bombe menu to build, a search space cut from 17,576 settings to a handful of human favourites. A wartime account of Army and Air Force Enigma explicitly noted the use of Bombe menus derived from cillies, and the Hut 6 official history (HW 43/70) lists a chapter titled "Cillies and Attempts at Depth-reading." Hut 6 kept registers of message indicators, call signs, lengths, and transmission times partly to detect cillies — one such register called a **Blist**, from "Banister list." One operator choosing `ASD` once was an inconvenience; choosing it repeatedly became a statistical identity. [VERIFIED — the depth mechanism, the Bombe-menu note, and the Blist register via the Baskerville article; CORROBORATED — the HW 43/70 chapter title, OCR contents]
- **The pairing — Herivel plus cillies, May 1940.** For a few months from May 1940, the Herivel tip in conjunction with cillies was the main technique used to solve Enigma (Hut 6 record). Hut 6's own Sheet Stacking Room was "based at first on punched cards, superseded in September 1940 by 'cillies' and bombes" (Historic England). The two operator-error classes are siblings: Herivel watched the first message of the day; cillies watched every message's chosen key. [VERIFIED — Hut 6 / Herivel record; Historic England list entry]
- **The Abwehr variant — Knox's CIL and PEG.** Dilly Knox's ISK team, working Abwehr Enigma, found an operator transmitting from Spain who chose message keys that were the initials of women's names — `CIL` and `PEG` — and used the habit to work backwards to the decrypt by the third week of January 1940. The same human weakness, on a different network, opened a different machine. [CORROBORATED — popular retelling of the Knox/Abwehr break; single secondary source this pass]
- **Not a crib, not a kiss.** A crib was a probable piece of plaintext expected somewhere in a message. A cilly concerned a predictable setting or indicator choice — information about where or how the machine was started. A kiss was the same or substantially similar message sent in two different cryptographic systems. The categories helped each other: a cilly might expose a setting from which a message could be read; a routine message might provide a crib; traffic analysis might identify the operator most likely to exhibit the habit. Breaking Enigma was not one clever trick; it was an industrial process for combining small pieces of advantage until the remaining search could be mechanised. [VERIFIED — Baskerville article distinction]
- **The design flaw, stated plainly.** The defenders designed randomness as a human responsibility without giving humans a reliable mechanism for producing it. Security procedure added cognitive effort to the operator's real task — getting the message through — and when the secure behaviour was slow, forgettable, or awkward, shortcuts emerged. Blaming the individual is incomplete; the deeper failure was procedural design. The machine behaved correctly. The procedure did not. [VERIFIED — Baskerville article]
- **Decoder-design note (Cillies → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Profile the chooser, not the choice.** One `ASD` is noise; `ASD` every day from the same call sign is a statistical identity. The Gauntlet's first screen on any specimen is a habit profile: log every free choice the specimen makes — seeds, nonces, defaults, first answers — and test the distribution against uniform. A human-shaped distribution is a fingerprint, and a fingerprint is a key. (2) **A predictable choice is a crib for the machine.** Cillies did not replace the Bombe; they fed it menus. The Gauntlet never asks one probe to break the specimen alone — each probe's job is to narrow the next probe's search, the way a cilly narrowed 17,576 settings to a dozen favourites. (3) **The operator is part of the key.** Enigma's keyspace ran to roughly 150 million million settings, and the operational process selected from twelve. Any specimen whose security rests on a human — or a human-shaped default — choosing well under load is already broken at the design level: the Gauntlet grades the procedure, not just the mechanism, and a control that works only when nobody is hurried is filed as a finding, not a pass. Where Banburismus weighed and Herivel watched, the cilly *named the clerk*. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run; CORROBORATED — the ~150 million million keyspace figure, Historic England via the Welchman record]

## Parkerismus — the reused column, or: the key the clerk filed twice

- **The flaw it exploited.** Enigma's daily settings came off a monthly setting sheet: columns of wheel orders, ring settings, and plugboard connections, one row per day. The sheets were drawn up in advance, and whoever drew them up re-used columns — a wheel order, a ring setting, a stecker column that had already appeared in a previous month's sheet. The machine was never touched; the paperwork was. A column re-used from a month Hut 6 had already solved is a column already known, not searched. [VERIFIED — *Cryptanalysis of the Enigma*, read first-party this pass, citing Welchman 1997, pp. 130, 131, 167]
- **What Parkerismus was.** The practice of re-using some of the columns of wheel orders, ring settings, or plugboard connections from previous months — and the analytical short-cut that followed from it. Bletchley Park christened it **Parkerismus** after Reg Parker, who had, through his meticulous record-keeping, spotted the phenomenon. The discovery was not a flash of mathematics; it was bookkeeping done well enough to notice that the enemy's paperwork repeated itself. [VERIFIED — *Cryptanalysis of the Enigma*, read first-party this pass]
- **The man.** Reginald H. Parker — Reg — worked in Hut 6's Intercept Control Room, the post where intercepted traffic arrived and was sorted before cryptanalysis began. The Hut 6 record lists him among the section's notable individuals as the discoverer of Parkerismus. [VERIFIED — *Hut 6* record, read first-party this pass; Welchman 1982, pp. 113, 131, 167, 168]
- **The exploit — a solved month becomes a partial key.** A monthly sheet's columns are not independent guesses. If a wheel-order column in the new month matches a column from a month already solved, that wheel order is known; the same holds for a ring-setting column or a stecker column. The short-cut compounds with the sibling sheet rules recorded in the same passage: no wheel order was repeated on a single monthly setting sheet, so once keys were being found regularly, possible wheel orders could be excluded by elimination; and on some networks no rotor could sit in the same slot as in the immediately preceding configuration, which cut the wheel orders to try. Parkerismus is the fourth member of that family of procedural economies — the sheet was a structured object, and its structure leaked. [VERIFIED — the re-use definition and the sibling rules, *Cryptanalysis of the Enigma*; the worked example of a matched column is this entry's reading of the recorded practice]
- **The quartet, complete.** With Parkerismus filed, the Bletchley "-ismus" set in this catalogue is complete: Banburismus weighed the traffic, Herivelismus watched the operators, Cillies named the clerk's choices, and Parkerismus filed the clerk's paperwork. All four are procedure, not wiring: none of them touches the Enigma's rotors. The difference is the direction of the leak — Banburismus weighed the traffic's statistics, Herivel watched the operator's hands, Cillies read the operator's choices, Parkerismus read the enemy's filing cabinet. Breaking Enigma was not one clever trick; it was an industrial process for collecting small procedural advantages until the remaining search could be mechanised. [VERIFIED — the four entries as filed in this catalogue; the summary judgement is this entry's own reading]
- **Decoder-design note (Parkerismus → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Keep the solved set.** Parker's break existed only because someone kept the solved months and compared them with the new ones. The Gauntlet's first filing rule is the same: every solved specimen, every broken default, every cracked configuration stays in the register, and every new specimen is checked against the register before a single fresh probe is spent. A solved problem that is not filed is a problem that has to be solved twice. (2) **The enemy's paperwork is part of the attack surface.** The monthly sheet was not the cipher, but it decided what the cipher would be. When a specimen's behaviour is configured from tables, templates, or reused defaults, the Gauntlet interrogates the configuration pipeline, not just the live specimen — a reused column is a known setting wearing a new date. (3) **Bookkeeping is a cryptanalytic instrument.** Parkerismus was discovered by meticulous record-keeping, not by a new idea. The Gauntlet's registers — probe logs, first-answer logs, choice distributions — are not administration; they are the instrument that notices the recurrence. Where Banburismus weighed, Herivel watched, and the cilly named the clerk, Parkerismus *filed the paperwork*. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]

## Yoxallismus — the E-rack that read a whole month, or: the letter the clerk could not stop typing

- **The problem it solved.** Offizier traffic — officers' messages — was enciphered on Enigma with a *second* setting for additional security: 26 set-ups, each represented by one letter A–Z and valid for a month. Breaking one Offizier message was never the prize; the prize was the month. The problem, as Hut 8 framed it, was blunt: "Given the wheel order, ring setting and message set-up — i.e. everything except the stecker — can the stecker be worked out without any knowledge of the content of the message?" If the answer was yes, one break opened the whole month's traffic. [CORROBORATED — *Cryptographic History of Work on the German Naval Enigma*, ellsbury.com]
- **The man.** Albert Leslie Yoxall (18 May 1914 – 30 September 2005), Hut 8, Naval Enigma, taken on as a "temporary junior administrative officer". He worked the Offizier problem and devised the method that took his name. In October/November 1942 he moved to Hut 7 to work on a Japanese naval cipher, where he made a significant contribution in identifying how the cipher permutations were constructed. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Leslie Yoxall]
- **The rediscovery.** In the late summer of 1941 Yoxall started work on the Offizier problem and re-discovered the method of the "E rack" — a known technique, but one whose importance in this connection had not been realised. He caused "a considerable sensation" by breaking an "example" set him, on a length of 80 letters — about a day after Turing, recognised by all as the authority on any theoretical matter connected with the machine, had stated his opinion that 200 letters constituted a theoretical minimum. Yoxall "must indeed have been inspired on this occasion as none of us ever succeeded in after days on a length of under 100 letters without some sort of crib." [CORROBORATED — *Cryptographic History of Work on the German Naval Enigma*]
- **The method — Dottery first, then Yoxallismus.** The first step was a Dottery: decode the message at the correct set-up with all letters assumed self-steckered; the result is gibberish, but of the 26 letters so assumed, 6 are in fact self-steckered, and the rows belonging to those 6 show dots distributed in accordance with language distribution, not random distribution — all 6 rows showing the same squares popular and unpopular, the most popular square being the Stecker of E. The second step, "known as a Yoxhallismus after its inventor" (the Hut 8 history spells it with two l's; the modern form is Yoxallismus), assumes *every* letter of the message to be an E — the Stecker of which is now known, so it can be encoded right through the message — and records the Stecker which each assumption implies. As E is very common, the assumption will often be correct, "and hence the squares representing true Stecker will fill up much more rapidly than the others." Part of the Stecker obtained, the message is decoded with partial Stecker; whenever a word can be guessed that is only partially decoded, further Stecker can be added, and the complete Stecker is soon obtained. On a message of more than 200 letters a Dottery was normally completed without much difficulty. [CORROBORATED — *The History of Hut Eight*, ellsbury.com]
- **The payoff.** The June Offizier was read (the June but not July Offizier having been pinched); Noskwith, in charge of Offizier research from the crib-room side, "finally succeeded in producing a right crib — another feat which we had thought might well prove impossible on such non-routine traffic" — and September Offizier was broken. "Once in, Yoxall's method proved itself in practice and the whole month's keys were read." [CORROBORATED — *Cryptographic History of Work on the German Naval Enigma*]
- **The quintet, not a quartet.** Parkerismus, filed this morning, closed the four-entry "-ismus" set as a quartet; Yoxallismus is the fifth member, and the one that worked a layer the other four never touched. Banburismus weighed the traffic, Herivelismus watched the operators, Cillies named the clerk's choices, Parkerismus filed the clerk's paperwork — and Yoxallismus read the officer's second setting, the layer above the daily key. The quartet framing stands as the record of one morning's filing; the set grows, and the growth is itself the lesson: a catalogue that calls itself complete has stopped looking. [VERIFIED — the five entries as filed in this catalogue; the framing is this entry's own reading]
- **Decoder-design note (Yoxallismus → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The commonest symbol is a crib you do not have to guess.** Yoxallismus never guessed a word; it guessed that the commonest letter would be common, and let frequency do the work a crib would have done. The Gauntlet's first probe of any specimen is its frequency profile — what it says most, what it never says — because a specimen that cannot stop saying one thing has already handed over a crib. (2) **One break must open the month.** The method was judged not by whether it read one message but by whether the month followed. A Gauntlet instrument is graded the same way: a probe that breaks one specimen and teaches nothing about the next is a parlour trick; a probe that opens the family is a method. (3) **A break nobody can repeat is a warning, not a triumph.** Yoxall's 80-letter break was never repeated under 100 letters without a crib — not even by Yoxall. A one-off break is filed as an existence proof, never as a procedure, and the Gauntlet's register marks it so: repeatable or it did not happen. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]

## Scritchmus — the chain that named the fast wheel, or: the rod the Banburist read the rotor by

- **The problem it solved.** Banburismus proper ranked the wheels — it said which wheels were probably in the machine, middle and right, and let the bombe do the rest. But ranking is not naming, and a bombe run still had to try every wheel order the ranking left open: 336 possible orders for three wheels chosen from eight, and a bombe that could test the 17,576 ring settings for one wheel order in 15 minutes — 60 runs in 24 hours, nearly five and a half days for all 336. Scritchmus was the part of the Banburismus procedure that could *identify* the right-hand (fast) wheel outright, by reading the distances between the day's indicator letters off the wiring of the wheel itself. [CORROBORATED — Banburismus record; The Turing Guide, Hosgood ch. 37]
- **The evidence — pairs that differ in one letter only.** Take two messages whose indicators differ only in the third letter. Their first two indicator letters were enciphered at the same rotor positions, so the two messages stand in depth up to the third letter — and the Banbury-sheet scoring says how far apart the two third letters stood on the right-hand wheel: bookings like "X = Q−2", "H = X−4", "B = G+3". Each booking is evidence that two key letters stood a given distance apart, though not which letters they were. The Banburist searched the deciban sheets for all distances with odds of better than 1:1 — scores of +34 or more — and kept only those. [CORROBORATED — Wikipedia, Banburismus, Scritchmus section; The Turing Guide]
- **The chain.** Where bookings share a letter they join, and the joined letters lie along a rod in their true order round the right wheel, each at its true distance from the others. From the three bookings above the Banburist could build a chain like `G--B-H---X-Q` — dashes for the unknown letters between, the known letters pinned at their measured gaps. One booking is weak evidence; a chain of them, each constraining the next, is a rod that only fits one rotor. [CORROBORATED — Wikipedia, Banburismus, Scritchmus section; garden.neap.art Banburismus explainer]
- **The test — lay the rod against the rotor.** The chain is compared at progressive offsets with the known letter-sequence of an Enigma rotor, and quite a few possibilities are discounted at once. And every booked pair tells one thing more: between the two messages' starts, the right wheel cannot have passed its notch — the place where it kicks the middle wheel on — because had it, the middle wheel would have moved for one message and not the other, and the two would never have lined up in depth at all. So each pair rules a stretch of the rod out, and what is left is where the wheel turns over. The wheels turned over at different letters, so that narrowed which of them could be on the right. Three of the eight navy wheels — VI, VII and VIII — turned over twice a turn, at Z and at M: with one of those on the right, a pair had half the room to stay in depth, fewer pairs lined up at all, and the rods came harder. [CORROBORATED — Wikipedia, Banburismus, Scritchmus section; garden.neap.art Banburismus explainer]
- **The payoff — 336 orders down to 18.** The Turing Guide's worked example: if Banburismus had precisely identified the middle wheel and established that the right-hand wheel was one of the three special navy wheels, then for each of the three possibilities for the right-hand wheel there were six of the eight wheels remaining for the left-hand wheel — 18 possible combinations, 18 bombe tests instead of the original potential of 336. Scritchmus did not break the day; it made the breaking affordable, the same way Banburismus did — by spending statistics before spending machine time. [CORROBORATED — The Turing Guide, Hosgood ch. 37]
- **The people.** Turing devised Banburismus; Hugh Alexander was regarded as the best of the Banburists; I. J. Good worked the theory alongside Turing; and Joan Clarke — a senior Hut 8 cryptanalyst, one of its longest-serving — became particularly associated with Scritchmus. The method's name, like Banburismus, wears the mock-Latin -ismus; the histories record the name and the method, and no settled etymology for "scritch" is given in the sources consulted this pass — it is filed as recorded, not explained. [CORROBORATED — the Alexander/Good/Clarke associations, Banburismus record as filed in this catalogue's Banburismus entry]
- **The sixth on the shelf.** With Scritchmus filed, the Bletchley shelf in this catalogue is six deep: Banburismus weighed the traffic, Herivelismus watched the operators, Cillies named the clerk's choices, Parkerismus filed the clerk's paperwork, Yoxallismus read the officer's second setting — and Scritchmus read the fast wheel off its own wiring. Five of the six wear the -ismus; Cillies is the one that never took the Latin. [VERIFIED — the six entries as filed in this catalogue; the framing is this entry's own reading]
- **Decoder-design note (Scritchmus → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Relative is enough.** Scritchmus never learned a single absolute letter — only distances between letters — and distances were enough to name the wheel. The Gauntlet's first structural probe asks for relations, not values: how far apart do two outputs stand, in what order, under what step — because a specimen that hides its values usually still leaks their geometry. (2) **A chain beats a point.** One booked distance is weak evidence; a chain of them, each constraining the next, is a rod that only fits one rotor. Probes should be designed to join: each answer should constrain the next question, and the register should keep the chain, not just the verdicts. (3) **The machine's own asymmetry is the tell.** The notch — a security complication the designers added — is what let Bletchley tell the wheels apart, and the double-notched wheels were harder precisely because they had less room to stay in depth. A specimen's hardest feature is usually its most identifying: the Gauntlet probes the asymmetry the designers were proudest of first, because that is where the fingerprint lives. Where Banburismus weighed and Yoxallismus counted the commonest letter, Scritchmus *measured the gaps*. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]

## The Clock Method — Różycki's clock, or: the wheel the indicator betrayed

- **The problem it solved.** Rejewski's grill method could already determine the right-hand rotor, but at a price: trying each possible rotor permutation at each of its 26 starting rotations, with the plugboard settings complicating every test. Jerzy Różycki's clock, devised at the Polish Cipher Bureau during 1933–1935, answered the same question with simple tests that the plugboard could not touch — and for the Poles, learning the rightmost rotor cut the rotor-order search space by a factor of three. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Clock (cryptography)]
- **The flaw it exploited — the doubled key.** The Germans did not send the message key in the clear, but they did something nearly as generous: they enciphered the three-letter message key twice. A key of ABL became ABLABL and was enciphered as a six-letter indicator, say PKPJXI — the doubled key, not the encrypted key sent twice. With about 60 messages on the same daily key, Rejewski's method of characteristics recovered the day's message keys outright (one carrier puts the figure at about 70), and weak clerk-chosen keys (CCC, WER) made the recovery easier still. The clock method started where that recovery ended: it knew the message keys and the ciphertext, and almost nothing else — not the plugboard, not the ring settings, not the rotor order, not the starting position. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Clock (cryptography); CORROBORATED — the ~70-message figure and the weak-key detail, Alchetron mirror of the same article]
- **The method — pairs that start the same.** In a day's traffic there might be about a dozen message pairs whose message keys start with the same two letters. Take such a pair and try both alignments of their ciphertexts: one alignment will use an identical polyalphabetic substitution, and from that alignment the cryptanalyst can read off a window of letters inside which the right-hand rotor's turnover must have fallen. A single pair bounds the turnover to a range; it does not name the rotor. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Clock (cryptography)]
- **The clock — turnovers as a dial.** The rotors turned over at different letters: rotor I at R, rotor II at F, rotor III at W, rotor IV at K, and every later rotor at A — the British mnemonic was "Royal Flags Wave Kings Above". Each pair's window admits only the rotors whose turnover letter falls inside it, and the windows intersect. One pair might say the turnover fell between B and U, leaving rotors I (R), II (F) and IV (K) viable; a second pair might say between M and C, leaving I (R), III (W) and V-onwards (A). Only rotor I satisfies both — so rotor I is the right-hand rotor. With a little luck, and a dozen pairs a day, the clock named the fast wheel without ever touching the plugboard. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Clock (cryptography), including the worked example]
- **The calendar that made it matter.** In the early 1930s the clock's answer was worth little, because the Germans used the same rotor order for three months at a time — determine it once, use it for a quarter. On 1 February 1936 the order began changing monthly; on 1 November 1936 it began changing daily. Each quickening raised the price of the grill method's brute trying, and raised the value of a test that named the fast wheel cheaply. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Clock (cryptography)]
- **The death — 15 September 1938.** The clock lived on the doubled indicator, and the doubled indicator died on a single day: 15 September 1938, when the Germans switched to per-message keys. The same change killed the cyclometer overnight — this catalogue's Rejewski entry records it. The clock did not fail; its food was withdrawn. No doubled key, no recovered message keys, no pairs that start the same — and the method that had named the fast wheel since the mid-1930s had nothing left to read. [CORROBORATED — the 15 September 1938 procedure change as filed in this catalogue's Rejewski entry; the clock's dependence on the doubled indicator per the Wikipedia method description]
- **The afterlife — Banburismus.** Różycki's clock was later elaborated by Alan Turing at Bletchley Park into Banburismus, the statistical weighing machine this catalogue filed earlier today; the British improved the method further, and it let them use their limited number of bombes more effectively against five to eight rotors. The clock is the root of the Bletchley shelf: the Polish test that read a wheel off its turnover, grown by Turing into a machine that read the whole day off its statistics. With it filed, the shelf is seven deep — one Polish root, six Bletchley branches. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Clock (cryptography); VERIFIED — the seven-entry shelf as filed in this catalogue]
- **Decoder-design note (Clock Method → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Read what the settings cannot hide.** The grill method fought the plugboard; the clock walked around it, testing only what the plugboard could not change. A Gauntlet probe should aim at the same class of fact: the property of the specimen that survives every configuration the specimen can choose — its turnover letter, not its plugboard. (2) **The intersection is the answer.** One window left three rotors; two windows left one. Probes should be designed to intersect, not merely to accumulate: each answer should cut the candidate set, and the register should record the cut, not just the observation. (3) **Record what a method eats.** The clock did not fail in 1938 — its input was withdrawn, and the method starved the same day. Every Gauntlet instrument is filed with its input dependency named, so that when a probe goes silent the register can say whether the specimen changed or the food ran out. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]

## Zygalski Sheets — the perforated net, or: the holes that only lined up once

- **The problem it solved.** On 15 September 1938 the Germans switched to per-message keys, and the cyclometer and the clock method died the same day — both had fed on the fixed daily ground setting, and the ground setting was now chosen fresh for every message. The doubled message key still went out over the air: six letters, the second three a repeat encipherment of the first three — and Henryk Zygalski, about October 1938, built a machine out of paper that could still read it. Where Rejewski's characteristics had needed sixty messages on one setting, Zygalski's sheets needed only a handful of messages that carried a particular accident. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Zygalski sheets; the 15 September 1938 change as filed in this catalogue's Rejewski entry]
- **The flaw it exploited — the female.** Take the six-letter indicator. If its first and fourth letters are the same, the product permutation AD has a fixed point — a 1-cycle — at the place where the message key's first letter was enciphered twice, three rotor steps apart. The same holds for the second and fifth letters (permutation BE) and the third and sixth (CF). The Poles called such a coincidence a "female": a rare, visible accident that only certain rotor positions can produce. A female does not name the setting — it vetoes most of them. [CORROBORATED — the female as a 1-cycle in AD/BE/CF, Borowska et al., "The Cryptanalysis of the Enigma Cipher," Advances in Computer Science Research vol. 10 (2013)]
- **The method — superposition.** For each of the six possible rotor orders, Zygalski made 26 perforated sheets, one for each starting position of the left (slowest) rotor. Each sheet carried a 26 × 26 matrix — the 676 possible starting positions of the middle and right rotors, duplicated horizontally and vertically (a–z, a–y) — with holes punched wherever a female could occur. The cryptanalyst took the sheets for the day's females, superposed them, and slid them against each other in a strictly defined program, each shift set by the intercepted messages' ground settings. With each added sheet the visible apertures thinned; with enough data a single aperture remained. Rejewski, who operated the device: "When the sheets were superposed and moved in the proper sequence and the proper manner with respect to each other, in accordance with a strictly defined program, the number of visible apertures gradually decreased. And, if a sufficient quantity of data was available, there finally remained a single aperture, probably corresponding to the right case, that is, to the solution. From the position of the aperture one could calculate the order of the rotors, the setting of their rings, and, by comparing the letters of the cipher keys with the letters in the machine, likewise permutation S; in other words, the entire cipher key." Like the cyclometer's card catalog, the whole procedure was independent of the number of plugboard connections — the plugboard could not touch it. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Zygalski sheets, including the Rejewski quotation; CORROBORATED — the working sets were made in triplicate, 3 × 26 sheets per rotor order, one set for each product AD, BE, CF, each sheet a 51 × 51 field square, Borowska et al.]
- **The manufacture — razor blades and a tenfold bill.** For security the sheets were made by hand, by the mathematician-cryptologists themselves, cutting the holes with razor blades. By 15 December 1938 only a third of the job was finished — and on that day the Germans introduced rotors IV and V. Six rotor orders became sixty, and the labor of making the sheets grew tenfold overnight. Poland could not out-build the re-arm race: the sheets were priced beyond the Bureau's budget, and the same arithmetic priced out the bombas. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Zygalski sheets]
- **The afterlife — Netz at Bletchley.** The sheets were part of what Poland handed over at Pyry on 25 July 1939, five weeks before the invasion. The British, at Bletchley Park, undertook two complete sets, made with perforators by a section headed by John R. F. Jeffreys. At Bletchley the sheets were known as Netz, from Netzverfahren, the "net method" — Welchman later remembered them as "Jeffreys sheets," though that name properly belonged to another catalog Jeffreys' section produced. The first set was finished in late December 1939; part of the second set reached the Polish cryptologists at PC Bruno outside Paris on 28 December; the rest was completed on 7 January 1940 and couriered to France by Alan Turing shortly after. "With their help," Rejewski wrote, "we continued solving Enigma daily keys" — and the sheets served the first wartime decryption of an Enigma message, on 17 January 1940. With the sheets filed, the Enigma-methods shelf in this catalogue stands eight deep — two Polish roots, six Bletchley branches. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Zygalski sheets]
- **The death — May 1940.** In May 1940 the Germans changed the message-key enciphering procedure completely (one Norwegian network excepted) and stopped the double encipherment. The sheets went dead overnight — the same death the clock method had died in 1938, and the same lesson: the method was never beaten, its food was withdrawn. The Herivel tip, filed earlier in this catalogue, could still be used, and carried Hut 6 until the bombes arrived. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Zygalski sheets; the 1 May 1940 change as filed in this catalogue's Herivelismus entry]
- **Decoder-design note (Zygalski → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **A hole is a veto, not a vote.** No single sheet names the answer; each sheet says where the answer is not, and the finding is the aperture that survives every veto. Design Gauntlet probes the same way: outputs that rule out are sturdier than outputs that claim — let the surviving aperture be the finding, and let positive claims come from a different instrument. (2) **Precompute the catalogue; spend the day on the stack.** The sheets cost months of razor-blade labor; using them cost minutes of sliding paper. The costly work is building the probe library and the twin baselines once; a sitting should be cheap — slide the sheets, count the apertures. (3) **A method dies when its food changes, not when it is beaten.** The sheets were never outsmarted; the doubled key was withdrawn and they starved the same day. Every instrument names its input dependency, so that when a probe goes silent the register can say whether the specimen changed or the food ran out. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]

## The Cyclometer — Rejewski's card catalog, or: the fingerprint that survived the plugboard

- **The problem it solved.** Rejewski's grill method could already recover the day's characteristic from the doubled key, but at a price: the grill was tedious, it leaned on sloppy clerk habits, and after it the Poles still faced a laborious search — a *Q*-catalog of 4,056 entries (26 × 26 × 6) eased part of it, but finding the ring settings could still require trying 17,576 possibilities. The grill worked well until 1 October 1936, the day the Germans stopped using six plugboard connections (*steckers*) and started using five to eight — more steckers could frustrate the grill outright. Marian Rejewski, "probably in 1934 or 1935," built a machine to replace the grill's toil with a lookup: the cyclometer, which catalogued the cycle structure of Enigma permutations. Two rotor banks at the top (one with its lid open), a rheostat at the left below, and an array of lamps and switches labelled with the letters at the right. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Cyclometer]
- **The flaw it exploited — the doubled key.** The Germans doubled the message key instead of sending the encrypted key twice: ABL became ABLABL and was enciphered as the six-letter indicator PKPJXI. Rejewski read the machine as six sequential permutations, A B C D E F, one per letter position — and because the first and fourth letters were the same plaintext letter, the second and fifth the same, the third and sixth the same, the composed permutations AD, BE and CF could be pieced together from the day's traffic. With enough messages — about sixty on the same daily key — the whole characteristic fell out in Cauchy cycle notation, for example AD = (pjxroquctwzsy)(kvgledmanhfib), BE = (kxtcoigweh)(zvfbsylrnp)(ujd)(mqa), CF = (yvxqtdhpim)(skgrjbcolw)(un)(fa)(e)(z). [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Cyclometer, including the worked 1930-manual example: wheel order II, I, III; ringstellung 24, 18, 22 (XMV); reflector A; plugboard A-M, F-I, N-V, P-S, T-U, W-Z; ground setting FOL; message key ABL → PKPJXI]
- **The insight — cycle lengths survive the plugboard.** Instead of indexing the catalog by the actual cycles, the Poles hit upon indexing it by the *length* of the cycles. The plugboard changed the identity of the letters in a permutation, but it did not change the lengths of the cycles — a stecker swaps two letters, and a swap conjugates the permutation, which preserves cycle structure. There are 101 possible patterns for the cycle lengths of one indicator permutation, and with three permutations in the characteristic about a million possible combinations (101³ = 1,030,301) — so the cycle lengths could serve as a hash into a table of the 105,456 possible settings. The odds were good that only one card — or a few — carried a given fingerprint. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Cyclometer]
- **The method — a fingerprint lookup.** From the day's traffic the cryptanalyst recovered the characteristic, calculated its cycle lengths — in the worked example, AD: 13; BE: 10 3; CF: 10 2 1 — and looked them up in the card catalog. The card named the wheel order (II, I, III) and the initial position of each wheel, without much work, and the method worked however many steckers the Germans were using. The catalog did not include the actual characteristic: the cyclometer indicated only membership in a cycle, not the order of letters within it — the fingerprint, never the face. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Cyclometer]
- **The recovery — the plugboard from the comparison.** The catalog did not disclose the plugboard settings, and for six plugs there are about 100 billion possible arrangements — trying them all was infeasible. Instead the cryptanalyst set an Enigma to the catalog's wheel order and positions, mapped out the unsteckered permutations A\* B\* C\* D\* E\* F\* by pressing each key and holding it while reading the lamp (holding the first key down keeps the machine from advancing the rotors), and compared the unsteckered characteristic against the day's real one. The differences read off the steckers directly: in the worked example, the plugboard cycles (un)(fa) of CF had to transpose with the unsteckered (vt)(mi); the singleton cycles showed "e" unsteckered while "w" and "z" were steckered together — and the comparison resolved to P-S, T-U, W-Z, N-V, A-M, F-I, exactly the day's plugboard. The only remaining secret was the ring positions (*Ringstellung*). [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Cyclometer, including the key-hold mapping procedure and the recovered stecker list]
- **The build — a year of labor, fifteen minutes a day.** The cyclometer prepared a catalog of the cycle lengths and numbers for all 17,576 rotor positions for a given rotor sequence, and with six possible sequences the card catalog comprised 6 × 17,576 = 105,456 entries. Preparation of the catalog, writes Rejewski, "was laborious and took over a year, but when it was ready... daily keys [could be obtained] within about fifteen minutes." The utility of the catalog was independent of the number of plug connections the Germans used — and of the reconstruction of message keys. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Cyclometer, including the Rejewski quotation]
- **The death — 15 September 1938, and the rebuild it survived once.** On 1 November 1937 the Germans changed the reversing drum, the reflector — and the Cipher Bureau had to start anew with a fresh card catalog, "a task," writes Rejewski, "which consumed, on account of our greater experience, probably somewhat less than a year's time." The cyclometer survived that death once. It did not survive the second: on 15 September 1938 the Germans changed entirely the procedure for enciphering message keys, and the card-catalog method became completely useless. The same change killed the clock method the same day — this catalogue's Clock Method entry records it — and it spurred the invention of Rejewski's cryptologic bomb and Zygalski's perforated sheets. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Cyclometer]
- **The afterlife — a working machine, rebuilt in 2019.** Using drawings made by Rejewski, Hal Evans and Tim Flack at the Department of Engineering, University of Cambridge, constructed a working version of the cyclometer in 2019. And with Rejewski's later cryptologic bomb, the cyclometer can be viewed as a predecessor to the Bombe that helped break Enigma later in the war at Bletchley Park. With it filed, the Enigma-methods shelf in this catalogue stands nine deep — three Polish roots, six Bletchley branches. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Cyclometer]
- **Decoder-design note (Cyclometer → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Index by the invariant, not the identity.** The plugboard could rename every letter in the characteristic, and the cyclometer never fought it — it indexed by cycle lengths, the one thing the adversary's renaming could not change. A Gauntlet probe should hunt the same class of property: the invariant of the specimen that survives every relabelling the specimen can perform — its cycle-length fingerprint, not its letter names. (2) **Precompute once; spend minutes per sitting.** The catalog cost over a year of labor and paid it back at fifteen minutes a day. The costly work is building the probe library and the twin baselines once; a sitting should be cheap — look up the fingerprint, read the card. (3) **A fingerprint is not a face.** The catalog named the wheel order and positions but never the characteristic itself, and never the plugboard — those still had to be recovered by comparison. A probe that returns a fingerprint has not returned the specimen: the register records what the instrument actually names, and the comparison step that turns the fingerprint into a reading is a separate instrument, filed separately. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]

## The Bomba Kryptologiczna — Rejewski's cryptologic bomb, or: the machine that ran all 17,576 settings at once

- **The problem it solved.** On 15 September 1938 the Germans changed entirely the procedure for enciphering message keys, and the cyclometer's card catalog became completely useless overnight — the same change killed the clock method the same day. The new procedure let each operator choose his own ground setting (*Grundstellung*) for every message and send it in the clear, then encipher the doubled message key from that setting. A catalog built for one daily ground setting had nothing to index on anymore. The Poles answered with two instruments at once: Zygalski's perforated sheets, filed in this catalogue, and Rejewski's cryptologic bomb — the *bomba kryptologiczna* — which stopped precomputing the search and mechanized it instead. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Cyclometer (the 15 September 1938 procedure change killing the card-catalog method and spurring the bomb and the sheets); Wikipedia, Cryptanalysis of the Enigma (the bomb method, invented in the autumn of 1938); quadibloc (ground settings chosen at random by the operator, and sent in the clear with each message)]
- **The flaw it exploited — the females.** The doubled key survived the procedure change, and with it the coincidence it made possible: one letter of the message key, doubled to protect it against transmission errors, could be enciphered to the same character at the first and fourth positions, the second and fifth, or the third and sixth — groups like WAVWHA, where the first symbol came out as W on the first and the fourth position. The Poles called these doublings "females" — Rejewski wrote they had designated them thus "for lack of a better idea" — and the modern term is "fixpoint." A female means the same plaintext letter was enciphered twice under rotor states three key-presses apart, and three females at the three spacings are enough to pin the day's setting. [VERIFIED — Link 2009, Cryptologia (the WAVWHA example, the 1–4 / 2–5 / 3–6 positions); CORROBORATED — the "for lack of a better idea" attribution, via Link's reading of Rejewski]
- **The insight — run the machine instead of reading the table.** The cyclometer had spent over a year of labor to answer in fifteen minutes; the bomba spent electricity to answer in about two hours. It consisted of three pairs of Enigma rotor sets driven by an electric motor via a planetary gear — six rotor sets in all, an electrically powered aggregate of six Enigmas — and instead of looking the day's setting up in a table, it turned all 17,576 possible rotor positions past the coincidence test and stopped when the test fired. The sheets needed about ten females to work; the bomba needed only three. [VERIFIED — Link 2009 (three pairs of Enigma rotor sets, electric motor, planetary gear); Wikipedia, Cryptanalysis of the Enigma (six Enigmas aggregate; exhaustive analysis of the 17,576 possible message keys; three females instead of about ten for the sheet method)]
- **The method — a stop on coincidence.** The operator "programmed" the bomba with three messages whose indicators carried females at 1–4, 2–5 and 3–6 respectively — in Link's reconstruction, GKD WAVWHA, JOT IWABWN and MDO OTWYZW, the first three letters of each being the *Grundstellung* in clear and the last six the encrypted doubled message key. The first pair of Enigmas was set to the indicators that had produced the coincidence at the first and fourth position, GKD and GKD+3 = GKG — the offset of three reflecting that in a female the same letter recurs three key-presses later — and the machine ran. When all three pairs simultaneously produced the same output letter, the bomba stopped: that rotor position was the day's setting. The cipher message transmitted the *Grundstellung* in the clear, so a match revealed the rotor order, the rotor positions, and the ring settings. [VERIFIED — Link 2009 (Figure 2 setup, GKD/GKG offset of three); Wikipedia, Cryptanalysis of the Enigma (the match revealing rotor order, positions and ring settings)]
- **The recovery — everything but the plugboard.** The match left exactly one secret standing: the plugboard permutation. Like the cyclometer before it, the bomba never named the steckers — they were recovered by comparison afterwards, setting an Enigma to the bomba's wheel order and positions and reading the plugboard off the differences between the unsteckered and the real characteristic, the procedure this catalogue's Cyclometer entry records in full. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Cryptanalysis of the Enigma (the only remaining secret was the plugboard permutation); the comparison procedure as filed in this catalogue's Cyclometer entry]
- **The build — six machines, one per wheel order.** Six *bomby* were quickly built by the AVA Radio Manufacturing Company (*Wytwornia Radiotechniczna AVA*) in Warsaw in November 1938, one for each of the then-possible wheel orders. A run took around two hours to determine the positions of the rotors. [VERIFIED — Link 2009 (six bomby, AVA, November 1938, one per wheel order); BCS / McCarthy (around two hours per run)]
- **The death — priced out in a month.** The bomba was useful only as long as three conditions were met: the indicator had to include the repetition of the message key; the number of rotors available had to be limited to three, giving six different wheel orders; and the number of plugboard leads had to remain relatively small, so that the majority of letters were unsteckered. Barely a month after delivery the Germans introduced two additional rotors for loading into the Enigma scrambler, increasing the number of wheel orders by a factor of ten — six became sixty, and building another 54 *bomby* was beyond the Poles' resources. On 1 January 1939 the number of plugboard leads was increased to ten. The Poles therefore had to return to manual methods, the Zygalski sheets. The bomba's working life was barely a month. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Bombe (the three conditions, the November 1938 delivery, the December rotor increase, the 54-machine price, the 1 January 1939 plugboard increase, the return to the sheets)]
- **The afterlife — the British Bombe, and a 2019 rebuild.** Alan Turing designed the British bombe on a more general principle — the crib, a stretch of predictable plaintext — and Gordon Welchman's diagonal board made it practical; the first, *Victory*, was installed at Bletchley Park on 18 March 1940, and a run through all 17,576 positions for one rotor order took about twenty minutes. The British machine was developed from the Polish bomba, and the lineage is the point: the bomba proved that six Enigmas wired together and spun through every position could find a day's key, and Turing's machine generalized the coincidence it hunted. No original *bomby* survive; Rejewski's papers of 1967 and 1979 carry the sketch and the description of how the machine worked, and in 2019 Jeremy McCarthy, a volunteer at the National Museum of Computing, recreated a working bomba in a mixture of hardware and software. With it filed, the Enigma-methods shelf in this catalogue stands ten deep — four Polish roots, six Bletchley branches. [VERIFIED — Wikipedia, Bombe (Turing 1939 design from the Polish bomba; Victory, 18 March 1940; ~20 minutes per rotor order); BCS (no originals survive; Rejewski's 1967/1979 papers; McCarthy's 2019 reconstruction)]
- **Decoder-design note (Bomba → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Brute force is a design, not a defeat.** When the table died, the Poles did not build a better table — they built a machine that re-ran the search live, at two hours a sitting. A Gauntlet probe that exhausts all 17,576 positions is a probe, not a failure of imagination: the register records the cost, and the cost is part of the finding. (2) **Three coincidences beat ten.** The bomba needed only three females where the sheets needed about ten — a sharper instrument needs less luck. Probe design should count the coincidences it needs: fewer, sharper, cheaper is a design goal, not a boast. (3) **A machine's life is its conditions.** The bomba lived exactly as long as its three conditions held and died the month the fourth and fifth rotors arrived. Every instrument carries its conditions on its face, and a reading from an instrument whose conditions have expired is a dead reading — version the instrument with the procedure it attacks, and retire it the day the procedure changes. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]
