## HPKE — Hybrid Public Key Encryption (RFC 9180), or: the one hybrid that replaced a zoo of them

- **The problem it solved.** Before HPKE there was no single interoperable hybrid: a zoo of non-interoperable ECIES variants — ANSI X9.63, IEEE 1363a, ISO/IEC 18033-2, SEC 1 — each with its own problems, relying on outdated primitives, lacking proofs of IND-CCA2 security, or failing to provide test vectors. HPKE, published February 2022 as an IRTF informational RFC from the Crypto Forum Research Group after twelve drafts, defines one construction with sufficient clarity to be interoperably implemented, and proves it IND-CCA2-secure under classical assumptions about the underlying primitives. [VERIFIED — RFC 9180 §1 (the ECIES zoo, the missing proofs and test vectors, the IND-CCA2 claim, the CFRG provenance); the twelve-draft count via Lipp]
- **The shape — three parts, one tuple.** A ciphersuite is a triple (KEM, KDF, AEAD), each chosen by a two-byte identifier from an IANA registry. The KEMs are all Diffie-Hellman: DHKEM(P-256, HKDF-SHA256) 0x0010, DHKEM(P-384, HKDF-SHA384) 0x0011, DHKEM(P-521, HKDF-SHA512) 0x0012, DHKEM(X25519, HKDF-SHA256) 0x0020, DHKEM(X448, HKDF-SHA512) 0x0021. The KDFs are HKDF-SHA256 0x0001, HKDF-SHA384 0x0002, HKDF-SHA512 0x0003. The AEADs are AES-128-GCM 0x0001, AES-256-GCM 0x0002, ChaCha20Poly1305 0x0003 — plus 0xFFFF, Export-only, reserved for applications that use only the Export interface and never encrypt. [VERIFIED — RFC 9180 §7, Tables 2–5]
- **The move — encapsulate, don't encrypt the key.** The traditional hybrid encrypts the symmetric key with the public key. HPKE inverts the phrasing: generate the symmetric key and its encapsulation with the public key. `Encap(pkR)` returns a fixed-length KEM shared secret and a fixed-length encapsulation of it; for DHKEM the encapsulation *is* the sender's ephemeral public key, so Npk equals Nenc — 32 bytes for X25519, 65 for P-256. The wire carries a public value, never the key itself. [VERIFIED — RFC 9180 §1 (the generate-and-encapsulate phrasing), §4 (Encap/Decap, Npk = Nenc for DHKEM)]
- **The four modes — one receiver key, three optional authentications.** Base (mode 0) encrypts to the holder of the recipient key and nothing more — anonymous sender, the usual hybrid. PSK (mode 1) mixes in a pre-shared key and its identifier, so the recipient learns the sender belonged to the PSK group. Auth (mode 2) adds the sender's static key pair through `AuthEncap`/`AuthDecap`, so the recipient is assured the secret came from the holder of that key. AuthPSK (mode 3) layers both. Every mode still takes the same `info` parameter — folded into key generation, e.g. identity information — and per-message `aad`. [VERIFIED — RFC 9180 §5.1, Table 1 (the four modes); the mode table via Lipp]
- **The context — one setup, many messages, and a second door.** Setup builds an encryption context holding a key, a base nonce, and an exporter secret; `Seal`/`Open` carry a sequence number, so nonces are derived per message and the context can encrypt a sequence. Single-shot `Seal`/`Open` cover one message. And `Export` derives almost-arbitrarily-long shared secrets from the exporter secret under an `exporter_context` — the second door, for when a fixed-size KEM secret is not enough: HPKE as a key-agreement machine, not just an encryption machine. [VERIFIED — RFC 9180 §5, §5.3, §6 (context, sequence numbers, Export); Lipp on Export]
- **The labels — domain separation is the design.** Every KDF call goes through `LabeledExtract`/`LabeledExpand`, which prefix the inputs with the version label "HPKE-v1" and a `suite_id` naming the ciphersuite ("HPKE" + the whole triple inside HPKE, "KEM" + the KEM inside DHKEM). The version is stamped into every derived key, so a future HPKE-v2 cannot cross-talk with v1 outputs — the labels are the boundary between versions, suites, and applications. [VERIFIED — RFC 9180 §4, §5.1 (LabeledExtract/LabeledExpand, suite_id, "HPKE-v1")]
- **The honest weakness — KCI in the auth modes, and the validation the RFC insists on.** The DHKEM `AuthEncap`/`AuthDecap` assurance is vulnerable to key-compromise impersonation: if the recipient private key `skR` is compromised, the assurance that the secret was generated by the holder of the sender key `skS` does not hold. Separately, senders and recipients MUST validate KEM inputs and outputs — P-256/384/521 points checked on-curve and not at infinity, X25519/X448 Diffie-Hellman outputs checked against the all-zero value, with failure aborting the operation. The authentication in Auth mode is real, but conditional on the recipient key staying secret. [VERIFIED — RFC 9180 §4.1 (the KCI caveat), §7.1.4 (validation requirements)]
- **Where it lives.** MLS (RFC 9420) — this catalogue's own MLS entry runs on HPKE throughout, and HPKE was named in the RFC's own introduction as built for MLS and TLS Encrypted ClientHello. Oblivious HTTP (RFC 9458) encrypts its requests with HPKE. COSE-HPKE (draft-ietf-cose-hpke-17, October 2025) carries it into the CBOR world this catalogue's COSE entry covers, supporting Base and PSK modes. The authors are Richard L. Barnes (Cisco), Karthik Bhargavan (Inria), Benjamin Lipp (Inria), and Christopher A. Wood (Cloudflare). [VERIFIED — RFC 9180 §1 (MLS and ECH as the named applications), authorship; CORROBORATED — OHTTP (RFC 9458) and the October 2025 COSE-HPKE draft status]
- **The post-quantum note.** Every KEM in RFC 9180 is classical Diffie-Hellman; the framework is deliberately KEM-agnostic, and §7.1.5 reserves the "Future KEMs" slot with security requirements for anything new. Post-quantum hybrids — ML-KEM layered into HPKE — are in draft work, not in the RFC. Until a PQ KEM is registered, HPKE is IND-CCA2 under classical assumptions only, and the catalogue's ML-KEM entry is the one that names the quantum horizon. [VERIFIED — RFC 9180 §7.1.5 (Future KEMs, security requirements); CORROBORATED — PQ hybrids in progress, not yet standardized]
- **Decoder-design note (HPKE → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Name the triple, not the product.** A ciphersuite is three independent choices — KEM, KDF, AEAD — and the Gauntlet's intake should record the same decomposition for any specimen, because a break in one primitive is not a break in the whole; a specimen graded as one blob hides which leg failed. (2) **Encapsulate, don't transport.** The wire carries an encapsulation — a public value — and never the key itself; a specimen whose wire carries its own key material has already confessed, whatever its cipher claims. (3) **Labels are the boundary.** "HPKE-v1" inside every KDF call is the version stamped into the key schedule; a specimen with no domain separation lets one context's keys bleed into another's. Test the boundary: replay one context's output into another's and watch whether the specimen notices. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the pre-HPKE ECIES zoo (ANSI X9.63, IEEE 1363a, ISO/IEC 18033-2, SEC 1) and its missing IND-CCA2 proofs and test vectors, the February 2022 CFRG publication and IND-CCA2 claim, the ciphersuite triple and every identifier in Tables 2–5 (DHKEM 0x0010–0x0012, 0x0020–0x0021; HKDF 0x0001–0x0003; AEAD 0x0001–0x0003, Export-only 0xFFFF), the generate-and-encapsulate move and Npk = Nenc for DHKEM, the four modes (base, PSK, auth, authPSK) and their authentication guarantees, the context with sequence numbers and the Export interface, the "HPKE-v1" labels and suite_id domain separation, the KCI caveat on DHKEM AuthEncap/AuthDecap and the §7.1.4 validation requirements, MLS and ECH as the RFC's named applications, the §7.1.5 Future KEMs slot, and the four authors and their affiliations; CORROBORATED — the twelve-draft count to publication, Oblivious HTTP's HPKE use, the October 2025 COSE-HPKE draft and its Base/PSK-only support, and post-quantum HPKE hybrids as in-progress draft work; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this entry's own doctrine, never run.]*

## age — the file encryption format with one cipher and no config options, or: the envelope that wraps its own key

- **The problem it solved.** GPG is a key-management system with an encryption tool attached: keyservers, trust models, algorithm menus, decades of options. age — designed by Filippo Valsorda and Ben Cartwright-Cox, specified at age-encryption.org/v1 under the C2SP umbrella — is the opposite bet: one AEAD (ChaCha20-Poly1305), one native public-key algorithm (X25519), one native password algorithm (scrypt), no config options, small explicit keys, UNIX-style composability. The reference implementation is Go (FiloSottile/age, BSD-3-Clause, repository opened May 2019); interoperable implementations exist in Rust (rage) and TypeScript (Typage). [VERIFIED — the age README (designers, spec link, "no config options", implementations); the C2SP age specification (the v1 format); the repository creation date]
- **The shape — two parts, one fresh key.** An age file is a textual header that carries the file key, plus a binary payload encrypted with it. Each file gets a fresh 128-bit file key — 16 bytes of CSPRNG output, never reused across files — and the whole file must be treated as binary and is not malleable without knowledge of the file key. The header is human-readable by design: a version line, one or more recipient stanzas, and a MAC. [VERIFIED — C2SP age specification, "Encrypted file format" and "File key"]
- **The header — every recipient gets its own wrapping.** The version line reads `age-encryption.org/v1`. Each recipient stanza starts with `->`, names its type and arguments, and carries a base64 body wrapped at 64 columns; every stanza wraps the same file key independently, so a file encrypted to ten recipients carries ten independent wrappings and any one identity unwraps it. The header ends with a `---` line carrying a base64 HMAC-SHA-256 over the whole header up to and including the `---` mark, keyed by HKDF-SHA-256(ikm = file key, salt = empty, info = "header") — so a tampered header is caught before any payload byte is read. Unknown stanza types MUST be ignored (grease tolerance), and non-native recipient types SHOULD use fully-qualified names such as `example.com/enigma`. [VERIFIED — C2SP age specification, "Header", "Recipient stanza", "Header MAC"]
- **The X25519 recipient — an ephemeral share per stanza.** An identity is 32 bytes of CSPRNG output, encoded as Bech32 with the human-readable part `AGE-SECRET-KEY-`; the recipient is X25519(identity, basepoint), encoded as Bech32 with HRP `age` (the familiar `age1...` string). Each stanza carries a fresh ephemeral share; the wrap key is HKDF-SHA-256(ikm = X25519(ephemeral secret, recipient), salt = ephemeral share || recipient, info = "age-encryption.org/v1/X25519"), and the stanza body is the file key sealed with ChaCha20-Poly1305 under an all-zero nonce. An all-zero shared secret aborts the unwrap. [VERIFIED — C2SP age specification, "The X25519 recipient type"]
- **The scrypt recipient — the passphrase door, and it stands alone.** A passphrase stanza carries a 16-byte salt and a decimal logN: the wrap key is scrypt(N = 2^logN, r = 8, p = 1, dkLen = 32, salt = "age-encryption.org/v1/scrypt" || salt, passphrase), and the body is the file key sealed the same way. The spec's worked stanza uses logN 18. The hard rule: an scrypt stanza, if present, MUST be the only stanza in the header — no mixing with other scrypt stanzas or any other type, because password-based encryption carries an implicit expectation of authentication that mixing would break, and implementations MUST reject mixed headers. [VERIFIED — C2SP age specification, "The scrypt recipient type"]
- **The payload — a STREAM you can seek.** The payload opens with a fresh 16-byte nonce; the payload key is HKDF-SHA-256(ikm = file key, salt = nonce, info = "payload"). The body is split into 64 KiB chunks, each encrypted with ChaCha20-Poly1305 under a 12-byte nonce built from an 11-byte big-endian chunk counter and a final-chunk flag byte (0x01 for the last chunk, 0x00 before it). This is the STREAM construction (ePrint 2015/189): streaming decryption must signal an error if the end of file arrives without a valid final chunk, the payload can be seeked by jumping in chunk increments, and the payload must never be modified without re-encrypting as a new file with a fresh nonce. [VERIFIED — C2SP age specification, "Payload"]
- **The plugin door — SSH keys, hardware tokens, post-quantum.** The two native types are the whole core spec; everything else is a plugin or an extension. The reference tool also encrypts to `ssh-rsa` and `ssh-ed25519` SSH public keys (decrypting with the private key file; ssh-agent not supported), and to GitHub users' listed SSH keys via `-R`. Hardware PIV tokens such as YubiKeys work through the age-plugin-yubikey plugin. Post-quantum hybrid keys (ML-KEM-768 × X25519) are built into age v1.3.0 and later: generate with `age-keygen -pq`, identities start `AGE-SECRET-KEY-PQ-1...`, recipients `age1pq1...` and run to roughly 2,000 characters. `age-inspect` reads a file's metadata — recipient types, post-quantum use, payload size — without decrypting it. [VERIFIED — the age README (SSH keys, plugins, post-quantum keys, age-inspect); CORROBORATED — the ML-KEM-768 × X25519 hybrid naming via the age-inspect example and independent implementation docs]
- **The honest weakness — encryption is not authentication of the sender.** age encrypts to a recipient; anyone holding the recipient's public key can produce a file that decrypts cleanly, so a decrypted file proves nothing about who wrote it — there is no sender signature in the format, and a recipient who needs provenance must add it outside age. Two more honest edges: the header is not encrypted, so the stanza types (and, for SSH recipients, an embedded public-key tag) are visible to anyone holding the file — the README warns SSH support makes it possible to track files encrypted to a specific public key — and ASCII armor is malleable unless the reader uses a strict PEM parser and enforces canonical base64, which the spec tells implementations to do. [VERIFIED — the C2SP age specification (header plaintext, armor malleability note); the age README (SSH tracking warning); CORROBORATED — the no-sender-authentication reading, standard for public-key file encryption]
- **Decoder-design note (age → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **One algorithm is a fingerprint.** A specimen that offers no algorithm menu — one AEAD, one KEM, one KDF — has removed the downgrade surface by construction; the Gauntlet's intake records the menu size alongside the algorithms, because a specimen with a menu is a specimen with a downgrade attack to test, and a specimen without one is not. (2) **The header is the interrogation surface.** age puts its recipient structure in readable text before a single payload byte: stanza types, counts, and (for SSH) identity tags are all visible without the key. A specimen whose envelope is readable is interrogable before it is decryptable — the Gauntlet reads the envelope first, counts the wrappings, and asks what each wrapping costs before it asks what the payload says. (3) **Grease is a doctrine, not a tolerance.** Unknown stanzas MUST be ignored — the format plans for recipients it has never met. A specimen that chokes on an unknown field has confessed its parser is brittle; the Gauntlet's first probe of any envelope is an unknown field, and the specimen that errors on it is graded on the error. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's own doctrine, never run.]

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the one-cipher/one-KEM/one-password design, the designers, the spec location, the reference and alternate implementations, the file-key rules, the header shape and MAC construction, the X25519 stanza construction and Bech32 encodings, the scrypt stanza construction and its no-mixing rule, the STREAM payload construction and its seek/error rules, the ASCII-armor construction, the SSH and plugin support, the post-quantum hybrid in v1.3.0+ with its key prefixes, and the SSH tracking warning; CORROBORATED — the ML-KEM-768 × X25519 hybrid naming and the no-sender-authentication reading; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's own doctrine, never run.]*

## Morse code (1837–1844) — the code with no secrecy in time, or: the set's named-but-unwritten second member

- **The gap this entry closes.** The Semaphore design note (2026-11-01) lists the catalogue's "no secrecy" control set as four channels — "Braille is touch, Morse is sound-in-time, semaphore is sight-in-space" — and the Chappe note closes the set as its fourth member. Morse, the set's second member, was named in that note and never written: grep-verified this pass, the catalogue carries 11 mentions of "Morse" and no entry — one-word references in the MVUEH, Bankrbot, ADFGVX, and Lorenz entries, a "Morse's wager" aside in the Huffman note, and the Semaphore note's own naming. This entry writes it. [VERIFIED — the Semaphore note's list; the grep]

- **The invention — Morse's numbers, Vail's alphabet.** Samuel F. B. Morse, a portrait painter turned inventor, conceived the electric telegraph in the 1830s on Joseph Henry's electromagnet work; his first code was numbers-only, a codebook of numbered words. Alfred Vail, who joined in 1837 and whose family financed the work, rebuilt it as the dot-and-dash alphabet the world actually used: each letter its own pattern of short and long pulses, the shortest codes given to the most frequent English letters (E a single dot, T a single dash) — frequency analysis baked into the code itself. Morse submitted the patent in 1837 ("The American Recording Electro-Magnetic Telegraph"). [VERIFIED — Library of Congress, Morse Papers; U.S. House history; CORROBORATED — the Vail frequency-weighting attribution, standard histories]

- **The first message — 24 May 1844.** Congress appropriated $30,000 in 1843 for an experimental line; Morse and Vail completed the roughly 38-mile Washington–Baltimore line in May 1844. On 24 May 1844 Morse, seated in the Supreme Court Chamber of the U.S. Capitol, tapped "WHAT HATH GOD WROUGHT" to Vail at the Mount Clare railroad depot in Baltimore — Numbers 23:23, chosen by Annie Ellsworth, daughter of Patent Commissioner Henry Leavitt Ellsworth. The paper tape survives in the Library of Congress. The first official signal had run three weeks earlier, 1 May: the Whig nomination of Henry Clay, sent from Annapolis Junction. [VERIFIED — Library of Congress; U.S. House history]

- **The shape — time is the alphabet.** International Morse (ITU-R M.1677-1) is a timing language, not a mark language: a dit is one unit, a dah three; the gap inside a letter is one unit, between letters three, between words seven. The symbol set is two marks and three silences — the silences carry as much of the message as the marks, and a reader who cannot time cannot read. Gerke's 1848 simplification (one dash length, uniform spacing) displaced American Morse's variable dashes and intra-character gaps; the German-Austrian telegraph network adopted it in 1851 and the Paris conference standardized it internationally in 1865. SOS — three dots, three dashes, three dots — was adopted at Berlin in 1906, in force 1908, and made famous by Titanic in 1912. [VERIFIED — ITU-R M.1677-1 timing; Library of Congress and House history for 1844; CORROBORATED — the Gerke 1848 / 1851 / Paris 1865 sequence, SOS 1906/1908, and Titanic 1912, standard histories]

- **The long afterlife — the code that refused to die.** Commercial maritime Morse ended 1 February 1999, when GMDSS replaced it for distress traffic — 155 years after the first message. It survives where the channel is cheapest: aviation navaids (VOR and NDB stations still broadcast their identifiers in Morse) and amateur radio, where operators still hold conversations in it by ear. A code with no secrecy is still in live service while every secret cipher in this catalogue's first section is a museum piece — because its channel, a beep and a silence, is the cheapest channel ever built. [CORROBORATED — the 1999 GMDSS retirement; the aviation-navaid and amateur-radio afterlife, standard references]

- **Decoder-design note (Morse → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Time is a symbol.** Morse's alphabet is durations and gaps; the marks alone decode nothing. A specimen that speaks in timing — packet gaps, blink rates, retry cadences, beacon intervals — is speaking Morse whether or not it knows the name, and the Gauntlet's first question of any timed channel is "what are the units" before it asks "what are the marks." (2) **The code leaks its own statistics.** Vail weighted code lengths by letter frequency, so the length table IS the frequency profile: the commonest letters are the shortest marks. A specimen whose encoding is visibly optimized for some distribution has confessed the distribution it expects — the interrogator reads the code's own economy as the plaintext's profile, and a specimen whose length table matches no natural distribution is either lying about its traffic or speaking a language the table was not built for. (3) **No secrecy means the attack surface is the channel.** Morse hides nothing, so its failures are all channel failures: a jammed wire, a spoofed sender, a mis-timed gap that turns one letter into two. A specimen whose channel is public must be graded on authentication, never on confidentiality — and the Gauntlet's first probe of any open channel is a forged correction in the channel's own tongue, because the correction signal is the thing to forge. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's own doctrine, never run.]

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the Morse/Vail/Henry roles, the numbers-only first code, the 1837 patent, the $30,000 appropriation, the 24 May 1844 first message and its wording, sender, receiver, and venue, the Annie Ellsworth / Numbers 23:23 provenance, the surviving Library of Congress tape, the 1 May Clay signal, and the ITU timing units; CORROBORATED — the Vail frequency-weighting attribution, the Gerke 1848 / 1851 / Paris 1865 sequence, SOS 1906/1908, Titanic 1912, the 1 February 1999 GMDSS retirement, and the aviation/amateur afterlife; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's doctrine, never run.]*

## The Borg cipher (1600s) — the Vatican medical manuscript in 34 signs, or: the book that waited four hundred years

- **The gap this entry closes.** The Borg cipher is the catalogue's most-cited unwritten cipher: the DESCRYPT note (2026-11-05 research loop) leans on it as the worked example of a machine-read historical cipher — 408 pages, Borg.lat.898, 34 symbols, a 500-symbol extract decoded in just over 29 minutes — but the cipher itself has no entry of its own. This entry writes it, and it also flags a date conflict the DESCRYPT note carried: that note said the Borg was "solved in 2014 by Megyesi's own team," while the sources read this pass put the decipherment in 2016 (Nada Aldarrab, Kevin Knight, Beata Megyesi). Adjudicated 2026-11-07 by the research loop — 2016 stands, the note is corrected. The 2016 date is filed here; the 2014 claim was handed to the research loop and adjudicated 2026-11-07 — no source supports 2014 (Wikipedia, citing Stockholm University and the ICDAR 2019 paper, and the BBC date the decipherment to 2016; the ACL 2021 paper cites Aldarrab's first automatic crack as 2017), so 2016 stands as settled and the DESCRYPT note's 2014 is corrected to 2016 in both files. [VERIFIED — the DESCRYPT note's reliance on the Borg as its example; the grep (no Borg entry before this one)]

- **The manuscript — 408 pages of medicine nobody could read.** The Borg cipher is an encrypted manuscript, probably from the 1600s, held at the Vatican Library as MSS-Borg.lat.898: 408 handwritten pages, the only unencrypted parts the first page in Arabic, some fragments and headings in Latin, and the last two pages in Italian. The contents, once read, are medical recipes for treating symptoms and diseases — hundreds of them, for dysentery, fever, and the rest, including the much-quoted "meat and broth of ravens for fluxes from the bowels." Scholars place its making in Northern Germany or Scandinavia in the 17th century. The inside cover carries the title "Itineris de septentrionales fructus" — "the fruit of a journey to the North" — and the manuscript is read as a copy of Montpellier H.505, a handwritten manuscript of Johannes van Heeck, one of the founders of the Accademia dei Lincei (1603). [VERIFIED — Vatican shelfmark, page count, languages, and medical contents via Wikipedia (Stockholm University and BBC as cited sources); CORROBORATED — the Northern Germany/Scandinavia origin and the ravens-broth recipe via BBC/AzerNEWS, June 2026; CLAIMED — the van Heeck / Montpellier H.505 attribution, Nick Pelling's reading on Cipher Mysteries, 2016, not independently verified this pass]

- **The cipher — 34 signs, and the word lengths given away.** The cipher uses 34 different characters: graphic signs (astrological and alchemical-looking marks among them) plus Roman letters with diacritics. There was no known key. One mercy for the attacker: the encipherer did not bother to disguise word lengths — word boundaries survive in the ciphertext, what the American Cryptogram Association calls an aristocrat cryptogram rather than a patristocrat — so the shape of the plaintext leaks through the symbols. An early hand attempt (Pelling, 2016) transcribed folios and ran them through a solver, and the solver said no: not Latin, not Italian, not Dutch — the failure was not the tool but the plaintext, 17th-century Latin used very differently from Caesar's, which the same tool decrypted with ease. The alphabet was recoverable almost in full by hand once the patterns were seen; the hard part was never the substitution, it was the language underneath it. [VERIFIED — the 34-character count and the graphic-signs-plus-diacritics composition via Wikipedia; CORROBORATED — the undisguised word lengths and the solver's failure on 17th-century Latin via Pelling's first-party account; CLAIMED — the exact "almost all of the alphabet by hand" extent, Pelling's own report]

- **The break — 2016, by machine translation, not by a key.** The Borg was decoded in 2016 by Nada Aldarrab, Kevin Knight, and Beata Megyesi, applying statistics-based translation techniques — the same machinery that had cracked the Copiale cipher — to the manuscript's symbols. No key was ever found; the cipher fell to language modelling over the symbol stream, the way a translation system learns a language it has never seen written in that script. The decoded text turned out to be the medical compendium described above: thousands of 17th-century treatments, of little medical value today and considerable historical value — a window into what late-medieval and early-modern medicine actually prescribed. The 2026 news is not a new break: the DESCRYPT chatbot re-decoded a 500-symbol extract of the already-solved Borg in just over 29 minutes, against weeks of manual work, and the honest reading (filed in the DESCRYPT note) is tool speed on known-plaintext ground truth — the tool earns its keep only when it produces a first reading of something still unread. [CORROBORATED — the 2016 decipherment, the three decoders, and the translation-technique method via Wikipedia (Stockholm University / ICDAR 2019 as cited sources) and the BBC, May–June 2026; the DESCRYPT 29-minute figure per the filed DESCRYPT note]

- **Decoder-design note (Borg → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The key is not the only way in.** The Borg fell with no key ever found — the attack was a language model over the symbol stream, not a key recovery. A specimen whose key is unrecoverable is not therefore unbreakable: the Gauntlet asks what the plaintext's language looks like before it asks where the key is hidden, and a specimen whose symbol stream carries a natural language's statistics is already half-open. (2) **Word lengths are a confession.** The encipherer left word boundaries visible, and every boundary is a free constraint on the plaintext — the solver's search space collapses by the shape of the words alone. A specimen that preserves any structural metadata — lengths, gaps, punctuation, timing — has handed the interrogator a skeleton to fit the flesh to, and the Gauntlet's first read of any ciphertext is its shape, before a single symbol is attacked. (3) **The solver can be right about the cipher and wrong about the language.** Pelling's tool failed on the Borg not because the cipher was strong but because its model of Latin was two thousand years out of date — 17th-century Latin is not Caesar's. A specimen's plaintext is a language with a date on it, and an interrogator who brings the wrong century's model will fail on a trivial cipher and blame the cipher. The Gauntlet grades its own language models alongside the specimen: a failed break is reported with the model that failed, not as a verdict on the cipher. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's own doctrine, never run.]

## Rongorongo (Rapa Nui) — the script that may be writing's fifth invention, or: the island that forgot how to read

- **The gap this entry closes.** Rongorongo is the catalogue's named-but-unwritten undeciphered script: the last two runs' "Next:" lines name it first among the remaining gaps, the UNDECIPHERED watch-list carries it only as a one-line table row ("Unsolved") and a passing mention in the Byblos entry, and grep-verified this pass the catalogue carries zero mentions of "Rongorongo" anywhere — no entry, no footnote, no aside. Phaistos Disc shares the gap and stays named for the next run. This entry writes Rongorongo. [VERIFIED — the grep; the "Next:" lines in the research log]

- **The corpus — two dozen wooden objects, none left on the island.** Twenty-six commonly accepted texts survive — the 2024 radiocarbon paper counts twenty-seven inscribed objects, and the count varies by scholar, 25 to 27. Most are flat tablets of irregular wood, sometimes driftwood, plus the Santiago Staff — a 126-cm chieftain's baton, the longest single text in the corpus — a bird-man statuette, and two reimiro chest ornaments. They are scattered in museums and private collections — Rome, London, Paris, Berlin, Washington, Santiago — and none remain on Easter Island. Only half are in good condition and authentic beyond doubt. The name is Rapanui roŋoroŋo — "to recite," "to chant out." The script was first noticed by outsiders in 1864, when the missionary Eugène Eyraud reported the tablets; writing had already ceased, and most tablets were lost or destroyed in the 1860s — the slave raids that carried off the island's learned men, then the missionary salvage that carried the survivors abroad. [VERIFIED — the 26-text count, the object types, the 1864 first notice, the 1860s loss; CORROBORATED — the 27-object count, the museum scatter, the "only half in good condition," the Eyraud attribution, the slave-raid cause]

- **The shape — reverse boustrophedon, and a sign list nobody agrees on.** Rongorongo is read bottom-to-top, left-to-right, rotating the tablet 180 degrees at the end of every line — reverse boustrophedon, the reader turning the wood like an ox turning at the field's edge. In a third of the tablets the lines sit in shallow fluting carved into the wood. The glyphs are outlines of human, animal, plant, artifact, and geometric forms, often joined into compounds. The sign inventory itself is disputed, which is the first problem any decipherer faces: Barthel's 1958 catalogue lists 632 sign shapes, which he parsed to about 120 basic glyphs; Pozdniakov reduced the inventory to 52 base glyphs covering 99.7% of tokens; Horley (2021) proposes 130 basic shapes. The classic corpus runs to roughly 15,000 glyphs — 14,906 across tablets A–S by the 2026 preprint count. [VERIFIED — the reading direction, the fluting, Barthel's 632 shapes and ~120 parse; CORROBORATED — the Pozdniakov 52, the Horley 130, the corpus size]

- **The two things that are known — a calendar and a genealogy.** Two passages have survived every challenge. In the mid-1950s Butinov and Knorozov, reading the small Santiago tablet, noticed triadic groups — every block of three glyphs beginning with the same sign, then a name, then a patronymic with a regular tail-like suffix — the shape of a genealogy. And Barthel spotted that two and a half lines of Tablet C, the Mamari tablet, read as a lunar calendar — a list of the nights of the moon; Guy (1990) developed it as an intercalation tool, a way to calculate when extra nights must be added to the month, and Valério (2024) calls the list an "artificial bilingual," the closest thing the corpus has to a Rosetta Stone. Nothing else is read: no continuous sentence of rongorongo has ever won general agreement, and whether the signs encode spoken Rapanui at all — full writing, or a mnemonic that cues a recitation learned by heart — is still open. [CORROBORATED — the genealogy pattern and the Mamari calendar; VERIFIED — no accepted continuous reading]

- **The 2024 date — wood older than contact.** Ferrara and colleagues, *Scientific Reports* 2024 (DOI 10.1038/s41598-024-53063-7), radiocarbon-dated four tablets held in Rome. Tablet D, the Échancrée, is wood of 1493–1509 CE — more than two centuries before Europeans reached the island in 1722; the other three are nineteenth-century wood (Tahua is European ash). The date is on the wood, not the carving — a fifteenth-century board can carry a nineteenth-century inscription — but it moves the invention question: the script could predate outside influence, which would make Rapa Nui one of only a handful of independent inventions of writing in human history, beside Mesopotamia, Egypt, China, and Mesoamerica. [CORROBORATED — the peer-reviewed dates and the wood identifications; the medium-vs-message caveat is this entry's own filing]

- **The claims that did not stick — and the 2026 preprint flood.** Steven Roger Fischer (1997) proposed the Santiago Staff records a creation chant in triadic procreation formulas; Guy and Pozdniakov showed the statistical patterns he identified arise from the script's structure rather than any specific content, and the field did not accept it. Davletshin (2012, 2022) proposed syllabic readings for individual glyphs by logogram substitution; no consensus followed. The 2026 preprint flood claims more: ALBA (March 2026) proposes 48 phonetic signs covering 93.6% of the classic corpus, and "Reading Rongorongo" (March 2026) an 89-entry dictionary covering 96.9% of tokens — both self-published, self-classified exploratory, neither peer-reviewed, and as of October 2026 no widely accepted continuous reading exists. A preprint proposing a solution is not a replicated decipherment. [CLAIMED — the Fischer, Davletshin, and 2026 preprint claims as claims; CORROBORATED — their non-acceptance, per the October 2026 survey]

- **Decoder-design note (Rongorongo → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The inventory is the first cipher.** Before any reading, the interrogator must decide what counts as a sign — Barthel's 120 against Pozdniakov's 52 against Horley's 130 is a two-and-a-half-fold disagreement on the alphabet itself. A specimen whose symbol inventory is disputed is graded on inventory discipline first: every claimed reading must name its sign list, and a reading that changes its inventory mid-attack is three readings, not one. (2) **One bilingual is worth a thousand statistics.** The Mamari calendar is the corpus's only anchor — a passage whose function is known before its reading. The Gauntlet's rule for undeciphered corpora: find the anchor first and grade every claimed reading against it before anything else; a reading that cannot reproduce the calendar is not a reading of the corpus, and a reading that reproduces only the calendar has proved one passage, not the script. (3) **Date the medium, not the message.** The 2024 radiocarbon dates date the wood, not the carving. A specimen's age claim must name what was dated — medium, ink, carving — and what it bounds; a date on the wrong layer is a false antiquity, and the Gauntlet treats any claim that slides from "the wood is old" to "the writing is old" as an undeclared inference, graded as one. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's own doctrine, never run.]

## Phaistos Disc (Crete, ~1700 BCE) — the stamped spiral that may not be a text at all

- **The gap this entry closes.** Phaistos Disc is the catalogue's last named-but-unwritten undeciphered script: grep-verified this pass, the name appears exactly once in each catalogue file — inside the Rongorongo entry's gap line, naming it as the next gap — and the UNDECIPHERED watch-list carries it only as a one-line table row ("Unsolved"), a passing mention in the watch-list's script survey, and the Unicode block note (U+101D0–U+101FF, Unicode 5.1). No entry, no footnote, no aside. This entry writes it. [VERIFIED — the grep; the "Next:" lines in the research log]

- **The corpus — one disc, no relatives.** Found July 3, 1908, by the Italian archaeologist Luigi Pernier in a basement storage room of the Minoan palace at Phaistos, on the south coast of Crete — room 8, building 101, northeast of the main palace — half-buried among charred bones and ashes, beside fragments of a Linear A tablet. A disc of fired clay, about 15–16 cm across and about 2.1 cm thick, stamped on both sides and fired to permanence; it now sits in the Heraklion Archaeological Museum. No other example of the script has ever been found: the corpus is one object, and every claim about the script is a claim about this disc alone. [VERIFIED — the date, the finder, the find-spot, the dimensions, the museum; CORROBORATED — the charred-bones deposit and the Linear A tablet found beside it]

- **The shape — a spiral stamped with movable type.** The disc carries 241 readable tokens — 122 on side A, 119 on side B — of 45 distinct sign types, grouped into 61 "words" (31 on A, 30 on B) by short vertical strokes; some counts give 242, the extra token an overstruck sign read differently by different scholars. The signs are pictographs — humans, animals, plants, tools — and they were not drawn: each distinct sign was pressed into the wet clay with its own pre-made punch, the earliest known instance of movable-type-like impression in writing. The spiral runs rim-to-centre and is conventionally read outside-in (groups numbered A1–A31, B1–B30 from the edge inward), though the reading direction itself is contested. Unicode 5.1 encodes the 45 signs at U+101D0–U+101FF. [VERIFIED — the counts, the 61 groups, the stamping, the Unicode block; CORROBORATED — the movable-type characterization, the outside-in convention, the 242nd token]

- **The count problem — Barber's wall.** In 1974 Elizabeth Barber proved mathematically that 241 tokens of 45 sign types is an insufficient corpus to verify any linguistic decipherment by statistical methods: the lock may not exist, and no statistics on this disc alone can prove a reading. There is no bilingual, no second specimen, and no agreed language family. The script matches neither Linear A — the contemporaneous Minoan administrative script, itself undeciphered but extensively attested — nor Linear B, deciphered by Michael Ventris in 1952, nor Cretan hieroglyphic; whether the signs are a syllabary, a logography, or an alphabet is assumed by each claimant, not shown. Louis Godart concluded in 1995 that decipherment may never be achieved. [CORROBORATED — Barber, Godart; VERIFIED — no bilingual, no second specimen, the Linear A/B distinction]

- **The claims that did not stick — and the 2026 trade-directory claim.** Wolfgang Reczko (2009) proposed a solar-eclipse calendar; Gareth Owens (2014) claimed a Minoan-language reading, a hymn to a mother goddess; a 2026 self-published analysis argues the disc is not a text at all but a database — a maritime trade directory, its 61 groups aligning with the roughly 55–65 confirmed sites of the Minoan trade network — and reads the positional distribution (only 19 of the 45 signs ever appear in first position) as field structure, not language. None of these has survived peer review, and no two independent researchers have converged on the same reading. A 2008 forgery claim was rejected by the consensus of working Minoan archaeologists: the excavation record, the Linear A tablet found beside the disc, and the scribe's own corrections — signs erased and re-impressed, which no forger would need — all point the other way. Thermoluminescence dating of the disc has never been performed. [CLAIMED — the Reczko, Owens, and 2026 readings as claims; CORROBORATED — their non-acceptance and the forgery-claim rejection]

- **Decoder-design note (Phaistos → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **One specimen is not a corpus.** n = 1 document, 241 tokens. The Gauntlet's rule for single-specimen corpora: every statistical claim must declare its sample size up front, and any "decipherment" verified only against the same 241 tokens that produced it is a fit, not a proof — Barber's wall is the pass bar, and a claim that does not clear it is graded as a pattern, never a reading. (2) **The stamp is the only ground truth.** The punches are physical tools with a stamping order, and the disc carries its own corrections — signs erased and re-impressed. A claimed reading that ignores which signs were overstruck, in what order, and where the corrections cluster has skipped the one layer of the specimen that cannot be argued with; the Gauntlet grades a reading against the correction map before the sign list. (3) **The medium is not the message.** Movable-type stamping is a fact about manufacture, not about language. A claim that slides from "stamped with type" to "therefore a printed text" — or from the spiral's geometry to a calendar, a directory, or a game board — has imported its conclusion; the Gauntlet separates how it was made from what it says and grades each on its own evidence. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's own doctrine, never run.]

*[Grade: VERIFIED — the one-passing-mention grep, the 1908 discovery, Pernier, the find-spot, the dimensions, the 241/45/61 counts, the stamping, the Unicode block, no bilingual, no second specimen, and the Linear A/B distinction; CORROBORATED — the charred-bones deposit and the Linear A tablet beside it, the movable-type characterization, the outside-in convention, the 242nd token, Barber's wall, Godart's 1995 verdict, and the non-acceptance of the Reczko, Owens, and 2026 claims plus the rejection of the 2008 forgery claim; CLAIMED — the Reczko calendar, the Owens hymn, and the 2026 trade-directory reading as claims; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's doctrine, never run.]*

## Cicada 3301 (2012– ) — the internet's recruitment puzzle, or: the test that never named its maker

- **The gap this entry closes.** Cicada 3301 is the catalogue's most-cited unwritten puzzle: grep-verified this pass, the name appears exactly once in each catalogue file — inside the steganography entry's tool lineage ("OutGuess (Cicada 3301's 2012–14 chain used it for image stego)") — and the UNDECIPHERED watch-list carries it only as a one-line table row ("~55 of ~75 pages unsolved; 2012/13 chains solved") plus a short note. No entry, no footnote, no aside. This entry writes it. [VERIFIED — the grep; the UNDECIPHERED table row]

- **The first winter — 2012: the image, the duck, the posters.** On 4 January 2012 (some accounts say 5 January) a black image with white text appeared on 4chan, signed only "3301": it was looking for "highly intelligent individuals" and promised a message hidden in the image. OutGuess steganography pulled a Caesar cipher out of it, which decoded to an image of a duck — "Woops! Just decoys this way" — whose own hidden layer pointed to the subreddit r/a2e7j6ic78h0j and a book cipher keyed to the medieval Welsh Mabinogion. The book cipher gave a Dallas phone number, (214) 390-9608, whose recorded message named three primes; two were the original image's own dimensions, 509 × 503, and with 3301 they multiplied to 845145127 — a website with a cicada image and a countdown. When the countdown ended at 17:00 UTC on Monday 9 January 2012, the site posted GPS coordinates: 14 physical poster locations across the world — Warsaw, Paris, Seoul, Sydney, Seattle, New Orleans, Hawaii, Moscow, Miami, and more — each poster bearing the cicada emblem and a QR code, each code leading on through further book ciphers (William Gibson's Agrippa, Crowley's Liber AL vel Legis) to a Tor hidden service and a final message. The handful who finished were contacted by email in February 2012; what they were told next has never been published in verified form. [CORROBORATED — the chain as reconstructed across multiple secondary accounts; the 4/5 January date variance filed, not resolved]

- **The second and third winters — 2013 and 2014: the books get harder.** A second image appeared on 4 January 2013 (some accounts say 5 January): a book cipher keyed to Crowley's Liber AL vel Legis, an MP3 credited to 3301 that opens with the sound of cicadas ("The Instar Emergence"), a bootable Linux disc, a table turning Anglo-Saxon runes into numbers, and new posters from Dallas to Moscow to Okinawa. Marcus Wanner — a teenager from near Roanoke, Virginia, who had finished the 2012 round — was the first to solve the 2013 round. The third round opened on Twitter in the first week of January 2014 ("Hello. Epiphany is upon you. Your pilgrimage has begun. Enlightenment awaits." — 4 January by Wikipedia's dating, 5–6 January by other accounts): its first step hid a book code keyed to Ralph Waldo Emerson's essay "Self-Reliance" (paragraph, sentence, word, letter), a later step a collage of William Blake's art, and the trail moved into runes read with a key released the year before. [CORROBORATED — the round structure and the Wanner solve; the January date variance filed, not resolved]

- **The Liber Primus — the book that stopped the hunt.** At the end of 2014 came the Liber Primus ("First Book"): a book of runes, released as the third round's final layer. Two of its pages were solved almost at once; the rest have not been read. The page count itself is disputed — the solvers' own count, given at DEF CON in August 2023, is 58 pages with 56 still unread after nine years; other accounts give 74 or 75 pages, with ~55–56 unread — and this entry files the discrepancy rather than picking a number: the book circulated in different paginations, and no single count is settled. What is settled is that no new round has followed the 2014 puzzle, by the solvers' own account, and the Liber Primus remains the hunt's open remainder. [CORROBORATED — the DEF CON 2023 solvers' count; CLAIMED — the 74/75-page counts as reported counts, with the variance filed]

- **The signature and the silence — the only ground truth the puzzle ever offered.** Every genuine clue carried a signature from the same OpenPGP key, 7A35090F, whose identity line reads "Cicada 3301 (845145127)" — the product of the first puzzle's own primes. In January 2016 the same Twitter account posted one more signed image ("Liber Primus is the way... its words are the map, their meaning the road, and their numbers the direction"), and on 29 April 2017 a user in the #cicadasolvers IRC channel found the last verified message, signed 4 April 2017: "Beware false paths. Always verify PGP signature from 7A35090F." An unsigned image pointing to Mojave Desert coordinates, posted to 4chan in early 2017, was treated as fake by the solvers for want of that signature. As of October 2026, no credible report of a newly signed message since April 2017, no confirmed identity, and no one who has proven authorship by signing with the key. The US Navy's 2014 Project Architeuthis copied the concept as a recruitment challenge — the puzzle's form, borrowed by the institution it was most often suspected of being. [CORROBORATED — the key, the 2016 and 2017 messages, the unsigned Mojave fake, the Architeuthis copy]

- **Decoder-design note (Cicada → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The signature is the specimen.** Cicada is the catalogue's cleanest intake test: a clue is genuine if and only if it verifies against 7A35090F — no provenance, no reputation, no plausibility substitutes. The Gauntlet's intake rule is the solvers' rule: unsigned is fake until signed, and a puzzle that arrives without its key is not a puzzle, it is a rumour wearing the puzzle's clothes. (2) **A solved round is not a solved puzzle.** 2012 and 2013 closed; 2014 did not — the Liber Primus is a separate specimen with its own verdict, and the rounds' solved status never transfers. The Gauntlet grades each layer on its own evidence and never lets a closed neighbour retire an open book. (3) **Grade the artifact, not the mythology.** Intelligence-agency recruitment, ARG, occult order — every theory of who built Cicada is SPECULATION, and the Gauntlet refuses the question: the specimen is the chain of ciphers, the posters, and the book, and its verdict is about what the chain does, not who laid it. A recruitment puzzle that never recruited anyone in public is still a cipher specimen; its silence is data about the specimen, not a hole to fill with a story. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's own doctrine, never run.]

## One-Time Pad (1917– ) — the cipher that cannot be broken and cannot be used, or: the secret that costs as much as the message

- **The gap this entry closes.** The one-time pad is the catalogue's most-cited unwritten cipher: grep-verified this pass, the phrase appears 15 times in the private catalogue and 14 in the public one, and every occurrence is a passing mention — the timeline's one-line note ("Shannon 1949: provably secure *if* pad is truly random, as long as the message, and used once"), the Venona entry's account of the pad's reuse, and a handful of cross-references. No entry, no footnote, no aside. The only cipher in the history of cryptography with a mathematical proof of unbreakability has no entry of its own. This entry writes it. [VERIFIED — the grep counts; the timeline line; the Venona entry]

- **The construction, and the four conditions that make it perfect.** A one-time pad encrypts by combining each plaintext symbol with a key symbol of equal length — modular addition on paper tapes, XOR in the modern telling — and the recipient combines again with the identical key to recover the message. That is the whole mechanism, and its security rests on four non-negotiable conditions: the key must be truly random; it must be at least as long as the message; it must remain completely secret; and every part of it must be used once, and only once. When all four hold, Claude Shannon's 1949 proof ("Communication Theory of Secrecy Systems") shows the ciphertext carries zero information about the plaintext — observing it does not change the attacker's probabilities for any possible original message. No amount of computing power, present or future, can break it, because there is nothing to compute: every possible plaintext of the same length is equally consistent with the same ciphertext. It is the only cipher in the catalogue with a proof of that strength, and the proof is information-theoretic, not computational — it does not depend on any hardness assumption surviving. [VERIFIED — the construction, the four conditions, and Shannon's 1949 perfect-secrecy proof, per multiple independent secondary sources this pass]

- **Vernam, Mauborgne, Shannon — three men, thirty-two years.** Gilbert Vernam, an engineer at AT&T, built the machine first: an automated teleprinter system combining the electrical representation of each character with a key tape, patented as US 1,310,719 (filed 1918, granted 1919), developed from 1917 work on securing teletype traffic. Vernam's tape was a key stream, but not yet a *random* one, and reuse was not yet forbidden. The decisive refinement came from Joseph Mauborgne of the US Army Signal Corps, credited alongside Vernam with the modern system in 1919: the key sequence must be genuinely random, and no part of it may ever be used twice — hence the name, and hence the pad: printed sheets of random digits, one page per message, torn off and burned after use. Thirty years later Shannon supplied what neither inventor had: the proof. His 1949 paper formalised perfect secrecy and showed the pad achieves it — and, by the same mathematics, that no cipher can achieve it with a key shorter than the message. The key must cost as much as the message, in length and in delivery, and that cost is the whole story of why the perfect cipher is almost never used. [VERIFIED — Vernam's 1917 development and the 1918/1919 patent dates, Mauborgne's 1919 random-and-never-reuse refinement, Shannon's 1949 proof; CORROBORATED — that no other cipher carries a comparable proof, per the standard secondary carriers]

- **Venona — the break that was not a break.** The one-time pad has never been broken. It has been *misused*, once, at scale, and the misuse is the most instructive failure in the catalogue. The full account sits in the timeline's Venona entry; the shape, in brief: under wartime pressure the Soviet pad producer generated some 35,000 pages of duplicated key, and duplicates were shipped to widely separated users. In 1944 Arlington Hall analysts isolated the "depth of two" — two messages encrypted under the same pad page — and the key cancelled out of the difference, leaving the XOR of two plaintexts for statistics and cribs to pick apart. Meredith Gardner read the first KGB message in February 1946; about 2,200 translations were eventually published, and KGB New York-to-Moscow traffic for 1944 was about 49% readable. The decrypts exposed the atomic spy rings — Klaus Fuchs, the Rosenbergs, Harry Gold — and the program ran, declassified, until the NSA released it in 1995. The algorithm was never at fault; the production control was. A one-time pad reused even once is not a weakened one-time pad. It is a different, breakable system that happens to look like one. [VERIFIED — the Venona figures and dates, as already filed in the timeline entry from NSA sources]

- **The hotline, and the deployments that survived the cost.** The deployments that worked are the ones where the cost was payable. The Moscow–Washington hotline, established in 1963 after the Cuban Missile Crisis, ran its first years on one-time tapes delivered through each side's embassy — a commercial machine, deliberately, so neither side had to reveal its high-grade ciphers to the other. Field agents carried paper pads through the Cold War, one page per message, burned after use. Numbers stations — the shortwave broadcasts of digit groups that still run today — are widely reported to carry one-time-pad traffic, the pad delivered by courier before the broadcast ever airs. Every deployment shares the same shape: the key travels first, by hand, over a channel already trusted, and the message follows later, over a channel that need not be. The pad does not remove the security problem. It relocates it, from the message to the key. [CORROBORATED — the 1963 hotline's one-time tapes and the commercial-machine choice, the paper-pad field practice, and the numbers-station use, per multiple secondary sources; the relocation framing is this entry's own]

- **The price, stated plainly.** Three costs, and one missing property. First, length: a gigabyte of message requires a gigabyte of key material, generated, stored, and delivered in advance — the key-distribution problem in its purest form, with no public-key shortcut, because encrypting the pad with another pad restates the problem. Second, custody: both ends need matching copies, delivered and stored without interception, copying, substitution, corruption, or loss, and every copy is a single point of total failure — whoever holds the pad can read everything and can forge everything. Third, the pad provides confidentiality and nothing else: it does not authenticate the sender and does not protect the integrity of the ciphertext. A malicious intermediary can flip bits in transit without either party noticing — the rewrite attack — because the pad carries no check on what it encrypts. And the boundary that matters most for the decoder: a keystream generated pseudorandomly from a short key is a stream cipher, not a one-time pad. The moment the key is shorter than the message, the proof dies, whatever the keystream's quality. Quantum key distribution is the modern attempt at the delivery problem — physics, not couriers, carrying the key — but it solves distribution, not length, not custody, and not authentication. [VERIFIED — the length cost, the custody requirement, the no-authentication/no-integrity property and the rewrite attack, and the stream-cipher boundary, per multiple secondary sources this pass; CLAIMED — quantum key distribution as the modern delivery attempt, a framing claim, not a deployment claim]

- **Decoder-design note (One-Time Pad → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Grade the key, not the cipher.** The mechanism is proven; there is nothing to attack in it, and the Gauntlet wastes no run on the mathematics. Interrogation targets the four conditions, and each is a falsifiable check: randomness (statistical tests on the key material), length (the key audit — a key shorter than the message is a different specimen), reuse (the depth scan — any two ciphertexts sharing key material re-grade the specimen on the spot), and custody (the chain-of-hands — who touched the pad, and when). A specimen that passes all four has nothing left to grade on secrecy, and the card says so. (2) **A two-time pad is a different specimen.** Reuse does not weaken the one-time pad; it converts it. The Gauntlet re-grades a reused pad as the system it has become — a depth-two additive stream with a reused keystream — and never lets the specimen keep the "unbreakable" label while standing on reused material. Venona is the standing example: the verdict on the cipher stayed VERIFIED while the verdict on the deployment failed, and the card carries both, separately. (3) **Perfect secrecy is not total security.** A specimen claiming "unbreakable" must state which property it claims, and the card grades the claimed property only. The pad's silence on authentication and integrity is not a flaw in the proof; it is a boundary on the claim. Any specimen that borrows the pad's aura — "unbreakable," "quantum-proof," "mathematically proven" — while selling a property the pad never promised is borrowing a verdict it has not earned, and the Fabrication Alarm fires on the borrowing, not on the mathematics. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's doctrine, never run.]

## Chaocipher (1918–2010) — the cipher that won on secrecy alone, or: the machine that mangled its own key

- **The gap this entry closes.** Chaocipher is the catalogue's most-cited unwritten cipher after the pad: grep-verified this pass, the name appears 7 times in the private catalogue and 5 in the public one, and every occurrence is a passing mention — the §(a) bullet that carries the whole story in miniature, and cross-references from the Kryha, SIGABA, Jefferson-disk, Playfair, and frequency-hopping entries. No full entry, no construction, no disclosure account. The cipher that survived ninety years on secrecy alone has no entry of its own. This entry writes it. [VERIFIED — the grep counts; the §(a) bullet; the cross-references]

- **The machine: two disks that rewrite themselves.** The Chaocipher is a hand machine of two disks, left and right, each carrying the 26 letters around its rim on removable tabs in a prearranged order — small enough, in Byrne's telling, to fit in a cigar box, and simple enough that "any person on earth" could use one. To encipher a letter: find the plaintext letter on the right disk and read the ciphertext letter off the left disk at the aligned position. Then, before the next letter, both alphabets are re-permuted by fixed rules — the left disk rotates to the ciphertext letter just produced and cycles its letters from the second position to the fourteenth, the right disk rotates to the plaintext letter and cycles its own span — so the cipher mangled its own key as it worked. Byrne's own terms for the anchor positions were *zenith* (first) and *nadir* (fourteenth). The consequence is the whole design: repeated plaintext never produces repeated ciphertext, because the alphabet that enciphered the first occurrence no longer exists by the second. It is dynamic substitution in mechanical form — the key is not a fixed mapping but a state, and the state moves on every letter. [VERIFIED — the two-disk construction, the locate-and-read step, and the per-letter permutation of both alphabets, per Rubin's July 2010 disclosure paper and the Wikipedia entry; CORROBORATED — the cigar-box size and the "any person on earth" claim, as filed in the §(a) bullet]

- **Byrne, the prizes, and ninety years of silence.** John Francis Byrne invented the Chaocipher in 1918 and spent more than three decades trying, unsuccessfully, to interest the US Signal Corps and the Navy in it. Frustrated, he published four challenge messages in his autobiography *Silent Years* (1953) — large amounts of plain and matching ciphertext, but never a description of the enciphering process — to bear out his contention that the system was "absolutely indecipherable," with cash prizes for a solution. (Rubin's disclosure paper dates the challenge presentation to 1954; the carriers disagree by a year, and the year is not load-bearing.) Nobody claimed the prize — not in the three months of the challenge, nor in the fifty-five years after it. Numerous professional cryptanalysts failed against the exhibits; whether official government agencies ever succeeded is unknown, on Rubin's own record. The first exhibit alone ran to 13,615 letters of ciphertext. For roughly ninety years the algorithm was a closely guarded secret known only to a handful of people, and the cipher's resistance was total — because nobody could see the machine. [VERIFIED — the 1918 invention, the failed approaches to the Signal Corps and Navy, *Silent Years*, the four challenge exhibits, and the 13,615-letter first exhibit, per Rubin 2010 and Cowan 2010; CORROBORATED — the unclaimed prizes and the failed professional attempts, per the same carriers]

- **The disclosure, and the break that followed in months.** In August 2009 Moshe Rubin located Byrne's daughter-in-law, Patricia Byrne; in May 2010 she donated all Chaocipher-related papers and artifacts to the National Cryptologic Museum at Ft. Meade. On July 2, 2010 Rubin published the first full public disclosure of the algorithm — "Chaocipher Revealed: The Algorithm" — and within weeks the ninety-year wall fell in pieces: in August 2010 Rubin deciphered Exhibit 1, working from the exhibit's known opening plaintext ("ALLGOODQQUICK…") and the key phrase "THINKTHINK" with its left/right alphabet pattern, deriving the starting wheel states; in December 2010 Michael J. Cowan published computer solutions to Exhibits 1 and 4. Exhibits 2, 3, and 5 remained unsolved at Rubin's writing — a partial break, honestly bounded, not a total one. The shape of the fall is the entry's lesson: ninety years of total resistance, then immediate partial reconstruction within months of disclosure. The defense was never the mechanism's strength. It was the mechanism's invisibility. [VERIFIED — the August 2009 location, the May 2010 donation, Rubin's July 2, 2010 disclosure, the August 2010 Exhibit 1 decipherment with its key phrase and pattern, and Cowan's December 2010 solution of Exhibits 1 and 4, per Rubin 2010 and Cowan 2010; CORROBORATED — that Exhibits 2, 3, and 5 stood unsolved at Rubin's writing]

- **The price, stated plainly.** Three costs, and one broken rule. First, the secrecy was the entire defense: the Chaocipher violates Kerckhoffs's principle in the most absolute form the catalogue holds — not "the key must stay secret" but "the *machine* must stay secret" — and the price of that violation is a cliff, not a slope. A cipher whose strength is its invisibility has no graceful degradation: the day the algorithm is published, the cipher goes from unbreakable to partially broken in weeks. Second, the machine was never adopted, so its field record is zero: its unbreakability was never tested in service, only in challenge, and a challenge the vendor controls is a weaker test than a war. Third, with the algorithm public, the system is weak by modern standards — deterministic per-letter permutation with known plaintext recovers the starting alphabets, exactly as Rubin's reconstruction did, and the key space is the pair of starting alphabets, not a secret the machine protects. The Chaocipher is the catalogue's purest experiment in mechanism secrecy, and the experiment's result is on the record: it works, for as long as the secret holds, and then it stops working all at once. [VERIFIED — the Kerckhoffs violation as a structural claim about the design, and the known-plaintext recovery of the starting alphabets, per Rubin's reconstruction; CLAIMED — "no graceful degradation" as a framing of the disclosure-to-break interval; SPECULATION — the field-record reading, this entry's own]

- **Decoder-design note (Chaocipher → Gauntlet).** Three rungs, growing the §(a) bullet's counter into doctrine. (1) **Self-mangling state dies under single-message analysis and only yields to sequence-level observation.** A specimen whose encoding function changes its own state per output — Chaocipher's wheels, a model's per-turn context, a container that re-keys per session — cannot be graded from one message, however long. The Gauntlet's interrogation of such a specimen is a sequence: many outputs, the state transition inferred from the series, exactly as Rubin's reconstruction worked from multiple exhibits, not one. A single-output fixture against a self-mangling specimen is a fixture that measures nothing. (2) **Mechanism secrecy has an expiry date, and the Gauntlet prices it.** "The algorithm is secret" is never accepted as a security property, only as a delay — and the delay is graded against the clock, not the brochure. Ninety years is a long delay and a short doctrine: the Chaocipher's cliff is the standing example that a secret mechanism is a depreciating asset, and any specimen whose defense is invisibility gets a card that says so, with the disclosure date as the expiry. (3) **The vendor's challenge is a free test protocol — and a partial break is still a break.** Byrne's unclaimed prizes are the Kryha rung's sibling: accept the challenge on the vendor's terms, work it, and return the keys. And the honest remainder matters as much as the break: Exhibits 2, 3, and 5 stood unsolved at Rubin's writing, so the card on the Chaocipher reads "Exhibits 1 and 4 broken, 2, 3, 5 standing" — never "Chaocipher broken" and never "Chaocipher unbroken." A specimen's verdict names exactly what fell and what stands. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's doctrine, never run.]

## Kryptos (1990– ) — the artist's cipher in the CIA courtyard, or: the sculpture that was solved everywhere except the last 97 letters

- **The gap this entry closes.** Kryptos is the catalogue's most-cited unwritten cipher after the pad and Chaocipher: grep-verified this pass, the name appears 6 times in the private catalogue and 7 in the public one, and every occurrence is a passing mention — the §(a) bullet that carries the whole story in miniature, and cross-references from the Grille, Taman Shud, Huffman, and Rosetta design notes. No full entry, no construction, no account of the 2025 turn that changed the specimen's status without breaking its cipher. The cipher that held 35 years against the NSA, the CIA, and the world has no entry of its own. This entry writes it. [VERIFIED — the grep counts; the §(a) bullet; the cross-references]

- **The sculpture: a lock with its key carved beside it.** Kryptos — Greek for "hidden" — is an S-shaped copper screen by Washington artist Jim Sanborn, built with retired CIA cryptographer Ed Scheidt, chairman of the CIA's own Cryptographic Center, and dedicated November 3, 1990, in the courtyard of CIA headquarters at Langley, Virginia. The screen carries about 1,800 letters; the ciphertext half, on the left as seen from the courtyard, is 869 characters — 865 letters and 4 question marks — holding four encrypted passages, K1–K4, one after another with no gap between them. The right half is a Vigenère tableau, flipped so it reads correctly only from behind the sculpture: the decode tool carved beside the lock. Sanborn said the sculpture contains a riddle within a riddle, solvable only after all four passages are deciphered — and hinted a fifth coded message will reveal itself then. [VERIFIED — the dedication date, the Scheidt collaboration, the 869-character count, the tableau, the riddle-within-a-riddle, per the Wikipedia entry and the Cipher Museum record]

- **The three solves: three systems, three solvers, one lesson in layers.** K1 is a Vigenère cipher on a KRYPTOS-scrambled alphabet, keyed PALIMPSEST — the word itself a manuscript scraped clean and written over, layers on layers. K2 is Vigenère again, keyed ABSCISSA. K3 is not substitution at all: a transposition that, unshuffled, paraphrases Howard Carter's 1922 account of breaking into Tutankhamun's tomb. The plaintexts: K1, "BETWEEN SUBTLE SHADING AND THE ABSENCE OF LIGHT LIES THE NUANCE OF IQLUSION"; K2, the invisible transmission, the Earth's magnetic field, the buried thing, "DOES LANGLEY KNOW ABOUT THIS? THEY SHOULD ITS BURIED OUT THERE SOMEWHERE X WHO KNOWS THE EXACT LOCATION? ONLY WW THIS WAS HIS LAST MESSAGE X THIRTY EIGHT DEGREES FIFTY SEVEN MINUTES SIX POINT FIVE SECONDS NORTH SEVENTY SEVEN DEGREES EIGHT MINUTES FORTY FOUR SECONDS WEST X LAYER TWO"; K3, "SLOWLY DESPARATELY SLOWLY THE REMAINS OF PASSAGE DEBRIS THAT ENCUMBERED THE LOWER PART OF THE DOORWAY WAS REMOVED WITH TREMBLING HANDS I MADE A TINY BREACH IN THE UPPER LEFT HAND CORNER AND THEN WIDENING THE HOLE A LITTLE I INSERTED THE CANDLE AND PEERED IN THE HOT AIR ESCAPING FROM THE CHAMBER CAUSED THE FLAME TO FLICKER BUT PRESENTLY DETAILS OF THE ROOM WITHIN EMERGED FROM THE MIST X CAN YOU SEE ANYTHING Q?" The misspellings — IQLUSION, UNDERGRUUND, DESPARATLY — are Sanborn's, deliberate. And the last word of K2 is itself a correction: the early readings gave WESTIDBYROWS; in 2006 Sanborn announced he had made an error and confirmed the plaintext reads WESTXLAYERTWO. Three solvers, in order of solving, not of telling: an NSA team led by Ken Miller with Dennis McDaniels and two unnamed analysts cracked all three in late 1992, within a month of Deputy Director William Studeman's formal challenge, and told no one for twenty years — the fact surfaced only in 2013, when Elonka Dunin obtained the NSA documents under FOIA; CIA analyst David Stein solved the same three in 1998 with pencil and paper across some 400 lunch hours, and his account stayed inside the intelligence community until July 1999; California computer scientist Jim Gillogly published the first public solutions in 1999, on a Pentium II. [VERIFIED — the keys, the plaintexts, the three solvers and their dates, the 2006 WESTXLAYERTWO correction, per the Wikipedia entry, the Cipher Museum record, and the NSA FOIA documents]

- **K4: 97 characters, and the system itself unknown.** The fourth passage is the whole specimen now: `OBKRUOXOGHULBSOLIFBBWFLRVQQPRNGKSSOTWTQSJQSSEKZZWATJKLUDIAWINFBNYPVTTMZFPKWGDKZXTJCDIGKUHUAUEKCAR` — 97 letters, verified this pass by count. The declassified NSA summary describes a fairly flat letter distribution with no long repeats, and reports autokey attempts without readable results. What makes K4 different from every other unsolved entry in this catalogue is that the artist kept handing over pieces of the answer, and the pieces did not help: in 2010 Sanborn revealed that positions 64–69 — ciphertext `NYPVTT` — decrypt to BERLIN; in 2014, positions 70–74 — `MZFPK` — decrypt to CLOCK; in 2020, positions 22–25 decrypt to EAST and positions 26–34 to NORTHEAST, which Sanborn said would be the last clue. Roughly a quarter of the plaintext, position-anchored, handed over free — and the system still would not crack, because nobody has identified the cipher system itself. In November 2025, at the International Spy Museum, Sanborn added that the clock is Berlin's World Clock, and that two events figure in the solution: a 1986 trip he took to Egypt, and the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989. [VERIFIED — the 97-character count and ciphertext, the flat distribution and failed autokey attempts per the NSA summary, the four clue releases and their positions, the November 2025 Spy Museum framing, per the Wikipedia entry and the October 2026 status check]

- **The 2025 turn: the break that wasn't a break.** On August 14, 2025, Sanborn published an open letter saying he would sell the K4 plaintext that November, near his 80th birthday. In September 2025, journalists Jarett Kobek and Richard Byrne found scraps of the K4 plaintext sitting in Sanborn's papers at the Smithsonian's Archives of American Art — misfiled years earlier during Sanborn's cancer treatment — not cryptanalysis, found in a box. Sanborn confirmed the scraps genuine and asked that they stay sealed; the Smithsonian agreed to seal the files for 50 years. On November 20, 2025, Sanborn's full Kryptos archive — the solution, the encryption tables, a prototype — sold at RR Auction for $962,500, against a $300,000–500,000 estimate, to an anonymous bidder; in June 2026 the venture firm Paradigm disclosed it was the buyer and launched a public Kryptos site with a ten-puzzle capture-the-flag challenge at $1,000 per solved puzzle. The specimen's status as of this writing: K4's plaintext is known to a small number of people and has never been published; the cipher itself has still never been broken by analysis. A July 2025 Zenodo paper claims a complete cryptogeographic solution — coordinates 38°57'06.9"N 77°08'44.6"W, timestamp 23:51 on November 9, 1989, the fall of the Berlin Wall — but the record as checked October 26, 2026 establishes no published, reproducible cryptanalytic solution, and the claim stands unreproduced. [CORROBORATED — the open letter, the Smithsonian find, the sealing, the auction price and buyer, per AP/RR Auction/Washington Post reporting as filed in the §(a) bullet and the October 2026 status check; CLAIMED — the July 2025 Zenodo solution, unreproduced]

- **Decoder-design note (Kryptos → Gauntlet).** Four rungs, growing the §(a) note's four into doctrine. (1) **The last layer changes the instrument.** K1 and K2 are Vigenère; K3 is transposition; K4 is something else entirely — three different systems in one specimen, and the solver who assumes K4 is Vigenère-with-another-key has already lost. Gauntlet standing rule: a specimen that yields in layers never promises the next layer uses the last layer's method. Re-derive the system class per layer; never inherit it. The Gauntlet's layering discipline is the Kryptos discipline: each chamber of a foreign specimen gets its own system identification, and a method that worked in chamber one is a hypothesis in chamber two, never a premise. (2) **Cribs are a budget, not a break.** Sanborn handed over roughly a quarter of K4's plaintext, position-anchored — BERLIN, CLOCK, EAST, NORTHEAST — and the system still would not crack, because cribs price the plaintext, not the mechanism. Gauntlet rule: known-plaintext is priced against the unknown system. A crib that does not name the system is calibration data, and a specimen that survives its own cribs has told you the mechanism is the unknown, not the message. (3) **Custody is the cipher's other flank.** K4's plaintext fell to an archive search, not cryptanalysis — the artist's own papers, misfiled during cancer treatment, sealed for 50 years, then auctioned for $962,500. Gauntlet rule, the §(a) note's third rung sharpened: interrogate the specimen's custody chain with the same rigor as its encoding. The leak that breaks a specimen is usually a filing error, not a mathematical one — and a sealed archive is embargoed knowledge, logged on the record as known-but-withheld, never pretended unknown, never treated as a break. (4) **A claimed solution is graded, not believed.** The July 2025 Zenodo paper claims the complete answer — coordinates, timestamp, event — four months before the archive sale, and the record as of October 2026 establishes no published, reproducible cryptanalytic solution. Gauntlet rule: a solution claim without a reproducible method is CLAIMED, and stays CLAIMED until the method reproduces. The auction price is not evidence, the author's confidence is not evidence, and the coordinates matching the Berlin Wall's fall is a consistency check, not a verification. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's doctrine, never run]
