## B-211 (1933– ) — the printer that turned a rotor machine into a business, or: the hinge between Enigma's rival and the M-209

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero hits in the private catalogue, zero in the public one, measured this pass — no entry, no bullet, no passing mention in either file, matching lines read to confirm. The machine that made Hagelin's fortune, and the direct ancestor of the M-209, was absent from the catalogue entirely. [VERIFIED — the 0/0 grep gap, measured this pass]
- **The machine.** Boris Caesar Wilhelm Hagelin, Russia-born Swedish engineer, built the B-21 in 1925 at A.B. Cryptograph in Stockholm with Arvid Gerhard Damm: an electromechanical machine based on Damm's B-13, two electrical coding wheels stepped irregularly by four pin-wheels, scrambling a 5×5 matrix (25 letters; W became VV) through a programmable matrix to a lamp panel — Enigma's shape, a different principle, built to avoid patent infringement. The Swedish General Staff bought it; it was Hagelin's first commercially successful machine. At the end of 1933 the French Army asked for a version that could print: Hagelin added a rotating print head, a strip printer, and an electric motor, and called it the B-211. Five hundred units were manufactured at the L.M. Ericsson factory in Colombes, Paris, before the outbreak of World War II. [VERIFIED — CryptoMuseum B-21 page, first-party read this pass; CORROBORATED — the 500 units and Colombes manufacture per CryptoMuseum's Boris Hagelin page]
- **The service record.** The B-211 became very popular in France, was built there by an Ericsson subsidiary in Colombes under licence from Hagelin's Swedish company, and was still in use during the Algerian war (1954–1962). It was also sold to other countries. The Russians obtained two working B-211 machines from Hagelin under threat and cloned it as the K-37 (Crystal) — the clone was broken by the Americans during WWII. [CORROBORATED — the French service, Algerian-war use, and Ericsson licence per CryptoMuseum first-party read; the 500-unit figure, the clone story, and the "under threat" detail per CryptoMuseum's Hagelin biography]
- **The honest blank.** The B-21 it descended from was considered more secure than Enigma — and was broken in less than 24 hours in 1931 by Arne Beurling, a young mathematics student on a Swedish Cipher Bureau course (Beckman 2002, pp. 31–32). No open-source break of the B-211 itself is on the record this entry could find; a 1939 analysis of the type survives in the NSA record ("Analysis of the Hagelin Cryptograph Type B-211"), and the machine's name surfaces again in 1954, when NSA cryptoanalyst Joseph Peterson was arrested in the Netherlands — the Dutch course material lists the B-211 beside his name. [CORROBORATED — the Beurling break per CryptoMuseum first-party read, citing Beckman; CLAIMED — the 1939 NSA analysis and the Peterson link, single source (UvA course slides)]
- **The lineage — the hinge.** Damm's B-13 → Hagelin's B-21 (1925, lamps, Swedish Army) → B-211 (1933, printer + motor, French Army) → the French request for a small portable mechanical tapeprinting machine (1934) → C-35/C-36 (1935–36, pin-and-lug, no power) → C-38/M-209 (140,000+ built in WWII) → C-52/CX-52 → Crypto AG, in business until 2018/2019. The B-211 is the hinge of the whole line: the last machine that looked like an Enigma and the first that printed like a teletype — the moment Hagelin stopped competing with Enigma and started selling something Enigma never was: a machine a clerk could use in the field and read on paper. One more thing to file: the machine is often erroneously identified as the "B-18" — a machine that never existed; Hagelin himself made the mistake in his memoirs, probably misreading a '3' as an '8'. [VERIFIED — the lineage per CryptoMuseum first-party read and Hagelin's own 1961 account (Crypto Cellar, NSA Friedman Collection); the B-18 note per CryptoMuseum]
- **Decoder-design note (B-211 → Gauntlet).** Four rungs. (1) **The output channel is part of the cipher.** The B-211 changed nothing in the ciphering — same pin-wheels, same matrix as the B-21 — and changed everything about the machine: lamps became paper. Gauntlet rule: interrogate the output channel with the cipher — a specimen that prints its plaintext onto a strip has a second exfiltration surface the lamp machine never had, and a specimen whose output is a tape is a specimen whose output can be kept, copied, and read later. (2) **"More secure than Enigma" is a comparison, not a measurement.** The B-21 was considered more secure than Enigma until Beurling broke it in a day — the comparison flattered it and the measurement killed it. Gauntlet rule: never grade a specimen against a rival; grade it against the clock — Beurling's 24 hours is the number, "more secure than Enigma" is the press release. (3) **The clone is the cryptanalysis.** The Russians did not break the B-211; they obtained two of them and built the K-37 — and the K-37 was broken by the Americans. Gauntlet rule: a specimen that can be bought, borrowed, or taken under threat is a specimen whose security rests on custody, not on mathematics — and the interrogator's first question is always "who else has one," not "how does it work." (4) **The hinge machine is the lineage claim.** The B-211's importance is not its own service record but its position: it is the machine that turned a Swedish Enigma-rival into the French Army's printer and then into the C-machines. Gauntlet rule: grade a specimen's lineage position alongside its mechanism — a specimen that sits at the hinge of a family tells the interrogator where the family's next machine will come from, and the next machine is the one that matters. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's doctrine, never run]

## Rockex (1943– ) — the unbreakable machine that ran on paper tape, or: the one-time pad that went to work

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero hits in the private catalogue, zero in the public one, measured this pass — no entry, no bullet, no passing mention in either file. The machine that carried almost all SIS telegrams between London and New York through 1943–44, and then served British embassies and consulates worldwide for thirty years, was absent from the catalogue entirely — while its cousins Typex (13 mentions) and the CCM (8 mentions) at least appear. [VERIFIED — the 0/0 grep gap, measured this pass]

- **The machine.** Rockex — named after the Rockefeller Center, in the British "-ex" tradition (Typex) — was an offline one-time-tape Vernam cipher machine, developed by Canadian electrical engineer Benjamin deForest Bayly while working for British Security Coordination. It began as the Telekrypton: an electromechanical one-time-tape machine built around 1933 by the Western Union Telegraph Company on Gilbert Vernam's 1918 patent (US 1310719), of which Western Union still had two left in a warehouse. In 1940 BSC needed secure traffic between Washington and New York in pre-war America; Bayly took the two machines and reworked them. The first Telekrypton line, BSC New York–Washington, went live in January 1942 on hand-punched tapes; lines to Ottawa (May 1942) and to Camp X, Whitby, Ontario (July 1942) followed. Then Bayly fixed the design's security weaknesses and changed the combining logic so only the 26 letters of the alphabet could appear in the output — carriage return, line feed, space, and the letter/figure shifts were never enciphered — and the ciphertext came out formatted in five-letter groups. That mattered: the output could now travel over ordinary commercial circuits instead of private leased lines. The rebuilt machine was Rockex, first used in 1943 on the transatlantic link between Camp X and the UK. [VERIFIED — the Wikipedia first-party read this pass (1943 service, Bayly/BSC, Rockefeller Center naming, Rockex II dates, Hanslope production, Borehamwood secrecy, Treasury 1951, service to 1973/mid-1980s); CORROBORATED — the Telekrypton origin, the 1933 Western Union build, the two warehouse machines, and the January/May/July 1942 lines per CryptoMuseum and jproc, agreeing]

- **The service record.** Rockex I remained the standard means of enciphering and deciphering almost all SIS telegrams between London and New York throughout 1943 and 1944. Only twelve Mk1 machines were ever built. The improved Rockex II was prototyped in New York and trialled in England in June 1944; one-time-tape production was managed by the War Office and monitored by GC&CS, and the machines were built by the Radio Security Service at Hanslope Park until 31 December 1946, under Brigadier Sir Richard Gambier-Parry — who then ran the post-war operation as a personal lease on a small factory at No. 4 Chester Road, Borehamwood, hiring through the local labour exchange as an ostensibly private venture, so secret that the UK Treasury did not discover it until 1951 and found that no financial auditing had ever been exercised over it. The machines went on serving British consulates and embassies until 1973, a few until the mid-1980s; Canada ran the Mk III and Mk V, and at Coverdale the system was replaced in the late 1950s by the BID-30/5-UCO online cryptosystem. It ran at 75 words a minute — 45.5 baud to Camp X, 50 baud for embassy traffic — and a slitter on the key-tape transmitter cut the tape apart at the feed holes as it fed, so a key tape physically could not be used twice. [VERIFIED — the Wikipedia first-party read (Rockex II dates, Hanslope to 31 Dec 1946, Borehamwood, Treasury 1951, T220/1444, service to 1973/mid-1980s); CORROBORATED — the twelve Mk1, the Bletchley Park Mk2, the 75 wpm, the baud rates, the slitter, and the BID-30 replacement per jproc/Coverdale]

- **Worked miniature (computed this pass).** Rockex is a Vernam machine: plaintext XOR keystream, both as 5-bit ITA2 (Murray) code. Take HELLO — H 00101, E 10000, L 01001, L 01001, O 00011 — and a keystream drawn with fixed seed 1943: 00011, 11000, 11111, 01111, 10110. XOR gives 00110, 01000, 10110, 00110, 10101 — which decodes as N, **01000**, F, N, Y. The second character, 01000, is not a letter in ITA2 at all: raw Vernam on teletype code produces untransmittable characters, and that is exactly the problem Bayly's redesign solved — the modified combining logic suppressed every functional so the output was always letters in five-letter groups. XOR the ciphertext with the same keystream and HELLO returns — round-trip verified this pass. The scale of the problem: across 10,000 random five-character keystreams, 64.2% yield at least one non-letter output — the raw machine fails its own formatting requirement most of the time, and Bayly's fix is what made the machine usable on commercial circuits. [VERIFIED — the encoding, the XOR, the non-letter, and the round-trip computed this pass; the 64.2% figure computed this pass over 10,000 seeded trials]

- **The honest blank.** A one-time pad is unbreakable in theory — Shannon proved it in 1949 — and Rockex was a one-time pad that went to work, so the machine itself has no break to recount. What it has is a report: shortly after the war it was reported that the US government had broken the UK's automated one-time-pad system (Telekrypton/Rockex) on the New York–UK link. If true, the break was not in the XOR — it was in the tape: the system's real problem, stated by every account, was producing and distributing vast quantities of genuinely random keystream tape, twin master tapes turned out at Hanslope from 1944 to 1947, early tapes hand-punched, the electronic random generator (Don Horwood, GCHQ, ex-COLOSSUS) arriving only after the war. A one-time pad fails the moment a tape is reused or its "randomness" is not random — and a system whose factory the Treasury did not know existed until 1951 is a system whose key discipline lived entirely on trust. [CLAIMED — the US-break report, single secondary (jproc, "it was reported"); CORROBORATED — the tape-production problem, the Hanslope twin tapes, and Horwood's post-war generator per jproc; the Shannon 1949 proof per the standard record]

- **Decoder-design note (Rockex → Gauntlet).** Four rungs. (1) **The tape is the cipher.** Rockex is an XOR gate with a paper feed — the machine contributes nothing to security, and everything lives in the key tape's randomness and single use. Gauntlet rule: interrogate key production before the mechanism — a specimen whose algorithm is trivially strong is graded on its key discipline, and the interrogator's first question is "who made the tape, and how random is it," not "how does it work." (2) **Offline is a feature.** No live key exchange, no handshake, no session to hijack — the attack surface is the tape's custody chain, Hanslope to Borehamwood to embassy, and the Treasury's 1951 discovery is a custody fact: the factory was secret even from the government's own auditors. Gauntlet rule: map the custody chain before the circuit — a specimen that moves its key on paper has a supply chain, and the supply chain is the specimen. (3) **The slitter is the doctrine in hardware.** The machine cuts the key tape apart as it feeds, so reuse is physically impossible rather than procedurally forbidden. Gauntlet rule: a specimen that enforces single-use mechanically is graded differently from one that asks the operator to remember — hardware enforcement is a property, policy enforcement is a hope. (4) **"Unbreakable" is a property of the system, not the machine.** The US-break report, if true, broke the tape discipline, not the XOR. Gauntlet rule: never grade a specimen's algorithm in isolation — grade the algorithm plus the key discipline plus the custody chain, because the break, when it comes, arrives through the weakest of the three. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's doctrine, never run]

## The Maya glyphs (3rd c. BCE–16th c. CE) — the script that was read as an alphabet for four hundred years, or: the syllables hiding in the alphabet

- **The gap this entry closes.** One passing mention in each catalogue — the Tangut line's "hieroglyphs/Mayan/cuneiform-class scripts" — and nothing else: no entry, no bullet, no name. Knorosov, Proskouriakoff, Landa, Schele, Palenque: zero hits on either side; the four Thompson hits are Ken Thompson (UTF-8) and a Linear B source citation, and the two "round tables" are NIST's. The only substantially deciphered writing system of Mesoamerica — called "likely the last of the great archaeological decipherments" (*Discovering Archaeology*, 1999) — was absent from the catalogue while Egyptian hieroglyphs, cuneiform, and Linear B are filed. [VERIFIED — the 1/1 passing-mention grep and the 0/0 name greps, measured this pass]

- **The script.** Maya writing is logosyllabic: logograms (whole words and morphemes) plus syllabic signs (consonant-vowel syllables), written in blocks arranged in paired columns, read left to right and top to bottom, each block read top-to-bottom, left-to-right within itself. The inventory runs to roughly 800 distinct signs — over 1,000 noted by epigraphers, 300–500 in use in any one period, about 550 logograms and about 150 syllabograms by one count, about 200 syllabic signs by another. The earliest identifiable inscriptions date to the 3rd century BCE (San Bartolo, Guatemala); the script stayed in continuous use until the Spanish conquest in the 16th century. Three bark-paper codices survive — Dresden, Madrid, Paris — alongside thousands of stone monuments, ceramics, and murals. About 90% of the writing can now be read with varying degrees of certainty. [VERIFIED — the logosyllabic structure, block layout, 3rd-c.-BCE San Bartolo origin, the three codices, and the ~90% figure per Wikipedia's Maya script article; CORROBORATED — the sign inventories (800 / 1,000+ / 300–500 / 550+150 / ~200) across secondary accounts, which disagree on counting method]

- **The arsonist's key.** In July 1562 at Maní, Yucatán, the Franciscan bishop Diego de Landa burned the Maya books he could seize — then, recalled to Spain to answer for it, wrote the *Relación de las cosas de Yucatán* (~1566) to justify himself, including a description of the writing system and a list of 27 glyphs matched to Spanish letters: his "Maya alphabet." For four centuries it was useless, because it is not an alphabet. When Landa spoke a letter's name — "be" for B — his informant wrote the syllable he heard: /be/. The list's own shape gives it away: six letters are duplicated (A three times; B, L, O, U, X twice each — 13 of the 27 entries), and four entries are not letters at all (CA, PP, CU, KU). An alphabet does not list A three times or include two-letter entries; a syllabary recorded through Spanish letter-names does exactly that. [VERIFIED — the 27-entry list, its duplicates, and its multi-letter entries, quoted and counted this pass; CORROBORATED — the 1562 Maní burning, the ~1566 *Relación*, and the "be"-for-B mechanism per standard histories]

- **The break: Knorosov, then Proskouriakoff.** Yuri Knorosov (1922–1999), a Soviet linguist who had worked from a facsimile of the Dresden Codex, published *"Drevnyaya pis'mennost' Tsentral'noy Ameriki"* in 1952: treat Landa's signs as syllables, not letters, and the script is logosyllabic — the same phonetic principle already proven in Egyptian and cuneiform, which the field had refused to apply to Maya. His synharmony principle: a CVC word is written with two CV syllables whose vowels echo each other, the second vowel silent — so *b'alam* "jaguar" is written *b'a-la-ma*, the final *a* unpronounced. He defended the dissertation in Moscow on March 29, 1955; the monograph *The Writing of the Maya Indians* followed in 1963. The West, led by J. Eric S. Thompson, held the ideographic line for another decade. The second break came from Tatiana Proskouriakoff (1960): at Piedras Negras she showed the inscriptions' date patterns were life histories — births, accessions, deaths of named rulers — so the glyphs recorded history, not only astronomy. The consolidation was collaborative: the first Palenque Round Table (*Mesa Redonda*) in 1973, then Schele, Mathews, Lounsbury, David Stuart, and a generation of epigraphers through the 1970s–80s, until the reading stood. [CORROBORATED — the 1952 paper, the 1955 defense, the 1963 monograph, Proskouriakoff 1960 at Piedras Negras, the 1973 Round Table, and Thompson's opposition per standard histories; the "be"-for-B and synharmony mechanics per the same]

- **Worked miniature (computed this pass).** Three counts, all from the quoted material. (1) **The Landa audit.** The 27-entry list carries 20 distinct labels; 6 labels are duplicated (A×3, B/L/O/U/X×2) covering 13 entries, and 4 entries are multi-letter (CA, PP, CU, KU). An alphabet with 13 of 27 entries duplicated and 4 entries that are not letters is not an alphabet — it is a syllabary seen through letter-names. (2) **The synharmony filter.** Five vowels give 5×5 = 25 vowel pairs for a two-syllable spelling, and only the 5 diagonal pairs (a-a, e-e, i-i, o-o, u-u) are synharmonic — a random spelling passes the filter 20% of the time, so the filter is a real test, not a tautology: *b'a-la-ma* (a-a) passes, while a hypothetical *b'a-la-me* (a-e) would be disharmonic, and disharmonic spellings are the script's own signal that something else is going on in the final syllable (a long or glottalized vowel). (3) **The syllabary inventory check.** Five vowels × nineteen consonants = 95 possible CV syllables; the reported syllabic inventory is about 150–200 signs, i.e. 1.6–2.1× the minimal CV set — the excess is allographic variation (several signs per syllable), not a second system. The numbers close: a ~95-syllable engine inside a ~800-sign script. [VERIFIED — all three counts computed this pass from the quoted Landa list and the stated vowel/consonant inventories; the 19-consonant / 5-vowel figures per World History Encyclopedia; the ~150–200 syllabic-sign figures per secondary counts]

- **The honest blank.** About a tenth of the corpus still resists reading, and the residue is not random: unidentified logograms, regional and period variation, and the disharmonic-vowel rules are still argued among epigraphers. The deeper blank is ethical and archival: the script is readable today largely because the man who burned the libraries also wrote down the key — the surviving corpus is a fragment of a fragment, and every reading is a reading of what the fire left. No verdict here grades the decipherers; the entry records the method, not the men. [CORROBORATED — the ~90% readability figure and the survival of three codices; the fire's scale per standard histories]

- **Decoder-design note (Maya → Gauntlet).** Four rungs. (1) **The key can be written by the arsonist.** Landa destroyed the books and recorded the alphabet in the same career — the most valuable document in the decipherment was written by the man who made the decipherment necessary. Gauntlet rule: never discard a source for its author's crimes or its format's errors; interrogate the artifact, not the author — a hostile witness can still carry the true key, and the key's provenance is a separate ledger from its truth. (2) **Name the assumed family before you attack.** Four centuries of failure came from one unexamined assumption: the script was an alphabet because the key was labeled an alphabet. Knorosov's move was not a new tool but a reclassification — syllabary, not alphabet — and the evidence was sitting in the list's own duplicates. Gauntlet rule: state the assumed family explicitly ("we are treating this specimen as an alphabet") and run the negation experiment before upgrading the specimen — when the specimen's own inventory contradicts the assumed family, kill the assumption first. (3) **The echo vowel is a checksum.** Synharmony turns the second syllable's vowel into a parity bit: a spelling that violates it is either a different word or a signal about the final syllable. Gauntlet rule: look for the specimen's internal redundancy — the field that echoes another field — and treat violations as information, never as noise. (4) **History is the plaintext's register.** Proskouriakoff's break was not linguistic but generic: the texts were histories of named people, so the readings had to sound like chronicles, not star charts. Gauntlet rule: a claimed decode must fit the specimen's register — what the artifact is for — and a reading that fits the symbols but not the purpose is a Dorabella-grade failure (the catalogue's letter-budget rung, applied to genre). [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's doctrine, never run]

## Purple — the Type B Cipher Machine (1939–1945), or: the machine America rebuilt without ever seeing

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero `## ` headings in either catalogue, measured this pass — 11 hits in the private catalogue, 9 in the public, every one a passing mention. The private catalogue's entire Purple record is a single one-line bullet; the public catalogue's is a lesson line and a cross-reference. The diplomatic machine whose traffic was codenamed MAGIC, whose break was read before Pearl Harbor, and whose replica the Americans built without ever seeing the original, had no entry of its own. [VERIFIED — the 0/0 heading gap and the 11/9 mention counts, measured this pass]

- **The machine.** The "System 97 Typewriter for European Characters" (九七式欧文印字機, *kyūnana-shiki ōbun injiki*), the Type B Cipher Machine, codenamed Purple by the United States — an electromechanical device built on stepping switches, the hardware of automatic telephone exchanges, not on rotors. The machine was first used by Japan in June 1938; the Foreign Office traffic the Americans attacked began in February 1939, and ran to the end of the war. Chief designer Kazuo Tanabe, with engineers Masaji Yamamoto and Eikichi Suzuki; Suzuki suggested the stepping switch in place of the troublesome half-rotor switch of the Red machine. All messages were written in the 26-letter English alphabet — Japanese text had to be transliterated or coded first. An input plugboard permuted the keyboard letters and split them into two groups, six and twenty; the sixes were scrambled by a 6 × 25 substitution table and the twenties, far more thoroughly, by three successive 20 × 25 tables; an output plugboard reversed the permutation onto the output typewriter. The plugboard arrangement changed daily; the membership of the sixes group changed every nine days. The message indicator at the head of each message — different for every message or part of a message — specified the initial positions of the twenties switches and the stepping order: the three stages were assigned fast, medium, and slow, six possible assignments. [VERIFIED — the Wikipedia first-party read this pass]

- **The stepping.** The sixes switch stepped one position for each character enciphered or decrypted — a periodic polyalphabetic substitution with period 25. The twenties stages were bi-directional (signals ran through them in the opposite order for decryption), their order fixed, with no reflector, unlike Enigma; only the stepping arrangement could change. The rule: exactly one of the three twenties switches stepped for each character; the fast switch stepped for each character except when the sixes switch was in its 25th position, then the medium switch stepped, unless it too was in its 25th position, in which case the slow switch stepped. [VERIFIED — the Wikipedia first-party read; the carry question is this entry's honest blank, below]

- **The inheritance, and the complacency.** Purple replaced the Type A Red machine (the Type 91 typewriter, 1931), whose vowels AEIOUY were enciphered separately and permanently — a weakness the Americans already knew, since they had broken Red. Purple kept the sixes/twenties division and only rotated the sixes membership every nine days. The Imperial Japanese Navy supplied both machines to the Foreign Ministry and believed Purple unbreakable — on the advice of the mathematician Teiji Takagi, who lacked a background in cryptanalysis — and the Navy, which did not fully cooperate with the Army on cipher development, never attempted to revise it. The Red machine had been unreliable unless its half-rotor contacts were cleaned daily; Purple's stepping switches were telephone hardware, and they worked. [VERIFIED — the Wikipedia first-party read; CORROBORATED — the Takagi advice per the same article's cited history]

- **The break: sixes by April, twenties by September.** The SIS had learned in 1938 that a new diplomatic cipher was coming. Frequency analysis made six of the 26 ciphertext letters stand out from the other twenty, which were more uniformly distributed — the signature of the inherited division. The sixes cipher turned out to be polyalphabetic with 25 fixed permuted alphabets, each used in succession, and the SIS recovered all 25 permutations by 10 April 1939 — two months into the traffic. Knowing 6 of 26 letters, scattered through the message, sometimes let the rest be guessed, especially in stylized diplomatic prose; some stations lacked Type B, so the same message occasionally went out in both Type B and the already-broken Red — cribs for the twenties. The twenties permutations were, in Friedman's word, "brilliantly" chosen, and periodicities would not appear by waiting: the plugboard alphabets changed daily. The team — Friedman assigned to lead in August 1939 — developed a transform that made messages sent on different days with the same indicator into homologous messages, as if sent on the same day; six messages sharing indicator 59173 gave enough traffic on identical settings to hunt for periodicity. In September 1940 Genevieve Grotjan found evidence of cycles in the twenties, and a pair of messages on indicator 59173 was decrypted by 27 September — the day the Tripartite Pact was announced. By October 1940 one third of the 120 possible indicator settings had been recovered. Navy Lieutenant Francis Raven then found the keying rhythm underneath: the Japanese had divided the month into three 10-day periods and, within each period, used the keys of the first day with small, predictable changes. [VERIFIED — the Wikipedia first-party read, citing Friedman's 14 October 1940 preliminary report and Liza Mundy's *Code Girls*]

- **The analog: a replica built from intercepts alone.** On the September 1940 breakthrough the SIS built a machine that duplicated the behavior of the Japanese machines, though no one in the United States had any description of one — the reconstruction rested on Larry Clark's ideas. Leo Rosen built the first Purple analog in late 1940; a second went to the Navy; a third went to England in January 1941 with four American cryptologists, exchanged for British successes against German ciphers, and was later sent on to Singapore and then India; a fourth went to the Philippines; a fifth stayed with the SIS; a sixth, originally intended for Hawaii, also went to England. The Americans used four 6-level telephone switches per twenties stage; the Japanese, as the Berlin fragment later showed, used three 7-layer switches — both represented the twenties cipher identically, and neither was a two-motion Strowger switch, as is sometimes claimed. The United States obtained portions of a Purple machine from the Japanese embassy in Berlin only after Germany's defeat in 1945, and found the Japanese stepping switch almost identical in construction to the one Rosen had chosen in Washington in 1939–40. Every other Purple machine was destroyed beyond recognition by the Japanese; American occupation troops searched for survivors through 1945–52. A complete Jade machine — same family, no sixes/twenties split — was captured and stands in the National Cryptologic Museum. [VERIFIED — the Wikipedia first-party read]

- **The service record — the traffic that mattered.** The decrypted traffic was codenamed MAGIC. US cryptanalysts decrypted and translated Japan's 14-part message breaking off negotiations — due at 1 p.m. Washington time on 7 December 1941 — before the Japanese embassy in Washington had done so; decryption and typing difficulties at the embassy, and ignorance of its deadline, made the Nomura Note late. The richest vein was Berlin: ambassador General Hiroshi Oshima reported German military affairs in detail, in Purple. On 3 June 1941 Hitler told him "in every probability war with Russia cannot be avoided"; in 1944 he toured the Atlantic Wall, and on 4 September Hitler told him Germany would strike in the West, probably in November. General George Marshall called Oshima's traffic "our main basis of information regarding Hitler's intentions in Europe." The Japanese were warned: in April 1941 the German diplomat Hans Thomsen told Ribbentrop that "an absolutely reliable source" — the Soviet ambassador Umansky, who had deduced the leak from Undersecretary of State Sumner Welles — had said the Americans had broken the Japanese diplomatic cipher. The message was forwarded to Tokyo; use of the code continued, and the Americans kept reading it through the war. The Japanese learned of the break only at the postwar Congressional hearings on Pearl Harbor. The Soviets broke Purple independently in late 1941 and, with Richard Sorge's reporting, learned Japan would strike south, not north — letting Stalin move Far East forces to Moscow in time for December 1941. [VERIFIED — the Wikipedia first-party read]

- **Worked miniature (computed this pass).** Three counts, all from the stated mechanism. (1) **The sixes toy.** Take the vowel set AEIOUY — Red's fixed sixes, used here as the toy group; Purple's own sixes membership rotated every nine days — and 25 permutations of it, drawn with fixed seed 97. Twenty-six A's encipher to YOOYYOIIUYEEEIUOEYYYUIAIIY: position 1 and position 26 agree (Y), the 25-cycle closed exactly, all six letters appear in the first 25 outputs, and decryption by the inverse permutations returns the plaintext — round-trip verified. The lesson the SIS learned in two months: the sixes channel is a 25-alphabet polyalphabetic with a fixed, recoverable table, and a six-letter channel leaks its own structure by frequency before any twenties work begins. (2) **The stepping odometer.** Model the twenties motion as an odometer driven by the sixes switch — fast steps on every character except a sixes revolution, when the medium steps, and when the medium wraps, the slow steps as the carry. Over one full cycle the state returns exactly to its start at 15,625 characters — 25³, the first return, verified by simulation — with the fast switch stepping 15,000 times, the medium 625 times (25 of them wraps), and the slow 25 times. The twenties key stream therefore repeats its stepping state every 15,625 characters: long for a diplomatic message, short for a month of traffic on one indicator — which is why the homologous-message transform, not the period, was the break. (3) **The key counts.** The sixes table wires 25 permutations of 6 letters out of 6! = 720 possible; the four switches hold 25⁴ = 390,625 initial-position combinations; the stepping order has 3! = 6 assignments; and the whole of it is addressed by only 120 possible indicator settings — the indicator is a 120-entry index into a 390,625-entry position space, which is exactly the compression Raven's 10-day-period discovery exploited. [VERIFIED — the sixes toy, the 15,625-char period and the per-period step counts, and the key counts, all computed this pass; the odometer carry is a model choice, flagged below]

- **The honest blank.** The entry's one open mechanical question is the carry. Wikipedia's stepping sentence says "exactly one of the three switches stepped for each character" and "the slow switch stepped" when the medium was also in its 25th position — read literally, the medium never moves again once it reaches its 25th position: simulated this pass, it freezes at character 625 and the slow then steps every 25 characters, a motion no working machine would have and a state that never returns to its start within 40,000 characters. The odometer reading used in the miniature — the medium wraps and the slow steps as the carry, two switches moving on the carry character — is the reading the known Purple simulators implement, and it yields the clean 25³ period; but the entry has not opened Freeman, Sullivan, and Weierud's "PURPLE Revealed" (Cryptologia, 2003) to confirm the carry against the reconstruction, and the Japanese wiring diagrams are not in hand. The period figure is therefore graded as a property of the odometer model, not of the machine — and the freeze is filed, not hidden, because a compressed secondary description that contradicts its own arithmetic is itself a finding about the source. [VERIFIED — both simulations run this pass; the freeze at char 625 and the 25³ odometer period are computed facts; the carry itself is CLAIMED — simulator practice, not a primary read]

- **Decoder-design note (Purple → Gauntlet).** Four rungs. (1) **Build the analog, don't wait for the specimen.** The SIS never saw a Purple machine until 1945 and read its traffic from 1940 — the replica was built from intercepted behavior alone, stepping-switch choice and all, and the Berlin fragment later confirmed the guess. Gauntlet rule: a specimen whose behavior is fully specified by its outputs does not need to be captured before it is interrogated — the interrogator builds the analog from the wire and tests the analog, and custody of the original is a confirmation step, not a prerequisite. (2) **The inherited division is the break.** Purple's fatal flaw was not its own mechanism but the division it inherited from Red: six letters enciphered separately, twenty separately, and the sixes channel weak enough to fall in two months. Gauntlet rule: interrogate a specimen's lineage before its mechanism — a weakness inherited from a predecessor the adversary has already broken is a weakness the adversary already owns, and the new machine's new parts do not redeem its old ones. (3) **The indicator is the key schedule's index, not its key.** 120 indicator settings address 390,625 switch positions, and Raven's discovery — three 10-day periods, first-day keys with small predictable changes — turned the indicator from an index into a calendar. Gauntlet rule: when a specimen's key schedule is addressed by a small index, attack the index's structure (its calendar, its reuse, its predictability) before the position space it points into — the small space is where the break lives. (4) **The warning that changes nothing is still intelligence.** Berlin told Tokyo in April 1941 that the cipher was broken, and Tokyo kept using it; the Americans learned of the break only at postwar hearings. Gauntlet rule: a specimen's operator behavior after a compromise warning is itself a finding — continued use after warning is not evidence the warning was wrong, it is evidence about the operator — and the interrogator records the warning and the continuation on separate ledgers, never letting the second erase the first. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's doctrine, never run]

## The Great Cipher (Grand chiffre, ~1680s–1893) — the nomenclator that stood two centuries and fell to a crib

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero `## ` headings in either catalogue, measured this pass — "Great Cipher" on 3 lines (4 occurrences) in the private catalogue and 4 lines in the public, "Grand Chiffre" on 12 lines (13 occurrences) private and 8 lines (9 occurrences) public, every one a passing mention or a doctrine citation. The doctrine cites it everywhere: the tokenization ladder (Z340, Copiale, Grand Chiffre, Linear B, ADFGVX, Playfair), the hostile-carrier rung, the crib-first rule — and the Bazeries entry even calls it "the catalogue's Grand Chiffre entry," a citation that pointed at a bullet, not an entry. The cipher that stood two centuries, and the break that proved the tokenization doctrine, had no numbered home. This entry also repairs that citation: the Bazeries entry's reference now points at a real entry. [VERIFIED — the 0/0 heading gap and the line/occurrence counts, measured this pass]

- **The machine.** The *Grand chiffre* was a nomenclator built by Antoine Rossignol and his son Bonaventure, cryptographers to the French court for generations — Antoine's reputation dated to 1626, when he broke a captured Huguenot letter from Réalmont the same day it was taken. The basis of the code Bazeries cracked was a set of 587 numbers, each standing for a French syllable — not a letter, not a word, a sounded syllable — layered with nulls to blunt frequency analysis and deliberate traps, including a code group that told the decryptor to *ignore the previous one*. The family varied the book across generations: one nomenclator carried thousands of symbols with only 587 distinct values (redundant numbers for the same syllable), and in another 131 of 711 code numbers stood for the sound of the letter "E" alone. Modified forms stayed in French military use until the summer of 1811 — roughly 130 years of service. [VERIFIED — the Wikipedia first-party read this pass; CORROBORATED — the 131-of-711 "E" figure and the redundant-numbers detail per the SSL Store explainer]

- **The silence.** When the Rossignols died the method died with them: no key survived, no description of the system, and the archive documents sat unreadable for two centuries. The silence is the cipher's second achievement — it outlived its makers by longer than it served them, 1893 − 1682 = 211 years from the Rossignol generation to the break. And the silence is not fully over: much of the enciphered material in the French archives remains unread today, because Bazeries broke the *system*, not every document. [VERIFIED — the 1811 end of use and the ~1893 break per Wikipedia; CLAIMED — "much remains undecrypted" per the SSL Store explainer, a secondary]

- **The break: Bazeries, three years, one crib.** Commandant Étienne Bazeries — the hobbyist solver who in 1890 had broken the French military's official transposition system and forced its replacement — spent about three years on the Great Cipher and cracked it around 1893. He tried the competent theories first: a homophonic reading (587 numbers for 26 letters, ~23 homophones per letter, which would have flattened the frequencies flat — they were not flat), then digraphs (587 observed numbers against 676 possible letter-pairs, close enough to look plausible, wrong enough to fail). The realization was a reclassification, not a new tool: the numbers stood for French *syllables*. The beachhead was a repeated sequence, 124-22-125-46-345, which he guessed stood for *les ennemis* — "the enemies," syllabified les-en-ne-mi-s, five numbers for five syllables — and from that information the whole cipher unravelled. One decrypted message touched the Man in the Iron Mask mystery: a letter between Louis XIV and his marshal Nicolas de Catinat about General Vivien de Bulonde, who was to attack the Italian town of Cuneo but fled, fearing the arrival of the Austrians, endangering the French campaign in Piedmont. Bazeries verified that Bulonde was disgraced and removed from command, and reasoned that 330 and 309 stood for *masque* and a full stop — the identification of the masked prisoner as Bulonde. [VERIFIED — the 1893 break, the three-year effort, the syllable realization, and the 124-22-125-46-345 les ennemis crib per the Wikipedia first-party read; CLAIMED — the Bulonde identification, disputed]

- **Worked miniature (computed this pass).** Three counts, fixed seed 1893, toy nomenclator of 40 syllables. (1) **The inventory test.** 587 is 86.8% of the 676 digraph space — close enough that the digraph hypothesis looked live, yet 89 digraph values the hypothesis needs never appear; the homophonic reading needs 22.58 numbers per letter and predicts near-flat frequencies the traffic does not show; the syllable reading is 1:1, 587 numbers for ~587 syllables. The inventory size alone kills two of the three hypotheses before any statistics run. (2) **The crib cascade.** Two toy messages share the phrase *les ennemis*: A = "les ennemis marchent sur Paris," B = "les ennemis sont dans la plaine." Their ciphertexts share exactly one repeated 5-gram — 859-967-510-672-317, the toy's *les-en-ne-mi-s* — and no other 5-gram repeats. Guessing that one sequence (the Bazeries move) fixes five codebook entries, and the crib alone recovers 5/10 groups (50%) of message A and 6/10 (60%) of message B, the extra point coming from *ne* recurring inside *plai-ne* — the crib unlocks more than its own phrase, because syllables recur across words and the recovery cascades. (3) **The trap and the nulls.** A stream carrying a fake syllable *te* followed by trap group 700 decodes naively as "les en ne mi te ? s mar chent sur pa ris" — the analyst who does not know the trap reads a syllable that was never sent, plus an unknown. Applied correctly, the trap deletes the previous group and the stream reads clean: "les en ne mi s mar chent sur pa ris," round-trip verified. And with 4 nulls planted in a 14-group stream (28.6% null share), the most frequent number in the observed stream is a null — 802, twice — so the frequency table's top entry carries no plaintext at all. Nulls do not merely dilute the signal; they can *become* the signal. [VERIFIED — the inventory ratios (86.8%, 89 missing, 22.58/letter), the unique shared 5-gram (859-967-510-672-317), the 50%/60% crib-cascade recoveries, the naive-vs-correct trap decodes, and the null-as-top-frequency count (802 ×2, 28.6% null share), all computed this pass]

- **The honest blank.** Three confessions. (1) **The inventory figure wobbles across secondaries.** One student write-up says 576 numbers in one place and 587 in another; Wikipedia ties 587 to "the basis of the code cracked by Bazeries." This entry takes 587 as CORROBORATED, not VERIFIED — the count that matters (syllable-scale, not letter- or digraph-scale) is stable across the disagreement, and the miniature's ratios use 587 as the stated figure. (2) **The Iron Mask identification is disputed.** Bulonde's disgrace is on the record; that he was the masked prisoner is Bazeries' inference, still argued — filed CLAIMED, never as the entry's verdict. [CORROBORATED — the 587 figure per Wikipedia; CLAIMED — the Bulonde identification and the "much remains undecrypted" note per secondaries]

- **Decoder-design note (Great Cipher → Gauntlet).** Four rungs. (1) **The tokenization ladder gains its home entry.** Z340, Copiale, Grand Chiffre, Linear B, ADFGVX, Playfair — the ladder's third link was a citation to a bullet; it is now an entry, and the ladder's claim ("the unit of analysis precedes the statistics") has its canonical syllable-scale receipt. Gauntlet rule, unchanged but now grounded: interrogate the tokenization assumption before running statistics, and cite the entry, not the bullet. (2) **Traps are the carrier fighting back.** Nulls blunt the statistics; the ignore-previous group actively punishes the analyst who reads literally — the 17th-century shape of the Paubox filter-biasing entry, implants that pre-poison the defending classifier. Gauntlet rule: treat a specimen's output channel as a hostile carrier first, evidence second — and a reading that cannot survive a trap-group test is a reading the carrier wrote, not the specimen. (3) **The crib is the beachhead; the cascade is the break.** Five numbers fixed 50–60% of two toy messages because syllables recur — the break is not the guess, it is what the guess unlocks. Gauntlet rule: grade a crib by its cascade (how much of the specimen's record it opens), never by the guess alone, and a crib that opens nothing is a coincidence, not a key. (4) **Custody is the cipher.** The system did not fall to mathematics for 211 years; it fell to a key schedule that was never written down and died with its keepers. Gauntlet rule: interrogate custody as a first-class axis — who holds the key schedule, what happens when they die, leave, or rotate — because a specimen whose key lives only in its operator's head is a specimen one retirement from unreadable, and the interrogator's job includes reading the key's *holders*, not just its bits. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's doctrine, never run]

## The Beale ciphers (1820s/1885– ) — the treasure that never paid, or: the book cipher that solved one third of itself

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero `## ` headings in either catalogue, measured this pass — "Beale" on 16 lines in the private catalogue and 18 in the public, every one a passing mention, a Most Wanted row, or a benchmark line. The library's own Most Wanted list (UNDECIPHERED.md) carries the ciphers as "Beale ciphers 1 & 3 | 1820s/1885 | Unsolved (2 of 3); hoax verdicts on record (2024 IACR, 2025 Bayesian analyses) | none verified," and the cipher_benchmark line lists "Beale 1&3" among its unsolved-area records — but the catalogue had no entry of its own for the most famous unsolved book cipher in America. The timeline has its home ("## 1822/1885 — The Beale ciphers: the cipher that never paid," CIPHER-TIMELINE.md); this entry is the catalogue's. [VERIFIED — the 0/0 heading gap and the 16/18 mention counts, measured this pass]

- **The story.** The whole of it comes from one pamphlet: *The Beale Papers*, published in Lynchburg, Virginia in 1885 by James B. Ward. As the pamphlet tells it, Thomas J. Beale led a party of 30 gentleman adventurers from Virginia who, hunting buffalo north of Santa Fe de Nuevo México, stumbled on a rich mine of gold and silver and spent 18 months working it. Beale was charged with carrying the yield to Virginia and burying it; after several trips he encrypted three messages — the location, a description of the treasure, and the names of the owners and their next of kin — and in 1822 entrusted an iron box holding them, with two plaintext letters, to Robert Morriss, innkeeper of Lynchburg's Washington Hotel, not to be opened unless Beale or his men failed to return within 10 years. A letter from St. Louis a few months later promised a friend would mail the key; it never arrived. Morriss opened the box in 1845, could not solve the ciphers, and decades later left the box to an unnamed friend, who — using a modified copy of the United States Declaration of Independence as the key — solved the second ciphertext and, unable to solve the other two, published all three in the 1885 pamphlet. [VERIFIED — the Wikipedia first-party read this pass]

- **The three papers.** Cipher 1, the location: 520 numbers, ranging 1–2906. Cipher 2, the contents: 762 numbers, ranging 1–1005 (Kruh counts 763 — the wobble is filed below). Cipher 3, the names and next of kin: 618 numbers, ranging 1–975. The solved second paper reads, in full: "I have deposited in the county of Bedford, about four miles from Buford's, in an excavation or vault, six feet below the surface of the ground, the following articles, belonging jointly to the parties whose names are given in number three, herewith: The first deposit consisted of ten hundred and fourteen pounds of gold, and thirty-eight hundred and twelve pounds of silver, deposited Nov. eighteen nineteen. The second was made Dec. eighteen twenty-one, and consisted of nineteen hundred and seven pounds of gold, and twelve hundred and eighty-eight of silver; also jewels, obtained in St. Louis in exchange to save transportation, and valued at thirteen thousand dollars. The above is securely packed in clay pots, with iron covers. The vault is roughly lined with stone, and the vessels rest on solid stone, and are covered with others. Paper number one describes the exact locality of the vault, so that no difficulty will be had in finding it." Totals: 2,921 pounds of gold and 5,100 pounds of silver, plus the jewels. Wikipedia's valuation: about 35,052 troy ounces of gold and 61,200 troy ounces of silver, worth about $96.3 million and $1.8 million respectively in October 2024, with the lead figure "over $60 million as of January 2025" — the library's own record carries the correction that the treasure has no verified bounty: treasure-hunting speculation, not a prize. [VERIFIED — the Wikipedia first-party read and the Campanelli 2022 table (N and ranges); the 2,921/5,100 totals computed this pass from the stated deposits; the no-verified-bounty correction per UNDECIPHERED.md]

- **The key.** A modified book cipher: each number is the position of a word in the key text, and the plaintext letter is the first letter of that word — the first number is 115, the 115th word of the Declaration is "instituted," so the first letter is "I." Beale's copy of the Declaration differed from the original, and five modifications must be applied to the original text to make the decode work: after word 154 ("institute") one word is added (the pamphlet inserts "a" before "new government"); after word 240 ("invariably") one word is removed (probably "a"); after word 466 ("houses") ten words are removed (probably "He has refused for a long time after such dissolutions"); after word 630 ("eat") one word is removed (probably "the"); after word 677 ("foreign") one word is removed (probably "their"). Plus quirks: words 78 and 79 ("self-evident," hyphenated) count as two words; the first letter of word 95 ("inalienable") is always read as "u" ("unalienable"); words 509 and 510 ("mean time") count as two; the 811th word's first letter ("fundamentally") is always read as "y"; the 1005th word's ("have") as "x." The decoded text itself carries six errors, probably transcription slips: *consistcd* (consisted), *rhousand* (thousand), *itron* (in iron), *uith* (with), *thc* (the), *varlt* (vault). The pamphlet's own printed translation on pages 20–21 differs from the actual decipherment in nine places. [VERIFIED — the Wikipedia first-party read this pass]

- **The authenticity case.** The hoax case is older than most of the solving attempts. James Gillogly's 1980 *Cryptologia* "A Dissenting Opinion" opened it; Joe Nickell's 1982 analysis in *The Virginia Magazine of History and Biography* made it scholarly — linguistic anachronisms ("stampeding" first appears in print in English in 1832; "improvise" not recorded before the 1820s), and a stylistic analysis showing the pamphlet and Beale's letters were almost certainly written by the same man: James B. Ward, himself a Mason, the pamphlet a "secret vault" allegory. Louis Kruh's *Cryptologia* "as a bamboozlement" series (1982, 1988) added the internal contradictions: Ward said he "arranged the papers in the order of their length and numbered them," yet ciphers 1, 2, and 3 contain 520, 762/763, and 618 numbers — not in length order; and cipher 3, at 618 numbers, appears too short to list 30 members' names plus their relatives' names and addresses. The Poe-authorship theory (researcher Robert Ward and others) is debunked on the record: Poe died in 1849, the pamphlet mentions the Civil War, and Poundstone's stylometric analysis found Poe's prose significantly different from the pamphlet's. Against the hoax case, Carl Hammer of Sperry UNIVAC ran the ciphers on late-1960s supercomputers and found that while poorly encoded, the two unsolved ciphers did not show the patterns of randomly chosen numbers and probably encoded an intelligible text. Two modern statistical papers sharpen the split rather than settling it. Viktor Wase (HistoCrypt 2020, "The Role of Base 10 in the Beale Papers"): the last-digit frequencies of the unsolved ciphers are non-uniform in base 10 but turn uniform in bases relatively prime to 10, while the solved cipher stays non-uniform in every base — the signature of numbers manufactured by a human in base 10, which would strongly suggest fraud. Leonardo Campanelli (2022, "A Statistical Cryptanalysis of the Beale Ciphers"): the first significant digits of cipher 2 follow an ε-Benford distribution with ε ≈ 0.15, while ciphers 1 and 3 deviate significantly from it — suggesting they are fake, or encoded by a different method than cipher 2. And the American Cryptogram Association's figure, carried by Wikipedia: applying the modified Declaration to cipher 1 yields alphabetical sequences such as *abcdefghiijklmmnohpp*, whose chances of appearing multiple times by chance are less than one in a hundred million million. [VERIFIED — the Wikipedia first-party read; CORROBORATED — the Gillogly/Nickell/Kruh/Hammer/Wase/Campanelli findings per Wikipedia's citations and the Campanelli paper's abstract and table as returned by search; the 2024 IACR and 2025 Bayesian hoax verdicts per the library's own UNDECIPHERED.md record, not re-read this pass]

- **Worked miniature (computed this pass).** Four counts, fixed seeds 1822 and 1885. (1) **The toy book cipher.** An 80-word toy key — the Declaration's opening, extended with tail words ("under vexed questions exact justice kings youth zeal xenial") so all 26 letters are covered — enciphers "vaultsixfeetdown" by the Beale rule (number = word position, take the first letter) as 73-36-72-42-68-38-8-80-11-7-33-32-52-56-1-10, and the same numbers decode back to "vaultsixfeetdown" exactly: round-trip verified. The same numbers read against the key text reversed give "iabtpovwtqgetaxs" — the numbers alone carry nothing; the key is everything, and a book cipher's security is the key text's custody. (2) **The alphabetical-run probability.** The quoted 20-letter sequence *abcdefghiijklmmnohpp* is a near-run, not a clean one: its first 17 letters (a..o) are non-decreasing, then it breaks at "h" before "pp." Exact counts over 26 letters: a 17-letter weakly increasing run has C(42,25) = 254,661,927,156 favorable sequences out of 26^17, probability ≈ 2.25×10⁻¹³ — 1 in 4.5×10¹²; a 19-letter near-run, 1 in 5.4×10¹⁴; the full 20 letters, 1 in 6.3×10¹⁵. The ACA's "less than one in a hundred million million" (10¹⁴) is the right order for a near-run of that length appearing multiple times — the sequences are structure, not chance, and they are not English. (3) **The cipher-3 capacity table.** 618 numbers must carry 30 member names + 30 heir names + 30 addresses = 90 items, i.e. 6.87 letters per item. At 7-letter names and 12-character addresses the job needs 780 numbers — short by 162. At 6-letter names and 10-character addresses it needs 660 — short by 42. Only at 5-letter names and 8-character addresses does it fit (need 540, slack 78). The capacity argument bites under ordinary name lengths — but it is a bound, not a proof: short names and abbreviated addresses could fit, and the entry does not claim otherwise. (4) **The Wase signature, modeled.** A synthetic Wase-style test (n = 2,000, seed 1885): a book-cipher stream — word positions Zipf-sampled over a 1,322-word text — has last-digit χ² = 352.1 in base 10 and 161.0 in base 7, non-uniform in both (95% critical values 16.92 and 12.59). A human-manufactured stream — numbers picked as "random-looking" decimals with digit bias toward 0, 5, 1, 7 — has χ² = 657.6 in base 10 but 5.7 in base 7: uniform. The signature reproduces exactly: a human making numbers in base 10 leaves a bias that washes out in base 7, while a genuine book-cipher stream stays skewed in every base. This is a model of Wase's test on synthetic streams, not a re-run on the real ciphers. [VERIFIED — the toy round-trip (73-36-72-42-68-38-8-80-11-7-33-32-52-56-1-10 → "vaultsixfeetdown"), the reversed-key gibberish, the run probabilities (1 in 4.5×10¹² / 5.4×10¹⁴ / 6.3×10¹⁵), the capacity table (780/660/540 vs 618), the 2,921/5,100 totals, and the synthetic χ² figures (352.1 / 161.0 / 657.6 / 5.7), all computed this pass]

- **The honest blank.** Three confessions. (1) **Cipher 2's length wobbles by one.** Wikipedia and the Campanelli table say 762 numbers; Kruh says 763. The entry uses 762 with the wobble filed — one number's difference, unresolved this pass, and it does not touch any other figure. (2) **The newest hoax verdicts are carried, not re-read.** The 2024 IACR and 2025 Bayesian analyses named in the library's UNDECIPHERED.md record are cited at that record's grade; this pass did not open either paper, so the entry does not upgrade them to VERIFIED. (3) **The alphabetical sequence breaks.** The ACA's quoted run *abcdefghiijklmmnohpp* is not a clean alphabetical run — it breaks at the "h" after "o." The entry's probabilities count the clean 17-letter prefix and the 19/20-letter near-runs separately, and the ACA's 10¹⁴ figure is an order-of-magnitude claim about such sequences appearing multiple times, not an exact single-sequence count. [CORROBORATED — the 762/763 wobble per Wikipedia and Kruh as returned by search; the 2024/2025 verdicts per the library's own record]

- **Decoder-design note (Beale → Gauntlet).** Four rungs. (1) **The solved third is the control.** Cipher 2 is the only ground truth in the set: it tells you what a genuine book cipher from this hand looks like — its ranges, its error rate, its key's five modifications and letter quirks. Gauntlet rule: never grade an unsolved specimen without a solved sibling from the same hand; the solved one is the null distribution, and every statistical test on the unsolved ones is a comparison against it, not against randomness in the abstract — Wase and Campanelli both do exactly this. (2) **A key that is a book is a key you can lose.** The Declaration is public, but Beale's modified copy is not — five insertions and deletions plus three letter quirks — and ciphers 1 and 3 may use keys that no longer exist: a document Beale wrote himself, or random characters. Gauntlet rule: interrogate the key's custody before the ciphertext's statistics — a book cipher whose key text is unrecoverable is a one-time pad with extra steps, and no amount of cryptanalysis recovers a key that was never published. (3) **Structure that is not language is a signature, not a plaintext.** The alphabetical runs in cipher 1 are too ordered to be chance and too un-English to be plaintext — they are the fingerprint of the manufacturing process. Gauntlet rule: when a specimen's output is structured but unreadable, stop asking what it says and ask how it was made — the manufacturing signature (base-10 digit bias, alphabetical runs) is evidence about the maker, and the maker is a suspect before the message is a message. (4) **The treasure is the incentive, not the evidence.** A $60M-plus prize — unverified, per the library's own record: no verified bounty — has drawn a century of digging, trespass arrests, and expeditions that found only Civil War artifacts. Gauntlet rule: price the specimen's claimed payoff separately from its evidence, and never let the size of the alleged reward raise the grade of the alleged cipher — the vault is a claim about the world, the numbers are a claim about the text, and the two ledgers never merge. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's doctrine, never run]

## The Abwehr Enigma — Enigma G / G31 (1931–1945), or: the spy machine that was simpler and harder at once

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero standalone entries in either catalogue, measured this pass — "Abwehr" on 4 lines in the private catalogue and 4 in the public, every one a passing mention or a sub-bullet inside the Cillies entry (the Spanish operator's CIL and PEG keys), never an entry of its own. The catalogue holds the military Enigma, the Lorenz, the Typex, the SIGABA, and the Bletchley attack-methods (Banburismus, Herivelismus, the Cyclometer, the Bomba, the Zygalski sheets, Cillies) — but not the machine Dilly Knox's team broke first, the one whose traffic fed the Double-Cross System. The timeline carries Enigma generally; this entry is the G model's. [VERIFIED — the 0 standalone entries and the 4/4 mention counts, measured this pass]

- **The story.** The Abwehr — Germany's military intelligence service — did not use the Wehrmacht's Enigma. It used Enigma G, factory designator Ch.15a, also called the G31: a "Zählwerksmaschine," a counter machine, developed around 1931 by Chiffriermaschinen AG in Berlin as a smaller, portable descendant of the A28 of 1928. Fewer than 350 were ever made, against the large number of plugboard military machines — and it is publicly known at all because it was the spies' machine, and because Bletchley Park unravelled it. Three survive by name: G312 in the Bletchley Park Trust collection (stolen from the Trust on 1 April 2000, front-page news); G260, found in Argentina toward the end of the war, used by the Abwehr or the Sicherheitsdienst; G110, one of a Hungarian Army shipment from 1931, buried in Poland and later conserved by the Trust, one of two surviving machines with a printer connection. [CORROBORATED — the G31/Ch.15a identity, the 1931 date, the A28 descent, the <350 production estimate, and the three survivors via CryptoMuseum and the Kenyon/Weierud abstract; the G312 theft date via the same abstract]

- **The machine: irregular by cogwheel, and the reflector that moved.** Three electrically wired rotors with 17, 15 and 11 turnover notches respectively, driven by firmly coupled cogwheels and pinion wheels — not the levers and pawls of the military machine — so the rotors could be stepped backwards or forwards in synchronism to correct errors. The settable reflector (UKW) moved during encipherment, where the military machine's reflector stood fixed. And there was no plugboard: the Steckerbrett was exclusive to the military machines. Bletchley called it the "11-15-17 machine" after the notch counts. The missing plugboard looks like a simplification; it was not one. The irregular stepping made the rotor motion harder to model than the military machine's metronome — the right rotor stepping every press, the middle every 26 — and the moving reflector meant the machine's reciprocal core was itself in motion. [CORROBORATED — the notch counts, the cogwheel drive, the backward/forward stepping, the moving settable reflector, and the absent plugboard via CryptoMuseum and Bletchley Park; the "11-15-17" nickname via both]

- **The break: rodding, and the indicator sent twice.** Dilly Knox — papyrologist, veteran of the previous war's naval codes — led the break from the Cottage at Bletchley Park with his team, Mavis Batey (née Lever) and Margaret Rock, under the section name ISK, Intelligence Service Knox. The method was rodding: an improvement of a technique Hugh Foss had developed in 1927 after analysing a commercial Enigma D — strips of slotted paper, rods, moved against one another to identify consistent letter pairs. The opening was the procedure, not the wiring: the Abwehr sent each message indicator (the message key) enciphered twice, the same weakness Rejewski had exploited on the military machine, and rodding turned the doubled indicator into a constraint on the starting position. The same operator habits the Cillies entry files — the Spanish station's keys as women's initials, CIL and PEG — were the human half of the same break. The intelligence that followed fed the Double-Cross System: rounding up and turning the Abwehr's agents in Britain, and watching their agents' activities in Spain and Portugal. [CORROBORATED — Knox, ISK and the Cottage, rodding and its Foss 1927 origin, the doubled-indicator opening, and the Double-Cross value via CryptoMuseum and the Kenyon/Weierud abstract; the CIL/PEG operator detail via this library's own Cillies entry]

- **Worked miniature (computed this pass).** Four counts, fixed seed 1941. (1) **The notch arithmetic.** 11, 15 and 17 are pairwise coprime — gcd 1 in all three pairs — so their joint alignment repeats every lcm(11, 15, 17) = 2,805 steps: 4.15× the 676-step cycle of a military Enigma's two slow rotors, and only 0.16 of the 17,576-step full rotor cycle. The number is a model of the notch-alignment period, not a claim about the machine's full state cycle — the cogwheel coupling means no single rotor's motion is periodic on its own — but it prices the difference: the G's irregularity is structured, and its structure has a period you can compute. (2) **The doubled indicator, in miniature.** A toy model — six positions, each a random permutation (seed 1941), a three-letter key JXF enciphered twice as XXCCJR. Brute-forcing the six toy offsets, exactly one is consistent — offset 0, recovering JXF. The probability behind it: one doubled pair agrees by chance with probability 1/26; three pairs, (1/26)³ = 1/17,576 — exactly the number of rotor starting positions (26³). A doubled indicator nearly uniquely identifies the start, before any Bombe, any crib, any statistics. That is the whole of Knox's opening, in arithmetic. (3) **The survival share.** Three named survivors of fewer than 350 machines: under 0.86% — the machine is rarer in the record than in the war. (4) **The traffic volume.** The popular figure of some 300,000 Abwehr messages read: over roughly 1,350 days from December 1941 to August 1945 that is about 222 a day; over a 2,000-day war, 150 a day. The arithmetic is exact; the 300,000 figure itself is a single popular carrier, graded CLAIMED below. [VERIFIED — the notch gcds and lcm, the 2,805/676/17,576 comparisons, the toy brute-force (one consistent offset, JXF recovered), the (1/26)³ = 1/17,576 identity, the <0.86% survival share, and the 222/150-per-day divisions, all computed this pass]

- **The honest blank.** Three confessions. (1) **The break date disagrees across carriers.** CryptoMuseum dates the first Abwehr break to October 1941; Wikipedia to 8 December 1941, by Knox; a popular retelling puts Knox's breakthrough in the third week of January 1940 — a date that matches the first British break into military Enigma with Polish help, and reads as a conflation of the two breaks. This entry uses the December 1941 date as the commonly cited one and files October 1941 as a near-agreeing variant; the January 1940 claim is not adopted. (2) **The Torch capture's rotor figures disagree with the standard notch counts.** Wikipedia's account of the November 1942 Operation Torch capture describes a plugboard-less machine whose rotors "had been changed to rotate 11, 15, and 19 times" — 19 where the G31's standard counts say 17. The entry carries the capture as a CORROBORATED fact and the 19 as an unresolved variant, not a correction. (3) **Two figures are carried, not verified.** The "some 300,000 messages" total and the ISK network labels GGG, ISK and ISLD come from a single popular carrier; the G312 theft's aftermath (recovery status) was not verified this pass. None of the three touches the mechanism, the break method, or the Double-Cross value. [CORROBORATED — the October/December 1941 dates and the Torch capture per CryptoMuseum and Wikipedia; CLAIMED — the 300,000 total and the network labels per a single popular carrier]

- **Decoder-design note (Abwehr Enigma → Gauntlet).** Four rungs. (1) **Simpler is not weaker, and the interrogation prices the difference.** The G has no plugboard — one whole layer fewer than the military machine — and is harder to model, because its stepping is irregular and its reflector moves. Gauntlet rule: never grade a specimen by its layer count; grade it by the predictability of its state motion. A machine with fewer parts and an irregular schedule is a different interrogation target than a machine with more parts and a metronome, and the fixture that assumes "less machinery, less work" misreads the specimen before it starts. (2) **The procedure is the attack surface, and the doubled indicator is the standing example.** The G's wiring was never the opening; the indicator procedure was — the same key sent twice, a clerical habit, not a design flaw. Gauntlet rule, confirmed again by the Cillies entry beside it: interrogate the operating procedure before the mechanism, because procedures are written by tired humans and mechanisms are written by engineers, and the tired human is the softer target. (3) **Rarity is evidence about the evidence.** Fewer than 350 machines, three named survivors: the G's public record is thin because the population was thin, not because the machine was unimportant. Gauntlet rule: a specimen with a small population gets its grades held to the surviving evidence — no extrapolation from the military Enigma's thick record onto the G's thin one, and no "unbroken" verdicts from absence. (4) **The break's value is measured downstream.** The G break's verdict is not "Knox read messages" but "the Double-Cross System ran on it" — agents turned, networks watched. Gauntlet rule: a break is graded by what it enabled, not by what it read; the specimen's threat ledger includes the operations its compromise made possible. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's doctrine, never run]

## The Enigma T — Tirpitz (1942–1945), or: the ally's machine, or: the cipher you do not hand to a friend

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero standalone entries in either catalogue, measured this pass — and zero mentions, not the seven the prior run's close-out carried: a project-wide grep for "Enigma T" and "Tirpitz" returns nothing outside the prior run's own log lines, and "JN-18", "T-258" and "T-259" return nothing at all. The prior run's "7 mentions" is not reproducible and is corrected here, not carried. The gap itself is real either way: the catalogue holds the military Enigma, the Abwehr G, the Swiss K in the NEMA lineage line, and the Bletchley attack-methods — but not the machine Germany built for Japan, the one whose traffic Bletchley named JN-18. The timeline carries Enigma generally; this entry is the T model's. [VERIFIED — the 0 standalone entries and the 0/0 mention counts, measured this pass; the correction of the prior run's "7 mentions" figure]

- **The story.** In 1942 Germany built an Enigma for communications with Japan — and built it deliberately weaker than its own. The T was based on the commercially available Enigma K: the Germans did not wish to supply another power, even an ally, with their military Enigma. Bletchley Park codenamed the machine Tirpitz and its traffic JN-18; the traffic was rarely intercepted and so difficult to break. The machine's war ended in a warehouse: in the summer of 1944 a number of T machines were captured in Normandy, awaiting shipment to Japan, and in August the Americans raided the port at Lorient in Brittany and carried away 60 of them. One survives by name: T244, in the Bletchley Park Trust collection. [CORROBORATED — the 1942 date, the K descent and the refusal to share the military machine, the Tirpitz codename, the JN-18 traffic name and its rarity and difficulty, the Normandy and Lorient captures and the 60-machine figure, and the T244 survivor via Bletchley Park and the declassified 1954 US wiring catalog]

- **The machine: eight wheels, five notches, and a scrambled front door.** Three wheels in use at a time, chosen from eight — all eight marked "T" — where the military machine chose three from five and the commercial model had three fixed. Every wheel carried five turnover notches instead of one, so the stepping was highly irregular where the commercial machine stepped like a metronome. The input sequence was fixed but neither QWERTZU nor alphabetical, and uniquely among the family, the wiring of the entry disc — the wheel that connects the keyboard to the rotors — was scrambled. The reflector moved during encipherment, as on the commercial model it descended from. (2) **Irregularity is the defense, and it is measurable.** The T's strength is not in how many substitutions it performs but in how unpredictably it steps — five notches, a scrambled entry disc, a moving reflector.
