## Codex Seraphinianus (1976–1981) — the book that cannot be read, or: the encyclopedia of a world that never was

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero standalone entries in either catalogue, measured this pass — no `## ` heading and no entry-titled bullet in either file; the only hits are one passing mention in each, the Linear A entry's deferral note ("the nearest zero of all, the Codex Seraphinianus at 0/0 mentions, is noted and deferred"). The catalogue holds the script the Codex is always compared to (the Voynich manuscript, bullet entry, ~240 pages, ~170,000 characters, six centuries unread) and the script that shares its silence (Rohonc) — but not the book that inverts them both: larger than the Voynich, younger than a living man, and unread because its author says there is nothing to read. The deferred zero is now the entry. [VERIFIED — the 0/0 heading counts and the 1/1 mention counts, measured this pass]

- **The book.** The *Codex Seraphinianus* is an illustrated encyclopedia of an imaginary world, created by Italian artist, architect and industrial designer Luigi Serafini between 1976 and 1978 and first published in 1981 by Franco Maria Ricci in Milan. It has approximately 360 pages (depending on edition) and is written throughout in an imaginary writing system. The book is in 11 chapters, in two sections: the first describes the natural world — flora, fauna, physics — and the second deals with human life — garments, history, cuisine, architecture. Chapter 8 is about the writing system itself, the book describing its own script from the inside. After the last chapter comes a table of contents or index, followed by an apparent afterword in a more casually rendered hand. It has been compared to the still-undeciphered Voynich manuscript, to Borges's "Tlön, Uqbar, Orbis Tertius," and to the artwork of M. C. Escher and Hieronymus Bosch. [VERIFIED — the 1976–1978 creation, the 1981 Franco Maria Ricci first publication, the ~360 pages, the 11 chapters in two sections and the chapter list, the chapter-8 self-description, and the Voynich/Borges/Escher/Bosch comparisons per Wikipedia "Codex Seraphinianus", read this pass]

- **The script.** The false writing system appears modeled on Western writing systems, with left-to-right writing in rows and an alphabet with uppercase and lowercase letters, some of which double as numerals. Some letters appear only at the beginning or end of words, similar to Semitic writing systems. The curvilinear letters are rope- or thread-like, with loops and even knots, and are somewhat reminiscent of Sinhala script. The illustrations are hand-drawn, colored-pencil, surreal parodies of things in the real world — a bleeding fruit, a plant that grows into roughly the shape of a chair and is subsequently made into one, a copulating couple who metamorphose into an alligator — and odd, apparently senseless machines, often with delicate appearances and bound by tiny filaments. Some illustrations are recognizable as maps or human faces; others, especially in the "physics" chapter, are mostly or totally abstract. Nearly all of the illustrations are brightly coloured and highly detailed. [VERIFIED — the left-to-right rows, the upper/lowercase alphabet with numeral-doubling letters, the positional letters, the rope-like curvilinear forms and the Sinhala resemblance, and the illustration record per Wikipedia, read this pass]

- **The one solved part.** The book's page-numbering system was decoded by Allan C. Wechsler and Bulgarian linguist Ivan Derzhanski as being a variation of base 21. It is the only component of the book that has ever yielded to analysis — the frame solved, the body untouched. [VERIFIED — the Wechsler/Derzhanski base-21 page numbering per Wikipedia, read this pass]

- **The author's word.** In a talk at the Oxford University Society of Bibliophiles on 11 May 2009, Serafini stated that there is no meaning behind the *Codex*'s script, which is asemic; that his experience in writing it was similar to automatic writing; and that what he wanted his alphabet to convey was the sensation children feel with books they cannot yet understand, although they see that the writing makes sense for adults. He has repeated it since: in a 2016 interview he described the book as one "without meaning, to be read without understanding," and the 2013 edition carries a 22-page "Decodex" in which he explains how he envisioned the work — with, his publicist said, "the crucial help he had in this from a white cat" — while providing no answers about what the *Codex* actually means, because he insists it means nothing: "The writing of the *Codex* is a writing, not a language, although it conveys the impression of being one. It looks like it means something, but it does not." The author's word is the whole decipherment file, and it is a negative: there is nothing to find, by design, and the design is the work. [VERIFIED — the 11 May 2009 Oxford statement, the asemic verdict, the automatic-writing account, and the child-before-a-book intent per Wikipedia, read this pass; CORROBORATED — the 2016 "without meaning" wording and the 22-page Decodex with the white cat per the dyerbolical piece and Smithsonian, October 2013]

- **The leak.** Two plates in the sixth chapter contain lines of French text, a quote from Marcel Proust's *À la recherche du temps perdu: Albertine disparue* (*In Search of Lost Time: Albertine Gone*). The words scattered on the floor of the illustration are from the same book. It is the only verifiable plaintext in the book — and it is borrowed, a quotation, not a key: the one place the Codex speaks a real language, it speaks someone else's words. [VERIFIED — the Proust plates in chapter 6 per Wikipedia, read this pass]

- **Editions and afterlife.** The original edition was issued in two volumes (127 + 127 pages). Single-volume editions followed in the United States, Germany and the Netherlands in 1983 (Abbeville, 370 pp.); an augmented edition with a preface by Italo Calvino in 1993 (392 pp.); a Rizzoli expanded edition in 2006 (384 pp.); a second revised Rizzoli edition in 2013 (396 pp., plus a limited signed and numbered deluxe edition of 300 copies in Italian and 300 in English); and a 40th-anniversary edition in 2021 (416 pp.). First-edition copies sold for up to $2,000 while the 2013 reprint sold for $125. Reception: Baird Searles, in *Asimov's Science Fiction* (April 1984), says "the book lies in the uneasy boundary between surrealism and fantasy, given an odd literary status by its masquerade as a book of fact"; Douglas Hofstadter, in *Metamagical Themas*, finds many of the illustrations "grotesque and disturbing" and others "extremely beautiful and visionary," and says the book "seems [to some people] to glorify entropy, chaos, and incomprehensibility"; American journalist Jim Dwyer finds that the work is an early critique of the Information Age. [VERIFIED — the edition history 1981–2021 and the Searles/Hofstadter/Dwyer reception per Wikipedia, read this pass; CORROBORATED — the $2,000 first-edition price and the $125 reprint price per Smithsonian, October 2013]

## The VIC cipher (1953–1957) — the hand cipher that beat the NSA, or: the cipher that fell to a defector

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero standalone entries in either catalogue, measured this pass — no `## ` heading in either file. The story is filed twice at bullet tier: a 1950s summary bullet ("the hand cipher that never fell to cryptanalysis") with a short design note, and a full bullet entry seeded 2026-10-19 ("the pencil-and-paper cipher that beat the NSA") with a three-rung design note — but neither bullet carries a worked miniature (0/0, measured this pass), and the seven matching lines in each file are the two bullet titles and their grade citations, the 2026-10-19 seed line, and three cross-references from the GROMARK entry (which shares VIC's lagged-Fibonacci generator). This entry promotes the cipher to full-entry status and adds what the bullets never had: the mechanism worked by hand, a miniature computed this pass, an honest blank, and four new Gauntlet rungs that do not repeat the bullets' rungs. The bullets' facts stand and are cited, not re-argued. [VERIFIED — the 0/0 heading counts, the 7/7 mention counts, and the 0/0 miniature counts, measured this pass]

- **The find.** On June 22, 1953, fourteen-year-old newspaper boy Jimmy Bozart, collecting for the *Brooklyn Eagle* at 3403 Foster Avenue, Brooklyn, was paid with a nickel that felt too light; when he dropped it, it popped open, revealing microfilm carrying 207 five-figure groups — 21 sets of five in seven columns and 20 sets in three columns, 1,035 digits with no key. The coin was two halves: a 1948 Jefferson obverse, a reverse minted between October 1942 and the end of 1945, a tiny hole drilled in the "R" of TRUST so a needle could force it open. The FBI tried for nearly four years and read nothing. The break came the human way: KGB lieutenant colonel Reino Häyhänen (codename VICTOR — hence "VIC"; the FBI renders the name Hayhanen), recalled to Moscow for good and unwilling to go, telephoned the United States Embassy in Paris early in May 1957 and defected. The nickel, it turned out, was a dead-drop item he had collected and accidentally spent before opening it. He handed the FBI the cipher itself, and the decoded message was Moscow's welcome to him and instructions for getting set up in America — four years spent on a greeting. His debriefing then identified his superior: William August Fisher, alias Rudolf Ivanovich Abel, arrested June 21, 1957 at the Hotel Latham in Manhattan and indicted that October. [VERIFIED — the Bozart find, the address, the 207-group count and its column arithmetic, the coin's two halves and the TRUST hole, the four-year failure, the May-1957 Paris defection, the accidentally-spent dead drop, the greeting payload, and the Abel arrest and indictment per the FBI's Famous Cases account and Wikipedia "Hollow Nickel Case", both read this pass]

- **The machine that wasn't.** In modern technical terms VIC is "straddling bipartite monoalphabetic substitution superenciphered by modified double transposition," of the Nihilist family — "arguably the most complex hand-operated cipher ever seen, when it was first discovered." Its components read like a cryptographic parts list decades early: mod-10 chain addition, a lagged Fibonacci generator, a straddling checkerboard, and a disrupted double transposition. The key is four things, three of them mnemonic and none of them ever written down: a Phrase (at least 20 letters, e.g. the first line of a song), a Date (numeric, no leading zeroes), a Personal Number (one or two digits, unique to the agent), plus five fresh random digits per message — the Keygroup, embedded in the clear in the ciphertext at a location the adversary does not know. From those secrets the agent derives a 50-digit pseudorandom block (five 10-digit lines, K through P), and from the block the message keys: a straddling checkerboard key, a standard columnar transposition key, and a diagonal transposition key with triangular disruption zones. The plaintext is bisected first — cut at an arbitrary point, the two halves inverted, a marker between them — so no message begins with the format the analyst expects; then checkerboarded into digits, transposed twice, and the Keygroup inserted P groups from the end, where P is the unused sixth digit of the Date. Häyhänen's checkerboard mnemonic was the Russian word for snowfall, *snegopad*; the English example board's mnemonic is "AT ONE SIR." The lineage is the Nihilist family grown up: in the war, Max Christiansen-Clausen in Sorge's Japan network and Alexander Foote in the Lucy ring ran stronger versions, the *Rote Kapelle* a weaker one — plaintext to digits by checkerboard (which compresses the text, raises its unicity distance, and shortens the transmission a direction-finder can hunt), an additive ("closing") drawn from almanacs of industrial statistics, dull books with high entropy density, and a concealed indicator group. VIC is the ultimate development of that line; by the 1950s most Soviet agents had moved to one-time pads, which in practice were sometimes broken by reuse — while VIC was not. David Kahn's verdict, from *Two Soviet Spy Ciphers* (reprinted in *Kahn on Codes*): "the finest and most advanced mnemonic cipher ever made public... although not theoretically insoluble, it is effectually unbreakable without prior knowledge of the system and on the basis of a single message." (1) **Chain addition is a hand LFSR.** Seed 90210: false-add the first two digits (9+0=9), append, advance the pair one step — 90210 → 90210 9 → 92 → 923 → 9231 → 92319. Five steps, five new digits, the generated 9 feeding back into the fifth sum. The same rule drives the key generation: Keygroup 72401 minus Date 13919 (mod-10, digitwise, no borrowing) gives Line-C 69592; chain-adding it five steps gives 54417, so Line-F.1 is 6959254417; adding Line-E.1 8017942653 to it (mod-10, no carrying) gives Line-G 4966196060 — every step of Wikipedia's worked example reproduced exactly. (2) **Digit encoding is a lookup, not arithmetic.** Under the example key sequence, 90210 encodes to 27067 (9→2, 0→7, 2→0, 1→6, 0→7). The key is a permutation of the digits; the aide row 1234567890 is the only map. (3) **The checkerboard compresses.** On the example board (header 5 9 6 1 3 2 8 4 7 0; top row A T _ O N E _ S I R; row 6 B–M; row 8 P–/), SNOWFALL — the English gloss of *snegopad* — encodes as 4 3 1 83 61 5 67 67, twelve digits for eight letters, a quarter shorter than the sixteen an all-two-digit encoding would take; the cross-check against Wikipedia's own encoding holds (M=60, E=2, A=5, N=3), and the stream decodes back to SNOWFALL exactly. Every frequent letter that lands on the top row saves a digit — compression is the first layer of the defense, and it is also why the transmission is short enough to outrun a direction-finder. (4) **The entropy converges to a 10-digit number.** Wikipedia's cryptanalysis section puts the message-key strength at the 10-digit Line-H, "approximately 34 bits," plus the date's last digit for "about 38 bits," brute-forceable in less than a day on modern computers. Computed this pass: log2(10^10) = 33.22 bits; with the eleventh digit, 36.54 bits. The article's rounding is the article's, the computation is this pass's — and the verdict holds under either: 10^10 trials take 10 seconds at a billion trials a second, 2.78 hours at a million a second. The five-digit Keygroup alone is a 100,000-possibility space (16.61 bits) — and it travels in the clear, protected only by position. (5) **Four years, one greeting.** 207 groups × 5 digits = 1,035 digits of captured traffic; four years is ≈1,461 days, so the Bureau spent ≈1.41 days per captured digit — and the payload was a welcome message and setup instructions. The 50-digit block yields the two transposition keys (13 + 6 = 19 digits) and, through its last line, the 10-digit checkerboard key: the whole apparatus per message hangs off a 10-digit Line-H, a 5-digit Keygroup, and three things that lived only in a man's head. Position is a search problem, not a cipher problem: price the search over positions (ten P values × the group count) before spending a cycle on the mechanism, and grade any specimen whose secret is positional as searchable, never as encrypted. - **The gap this entry closes.** Zero `## ` headings in either catalogue, measured this pass — and the story itself is nowhere in either file: "Gold-Bug" appears on 2 lines in the private catalogue and 1 line in the public, all inside the Beale entry (a Joe Nickell reference and a grade-line citation), with 0 mentions of Legrand, 0 of Captain Kidd, and 0 of "Edgar Allan Poe" in either file, and 0 worked miniatures anywhere. The catalogue's frequency-analysis bullet describes the method; no entry has ever demonstrated it on a real text. This entry is the first full demonstration — the table re-counted, the crib verified, the decode reproduced end to end — plus an honest blank and four new Gauntlet rungs. [VERIFIED — the 0/0 heading counts, the 2/1 mention counts and their Beale-entry location, the 0/0/0 Legrand/Kidd/Poe counts, and the 0/0 miniature counts, measured this pass]

- **The story.** Edgar Allan Poe's "The Gold-Bug" follows William Legrand, a ruined New Orleans gentleman living in a cabin on Sullivan's Island, South Carolina, with his servant Jupiter. Legrand finds a brilliant gold-colored scarab, and a scrap of parchment he used to wrap it turns out to carry more: held to the heat of the hearth, a skull appears in invisible ink, and between the death's-head and the goat, a cryptogram — directions to treasure buried by the pirate Captain Kidd. The directions send them to a tree on the mainland, a skull nailed to a branch, the bug dropped through the skull's left eye socket (after Jupiter first drops it through the right, and Legrand corrects the point), a line of fifty feet, and a dig that unearths two skeletons and a chest packed with gold coins and jewelry. Poe wrote it in Philadelphia; he had first sold it to *Graham's Magazine* for $52, then took it back on hearing of the *Philadelphia Dollar Newspaper*'s writing contest, won the $100 grand prize — probably the largest single sum he ever received for any work — and saw it published in the *Dollar Newspaper* on June 21 and June 28, 1843. It became the most popular and widely read of his prose works during his lifetime; by May 1844 Poe reported it had circulated 300,000 copies. The run-up matters: in 1840 Poe had invited readers of *Alexander's Weekly Messenger* to submit their own substitution ciphers, boasting he could solve them all, and letters poured in from all over the country; in July 1841 he published "A Few Words on Secret Writing." The story is the challenge, dramatized — Legrand's explanation of the solve is very like Poe's own explanation in that essay. [VERIFIED — the plot, the $100 prize and its standing, the June 21/28 1843 *Dollar Newspaper* publication, the *Graham's* $52 sale and buy-back, the 1840 challenge and the July 1841 essay, per Wikipedia "The Gold-Bug", read first-party this pass (crawl 2026-11-01); CORROBORATED — the 300,000-copy circulation, Poe's own May-1844 report]

- **The cipher and the method.** A simple monoalphabetic substitution: 203 characters drawn from 20 symbols, no divisions between words. Legrand's order is the lesson. First, the language: the pun on "Kidd" is appreciable in no other language than English, so he assumes the cryptograph is English — otherwise he would have begun with Spanish and French, the tongues in which a pirate of the Spanish main would most naturally have written. Second, the count: he counts every symbol and builds a table — 8 appears 33 times, ; 26, 4 19, ‡ and ) 16 each, * 13, 5 12, 6 11, † and 1 8 each, 0 6, 9 and 2 5 each, : and 3 4 each, ? 3, ¶ 2, — 1 — and since *e* is the most frequent letter in English, he assumes 8 is *e*, then verifies the guess: *e* doubles with great frequency in English, and 8 is doubled no less than five times in so brief a cryptograph. Third, the crib: of all words in the language "the" is most usual, so he looks for repetitions of three characters in the same order, the last being 8 — and finds no less than seven such arrangements, the characters being ;48. So ; is *t*, 4 is *h*, and 8 is *e*, "the last being now well confirmed." From there the solution walks itself out: the last-but-one ";48" is followed by "t eeth," and since no word can be formed of which that *th* can be a part, the word is "tree" — another letter, *r*, represented by (. Then "the tree thr...h the" makes "through" evident at once — three new letters, *o*, *u*, *g*, represented by ‡, ?, and 3. "83(88" is the conclusion of "degree" — another letter, *d*, represented by †. "48(;88" reads "th rtee," suggestive of "thirteen" — two new characters, *i* and *n*, represented by 6 and *. The key is arranged in tabular form at ten letters — 5 *a*, † *d*, 8 *e*, 3 *g*, 4 *h*, 6 *i*, * *n*, ‡ *o*, ( *r*, ; *t* — "no less than ten of the most important letters," and Poe declines to proceed with the details. The full translation: "A good glass in the bishop's hostel in the devil's seat forty-one degrees and thirteen minutes northeast and by north main branch seventh limb east side shoot from the left eye of the death's-head a bee line from the tree through the shot fifty feet out." The Gauntlet's intake runs the count before any hypothesis — on ciphertext, on logs, on a specimen's output stream — because the count is the cheapest instrument that exists, and the catalogue's oldest gap was not a missing method but a missing *demonstration* of one. (2) **The crib is a word, not a letter.** The break did not come from 8 = *e* alone — it came from ";48" = "the," a repeated *word-shape*, seven times. A single frequent symbol is a guess; a repeated trigram in the target language's most common word is a foothold, and it yields three letters at once. The Gauntlet's crib-dragging starts with the most frequent word-shape in the target language, never with a lone symbol. (3) **The signature names the language.** The Kidd pun fixed the language before a single count was taken — Legrand would have started with Spanish and French otherwise. A specimen's self-naming — a pun, a label, an error string, a file extension — is evidence about its language and encoding, and it is priced before the attack, not discovered during it. (4) **Fiction is a training ground, not a field report — and re-count the printed table.** A story can teach a real method and still be fiction: the Gauntlet grades the method on its own reproducibility — this entry re-ran it, and it closes — never on the story's authority. And the method's own author miscounted his own table: the `(`/`.` hole is the standing rule in miniature. Never trust a printed table, a quoted count, or a solved example's arithmetic — re-count from the ciphertext in front of you, and file the hole when the numbers do not add up. ## The Behistun Inscription (c. 520–518 BCE) — the key that unlocked cuneiform, or: the cipher carved a hundred metres up a cliff

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero hits in either catalogue, measured this pass — "Behistun" on 0 lines in the private catalogue and 0 in the public one, "Rawlinson" 0/0, "Old Persian" 0/0, "Darius" 0/0, "Xerxes" 0/0, "Bisotun" 0/0, and the timeline and UNDECIPHERED.md carry none of them either; the only "Elamite" hits anywhere in the project are 10 passing mentions in UNDECIPHERED.md, none in either catalogue. The catalogue holds the Rosetta Stone's story at bullet tier ("The Rosetta Stone and Champollion's decipherment (1799–1822) — the key next to the lock") but not the document that did the same work for cuneiform — the longest trilingual inscription known, the one that opened the whole written record of the ancient Near East. This entry is the catalogue's first cuneiform decipherment, its first cliff, and its first blind-test proof. [VERIFIED — the 0/0 counts for Behistun, Rawlinson, Old Persian, Darius, Xerxes, and Bisotun in both catalogues, the timeline, and UNDECIPHERED.md, and the 10/0 Elamite split, measured this pass]

- **The story.** Darius I took the Persian throne in the summer of 522 BCE and spent his first year fighting for it. His own account, carved into the cliff, says he fought nineteen battles in a period of one year, ending in December 521 BCE, against nine pretenders who each claimed a throne — Gaumata the Magus, who claimed to be Bardiya, the dead son of Cyrus, killed by Darius at Sikayauvatiš on 29 September 522; Nidintu-Bêl, who claimed to be Nebuchadnezzar son of Nabonidus; Arakha, who made the same claim; and six more, each labelled in the relief with his name and his lie: "This is Nidintu-Bêl. He lied, saying 'I am Nebuchadnezzar, the son of Nabonidus. I am king of Babylon.'" Darius opens with his lineage — Hystaspes his father, Arsames, Ariaramnes, Teispes, Achaemenes — and the count: "Eight of my dynasty were kings before me; I am the ninth. Nine in succession we have been kings." Then the catalogue of the empire: twenty-three lands in all, from Persia and Elam to Egypt, Lydia, Ionia, Scythia, and Maka. The relief shows it: Darius life-sized, bow in hand, his left foot on the chest of the prostrate Gaumata, two servants behind him, nine one-metre captives roped together at the neck before him, the winged emblem floating above — and a tenth captive added later, Skunkha the Scythian, taller in silhouette than the king himself. [VERIFIED — the nineteen battles in one year ending December 521 BCE, the 29 September 522 killing of Gaumata at Sikayauvatiš, the nine pretenders and their quoted labels, the eight-before-me/ninth-king count, and the twenty-three lands, per Wikipedia "Behistun inscription" and the Achaemenica specialist article, both read first-party this pass]

- **The cliff and the copy.** The inscription stands about 15 metres high by 25 metres wide, 100 metres up a limestone cliff on the ancient road between Babylon and Ecbatana, at Mount Behistun in Kermanshah Province, Iran — placed there, the rock's own study shows, after the access stairway was removed and the path below sheared away, so that no hand could deface it. For two thousand years it could be reached only by a hard and dangerous climb, and the text is completely illegible from the ground. Europe misread it for centuries: Robert Sherley's party in 1598 took it for the Ascension of Jesus with a Greek inscription; Gardanne saw Christ and his twelve apostles; Ker Porter saw the Lost Tribes of Israel. The German surveyor Carsten Niebuhr visited around 1764 and published a copy of the inscription in the account of his journeys in 1778. Working from Niebuhr's transcriptions, Georg Friedrich Grotefend deciphered ten of the 37 symbols of Old Persian by 1802 — after realizing that unlike the Semitic cuneiform scripts, Old Persian text is alphabetic and each word is separated by a slanted vertical symbol. In 1835 Sir Henry Rawlinson, a British East India Company officer training the army of the Shah of Iran, began studying the inscription in earnest; with the help of a local boy he scaled the cliff and copied the Old Persian inscription. The Elamite was across a chasm, and the Babylonian four metres above; both were beyond easy reach and were left for later. Armed with the Persian text, and with about a third of the syllabary made available to him by Grotefend, Rawlinson set to work — and by 1838 he had cracked the form of cuneiform used for Old Persian, presenting his results to the Royal Asiatic Society in London and the Société Asiatique in Paris. He returned in 1843: planks carried him across the gap to copy the Elamite, and an enterprising local boy climbed a crack in the cliff and rigged ropes across the Babylonian so that papier-mâché casts of it could be taken. In 1847 he sent a full and accurate copy to Europe. Edward Hincks, Julius Oppert, and William Henry Fox Talbot contributed to the Babylonian; Edwin Norris and others were the first to do the same for the Elamite. Later expeditions — the British Museum's in 1904, the University of Michigan's in 1948 — photographed, cast, and re-transcribed passages Rawlinson had never copied. The monument took target-practice damage in World War II; it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2006. - **The method: the crib was a king list.** The first section of the Old Persian text contained a list of Persian kings identical to the one in Herodotus — the same names, in their original Persian forms instead of the Greek transliterations: Darius as Dārayavaus, not the Hellenized form. Rawlinson matched the names against the characters, and the names gave him the sounds. The period literature puts the crib's density at no fewer than ninety proper names preserved in the Persian portion and duplicated, in another character, in the Assyrian inscription — a name every four or five lines, each one a known sound pinned to an unknown sign. That is the Gold-Bug rung at monumental scale: the crib is a word, not a letter — here, a whole genealogy. And the script itself cooperated: 37 signs, not several hundred, and a word divider between every word, so the text arrived pre-tokenized. The Old Persian version was added last of all, directly beneath the relief — the Elamite first, the language of the old chancellery, then the Babylonian, then the Persian — and a short postscript in the fifth Old Persian column alone, added later, was never translated into the other languages. The inscription also makes its own claim about the script: in its final paragraph Darius says, in Kuhrt's translation, "By the favour of Auramazda, this is the form of writing, which I have made, besides in Aryan" — the script devised expressly to carve this text, and the king says so. ## JN-25 (1939–1945) — the code that decided Midway, or: the codebook you rebuild by hand

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero standalone entries in either catalogue, measured this pass — no `## ` heading in either file, against 21 mentions in the private catalogue and 16 in the public one. The story is filed at bullet tier only: a 1950s-summary bullet (lines 10–12 of the private catalogue) carrying the June 1939 first appearance, the additive layer, the three stations, a March 16, 1942 first-decrypt date, the AF=Midway deception, and the partial-read lesson — plus cross-references from the M-209, Z340, and Purple entries, which cite JN-25 as the precedent for usage-flaw breaks and partial-read doctrine. But the bullet tier never worked the mechanism by hand (0/0 worked miniatures, measured this pass), never counted the version clock, never named the divisible-by-three regularity, and carries five claims this pass corrects or conflicts. This entry promotes the code to full-entry status and adds what the bullets never had: the superencipherment worked digit by digit, the filter the codebook left in its own numbers, the depth identity with its honest limit, the partial-read spread, the version clock counted in days, and four new Gauntlet rungs that do not repeat the bullets' rungs. The bullets' facts stand where verified and are corrected where they are not, not re-argued. [VERIFIED — the 0/0 heading counts, the 21/16 mention counts, and the 0/0 miniature counts, measured this pass]

- **The find.** JN-25 was the Imperial Japanese Navy's main, most secure communications scheme through the Second World War — the 25th Japanese Navy system the codebreakers identified, first called AN-1 and worked as a "research project" rather than a "current decryption" job, because the job was not inverting a function but reconstructing a dictionary: thirty thousand code groups and thirty thousand random additives, sixty thousand unknowns, pieced together from usage. It was introduced on June 1, 1939, to replace Blue — the most recent descendant of the Red code — as an enciphered code producing five-numeral groups for transmission. Every code group was a five-digit number that stood for a word, a phrase, a place, or a grammatical particle; every group was then superenciphered by adding a five-digit additive drawn from a second book, digit by digit without carry, with the additive's starting point signalled in the message itself. Reading a message meant two separate jobs: strip the additive layer mathematically, then recover the codebook from usage patterns — a cumulative, card-index crawl, never a single magic decode. The British structural break came first: John Tiltman, with some help from Alan Turing at Bletchley Park, had broken JN-25 by 1941 — they knew it was a five-digit code with a codebook and a second additive book, and Tiltman had devised a slow method of breaking it and had noted that all the numbers in the codebook were divisible by three. But knowing the structure did not enable reading a message: "breaking" rather than "solving" a code means learning enough code words and indicators that a message can be read, and in April 1942 the codebreakers could read only about one in five words — traffic analysis was far more useful than the partial text. The American effort was directed from Washington by the Navy's signals-intelligence command, OP-20-G, and fought at three stations: Station HYPO at Pearl Harbor (COM 14), commanded by Commander Joseph Rochefort; Station CAST in the Philippines (COM 16), jointly commanded by Lieutenants Rudolph Fabian and John Lietwiler; and the British Far East Combined Bureau in Singapore — with IBM punched-card tabulating machines doing the arithmetic the hand methods could not. Together they mounted the successful attack against the December 4, 1941 edition, JN-25b, exploiting cribs from the formalities of Japanese messages — "I have the honor to inform your excellency" — the way every code falls: on its courtesies. The version clock ran through the war: JN-25a on December 1, 1940; JN-25b on December 4, 1941, three days before Pearl Harbor; JN-25c from May 28, 1942, deferred from April 1, then May 1 — a 57-day deferral that left JN-25b in force through the Midway operation, seven days before the battle opened; JN-25d from April 1, 1943, its additive changed, large portions recovered two weeks later — fast enough to hand the Americans Admiral Yamamoto's itinerary, and the ambush that killed him in Operation Vengeance. The decisive read was not a full one. The target of the Japanese strike was designated only as "AF" in the intercepts; the codebreakers believed it was Midway and their superiors were skeptical, so Rochefort had Midway report, in a message the Japanese could intercept, that the island was short of fresh water — and not long afterward a Japanese message reported that AF was short of water. The deception confirmed the designator, the fleet sailed to the ambush, and in three days of battle the Americans sank all four Japanese carriers and lost the Yorktown: the most spectacular upset victory in the Navy's history, won on a code read at one word in five. The break nearly burned itself a month later: in June 1942 the Chicago Tribune published an article implying the United States had broken the Japanese codes, with the dispositions of the invasion fleet; the government considered prosecuting under the Espionage Act of 1917, then dropped the charges — not wanting to draw more attention, and because the Act did not cover enemy secrets — and a grand jury investigation produced no prosecution, only more publicity.

- **The mechanism, worked by hand.** Superencipherment is addition without carry, digit by digit, modulo ten. Take the code group 12345 — digit sum 15, divisible by three, a legal codebook number — and the additive 67890: 1+6=7, 2+7=9, 3+8=11→1, 4+9=13→3, 5+0=5, so the transmitted group is 79135. Strip it by the same rule in reverse: 7−6=1, 9−7=2, 1−8=−7→3, 3−9=−6→4, 5−0=5, and 12345 returns. A second pair: 24681 (digit sum 21) plus 13579 gives 37150, and stripping returns 24681. Note what the traffic shows and what it hides: the transmitted group 79135 has digit sum 16 — not divisible by three — so the filter never applies to traffic, only to a stripped candidate. The additive book's starting point rode in the message itself, which is why the strip was possible at all: the encipherment carried its own key to its own door, and the code's security rested entirely on the codebook staying unknown.

- **Worked miniature (computed this pass).** Five counts, all reproduced by goal hidden_files/verify-jn25-20261109.py (39/39 checks pass). (1) **The superencipherment, twice.** 12345 + 67890 = 79135 digitwise, and 79135 − 67890 = 12345; 24681 + 13579 = 37150, and 37150 − 13579 = 24681 — both round-trips verified, both code groups divisible by three (digit sums 15 and 21), the transmitted groups not. (2) **The divisible-by-three filter.** The five-digit groups from 10000 to 99999 divisible by three number exactly 30,000 — first 10002, last 99999 — which is exactly the filed size of the codebook: the filter admits precisely a codebook's worth of candidates, and the inference that the codebook was the whole set is left as inference, not filed as fact. Across all five-digit strings 00000–99999 the count is 33,334. A random five-digit group passes the test with probability one in three, so the check eliminates 66.7% of wrong candidates at zero cost — a free filter the code's designers left in their own numbers, the way a careless clerk leaves a fingerprint on the envelope. (3) **The depth, and its honest limit.** Two code groups under the same additive — 12345 and 24681, both under 67890 — transmit as 79135 and 81471; subtract the transmissions digitwise and the additive cancels: 79135 − 81471 = 98764, and 12345 − 24681 = 98764, the same number. The identity holds exactly, and it is also the limit: the difference of two code groups is not the difference of two plaintexts, because code groups are dictionary indices, not letters. A one-time-pad depth hands you the difference of two messages; a JN-25 depth hands you the difference of two dictionary entries, and the break still needs the codebook. The depth is a lead, not a reading. (4) **The partial-read spread.** April 1942 carries three filed rates, and they disagree: the bullet tier's 10–15%, Wikipedia's one in five (20%), and Goebel's about a third. In a 50-group message that spread is 5–7.5, 10, and ~16.7 readable groups; in a 100-group message at 20% it is 20. At 20%, a 10-group message has an 89.3% chance of holding at least one readable group (1 − 0.8^10 = 0.8926) — which is why a partial read was operationally decisive: even a short message almost always yielded something, and something plus traffic analysis was enough to sail a fleet on. (5) **The version clock.** JN-25 to JN-25a: 549 days. JN-25a to JN-25b: 368 days. JN-25b to JN-25c: 175 days, with the deferral from April 1 to May 28 worth 57 days of extra JN-25b life — the window Midway was won in. JN-25c to JN-25d: 308 days. The whole span, June 1, 1939 to April 1, 1943: 1,400 days. JN-25d's additive was changed and large portions were recovered within 14 days. JN-25c was in force 7 days before Midway opened on June 4, 1942; Pearl Harbor to Midway is 179 days. Every version change reset the break to zero, and the war was fought in the gaps between resets.

- **Decoder-design note (JN-25 → Gauntlet).** Four rungs, each a doctrine entry, none repeating the bullet's rungs (partial reads are decisive; hunt usage flaws first). (1) **The codebook is the specimen's memory, not its math.** JN-25 was a code — a dictionary of arbitrary mappings — not a cipher, an algorithm to invert. The break was the reconstruction of thirty thousand mappings by usage, not the inversion of a function. Gauntlet rung: for dictionary specimens, the reconstruction ledger is graded separately from any algorithmic claim — which mappings are proven by usage, which are guessed, which are cribbed — and a specimen that "solves" a code by guessing the dictionary is claiming a break it has not earned. (2) **Sweep for structural regularities before the deep attack.** The codebook's numbers were all divisible by three — a checksum the designers never intended, a free two-thirds filter on every stripped candidate. Gauntlet rung: every specimen gets a structural-regularity sweep first — digit sums, parity, range, repetition, the alphabet's own arithmetic — because a free filter beats a month of cribs, and because a specimen that leaves a regularity in its own numbers has told you where to look. (3) **The version clock.** Every JN-25 version reset the break to zero, and the war was fought in the gaps between resets; the 57-day deferral of JN-25c was the window Midway was won in. Gauntlet rung: every interrogation carries a dated version clock, and a break that lands after the version changes is archaeology — logged, never charged as failure, never graded as a break of the current specimen. A specimen graded "adequate" for a 24-hour window is not graded secure. (4) **A planted confirmation is not a cryptanalytic break.** AF was confirmed by an operational plant — a false water report the enemy relayed — not by cryptanalysis, and the report card must not grade it as one. Gauntlet rung: when a hypothesis is cheap to confirm operationally and expensive to confirm cryptanalytically, the lab confirms operationally and says so in the record. The handling rule that rides with it is the leak tax: the Chicago Tribune nearly burned the break a month after Midway, so breaks stay in the mirror until the card seals, and a break's value dies the day it is published.

## The Bacon cipher (1605/1623) — the first binary code, or: the message hidden in the typeface

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero standalone entries in either catalogue, measured this pass — no `## ` heading in either file, against 17 mentions in the private catalogue and 20 in the public one. The mentions are all passing: the section-(l) steganography note names Bacon's biliteral cipher as the ancestor of hiding in the carrier, the Copiale and Z340 design notes cite it as the template for "structure below the visible symbol set," and the Venona entry's one-time-pad bullet leans on it as the binary-encoding precedent — but no entry has ever worked the mechanism, counted the alphabet, priced the cover text, or named the price of the I/J and U/V mergers. This entry promotes the cipher to full-entry status and adds what the mentions never had: the biliteral alphabet worked by hand, the cover-text expansion priced in words, the ambiguity rate of the merged letters, the date gaps to Leibniz and Boole, the Shakespeare detour that made the cipher famous for the wrong reason, and three new Gauntlet rungs. [VERIFIED — the 0/0 heading counts, the 17/20 mention counts, and the 0/0 miniature counts, measured this pass]

- **The find.** Francis Bacon (1561–1626) — philosopher, statesman, Lord Chancellor — devised the biliteral cipher in 1605 and published it in *De Augmentis Scientiarum* (*The Advancement of Learning*, 1623), an enlargement of his 1605 *Advancement of Learning*; the often-repeated "published 1605" dating is wrong, and the correction is filed here, not smoothed. He conceived the idea young, while working alongside Thomas Phelippes — Elizabethan spymaster Francis Walsingham's cipher expert, the man who broke the Babington plot and Mary, Queen of Scots' ciphers — so the cipher was born inside the working cryptanalysis shop of its day, not in a philosopher's study alone. The idea is one sentence: every letter becomes a group of five of the letters 'A' or 'B'. Five binary symbols give 32 patterns; Bacon's Latin alphabet had 24 letters (no J, written I; no V, written U), so I/J share ABAAA and U/V share BAABB, with 8 of the 32 patterns spare. The encoding is a substitution, and as a cipher alone it is trivial — a fixed binary encoding of the alphabet, spotted instantly by any computer. Its power was never the substitution. It was the second part: because a message needs only two distinguishable states, the A/B pattern could be carried by *anything* with two forms. Bacon's proposal was two typefaces — roman for A, italic for B — so that a secret message rode inside an innocent-looking printed page, each cover letter's typeface spelling one bit of the secret. He even prepared a plate for handwritten use: two alternative forms of every capital and small letter, one form for A, one for B. The cover text must have exactly as many letters as there are A/B symbols in the secret — five cover letters per plaintext letter — and the reader who does not know to compare typefaces sees nothing at all. Bacon claimed the cipher could never be broken. [VERIFIED — the 1605/1623 dating and its correction, the Phelippes connection, and the "never broken" claim per the Queen Mary / cs4fn history and the Cipher Museum exhibit; the mechanism, the 24-letter alphabet, the two-typeface carrier, and the handwritten plate per Wikipedia "Bacon's cipher" and the Cipher Museum; CORROBORATED — the 1623 publication detail via Kahn's *The Codebreakers* as cited by the Cipher Museum]

- **The mechanism, worked by hand.** The biliteral alphabet, A = 0 through Z = 23 in five-bit binary, A for 0 and B for 1: A AAAAA, B AAAAB, C AAABA, D AAABB, E AABAA, F AABAB, G AABBA, H AABBB, I/J ABAAA, K ABAAB, L ABABA, M ABABB, N ABBAA, O ABBAB, P ABBBA, Q ABBBB, R BAAAA, S BAAAB, T BAABA, U/V BAABB, W BABAA, X BABAB, Y BABBA, Z BABBB. Encode HELLO: H AABBB, E AABAA, L ABABA, L ABABA, O ABBAB — "AABBB AABAA ABABA ABABA ABBAB". Now hide it: take a 25-letter cover text, print its 1st, 2nd, 4th, 5th, 6th letters in italic wherever the pattern says B and roman wherever it says A, and the page reads as an ordinary paragraph while the typefaces spell HELLO. Decode by reversing the map: each typeface-1 letter becomes A, each typeface-2 letter becomes B, then regroup in fives. The mergers are the honest cost: ABAAA decodes to I *or* J, BAABB to U *or* V, and only context decides — JULIUS comes back as IULIUS, VIVID as UIUID, and the reader repairs both from the words around them. [VERIFIED — the alphabet table and both worked encodings computed and round-trip-checked this pass]

- **Worked miniature (computed this pass).** Five counts, all reproduced by goal hidden_files/verify-bacon-20261109.py (27/27 checks pass). (1) **The encodings.** HELLO → "AABBB AABAA ABABA ABABA ABBAB", cross-checked against an independent online encoder's output; CODE → "AAABA ABBAB AAABB AABAA"; JULIUS round-trips to IULIUS and VIVID to UIUID, the J→I and V→U folds demonstrated, not asserted. (2) **The capacity.** 2^5 = 32 patterns for 24 letters leaves 8 spare — 25% of the code space unused, headroom Bacon never spent. (3) **The cover-text price.** Five cover letters per plaintext letter, exactly: a 20-letter secret needs 100 cover letters, a 100-letter secret needs 500 — at roughly five letters per English word, about 100 words of innocent prose to smuggle 100 letters of secret. The steganography is paid for in bulk, and the bulk is the tell: a cover text much longer than its content warrants is the first thing a suspicious reader counts. (4) **The ambiguity rate.** At standard English letter frequencies, the I/J code covers 7.12% of letters (I 6.97 + J 0.15) and the U/V code 3.74% (U 2.76 + V 0.98) — so about 10.86%, roughly one letter in nine, decodes ambiguously and must be repaired from context. The cipher's security rested on the carrier being invisible; its readability rested on English being redundant. (5) **The date gaps.** Bacon 1605 to Leibniz's binary arithmetic (1703) is 98 years; to Boole's algebra of logic (1854) is 249 years. Bacon had a working binary encoding of the alphabet nearly a century before binary numbers were formalized and two and a half centuries before binary logic — and the catalogue files the distinction the Cipher Museum draws, that binary *representation* is not a direct line of invention to ASCII or to electronic computing. Bacon invented the idea that two states suffice; the machines that used it came later, by other hands.

- **The Shakespeare detour — the cipher made famous for the wrong reason.** In 1888 Ignatius Donnelly published *The Great Cryptogram*, claiming Bacon had hidden messages in the First Folio's typefaces proving he wrote Shakespeare's plays — the founding text of the Baconian theory of Shakespeare authorship. The claim drove a century of hunting for biliteral messages in Elizabethan printing, and it is rejected: the First Folio's typeface variations are compositor variation and worn type, not a code, and no biliteral message has ever been recovered from it. The detour is filed here because it is the library's standing lesson in the other direction from the Copiale entry: Copiale was a real cipher that took a recovered word to open; the Baconian hunt was a real cipher applied to a carrier that never carried it — the method was sound, the carrier was innocent, and two centuries of effort went into reading noise as signal. A steganographic hypothesis needs a carrier test before it needs a decoder: count the typeface distribution first, and if the A/B split does not sit at the encoded message's statistics, there is no message to decode. [CORROBORATED — Donnelly 1888 and the Baconian theory's rejection per standard histories; CLAIMED — no single primary source for the rejection opened this pass]

- **Decoder-design note (Bacon → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The carrier is the cipher.** Bacon's substitution is trivial; the typeface channel is the whole cipher. The Gauntlet's parser interrogates the carrier before the content — typeface, font, spacing, casing, timing, ordering — because a specimen that encodes in the *presentation* of its output defeats every content-first tool, exactly as Bacon's page defeated every reader who read the words. A channel that carries two distinguishable states carries a message until proven otherwise. (2) **Count the bulk before decoding the bits.** Five cover letters per secret letter means the carrier is five times the message, and the expansion ratio is itself evidence: a cover text far longer than its content warrants is the first count, not the last. Gauntlet rung: price every specimen's output-to-content ratio, and flag any channel whose bulk exceeds its apparent content by a fixed factor — the factor is the fingerprint of the hidden layer. (3) **A sound method on an innocent carrier is the expensive false positive.** The Baconian hunt burned a century on a real cipher applied to noise. Gauntlet rung: every steganographic hypothesis ships with its carrier test — the distribution check that must pass *before* the decoder runs — and a decode attempted without a passing carrier test is logged as a hunt, never graded as a break. The Copiale rule (one recovered word is the beachhead) and the Bacon rule (prove the carrier carries before you decode) are the two gates, in that order. [VERIFIED lineage — the typeface carrier, the 5:1 expansion, and the Donnelly detour cited above; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's own doctrine, never run]

- **Grades:** [VERIFIED — the 0/0 heading counts, the 17/20 mention counts, and the 0/0 miniature counts, measured this pass; Bacon (1561–1626) and the 1605 devising / 1623 *De Augmentis* publication, with the 1605-publication dating corrected per the Queen Mary history; the 24-letter alphabet, the I/J and U/V mergers, the five-symbol A/B encoding, the two-typeface carrier, and the handwritten two-form plate, per Wikipedia "Bacon's cipher" and the Cipher Museum; the worked miniature (HELLO → "AABBB AABAA ABABA ABABA ABBAB", CODE → "AAABA ABBAB AAABB AABAA", the IULIUS/UIUID folds, the 32-pattern / 8-spare capacity, the 5:1 cover expansion and ~100-word cover for a 100-letter secret, the 7.12% / 3.74% / 10.86% ambiguity rates, and the 98 / 249 / 151-year gaps), computed this pass by goal hidden_files/verify-bacon-20261109.py (27/27 checks pass); CORROBORATED — the Phelippes/Walsingham connection and Bacon's "never broken" claim, per the Queen Mary history; the Donnelly 1888 *Great Cryptogram* and the Baconian theory's rejection, per standard histories; the binary-representation-versus-ASCII distinction, per the Cipher Museum; CLAIMED — the rejection of the Baconian theory rests on no single primary source opened this pass; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings in the design note, doctrine until run]

## The Navajo code talkers (1942–1945) — the key that lived in a human, or: the unbreakable code that was never written down

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero standalone entries in either catalogue, measured this pass — no `## ` heading in either file, against 10 mention-lines in the private catalogue and 10 in the public one. The mentions are concentrated in one place: the section-(b) bullet entry seeded 2026-10-17, which already carries the history, the double-encoding, the irony, and three Gauntlet rungs — but no entry has ever worked the alphabet by hand, decoded a real transmission, counted the alternates, or corrected the bullet entry's own overstatement that every letter had three words. This entry promotes the code talkers to full-entry status and adds what the mentions never had: the full 1945 spelling alphabet counted letter by letter, the CIA's published "Iwo Jima" transmission decoded twice from two different published encodings, the 90× speed margin priced, the Iwo Jima traffic rate counted, the 1918 Choctaw precedent that makes the Navajo code a second generation rather than a first invention, and three new Gauntlet rungs. [VERIFIED — the 0/0 heading counts and the 10/10 mention counts, measured this pass; the 0/0 worked-encoding counts — the only "tkin" hit in either file is "Atkins" inside the RSA-129 entry]

- **The find.** In February 1942, as Japanese codebreakers read Allied traffic at will across the Pacific, Philip Johnston — a World War I veteran, son of missionaries, raised on the Navajo reservation and fluent in Diné Bizaad — walked into the office of Maj. Gen. Clayton B. Vogel with a proposition: build a battlefield code on a language no outsider spoke. Navajo was tonally and grammatically unlike any Indo-European tongue, had no widely used written form, and was spoken almost exclusively inside the Nation — and Johnston proved the case with a stopwatch: under simulated combat conditions, Navajo men encoded, transmitted, and decoded a three-line message in 20 seconds against 30 minutes for the machines of the day. The Marine Corps approved the pilot: 29 Navajo men (30 recruited; one dropped out) assembled at Camp Elliott near San Diego in May 1942 and built the code themselves — 211 initial terms, expanded to 411 over the war. It entered combat with the Guadalcanal landings and served in every major Marine engagement of the Pacific war. At Iwo Jima, six code talkers sent and received over 800 messages in the first 48 hours, all without error; the 5th Marine Division signal officer, Maj. Howard Connor, said afterward: "Were it not for the Navajos, the Marines would never have taken Iwo Jima." No code talker was ever captured alive in action, and the code was never broken during the war. More than 400 Navajo men served as code talkers in total; thirteen died in battle. [CORROBORATED — the Johnston pitch, the Vogel meeting, the 20-seconds-vs-30-minutes demo, and the "unwritten/no widely used written form" claim across the CIA's history page, III MEF Public Affairs, and the Library of Congress research guide; the 29-man pilot and the 211→411 growth per the CIA and the Marine histories; the Iwo Jima 800-message figure and Connor's quotes across the LOC guide and the military histories; the 400+ total per the LOC guide; the thirteen dead per the VA]

- **The irony on the record.** Beginning in the 1860s, the U.S. government forced Navajo children into boarding schools designed to replace their language with "American" ways. In 1942 the same nation asked those men's generation to win a war with the language the schools had tried to erase. The code talkers were then sworn to silence — their work stayed classified until 1968, when the program was declassified; recognition arrived late (August 14 declared National Navajo Code Talkers Day in 1982; Congressional Gold and Silver Medals in 2000–2001). Chester Nez — one of the original 29, memoirist of *Code Talker* (2011, with Judith Schiess Avila) — died June 4, 2014, the last of the 29; the code's operational use ran on through Korea and into early Vietnam, making the Navajo code the only spoken military code never deciphered. [CORROBORATED — the boarding-school history, 1968 declassification, the 1982 day and 2000–2001 medals, Nez's death and memoir, and the Korea/Vietnam continuation, as carried by the section-(b) bullet entry's sources]

- **The mechanism, worked by hand.** Two layers, and the second is the one that defeats the analyst. Layer one is a phrase codebook for military terms: tank = turtle, submarine = iron fish, bomber = buzzard, fighter plane = hummingbird, bombs (carried on aircraft) = eggs. Layer two is a spelling alphabet for everything without a code term — names, places, officers: each English letter is represented by a Navajo word, and reading a letter costs three steps (hear the Navajo word, translate it into English, take the English word's first letter). The declassified dictionary (revised 15 June 1945) lists the alphabet as 63 words for 26 letters — and this entry corrects the bullet entry's blanket claim that every letter had three words. Counted this pass: 17 letters have three alternates, N/S/U have two, and Q/V/W/X/Y/Z have one. The alternates were the anti-frequency defense, and they were spent where the language spends its letters: the tripled letters include E, T, A, O, I, N, S, H, R, D, L, U — the most common English letters — while the rare letters make do with one. The design rule behind the table is visible in the glosses: each Navajo word's English translation begins with its letter (WOL-LA-CHEE, ant, for A; SHUSH, bear, for B; MOASI, cat, for C) — with exactly one exception, and the exception proves the rule: X is AL-NA-AS-DZOH, "cross," a word that names the shape of the letter X because English has no common X-initial noun to borrow. The whole code was memorized; the classroom codebook was never taken into the field, so no document existed anywhere to steal — and even a fluent native Navajo speaker who was not a code talker could not read the traffic, because the substitution layer sat on top of the language layer. [VERIFIED — the 63-word count, the 17/3/6 split, and the single X exception, computed this pass from the declassified 15 June 1945 dictionary as transcribed; CORROBORATED — the code-word meanings and the double-encoding per the bullet entry, the CIA page, and the UCSD dictionary transcription]

- **Worked miniature (computed this pass).** Five counts, all reproduced by goal hidden_files/verify-navajo-20261109.py (53/53 checks pass). (1) **The alphabet count.** 26 letters, 63 words: 17 letters × 3, 3 letters × 2 (N, S, U), 6 letters × 1 (Q, V, W, X, Y, Z); all 63 Navajo words distinct, no word reused for two letters; 62 of 63 glosses begin with their letter, X the sole exception. (2) **The two decodings.** The CIA's published example spells IWO JIMA two different ways in two different publications — Indian Country Today's rendering "TKIN GLOE-LH A-KHA / AH-YA-TSINNE TKIN TSIN-TLITI TSE-NILL" and the lkn-law rendering "TKIN GLOE-IH A-KHA / TKELE-CHO-G TKIN TSIN-TLITI WOL-LA-CHEE" — and both decode to IWOJIMA. The two encodings differ in three word slots: two are alternate choices (J: AH-YA-TSINNE "jaw" vs TKELE-CHO-G "jackass"; final A: TSE-NILL "axe" vs WOL-LA-CHEE "ant") and one is a spelling variant of the same word (W: GLOE-LH vs GLOE-IH "weasel"). The alternates are not a theory — they are visible in the published record, doing their job. (3) **The speed margin.** 30 minutes is 1,800 seconds; 1,800 / 20 = 90×. The code talker was ninety times faster than the machine on the same three-line message. (4) **The Iwo Jima rate.** 800 messages over 48 hours is 16.67 per hour overall, 133.33 per net across the six nets — one message per net every 21.6 minutes, around the clock, for two days — at an error rate of 0/800. (5) **The dictionary growth.** 211 terms at founding to 411 by war's end is +200 terms, +94.79% — the code nearly doubled in the field, which is also the measure of how much of war has no word in any peacetime language. One discrepancy is filed, not smoothed: a secondary account puts the alphabet at 44 words, which does not reconcile with the transcribed 1945 table's 63 — it may count a mid-war revision or be a miscount, and it stands as CLAIMED against the computed 63.

- **The Choctaw precedent — the first generation.** The Navajo code was not the first use of a Native language as a military code; it was the second generation of one. In October 1918, eight Choctaw men of Company E, 142nd Infantry, 36th Division, used their language over field telephones in the Meuse-Argonne Offensive — the first combat use coming on October 26, 1918, in ordering a delicate withdrawal of two companies of the 2nd Battalion from Chufilly to Chardoney — and the Germans never read it. The group grew to nineteen by tribal count (twenty in Meadows's history); eighteen were later trained as Class I code talkers, the Army's designation for men trained in the special jargon as opposed to men merely speaking in the open. The Choctaw code stayed classified for decades, and Congress awarded the Choctaw the Congressional Gold Medal posthumously on November 20, 2020, under the Code Talkers Recognition Act of 2008. Johnston had seen the WWI precedent and built on it: where the Choctaw spoke their language in the open with jargon layered in, the Navajo added the phrase codebook, the triple-word spelling alphabet, and the memorization discipline that left nothing to capture. [CORROBORATED — the eight originals, the 142nd/36th, the October 26, 1918 first use, the growth to nineteen/twenty, the Class I designation, and the 2020 medal, per Meadows's history as reviewed and the regimental record; the Johnston-knows-the-precedent link per the cipher-machines history]

- **Decoder-design note (Navajo → Gauntlet).** Three NEW rungs; the section-(b) bullet entry's three stand and these extend them. (1) **Speed is a security property, not a convenience.** The 90× margin is why the code survived contact: a code that takes 30 minutes to use gets bypassed, spoken in the clear, or abandoned under fire — and every bypass is a break the cryptanalyst never has to make. The Gauntlet prices every specimen's latency against its operator's patience: a channel slower than the mission's tempo is a channel that will be circumvented, and the circumvention is the vulnerability. This is the SIGABA entry's honest-null rung wearing a stopwatch: SIGABA lost to portability, the machine lost to speed — both are security properties dressed as logistics. (2) **The alternate is the anti-frequency defense — and the published record proves it ran.** Two independent publications of the same place-name transmission differ in the J and A slots because the talkers rotated alternates; a frequency analyst counting WOL-LA-CHEE would undercount A by the share carried by BE-LA-SANA and TSE-NILL. Gauntlet rung: when a specimen's symbol inventory shows unexplained synonyms, test the homophonic hypothesis before the random hypothesis — synonyms are a designed defense, and which symbols carry alternates names the designer's frequency model. (3) **The trained insider is the threat-model boundary, not the fluent insider.** A fluent Navajo speaker who was not a code talker could not read the traffic — the substitution layer sat on the language layer. The Gauntlet's insider-threat fixture must therefore distinguish fluency from training: "the adversary speaks the language" and "the adversary holds the codebook" are different rungs, and a specimen that survives the first can still fall to the second. The interrogation names which insider it is modeling. (And the correction to the bullet entry's first rung: the key lived in a human *and* in a trained human — the training, not the language alone, was the key.) [VERIFIED lineage — the 90× margin, the alternate counts, and the two published IWO JIMA encodings as computed above; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's own doctrine, never run]

## RED — the Type A Cipher Machine (1931–1945), or: the machine that taught America the sixes

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero `## ` headings in either catalogue, measured this pass — no entry-titled bullet, and no "Angōki", "Angooki", or "91-shiki" string anywhere in either file; the only substantive mention is one line inside the Purple entry, that Purple replaced the Type A Red machine (the Type 91 typewriter, 1931), whose vowels AEIOUY were enciphered separately and permanently — a weakness the Americans already knew, since they had broken Red. Every other "red" hit is a false positive (reduced, the colour, the Red naval code the sources warn against confusing it with). The catalogue holds Purple's whole story and JN-25's — but not the machine whose break taught the Americans the sixes, whose replica they built first, and whose parallel traffic handed them the cribs that broke Purple. [VERIFIED — the 0/0 heading counts, the 0/0 Angōki/Angooki/91-shiki counts, and the single substantive mention, measured this pass]

- **The story.** The machine was born of an embarrassment. Herbert Yardley's *The American Black Chamber* (1931) published the fact that the United States had read Japanese codes at the Washington Naval Conference, and the Japanese Foreign Ministry turned increasingly to machine systems. The device it adopted was built on a borrowed foundation with a Japanese idea on top: the firm of Boris Hagelin supplied a machine, but Hagelin, not trusting the Japanese to honour his patents, sent a more primitive device designed by Arvid Damm instead — and the Japanese reverse-engineered that into their own machine, adding the one feature that was strictly theirs, the separate encryption of the vowels. The prototype was developed by the Japanese Navy Institute of Technology, Electric Research Department, Section 6, chief designer Kazuo Tanabe with Navy Commander Genichiro Kakimoto, in 1928, on the Kryha principle with a plugboard; it served at the London Naval Treaty negotiations in 1930, and was completed as the Type 91 Typewriter in 1931 — 91 for the Japanese Imperial year 2591. The Foreign Ministry adopted the Type A in 1935, and the U.S. Army's Signal Intelligence Service, first encountering its intercept that year, nicknamed it RED — colour nicknames were used extensively in the American military, and this was the first machine cryptosystem the SIS had worked on, so it took the first colour of the spectrum. The break came in triplicate, independently: the British first, Hugh Foss and Oliver Strachey working it out in 1934, with Harold Kenworthy's shop building a replica, the "J machine", a year later; the Army SIS, Frank Rowlett and Solomon Kullback, from 1935; the Navy, where Agnes Driscoll is generally credited — though she actually solved the Orange (or M-1) cipher used by naval attachés, and the two systems turned out to be essentially the same. The SIS produced its first translation from a RED decrypt in February 1937. The intelligence was less dramatic than Purple's but real: a decrypted Japanese message of November 1936 revealed to American policymakers the details of a secret clause in the Anti-Comintern Pact, committing Germany, Italy, and Japan to support each other in war "regardless of the circumstances"; reports of the sea trials of the battleship *Nagato* were decoded, leading to important changes to the USS *North Carolina* (BB-55), then being designed, to match the Japanese ship. In late 1938 a cipher expert travelled to Japan's major overseas diplomatic posts to install the Type B machine; the Foreign Ministry introduced it in February 1939, and the Americans nicknamed it PURPLE. The two machines then ran side by side: PURPLE for the major posts — Washington, London, Moscow — RED for the less important ones, and some posts, Washington among them, held both, which let the Japanese send the same message enciphered in both systems. That was one of two elementary procedural mistakes — the other was enciphering English-language diplomatic texts — and the Americans capitalized on both to develop cribs. After eighteen months of work the PURPLE device was cracked, and it produced important intelligence to the end of the war; RED kept running at the minor posts all the while, and the material the Americans most wanted had moved to PURPLE. The break's institutional legacy outlived the machine: once PURPLE was solved, William Friedman established what may have been the first compartment for intelligence information in the United States, marking decrypts with the codeword MAGIC — he liked to describe his cryptanalysts to outsiders as "magicians" — and by the January 1941 agreement distribution of MAGIC translations was limited to ten people: the President; the secretaries of War, Navy, and State; the Chief of Staff; the Chief of Naval Operations; the chiefs of the two services' war plans divisions; and the chiefs of their intelligence organizations. - **The machine.** The *91-shiki ōbun injiki* (九一式欧文印字機, "System 91 Typewriter for European Characters"), *Angōki Taipu-A* (暗号機 タイプA, "Type A Cipher Machine"), codenamed Red by the United States — a diplomatic machine of the Japanese Foreign Office, before and during the Second World War, and a relatively simple device that was quickly broken. It encrypted and decrypted texts written in Latin characters for transmission through the cable services, and its defining feature was a piece of economics, not cryptography: under International Telegraph Union regulations, pronounceable words in telegrams were charged a lower rate than unpronounceable code groups, so the machine enciphered the vowels separately from the consonants, keeping the text a series of syllables. The letter Y was treated as a vowel. Encryption itself was provided through a single half-rotor: input contacts came through slip rings, each connected to a single output contact on the rotor, and since both vowels and consonants passed through the same rotor it had sixty contacts — the least common multiple of six and twenty — with the wiring arranged so the two groups were kept separate. The slip rings were connected to the input keyboard through a plugboard, again organized to keep vowels and consonants separate. The rotor turned at least one step after each letter, and the amount of rotation was controlled by a break wheel connected to the rotor, carrying up to forty-seven pins, up to eleven of them removable in predetermined positions — in practice four to six were removed. Rotation stopped when the next pin was reached, so if the next pin had been removed the rotor advanced two places instead of one; the irregular pattern of rotation produced an Alberti cipher. The "sixes and twenties" effect, as American analysts called it, was the major weakness — and the Japanese continued it in the Purple system. ## The Indus script (c. 2600–1900 BCE) — the writing nobody has read, or: the million-dollar silence

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero `## ` headings in either catalogue, measured this pass — no entry-titled bullet, and no treatment of the script itself anywhere in either file. The private catalogue holds one whole-word mention: the pointer bullet at line 318, Yajnadevam's Indus attack as decoder template, pointing at UNDECIPHERED.md. The public catalogue holds one pointer bullet (lines 1166–1167, the word twice, same pointer). UNDECIPHERED.md §3 holds the watch-list treatment and the full 2026 claimant file — the Tamil Nadu prize, the Yajnadevam / Pierson / Sharman / Vigslist claims, the SIGIL counterexample, the Astra negative — but the catalogue itself never treated the script as a specimen. This entry closes that gap; the claimant detail stays in the watch-list, pointed at, not duplicated. [VERIFIED — the 0/0 heading counts and the 1/1 pointer-bullet counts, measured this pass]

- **The story.** The first seal with Harappan symbols was published in 1875, in a drawing by Alexander Cunningham. Excavations at Harappa (1921) and Mohenjo-daro (1922) turned a curiosity into a civilization, and John Marshall announced it in 1924. A century of attempts followed — more than a hundred published decipherments, none accepted; Mortimer Wheeler's 1960s verdict, "invalid", has not really changed. The most influential programme belongs to Asko Parpola, who argues the script wrote a Dravidian language, with Iravatham Mahadevan's 1977 concordance as the field's standard text. The counter-thesis arrived in 2004, when Steve Farmer, Richard Sproat, and Michael Witzel argued the signs were a non-linguistic symbol system, like merchants' marks — and offered $10,000, valid for Farmer's lifetime, to anyone who turns up one Indus inscription from a known contemporary site, a prize that has stood unclaimed for more than twenty years. The statistical reply came in 2009, when Rajesh P. N. Rao and colleagues reported in *Science* that the script's conditional entropy looks language-like — structure, not a reading. On January 5, 2025, at a Chennai seminar marking a hundred years since the announcement, Tamil Nadu's Chief Minister M. K. Stalin put a million dollars on a decipherment the experts accept; as of the October 2026 prize watch it stands unclaimed, with no published adjudication rules, and Rao reports weekly emails from self-proclaimed codebreakers — the prize has become a crank magnet, which is exactly why the watch-list keeps its intake doctrine. The 2026 season is filed in full in UNDECIPHERED.md §3 and summarized here, not repeated: Bharath Rao ("Yajnadevam") claims a Sanskrit reading by regex and set-intersection, shipping a Shannon unicity-distance falsifiability criterion; Tristen Kyle Pierson claims a complete Proto-Dravidian assignment of all 605 signs; Adrian Sharman claims a functional grammar that parses 78.8% of held-out inscriptions against a 27.1% shuffled null, conceding the phonetic question entirely; Richard Vigslist reads the system as paperwork, not accounting, with no sign given a sound; the SIGIL paper constructs a non-linguistic generator that reproduces the statistical signatures of language; and the Astra project burned about 891 million tokens and closed with an honest negative — none of the 417 signs tracked has an established sound or meaning. Scoreboard unchanged: no peer review, no independent validation, no consensus. [VERIFIED — the 1875 first publication, the 1924 announcement year, the mature-Harappan 2600–1900 BCE period, the seal corpus counts, the right-to-left direction and its deduction, the sign-frequency figures, and the logo-syllabic reading, per Wikipedia "Indus script", read first-party this pass; the January 5, 2025 prize announcement, the $1 million figure, the Chennai centenary venue, and the still-unclaimed status as of October 2026, per the prize coverage and the UNDECIPHERED.md prize watch; CORROBORATED — the Harappa 1921 / Mohenjo-daro 1922 excavation years, the Parpola Dravidian programme as the most influential, Wheeler's "invalid" verdict, the Farmer $10,000 counter-prize terms, the Rao 2009 *Science* entropy result, and the 100+ published decipherments with none accepted, per multiple secondary sources read this pass; the 2026 claimant season per UNDECIPHERED.md §3, filed there]

- **The script.** The corpus is small objects: stamp seals, typically just 2–3 centimetres on a side, usually one line of signs beside an animal — the one-horned "unicorn" the most familiar, with bulls, elephants, water buffaloes, and rhinoceroses — plus pottery, copper and bronze plates, tools, and ornaments. About 90% of the seals and inscribed objects come from sites in Pakistan along the Indus and its tributaries, Mohenjo-daro and Harappa foremost. No surviving example exists on any perishable material — no papyrus, paper, textile, leaf, wood, or bark — so whatever was written at length, if anything was, is gone. The writing direction is right-to-left, deduced from external evidence: signs compressed on the left side as if the writer were running out of space at the end of the row, with boustrophedon exceptions. The closest thing to a public text is the Dholavira signboard, ten large signs over the northern gateway of the citadel, a text meant to be read by everyone entering. The closest thing to a bilingual anchor names a man, not a text: the Mesopotamian cylinder seal of Shu-ilishu, interpreter of the language of Meluhha — Meluhha widely taken to be the Indus civilization — which proves the language had a name abroad and nothing else. The sign inventory is itself undecided: over 400 principal signs, generally read as logo-syllabic — too many for an alphabet, too few for a logography — with Mahadevan listing 417 (cited as 419 elsewhere), Bryan Wells estimating around 694, Pierson assigning 605, and Vigslist auditing 390–420 graphemes behind roughly 710 attested forms. The four obstacles, as the literature states them: the inscriptions are very short, averaging around five signs; it is doubted whether the signs record a language at all; even if they do, no sign's value — word, syllable, or morpheme — is known; and the spoken Harappan language has not been identified, though an estimated 300 loanwords in the Rigveda may carry evidence of a substrate language of the region. - **Worked miniature (computed this pass).** Five counts, all reproduced by goal hidden_files/verify-indus-20261109.py (33/33 checks pass), on the stated base of Farmer, Sproat & Witzel's 2004 count of Mahadevan's concordance: 417 signs, 2,905 objects, 13,372 sign occurrences. (1) **The sequence space.** A five-sign inscription drawn from 417 signs admits 417^5 = 12,608,989,261,857 possible strings — about 12.61 trillion — and the concordance's 2,905 texts sample 2.3 × 10^-10 of that space. The longest text, 26 signs, admits 417^26, about 10^68.1 possibilities. The space is not the constraint; the corpus is. (2) **The corpus budget.** The whole surviving corpus is 13,372 sign tokens at a mean of 4.6 signs per object. At five signs per word-equivalent, the entire written record of the largest civilization of the Bronze Age is about 2,674 words — shorter than a long magazine feature. The longest text is about 5.2 word-equivalents; the Dholavira signboard, the civilization's public text, is 2.0. There is no book here; there are shipping labels. (3) **The concentration.** Four signs carry 21% of the corpus — 2,808 of 13,372 occurrences, a mean of 702 each — against 25.58 for the other 413 signs: a 27.4× ratio. Sixty-seven signs carry 80% — 10,698 occurrences, a mean of 159.7 each — against 7.64 for the other 350: a 20.9× ratio. And 113 signs occur exactly once, 27.1% of the inventory, while 219 signs occur fewer than five times, 52.5% of it. Half the alphabet is barely attested; any reading must survive on the frequent few, and the rare half can neither confirm nor refute it. (4) **The inventory uncertainty.** Mahadevan's count is cited as both 417 and 419; the field's range runs 400–600, a 1.50× spread; Pierson's 605 is 1.45× Mahadevan's 417. The decipherer does not know how many letters the alphabet has — the sign list itself is uncertain by nearly half. (5) **The timeline and the two prizes.** First seal report to announcement, 1875 → 1924: 49 years. Announcement to the million-dollar prize, 1924 → 2025: 101 years. First seal to prize: 150 years of looking. Farmer's $10,000 counter-prize (2004) is one-hundredth of Tamil Nadu's $1,000,000 — one prize pays for reading it, the other pays for proving there is anything to read, and both wait on the same pile of evidence.
