- **The honest blank.** Five confessions. (1) Whether the script records language at all is unresolved: the Farmer thesis stands, the Rao entropy result answers structure and not reading, and the SIGIL counterexample shows a non-linguistic generator reproducing the statistical signatures of language. (2) The language family is unidentified: Dravidian is the most argued (Mahadevan, Parpola, Zvelebil), Indo-Aryan, Austroasiatic, and a lost family are all proposed, and the ~300 Rigvedic loanwords suggest a substrate, not an identity. (3) The counts themselves vary by citation and are filed, not smoothed: 417 vs 419 signs in citations of the same concordance, 2,905 vs 2,906 objects, 26 vs 17 signs for the longest text (Farmer et al. count 17 as the longest on a single seal surface; the commonly cited 26-sign figure is a pottery inscription, not a seal face). (4) The Dholavira signboard's ten signs have no agreed reading, and no sign anywhere has an established sound or meaning — the Astra negative (417 signs tracked, none established) is the current state of the art. (5) The prize has no published adjudication rules: "to the satisfaction of archaeological experts" is the whole criterion, and no winner, no shortlist, and no judging panel have been announced as of the October 2026 prize watch.

- **Decoder-design note (Indus → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The corpus is the intake form.** Before any decipherment claim, the Gauntlet demands the corpus arithmetic: how many tokens, how long is the longest text, how many signs carry the load. A claim that cannot state its corpus budget is not a claim — it is a wish. (Indus: 13,372 tokens, longest 26 signs, four signs carry a fifth.) (2) **The bilingual is the receipt; the falsifiability criterion is the substitute.** A decipherment with no bilingual and no long text must ship the conditions under which it is wrong — Yajnadevam's unicity-distance test is the template — and the Gauntlet runs the SIGIL test first: can a non-linguistic generator produce the same statistics? If yes, the statistics prove nothing, and the claim waits. (3) **The negative control is a result.** Astra burned about 891 million tokens and closed with "no sign has an established sound" — the Gauntlet files a clean negative as a result, not a failure. A method that cannot say "I don't know" cannot be trusted when it says "I know"; the honest nulls (Sharman's 33 killed hypotheses) are intake, not embarrassment. ## The Pigpen cipher (18th century) — the cipher you can read without breaking, or: the grid that hid in plain sight

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero `## ` headings in either catalogue, measured this pass — no entry-titled bullet, and no "Pigpen", "Rosicrucian", "tic-tac-toe", or "Napoleon cipher" string anywhere in either file; the single "Masonic" hit per file sits inside the Beale ciphers entry, a Masonic-allegory reading of the Beale story, not a cipher treatment. The catalogue holds the substitution ciphers Pigpen is always shelved beside — Atbash, the Bacon cipher, Playfair, the Beale ciphers — and the machine ciphers of the lodges' century, but not the one geometric substitution a child learns in an afternoon and a prisoner used in a war. The thinnest zero of all, measured this pass. [VERIFIED — the 0/0 heading counts and the 0/0 mention counts for Pigpen/Rosicrucian/tic-tac-toe/Napoleon-cipher, and the 1/1 Masonic hits identified as the Beale allegory reading, measured this pass]

- **The story.** Nobody knows who invented it, and the catalogue says so plainly. The origin stories pile up — Hebrew rabbis, the Knights Templar in the Crusades, a 16th-century individual saving his personal notes — and none of them is pinned down. The first hard date is 1531, when Cornelius Agrippa described an early form in *De Occulta Philosophia*, the "Kabbalah of the Nine Chambers": a Hebrew-alphabet grid system used for religious symbolism, not for keeping secrets. The first confirmed secret-keeping use belongs to the Freemasons, who took the system up in the early 18th century to keep their records of history and rites private and for correspondence between lodge leaders — so thoroughly that the cipher is still called the Freemason's cipher. The system then turns up wherever people needed a secret they could draw with a stick: on July 7, 1730, the French pirate Olivier Levasseur threw a scrap of pigpen writing overboard as he went to the gallows, allegedly holding the whereabouts of his treasure — never found, speculated to lie in the Seychelles, and the scrap's exact configuration was never determined. An early stone in Trinity Church Cemetery in New York City, which opened in 1697, carries a pigpen inscription that deciphers to "Remember death" — memento mori, carved where everyone could see it and almost no one could read it. George Washington's army held documentation of the system with a much more randomized alphabet. During the American Civil War, Union prisoners in Confederate prisons used it; in December 1863 one prisoner's pigpen letter stumped the Union army's own cryptographers. - **The cipher.** A geometric monoalphabetic substitution: every letter becomes a fragment of a grid. The standard Masonic key lays the alphabet across four diagrams in reading order — two tic-tac-toe grids and two diagonal crosses. Grid one, undotted, holds A through I; grid two, the same shapes with a dot in each cell, holds J through R; cross one, the four wedges of an X, holds S through V; cross two, the same wedges dotted, holds W through Z. To encipher a letter you draw the lines that surround its cell: A, top-left corner, is the right and bottom lines; E, the centre, is a closed box; the dot tells you which of the two identical diagrams you are in. Thirteen shapes, doubled by the dot, make twenty-six glyphs. The variants reorder the diagrams — grid, cross, grid, cross instead of grid, grid, cross, cross — or drop the crosses entirely for three grids with one and two dots and an ampersand in the last cell, the Newark variant swapping dots for short lines; the 17th-century Rosicrucian form used a single nine-cell grid with one to three dots per cell, the dot's position — left, centre, or right — naming which of the three letters in that pen was meant; and the Templar form builds its glyphs from a Maltese cross, a cipher most likely of 18th-century Neo-Templars rather than the 12th-to-14th-century order. ## The Quipu (c. 2600 BCE– ) — the knots that kept an empire, or: the writing you read with your hands

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero `## ` headings and zero mentions of quipu, khipu, or quipucamayoc in either catalogue, measured this pass — the thinnest zero of all, measured this pass. The catalogue already holds the undeciphered scripts a decoder reaches for first — Maya glyphs, Linear A, the Indus script, Rongorongo, the Phaistos Disc — and the Rosetta Stone and Linear B as bullets, but not the one writing system that is not written at all: no ink, no incision, no surface. An empire of perhaps ten million people, administered for a century without a single written word, on string. [VERIFIED — the 0/0 heading counts and the 0/0 mention counts for quipu/khipu/quipucamayoc, measured this pass]

- **The story.** The word is Quechua for "knot": *quipu* is the Spanish spelling, *khipu* the Quechua one, and the catalogue uses both. A quipu is a record-keeping device of knotted cotton or camelid-fiber cords — a main cord with pendant cords hanging from it, subsidiary cords hanging from those, anywhere from a few cords to several thousand. Objects unambiguously identifiable as quipus first appear in the archaeological record in the 1st millennium CE, likely Wari; they ran the administration of the Kingdom of Cusco in the 13th to 15th centuries and then of the Inca Empire (1438–1533), flourishing across the Andes from about 1100 to 1532 — tax obligations, census records, calendrical information, military organization, and possibly stereotyped historical annales. The men who read them were the *quipucamayocs*, the khipu specialists; in the early Spanish years their bookkeeping was summoned into court and recognised as valid documentation of past payments. After the conquest the Spanish destroyed many quipus as idolatrous, then adapted the survivors to colonial administration and fused them with writing into quipu boards for tracking religious duties — and in some Andean villages the cords never stopped being used. The survivors are scattered: Gary Urton's 2003 estimate was about 600 extant quipus; the Khipu Database Project he built with Carrie Brezine counts 751 reported; a 2021 survey of museum and private inventories puts known extant pre-Columbian quipus at just under 1,400, of which the Open Khipu Repository holds 702 with publicly available data as of January 2026. The largest single collection — 298 quipus — sits in the Ethnological Museum of Berlin, an ocean from the mountains that made them. [VERIFIED — the Quechua meaning and both spellings, the cord construction and cord counts, the Wari first appearance, the Cusco and Inca dates and administrative uses, the quipucamayoc court standing, the destruction and the colonial adaptation and boards, the 600 / 751 / just-under-1,400 / 702 figures and the Berlin 298, per Wikipedia "Quipu", read first-party this pass]

- **The system.** The numbers are the solved part, and they were solved by reading, not by guessing. Leslie Leland Locke is credited with first demonstrating that the knots encode numbers in base-10 positional notation; Marcia and Robert Ascher, building on Locke from the late 1960s, analysed several hundred quipus and showed most of the information recorded is numerical and systematically interpretable. Three knot types do the work: simple overhand knots, long knots (an overhand knot with extra turns), and figure-eight knots, with a rare fourth — a figure-eight with an extra twist, the "EE" knot. On a cord, knots cluster at registers along its length, each register a power of ten, the ones position at the bottom. Digits in the tens and higher are clusters of simple knots; in the ones position, 2–9 is a long knot with that many turns and 1 is a figure-eight; zero is the absence of a knot in that position. So 731 is 7 simple, 3 simple, figure-eight; 804 is 8 simple, gap, long-4; 1493 is 1 simple, 4 simple, 9 simple, long-3; and one cord can hold several numbers in sequence — 107 followed by 51 is 1 simple, gap, long-7, 5 simple, figure-eight. The reading is proved by the quipus themselves: cords regularly contain the sums of the next *n* cords, and sometimes sums of sums — a relationship that would be wildly improbable if the knot values were being misread. Beyond numbers sit the *number labels*: digit strings used as codes rather than quantities. Carrie Brezine hypothesised that a particular three-number label at the start of some quipus refers to Puruchuco, like a ZIP code. The August 12, 2005 *Science* report by Urton and Brezine, "Khipu Accounting in Ancient Peru", may represent the first identification of a quipu element for a non-numeric concept: a sequence of three figure-eight knots at the start of a quipu that seems to be a unique signifier — a toponym for Puruchuco, or the name of the quipu keeper, or its subject matter, or even a time designator. Three knots, four live readings, and the paper says so. - **The phonetic turn.** For decades the standing view was that quipus are not glottographic writing — no phonetic referent, no link to Quechua. Sabine Hyland broke that consensus from the field, not the archive. In July 2015 she examined two 18th-century khipus guarded by the village of San Juan de Collata in the Peruvian Andes — letters exchanged by local leaders during a revolt against Spanish authority, the only Andean phonetic khipus ever identified — and published the partial decipherment in *Current Anthropology* 58(3) in 2017, "Writing with Twisted Cords: The Inscriptive Capacity of Andean Khipu Texts". The pendants come in 95 different combinations of colour, fibre type, and direction of ply — inside the 80-to-800-symbol range of logosyllabic writing systems — and Hyland reads them as logosyllabic, each pendant a phonetic syllable, like Classic Mayan. The decipherment turned on the signatures: assuming the first khipu was signed at the end with the lineage name *Alluka*, its last three pendants should sound out A, LLU, KA — the last pendant blue, and the local word for blue is *ankas*, perhaps the KA. The same cords on the second khipu then read A, KA, and its final pendant, a golden-brown vicuña fibre the locals call *paru*, supplies PAR: *Yakapar*, the other lineage of the revolt — a name the written record independently attributes to the khipu's sender. Two lineage names, read phonetically, the first phonetic decipherment of any khipu. Hyland's programme has since also deciphered the meaning of knot direction and of ply direction in khipus, and the two most common colour patterns; and in 2011 a possible match between six colonial-era Santa Valley quipus and a Spanish colonial document from the same region was identified — the strongest Rosetta-like connection currently known. - **The story.** "The Adventure of the Dancing Men" — Arthur Conan Doyle, first published in *The Strand Magazine* in December 1903 (United States: *Collier's*, 5 December 1903), original title "The Dancing Men", collected in *The Return of Sherlock Holmes* (United States February 1905, United Kingdom March 1905). Hilton Cubitt of Ridling Thorpe Manor, Norfolk, brings Holmes a paper of absurd little figures: his American wife Elsie Patrick had made him promise never to ask about her past — "very disagreeable associations" in Chicago — and now the figures arrive, first mailed from the United States, then chalked around the house, and Elsie is terrified and will not explain. Holmes reads them as a substitution cipher and cracks them by frequency analysis — but the last message sends him rushing to Norfolk too late: Cubitt dead of a bullet to the heart, Elsie gravely wounded by a gunshot to the head. Inspector Martin reads murder-suicide with Elsie the prime suspect; Holmes proves a third person. The sender is Abe Slaney, Elsie's former fiancé, a deadly criminal from Chicago, come to take her back; her father headed the Chicago gang — "the Joint" — that invented the cipher. Cubitt had fired the first shot, so Slaney's hanging sentence is reduced to penal servitude; Elsie recovers and spends her life helping the poor. One of only two Holmes short stories in which the client dies after seeking his help (the other: "The Five Orange Pips"). [VERIFIED — the December 1903 Strand / 5 December 1903 Collier's publication, the 1905 collection dates, the Ridling Thorpe plot, the deaths, the third-person proof, Slaney's identity and sentence, Elsie's recovery, and the two-stories distinction, per Wikipedia "The Adventure of the Dancing Men", read first-party this pass]

- **The cipher.** A monoalphabetic substitution: each stick man, in a distinct dancing pose, stands for one letter of the alphabet. The figures carry no spaces; instead, a man at the end of a word holds a small flag — the flag is the word boundary, the only segmentation the reader gets. Its security was steganography, not mathematics: the inventor expected it "would pass as a child's scrawl", which is exactly what Cubitt first took it for. Only 18 letters appear in the story's messages; F, J, K, Q, U, W, X, Z never occur and have no known figures. The cipher was inspired by a visit to the Hill House Inn in Happisburgh, on the North Norfolk coast. It arrives as two more short sentences and one message that "appeared — since there was no flag — to be a single word": five letters, E's second and fourth — "It might be 'sever,' or 'lever,' or 'never'" — and as a reply to an appeal, NEVER is far the most probable, giving N, V, and R. Then the name: a combination with two E's and three letters between, forming the termination of the message "three times repeated", must be "ELSIE" — giving L, S, and I. The word before it has four letters and ends in E — "surely the word must be 'COME'" — giving C, O, and M. With those ten letters the first message renders ".M .ERE ..E SL.NE."; "the first letter can only be A" (it occurs three times), "and the H is also apparent in the second word" — "AM HERE A.E SLANE." — "or, filling in the obvious vacancies in the name: AM HERE ABE SLANEY." Holmes cables his friend Wilson Hargreave of the New York Police Bureau about the name; the reply: "The most dangerous crook in Chicago." Holmes then writes his own dancing-men message — "COME HERE AT ONCE" — and has it delivered to Slaney at Elrige's Farm, knowing Slaney will believe it came from Elsie; Slaney walks into the manor and is seized. ## The Myszkowski transposition (1902) — the cipher that called itself undecipherable, or: the keyword that repeats itself

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero `## ` headings and zero mentions of "Myszkowski" in either catalogue, measured this pass — the thinnest zero of all, measured this pass. The catalogue holds the rest of the transposition family — rail fence, scytale, columnar, double transposition, disrupted transposition, grilles — and the fractionation family that transposition feeds (Bifid, Trifid, ADFGX/ADFGVX), but not the one variant whose entire novelty is a repeated letter in the keyword. [VERIFIED — the 0/0 heading counts and the 0/0 mention counts for Myszkowski/myszkowski, measured this pass]

- **The story.** Émile Victor Théodore Myszkowski, a retired French Army colonel, published *Cryptographie indéchiffrable* — *Indecipherable Cryptography*, subtitle *basée sur de nouvelles combinaisons rationelles* (*based on new rational combinations*) — in Paris in 1902, Société Française d'Imprimerie et de Librairie, 15 Rue de Cluny. The book described a cipher of his own invention and claimed, incorrectly, that it was undecipherable — secure against unauthorised attempts to read it. The cipher was a form of repeated-key transposition. The claim did not survive: a transposition is a permutation, and a permutation keeps the plaintext's letter frequencies intact, which is exactly how a cryptanalyst detects it. [VERIFIED — the author, rank, book title, subtitle, 1902 date, Paris publisher and address, and the "claimed (incorrectly) was undecipherable" wording, per Wikipedia "Cryptographie indéchiffrable", read first-party this pass; the frequency-preservation point per Wikipedia "Transposition cipher", Detection and cryptanalysis, read first-party this pass]

- **The system.** A variant of columnar transposition, and the variant is one rule. The keyword must have recurrent letters — a keyword with no repeats is just ordinary columnar transposition, and the catalogue's ZEBRAS example already covers that. The keyword's letters are numbered by alphabetical rank, and recurrent letters are numbered identically: TOMATO yields the keystring 432143. (Usual practice treats later occurrences as if they were the next letter in alphabetical order — TOMATO yielding 532164 — which is the ordinary columnar key, not Myszkowski's.) The plaintext is written row-wise into a grid as many columns wide as the keyword is long. Columns are then read off in rank order, and the tie rule is the cipher: a column whose number is unique is transcribed downward; columns sharing a number are transcribed left to right, row by row. The canonical example, keyword TOMATO, plaintext WEAREDISCOVEREDFLEEATONCE: keystring 4 3 2 1 4 3; grid rows WEARED / ISCOVE / REDFLE / EATONC / E; read-off rank 1 (column 4, down): ROFO; rank 2 (column 3, down): ACDT; rank 3 (columns 2 and 6, left to right): EDSEEEAC; rank 4 (columns 1 and 5, left to right): WEIVRLENE; ciphertext ROFOA CDTED SEEEA CWEIV RLENE. [VERIFIED — the recurrent-letter requirement, both keystrings, the unique-down / recurring-left-to-right rule, the grid, and the grouped ciphertext, per Wikipedia "Transposition cipher", Myszkowski transposition, read first-party this pass]

- **The worked miniature (computed this pass).** Six counts, all reproduced by goal hidden_files/verify-myszkowski-20261110.py (20/20 checks pass). (1) **The keystrings.** TOMATO derives to 432143 under the Myszkowski rule and 532164 under usual practice; BANANA derives to 213131; ZEBRAS, with no repeats, derives to 632415 either way — the tie rule only bites when a letter repeats. (2) **The canonical example, re-run.** Encryption of WEAREDISCOVEREDFLEEATONCE under TOMATO reproduces Wikipedia's ciphertext exactly — ROFOACDTEDSEEEACWEIVRLENE, grouped ROFOA CDTED SEEEA CWEIV RLENE, 25 letters — and decryption round-trips it back to the plaintext. (3) **A fresh example.** Keyword BANANA, plaintext MEETMEATTHEOLDMILLATMIDNIGHT (28 letters): ciphertext ETETHODILTINGTMALAIEMTEMLMDH, decryption round-trips. (4) **The keyspace.** A Myszkowski keystring is a weak ordering of the keyword's letters — ranks with ties allowed — so the count of distinct keystrings for a keyword of length n is the ordered Bell (Fubini) number: 1, 3, 13, 75, 541, 4683, 47293, 545835 for n = 1..8. At n = 6 that is 4683 against 720 plain permutations — 6.5× the keyspace of ordinary columnar transposition at the same keyword length, and 47293 at n = 7. (5) **The pattern count.** TOMATO's repeat pattern — two pairs and two singles, (2,2,1,1) — admits 180 distinct keystrings: 6!/(2!2!). The keyword's shape, not just its length, sets the keyspace. (6) **The frequency receipt.** The ciphertext is a permutation of the plaintext — E occurs 7 times in both — which is the detection the entry's story turns on: the "undecipherable" cipher announces itself as a transposition to anyone who counts. And the tie rule's direction matters: reading the tied columns down instead of left to right gives ROFOACDTESEADEECWIREEEVLN, which is not the ciphertext — the row-wise read is load-bearing, not a formatting choice. [VERIFIED — all counts, renders, and keyspace figures computed this pass by verify-myszkowski-20261110.py, 20/20 checks pass]

- **The honest blank.** Three confessions. (1) The "undecipherable" claim is filed as wrong on the mechanism's own terms — a permutation preserves frequencies, and the same article's Detection section says so — but no break narrative for Myszkowski specifically was read this pass: no named cryptanalyst, no date, no worked break. The claim's falsity is structural, not historical. (2) No operational use was found in the sources read this pass: no army, service, or agent is recorded as having fielded the cipher — it lived in the book and then in the textbooks, and the catalogue does not invent a service history for it. (3) The Kahn citation is carried, not opened: the transposition article cites David Kahn's *The Codebreakers* (pp. 301–304, 535, 539) for the columnar history and the Myszkowski passage, and this pass read the article, not Kahn. [CLAIMED — nothing in this section rises above the grades stated]

- **Decoder-design note (Myszkowski → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The key's shape is the first thing to inventory.** A repeated letter in a keyword is not a flaw in the key — it is a structural tell that forces a row-wise read and changes the read order of whole columns. The Gauntlet inventories a specimen's key-shape — ties, repeats, degeneracies — before its content, because the shape constrains the read before any letter is placed. (2) **Keyspace arithmetic is not security.** 4683 keystrings at n = 6 is 6.5× the plain columnar count, and the cipher is still a permutation: frequency profile intact, anagramming still works, depth still bites. A specimen that boasts a bigger keyspace has changed the counting, not the attack — the Gauntlet grades the attack surface, never the keyspace number alone. (3) **A title is a claim, not evidence.** A book called *Indecipherable Cryptography* grades itself in its own title, and the claim was wrong. The Gauntlet treats a specimen's self-description — its name, its manual, its marketing — as a claim to test, never as evidence: the Beale rung and the Voynich self-graders' rule, confirmed a third time. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's doctrine, never run]

## The Ogham alphabet (c. 4th–10th centuries) — the writing on the edge of the stone, or: the key that never got lost

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero `## ` headings and zero mentions of "ogham" in either catalogue, measured this pass — the thinnest zero of all, measured this pass. The catalogue holds Linear A and Linear B, the undeciphered scripts, the fractionation family, and the rotor machines — but no entry for the one alphabet whose own origin story is a cipher debate, and no entry for a script that was never lost at all. (The next zero stands named for a later loop: "runic" is 0/0 headings in both catalogues, and the six "rune" substring hits are false positives and passing mentions — Székely runes inside the Voynich entry, Cicada's *Liber Primus* as a "book of runes" — not an entry.) [VERIFIED — the 0/0 heading counts and the 0/0 mention counts for ogham/Ogham in both catalogues, measured this pass]

- **The story.** Ogham is an Early Medieval alphabet used to write Primitive Irish in the "orthodox" stone inscriptions of the 4th to 6th centuries AD, and later Old Irish in the scholastic inscriptions of the 6th to 9th centuries; the article's infobox dates the script c. 4th–10th centuries. Roughly 400 orthodox inscriptions survive on stone monuments throughout Ireland and western Britain — the article's lead figure; its Corpus section says roughly 380, a twenty-inscription disagreement inside one article, carried in the honest blank below. The bulk are in southern Munster: Cork and Kerry hold 60% of all Irish ogham stones, over one-third of the total sits in County Kerry alone, most densely in the former kingdom of Corcu Duibne, and the largest number outside Ireland is in Pembrokeshire, Wales. The inscriptions usually consist of personal names written in a set formula — X MAQI Y MUCOI Z, "of X, son of Y, of the tribe of Z" — and the Ballaqueeney stone on the Isle of Man reads BIVAIDONAS MAQI MUCOI CUNAVA[LI], "of Bivaidonas, son of the tribe Cunava[li]". The stone commemorating Vortiporius, a 6th-century king of Dyfed, is the only ogham inscription bearing the name of an identifiable individual. And the script's defining fact for this catalogue is an inversion of every other decipherment story here: ogham was never lost. The alphabet survived in the manuscripts — the *Auraicept na n-Éces* ("The Scholars' Primer") and *In Lebor Ogaim* ("The Ogam Tract") — so the stones were readable the moment the manuscript key was laid beside them. There was no Ventris moment, no forty-year silence: the key outlived the lock. Ogham was still being used for notes in manuscripts down to the 16th century, and a modern ogham inscription stands on a gravestone dated 1802 at Ahenny, County Tipperary. [VERIFIED — the period, the two corpus counts, the Munster/Kerry/Pembrokeshire distribution, the formula and the Ballaqueeney reading, the Vortiporius singularity, the manuscript survival and the 16th-century use and the 1802 stone, per Wikipedia "Ogham", read first-party this pass]

- **The system.** The alphabet originally consisted of twenty letters, the *Beith-luis-nin*, divided into four groups — *aicme*, "family" — of five, by stroke angle and direction. *Aicme beithe*, the B group (B L F S N), takes right-side/downward strokes; *aicme hÚatha*, the H group (H D T C Q), takes left-side/upward strokes; *aicme muine*, the M group (M G NG Z R), takes oblique crossing strokes; *aicme ailme*, the A group (A O U E I), takes notches or perpendicular crossing strokes on the stemline itself. Every letter is one to five strokes: the aicme is the position, the count is the letter, so the whole alphabet is a 4×5 tally grid. On a standing stone the script is carved into the edge — the *droim* or *faobhar* — which forms the stemline, and the text is read beginning from the bottom left-hand side, continuing upward along the edge, across the top and down the right-hand side. Five additional letters, the *forfeda*, were later introduced mainly in the manuscript tradition; of them only the first, *éabhadh*, regularly appears in inscriptions, mostly with the value K in the word *koi* ("here"), and the last, *eamhancholl*, appears in no orthodox inscription at all. A letter for P is conspicuously absent — the phoneme was lost in Proto-Celtic, and no sign was needed until Latin loanwords arrived — while a letter for the labiovelar Q (*ceirt*) survives for a phoneme already lost in Old Irish: the alphabet is designed for a language older than its stones. The *Ogam Tract* also gives a variety of some 100 variant or secret modes of writing ogham — 92 in the Book of Ballymote — so the alphabet carried its own cipher modes inside its own teaching text. Unicode took ogham in September 1999 with version 3.0, block U+1680–U+169F, ISO 15924 Ogam (212). [VERIFIED — the four aicmí and their stroke directions, the 1–5 stroke rule, the droim reading order, the forfeda record, the missing P and the surviving Q, the ~100/92 secret modes, and the Unicode block, per Wikipedia "Ogham", read first-party this pass]

- **The worked miniature (computed this pass).** Seven counts, all reproduced by goal hidden_files/verify-ogham-20261110.py (31/31 checks pass). (1) **The tally grid.** Each aicme sums to 1+2+3+4+5 = 15 marks, so the whole twenty-letter alphabet costs 60 marks — four aicmí of fifteen. (2) **The formula words.** MAQI is 12 marks (M 1 oblique, A 1 notch, Q 5 left, I 5 notches); MUCOI is 15 (M 1, U 3, C 4, O 2, I 5). (3) **The Ballaqueeney stone, re-run.** BIVAIDONAS MAQI MUCOI CUNAVA[LI] is 27 letters and 80 marks: BIVAIDONAS 29 (V written with the F letter, Primitive Irish having no V — the read-back is BIFAIDONAS), MAQI 12, MUCOI 15, CUNAVALI 24; every word round-trips through the encode/decode mapping. (4) **The name that does not fit.** KODAKAI cannot be carved in the orthodox twenty: K is absent and needs the forfid *éabhadh*, while O, D, A, I are all present — the catalogue's own name arrives a millennium late for its own alphabet. (5) **The corpus disagreement.** The article's lead says roughly 400 orthodox inscriptions and its Corpus section says roughly 380 — a 20-inscription gap inside one article, about five percent. (6) **The secret-mode count.** The Ogam Tract's ~100 variant modes against the Book of Ballymote's 92 — a difference of eight modes between the two counts. (7) **The tree audit.** Of the twenty letter names, eight at most are tree names by McManus's count, and only five are comprehensible without glosses in the *Auraicept* itself — the "Celtic tree alphabet" is a minority of the names. [VERIFIED — all counts, renders, and round-trips computed this pass by verify-ogham-20261110.py, 31/31 checks pass]

- **The honest blank.** Four confessions. (1) The origin is genuinely unsettled, and the entry files the debate, not a verdict. The cryptic-alphabet school (Carney, MacNeill) holds ogham was created as a secret means of communication against the authorities of Roman Britain — political, military, or religious reasons — and the article notes the serious threat of Roman invasion may have spurred it. The Christian-community school (McManus) holds it was invented by the first Christian communities in early Ireland for a unique alphabet of their own. A third hypothesis (Thurneysen, Vendryes) derives the letter forms from a tally-mark counting system built on fives and twenties. A fourth (Macalister) — finger signals invented by Gaulish druids in Cisalpine Gaul around 600 BC — is largely rejected by later scholars. On the template, the Latin alphabet is the primary contender, with Elder Futhark and Greek holding supporters, and Düwel (1968) points out a similarity with ciphers of Germanic runes; the article's own infobox lists the parent system as "Unknown (possibly a cipher of Latin script)". (2) The "Celtic tree alphabet" is a medieval gloss plus a modern popularization, not the original naming. The tree reading was popularized by Robert Graves in *The White Goddess*; McManus dates the tree idea to the Old Irish period, centuries after the letters were named, arising because the letters were called *feda*, "trees", for their shape. Only five names need no gloss in the *Auraicept* — beith "birch", fearn "alder", sail "willow", dair "oak", coll "hazel" — and McManus adds at most three more (onn "ash", idad probably "yew", ailm possibly "pine"). The rest are not trees at all: uath is "horror, fear", tinne is "ingot", gort is "field", ruis is "red", úr is "earth, clay, soil", and eadhadh is of unknown meaning. (3) The Pictish ogham inscriptions remain undeciphered: the Lunnasting stone and its kin record fragments of what is probably Pictish, Cox (1999) has argued for Old Norse, and others remain unconvinced — the language is still the subject of debate. (4) The corpus count disagrees with itself — roughly 400 in the lead, roughly 380 in the Corpus section — and this pass read the article, not the underlying corpus, so no count is certified above the article. [VERIFIED — the four schools and the Macalister rejection, the Latin-template preference, the Düwel cipher note, and the "possibly a cipher of Latin script" parent-system line, per Wikipedia "Ogham"; the tree audit (5 without glosses, 8 at most) per McManus as carried by the article; the Pictish undeciphered status and the Cox debate per the article; CLAIMED — the legendary accounts (Fenius Farsa after Babel; Ogma's invention; the first message of seven b's on a birch warning Lug) as carried by the article, not opened this pass]

- **Decoder-design note (Ogham → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **A surviving key inverts the problem.** Ogham was never broken — it was remembered. The Gauntlet's first question for any unknown script is whether a key survives beside the lock: a manuscript, a bilingual, a crib. A surviving key turns a decipherment into a lookup, and the specimen's difficulty moves from the code to the carrier — the stone's edge, the formula, the names. The Rosetta rung said the same from the other side; ogham is the case where the key never left. (2) **A tally is a coordinate system.** Four aicmí by five positions is a 4×5 grid, and every letter is an address: position first, count second. The Gauntlet inventories a specimen's coordinate structure before its content, because the address space bounds the message space — sixty marks for twenty letters is a budget, and a specimen that spends it differently is telling you its alphabet. (3) **A name is not a meaning.** The tree alphabet is a gloss that stuck: the letters' names are claims about the letters, not the letters themselves, and only eight of twenty survive the audit. The Gauntlet treats any naming layer — tree names, code names, marketing — as a claim to test, never as evidence: the Myszkowski title rung, confirmed a fourth time. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's doctrine, never run]

The catalogue holds the undeciphered scripts, the fractionation family, the rotor machines, and now Ogham — but no entry for the one writing system in recorded history invented single-handedly by a man who could not read at all, and no entry for a script whose key was never lost because it was never hidden: it was taught, in the open, to a six-year-old girl first. - **The story.** Sequoyah — ᏎᏉᏯ, Se-quo-ya, in English George Gist or George Guess — was a Cherokee silversmith, born around 1770 in the Overhill town of Tuskegee on the Little Tennessee River, who could not read or write English. Around 1809, impressed by the "talking leaves" of European written languages — paper that spoke across distance — he began work on a writing system for Cherokee, and worked at it for twelve years. His first attempt was a logogram for every word, abandoned when the count ran into the thousands; his second attempt was the breakthrough: Cherokee syllables are finite, and each one could have its own sign. The work was done in the open and in the face of it: neighbours whispered witchcraft, and his wife is said to have burned his first papers, believing them sorcery. In 1821 he finished — 86 characters, each a syllable — and taught his first pupil, his six-year-old daughter Ayoka. The demonstration is the catalogue's purest interrogation scene: as the story goes, Sequoyah was charged with witchcraft and brought before a town chief, who tested his claims by separating him and his daughter and asking them to communicate through the marks alone; by the trial's end the officials were convinced, and their question was not punishment but "Can you teach us how to read?" The council approved the syllabary's dissemination in 1821, and within months the Nation was mostly literate; by 1825 the majority of Cherokees could read and write in their new orthography, and the National Council formally adopted it the same year. In 1824 the General Council had already awarded Sequoyah a large silver medal — "Presented to George Gist by the General Council of the Cherokee for his ingenuity in the invention of the Cherokee Alphabet" — which he is said to have worn for the rest of his life and to have been buried with. The press followed the people: on February 21, 1828, the first issue of the *Cherokee Phoenix* appeared at New Echota, the first newspaper published by Native Americans in the United States and the first published in a Native American language, edited by Elias Boudinot with type cast by Samuel Worcester; it ran until the Georgia Guard seized the press in 1834. And the invention travelled: in the 1960s evidence emerged that the Cherokee syllabary provided a model for the design of the Vai syllabary of Liberia, which emerged about 1832–33 — one invented script seeding another across an ocean. Sequoyah died in August 1843 at San Fernando de Rosas in Mexico, seeking Cherokee bands who had fled there, twenty-two years after he finished his syllabary. Four years later a botanist in Vienna named the tallest trees on earth for him — or so the story goes, and the naming is still argued. - **The system.** The modern syllabary is 85 characters, each a distinct syllable, arranged in Worcester's recitation order: six vowels first (a e i o u v, where v is the nasal mid-central vowel), then twelve consonant rows — g/k, h, l, m, n/hn, qu, s, d/t, dl/tl, ts, w, y — each row running across the six vowel columns. The shapes are borrowed and the code is new: the letters resemble Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, and Glagolitic characters, but no character carries its borrowed sound — a decoder's warning made flesh, the shape is not the cipher. The system is deliberately lossy in exactly the ways a syllabary can afford: voiced and unvoiced consonants are generally not distinguished (there is no separate ko — the g row gives go only, and ke, ki, ku, kv do not exist at all); long vowels are not distinguished; syllables ending in a vowel, h, or a glottal stop are not differentiated, so one sign Ꮡ stands for both suú "six" and súh "fishhook"; consonant clusters take an inserted vowel, so ᏧᎾᏍᏗ spells tsu-na-s-di for juunsdi̋, "small (plural), babies"; tones are unmarked, and the reader supplies them from context. Two print-shop edits mark the system's history: in 1828 Boudinot reordered the chart and dropped the 86th character entirely — the obsolete mv, Ᏽ — and in 1834 Worcester inverted the do character Ꮩ so it could not be confused with go Ꭺ, the old form an upside-down V, the modern form a V. Otherwise the characters remained remarkably invariant until twentieth-century typesetting. Sequoyah also proposed a numeral system in the late 1820s — unique signs for 1 through 19, tens for 20 through 100, a ciphered-additive structure for larger numbers — but it was never adopted and never typeset, and as of Unicode 17.0 the numerals are still not encoded. The syllabary itself reached Unicode in September 1999 with version 3.0, block U+13A0–U+13FF, and lowercase letters followed in June 2015 with version 8.0, the Supplement at U+AB70–U+ABBF — though the lowercase is almost never used, and Cherokee remains essentially unicameral in practice. - **Decoder-design note (Cherokee → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The hardest encoder has no key at all.** Sequoyah was illiterate in every script he had seen — he had no key, no teacher, no bilingual, only the observation that paper could speak. The Gauntlet's first question for a specimen is usually "what key does it hold"; the Cherokee rung inverts it: ask what the specimen can build with no key, because an agent that can invent its own code from observation alone is a different class of specimen from one that merely applies a given cipher. (2) **Borrowed shapes, new code.** The syllabary's letters look like Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, and Glagolitic — and none of them means what its shape means elsewhere. The Gauntlet treats any familiar shape as a trap: the interrogator who reads a borrowed glyph by its home value is the analyst who reads the tree names as the letters, the Ogham rung confirmed a second time. (3) **The demonstration is the protocol.** The trial separated the encoder from the decoder and asked them to communicate through the marks alone — that is a gauntlet run in period dress, and it is the cheapest proof in the catalogue: two parties, one channel, no shared key beyond the marks themselves, and the question "can you teach us" as the verdict. A specimen that passes a separated demonstration has proven its code in the only way that counts — by surviving the separation. ## The Glagolitic alphabet (c. 862–863) — the word made letters, or: the alphabet that died twice and still speaks

- **The story.** Cyril of Thessalonica, a Christian monk, created the alphabet in the ninth century — 862 or 863 — to translate Greek liturgical texts into Old Church Slavonic, a language the Greek and Latin alphabets could not write. He and his brother Methodius were sent by the Byzantine emperor to Great Moravia at the request of Prince Rastislav, who wanted to weaken his country's dependence on East Frankish priests; the alphabet was used between 863 and 885 for government and religious documents and books, and at the Great Moravian Academy the missionaries founded. The mission died with its patrons: in 885 Pope Stephen V issued a bull restricting services to Latin or Greek, Svatopluk I persecuted the students of Cyril and Methodius, and in 886 Wiching, the East Frankish bishop of Nitra, banned the script and jailed two hundred followers of Methodius. The survivors carried the alphabet south: Clement, Naum, Angelar, Sava, and Gorazd reached the First Bulgarian Empire, where Boris I received them and founded the Ohrid and Preslav literary schools. There the alphabet met its child: Early Cyrillic was developed gradually in the Preslav school by scribes who incorporated some Glagolitic letters into the Greek alphabet, and in 893 a great assembly of notables summoned by Boris chose Cyrillic — the Glagolitic alphabet gradually ceased to be used in Bulgaria over the next two centuries, though passages written in it appear in Cyrillic manuscripts until the end of the fourteenth century. Its second life was Croatian. The rounded form gave way to the angular, squared form of the Adriatic coast; the Baška tablet, conventionally dated to about 1100 and found on Krk, is its great stone witness; in 1248 Pope Innocent IV granted Bishop Philip of Senj the unique privilege of using the Slavonic language and this script in the Roman Rite liturgy; Hrvoje's Missal was illuminated in Split in 1404; and the 1483 *Missale Romanum Glagolitice* was the first printed Croatian Glagolitic book. The script survived the Ottoman incursions, the Counter-Reformation, and the confiscation of its only printing press, kept alive by rural chapters and island notaries — the final Glagolitic entry in the Omišalj parish baptismal register is dated 1817, and a lay Glagolite was still keeping a journal in it in 1832 — and it survived into the twentieth century on Krk and in the Zadar archipelago, where its area even expanded in the early 1900s before Vatican II confined its regular use to a few monasteries. It also carries a false provenance worth more than a true one: in the thirteenth century Croatian scribes ascribed the alphabet's invention to St. Jerome — "Hieronymian" — a compatriot born on the Dalmatian border, and the legend was used to defend Slavonic writing and liturgy against Rome; it spread so far that the Emperor Charles IV believed it, and the epoch of traditional attribution to Jerome ended only probably in 1812. Today the alphabet is on the Croatian one, two, and five euro cent coins, and it was the writing system of the world of *The Witcher* video games from 2007 to 2015 — a dead liturgical script, still speaking. [VERIFIED — the 862/863 creation, the Moravian mission and its dates, the 885 bull, the 886 ban and the two hundred jailed, the Bulgarian schools, the 893 assembly, the Baška tablet date, the 1248 privilege, Hrvoje's Missal 1404, the 1483 first printed book, the 1817 register entry, the 1832 journal, the Jerome legend and its 1812 end, the euro coins, and the Witcher use, per Wikipedia "Glagolitic script", read first-party this pass]

- **The system.** The alphabet known today has forty-one letters — the article's own table prints forty-two rows, and the discrepancy is filed in the honest blank below. Twenty-four of the forty-one probably derive from graphemes of the medieval cursive Greek small alphabet, given an ornamental design; the rest are the alphabet's own invention or borrowings from further afield — *sha* Ⱎ, *tsi* Ⱌ, and *cherv* Ⱍ are proposed from the Hebrew shin and tsadi, *zhivete* Ⰶ from the Coptic janja — and one widely discussed theory, that all the letters were constructed from the Christian symbols cross, circle, and triangle, could not be proven as a general design principle, though the symmetric pair *i* Ⰻ and *slovo* Ⱄ, which together form the abbreviation of the nomen sacrum *Isusъ*, "Jesus", is accepted as deliberate construction. The name is the word: *glagolŭ* means "utterance" or "word", *glagoljica* developed in Croatia around the fourteenth century from *glagolity*, those who used the Slavonic liturgy, and the alphabet is also called *azbuka* acrophonically, from the names of its first two letters, on the model of alpha plus beta. The letters name themselves into a sentence — the acrostic is computed in the miniature below. The alphabet has two hands: the original rounded form of Bulgaria and Macedonia, and the angular, squared form of Croatia, plus a cursive form developed for notaries; the majuscule served inscriptions and higher liturgical uses, the minuscule religious and secular documents alike. For numbers, the Glagolitic numerals assign values by native alphabetic order — unlike Cyrillic numerals, which inherited their values from the corresponding Greek letters — so Ⰰ is one, Ⰱ is two, and so forth, combined additively, highest value at the left, with the teens eleven through nineteen written in reverse order, ones before tens, as Slavic lexical numerals demand; numbers are set apart with dots or a titlo over the letters. The alphabet reached Unicode in March 2005 with version 4.1, block U+2C00–U+2C5F, and the combining letters of the Glagolitic Supplement, U+1E000–U+1E02F, followed in June 2016 with version 9.0; its ISO 15924 code is Glag (225). And the Cherokee link closes the loop: Sequoyah's borrowed shapes included letters that look like Glagolitic — and, as #161 recorded, none of them means what its shape means elsewhere. - **Decoder-design note (Glagolitic → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The alphabet with two hands.** Rounded and angular are the same code in two shapes, and a cursive besides — the Gauntlet that mistakes a hand for a cipher fails the specimen, and the interrogator who reads a borrowed shape by its home value is the analyst who reads the tree names as the letters, the Cherokee rung confirmed a third time. (2) **The name is the key.** *Glagol* is "word"; the letters name themselves into a sentence; the alphabet documents itself. The Gauntlet's question is whether the self-documentation is the code or a story told about it — and the Jerome legend is the caution: a false provenance protected a true script for six centuries, so provenance and content are separate interrogations, graded separately, and a script can be real while its story is false. (3) **The alphabet that died twice.** It was replaced in the east by an assembly vote and survived in the west by a papal privilege and a coastline — survival is a property of institutions, not of codes. And it had a cryptographic afterlife: in the Cyrillic world its later use was mostly cryptographic, in miscellanies and gospels where Glagolitic passages hid inside Cyrillic books — a dead liturgical script becomes a living cipher. The Gauntlet's final question for any specimen is language or code — and whether the answer changes when the users change. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's doctrine, never run]

## The Scytale (c. 7th–4th c. BC) — the stick that was the key, or: the cipher that may never have been a cipher

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero `## ` headings for Scytale in either catalogue, measured before this entry was written — and twenty-seven case-insensitive occurrences in the private catalogue against twenty-six in the public (six capital "Scytale" and one "Skytale" each side, the rest lowercase), all of them inside the seed bullet filed 2026-10-18 and the cross-references it spawned: the McCormick rung, the key-custody ladder, the Cherokee and Glagolitic gap notes. It is the most-discussed never-entered item in the archive: the oldest cipher device in the record, cited everywhere, filed nowhere. A correction rides with the gap: entries #161 and #162 both carry the figure "Scytale 52/50 mentions", and that figure does not reproduce under the counting used here — grep -o, case-insensitive, per catalogue file, counted this pass at 27/26, and no combination tested (catalogue plus research log, 30/29; whole project, 62 occurrences) reaches 52/50; the method behind the earlier figure was not recorded, so this entry re-baselines the count with the method stated. Behind Scytale, Voynich carries thirty occurrences in the private catalogue and twenty-eight in the public, still with no heading — discussed, never entered. [VERIFIED — the 0/0 heading counts and the 27/26 occurrence counts, measured this pass before this entry was written; the 30/29 and 62 totals, measured the same way]

- **The story.** The scytale (Greek σκυτάλη, "baton, cylinder", also transliterated skytale) is the oldest cipher device in the archive by a wide margin. From indirect evidence it was first mentioned by the Greek poet Archilochus, who lived in the seventh century BC; other Greek and Roman writers mentioned it in the following centuries, but it was not until Apollonius of Rhodes, in the middle of the third century BC, that a clear indication of its use as a cryptographic device appeared. The first description of how it operated comes from Plutarch (50–120 AD), *Life of Lysander* 19.5–7: when the ephors send out an admiral or a general, they make two round pieces of wood exactly alike in length and thickness, keep one themselves, and give the other to the envoy; whenever they wish to send some secret and important message, they make a scroll of parchment long and narrow, like a leathern strap, and wind it round their scytale, leaving no vacant space, covering its surface all round with the parchment; they write what they wish on the parchment as it lies wrapped about the scytale, then take the parchment off and send it, without the piece of wood, to the commander — who cannot get any meaning out of it, since the letters have no connection but are disarranged, unless he takes his own scytale and winds the strip about it, so that when its spiral course is restored perfectly he reads around the staff and discovers the continuity of the message. "And the parchment, like the staff, is called scytale, as the thing measured bears the name of the measure." Aulus Gellius (*Attic Nights* 17.9.6–16) and Ausonius (*Epistles* 28.23–27) carry the same tradition. The commanders named in the record as users are Lysander, Clearchus, and Agesilaus, in the window from the outbreak of the Peloponnesian War in 431 BC to the Battle of Leuctra in 371 BC. [VERIFIED — the Archilochus/Apollonius dating frame, the Plutarch passage in Perrin's translation, and the Gellius/Ausonius tradition, per Wikipedia "Scytale", read first-party this pass; CORROBORATED — the three commanders and the 431–371 window, per García Pinto, "The Spartan Scytale", Ancient Warfare XIV-3, via its academia.edu excerpt]

- **The system.** Pure transposition: the message's letters rearranged, nothing substituted. The model the miniature uses — the standard modern reconstruction, and the one that reproduces the literature's own worked examples exactly — is a grid: the staff's circumference is the number of letters per turn (C); the message is written row-wise into R turns of C letters; the unwound strip reads column-wise, and that column-wise reading is the ciphertext. The diameter *is* the key, and it is a small key: anyone who has heard of the method and can try rod sizes can brute-force it by steadily varying the diameter — "a kind of brute-force attack". A message too short to fill the grid evenly takes padding letters — X in the literature's example. The strip is the ciphertext; the staff never travels. [VERIFIED — the grid model reproduces Wikipedia's two worked examples exactly, computed this pass; CORROBORATED — the diameter-as-key and the brute-force-by-diameter, per the seed bullet's Poritz citation]

- **The worked miniature (computed this pass).** Seventy-two checks, all reproduced by goal hidden_files/verify-scytale-20261110.py (72/72 pass). (1) **The literature's own examples, re-run exactly.** "Meet us at the park today" — twenty letters, spaces out — at five letters a turn encodes to MSETEAPOETADTTRAUHKY, Wikipedia's "Mseteapoetadttrauhky" to the letter; "Iotoctydamoaneuynetx" at five a turn decodes to "I cannot meet you today", the trailing X discarded as padding. (2) **The Spartan message.** "Enemy attacks at dawn tomorrow" — twenty-six letters, the figure text in García Pinto's article — encoded at five staff sizes: four letters a turn, seven turns, two pads: EYAAWMONACTNOWETKDTRXMTSAORX; five a turn, six turns, four pads: EAKAMWNTSWOXETANRXMATTRXYCDOOX; six a turn, five turns, four pads: ETATONTTOWEADMXMCAOXYKWRXASNRX; seven a turn, four turns, two pads: ETDONAARECWRMKNOYSTWAAOXTTMX; eight a turn, four turns, six pads: EAWONCNWEKTXMSOXYAMXATOXTDRXTARX. Every one decodes back exactly, and every one is a pure rearrangement of the same twenty-six letters plus padding — transposition only, verified by multiset. (3) **The brute force, counted.** For a twenty-six-letter strip the candidate diameters are two through twenty-five — twenty-four candidates, all twenty-four giving distinct ciphertexts — and trying every diameter against each encoded strip recovers the message at exactly one diameter and no other. The keyspace is log2(24), about 4.58 bits — about the size of Caesar's twenty-five shifts at 4.64 bits. The oldest cipher in the archive has a keyspace the size of the simplest. (4) **The catalogue's own name.** KODAKAI, seven letters: three a turn gives KAIOKXDAX; four a turn gives KKOADIAX — round-trips both ways. (5) **The timeline.** Four centuries from Archilochus's seventh century to Apollonius's mid-third; about four more to Plutarch; one thousand eight hundred seventy-eight years from Plutarch's death (about 120) to Kelly's paper in 1998; twenty-two years from Kelly to Diepenbroek's defence in 2020; sixty years across the 431–371 window; twenty-eight years from Kelly to this loop. [VERIFIED — all ciphertexts, round-trips, brute-force uniqueness, keyspace bits, and intervals computed this pass by verify-scytale-20261110.py, 72/72 checks pass]

- **The honest blank.** Six confessions. (1) The 52/50 mention figure in entries #161/#162 does not reproduce — see the gap note; the re-baselined count is 27/26, method stated. (2) No staff and no strip survives: everything about the device's physical form comes from writers centuries after its supposed use — Plutarch and Gellius both write in the second century AD about fifth- and fourth-century Sparta. (3) The three accounts — cipher (Plutarch), authenticator (Russel 1999), myth (Kelly 1998) — are unresolved in the record; Diepenbroek's 2020 Bristol dissertation argues the other way, that the cryptographic principles of the scytale are no less complex than some twentieth-century transposition ciphers, but a dissertation arguing is not a second lab reproducing. (4) The grid model is a reconstruction: Plutarch describes a spiral winding, and the row-and-column grid is the modern reading of it — the miniature proves the model reproduces the literature's examples, not that Spartans used the model. (5) The brute-force count assumes the attacker knows the method and the strip length; a strip intercepted without that knowledge is a harder problem, and the count says nothing about it. (6) The KODAKAI renderings depend on the padding convention — X is the literature's pad letter, not a Spartan one. [VERIFIED — the 27/26 re-baseline and the no-surviving-artifact limit, per the sources as read this pass; CORROBORATED — the Diepenbroek dissertation's existence and its abstract's claim, via its academia.edu listing, full text not opened this pass]

- **Decoder-design note (Scytale → Gauntlet).** Three rungs, carried forward from the seed bullet of 2026-10-18 and now filed as the entry's own — with the miniature's receipts behind them, so the "small key" claim is now a number, not an assertion. (1) **The tokenization doctrine's oldest ancestor.** The scytale is pure transposition — the first entry in this catalogue that is *only* transposition, two thousand years before the Z340's transposition layer and the Grand Chiffre's traps: "structure before substitution" begins here. The Gauntlet's re-chunking and re-ordering interrogation precedes substitution analysis because the oldest cipher in the archive already defeats the analyst who runs statistics first. (2) **The key is a physical dimension.** The M-94's wheel order, the M-138's strip selection, the M-209's cage configuration — and two millennia before them, the scytale's diameter. Every era's key lives in a physical parameter first and a symbol string second. Gauntlet operator-stage: format parameters (block size, key length, IV width, stepping cadence) are interrogated as key material, never accepted as constants. And the parameter's size is now counted: twenty-four candidate diameters, 4.58 bits — a keyspace the size of Caesar's, which is why the brute-force rung is a fixture, not a warning. (3) **Authenticate ≠ encrypt — state the claimed property first.** Kelly may be right, Russel may be right, or Plutarch may be right — and the report-card discipline does not need the answer to hold its rule: the card states the specimen's *claimed* security property (confidentiality, integrity, authenticity) before grading whether the specimen meets it. A "break" measured against a property the specimen never promised is a fabrication class under the Fabrication Alarm — the analyst's version of cracking a lock that was never engaged. ## The Voynich manuscript (Beinecke MS 408, parchment 1404–1438) — the book that behaves like a language and yields like a stone

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero `## ` headings for Voynich in either catalogue, measured before this entry was written — and twenty-nine case-insensitive occurrences in the public catalogue against thirty-one in the private, all of them in the UNDECIPHERED roster and the cross-references it spawned. It is the most-discussed never-entered item left in the archive after the Scytale: the most studied unread book in the world, cited everywhere, filed nowhere. The count reconciles exactly with entry #163, which measured thirty in the private catalogue and twenty-eight in the public before it was written and then added one "Voynich" mention to each side — 28 + 1 = 29, 30 + 1 = 31, measured this pass by grep -o, case-insensitive, per catalogue file. The full claim-by-claim record already lives in library/UNDECIPHERED.md (items a–l plus the prior roster, Oct 14–Nov 1, 2026); this entry is the catalogue's first filing, not the project's first word on it. [VERIFIED — the 0/0 heading counts and the 29/31 occurrence counts, measured this pass before this entry was written; the 28/30 → 29/31 reconciliation, computed this pass]

- **The story.** The Voynich manuscript (Beinecke MS 408) is an illustrated codex, hand-written in an undeciphered script called Voynichese, on vellum radiocarbon-dated at the University of Arizona in 2009 to 1404–1438 — a thirty-four-year span, six centuries back. About 240 of at least 272 pages survive (about 88 percent; thirty-two pages missing), in 18 quires of an original 20, measuring 23.5 by 16.2 by 5 centimetres. The first confirmed owner was Georg Baresch, a seventeenth-century Prague alchemist; a letter from Jan Marek Marci to Athanasius Kircher, written in 1665 or 1666 and found inside the covers, is the earliest information about its existence. The book is named for Wilfrid Voynich, the Polish book dealer who purchased it in 1912 — two hundred and forty-six years after Marci's letter — and it has been held at Yale's Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library since 1969; Yale published the entire manuscript online in 2020, fifty-one years later. It has been studied by professional and amateur cryptographers including the codebreakers of both world wars — Prescott Currier, William Friedman, Elizebeth Friedman, John Tiltman — all unsuccessful. It has never been demonstrably deciphered, and none of the proposed hypotheses has been independently verified. By its illustrations it falls into six sections: herbal (126 pages), astronomical (17), balneological (20), cosmological (14, including the six-page Rosettes foldout), pharmaceutical (16), and recipes (25), with eight pages of text only; none of the plants depicted is unambiguously identifiable. The text runs left to right in a script of twenty to twenty-five characters, with no obvious punctuation, in a smooth ductus that gives the impression the symbols were not enciphered — no delay between characters, as written encoded text would show. The count stands at about 37,919 word tokens, 8,114 unique word types, over 170,000 characters. Transcription alphabets exist to make it machine-readable — the Extensible Voynich Alphabet (EVA), and before it William Friedman's First Study Group in the 1940s, transcribing each line to an IBM punch card. The handwriting is the work of up to five scribes, by Lisa Fagin Davis's reading of small stylistic tells that vary between sections but not within them — a community's book, not a lone genius's, and not, on that evidence, a single unwell mind's hoax. [VERIFIED — the radiocarbon span, page counts, dimensions, ownership chain, 1912 purchase, 1969 Beinecke holding, 2020 online publication, the failed codebreakers, the section page counts, the token/type/character counts, the script size, the EVA and punch-card transcriptions, and the five-scribe reading, per Wikipedia "Voynich manuscript", read first-party this pass]

- **The system.** What the text does, whether or not it means anything. The word frequencies follow Zipf's law: the most frequent word appears roughly twice as often as the second-most-common, and three times as often as the third; the mix of word lengths and the ratio of unique words to total words resemble languages around the world. Practically no word has fewer than two letters or more than ten. The words follow positional laws: certain characters must appear in each word (like English vowels), some characters never follow others, some occur only at the beginning of a word, some only in the middle, some only at the end (like Greek final sigma); the morphology suggests a three-part word structure of prefix, root or midfix, and suffix, with particular characters likelier in particular fields. The language of the manuscript differs from known human languages in spelling — too many letters repeated in the same order, both within words and across neighbouring words — and the same common word appears up to five times in a row. Words differing by only one letter repeat with unusual frequency, which is why single-substitution decipherings yield babble-like text; Elizebeth Friedman in 1962 called such statistical analyses "doomed to utter frustration". Second-order conditional entropy (h2) sits around 2, against 3 to 4 for natural languages: Voynichese character sequences are far more predictable than a language's, and Bowern and Lindemann conclude its statistical properties are not consistent with a substitution cipher or a polyalphabetic cipher — it is likely an encoded natural language or a constructed language, written by two methods at least, in two "languages": Voynich A in the herbal and pharmaceutical parts, Voynich B in the balneological, some medicinal and herbal, and the astrological sections, with substantially different most-common vocabularies. The different sections have different sets of overrepresented words, as chapters on different subjects would. The intake bar for any claim about this book is now a number, set by the Caniatti and Claude falsification suite (Oct 2026, roster item g): homophonic substitution with spaces in fourteen languages recovers 69–98 percent real words on controls against at most 36 percent on Voynich; a spaceless simulated-annealing solver with a 5-gram Latin model on nine million letters recovers 98–100 percent of keys on 56 + 71 positive controls and never reliably rises above negative controls on Voynich across four glyph-countings, nine grouping levels, seventy-one languages, and backwards reading; ordered anagrams show glyph order inside words is language-like, not anagram-like; plant-name cribs that recover a planted name in the first word of a control page find no trace in Voynich; Bax (2014) is refuted outside derivation pages (p = 0.14); and two formally positive outcomes were exposed as artefacts, one reproduced on shuffled Voynich. Calibrated controls, published negatives, no self-grading. [VERIFIED — the Zipf ratios, word-length bounds, positional laws, three-part structure, the five-in-a-row repetition, the Friedman 1962 verdict, and the h2 ≈ 2 finding with its substitution/polyalphabetic exclusion, per Wikipedia, read first-party this pass; CORROBORATED — the Caniatti falsification suite's figures, per the roster as filed in library/UNDECIPHERED.md]

- **The worked miniature (computed this pass).** Twenty-nine checks, all reproduced by goal hidden_files/verify-voynich-20261110.py (29/29 pass). (1) **The roster's own numbers, re-added.** Hoeben's f57v architecture: seventeen to the fourth power is 83,521 joint register configurations, and six times that is 501,126 pair-order tests. Honeycutt's reader studies: 828 complete receiving labels plus 429 component forms is 1,257 receiving references; twenty-eight profiles against 303 figures is an 8,484-pair matrix, and 7,832 unassessable plus 606 source-ineligible plus 46 partial compatibilities is 8,484 again — the 46 partials are about 0.54 percent of the matrix. Zuger's Glagolitic claim: 94.7 percent of 37,793 tokens is 35,790 tokens covered. Ferreira's f84r split: 50.64 plus 49.36 is 100.00. Section pages: 126 + 17 + 20 + 14 + 16 + 25 is 218; plus the eight text-only pages is 226 — fourteen pages short of 240, the foldout-counting ambiguity, stated not smoothed. [VERIFIED — all sums, products, ratios, and intervals computed this pass by verify-voynich-20261110.py, 29/29 checks pass]

- **The honest blank.** Six confessions. (1) No decipherment is verified: every complete-reading claim on the roster — Zuger's angular Glagolitic Croatian at 94.7 percent morphological coverage, Hafner's archaic Middle Welsh herbal, Funchal's five-family structural reading, Ortiz Velazquez's analog decision engine, Zsiros's mining-installation reading, Shlygin's spy hypothesis — is CLAIMED, single-lab, no peer review, no independent replication on held-out folios. (2) The manuscript may not be a cipher at all: Bowern's exclusion of substitution and polyalphabetic ciphers means the "cipher" framing itself is unproven, and this catalogue files the book as an undeciphered writing system, not as a cipher with a missing key. (3) The book has likely been read in the wrong page order for centuries: Layfield and Davis (Digital Medievalist, peer-reviewed, Oct 2026) found attached pages scoring highly for coherence across many intervening pages, and the folded sheets were likely stacked as loose singulions and mis-bound in the mid-to-late 1400s — illustrations of streams and pipes that run into the gutter and fail to match across a spread join up once the pages are treated as a loose stack. Any reading that depends on page order inherits that error. (4) The only on-record known-name decryption attempt failed: the three faded columns in the right margin of f.1r — the Roman alphabet, a series of Voynich characters, and a second Roman alphabet offset by one letter, in a hand matching Marci — do not work. The honest null constrains the easy-substitution hypothesis more than another modern claim constrains anything. (5) Ferreira's H = 0.4999 is unresolved — see the miniature; the entropy figure cannot be reproduced from the split as stated. (6) This entry adds no new evidence about the manuscript; it files the roster's record, with the miniature's arithmetic as its only new computation. ## The AMSCO cipher (19th century; first book mention 1939) — the transposition that counts one-two, one-two, or: the cipher named after its inventor

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero occurrences of "Amsco" in either catalogue — no heading, no bullet, no mention — measured this pass by grep -o, case-insensitive, per catalogue file (0 in the private catalogue, 0 in the public), against a shelf where its neighbours are all filed: columnar transposition (12 occurrences private, 11 public), double transposition (12/11), rail fence (8/5), Atbash (15/15). Three named hand ciphers share the absence — AMSCO, Slidefair, Cadenus, each 0/0 — and AMSCO is filed first because it carries a named inventor, a book mention, and three published worked examples to verify against. Route transposition shares the absence too (0/0) and is noted, not filed, here. [VERIFIED — the 0/0 counts and the neighbour counts, measured this pass]

- **The story.** AMSCO is an incomplete columnar transposition invented by American Cryptogram Association member A. M. Scott — the name is his initials — and mentioned in Helen Fouché Gaines's *Cryptanalysis: A Study of Ciphers and Their Solution*, first published as *Elementary Cryptanalysis* in 1939 (Gaines, 1888–1940). dCode dates the cipher to the 19th century. It differs from regular incomplete columnar transposition in one twist: the plaintext is written into the block alternately in pairs and single letters — digraphs and singletons in a 1-2 or 2-1 cutting sequence — and the columns are then read off vertically in key order. It lives on in cryptogram magazines, puzzle hunts, and codebreaking challenges, and in every modern cipher toolkit (Boxentriq, dCode, CryptoCrack) — a pencil-and-paper cipher that survived into the solver age because its irregular grid defeats the eye even though it preserves every letter frequency exactly. [VERIFIED — the Scott invention, the Gaines 1939 first book mention, and the 1-2 cutting rule, per CryptoCrack, read first-party this pass; the 19th-century dating and the initials, per dCode, read first-party this pass; CORROBORATED — the magazines-and-puzzle-hunts habitat, per Boxentriq, read first-party this pass]

- **The system.** A key is selected, which determines the width of the block; the plaintext is written into the block horizontally below the key, with both rows and columns alternating between digraphs and single letters; each column is then read off vertically to form the cipher, the order of reading set by the numeric order of the keyword. No null letters need fill an empty or incomplete cell — the grid's last row is simply ragged. Decryption rebuilds the grid from the column lengths (the cutting sequence fixes how many characters each cell holds) and reads row by row. The solving method is brute-force search over key orders (CryptoCrack), and the search grows factorially with the width (Boxentriq) — the whole security of the cipher is the key space, since the letter multiset passes through untouched. The cutting sequence can be more complex than 1,2: dCode shows a (3,2,1) cutting sequence, where the cell sizes rotate across rows.
