## The Slidefair cipher (1939; Gaines's own invention) — the digram cipher worked on a slide, or: the cipher that slides its alphabets

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero `## ` headings for Slidefair in either catalogue, measured this pass — and exactly two case-insensitive occurrences per catalogue, both of them inside the AMSCO entry's sibling-gap sentence, naming Slidefair as one of the three named hand ciphers sharing the absence. The shelf around it is fully filed: Playfair carries one heading and 61 occurrences in the private catalogue against 58 in the public, Vigenère 132/131, Gaines herself 15/14. Cadenus and route transposition share the 2/2, 0-heading state and wait their turn. Slidefair is filed now because it is the only one of the three whose inventor is named, whose description survives in the inventor's own book, and whose worked examples — the inventor's and a modern toolkit's — both re-encrypt exactly. [VERIFIED — the 0/0 heading counts and the 2/2 occurrence counts for Slidefair, Cadenus, and route transposition, and the neighbour counts, measured this pass]

- **The story.** The Slidefair cipher was invented by Helen Fouché Gaines (1888–1940) and described in her book *Cryptanalysis: A Study of Ciphers and Their Solution*, first published as *Elementary Cryptanalysis* in 1939 — the same book that carries the AMSCO cipher's first mention, so the two entries share a provenance and a shelf. Gaines presents it in Chapter XIX, "Polyalphabetical Encipherment Applied by Groups," as Figure 165, and in her own words it is "the writer's own contribution, accomplished with a slide" — the slide in the example was the Saint-Cyr slide. The American Cryptogram Association kept it alive as a cipher-exchange type: its journal index lists a decrypting method by DUNFEL (Apr–May 1945), a probable-word method by CAGLIOSTRO (Apr–May 1951), a two-part "Tackling the Untipped Slidefair" by CERE E. US (Jul–Oct 1998), and a Porta Slidefair solved with the PhoeBee by HONEYBEE (Jul–Aug 1998) — and Gaines's own book sets its students a Slidefair practice cryptogram, No. 152 by PICCOLA, with the probable word DESCENT. [VERIFIED — the invention, the book, the chapter and figure, and Gaines's own words, per the Gutenberg text of *Elementary Cryptanalysis*, read first-party this pass; CORROBORATED — the ACA habitat and the Porta variant, per the ACA's *Cryptogram* index, read first-party this pass]

- **The system.** The plaintext is marked off into letter pairs and enciphered pair by pair against a Vigenère, Beaufort, or Variant table; the keyword defines the period and the alphabets used — one key letter per pair, so a nine-letter keyword is a period of nine pairs, eighteen letters. If the plaintext has an odd number of letters a null such as X is added to complete the last pair. The rule, in Gaines's words: bring the key letter's alphabet into position on the slide; find the pair's first letter in the upper alphabet and its second letter in the lower one; imagine them standing at the two ends of a diagonal, and substitute the two letters from the two ends of the corresponding cross-diagonal, taking the upper one first. Where the two plaintext letters happen to coincide — the same column — use the two letters which have also coincided immediately to their right. In table arithmetic, with the key letter k, the upper alphabet plain and the table body as written: Vigenère gives c1 = p2 − k, c2 = k + p1; Beaufort gives c1 = k − p2, c2 = k − p1; Variant gives c1 = p2 + k, c2 = p1 − k (all mod 26); and in the same-column case c1 = p1 + 1 with c2 read one step right in the key row. Decipherment inverts the rectangle, and the same-column case is detected from the ciphertext pair itself (for Vigenère, when c2 − c1 equals the key letter). The key space for a keyword of length n is 26^n — 26^9, about 5.4 × 10^12, for the nine-letter keyword in the worked example — though repeated key letters shrink the distinct alphabets actually used (SLIDEFAIR uses eight). [VERIFIED — the mechanism, the null rule, and the coincidence rule, per CryptoCrack, read first-party this pass, and per Gaines's own description, read first-party this pass; the table arithmetic is this entry's formalisation, verified by the miniature]

- **The worked miniature (computed this pass).** One hundred twenty-two checks, all reproduced by goal hidden_files/verify-slidefair-20261110.py (122/122 pass). Three published examples, re-encrypted from the algorithm — not re-asserted. (a) **Gaines's own example, Fig. 165** (Chapter XIX, pp. 198–199): key HERCULES (8 letters, 7 distinct), plaintext SE ND DI AM ON DS TO AM ST ER DA MM ON DA YW EE KW IT HO UT FA IL (44 letters, 22 pairs) encrypts to XZ ZR RU KC TI HO KX US MZ NI JU KO TI PO SC MW PR PM XY RW GZ AT (22 pairs) — every pair reproduced, including the last six, where the plaintext KW IT HO UT FA IL becomes PR PM XY RW GZ AT. (b) **CryptoCrack, Vigenère**: key SLIDEFAIR, plaintext "If you do a job too well, you'll get stuck with it" (37 letters, plus the null X, 38 letters, 19 pairs) encrypts to NA DJ VC XR KN OG PP XF UC WQ AF YT QH PW XZ WK LQ RY FL (19 pairs); the same-column pairs land exactly as published — OO under A becomes PP, WE under I becomes XF. (c) **CryptoCrack, Beaufort**: the same plaintext and key encrypt to NK XN FO DP QV ME MM EM GG EU AR CX KZ LM DL EQ PA JK VZ (19 pairs), with no same-column pair in the run. (d) **CryptoCrack, Variant**: the same plaintext and key encrypt to XQ ZN LM DL SF YW PP MO CU GG WJ OD WB XO HP WK BA ZQ PB (19 pairs); OO under A again becomes PP by the same-column rule. (e) **Gaines's coincidence rule, direct**: EL under the H-alphabet of the Saint-Cyr slide becomes FM, exactly as she states — E sits at upper position 4 and L at lower position 4 under shift 7, and the letters immediately to their right are F and M. (f) **Round trips**: decrypting each of the three CryptoCrack ciphertexts under its table returns the 38-letter plaintext exactly. (g) **The involution**: on every normal pair, enciphering twice returns the plaintext — the Slidefair, like the Playfair, is its own inverse except on same-column pairs, where a second application shifts one step further (OO under A goes PP, then QQ). History: Gaines was 51 when the book first appeared (1939 − 1888) and died the year after (1940 − 1939 = 1); 87 years have passed since that appearance (2026 − 1939). [VERIFIED — all re-encryptions, round trips, the coincidence check, the involution, and the intervals computed this pass by verify-slidefair-20261110.py, 122/122 checks pass]

- **The honest blank.** Five confessions. (1) The name's etymology is unsourced: "Slidefair" reads as slide + Playfair, but Gaines never explains the name in the passage read, and no second source for the naming was read this pass — this entry does not assert it. (2) The Porta table variant is named in the ACA index (HONEYBEE, Jul–Aug 1998) but no Porta Slidefair worked example was read first-party; the fourth table is named, not verified. (3) The ACA decrypting articles (DUNFEL 1945, CAGLIOSTRO 1951, CERE E. US 1998) are index entries only — none was read first-party, so no solving method beyond the periodic structure is filed here. - **Decoder-design note (Slidefair → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The digram is the unit.** Slidefair defeats every unigram test by construction: a single letter takes different substitutes depending on its partner and its position in the pair, so letter frequencies come back scrambled. The Gauntlet's statistical rungs must test at the digram level — digram frequencies, contact charts — or they will report "random" where the structure is merely paired. Gaines's own book ships a digram-frequency chart for exactly this reason. (2) **The period is counted in pairs, not letters.** A nine-letter keyword is a period of nine pairs and eighteen letters; a Kasiski-style period probe that counts in letters will find the period doubled and chase a phantom. The Gauntlet's periodicity rung must count its repeats in the cipher's own unit — pairs here, cells in AMSCO, letters in Vigenère. (3) **The coincidence is the tell.** When a known plaintext pair lands in the same column, the ciphertext pair is the plaintext pair shifted one step right — and the key letter is exposed: for Vigenère, p2 = p1 + k, so k = p2 − p1. One known same-column pair determines its key letter outright, and the involution means a known ciphertext pair under a known key letter decrypts itself. The Gauntlet's crib rung should hunt the coincidence first: it is the cheapest key recovery in the whole digram family, and it is also the specimen's fingerprint — a cipher that never produces a same-column pair in long text is not a Slidefair. [CORROBORATED lineage — the digram statistics and the periodic structure, per Gaines and CryptoCrack as read this pass; SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's doctrine, never run]

## The Cadenus cipher (1925; Soudart & Lange) — the double transposition on twenty disks, or: the cipher that must count in twenty-fives

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero `## ` headings for Cadenus in either catalogue, measured this pass — and exactly five case-insensitive occurrences per catalogue, all five of them inside the AMSCO and Slidefair entries' gap and grades sentences: two in the AMSCO entry (its gap sentence and its grades bracket), three in the Slidefair entry (its gap sentence, the verification bracket inside that sentence, and its grades line). The transposition shelf around it is fully filed: columnar transposition 17 occurrences in the private catalogue against 16 in the public, double transposition 13/12, rail fence 10/7, AMSCO 22/22, Slidefair 25/25. Route transposition shares the 5/5, 0-heading state and waits its turn. Cadenus is filed now because its description survives in two independent worked examples — a modern toolkit's and the ACA's own type sheet — and both re-encrypt exactly under one rule. [VERIFIED — the 0/0 heading counts and the 5/5 occurrence counts for Cadenus and route transposition, and the neighbour counts, measured this pass]

- **The story.** The Cadenus cipher is a double transposition cipher described in *Traité de Cryptographie* by Emile-Arthur Soudart and André Lange, published in 1925. Soudart was Chief of the French Army's Cipher Section and Lange his assistant. The system used twenty numbered disks arranged on a common axle, with space to write the message on the edge of each disk — though it converts easily to a pencil-and-paper method. The American Cryptogram Association kept it as a cipher-exchange type, its one-page type sheet (no. 38) capping the period at six. One hundred one years have passed since the book appeared (2026 − 1925). [CLAIMED — the 1925 book, the authors and their roles, and the twenty disks, per CryptoCrack, read first-party this pass; the book itself was not opened; VERIFIED — the ACA type sheet, its period cap, and its sheet number, per the ACA sheet read first-party this pass]

- **The system.** Choose a keyword whose length is the message length divided by twenty-five, and write the plaintext horizontally in a block below the key — twenty-five rows, one column per key letter. The keyword does two jobs at once: its letters in alphabetical order give the order the columns are read, and each column is read starting at a row fixed by its keyword letter. The row is found in a twenty-five-letter key column written beside the block: A first, then Z down to B, with V and W sharing one cell. The keyword letter at the top of a column is found in that key column, and the column is read starting at that row, wrapping to the top — so a column topped by A starts at row one and a column topped by C starts at row twenty-four. The cipher block is then read off by rows. The limitation is absolute: the message length must be a multiple of twenty-five, padded if needed — the CryptoCrack example pads with xx. Two transpositions ride in one pass: the columns are permuted, and each column is cyclically rotated — which is why CryptoCrack calls it a double transposition and the ACA sheet calls it a columnar tramp. The key space for a four-letter keyword is 358,800 distinct-letter keywords (26 × 25 × 24 × 23), or 456,976 if repeated letters were allowed — though a repeated letter would leave the column order tied, so working keywords are distinct-letter; the ACA's period cap of six gives 165,765,600 distinct-letter keywords at most. [VERIFIED — the mechanism, the key column, and the key-space arithmetic, per the ACA sheet and CryptoCrack as read this pass and the miniature; CLAIMED — the twenty-disk apparatus, single-source]

(b) **ACA sheet, key EASY**: plaintext "A severe limitation on the usefulness of the Cadenus is that every message must be a multiple of twenty-five letters long." (100 letters); column order 2134; key-column positions A = 1, E = 22, S = 8, Y = 3; the sheet's own prose is confirmed — the first plaintext column begins its rotation with its twenty-second letter, Y — and the cipher block read by rows gives SYSTR ETOMT ATTLU SOATL EEESF IYHEA SDFNM SCHBH NEUVS NPMTO FAREN USEIE EIELT ARLME NTIEE TOGEV ESITF AISLT NGEEU VOWUL — every row reproduced. (c) **Round trips**: un-rotating and un-permuting each cipher block returns its plain block exactly. (d) **Pure transposition**: both ciphertexts are letter-for-letter permutations of their plaintexts, so unigram frequencies survive untouched. The printed block is right and reproduces exactly; the prose is stale or mistaken, and this entry files the block, not the prose. - **Decoder-design note (Cadenus → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The length is the tell.** A Cadenus ciphertext is always a multiple of twenty-five letters, and its block is always twenty-five rows deep — the Gauntlet's length rung should flag a multiple-of-twenty-five ciphertext as Cadenus-shaped before any other test runs, the way it flags even lengths for a digram cipher. (2) **The rotation is the fingerprint.** Each cipher column is a cyclic rotation of a plaintext column, and the rotation is not free: it is the key-column position of the column's keyword letter. A crib placed in a column therefore constrains its rotation to one of twenty-five starts, and a known keyword letter fixes it outright — the Gauntlet's crib rung should test column rotations, not just column permutations, or it will miss the key entirely. (3) **The double transposition defeats single-transposition solvers.** A solver that only permutes columns can never reach the plaintext, because every column is also rotated; the Gauntlet must test permutation and rotation jointly, and a specimen that reports "unsolved" on a Cadenus after a column-only attack has shown a gap in its solver, not in the cipher. ## The route transposition cipher (1916; Hitt's six patterns) — the transposition that walks the grid, or: the cipher whose key is a path

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero `## ` headings for route transposition in either catalogue, measured this pass — and exactly eight case-insensitive occurrences per catalogue, all eight of them inside the AMSCO, Slidefair, and Cadenus entries' gap and grades sentences: AMSCO gap 1 + grades 1, Slidefair gap 2 + grades 1, Cadenus gap 2 + grades 1. The transposition shelf around it is fully filed: columnar transposition 19/18, double transposition 19/18, rail fence 12/9, AMSCO 26/26, Slidefair 29/29, Cadenus 25/25. Route transposition is filed now because its description survives in two independent worked sources — the ACA's own Young Tyros page and the Wikipedia route-cipher section — and every published reading re-encrypts exactly under one route library. [VERIFIED — the 0/0 heading counts and the 8/8 occurrence counts and the neighbour counts, measured this pass by grep -o, case-insensitive]

- **The story.** Classic route transposition is the plain-vanilla form of geometric transposition: the plaintext is written into a complete square or rectangle by one route and read out by another. There are six basic patterns — orthogonal, diagonal, spiral, orthogonal boustrophedon, diagonal boustrophedon, crab spiral — and, except for the crab spirals, which were added later, they were introduced in 1916 by Colonel Parker Hitt in his *Manual for the Solution of Military Ciphers*, as summarized by THEANO in the November/December 2005 *Cryptogram*. Each pattern yields eight routes by reflection and transposition, so there are 48 ways to enter characters and 47 ways to remove them: 48 × 47 = 2,256 route transposition ciphers from the six patterns alone. "In by rows and out by columns" is the plain-vanilla case — the basic orthogonal route in, its transposition out. The ACA's own guidelines cap the grid at an 8 × 8 square or an 8 × 10 rectangle, and the letter X is often used as a null to complete the rectangle. A variation, the Union Route Cipher of the American Civil War, transposed whole words instead of individual letters; sensitive words were first concealed by code, and null words — often chosen to make the ciphertext humorous — padded the grid. [VERIFIED — the six patterns, Hitt 1916, THEANO 2005, the 48 × 47 arithmetic, the ACA size caps, and the Union variant, per Christensen, the Young Tyros page, and Wikipedia, read first-party this pass]

- **The worked miniature (computed this pass).** 103 checks pass in goal hidden_files/verify-route-transposition-20261110.py. (a) **The 25-letter route table (Young Tyros).** Plaintext "A ROUTE TRANSPOSITION CIPHER" in a 5 × 5, all eleven published readings reproduced exactly — rows plain, alternating, and reversed; columns plain, alternating, and reversed; clockwise spiral; counter-clockwise spiral; diagonal plain, alternating, and reversed. Two conventions the table quietly mixes: the clockwise spiral winds INWARD from the top-left corner, while the counter-clockwise spiral winds OUTWARD from the center — the table's two spirals are not the same walk reversed, and a solver that assumes one convention for both will misread the second. The diagonal rules, reconstructed from the strings: anti-diagonals, read bottom-left-to-top-right for plain, top-right-to-bottom-left for reversed, alternating from the second diagonal. (b) **The two riddle grids.** "WARLF HSWSL AFHAI TOENE HUEDS" read by columns gives "WHATHASFOURWHEELSANDFLIES". "TEGAB ROCOR UVXNA CERHG KWITA" read by columns is the ciphertext, and the clockwise spiral in from the lower-right corner gives "AGARBAGETRUCKWITHNOCOVERX" — the plaintext plus null X. (c) **RT-1 solved.** The published exercise "Abe Lincoln at Gettysburg (25)" — ciphertext FCNER OODNS URSYA REEEG SAVAO — brute-forced over every fill × read route this pass: exactly two routes hit, the transpose twins (rows-in/cols-out and cols-in/rows-out), both yielding "FOURSCOREANDSEVENYEARSAGO". ## The runic alphabet (Elder Futhark, c. 2nd–8th c. CE) — the letters that were also a cipher, or: the script whose name means secret

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero `## ` headings for runic, rune, or futhark in either catalogue, measured this pass — and one "runic" hit per catalogue, the Ogham entry's own sentence naming this zero ("runic" is 0/0 headings in both catalogues). "Elder Futhark" 1/1 (the Ogham honest blank), "Younger Futhark" 0/0, "Futhark" 2/2 (both inside the Ogham entry), "ætt" 0/0. A correction rides with the gap: the Ogham entry's gap sentence counted six "rune" substring hits, but re-measured this pass the six pre-Ogham lines alone carry seven occurrences — line 9004 carries two — so the six was a line count, and the occurrence count stands corrected here at eleven. The writing-system shelf around it is fully filed: Ogham, Cherokee, Glagolitic, Linear A, the Maya glyphs, the Indus script, the Dancing Men, and Myszkowski each carry one heading in each catalogue. Runic is filed now because it is the zero the Ogham entry named for a later loop — and because it is the one alphabet whose own name means "secret". [VERIFIED — the 0/0 heading counts and the 1/1, 11/11, 1/1, 0/0, 2/2, 0/0 occurrence counts and the neighbour heading counts, measured this pass by grep -o, case-insensitive, before this entry was written]

- **The story.** The name gives the game away before the alphabet does: "rune" stems from a Proto-Germanic form reconstructed as *rūnō*, translatable as "secret, mystery; secret conversation; rune" — Gothic *rūna* "secret, mystery, counsel", Old English *rūn* "whisper, mystery, secret, rune", Old Norse *rún* "secret, mystery, rune". The earliest Germanic epigraphic attestation is the Proto-Norse *rūnō* on the Einang stone (AD 350–400) and the Noleby stone (AD 450). The article's own gloss is the decoder's warrant: "The name *rune* itself, taken to mean 'secret, something hidden', seems to indicate that knowledge of the runes was originally considered esoteric, or restricted to an elite" — and the 6th-century Björketorp Runestone says it outright in Proto-Norse: *Haidzruno runu* — "I, master of the runes, conceal here runes of power." The Elder Futhark is the oldest form of the runic alphabets, used by Germanic peoples from the 2nd to the 8th centuries for inscriptions on jewellery, amulets, tools, weapons, and runestones. It has 24 runes, often arranged in three groups of eight, each group called in modern times an *ætt* (Old Norse "lineage"), and it takes its name from the first six rune sounds: F, U, Þ, A, R, K. The earliest known sequential listing dates to c. 400 AD on the Kylver Stone in Gotland; the 6th-century Vadstena and Mariedamm bracteates show the division into three ættir. The reading of the Elder Futhark was forgotten and was not recovered until 1865, when the Norwegian scholar Sophus Bugge deciphered it — 1,465 years after the Kylver listing. In Scandinavia the script was simplified to the 16-letter Younger Futhark from the late 8th century, while the Anglo-Saxons extended it into the futhorc; the Latin alphabet replaced runes by around AD 700 in central Europe and 1100 in Scandinavia, but runes persisted for specialized purposes in rural Sweden — Dalarna, runic calendars — until the early 20th century. There are some 350 known Elder Futhark inscriptions, 81 from the South and 267 from Scandinavia. [VERIFIED — the *rūnō* etymology, the Einang/Noleby attestations, the Björketorp curse, the 24-rune/three-ætt structure, the Kylver and bracteate listings, the Bugge 1865 decipherment, the Younger simplification, the replacement dates, the Dalarna persistence, and the ~350-inscription count, per Wikipedia "Runes" and "Elder Futhark", read first-party this pass]

- **The cipher system.** Cipher runes, or cryptic runes, are the cryptographical replacement of the letters of the runic alphabet — and the replacement is an address, not a substitution. Every form is built on one principle: give the number of the *ætt* and the number of the rune within the *ætt*. In the Younger Futhark's 16 letters, the Icelandic tradition calls the three groups Freyr's *ætt* (f, u, þ, ã, r, k), Hagal's *ætt* (h, n, i, a, s), and Tyr's *ætt* (t, b, m, l, R) — and to make the inscription harder, Freyr's and Tyr's ætts change places, so group one is group three and vice versa. The **branch runes** hang strokes on a vertical stem, branching upwards: strokes on the left indicate the *ætt*, strokes on the right the order within the *ætt*. The **tent runes** hang strokes on the four arms of an X: each X represents two runes, read clockwise starting with the top-left arm, the strokes on the first arm giving the *ætt* — the rows are (1) *fuþarkgw*, (2) *hnijæpzs*, (3) *tbemlŋod* — and the strokes on the second arm the order within that *ætt*. There are variants: inverting the numbers, counting the ætts and the runes within them backwards; **tree runes** and **hook runes** are like branch runes, with the strokes pointing downward diagonally and curving downward respectively; and the forms mix, as in the phrase *ek vitki*, where *ek* is written in straightforward branch runes but *vitki* is written with the ætts as hooks and the order as branches. Several runestones use such devices of obscuring the inscription, especially in Orkney. The knowledge was best preserved in Iceland, where 17th–18th-century scholars produced several treatises — most notably Jón Ólafsson's *Runologia* (1705–1779), written in Copenhagen in 1732–52 and now preserved in the Arnamagnæan Institute. His treatise presents the Younger Futhark in the Viking Age order, with the m-rune preceding the l-rune — a detail of paramount importance, because in the 13th century the two runes changed places through the influence of the Latin alphabet, where *l* precedes *m*. A comparable system of letter modification is the Ogham "scales" recorded in the Ogam Tract — the same device, one alphabet over, in the entry that named this zero. [VERIFIED — the address principle, the three Younger ættir and the Freyr↔Tyr swap, the branch/tent/tree/hook forms and the *ek vitki* mixing, the Orkney stones, the Jón Ólafsson preservation and the l/m order trap, and the Ogham-scales parallel, per Wikipedia "Cipher runes", read first-party this pass]

- **The worked miniature (computed this pass).** 72 checks pass in goal hidden_files/verify-runic-20261110.py. (a) **The inventory.** The cipher article's rows are (1) *fuþarkgw*, (2) *hnijæpzs*, (3) *tbemlŋod*: three groups of eight, 24 distinct letters, and the first six spell FUTHARK. The row order is not stable across witnesses: the cipher rows differ from the Kylver row (*fuþarkgw hnijpïzs tbemlŋdo*) at exactly four positions — the ï/p swap in ætt 2 and the o/d swap in ætt 3 — and from the Elder Futhark article's own table (*hnijïpzs; tbemlŋdo*) at exactly two, the o/d swap. The "standard" row is a composite of two witnesses; the miniature uses the cipher article's rows because that article defines the cipher system. (b) **Branch runes.** KODA encodes as (1,6), (3,7), (3,8), (1,4) — K in ætt 1 position 6, O in ætt 3 position 7, D in ætt 3 position 8, A in ætt 1 position 4 — for 7 + 10 + 11 + 5 = 33 strokes, and decodes back exactly. FUTHARK encodes as the staircase (1,1), (1,2), (1,3), (1,4), (1,5), (1,6) — 27 strokes, the alphabet's own name walking down its first ætt. Under the inverted-counting variant, K is (3,3) — and (3,3) under straight rules reads as *e*, not K: the reader must know the convention, and the convention is nowhere on the stone. (c) **Tent runes.** The pair (K,O) is one X with arms (1,6,3,7); (D,A) is (3,8,1,4); both decode back exactly, and a full 24-rune row takes 12 X's. (d) **Rök, re-derived.** The Rök runestone's printed Unicode transliteration carries 30 coordinate pairs in the ciphered tail — 11 distinct — and all 30 resolve to the printed runes under the Younger Futhark ættir with Freyr's and Tyr's ætts swapped: [3:3 = ᚦ], [2:2 = ᚿ], [2:3 = ᛁ], [1:1 = ᛐ], [3:2 = ᚢ], [1:4 = ᛚ], [3:5 = ᚱ], [2:5 = ᛌ], [2:4 = ᛆ], [3:6 = ᚴ], [1:3 = ᛙ]. Without the swap, 17 of the 30 mis-resolve — and [3:6] is undecodable outright, because the unswapped group 3, Tyr's ætt, holds only five runes. The four group-2 pairs are unaffected, because Hagal's ætt stays group 2 either way. (e) **Displacement.** The stone's second encryption is displacement, a Caesar shift: on the 24-letter Elder row, RUN shifted +3 is WRÏ — R(5)→W(8), U(2)→R(5), N(10)→Ï(13) — and brute force over all 24 shifts recovers RUN at exactly shift 3. (f) **Unicode.** The Runic block is U+16A0–U+16FF, 96 code points, added in Unicode 3.0 (September 1999) with 81 symbols — 75 letters (U+16A0–U+16EA), 3 punctuation marks, 3 calendar symbols; all 24 Elder glyphs ᚠ ᚢ ᚦ ᚨ ᚱ ᚲ ᚷ ᚹ ᚺ ᚾ ᛁ ᛃ ᛇ ᛈ ᛉ ᛊ ᛏ ᛒ ᛖ ᛗ ᛚ ᛜ ᛞ ᛟ are named RUNIC LETTER and sit inside the block, as do all 11 of Rök's coordinate glyphs. [VERIFIED — the inventory, the row discrepancies, the branch/tent encodings and round trips, the 30 Rök coordinates and the swap test, the displacement brute force, and the Unicode arithmetic, computed this pass by verify-runic-20261110.py, 72/72 checks pass]

- **The Rök runestone.** The stone that proves the system was used, not just described: the Rök runestone (Ög 136), carved in the early 9th century by the runemaster Varinn — 2.4 metres tall, 5.1 tons, found built into a church wall in the 19th century — carries the longest extant pre-Christian runic inscription, around 760 characters, and is considered the first known piece of written Swedish literature. The inscription is partially encrypted in two ways: by displacement (Caesar cipher) and by using special cipher runes; it is intentionally challenging to read, using kennings in the manner of Old Norse skaldic poetry. Starting with the Ingold part, the text becomes increasingly hard to read: where the first part is written in the 16 common short-twig runes of the Younger Futhark, Varinn switches over to the older 24-type Elder Futhark and cipher runes — and the stone's uppermost row features tent runes, with a hook rune centered in the bottom row. The obscurity may perhaps even be part of a magic ritual. [VERIFIED — the Ög 136 identity, the Varinn attribution, the dimensions and the church-wall find, the ~760 characters, the twofold encryption, the short-twig-to-Elder switch, and the tent/hook placement, per Wikipedia "Rök runestone", read first-party this pass]

(5) The ætt names Freyr, Hagal, and Tyr are the Icelandic tradition's names for the Younger Futhark groups; what the Elder groups were originally called remains unknown. (6) No runic break is filed here: Rök's coordinates were re-derived from the article's own printed resolutions, which is verification, not cryptanalysis, and no solving procedure was run against any cipher-rune text. - **Decoder-design note (Runic → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The coordinate is the cipher.** Cipher runes replace the letter with its address — ætt, then position. A specimen whose output looks like small-number pairs (counts, indices, coordinates) is first tested as an address cipher, not as noise: do the pairs index a known row before asking whether they are values? The Gauntlet's fixture map gains the address test as a standing first step for pair-shaped traffic. (2) **The row order is key material.** The Freyr↔Tyr swap and the 13th-century l/m swap both change every resolution, and the row order lives in a tradition (Jón Ólafsson's treatise) or a stone (Kylver), not in the message. A specimen's index table is interrogated as key material — who fixed the order, when did it change, what breaks if two entries swap — and the fixture carries the row version alongside the ciphertext. The Rök check is the calibration: 17 of 30 coordinates fail under the wrong row, and one becomes undecodable. (3) **Obscurity is the threat model, not strength.** Twenty-four shifts, sixteen symbols, thirty coordinates — all brute-forceable in seconds; Varinn's goal was display and delay ("intentionally challenging to read"), not secrecy against a determined reader. Gauntlet verdicts carry the maker's intent alongside the finding: a display cipher graded as if it were a secrecy cipher is a category error, and a secrecy claim on a display mechanism is the specimen's own confession. ## The straddling checkerboard (Soviet field practice, 1940s–1950s) — the board that straddles the digit, or: the Polybius square that learned to count

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero `## ` headings and zero bullet entries for "straddling checkerboard" in either catalogue, measured this pass — and eight case-insensitive occurrences per catalogue, all eight of them passing mentions inside the VIC and Nihilist entries (VIC's "straddling bipartite monoalphabetic substitution", the Nihilist entry's "straddling checkerboard" as the hardened substitution in the Soviet improvements, the two-square entry's family placement). "Checkerboard" alone is 17/17; "straddling" alone is 12/12, the other four being the VIC entry's "straddling bipartite" phrasing. The shelf around it is fully filed: VIC 1/1 headings, Nihilist (bullet entry, 1880s), Polybius (bullet entries), fractionation 24/30, the Delastelle private bullet entry (Bifid/Trifid). The component that carries the whole Soviet line — the board that turns letters into digits before any additive or transposition touches them — never got its own entry. It is filed now because its description survives in three independent worked sources that all re-encode exactly: the Wikipedia VIC article, John Savard's quadibloc, and the Crypto Wiki VIC page. [VERIFIED — the 0/0 heading counts, the 0/0 bullet-entry counts, and the 8/8, 17/17, 12/12 occurrence counts and the neighbour counts, measured this pass by grep -o, case-insensitive, before this entry was written]

- **The story.** The straddling checkerboard is not a cipher. It is a component — the front end of the Soviet pencil-and-paper line that runs from the 1880s Nihilist cipher through the wartime spy rings to VIC. During World War II, several Soviet spy rings communicated with Moscow Centre using ciphers that were evolutionary improvements on the basic Nihilist: a very strong version was used by Max Christiansen-Clausen in Richard Sorge's network in Japan and by Alexander Foote in the Lucy spy ring in Switzerland, and a slightly weaker version by the *Rote Kapelle* network. In both versions the plaintext was first converted to digits by a straddling checkerboard rather than a Polybius square. The ultimate development was VIC, used in the 1950s by Reino Häyhänen, codenamed "VICTOR" — the cipher found on microfilm inside a hollowed-out nickel by a newspaper boy in 1953, which the NSA could not break until Häyhänen defected in 1957 and explained it. By then most Soviet agents had moved to one-time pads; VIC survived where reused one-time-pad pages did not. No inventor is named for the board itself in any source read this pass: it enters the record as Soviet field practice, not as a patented device. [VERIFIED — the Sorge/Clausen, Lucy/Foote, and Rote Kapelle deployments and the hollow-nickel find and the 1953–1957 NSA record, per the Wikipedia VIC article, read first-party this pass; CLAIMED — the "no inventor named" negative, a statement about the sources read this pass, not about history]

- **The system.** Ten columns headed by the digits 0–9, in a keyed order (the header is key material — see the miniature). The second row holds the eight most frequent letters, memorized through a mnemonic: "AT ONE SIR" in the Wikipedia example, "a sin to err" (dropping the second r) in the wartime telling, "snegopad" (Russian for snowfall) for Häyhänen's Cyrillic board, "ESTONIA-R" in the Crypto Wiki telling. The two header digits left blank in that row become the labels of the two lower rows, which hold the remaining eighteen letters plus full stop and the numbers-shift symbol "/" — twenty-eight symbols in thirty cells, two cells spare. A top-row letter costs one digit; a lower-row letter costs two, row digit first. The code has the prefix property: no single-digit code is a row label, so a digit stream parses left-to-right with no separators and no ambiguity — the first digit of each symbol says whether the symbol is one digit or two. Numbers are sent by a shift: "/" opens number mode, each plaintext digit is sent three times, "/" closes it (see the honest blank for the dispute over "three"). Two purposes ride on the one board: compression — the frequent letters shrink to a single digit, so the message gets shorter and the radio operator shuts down sooner, out from under enemy direction finders — and diffusion — the digit stream is what the additive and the transpositions then work on, so the letter never meets the cipher as a letter. The wartime additive came from almanacs of industrial statistics, chosen because the books looked dull enough not to arouse suspicion if an agent was searched; the figures are not uniformly distributed (Benford's law: an excess of 0 and 1), but they were never successfully cryptanalysed in practice. [VERIFIED — the board layout, the 28-in-30 count, the prefix property, the four mnemonics, the number-shift mechanism, and the almanac additive with its Benford caveat, per the Wikipedia VIC article and quadibloc, read first-party this pass; CORROBORATED — the compression rationale (shorter transmissions, higher unicity distance) per the Wikipedia history section]

- **The worked miniature (computed this pass).** 53 checks pass in goal hidden_files/verify-straddling-checkerboard-20261110.py. (a) **Three boards, one shape.** The Wikipedia board (header 5 9 6 1 3 2 8 4 7 0, from VIC's [Line-S]; top AT ONE SIR; rows 6 and 8), the quadibloc board (header 9 8 2 7 0 1 6 4 3 5; same top row; rows 2 and 6), and the Crypto Wiki board (header 0–9 in order; top ESTONIA-R; rows 2 and 6, with "/" in row 6). Each holds exactly 28 symbols with distinct codes, eight single-digit codes, and a prefix-free code — the two row labels are exactly the two header digits the top row leaves blank. (b) **The Wikipedia example, re-encoded.** The message "Attack at dawn. By dawn I mean 0500. Not 0915 like you did last time." is bisected and the halves swapped — "mean 0500. Not 0915 like you did last time./Attack at dawn. By dawn I" — and the board turns it into digits: M=60, E=2, A=5, N=3, then the shift, the tripled digits "000 555 000 000" for 0500, the shift back, "."=87, "Not"=319, the shift, "000 999 111 555" for 0915, the shift back, and on through "like you did last time." to the marker and "Attack at dawn. By dawn I". Encoding the bisected message *without* the "/" marker reproduces the article's printed final code digit for digit: "60253 80000 55500 00008 08731 98000 09991 11555 80677 64288 18666 76667 54997 60287 59956 96459 66583 38765 88665 8337" — 99 digits, exact. Encoding it *with* the marker gives 101 digits, first differing at index 70, where the marker's own code "80" sits. A mode-aware decoder (a "/" followed by three identical digits is a shift; a "/" followed by letters is the marker) recovers the message exactly from either stream, and both round-trip. (c) **The other two published examples.** Quadibloc's "SENDMONEY" → "410222570166" (S=4, E=1, N=0, D=22, M=25, O=7, N=0, E=1, Y=66), round trip exact. The Crypto Wiki's "ATTACKATDAWN" → "3113212731223655" (A=3, T=1, C=21, K=27, D=22, W=65, N=5), round trip exact; adding the key number 0452 digit-wise mod 10 gives "3565257935743007", and reading those digits back through the same board gives "ANWHRSANROAEER" — the published superencipherment, reproduced. (d) **The compression, priced.** "ATTACKATDAWN" is 12 letters into 16 digits, not 24; "SENDMONEY" is 9 into 12, not 18; the Wikipedia message's 44 letters take 61 digits, not 88 — 27 of its 44 letters sit in the top row and cost a single digit. (e) **The header is key material.** "ATTACKATDAWN" under the three boards gives three different digit strings — "5995696459665833", "9889282498229600", "3113212731223655" — the same plaintext, three boards, no shared digit. A standard-construction board (header a permutation of 0–9, top row any 8 of 26 letters in any order, lower rows alphabetical) has 10! × P(26,8) = 228,581,479,526,400,000 possibilities; freeing the lower rows multiplies by 20!. - **Decoder-design note (Straddling checkerboard → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The prefix property is the parse rule, and it is the first test on any digit stream.** A specimen whose output is digits parses left-to-right with no separators only if its code is prefix-free — and the straddling board's whole design is that property. The Gauntlet's digit-stream rung tries the prefix parse before anything else: find the two digits that only ever open a pair, and the board's skeleton is already half-drawn. A stream that will not prefix-parse is not a checkerboard, and a fixture that assumes separators where the code needs none is a fixture that misread the specimen. (2) **The header is key material, never a default.** Three boards, one plaintext, three digit strings with nothing shared — and the Wikipedia board's header is itself derived from VIC's key generation ([Line-S]), not chosen. A specimen's digit header is interrogated as key: who generated it, from what, and what changes if two digits swap. A board read as "0–9 in order" when its header is scrambled is a specimen graded against the wrong key. (3) **One symbol, two jobs, is a design smell — flag it, don't smooth it.** "/" is the numbers-shift and the bisection marker and the same code does both; the article's own example trips over the collision (the marker vanishes from the final code; the blind-toggle decoder dies on it). Gauntlet rule, standing: a specimen that overloads one symbol with two meanings is flagged at intake, and the fixture that decodes it must state its disambiguation rule out loud — lookahead, context, or position — before it trusts its own parse. Compression is the fourth rung's warning, carried free: the board shortens the message before it enciphers it, so the specimen's length and its letter frequencies are both hidden at once — grade the compression stage separately from the cipher stage, or the fixture will price a short ciphertext as a strong one. ## The Trifid cipher (Delastelle, 1901–1902) — the cube that diffuses, or: the first practical trigraphic substitution

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero `## ` headings for "Trifid" in either catalogue, measured this pass — and eleven case-insensitive occurrences in the private catalogue against six in the public, all of them passing mentions: the private Delastelle bullet entry carries five (its heading bullet, its cube bullet, its grade line — lines 2411, 2413, 2417), the Four-square bullet and its design note carry one each (lines 2447, 2452), the family-placement bullet and the Nihilist design note carry one each (lines 3156, 3173), and the Myszkowski and straddling-checkerboard gap sentences carry one each (lines 9754, 9952) — nine lines, eleven occurrences. The public catalogue carries six, one each on lines 6995, 7000, 7874, 7891, 14225, 14423: it does not mirror the Delastelle bullet entry at all, which is why its count is lower. The shelf around it is fully filed: Bifid shares the same bullet entry and the same 0-heading state (Bifid remains the standing zero after this entry), the fractionation family (ADFGX/ADFGVX) carries headings, and the straddling checkerboard — the component that feeds fractionated systems — was filed as entry #170. The cipher that gave the fractionation family its third dimension never got its own entry. [VERIFIED — the 0/0 heading counts and the 11/6 occurrence counts and the per-line counts above, measured this pass by grep -o, case-insensitive, before this entry was written]

- **The story.** Félix Marie Delastelle (1840–1902), a French amateur cryptographer, wrote his *Traité Élémentaire de Cryptographie* in 1901; it was published in Paris by Gauthier-Villars in 1902, the year of his death. The treatise introduced fractionation with the Bifid and then extended it to three dimensions with the Trifid. The cipher exists because twenty-seven is the smallest cube that holds an alphabet: Delastelle's own argument (p. 101, quoted in the Trifid cipher article) is that *n* objects combined in trigrams give *n*³ — two would give only 2³ = 8 trigrams, four would give 4³ = 64, but three give 3³ = 27, so "three is the only value for *n*". The name means "divided into three parts" (Oxford English Dictionary, via the article), and the article's long-standing characterization calls the Trifid the first practical trigraphic substitution. [CORROBORATED — Delastelle's biography and treatise dates via the Trifid cipher article and this catalogue's Delastelle bullet entry; the n³ argument and the OED gloss via the article, which cites Delastelle pp. 101–103; the treatise itself not opened first-party this pass; the "first practical trigraphic substitution" sentence is carried in mirrors of the article and does not appear in the current page text read this pass]

- **The system.** A 27-letter mixed alphabet — keyword letters in order, then the remaining alphabet, then one extra symbol — populates a 3×3×3 cube; each letter takes the Cartesian coordinates of its cell as a trigram, 111 through 333 (layer, row, column). Delastelle's own 27th symbol is "+"; other working sources use "." (Practical Cryptography) and "#" (CryptoCrack and the ACA) — the 27th symbol is a per-source convention, not a fixed part of the cipher. Encryption divides the plaintext into groups of fixed size (Delastelle's examples use 5 and 7), writes each letter's trigram vertically beneath it, reads the digits horizontally across the group, regroups them into triplets, and reads the triplets back through the cube. Decryption reverses the procedure. The group size should be coprime to 3 for maximum diffusion, and an enciphering error is confined to its group (Gaines p. 210, via the article). Keyspace: 27! ≈ 1.09×10²⁸ (computed this pass). The ACA carries Trifid as a cipher type (120–150 letters, *The ACA and You* handbook pp. 83–84) with "#" as its 27th character; ANCHISES's Trifid Relations script (Jan–Feb 2008 Computer Column, cryptogram.org, read first-party this pass) works cribbed Trifids at period 9 (ND2003 E-21, ciphertext PP#TNPAUF, crib "aininitss") and period 7 (MA2021 E-17). [CORROBORATED — cube mechanics and group sizes via the Trifid cipher article citing Delastelle pp. 101–103 and Gaines; the 27th-symbol variation via the three worked sources below; ACA habitat via the handbook listing and the ANCHISES script read first-party this pass]

- **The worked miniature (computed this pass).** 22 checks pass in goal hidden_files/verify-trifid-20261110.py. (a) **Delastelle's own example, via the article.** Key FELIX MARIE DELASTELLE → mixed alphabet FELIXMARDSTBCGHJKNOPQUVWYZ+; plaintext "aide-toi, le ciel t'aidera" (punctuation dropped, twenty letters), period 5 → FMJFV OISSU FTFPU FEQQC; the three digit rows match the article's table exactly, and the cube spot-checks (F = 111, M = 123, + = 333). (b) **Practical Cryptography.** Key EPSDUCVWYM.ZLKXNBTFGORIJHAQ ("." as 27th); "DEFEND THE EAST WALL OF THE CASTLE." (twenty-nine characters, the final "." enciphered), period 5 → SUEFE CPHSE GYYJI XIMFO FOCEJ LBSP; all three digit rows match the page exactly (row 1 ends 3 1 2 2 1 2), including the short four-letter final group. (c) **CryptoCrack.** Keyword RALPHEMERSON → keyed alphabet RALPHEMSONBCDFGIJKQTUVWXYZ# ("#" as 27th); "THEONLYWAYTOHAVEAFRIENDISTOBEONE", period 7 → QPTISKM UQPUBBW QBHPVWL FMBYQAJ AEEU. All three decrypt back exactly. (d) **Structure, measured not asserted.** At period 3, every full-group ciphertext trigram is single-row — all eighteen trigrams across six groups draw their three digits from one coordinate row, so the row partition survives; at period 5, group 1's second trigram draws from rows 1 and 2, so the coordinate identity is destroyed — that is what "coprime to 3 for maximum diffusion" means, measured. Diffusion is per-coordinate: changing a plaintext letter to one differing in all three coordinates moves exactly three ciphertext letters (A = 131 → B = 213, measured at periods 3 and 5 alike); changing it to one differing in a single coordinate moves exactly one (L = 113 → M = 123). One corrupted ciphertext letter damages at most three plaintext letters, all inside its own group — corrupting the first letter of the aide-toi ciphertext leaves groups 2–4 plaintext intact. Keyspace 27! = 10,888,869,450,418,352,160,768,000,000 (≈1.09×10²⁸), computed exactly.

- **The honest blank.** Five confessions. (1) Delastelle's *Traité* was not opened first-party this pass — the aide-toi example and the pp. 101–103 citations arrive via the Trifid cipher article. (2) The "first practical trigraphic substitution" characterization is carried in mirrors of that article and does not appear in the current page text read this pass. (3) The Alchetron/Crypto Wiki variant example — "TREATY ENDS BOER WAR." with the period as the 27th character — was not re-encrypted this pass; it is noted, not verified. (4) The cryptanalysis literature (LANIKI Lecture 17, cited by Practical Cryptography; the Jan–Feb 2008 Computer Column article text behind the ANCHISES script) was not read this pass — only the script itself was opened. (5) A self-caught error from this pass: an early draft of the verify script asserted that a period divisible by 3 collapses the cipher to a fixed monoalphabetic substitution — the script itself refuted it (A → B at period 3 still moves three ciphertext letters), and the entry states the true property (row segregation) instead. The draft assertion is preserved in the script's comments as the refuted claim.

- **Decoder-design note (Trifid → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Fractionation means the unit of analysis is the coordinate stream, not the letter.** The letter is a recombination; letter-frequency analysis sees only recombined output. Gauntlet port: when a specimen's output shows each output symbol depending on several input symbols, split the attack into coordinate streams before touching letter frequencies. (2) **The period's arithmetic is a fingerprint.** A period coprime to 3 mixes coordinate rows; a period divisible by 3 segregates them — and the segregation is measurable from ciphertext alone, because a single-row trigram preserves the row partition. Gauntlet port: probe a specimen's block size against small moduli; a period that preserves a partition under regrouping is a structural tell, and it splits one cube problem into three row problems. (3) **Error confinement is tamper localization.** One wrong ciphertext letter damages at most three plaintext letters, all inside one period group — the group is a blast wall. Gauntlet port: corrupt one symbol deliberately and watch where the damage stops; the boundary is the design — and a specimen that does NOT confine errors is confessing a chaining mode. Either way, the damage map is the interrogation.

## The Bifid cipher (1901) — the letter split in two, or: the cipher that dissolved the letter

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero `## ` headings for "Bifid" in either catalogue, measured this pass — and eighteen case-insensitive occurrences in the private catalogue against twelve in the public, all of them passing mentions: the private Delastelle bullet entry carries seven (its heading bullet two, its Bifid bullet, its Trifid bullet, its Shannon bullet, its design note, its grade line — lines 2411:2, 2412, 2413, 2414, 2415, 2417), the Solitaire design note carries one (line 2425), the Four-square bullet and its design note carry one each (lines 2447, 2452), the family-placement bullet and the Nihilist design note carry one each (lines 3156, 3173), and the Myszkowski, straddling-checkerboard and Trifid gap sentences carry one, one and two (lines 9754, 9952, 9970:2) — sixteen lines, eighteen occurrences. The public catalogue carries twelve, two each on lines 6971 and 14441 and one each on lines 6995, 7000, 7874, 7891, 14225, 14423, 14443, 14455: it does not mirror the Delastelle bullet entry at all, which is why its count is lower. The shelf around it is fully filed: the Trifid — the cipher that gave the fractionation family its third dimension — was filed as entry #171 this same day; four-square, Delastelle's third answer to the same enemy, travels as a bullet entry; ADFGX/ADFGVX carry headings; the straddling checkerboard, the component that feeds fractionated systems, was filed as entry #170. The cipher that gave the fractionation family its first dimension — the one Shannon canonized as §10 without naming its inventor — never got its own entry. [VERIFIED — the 0/0 heading counts and the 18/12 occurrence counts and the per-line counts above, measured this pass by grep -o, case-insensitive, via goal hidden_files/verify-bifid-20261110.py, before this entry was written]

- **The story.** Félix Marie Delastelle (1840–1902), a French amateur cryptographer, wrote his *Traité élémentaire de cryptographie* in 1901; it was published in Paris by Gauthier-Villars in 1902, the year of his death. The Bifid is the first of the fractionation ciphers in that volume — the Trifid, its three-dimensional extension, follows in the same pages — and the name says the mechanism: Latin *bifidus*, "divided in two", from *bi-* (two) + *findere* (to split), the same construction as the Trifid's "divided into three parts". The cipher was never fielded: Practical Cryptography's standing note is that it "has never been used by a military or government organisation, only ever by amateur cryptographers" — and the amateurs kept it. The American Cryptogram Association carries Bifid as a cipher type (125–150 letters, *The ACA and You* handbook pp. 37–38), with two descendants in the same handbook: CM Bifid, the conjugated-matrix variant (pp. 41–42), first printed in the Jan–Feb 1960 *Cryptogram* and thought to have been developed some fifteen years earlier, and Twin Bifid (pp. 85–86, 100–150 letters each). [CORROBORATED — Delastelle's biography and treatise dates via this catalogue's Delastelle bullet entry and the Trifid entry; the etymology via Wiktionary and Etymonline; the never-fielded standing via Practical Cryptography; the ACA habitat via the handbook's contents listing; the CM Bifid history via CryptoCrack's cipher guide]

- **The system.** A 25-letter mixed alphabet — keyword letters in order, then the remaining alphabet, one extra symbol dropped — fills a 5×5 Polybius square; English practice merges I with J. Each plaintext letter takes its (row, column) coordinates, written vertically beneath the message; the coordinate stream is then read off horizontally — all the row-coordinates, then all the column-coordinates — and re-paired into letters through the same square. Messages are enciphered in blocks of fixed length, the period, which is part of the key. Every ciphertext letter depends on two plaintext letters, so the Bifid is a digraphic cipher, like the Playfair — and single-letter frequency analysis, the killer of all monoalphabetic systems, finds nothing to bite on: the letter boundary has been dissolved. Keyspace: 25! = 15,511,210,043,330,985,984,000,000 (≈1.55×10²⁵, 83.7 bits), computed exactly this pass — but fewer distinct ciphers than tables, because the same permutation applied to both rows and columns yields the same cipher (Machiavelo & Reis 2006); the simultaneous-permutation orbit count is 25!/120 = 129,260,083,694,424,883,200,000, derived this pass from the paper's stated equivalence. The period's parity decides the cryptanalysis: for even periods *p*, ciphertext letters at a distance of *p*/2 are influenced by two plaintext letters, so bigram statistics can find the period; for odd *p*, they are influenced by three, so the break needs trigram statistics and more text — which is why most authors recognize odd periods as the stronger, though Bow (1960) argued against it. Machiavelo & Reis (DCC-2006-1) put the period normally above 6 and give a fully automated ciphertext-only attack — period found by a statistical function, key-table generated from it — feasible given enough text. [CORROBORATED — the square mechanics and the period-detection rule via the Bifid cipher article and Practical Cryptography; the never-fielded standing and the period-5 worked example via Practical Cryptography; the orbit equivalence, the period-above-6 norm, the Bow dissent and the automated attack via Machiavelo & Reis 2006 as summarized; the ACA habitat via the handbook contents listing]

(twenty-nine letters) → FFYHMKHYCPLIASHADTRLHCCHLBLR; the step-1 row and column strings match the page exactly, and the ciphertext decrypts back exactly. (c) **Rosetta Code.** Alphabetical square (I/J merged), "ATTACKATDAWN", one block of twelve → DQBDAXDQPDQH; both digit rows match the page exactly, and the ciphertext decrypts back exactly. (d) **multiwingspan.** Keyed square MXTSVGWBCFNDRZLOYQAPIHKUE, "THESECRETISOUT", one block of fourteen → VIHLVSIDUULNOQ; both digit rows match the page exactly, and the ciphertext decrypts back exactly. (e) **This catalogue's own bullet miniature.** HELLO, alphabetical square, period 5 → FNNVD; decrypts back exactly. (f) **Structure, measured not asserted.** Period 1 is the identity — a block of one letter pairs its own row and column straight back together. The period is key material: FLEEATONCE at period 5 → UAIEYYDINS, at period 10 → UAEOLWRINS, two different ciphers from one square and one message. At even periods 2 through 8, every ciphertext letter is coordinate-pure — both its digits come from the row stream or both from the column stream; at odd periods 3 through 9, exactly one letter per block is mixed, the one straddling the midpoint (position (*p*−1)/2). The half-period parent rule holds exactly: at even *p*, ciphertext letters at distance *p*/2 share precisely the same two plaintext parents; at odd *p*, letters at distance floor(*p*/2) or ceil(*p*/2) jointly have three parents. Diffusion is per-coordinate: changing the first plaintext letter in one coordinate moves exactly one ciphertext letter (position 0), in both coordinates moves exactly two (positions 0 and 5); changing the middle letter in one coordinate moves one (position 7), in both moves two (positions 2 and 7). One corrupted ciphertext letter damages at most two plaintext letters, all inside its own group — corrupting a letter in the castle example's second group damages exactly one plaintext letter, inside that group; corrupting the first letter of the Wikipedia example damages two, both inside the block.

- **Decoder-design note (Bifid → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The period's parity is a fingerprint you can read from the parents.** Even period → half-period-separated letters share exactly two parents, so bigram statistics find the period; odd → three parents, so the break needs trigram statistics and more text. Gauntlet port: when a specimen batches its work, test the batch size's parity by the parent count at half-distance; the parity tells you how much text the break needs — and a specimen that chose an even batch size has already told you its cheaper attack. (2) **One coordinate is one confession.** Changing a plaintext letter in one coordinate moves one ciphertext letter; in both, two — the movement count is the diffusion order, measured not asserted. Gauntlet port: perturb one input coordinate at a time and count the output movement; a specimen whose single-coordinate change moves the whole output is confessing chaining, not fractionation — and the count is the interrogation, not the designer's story. (3) **The honest keyspace is the orbit count, not the table count.** 25! tables, 25!/120 ciphers — the same permutation on rows and columns is the same cipher. Gauntlet port: when a specimen claims a keyspace, ask which keys are secretly the same key; a specimen that counts tables is overstating its strength by the symmetry factor, and the interrogation prices the symmetry before it prices the key.

## The Ragbaby cipher (1955; SHERLAC) — the cipher whose key is the word count, or: the polyalphabetic that never repeats

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero `## ` headings for "Ragbaby" in either catalogue, measured this pass — and zero case-insensitive occurrences in either catalogue, and zero for "SHERLAC" in both: the cipher does not exist in this library in any form, not even as a passing mention. The shelf around it is fully filed: the keyword-cipher family travels as bullet entries; the ACA habitat is filed (the Bifid's handbook standing, the CM Bifid and Twin Bifid descendants); the fractionation family just closed its first two dimensions as entries #171 and #172. The Ragbaby is the American Cryptogram Association's own invention — born in its own magazine, solved by its own methods — and the catalogue never filed it. [VERIFIED — the 0/0 heading counts and the 0/0 occurrence counts and the 0/0 SHERLAC counts, measured this pass by grep -o, case-insensitive, via goal hidden_files/verify-ragbaby-20261110.py, before this entry was written]

- **The story.** The Ragbaby cipher was invented by the ACA member SHERLAC and first described in the Jul–Aug 1955 edition of the ACA's magazine *The Cryptogram*. It is a puzzle cipher, not a military one: it lives in the ACA's solving tradition, where its listed solving methods are hill climbing and dictionary keyword search. Seventy-one years after its description it has no field history, no military use, and no famous break — its whole career is the puzzler's page, which is exactly why the catalogue files it: the Ragbaby is the clearest small example of a polyalphabetic whose key is not a repeated word but the message's own shape. [CORROBORATED — the inventor, the Jul–Aug 1955 first description, and the solving methods via CryptoCrack's Ragbaby guide; the 1955 dating and the magazine venue via the same source]

- **The system.** Two ingredients, one secret. (1) A keyed 24-letter alphabet: the keyword's letters in order with repeats removed, then the remaining alphabet in order — I/J merged (J becomes I) and W/X merged (X becomes W), so the alphabet holds 24 letters and J and X never appear. (2) A number key written under the plaintext, word by word: under the first word the numbers run 1, 2, 3, …; under the second word they start at 2 and run 2, 3, 4, …; under the third they start at 3 — the shift for the letter at position *p* (1-based) of word *w* is *w* + *p* − 1, counted forward that many places in the keyed alphabet, wrapping at the end. Word divisions are preserved in the ciphertext. The number key carries no secret at all: given the word lengths, every shift is public — the *only* secret is the keyed alphabet, which makes the Ragbaby a monoalphabetic substitution with position-dependent offsets, not a true polyalphabetic with an independent key stream. Keyspace: 24! = 620,448,401,733,239,439,360,000 (≈6.20×10²³, 79.0 bits) in theory — but the alphabet is keyword-built, and for the short keywords the sources name (4–7 letters) the ordered-keyword bound is P(24,4) + P(24,5) + P(24,6) + P(24,7) = 1,846,628,784 (≈1.85×10⁹, 30.8 bits), and a dictionary keyword search is the listed break — the honest keyspace is the dictionary, not the factorial. [CORROBORATED — the alphabet construction, the number-key rule, and the solving methods via CryptoCrack and the CWU walkthrough; the 24-letter merge rule via both; VERIFIED — the shift formula against the published number key, the 24! arithmetic, and the P(24,4..7) bound, computed this pass]

- **The worked miniature (computed this pass).** 21 checks pass in goal hidden_files/verify-ragbaby-20261110.py. (a) **CryptoCrack.** Keyword FRANKLIN → dedup FRANKLI → keyed alphabet FRANKLIBCDEGHMOPQSTUVWYZ; "WELL DONE IS BETTER THAN WELL SAID", number key 1234 2345 34 456789 5678 6789 78910 → YHCD GSBP DW GPFRTE ZTDG NSMO FEPU; the published number key is reproduced exactly by the shift formula, and the ciphertext decrypts back exactly. (b) **CWU.** Keyword TREENUT → dedup TRENU → keyed alphabet TRENUABCDFGHIKLMOPQSVWYZ; "THIS IS THE ONLY EXAMPLE" → RKMZ LY NMC VDVA CNIZETK, re-encrypted exactly — the walkthrough's per-letter steps (t→R, h→K, i→M, s→Z; i→L, s→Y; t→N, h→M, e→C) all check out, and the full string matches. (c) **This catalogue's own miniature.** Keyword KODAKAI → KODAIBCEFGHLMNPQRSTUVWYZ; "MEET AT DAWN" → NGHY BW BEDU; decrypts back exactly. (d) **Structure, measured not asserted.** The smear is total: in the FRANKLIN example the plaintext E enciphers to four different letters (H, P, S, T) and L to four (C, D, M, O), and *every* repeated letter in the message smears to more than one ciphertext letter — raw frequency analysis finds nothing to bite on, but position-conditioned analysis would. The word-length leak is exact: ciphertext word lengths equal plaintext word lengths in both published examples (7/7 words, 5/5 words) — the shape of the message rides in the clear. A one-letter word shifts by exactly its word index (three one-letter words under FRANKLIN encipher A → N, K, L for words 1, 2, 3). The merge is lossy: X and W encipher identically, so "EXAMPLE" decrypts back as "EWAMPLE" — the receiver must disambiguate J/I and X/W from context, a cost the 24-letter alphabet charges on every message that uses them. One corrupted ciphertext letter damages exactly one plaintext letter — the error confinement of a system with no chaining.

- **The honest blank.** Six confessions. (1) The name's etymology was not established this pass — no source consulted says why SHERLAC called it "Ragbaby", and none is asserted here. (2) A second source (CipherChronicle) dates the cipher's popularity to "American puzzling circles in the early 20th century" — against the sourced 1955 first description; the two datings were not adjudicated, and the 1955 date is the one carried. (3) The alphabet merge has a variant: CryptoCrack and the CWU walkthrough merge I/J and W/X, while CipherChronicle merges I/J and U/V — the U/V variant was not verified, and this entry follows the ACA-tool sources. (4) The Jul–Aug 1955 *Cryptogram* issue was not opened first-party this pass — the inventor and dating arrive via CryptoCrack. (5) SHERLAC's identity beyond the ACA handle was not established. (6) One self-caught error this pass: the first verify run failed the TREENUT decrypt — the script expected "EXAMPLE" back, and the cipher correctly returns "EWAMPLE", because X merges to W on encryption; the check was wrong, the cipher was right, and the lossy merge is now a measured finding rather than a failed test.

- **Decoder-design note (Ragbaby → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The key that isn't a key.** The number key is fully determined by the word lengths — it carries zero secret, and the only secret is the keyed alphabet. Gauntlet port: when a specimen's "key" decomposes into public structure plus one secret, price the secret alone; a specimen that counts its public structure as key material is overstating its strength by exactly the structure's share, and the interrogation separates the two before it prices either. (2) **Position-dependence is the smear.** The same letter enciphers four ways by word position, so flat frequency analysis fails — but position-conditioned analysis recovers the alphabet. Gauntlet port: before grading a channel's output statistics as flat, test them conditioned on position; a specimen whose unigram flatness dissolves under position-conditioning is smearing, not random — and the conditioning that dissolves it is the interrogation. (3) **Word lengths are the leak.** The ciphertext preserves word boundaries exactly, so the word-length pattern rides in the clear. Gauntlet port: count the structural leakage a specimen preserves — lengths, boundaries, counts — before pricing its content secrecy; a specimen that hides content but ships structure has already told you the shape of the message, and the shape is the interrogation's first question.

## The Lamport one-time signature (1979) — the signature that is only a hash function, or: the seal whose key is two piles of random numbers

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero case-insensitive occurrences of "Lamport" in either catalogue, measured this pass — and zero in either research log: the scheme does not exist in this library in any form, not even as a passing mention. The shelf around it is fully filed, which is what makes the zero loud: the descendants are all on record — ML-DSA (FIPS 204), SLH-DSA / SPHINCS+ (FIPS 205), XMSS (RFC 8391), LMS (RFC 8554), and the Merkle tree that makes one-time keys many-time — while the root they all grow from was never filed. The Lamport one-time signature is the ancestor of the entire hash-based signature lane: the scheme that proved a digital signature needs nothing but a one-way function. [VERIFIED — the 0/0 occurrence counts in both catalogues and both research logs, measured this pass by grep -o, case-insensitive, via goal hidden_files/verify-lamport-20261110.py, before this entry was written]

- **The story.** The original version was first published in Diffie and Hellman's 1976 "New Directions in Cryptography"; Leslie Lamport published the improved approach in October 1979 as "Constructing Digital Signatures from a One Way Function" (SRI International, CSL-98). The idea is almost offensively simple, which is the point: a signature scheme built from nothing but a hash function has no trapdoor to steal, no number theory to break, and no structure for a quantum computer to exploit beyond Grover's generic square-root speedup — the reason the hash-based lane survived the NIST post-quantum standardisation as the backup on different math. Lamport himself never deployed it as a product; it is a primitive, not a system — and every hash-based signature since is a compression, a tree, or a state-removal built on top of it. [CORROBORATED — the 1976 first publication and the October 1979 SRI report, per Wikipedia's Lamport-signature page, read first-party this pass; the NIST backup framing from this library's ML-DSA and SLH-DSA entries]

- **The system.** One hash function, one rule: never sign twice. (1) Key generation: pick 256 pairs of random 256-bit numbers — 512 numbers in total — and hash each one; the 512 random numbers are the private key, the 512 hashes are the public key. (2) Signing: hash the message to a 256-bit digest, and for each bit reveal one number from the matching pair — the first number if the bit is 0, the second if it is 1. The signature is 256 revealed numbers. (3) Verification: hash each revealed number and check it against the public key's matching entry; all 256 must match. The unused half of the private key must then be destroyed — a signature publishes exactly half the secret, and a second signature under the same key publishes half of what remains. Sizes, measured this pass: private key 16,384 bytes (16 KiB), public key 16,384 bytes, signature 8,192 bytes (8 KiB) — to sign a 32-byte digest. Lamport's 1979 improved variant may publish both, one, or neither number from any pair, buying the same strength from a shorter key; the Winternitz compression, which signs multi-bit chunks instead of single bits, shrinks keys and signatures further at the cost of more hashing — the size ladder that runs from Lamport through WOTS+ to SPHINCS+. [VERIFIED — the mechanism, the 16 KiB / 16 KiB / 8 KiB sizes, and the one-time rule, computed this pass; CORROBORATED — the 1979 improved variant and the Winternitz compression, per Wikipedia's Lamport-signature page]

- **The worked miniature (computed this pass).** 17 checks pass in goal hidden_files/verify-lamport-20261110.py (SHA-256, deterministic seed, full 256-bit keys — no toy scale). (a) **Sizes.** Private key 512 × 32 bytes = 16,384; public key the same; signature 256 × 32 = 8,192 — the textbook figures, reproduced exactly. (b) **Sign and verify.** Message "KODAKAI" signs and verifies; flipping one byte of the first signature element fails verification; signing the neighbouring message "KODAKAJ" and presenting the first message's signature fails — the signature is bound to the digest, not the message text. (c) **The one-signature leak, exact.** After one signature, exactly 256 of 512 preimages are revealed — 50.0%, no more and no less: half the private key is public by construction, and the other half is the entire remaining security. (d) **The two-signature misuse, measured.** Signing a second message ("DECODER") with the same key reveals 385 of 512 preimages — 75.2% of the private key gone. The two digests differ in 129 of 256 bit positions, and the revealed count is exactly 256 + 129: every agreeing position contributes one preimage, every differing position contributes both. (e) **The forgery.** A hybrid digest — the first digest with its first five differing positions flipped to the second digest's bits — differs from both signed digests, and a signature assembled *only* from already-revealed preimages verifies for it. The forgeable-digest count for these two signatures is 2^129: at every differing position either bit is signable, at every agreeing position only the shared bit is. Honest layer: the forgery lives at the digest layer — a signature that verifies for a digest never signed. Finding an actual *message* whose digest equals the hybrid is a separate preimage problem, and this pass forges no message. (f) **Determinism.** Rebuilding the keypair from the same seed reproduces the identical public key — the miniature is re-runnable, not a one-off.

- **The honest blank.** Five confessions. (1) The 1976-versus-1979 dating is carried as Wikipedia states it — the original version in Diffie-Hellman 1976, the improved approach in Lamport's October 1979 report — and the 1976 paper itself was not opened first-party this pass. (2) Lamport's improved variant (publish both, one, or neither per pair) and the Winternitz compression are described, not implemented or measured, this pass. (3) The 2^129 forgeable-digest count is for these two digests (129 differing positions measured); the expectation for random digests is 128, and this run's 129 is one draw, not a law. (4) The quantum figures — Grover halving preimage security, 256-bit elements for 128-bit quantum security — come from Wikipedia's security-parameters section, not from a derivation this pass. (5) No field deployment is claimed for Lamport itself: it is a primitive with no production history of its own, and its descendants (XMSS, LMS, SPHINCS+) carry the deployment record, already filed in this library.

- **Decoder-design note (Lamport → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The one-time rule is the whole security.** Reuse is not a flaw in the scheme — it is the scheme's boundary, and crossing it leaks 75% of the key in two signatures and forges digests by the billions. Gauntlet port: stateful-versus-stateless is a first-class interrogation question, asked before any other: a specimen whose safety depends on never repeating a state must be asked how it *enforces* that — and "the operator promises" is not an enforcement, it is a hope with a key attached. The SPHINCS+ entry's prehistory (stateful XMSS/LMS, stateless SPHINCS+ as the escape) is this rung's filed precedent. (2) **Size is the price of hash-only security.** 16 KiB of key and 8 KiB of signature to sign 32 bytes — the most expensive signature in the library per signed byte, and the cheapest in assumptions. Gauntlet port: price a specimen's overhead against the traffic it must carry, not against the abstract; a primitive that is secure but unaffordable at the channel's volume is a failed fit, not a failed primitive — and the interrogation says which one it is. (3) **Name the layer of the forgery.** The hybrid digest verifies, but no message was forged — the finding lives at the digest layer, and claiming a forged message would overstate it by exactly one preimage search. Gauntlet port: every forgery claim names its layer — digest, message, session, identity — before it is graded; a verification that passes at a lower layer is a finding about the key, never a forged message, until the layer above is also crossed.
