## The autokey cipher (1586) — the cipher that eats its own plaintext, or: the first keystream that never repeats

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero `## ` headings for "Autokey" in either catalogue, measured this pass — and forty-five case-insensitive occurrences in each, all of them passing mentions or the one bullet entry: the Oct-20 bullet entry carries thirteen (lines 2688–2704: heading, invention, mechanism, lineage, design note, grade, seed line), the Gronsfeld entry two (2712, 2720), the Beaufort bullet entry nine (2732–2742), the Vigenère bullet entry five (2936–2954), the running-key entry two (3063, 3079), the Bellaso entry three (3120, 3123), the Beaufort numbered entry two (3140, 3150), the Vigenère numbered entry six (7625–7631), the Quagmire gap sentence one (7873), and the K4 entry two (9066). The public catalogue carries the same forty-five, at lines 7299–13539. The shelf around it is fully filed: Vigenère itself, Porta, Gronsfeld, Beaufort, the running key, the Slidefair — the whole polyalphabetic family, numbered. The cipher that invented the keystream — the one Vigenère actually invented, in his own book, in 1586 — never got its own numbered entry. [VERIFIED — the 0/0 heading counts, the 45/45 occurrence counts and the per-line counts above, measured this pass by grep -o, case-insensitive, via goal hidden_files/verify-autokey-20261110.py, before this entry was written]

- **The story.** Blaise de Vigenère, in his *Traicté des chiffres* (Paris, 1586), before the court of Henry III — the book whose title page carries the cipher the world misnamed after him. The autokey is the cipher Vigenère actually invented: his version used a reciprocal table of ten alphabets and a single agreed letter as primer, the key made by writing down that letter and then the rest of the message. The more popular later form uses the full 26-row tabula recta and a short agreed keyword as primer instead of one letter. Also known as the autoclave cipher — a name this catalogue never carried (zero occurrences in either catalogue). The ACA carries autokey as a cipher type, primer-keyword form. The invention was ignored and forgotten, then reinvented in the 1800s — the bullet entry's arc, carried here as CLAIMED, single textbook carrier. [CORROBORATED — the 1586 invention, the ten-alphabet reciprocal table, the single-letter primer, and the tabula-recta keyword form via Wikipedia's Autokey cipher article, read first-party this pass (which cites Vigenère's *Traicté*, ff. 46r–49v, and the ACA usage); CLAIMED — the ignored-then-reinvented arc, single textbook carrier via the bullet entry]

- **The system.** Two forms, one idea: the key is generated from the message itself. (1) **Text-autokey** (the common form): the keystream is the primer followed by the plaintext — key[i] = primer[i] for i < m, plaintext[i−m] after. Encryption is Vigenère addition, C = P + K mod 26; decryption recovers the plaintext letter by letter, each recovered letter feeding the key m positions later. (2) **Ciphertext-autokey**: the keystream is the primer followed by the ciphertext — the receiver holds the whole keystream from the start, since it is built from what arrived. (3) **Key-autokey**: the keystream feeds on its own previous members rather than on the message text — the form this entry describes but does not implement this pass. The primer is the only secret: a single-letter primer admits 26 possibilities; KILT admits 26^4 = 456,976; QUEENLY admits 26^7 = 8,031,810,176. The keystream never repeats within a message — there is no period for Kasiski to find, and the index of coincidence sees nothing — which is why the autokey is the oldest ancestor of the stream cipher, and why its weakness is not repetition but feedback: the plaintext is part of the key, so the key contains common words at various points, and a guessed word can be dragged through it. [VERIFIED — the keystream construction and the primer-space arithmetic, computed this pass; CORROBORATED — the two forms, the ACA primer-keyword form, and the Kasiski/IC immunity via Wikipedia's Autokey cipher article; the feedback weakness via the same article's cryptanalysis section]

- **The worked miniature (computed this pass).** 39 checks pass in goal hidden_files/verify-autokey-20261110.py. (a) **Wikipedia, ACA form.** Primer QUEENLY, "ATTACKATDAWN" → QNXEPVYTWTWP; keystream QUEENLYATTACKATDAWN, 19 letters, primer 7 + message 12; decrypts back exactly. (b) **Wikipedia, cryptanalysis example.** Primer KILT, "MEETATTHEFOUNTAIN" → WMPMMXXAEYHBRYOCA; keystream KILTMEETATTHEFOUN; decrypts back exactly. (c) **This catalogue's own bullet miniature, reproduced.** Primer D, "ATTACKATDAWN" → DTMTCMKTWDWJ; decrypts back exactly — the Oct-20 seed's single example, re-encrypted, not re-asserted. (d) **The crib-drag, reproduced.** Decrypting WMPMMXXAEYHBRYOCA with the guessed word THE slid through the key at offsets 0, 1, 2 gives "dfl tft eta fax yrk", "tii tqt hxu oun fhy", "wfi eqw lrd iku vvw" — exactly Wikipedia's three rows; the wrong alignments read as noise, the right one reads as words. (e) **The cascade, measured.** Guessing THE as plaintext at positions 6–8 reveals the key at 10–12 (key[i+4] = plaintext[i]) — which is THE again — and that decrypts ciphertext 10–12 to OUN, which is the key at 14–16, decrypting to AIN; backwards, the key at 6–8 is ETA, decrypting ciphertext 2–5 to ETA. One three-letter guess reaches 15 of 17 letters; only M@0 and E@1 stay hidden. (f) **Error propagation, measured — and Wikipedia's loose sentence corrected.** Corrupting one ciphertext letter under the 4-letter primer KILT breaks exactly positions 5, 9, 13 — one residue class mod 4, three of seventeen letters, not the remainder. Under Vigenère's single-letter primer D, the same corruption breaks every later letter (positions 5–11) — the stride is the primer length, so "a single mistake renders the rest unintelligible" is true of Vigenère's original and overstated for the keyword form. Flipping one plaintext letter in encryption changes the ciphertext at that position and m positions later (5 and 9 for KILT; only the last letter when the flip is final). (g) **Ciphertext-autokey, same primer, same message.** KILT + MEETATTHEFOUNTAIN → WMPMWFITAKWNNDWVA, a different cipher from (b); one corrupted ciphertext letter damages exactly two plaintext letters (positions 5 and 9) — bounded, because the keystream is built from what arrived, not from what is being recovered.

- **The honest blank.** Five confessions. (1) Vigenère's *Traicté des chiffres* was not opened first-party this pass — the 1586 dating, the ten-alphabet table, and the ff. 46r–49v locus arrive via Wikipedia's article and its references. (2) The "ignored and forgotten, then reinvented in the 1800s" arc is CLAIMED, single textbook carrier via the bullet entry — not re-sourced this pass. (3) Key-autokey is described, not implemented or measured: no keystream-generation rule for it is asserted here. (4) The ACA's autokey solving practice (crib-dragging as actually done by solvers) is carried from Wikipedia's cryptanalysis section, not from the ACA handbook text. (5) One self-caught error this pass — the verify script's first run failed four checks, and three were the script's own wrong expectations (bullet-block count 13 not 8; keystream truncation; encryption-flip stride m not 1); the fourth was the real finding: decryption error propagation runs down one residue class mod m, and the entry now states the measured rule instead of Wikipedia's loose sentence.

- **Decoder-design note (Autokey → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The keystream's parentage is the first question.** A specimen whose key is generated from its own traffic has no period to find — Kasiski and IC are dead on arrival — and the interrogation starts instead with the feedback question: what feeds the keystream, the plaintext, the ciphertext, or the key itself? The parentage decides the whole attack: plaintext-feed gives crib-dragging and the cascade; ciphertext-feed gives bounded damage and no cascade; key-feed gives a generator to price. Name the parent before pricing the key. (2) **Error propagation is the fingerprint of the feed.** Corrupt one symbol and count the damage: one residue class mod m means plaintext-feed with primer length m; exactly two positions means ciphertext-feed; everything after means a single-letter primer or a chained feed. The damage map measures the construction without ever seeing the key — and a specimen that claims a long primer but damages like a short one has confessed its real primer length. (3) **The primer is the whole secret, priced alone.** 26 for one letter, 456,976 for four, 8.03 billion for seven — and the rest of the keystream is the message, which the analyst already has in part the moment any crib lands. A specimen that counts its keystream length as key material is overstating its strength by exactly the message's share; the interrogation prices the primer and treats the rest as known-plaintext waiting to happen.

## The Beaufort cipher (1857) — the admiral's subtraction, or: the cipher that comes home by itself

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero `## ` headings for "Beaufort" in either catalogue, measured this pass — and ninety-four case-insensitive occurrences in the private catalogue against ninety-three in the public, all of them passing mentions or the two bullet entries: the Oct-20 bullet entry carries thirty-seven (lines 2730–2748: heading, invention, mechanism, variant, miniature, weaknesses, design note, grade, seed line), the Oct-27 numbered bullet entry thirty-three (3144–3158), the autokey gap sentence three (10050), the Vigenère numbered entry three (7629), the M-209 numbered entry seven (9154:1, 9156:4, 9164:2), the Slidefair grades four (9892:2, 9894:1, 9900:1), and the remaining seven in the M-209 cage bullet (2285), an Enigma weakness line (2776), the M-209 bullet (2836:2, 2846:1, 2850:1), and the Vigenère bullet lineage (2952). The public catalogue carries the same ninety-three at lines 7341–14523; the single difference is the Enigma weakness line, whose public counterpart carries no Beaufort mention. The shelf around it is fully filed: the whole polyalphabetic family now numbered — Alberti, Trithemius, Bellaso, Vigenère, autokey (#175, this morning), running key, Porta, Gronsfeld, GROMARK — and the subtraction that made the cipher its own mirror never got its own numbered entry. - **The story.** Sir Francis Beaufort (27 May 1774 – 17 December 1857), Irish-born Royal Navy officer, Hydrographer of the Navy 1829–1855 — twenty-six years, longer than anyone before or since — and the man who numbered the wind: the Beaufort scale, written into his journal from 1805. The cipher that carries his name was published after his death in 1857 as a small card titled *Cryptography, A System of Secret Writing*, sold for sixpence in England as a system for sending secret messages by telegraph or by postcard. The name is the family's second misattribution: the construction is credited by secondary sources to the Italian Giovanni Sestri in 1710, a century and a half before Beaufort's card — Beaufort's contribution was the neat, practical, printed form a naval officer could carry. Beaufort himself wrote portions of his own letters and journals in personal cipher; the deciphered writings revealed family and personal problems. The cipher's long life was a life of convenience: the Hagelin M-209 rotor machine embodies the Beaufort principle in brass, and the U.S. National Security Agency's DIANA one-time-pad system — the manual table carried by U.S. Special Forces in Vietnam — is a Beaufort table. [CORROBORATED — the 1774–1857 dates, the 26-year hydrographer tenure, and the personal-cipher correspondence via the Wikipedia Francis Beaufort entry read first-party this pass; the 1857 posthumous sixpenny card and its title via Martin Gardner's *Codes, Ciphers, and Secret Writing* (archive.org first-party text) and the Boxentriq Variant Beaufort history; the Sestri 1710 origin via the vectree and calcoolator Beaufort histories; the M-209 and DIANA deployments via the Wikipedia Beaufort cipher article read first-party this pass]

- **The system.** Two conventions, one cipher — and this entry states both, because confusing them is the one-sign trap at the level of the formula itself. The catalogue's convention, carried from the bullet entry and the CryptoCrack carrier: C = K − P mod 26, Vigenère's addition with the plaintext's sign flipped. Wikipedia's tableau convention, read first-party this pass: C = (51 − K − P) mod 26, i.e. (25 − K − P) mod 26 in 0-indexed letters. The two agree up to Atbash of the key — Beaufort(P, K) = Wiki-Beaufort(P, Atbash(K)) for every letter pair, verified exhaustively this pass — so they are the same system under different key labelling, and a fixture that assumes one and meets the other mislabels every letter while still passing its own round-trip test. Both are reciprocal: K − (K − P) = P, and (25 − K − (25 − K − P)) = P. The Variant Beaufort is the third member: C = P − K, Vigenère's addition with the key's sign flipped instead — not reciprocal, decryption adds the key back. Keyspace 26^n for a key of length n, the same as Vigenère — WIND admits 26^4 = 456,976 keys — and a repeating key still has period n: Kasiski and the index of coincidence apply unchanged, because Beaufort is Vigenère with a sign change and nothing else. [VERIFIED — the two formulas, the Atbash equivalence over all 676 letter pairs, both involutions, and the 26^4 keyspace, computed this pass; CORROBORATED — the tableau procedure and the Variant definition via the Wikipedia Beaufort cipher article and the Boxentriq Variant history read first-party this pass]

- **The worked miniatures (computed this pass).** 29 checks pass in goal hidden_files/verify-beaufort-20261110.py. (a) **The bullet miniature, reproduced.** BEAUFORT under WIND → VENJRUWK; re-enciphered under the same key it returns BEAUFORT exactly — the Oct-27 seed's single example, re-encrypted, not re-asserted. (b) **CryptoCrack's independent example.** Key C, plaintext H → Beaufort V; Variant → F — the one-sign trap in a single letter. (c) **This catalogue's own miniature.** KODAKAI under SEA → IQXSUAK, round trip exact; Variant gives SKDIGAQ, and adding the key back returns KODAKAI. (d) **The A-leak, measured.** K = P at every position gives all A's — KODAKAI under KODAKAI → AAAAAAA — and of the 676 possible (key, plaintext) pairs exactly 26 coincide, so a random Beaufort ciphertext carries an A at ~3.8% of positions that confesses the key letter outright. (e) **The A-column mirror.** Key letter A is Atbash: ABCXYZ under A → AZYDCB, and −P mod 26 holds for every letter — a column keyed by A is a reversed-alphabet column an analyst recognizes on sight. (f) **The period, demonstrated.** Sixteen A's under KEY → KEYKEYKEYKEYKEYK: constant plaintext prints the key in plain sight, period 3, the whole key recovered without analysis. (g) **The convention variance, measured.** Wikipedia's d-under-m example gives K under the tableau formula and J under the bullet formula; the bullet miniature under the tableau formula gives a different ciphertext, and the tableau formula with the Atbash key DMRW reproduces VENJRUWK exactly — the two conventions are one cipher, and the key's spelling is the only difference. (h) **The trigram count, derived — the bullet's carried number, now proven.** Wikipedia's table lists 126 trigrams (AAZ … RRR); every one sums to 25 mod 26 — AAZ, ABY, AMN ("man"), CIP ("pic"), RRR all check — because the Beaufort relation is K + M + C ≡ 25 (mod 26). Enumerated this pass: the sorted triples (a ≤ b ≤ c) number 3,276 in total, and every one of the 26 residues holds exactly 126 of them — 26 × 126 = 3,276 — so the Beaufort residue 25 holds 126, and the count is not a property of the cipher at all but of the alphabet: any residue would hold 126. The operators memorized 126 trigrams because there are only 126 unordered triples to memorize, whichever residue the cipher picks.

- **Decoder-design note (Beaufort → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **Name the convention before you grade the cipher.** Two formulas for one cipher, differing by Atbash of the key: a fixture that assumes C = K − P and meets a specimen running C = 25 − K − P will fail every letter and blame the specimen, when the specimen is Beaufort in the other spelling. The Gauntlet's formula-naming rule, from the bullet entry, is now a standing first probe: state the formula, state the key convention, and run the Atbash-key equivalence check before any grade — a specimen misidentified by one sign is graded against a cipher it never was. (2) **A leak that fires 1 time in 26 is a leak, priced in the open.** The A-leak is not a curiosity: every A in a Beaufort ciphertext is a position where the key is known, and a long message volunteers ~3.8% of its key for free. The Gauntlet's leak ledger prices confession rates, not just confession existence — a 1-in-26 leak over a thousand letters is forty free key letters. (3) **Reciprocity is a usability grade, not a security grade.** Beaufort outlived its security by a century in hand systems — M-209, DIANA — because one table and no direction meant fewer operator errors under fire. The Gauntlet grades deployability on its own ledger, and Beaufort is the standing case: the cipher operators can run correctly under stress survives in the field long after a stronger cipher they fumble is abandoned. The family's arc is now complete in full: disc, recta, countersign, misnamed square, autokey, running key, and the subtraction that made the cipher its own mirror.

- **The story.** Russian Nihilists in the 1880s — revolutionaries organizing terrorism against the tsarist regime — enciphered their traffic with a hand cipher built on a keyed Polybius square. The term later stretched: the article notes it is "sometimes extended to several improved algorithms used much later for communication by the First Chief Directorate with its spies." The descendants are the catalogue's own record: during World War II, several Soviet spy rings communicated to Moscow Centre with ciphers "essentially evolutionary improvements on the basic Nihilist cipher" — a very strong version run by Max Clausen inside Richard Sorge's network in Japan, and by Alexander Foote in the Lucy ring in Switzerland; a slightly weaker version by the Rote Kapelle. The line ends at VIC (1950s), Reino Häyhänen's hand cipher, "the ultimate development along these lines" — by then most Soviet agents were on one-time pads instead. Seventy years from a revolutionary's worksheet to a hollow nickel. [CORROBORATED — the 1880s origin line, the First Chief Directorate extension, and the Clausen/Sorge, Foote/Lucy, and Rote Kapelle deployments via the Wikipedia Nihilist cipher article read first-party this pass; the VIC endpoint via this catalogue's VIC entry]

- **The system.** Build a 5×5 Polybius square from a mixed-alphabet keyword (I/J merged — the square holds twenty-five letters). Convert both the plaintext and the keyword to two-digit row-column numbers, and add them together "in the normal way" — schoolbook arithmetic, no modulus — repeating the key numbers as required. Decryption subtracts the key numbers and reads the square back. The keyspace is the square: 25! = 15,511,210,043,330,985,984,000,000 ≈ 1.55×10²⁵ possible keyed squares (log₁₀ 25.19) — but a keyword-generated square is one choice of keyword, and the key that actually repeats over the message is the short keyword, not the square: RUSSIAN is seven letters over a twenty-letter message, period 7. The cipher's whole security argument is that the ciphertext is numbers, not letters — and its whole weakness is that the arithmetic is ordinary. [VERIFIED — the 25! arithmetic, computed this pass; CORROBORATED — the square-plus-normal-addition mechanism and the repeated-key rule via the Wikipedia article read first-party this pass]

- **The worked miniatures (computed this pass).** 49 checks pass in goal hidden_files/verify-nihilist-20261110.py. (a) **Wikipedia's canonical example, re-encrypted exactly.** ZEBRAS square — Z E B R A / S C D F G / H I K L M / N O P Q T / U V W X Y — plaintext DYNAMITE WINTER PALACE → 23 55 41 15 35 32 45 12 53 32 41 45 12 14 43 15 34 15 22 12; key RUSSIAN → 14 51 21 21 32 15 41, repeated to twenty; ciphertext by normal addition → 37 106 62 36 67 47 86 26 104 53 62 77 27 55 57 66 55 36 54 27 — all twenty sums exactly as printed in the article, and subtraction returns the plaintext exactly. (b) **The leak, measured on the canonical example.** Two of the twenty ciphertext numbers exceed 100 — 106 (Y 55 + U 51) and 104 (W 53 + U 51) — and both are fifth-row + fifth-row pairs, exactly as the article's cryptanalysis states. (c) **The census — the whole arithmetic, enumerated.** Over all 625 (plaintext, key) pairs, the achievable ciphertext sums are 81 of the 89 integers from 22 to 110; the eight that can never occur are 31, 41, 51, 61, 71, 81, 91, 101 — every sum ≡ 1 (mod 10), because each coordinate's digits run 1–5 and no two of them sum to 1 mod 10. Exactly 25 pairs produce a number over 100 (both coordinates from row 5: 5 × 5), and exactly two pairs produce 100 itself (45 + 55 and 55 + 45). The most frequent sum is 66, from 25 pairs. The ciphertext alphabet has holes, and the holes are part of the cipher. (d) **The hardening, run on the same message.** Digit-wise addition mod 10 — the WWII improvement, non-carrying addition — gives 37 06 62 36 67 47 86 26 04 53 62 77 27 55 57 66 55 36 54 27: no value over 100, no value containing the digit 1 anywhere in the census (digits are 1–5 + 1–5 mod 10), maximum 99. The subtract-100 fix gives exactly the same twenty numbers on this message — the two hardenings agree here, and diverge exactly when the units digits carry: 55 + 55 is 00 digit-wise and 10 by subtract-100. (e) **Both bullet miniatures, re-encrypted.** WINTER square, PALACE under FIRE → 74 34 56 37 55 27 (the Oct-20 seed, round trip exact); WINTER square, KODAKAI under SEA → 79 57 47 67 49 44 57 (the Oct-27 seed, round trip exact).

(1) **Enumerate the ciphertext alphabet before attacking the cipher.** The census is the fixture's first measurement for any numeric specimen: which values can occur, which can never occur, which are frequent. A Nihilist specimen that emits a 41 has confessed it is not Nihilist arithmetic — the holes are a free discriminator that costs nothing to check and fires before any key work begins. [VERIFIED — the 0/0 heading counts and the 0/0 mention counts for Hangul in both catalogues, measured this pass; the zero Hangul hits in the research log, TRICKS.md, TESTS.md, UNDECIPHERED.md, CIPHER-TIMELINE.md, and MATH-PHYSICS.md, measured this pass; the 2/1 "Sejong" counts with every hit the university, measured this pass; the 0/0 "featural" counts in both catalogues, measured this pass]

- **The story.** Sejong the Great, fourth king of Joseon (reigned 1418–1450), created the alphabet to give his people writing of their own. Korea wrote in Classical Chinese, with native phonetic systems (Idu, Hyangchal, Gugyeol, Gakpil) alongside — but Chinese characters were so ill-suited to Korean, and so numerous, that only privileged aristocrats (yangban), usually male, could read and write fluently. The alphabet was designed so that people with little education could learn to read and write, and the popular saying about it is the catalogue's cleanest learnability claim: "A wise man can acquaint himself with them before the morning is over; even a stupid man can learn them in the space of ten days." The project was completed in late December 1443 or January 1444 and described in 1446 in the document Hunminjeongeum — "The Correct Sounds for the Instruction of the People" — after which the alphabet itself was originally named; its companion commentary, the Hunminjeongeum Haerye ("Explanation and Examples"), also 1446, was discovered in 1940 and explains the design. The publication date, October 9, became Hangul Day in South Korea; the North's equivalent, Chosŏn'gŭl Day, is January 15. The name Hangul itself came later: coined by the linguist Ju Si-gyeong in 1912 — han, "great", plus geul, "script" — "Korean script". The alphabet faced the elite's opposition from the start: in the 1440s Choe Manri and other Confucian scholars held Hanja the only legitimate writing system and saw the new letters as a threat to their status; the letters entered popular culture anyway, used especially by women and writers of popular fiction. King Yeonsangun banned its study and publication in 1504, after a document criticizing him was published; King Jungjong abolished the Ministry of Eonmun in 1506. It revived with gasa and sijo poetry in the late sixteenth century and novels in the seventeenth; in 1796 the Dutch scholar Isaac Titsingh became the first to bring a Korean book to the Western world, and in 1832 the Oriental Translation Fund published his French translation. Nationalism, the Gabo Reformists, and Western missionaries carried it into official documents for the first time in 1894; school texts followed in 1895 and the Tongnip Sinmun in 1896, the first newspaper printed in Korean and English. After the Japanese annexation of 1910, Japanese became the official language; Korean was still taught in Korean-established schools, and the orthography was standardized in 1912 and again in 1930 — the second reform abolishing the vowel arae-a (ㆍ) — while Ju Si-gyeong's Korean Language Research Society (later the Hangul Society) published its Standardized System of Hangul in 1933. Japan banned Korean from schools in 1938 and outlawed all Korean-language publications in 1941. The definitive modern orthography was published in 1946, just after independence; North Korea's 1948 attempt to make the script perfectly morphophonemic with new letters, and Syngman Rhee's 1953 attempt to simplify it, were both abandoned within a few years; North Korea made Hangul its exclusive writing system in 1949 and banned Hanja completely. Today it is the official writing system of both Koreas and co-official in the Yanbian Korean Autonomous Prefecture and Changbai Korean Autonomous County in Jilin, China; the Hunminjeong'eum Society in Seoul tries to spread it to unwritten languages of Asia, and in 2009 the town of Baubau in Indonesia unofficially adopted it to write Cia-Cia — an attempt confirmed failed in October 2012. - **The system.** The letters are called jamo (자모). Modern orthography uses 24 basic letters: 14 consonants (ㄱ ㄴ ㄷ ㄹ ㅁ ㅂ ㅅ ㅇ ㅈ ㅊ ㅋ ㅌ ㅍ ㅎ) and 10 vowels (ㅏ ㅑ ㅓ ㅕ ㅗ ㅛ ㅜ ㅠ ㅡ ㅣ), plus 27 complex letters formed by combining them: 5 tense consonants (ㄲ ㄸ ㅃ ㅆ ㅉ), 11 complex consonants (ㄳ ㄵ ㄶ ㄺ ㄻ ㄼ ㄽ ㄾ ㄿ ㅀ ㅄ), and 11 complex vowels (ㅐ ㅒ ㅔ ㅖ ㅘ ㅙ ㅚ ㅝ ㅞ ㅟ ㅢ). Four letters of the original alphabet are gone: the vowel arae-a (ㆍ) and three consonants (ㅿ ㆁ ㆆ) — so the original count was 28, seventeen consonants and eleven vowels. The design is featural, and the Haerye says so in so many words: the five basic consonants diagram the speech organs — ㄱ is a side view of the back of the tongue raised toward the velum, ㄴ the tip of the tongue at the alveolar ridge, ㅁ the outline of the lips, ㅅ the teeth, ㅇ the throat — and the rest are derived by added strokes: aspiration (ㄱ→ㅋ, ㅈ→ㅊ, ㄷ→ㅌ, ㅂ→ㅍ), firm contact (ㄴ→ㄷ, ㅅ→ㅈ), release (ㅁ→ㅂ), doubling for tenseness (ㄱ→ㄲ). The letter ㅌ is the design in miniature: three strokes, each meaningful — the bottom stroke is alveolar like ㄴ ㄷ ㄹ, the middle is aspiration like ㅎ ㅋ ㅊ, the top is a plosive like ㄱ ㄷ ㅈ. The vowels are built from three elements: a horizontal line for the flat Earth, the essence of yin; a point for the Sun in the heavens, the essence of yang (a short stroke under the brush); a vertical line for the upright Human, mediator between Heaven and Earth — and the combinations give the rest: bright ㅗ ㅏ against dark ㅜ ㅓ, iotization by doubling the dot (ㅏ→ㅑ, ㅓ→ㅕ, ㅗ→ㅛ, ㅜ→ㅠ), and the compounds ㅘ = ㅗ+ㅏ, ㅝ = ㅜ+ㅓ, ㅐ = ㅏ+ㅣ. There is no letter for w or y: w is always analyzable as o or u before a or eo, and y is the doubled dot. The letters were named by Choe Sejin in 1527 (Hunmongjahoe): giyeok, nieun, digeut, rieul, mieum, bieup, siot, ieung, jieut, chieut, kieuk, tieut, pieup, hieuh. Letters are written in syllabic blocks — initial (choseong 초성), medial (jungseong 중성), and optionally final (jongseong 종성, the batchim 받침, "supporting floor") — so 한글 is spelled as blocks, not as the linear ㅎㅏㄴㄱㅡㄹ. A syllable with no initial consonant takes the null ㅇ as placeholder. Nineteen initials, twenty-one medials, twenty-seven non-empty finals (plus none): 11,172 possible blocks, and the block is written in a square the size of a Hanja character. In Unicode, the 11,172 precomposed syllables make up the Hangul Syllables block (U+AC00–U+D7A3); the jamo live at U+1100–U+11FF, U+3130–U+318F, U+A960–U+A97F, and U+D7B0–U+D7FF; its ISO 15924 code is Hang (286). The old names carry the politics: the elite called Hanja jinseo, "true letters", and supporters called the new script jeong'eum, "correct pronunciation", gungmun, "national script", and eonmun, "vernacular script". - **The story.** The Phoenician script is an abjad — a consonantal alphabet — used across the Mediterranean civilization of Phoenicia for most of the 1st millennium BC: 22 consonant letters, no vowels, written right to left. It was one of the first alphabets, and the first to have a fixed writing direction — while previous systems were multi-directional, Phoenician was written horizontally, right to left. It developed directly from the Proto-Sinaitic script of the Late Bronze Age, which was derived in turn from Egyptian hieroglyphs — but it was not invented by the Phoenicians: as Krahmalkov puts it, it was an adaptation of the early West Semitic alphabet to the needs of their own language, and the Phoenicians' contribution was the fixed form and the spread. The inscriptions on the Phoenician arrowheads at al-Khader near Bethlehem, dated c. 1100 BC, gave epigraphists the "missing link" between Proto-Canaanite and Phoenician. The Ahiram epitaph — engraved on the sarcophagus of King Ahiram in Byblos, one of five known Byblian royal inscriptions, its dating controversial — shows essentially the fully developed Phoenician script, and the name "Phoenician" is by convention given to inscriptions beginning in the mid-11th century BC. The conventional date of 1050 BC for the emergence of the script was chosen because there is a gap in the epigraphic record: there are not actually any Phoenician inscriptions securely dated to the 11th century, and the oldest inscriptions are dated to the 10th century. The Zayit Stone, 10th century BC, carries five letters in a row — waw, he, het, zayin, tet (𐤅𐤄𐤇𐤆𐤈) — the alphabet already fixed in its order. Beginning in the 9th century BC, adaptations thrived: Greek, Old Italic, and Anatolian scripts. The alphabet's attractive innovation was its phonetic nature — one sound, one symbol, only a few dozen symbols to learn — where cuneiform and Egyptian hieroglyphs employed many complex characters and required long professional training, which had restricted literacy to a small elite. The other reason was the maritime trading culture of Phoenician merchants, which spread the alphabet into North Africa and Southern Europe; inscriptions have been found at Byblos, Carthage, and across the Mediterranean basin. The simplicity let the common people learn to write, which upset the long-standing status of literacy as the exclusive achievement of royal and religious elites — scribes who used their monopoly on information to control the common population — and the appearance of Phoenician disintegrated many of those class divisions, although Assyria, Babylonia, and Adiabene would continue to use cuneiform for legal and liturgical matters well into the Common Era. According to Herodotus, the Phoenician prince Cadmus was accredited with introducing the Phoenician alphabet — *phoinikeia grammata*, "Phoenician letters" — to the Greeks, who adapted it to form their Greek alphabet; Herodotus claims the Greeks did not know of the Phoenician alphabet before Cadmus, and estimates that Cadmus lived 1,600 years before his time, while the historical adoption by the Greeks was barely 350 years before Herodotus. The Phoenician alphabet was known to the Jewish sages of the Second Temple era, who called it the "Old Hebrew" (Paleo-Hebrew) script. The Phoenician alphabet proper was used in Ancient Carthage until the 2nd century BC, when it was used to write Punic, and it became obsolete with the destruction of Carthage in 146 BC — cursive forms had increased over time, culminating in the Neo-Punic alphabet of Roman North Africa. The script was deciphered in 1758 by Jean-Jacques Barthélemy, from the Cippi of Melqart, the coins, and the Pococke Kition inscriptions — but its relation to the Phoenicians remained unknown until the 19th century, and it was at first believed to be a direct variation of Egyptian hieroglyphs, which Champollion deciphered in the early 19th century. Lebanon's inscribed objects, assembled by the General Directorate of Antiquities and displayed in the National Museum of Beirut, formed the basis of a nomination of the Phoenician alphabet to the Memory of the World International Register; UNESCO accepted the nomination in 2005, recognising the alphabet as documentary heritage of global importance. - **The system.** Twenty-two letters, in a fixed order that every descendant kept. The letters are acrophonic: each name is a word that begins with the letter's own sound, so the key is the vocabulary. 𐤀 Alp, "ox, head of cattle", [ʔ]; 𐤁 Bet, "house", [b]; 𐤂 Gaml, "throwing stick (or camel)", [ɡ]; 𐤃 Dalt, "door (or fish)", [d]; 𐤄 He, "window", [h]; 𐤅 Waw, "hook", [w]; 𐤆 Zen, "weapon", [z]; 𐤇 Het, "courtyard/wall (?)", [ħ]; 𐤈 Tet, "wheel", [tʼ]; 𐤉 Yod, "arm, hand", [j]; 𐤊 Kap, "palm of a hand", [k]; 𐤋 Lamd, "goad", [l]; 𐤌 Mem, "water", [m]; 𐤍 Nun, "serpent (or fish)", [n]; 𐤎 Samk, "pillar(?)", [s]; 𐤏 En, "eye", [ʕ]; 𐤐 Pe, "mouth (or corner)", [p]; 𐤑 Sade, "papyrus plant/fish hook?", [t͡sʼ]; 𐤒 Qop, "monkey/needle", [kʼ]; 𐤓 Rosh, "head", [r]; 𐤔 Shin, "tooth (or sun)", [ʃ]; 𐤕 Taw, "mark", [t]. The letters were originally incised with a stylus, so their forms are mostly angular and straight. As an abjad used to write a Semitic language, it leaves vowel sounds implicit — though late varieties sometimes used *matres lectionis* to denote some vowels — and the cuneiform that wrote a related Semitic language did indicate vowels, which suggests the Phoenicians simply accepted the model of the Egyptians, who never wrote vowels. The order is the ancestor of every abjad order after it: Hebrew alef bet gimel dalet he vav zayin het tet yod kaf lamed mem nun samekh ayin pe tsade qof resh shin tav is the same twenty-two in the same sequence, and Greek alpha beta gamma delta epsilon digamma zeta eta theta iota kappa lambda mu nu xi omicron pi san qoppa rho sigma tau keeps the order while repurposing the letters Greek did not need as consonants. The repurposing is the second invention: each such letter had its name shorn of its leading consonant, and the letter took the value of the now-leading vowel — *alp*, a glottal stop, became /a/; *he* became /e/; *het* became /eː/; *en* became /o/ (because the pharyngeality altered the following vowel); the two semi-consonants *waw* and *yod* became the high vowels /u/ and /i/. (Some dialects of Greek, which did possess /h/ and /w/, continued to use the Phoenician letters for those consonants as well.) The Ionic variant evolved into the standard Greek alphabet, and the Cumae variant into the Italic alphabets, including Latin. The Runic alphabet is derived from Italic; the Cyrillic alphabet from medieval Greek, with some letters based on Glagolitic forms. The Hebrew, Syriac, and Arabic scripts are derived from Aramaic — Arabic as a medieval cursive variant of Nabataean — and Ge'ez is from South Arabian. The Coptic alphabet is mostly the mature Greek alphabet of the Hellenistic period, with a few additional letters for sounds not in Greek at the time, based on Demotic. The Paleohispanic scripts — the indigenous semisyllabaries of Tartessian, Iberian, and Celtiberian — were deciphered in 1922 by Manuel Gómez-Moreno; Gómez-Moreno first pointed to a joined Phoenician-Greek origin, and following authors consider their genesis to have no relation to Greek. The notable inscriptions, by their KAI numbers: KAI 1, the Ahiram sarcophagus, Byblos, c. 1000 BC; KAI 14, the sarcophagus of Eshmunazar II, 5th century BC; KAI 15–16, the Bodashtart inscriptions, 4th century BC; KAI 24, the Kilamuwa Stela, 9th century BC; KAI 46, the Nora Stone, c. 800 BC; KAI 47, the Cippi of Melqart inscription, 2nd century BC; KAI 26, the Karatepe bilingual, 8th century BC; KAI 277, the Pyrgi Tablets, Phoenician-Etruscan bilingual, c. 500 BC; and the Çineköy inscription, Phoenician-Luwian bilingual, 8th century BC. The script's Unicode home is U+10900–U+1091F, ISO 15924 Phnx (115): 22 letters at U+10900–U+10915, six numerals — 𐤖 1, 𐤗 10, 𐤘 20, 𐤙 100, 𐤚 2, 𐤛 3 — at U+10916–U+1091B, and the word separator 𐤟 at U+1091F. (7) **The timeline.** 904 years of use, 1050 to 146 BC; 3,076 years from the conventional start to this entry; 2,758 years from the Ahiram sarcophagus (c. 1000 BC) to the 1758 decipherment — the alphabet unread for nearly three millennia; 268 years from decipherment to this entry; 21 years since the 2005 UNESCO recognition; 50 years from the al-Khader arrowheads (c. 1100 BC) to the conventional 1050 BC start; about 2,876 years from the Greek adoption (c. 850 BC) to this entry; 1,904 years from the fall of Carthage to Barthélemy's reading. (8) **The Greek repurposing census.** 6 of 22 letters became vowels (alp→a, he→e, het→ē, en→o, waw→u, yod→i); 16 stayed consonants — the vowels were not added, they were *found*, by shaving the consonant off the front of a name. (10) **The order check.** The Phoenician order matches the Hebrew order name for name across all 22, and the Greek order keeps the same 22 positions — alpha is alp's slot, epsilon is he's, eta is het's, omicron is en's, and digamma sits in waw's slot, the consonant Greek kept where it needed one. - **The honest blank.** Eleven confessions. (1) The 1050 BC date is conventional, not observed: it was chosen because there is a gap in the epigraphic record, and no Phoenician inscription is securely dated to the 11th century — the oldest are 10th century. (2) The Ahiram epitaph's dating is controversial, per the article's own hedge — the "fully developed" reading rests on a contested date. (3) "Invented by the Phoenicians" is wrong, per Krahmalkov as the article carries him: it was an adaptation of the early West Semitic alphabet, and the Phoenicians' contribution was the fixed form and the spread — the ancestor was itself a borrower. (4) Nine letter meanings carry the article's own question marks or alternatives — Het "courtyard/wall (?)", Samk "pillar(?)", Sade "papyrus plant/fish hook?", Qop "monkey/needle", Gaml "throwing stick (or camel)", Dalt "door (or fish)", Nun "serpent (or fish)", Pe "mouth (or corner)", Shin "tooth (or sun)" — the meanings are reconstructions, and the (?) is the article's, not this entry's. (5) Tet's wheel is a later glyph reading: the note says the glyph was taken to represent a wheel, but it possibly derives from the *nefer* hieroglyph and would originally have been called *tab*, "good" — the name and the picture disagree, and the entry carries both. (6) Nun's name and glyph disagree too: the name *nūn* is a word for "fish", but the glyph is presumably from the depiction of a snake, which would point to an original name *naḥash*, "snake" — the fish is the later name, the snake the earlier picture. (7) The ṣade name may be from *ṣd*, "to hunt" — a third name that might not mean what the table says. (8) He and ḥet continue *three* Proto-Sinaitic letters — *ḥasir* "courtyard", *hillul* "jubilation", and *ḫayt* "thread" — and the shapes and names crossed: the shape of *ḥet* continues *ḥasir* but the name continues *ḫayt*, while the shape of *he* continues *hillul* but the name means "window" — two letters built from three, with the wires crossed in the middle. (9) The Runic origin is disputed among three theories — Latin itself, some early Old Italic alphabet via the Alpine scripts, or Greek — and the article settles only that all three trace back to Phoenician; the path is unsettled, and this entry does not pick one. (10) Libyco-Berber as a child system carries a question mark in the infobox — the descent is uncertain, and the table's empty Libyco-Berber cells for most letters say the same. (11) The Cadmus story is Herodotus's telling, and his 1,600-year estimate is off by about 1,250 years against the roughly 350-year adoption the article dates — the founder is a story, not a date, and the entry carries him as told. - **Decoder-design note (Phoenician → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The alphabet that leaves the vowels out.** A specimen that omits information and still communicates is interrogated by its omissions: what it leaves out tells you what its readers already know. A code that omits vowels assumes a reader who speaks the language; a specimen whose omissions assume knowledge the interrogator lacks is hiding its key in the reader, not in the text — and the Gauntlet's missing-information probe asks what a specimen needs its reader to already know, because that need is the specimen's confession of its audience. (2) **The key is the vocabulary.** Every letter's name begins with its own sound — alp is ʔ because the word for ox starts with ʔ — so the key is not a table, it is the language itself. The Gauntlet's name probe asks a specimen to name its own parts and checks whether the names are the key: a specimen whose names encode their own values confesses its key to anyone who learns the names, and a specimen whose names are arbitrary is hiding its key behind a table somebody else must supply. (3) **The descent probe.** Twenty-two letters became every Western alphabet — the descendants are the specimen's confession. Trace what a specimen's children kept and what they changed: the parts every child kept are the load-bearing parts, and the parts every child changed are the accidents of one language. Greek kept the order and shaved six consonants into vowels; Hebrew kept the order and the consonants; Latin kept the order through two hand-offs. A specimen with no descendants has no descent evidence — and a specimen whose descendants all changed the same thing was wrong in the same place. - **The story.** The Georgian scripts are the three writing systems used to write the Georgian language: Asomtavruli, Nuskhuri, and Mkhedruli. Although the systems differ in appearance, their letters share the same names and alphabetical order and are written horizontally from left to right. Of the three, Mkhedruli — once the official script of the Kingdom of Georgia and mostly used for the royal charters — is now the standard script for modern Georgian and its related Kartvelian languages (Mingrelian, Svan, Bats, and Laz), whereas Asomtavruli and Nuskhuri are used only by the Georgian Orthodox Church, in ceremonial religious texts and iconography. Georgian scripts are unique in their appearance and their exact origin has never been established; in strictly structural terms, their alphabetical order largely corresponds to the Greek alphabet, with the exception of letters denoting uniquely Georgian sounds, which are grouped at the end. Originally consisting of 38 letters, Georgian is presently written in a 33-letter alphabet, as five letters are obsolete. The "living culture of three writing systems of the Georgian alphabet" was granted the national status of intangible cultural heritage in Georgia in 2015 and inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2016 (reference 01205). The origin of the Georgian script is poorly known, and no full agreement exists among Georgian and non-Georgian scholars as to when the script was created, who designed it, and the main influences on that process. The first attested version is Asomtavruli, which dates back to the 5th century; the other scripts were formed in the following centuries. Most scholars link the creation to the Christianization of Iberia, a core Georgian kingdom of Kartli: the alphabet was therefore most probably created between the conversion of Iberia under King Mirian III (326 or 337) and the Bir el Qutt inscriptions of 430, and it was first used for translation of the Bible and other Christian literature into Georgian, by monks in Georgia and Palestine. The oldest Asomtavruli inscriptions found so far date from the 5th century and are Bir el Qutt and the Bolnisi inscriptions. Professor Levan Chilashvili's dating of fragmented Asomtavruli inscriptions, discovered by him at the ruined town of Nekresi in the 1980s, to the 2nd or 1st century BC has not been accepted. A Georgian tradition first attested in the medieval chronicle *Lives of the Kings of Kartli* (c. 800) assigns a much earlier, pre-Christian origin to the alphabet and names King Pharnavaz I (3rd century BC) as its inventor; this account is now considered legendary and is rejected by scholarly consensus, as no archaeological confirmation has been found. Scholars such as Tamaz Gamkrelidze, A. Potskhishvili, and Z. Sarjveladze suggested the Pharnavaz account should be understood as the introduction of alloglottography in foreign scripts: Gamkrelidze argues Pharnavaz introduced writing on the basis of Aramaic script — the text synchronically translated from Georgian and written down in Aramaic by a specialist — while Potskhishvili argues Greek graphics were used instead. Another point of contention is the role of Armenian clerics: according to medieval Armenian sources and a number of scholars, Mesrop Mashtots, generally acknowledged as the creator of the Armenian alphabet, also allegedly created the Georgian and Caucasian Albanian alphabets. This tradition originates in the works of Koryun, a fifth-century historian and biographer of Mashtots, and has been quoted by Donald Rayfield and James R. Russell, but has been rejected by Georgian scholarship and some Western scholars who judge the passage in Koryun unreliable or even a later interpolation. The Armenian linguist Hrachia Acharian strongly defended Koryun as a reliable source and dated the invention to 408, four years after Mashtots created the Armenian alphabet (which he dated to 404). Ivane Javakhishvili concluded the Mashtots-creation version is a VI–VII century addition; the 5th-century Armenian historian Ghazar Parpetsi considers Mashtots the creator of only the Armenian alphabet; and Gamkrelidze argues a thorough linguistic analysis would have been necessary to create a new writing system for the language, while Mashtots did not know Georgian. Scholars have debated whether the alphabet was inspired more by the Greek alphabet or by Semitic alphabets such as Aramaic; recent historiography focuses on greater similarities with the Greek alphabet than in the other Caucasian writing systems, most notably the order and numeric value of letters. Some scholars have also suggested certain pre-Christian Georgian cultural symbols or clan markers as a possible inspiration for particular letters. Asomtavruli — the name means "capital letters", from *aso* "letter" and *mtavari* "principal/head", also known as Mrgvlovani "rounded" — is the oldest script, and despite its name this "capital" script is unicameral. From the 9th century, Nuskhuri started becoming dominant and Asomtavruli's role was reduced, though epigraphic monuments of the 10th to 18th centuries continued to be written in it, and in the majority of 9th-century manuscripts written in Nuskhuri, Asomtavruli was used for titles and the first letters of chapters; some manuscripts written completely in Asomtavruli can be found until the 11th century. In early Asomtavruli the letters are of equal height; Georgian historian and philologist Pavle Ingorokva believes the direction, like that of Greek, was initially boustrophedon, though the direction of the earliest surviving texts is from left to the right. In most Asomtavruli letters, straight lines are horizontal or vertical and meet at right angles; the only letter with acute angles is Ⴟ (*jani*). From the 7th century, the forms of some letters began to change and the equal height was abandoned, with letters acquiring ascenders and descenders. Coins of Queen Tamar of Georgia and King George IV of Georgia minted using Asomtavruli script date to 1200–1210 AD. Nuskhuri — the name comes from *nuskha*, meaning "inventory" or "schedule" — is the second script; soon augmented with Asomtavruli illuminated capitals in religious manuscripts, the combination is called Khutsuri, "clerical", from *khutsesi* "cleric", and was principally used in hagiography. Nuskhuri first appeared in the 9th century as a graphic variant of Asomtavruli; the oldest inscription is found in the Ateni Sioni Church and dates to 835 AD, and the oldest surviving Nuskhuri manuscripts date to 864 AD. Nuskhuri becomes dominant over Asomtavruli from the 10th century. Mkhedruli — literally "cavalry" or "military", from *mkhedari* meaning "horseman", "knight", "warrior" — is the third and current script. It first appears in the 10th century; the oldest Mkhedruli inscription is found in Ateni Sioni Church dating back to 982 AD, and the second oldest Mkhedruli-written text is found in the 11th-century royal charters of King Bagrat IV of Georgia. Mkhedruli was mostly used then in the Kingdom of Georgia for the royal charters, historical documents, manuscripts, and inscriptions, and was used for non-religious purposes only — the "civil", "royal", and "secular" script. It became more and more dominant over the two other scripts, though Khutsuri was used until the 19th century, and Mkhedruli became the universal writing system outside of the Church in the 19th century with the establishment and development of printed Georgian fonts. Asomtavruli is used intensively in iconography, murals, and exterior design, especially in stone engravings; Georgian linguist Akaki Shanidze made an attempt in the 1950s to introduce Asomtavruli into the Mkhedruli script as capital letters to begin sentences, as in the Latin script, but it did not catch on. Asomtavruli and Nuskhuri are officially used by the Georgian Orthodox Church alongside Mkhedruli, and Patriarch Ilia II of Georgia called on people to use all three Georgian scripts. The Georgian letter ⟨ვ⟩ is on the Wikipedia logo (lower left), and the Alphabetic Tower stands on the panorama of Georgia's port city of Batumi. - **The system.** Thirty-three letters, in a fixed order that all three scripts keep. The modern Mkhedruli alphabet: ა *ani* /ɑ/, ბ *bani* /b/, გ *gani* /ɡ/, დ *doni* /d/, ე *eni* /ɛ/, ვ *vini* /v/, ზ *zeni* /z/, თ *tani* /t/, ი *ini* /i/, კ *k'ani* /kʼ/, ლ *lasi* /l/, მ *mani* /m/, ნ *nari* /n/, ო *oni* /ɔ/, პ *p'ari* /pʼ/, ჟ *zhani* /ʒ/, რ *rae* /r/, ს *sani* /s/, ტ *t'ari* /tʼ/, უ *uni* /u/, ფ *pari* /p/, ქ *kani* /k/, ღ *ghani* /ɣ/, ყ *q'ari* /qʼ/, შ *shini* /ʃ/, ჩ *chini* /tʃ/, ც *tsani* /ts/, ძ *dzili* /dz/, წ *ts'ili* /tsʼ/, ჭ *ch'ari* /tʃʼ/, ხ *khani* /χ/, ჯ *jani* /dʒ/, ჰ *hae* /h/. Five vowels — ა ე ი ო უ — and twenty-eight consonants, including the ejective series კ პ ტ წ ჭ and the gutturals ღ ყ ხ. The letters double as numerals, in the Greek manner: ა=1, ბ=2, გ=3, დ=4, ე=5, ვ=6, ზ=7, თ=9, ი=10, კ=20, ლ=30, მ=40, ნ=50, ო=70, პ=80, ჟ=90, რ=100, ს=200, ტ=300, უ=400, ფ=500, ქ=600, ღ=700, ყ=800, შ=900, ჩ=1000, ც=2000, ძ=3000, წ=4000, ჭ=5000, ხ=6000, ჯ=8000, ჰ=9000 — and the obsolete letters hold the slots the modern alphabet dropped: ჱ *he* = 8, ჲ *hie* = 60, ჳ *vie* = 400 (the same value as უ), ჴ *qari* = 7000, ჵ *hoe* = 10000. The Society for the Spreading of Literacy among Georgians, founded by Prince Ilia Chavchavadze in 1879, discarded those five letters, which had become redundant: ჱ /e̞j/ was equivalent to ეჲ *ey*; ჲ /j/ appeared for the sound /j/ after a vowel but was dropped from the pronunciation and abolished from the spelling; ჳ /wi~vi/ came to be pronounced the same as ვი *vi* and was replaced by that sequence; ჴ /q/ came to be pronounced the same as ხ *khani* and was replaced by it; ჵ /oː/ was used for the interjection *hoi!* and is now spelled ჰოი, and is also used in Bats for the /ʕ/ or /ɦ/ sound. All but ჵ continue to be used in the Svan alphabet; ჲ is used in the Mingrelian and Laz alphabets as well, for the y-sound /j/. The number of Georgian letters used in other Kartvelian languages varies: Mingrelian uses 36 (the thirty-three current letters, one obsolete letter, and two additional letters specific to Mingrelian and Svan); Laz uses the same 33 plus that same obsolete letter and a letter borrowed from Greek, for a total of 35; Svan, when written, uses Georgian letters as utilized in Mingrelian, with an additional obsolete letter and sometimes diacritics for its many vowels. Mkhedruli has been adapted to languages besides Georgian, and some alphabets retained obsolete letters while others acquired additional ones: ჶ *fi* is used in Laz and Svan, and formerly in Ossetian and Abkhaz, for foreign names, and derives from the Greek letter Φ; ჷ *shva* is used for the schwa sound in Svan and Mingrelian, and formerly in Ossetian and Abkhaz; ჸ *elifi* is used for the glottal stop in Svan and Mingrelian and in the Tushetian dialect of Georgian, and is a reversed ⟨ყ⟩; ჹ *turned gani* was once used for [ɢ] in evangelical literature in Dagestanian languages; ჼ *modifier nar* is used in Bats and nasalizes the preceding vowel; ჺ *aini* is occasionally used for [ʕ] in Bats and derives from the Arabic letter ⟨ع⟩; ჽ *aen* was used in Ossetian, pronounced [ə]; ჾ *hard sign* was used in Abkhaz for velarization of the preceding consonant; ჿ *labial sign* was used in Abkhaz for labialization of the preceding consonant. The script was used for still more languages: Abkhaz until the 1940s, Circassian, Ingush, Chechen, and Avar historically, Ossetian until the 1940s, Persian, Armenian, Russian, and Turkish, and Azerbaijani used by Azeris in Georgia. In handwriting, only four letters are x-height, with neither ascenders nor descenders — ა, თ, ი, ო — thirteen have ascenders (ბ, ზ, მ, ნ, პ, რ, ს, შ, ჩ, ძ, წ, ხ, ჰ), thirteen have descenders (გ, დ, ე, ვ, კ, ლ, ჟ, ტ, უ, ფ, ღ, ყ, ც), and three have both ascenders and descenders (ქ, ჭ, and, in handwriting, ჯ; წ sometimes has both in handwriting). Several letters are similar and may be confused at first, especially in handwriting: ვ and კ differ by whether the top is a full arc or a vertical line; ვ and გ by whether the bottom is an open curve or a closed loop, as with უ and შ, and similarly ს and ხ; კ and პ by whether the letter is written below or above x-height and whether it is written top-down or bottom-up — and in Mtavruli, all letters have the same height and vertical positioning, so those differences disappear, and Კ and Პ can only be distinguished by the length and slight curving of the upper stroke; მ and ძ differ by ძ's vertical top. Mkhedruli is potentially a bicameral script, with capital letters called Mkhedruli Mtavruli, or simply Mtavruli: nowadays Mtavruli is only used in all-caps text in titles or to emphasize a word, though in the late 19th and early 20th centuries it was occasionally used, as in Latin and Cyrillic scripts, to capitalize proper nouns or the first word of a sentence, and contemporary Georgian script does not recognize capital letters — their usage has become decorative. Asomtavruli is often highly stylized, with ligatures, intertwined letters, and letters placed within letters; Nuskhuri likewise, with abbreviations for *nomina sacra* including diacritics called *karagma*, which resemble *titla* — abbreviating was a practical measure, widespread in manuscripts and hagiography by the 11th century, because writing materials such as vellum were scarce and precious; and Mkhedruli, in the 11th to 17th centuries, also came to employ digraphs to the point that they were obligatory. In punctuation, clusters of one, two, three, and six dots were introduced by Ephrem Mtsire in the 10th century to indicate increasing breaks in the text — one dot a minor stop, two dots special words, three dots a bigger stop, six dots the end of the sentence; starting in the 11th century, marks resembling the apostrophe and comma came into use, an apostrophe marking an interrogative word and a comma appearing at the end of an interrogative sentence; from the 12th century on, these were replaced with the semicolon (the Greek question mark); in the 18th century, Patriarch Anton I of Georgia reformed the system again, with commas, single dots, and double dots used to mark "complete", "incomplete", and "final" sentences; for the most part, Georgian today uses the punctuation as in international usage of the Latin script. The first Georgian script was included in Unicode Standard in October 1991 with the release of version 1.0; in creating the Georgian Unicode block, important roles were played by German Jost Gippert, a linguist of Kartvelian studies, and American-Irish linguist and script-encoder Michael Everson, who created the Georgian Unicode for the Macintosh systems, with significant contributions also made by Anton Dumbadze and Irakli Garibashvili. Georgian Mkhedruli script received an official status for being Georgia's internationalized domain name script for (.გე). Mtavruli letters were added in Unicode version 11.0 in June 2018; they are capital letters with similar letterforms to Mkhedruli, but with descenders shifted above the baseline, with a wider central oval, and with the top slightly higher than the ascender height. Georgian characters are found in three Unicode blocks: Georgian (U+10A0–U+10FF), where Mkhedruli occupies U+10D0–U+10FF and Asomtavruli U+10A0–U+10CF; Georgian Supplement (U+2D00–U+2D2F), which contains Nuskhuri; and Georgian Extended (U+1C90–U+1CBF), which contains the Mtavruli capitals. Mtavruli is defined as the upper case, but not title case, of Mkhedruli, and Asomtavruli as the upper case and title case of Nuskhuri. The script's ISO 15924 codes are Geor (240) for Georgian (Mkhedruli and Mtavruli) and Geok (241) for Khutsuri (Asomtavruli and Nuskhuri). Online, the Georgian letter ⟨ღ⟩ (*ghani*) is often used as a love or heart symbol, and ⟨ლ⟩ (*lasi*) is sometimes used as a hand or fist in emoticons. - **The honest blank.** Eleven confessions. (1) The origin is unknown, per the article's own opening: no full agreement exists among Georgian and non-Georgian scholars as to when the script was created, who designed it, and the main influences on that process — the entry carries three rival births and settles none of them. (2) The Pharnavaz account is legendary and rejected by scholarly consensus, with no archaeological confirmation — the entry carries him as told, in the *Lives of the Kings of Kartli* c. 800, not as a date. (3) The alloglottography reading of Pharnavaz is Gamkrelidze's argument, not a finding — and Potskhishvili's Greek-graphics alternative sits beside it, unresolved. (4) The Mashtots tradition rests on a passage in Koryun that Georgian scholarship and some Western scholars judge unreliable or even a later interpolation; Acharian's defence and his 408 date are his, Javakhishvili calls the version a VI–VII century addition, and Ghazar Parpetsi gives Mashtots only the Armenian alphabet. (5) Chilashvili's Nekresi dating to the 2nd or 1st century BC has not been accepted — the 430 floor stands. (6) The boustrophedon beginning is Ingorokva's belief; the earliest surviving texts run left to right, and the belief is the article's, not this entry's. (7) Jani's origin as a monogram of Christ, from ini and kani, is Machavariani's belief; and Pataridze's reading of its cross-like shape as the end of the alphabet carries the article's own caveat — Phoenician taw, Greek chi, and Latin X do not have that function in Phoenician, Greek, or Latin. (8) The "uniquely Georgian sounds grouped at the end" claim is structural: the evidence the article offers is the order and the numeric values, and the thousands break the Greek parallel — they run on Georgian-only letters, so the parallel proves the first 900 and stops there. (9) The numeral system has a duplicate — ჳ and უ both carry 400 — and the article notes it without saying which one a scribe used; the entry counts both and does not resolve the collision. (10) The five discarded letters' fates are dated to the 1879 reform, but the mergers that made them redundant (ჳ pronounced as ვი, ჴ as ხ) are not dated — the discard is an event, the mergers are a drift. (11) Mtavruli is only "potentially" a bicameral script — the article hedges, contemporary Georgian does not recognize capitals, and the 19th-century capitalization use is described as occasional. - **The story.** Tifinagh is a script used to write the Berber languages (Tamazight), descended from the ancient Libyco-Berber alphabet. Its infobox reads: script type abjad; period 6th century BCE; direction right-to-left, left-to-right, vertical writing, bottom-to-top; languages Berber; parent systems Egyptian hieroglyphs, Proto-Sinaitic, Phoenician alphabet with a question mark, Libyco-Berber alphabet; child system Neo-Tifinagh (20th century); ISO 15924 Tfng (120), Tifinagh (Berber); Unicode range U+2D30–U+2D7F. The traditional Tifinagh, sometimes called Tuareg Tifinagh, is still used by the Tuareg people of the Sahara — in southern Algeria, northeastern Mali, northern Niger, and northern Burkina Faso — for writing the Tuareg languages. Neo-Tifinagh, developed by the Berber Academy in the 1970s, is an alphabet that adapts Tuareg Tifinagh for broader use across North Africa, particularly for Kabyle and other Berber dialects. Tifinagh is one of three major competing Berber orthographies alongside the Latin and the Arabic alphabets, but outside of symbolic or cultural uses, the Latin script remains dominant for writing Berber languages in North Africa. The word *tifinagh* (singular *tafinəq*, from *ta-finəɣ-t*) is thought by some scholars to be a Berberized feminine plural cognate or adaptation of the Latin word *Punicus*, "Punic, Phoenician", through the Berber feminine prefix *ti-* and the root √FNƔ from √PNQ — so *tifinagh* could possibly mean "the Phoenician (letters)" or "the Punic letters". Others support an etymology involving the Tuareg verb *efnegh*, "to write". These are not mutually exclusive, however, as the Libyco-Berber concept of writing being borrowed from the Phoenicians has wide support among linguists and archaeologists. Before or during the ancient Berber kingdoms of Numidia (northern Algeria) and Mauretania (northern Morocco), between 202 BCE and 25 BCE, many inscriptions were engraved using the Libyco-Berber script, also known as Ancient Libyan, found in thousands of stone inscriptions and engravings throughout Morocco, northern Algeria, Tunisia, northern Libya, and the Canary Islands. The exact evolution of both Libyco-Berber and Tifinagh is still unclear. The latter writing system was widely used in antiquity by speakers of the largely undeciphered Numidian language, also called Old Libyan, throughout Africa and on the Canary Islands. The script's origin is uncertain, with some scholars suggesting it is related to, descended or developed from the Phoenician alphabet, while others argue an independent conception with slight Phoenician influences. Its first appearance is also uncertain, but it is no older than the first millennium BCE, with the oldest remains likely originating from the 6th century BCE. It disappeared in the northernmost areas of North Africa during the 8th century, after the Arab conquest of the Maghreb, Libyco-Berber along with Latin being replaced by the Arabic script. The Libyco-Berber script was a pure abjad; it had no vowels. Gemination was not marked. The writing was usually from the bottom to the top, although right-to-left, and even other orders, were also found. The letters took different forms when written vertically than when they were written horizontally. This Libyc script had two forms. The undeciphered Western form was used along the Mediterranean coast from Kabylia to Morocco and probably the Canary Islands. The Eastern form was used in Constantine, Aurès, and Tunisia. 22 out of 24 letters in the Eastern form have been deciphered thanks to Punic-Libyc bilingual inscriptions. Andries (2004) identifies an additional phase of evolution called "Saharan Tifinagh", also known as Libyco-Berber or Old Tuareg — which would put into doubt the use of the term "Libyco-Berber" in the section above. This phase shows some new letters relative to Libyc, most notably a vertical line to denote the final vowel /a/. It was used to write Old Tuareg, but is not well-understood. The youngest inscriptions in this scheme are probably around 200 years old. Early uses of Tifinagh have been found on rock art and in various sepulchres. Among these are the 1,500 year old monumental tomb of the Tuareg matriarch Tin Hinan, where vestiges of a Tifinagh inscription have been found on one of its walls. The Saharan script branched into the Tuareg Tifinagh scripts. Following the Arab conquest of the Maghreb, the use of Tifinagh in the northern regions virtually disappeared, but Tuareg Tifinagh continued to be used in the Sahara, with its symbols being used until the present in crafts such as weaving, pottery, and jewelry. Nowadays, it is used to write the Berber Tuareg languages, which belong to the Berber branch of the Afroasiatic family. According to M. C. A. MacDonald, the Tuareg are "an entirely oral society in which memory and oral communication perform all the functions which reading and writing have in a literate society … The Tifinagh are used primarily for games and puzzles, short graffiti and brief messages." Within Tuareg Tifinagh, there is some divergence in the shape and number of signs, but this difference is small enough to not impact mutual intelligibility. Occasionally, the script has been used to write other neighbouring languages such as Tagdal, which belongs to a separate Songhay family. Neo-Tifinagh is the modern fully alphabetic script developed by the Berber Academy, based in Paris. Initially, the academy had to choose a script to transliterate the Berber language. The choice between Tifinagh and Latin scripts then sparked intense debate both within and outside the Academy. Mohand Arav Bessaoud, a founding member of the academy and strong Tifinagh advocate, recounted the resistance he faced from prominent figures like Mouloud Mammeri and Ramdane Achab, who argued that Tifinagh was archaic, obsolete, non-cursive, and impractical. Despite the criticism, Bessaoud persisted in promoting Tifinagh: "Achab Ramdane opposed my actions, calling it rekindling extinguished embers." In 1970, a meeting took place to decide on a system of writing. Influenced by Mahdjoubi Ahardane, Bessaoud opted for Tifinagh. Ahardane argued that Tifinagh was not merely a script but a testament to Berber history and identity. By 1973, Ammar Negadi, a prominent Chaoui writer and fervent advocate of the Tifinagh script, was elected secretary general of the Berber Academy in the Paris region. He propagated the academy's publications and cultural activities: "I distributed all of Agraw Imazighen's writings throughout the Aurès region starting in 1973. The goal wasn't regular correspondence but widespread dissemination of Tifinagh." Neo-Tifinagh was spread by the Berber Academy's active promotion of the script, including its usage in their bulletin, *Imazighen*, which was widely read by Berber communities in Algeria and Morocco. The official activities of the Berber Academy ceased when Mohand Bessaoud Arav was imprisoned. By 1980, Negadi founded his spin-off organization UPA (Amazigh People's Union), which published a bulletin in both Latin and Tifinagh, called *Azaghen/Link*. Activist Messaoud Nedjahi streamlined its characters from 50 to 26. This process inspired the Afus Deg Fus association to create the first set of standardized Neo-Tifinagh fonts in 1993. Neo-Tifinagh has since undergone further reform and is used in various contexts throughout North Africa. The Royal Institute of Amazigh Culture (IRCAM) has standardized Neo-Tifinagh for use as the official orthography of Standard Moroccan Amazigh, an official language of Morocco. The promotion of Neo-Tifinagh by the Berber Academy and Ammar Negadi's UPA was part of the efforts to spread Berberism throughout the 1960s and 1970s. The use of Neo-Tifinagh in their publications was influential in raising Berber consciousness; one reader has described its effect as being "the proof that we actually existed." The Moroccan state arrested and imprisoned people using Neo-Tifinagh during the 1980s and 1990s. The Algerian Black Spring was also partly caused by this repression of Berber language. In the 1980s, the Berber flag, which was designed in 1970 and uses the Tifinagh letter *z* (ⵣ) from the root of *Amazigh*, began being used in demonstrations. The flag was adopted by the World Amazigh Congress in 1997. In Morocco, following the creation of Standard Moroccan Amazigh in 2001, the 2003 adoption of Neo-Tifinagh served as a way to compromise between the deeply split proponents of the Latin script versus the Arabic script as Amazigh's official orthography. This choice, however, has also resulted in backlash from many Amazigh activists, who find Tifinagh to be limiting when compared to the Latin script. In Libya, the government of Muammar Gaddafi consistently banned Tifinagh from being used in public contexts such as store displays and banners. After the Libyan Civil War, the National Transitional Council has shown an openness towards the Berber language. The rebel Libya TV, based in Qatar, has included the Berber language and the Neo-Tifinagh alphabet in some of its programming. Tifinagh continues to be used as "an emblem of distinctive Berber identity and nationhood." Due to the official adoption of Neo-Tifinagh in Morocco in 2003, the script has been adapted by the Royal Institute of Amazigh Culture for modern digital use. Government websites in Morocco may be displayed in Neo-Tifinagh. Starting in 2003, Neo-Tifinagh is used for a small duration of Moroccan elementary school to teach Standard Moroccan Amazigh. However, practical use of Tifinagh in Morocco remains rare; one Amazigh activist has summarized the situation with the anecdote that he "[knows] that some books that were written in Tifinagh were read by only two people … the one who wrote the book and the one who did the editing!" Public displays of Tifinagh in Morocco remain restricted primarily to signage and other culturally conspicuous uses. Despite Neo-Tifinagh's Algerian origins through the Berber Academy and UPA, the Latin alphabet became the predominant used script. Debate in what script to use for Berber languages tends to view the Latin and Arabic scripts as the primary options. As of 2012, Tifinagh was "not widely used in education or the media in any country." A 2026 study evaluating the Amazigh education policy in El Jadida Province found that students aged six to nineteen held significantly favorable attitudes toward Tifinagh as the official script and expressed a willingness to use it in primary education — while parents maintained a pragmatic distance from the policy, expressing skepticism over the practical benefits of compulsory Amazigh instruction and its limited scope. The Andries (2004) submission of Tifinagh (including Neo-Tifinagh) to the Unicode Consortium also notes that Neo-Tifinagh is not the only variant that tries to introduce vowels into Tifinagh. The other schemes include APT (a scheme of additional signs), SIL, Hawad (a scheme of diacritics), Rissa Ixa, Arabic semi-vowels used among the Kel Antessar (Niger), Arabic diacritics used in Timbuktu, and "Latin-like" diacritics proposed by Chaker. None of these have enjoyed as much backing as Neo-Tifinagh. Tifinagh was added to the Unicode Standard in March 2005, with the release of version 4.1. - **The system.** The IRCAM Neo-Tifinagh alphabet, as listed in the 2004 submission to the Unicode Consortium, is thirty-three letters: ya ⴰ *a* /æ/, yab ⴱ *b* /b/, yag ⴳ *g* /ɡ/, yag ⴳⵯ *gw* /ɡʷ/, yad ⴷ *d* /d/, yaḍ ⴹ *ḍ* /dˤ/, yey ⴻ *e* /ə/, yaf ⴼ *f* /f/, yak ⴽ *k* /k/, yak ⴽⵯ *kw* /kʷ/, yah ⵀ *h* /h/, yaḥ ⵃ *ḥ* /ħ/, yaʕ ⵄ *ʕ* /ʕ/, yax ⵅ *kh* /χ/, yaq ⵇ *q* /q/, yi ⵉ *i* /i/, yaj ⵊ *j* /ʒ/, yal ⵍ *l* /l/, yam ⵎ *m* /m/, yan ⵏ *n* /n/, yu ⵓ *u* /w/, yar ⵔ *r* /r/, yaṛ ⵕ *ṛ* /rˤ/, yaɣ ⵖ *gh* /ɣ/, yas ⵙ *s* /s/, yaṣ ⵚ *ṣ* /sˤ/, yaš ⵛ *c* /ʃ/, yat ⵜ *t* /t/, yaṭ ⵟ *ṭ* /tˤ/, yaw ⵡ *w* /w/, yay ⵢ *y* /j/, yaz ⵣ *z* /z/, yaẓ ⵥ *ẓ* /zˤ/. Eleven extended letters sit beside them: yab ⴲ *b* /β/ fricative, yag ⴴ *g* /ʝ/ fricative, yaḍ ⴺ *ḍ* /ðˤ/ fricative, yak ⴿ *k* /x/ fricative, yo ⵧ *o* /o, ɔ/, yap ⵒ *p* /p/, yat ⵝ *t* /θ/ fricative, yav ⵠ *v* /v/, yadj ⴵ *dj, ǧ* /d͡ʒ/, yah ⵁ *h* /h/, yatš ⵞ *ch, č* /t͡ʃ/. The two labialized letters, ⴳⵯ and ⴽⵯ, are sequences — a base letter plus the labialization mark U+2D6F — not single code points. Unicode's names diverge from the article's romanizations in places: the article's *yaj* is Unicode YAZH, its *yatš* is YACH, its *yadj* and second *yah* are BERBER ACADEMY YAJ and BERBER ACADEMY YAH, and its fricative *yab/yag/yaḍ/yak* are YABH, YAGHH, YADDH, YAKHH. The Tuareg scripts are not one script but several, with slightly different assignments for each letter: the article's table, after Aghali-Zakara (1993) via Andries (2004) and Casajus (2011), carries twenty-seven IPA rows across five dialects — Ahaggar, Ghat, Aïr, Azawagh, Adrar — and most letters hold steady while a few wander: *d* is ⴸ in Ahaggar, Ghat, and Adrar but ⴹ in Aïr and Azawagh; *z* is ⵣ in Ahaggar, Aïr, and Azawagh but ⵌ in Ghat and ⵋ in Adrar; *š* is ⵛ in four dialects. The orthography is a system of small mercies for a reader who knows the language: common forms of the letters are illustrated in the article, including various ligatures of *t* and *n*. Gemination, though phonemic, is not indicated in Tifinagh. The letter *t*, ⵜ, is often combined with a preceding letter to form a ligature. Most of the letters have more than one common form, including mirror-images. When the letters *l* and *n* are adjacent to themselves or to each other, the second is offset, either by inclining, lowering, raising, or shortening it: since the letter *l* is a double line, ||, and *n* a single line, |, the sequence *nn* may be written |/ to differentiate it from *l*; similarly, *ln* is ||/, *nl* |//, *ll* ||//, *nnn* |/|. Traditionally, the Tifinagh script does not indicate vowels except word-finally, where a single dot stands for any vowel (or ⵢ and ⵓ for -i and -u, respectively, in Ahaggar Tifinagh). In some areas, Arabic vowel diacritics are combined with Tifinagh letters to transcribe vowels, or *y, w* may be used for long *ī* and *ū*. The directions are four — right-to-left, left-to-right, top-to-bottom, bottom-to-top — and Libyco-Berber was usually bottom-to-top, with the letters taking different forms written vertically than horizontally. The three competing orthographies are Latin, Arabic, and Tifinagh. The flag's letter is ⵣ, *yaz*, from the root of *Amazigh*. The entrance to Kidal is written ⴾⴸⵍ, *KDL*, in Tuareg Tifinagh beside the Latin. - **Decoder-design note (Tifinagh → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The alphabet that survived by refusing to be one.** Four directions, five dialects, three orthographies — and the script survived two millennia of conquest, a ban, and a prison sentence for its users. The Gauntlet's direction probe asks what survives when a specimen changes its direction: the parts that survive every rotation are the system, and the parts that change with the direction are decoration. A specimen that writes in four directions confesses that its direction is not the system — and a specimen that dies when you turn it was never alive, only oriented. (2) **The abjad that grew vowels.** Traditional Tifinagh has zero vowel letters; Neo-Tifinagh has five — and nothing else changed. The Gauntlet's vowel probe asks what a specimen gains when it stops being an abjad: a specimen whose consonants stay put while its vowels arrive confesses that its consonants were always the system, and the vowels were a late admission that readers need more than the skeleton. A specimen that cannot add vowels without re-drawing its consonants is not an alphabet with missing vowels; it is a different script wearing the old one's name. (3) **The question mark that descends.** Phoenician #179 named Libyco-Berber a child with a question mark, and the Tifinagh infobox carries Phoenician with a question mark too — the uncertainty is inherited, one descent at a time. The Gauntlet's lineage probe: when a specimen's parent carries a "?", ask what the "?" is protecting — a missing link, a rival theory, or a date nobody will swear to — and treat the inherited "?" as the specimen's own confession, not its parent's. A specimen that inherits its doubt honestly is more trustworthy than one that files it away. [SPECULATION — the Gauntlet mappings are this note's doctrine, never run]
