- **The story.** The Thai script (Thai: อักษรไทย, RTGS: *akson thai*, pronounced [ʔàksɔ̌ːn tʰāj]) is the abugida used to write Thai, Southern Thai, and many other languages spoken in Thailand. Its infobox reads: script type abugida; creator Ramkhamhaeng the Great; period 1283–present; direction left-to-right; official script of Thailand; languages Thai and Southern Thai in standard form, and Lanna, Isan, Phu Thai, Pattani Malay, Urak Lawoi, Phuan and others in non-standard form; parent systems Egyptian hieroglyphs, Proto-Sinaitic, Phoenician, Aramaic, Brahmi, Tamil-Brahmi, Pallava, Old Khmer, Sukhothai, Thai; child system Tai Viet; sister system Fakkham; ISO 15924 Thai (352), Thai; Unicode range U+0E00–U+0E7F. The script as used to write Thai has 44 consonant symbols (Thai: พยัญชนะ, *phayanchana*), 16 vowel symbols (Thai: สระ, *sara*) that combine into at least 32 vowel forms, four tone diacritics (Thai: วรรณยุกต์ or วรรณยุต, *wannayuk* or *wannayut*), and other diacritics. Although commonly referred to as the Thai alphabet, the script is not a true alphabet but an abugida, in which the full characters represent consonants with diacritical marks for vowels; the absence of a vowel diacritic gives an implied 'a' or 'o'. Consonants are written horizontally from left to right, and vowels following a consonant in speech are written above, below, to the left or to the right of it, or a combination of those. The Thai script is derived from the Old Khmer script (Thai: อักษรขอม, *akson khom*), a sophisticated writing system rooted in the South Indian Pallava alphabet and a southern branch of the ancient Brahmi tradition. The Sukhothai script was the earliest Thai script developed from the Old Khmer script. The Ram Khamhaeng Inscription dated to 1292 is often cited as the script's first appearance, yet many scholars question its authenticity and reliability as historical evidence. However, according to the Wat Bang Sanuk Inscription (C.107) in Phrae province, several scholars proposed that the earliest Thai script could be dated back to 1219. The introduction of tone markers in the Thai script was an adaptation to record tonal features absent in the source languages such as Dravidian languages, Indo-Aryan languages and the Mon-Khmer (Austroasiatic languages) family. Although Chinese and other Sino-Tibetan languages have distinctive tones in their phonological system, no tone marker is found in their orthographies. Another addition was consonant clusters that were written horizontally and contiguously, rather than writing the second consonant below the first one. The vowel marks were written on the main line. However, the practices fell out of use not long after. The spelling–sound relationship is fairly complex. For many consonant sounds there are two different letters that both represent the same sound but cause a different tone to be associated — this stems from a major change (a tone split) that occurred historically in the phonology of the Thai language. At the time the Thai script was created, the language had three tones and a full set of contrasts between voiced and unvoiced consonants at the beginning of a syllable. At a later time, the voicing distinction disappeared, but in the process, each of the three original tones split in two, with an originally voiced consonant (the modern "low" consonant signs) producing a lower-variant tone, and an originally unvoiced consonant (the modern "mid" and "high" consonant signs) producing a higher-variant tone. Thai borrowed a large number of words from Sanskrit and Pali, and the Thai alphabet was created so that the original spelling of these words could be preserved as much as possible — so the alphabet has a number of "duplicate" letters that represent separate sounds in Sanskrit and Pali but which never represented distinct sounds in Thai. Some are used to indicate tone distinctions, and others are mostly or exclusively used in Sanskrit and Pali borrowings. The desire to preserve original Sanskrit and Pali spellings also produces a particularly large number of duplicate ways of spelling sounds at the end of a syllable, as well as a number of silent letters: Thai สามารถ (spelled *sǎamaarth* but pronounced *sa-mat* /sǎː mâːt/, with a silent r and a plain t represented using an aspirated consonant) "to be able" (Sanskrit समर्थ *samartha*), and Thai จันทร์ (spelled *chanthr* but pronounced *chan* /tɕān/ because the th and the r are silent) "moon" (Sanskrit चन्द्र *chandra*). Thai phonology dictates that all syllables must end in a vowel, an approximant, a nasal, or a voiceless plosive, so the letter written may not have the same pronunciation in the initial position as it does in the final position. Even though the high class letter *ho hip* ห is used to write the sound /h/, if the letter comes before a low class letter in a syllable, it becomes the silent *ho nam* and turns the initial consonant into high class. Thai letters do not have upper- and lower-case forms like Latin letters do. Spaces between words are not used, except in certain linguistically motivated cases. Minor pauses in sentences may be marked by a comma (Thai: จุลภาค or ลูกน้ำ, *chunlaphak* or *luk nam*), and major pauses by a period (Thai: มหัพภาค or จุด, *mahap phak* or *chut*), but most often are marked by a blank space (Thai: วรรค, *wak*). Thai writing also uses quotation marks (Thai: อัญประกาศ, *anyaprakat*) and parentheses, but not square brackets or braces. A *paiyan noi* ฯ (Thai: ไปยาลน้อย) is used for abbreviation. A *paiyan yai* ฯลฯ (Thai: ไปยาลใหญ่) is the same as "etc." Several obsolete characters indicated the beginning or ending of sections: a bird's eye ๏ (Thai: ตาไก่, *ta kai*, officially called ฟองมัน, *fong man*) formerly indicated paragraphs; an *angkhan kuu* ๚ (Thai: อังคั่นคู่) was formerly used to mark the end of a chapter; a *kho mut* ๛ (Thai: โคมูตร) was formerly used to mark the end of a document, but is now obsolete. Two of the consonants, ฃ (*kho khuat*) and ฅ (*kho khon*), are no longer used in written Thai, but still appear on many keyboards and in character sets. When the first Thai typewriter was developed by Edwin Hunter McFarland in 1892, there was simply no space for all characters, thus two had to be left out. Also, neither of these two letters correspond to a Sanskrit or Pali letter, and each of them, being a modified form of the letter that precedes it (compare ข and ค), has the same pronunciation and the same consonant class as the preceding letter, thus making them redundant. They used to represent the sound /x/ in Old Thai, but it has merged with /kʰ/ in Modern Thai. The inherent vowels are /a/ in open syllables (CV) and /o/ in closed syllables (CVC): ถนน transcribes /tʰ àn ǒn / "road". There are a few exceptions in Pali loanwords, where the inherent vowel of an open syllable is /ɔː/. The circumfix vowels, such as เ–าะ /ɔʔ/, encompass a preceding consonant with an inherent vowel: /pʰɔʔ / is written เพาะ, and /tɕʰ apʰɔʔ / "only" is written เฉพาะ. The characters **ฤ ฤๅ** (plus **ฦ ฦๅ**, which are obsolete) are usually considered as vowels, the first being a short vowel sound, and the latter, long; the letters are based on vocalic consonants used in Sanskrit, given the one-to-one letter correspondence of Thai to Sanskrit, although the last two letters are quite rare, as their equivalent Sanskrit sounds only occur in a few, ancient words and thus are functionally obsolete in Thai. As alphabetical entries, ฤ ฤๅ follow **ร**, and themselves can be read as a combination of consonant and vowel, equivalent to รึ (short) and รือ (long) (and the obsolete pair as ลึ, ลือ), respectively. Moreover, **ฤ** can act as **ริ** as an integral part in many words mostly borrowed from Sanskrit such as ก**ฤ**ษณะ (*kritsana*, not *kruetsana*), **ฤ**ทธิ์ (*rit*, not *ruet*), and ก**ฤ**ษดา (*kritsada*, not *kruetsada*). It is also used to spell อังก**ฤ**ษ *angkrit* England/English. The word **ฤ**กษ์ (*roek*) is a unique case where **ฤ** is pronounced like **เรอ**. In the past, prior to the turn of the twentieth century, it was common for writers to substitute these letters in native vocabulary that contained similar sounds as a shorthand that was acceptable in writing at the time — for example, the conjunction 'or' (Thai: หรือ /rɯ̌ː/ *rue*) was often written Thai: ฤ. This practice has become obsolete, but can still be seen in Thai literature. Thai was added to the Unicode Standard in October 1991 with the release of version 1.0. It is a verbatim copy of the older TIS-620 character set which encodes the vowels เ, แ, โ, ใ and ไ before the consonants they follow, and thus Thai, Lao, Tai Viet and New Tai Lue are the only Brahmic scripts in Unicode that use visual order instead of logical order. Thai characters can be typed using the Kedmanee layout and the Pattachote layout. The classes reflect the sounds the letters originally corresponded to in Old Thai: "middle" sounds were voiceless unaspirated stops; "high" sounds, voiceless aspirated stops or voiceless fricatives; "low" sounds, voiced — subsequent sound changes have obscured the phonetic nature of the classes. Today, the class of a consonant without a tone mark, along with the short or long length of the accompanying vowel, determine the base accent (พื้นเสียง, *phuen siang*). Middle class consonants with a long vowel spell an additional four tones with one of four tone marks over the controlling consonant. In the phonetic table, Thai distinguishes three voice/aspiration patterns for plosives — unvoiced unaspirated, unvoiced aspirated, voiced unaspirated — where English has only two; in the velar series there is a /k/, /kʰ/ pair and in the postalveolar series the /tɕ/, /tɕʰ/ pair. The 44 consonants provide 21 sounds in initial position; the finals collapse: at the end of a syllable all plosives are unvoiced, unaspirated, and have no audible release; initial affricates and fricatives become final plosives; the initial trill (ร), approximant (ญ), and lateral approximants (ล, ฬ) are realized as a final nasal /n/. Only 8 ending consonant sounds, as well as no ending consonant sound, are available in Thai pronunciation. Among these consonants, excluding the disused ฃ and ฅ, six (ฉ, ผ, ฝ, ห, อ, ฮ) have never been attested as a final. When ย ends a syllable it is usually part of the vowel; when ว ends a syllable it is always part of the vowel. อ is a special case: at the beginning of a word it is used as a silent initial for syllables that start with a vowel, and the same symbol is used as a vowel in non-initial position. The lower curves of the letters ญ and ฐ are removed when certain letters are written below them. Twenty-one vowel symbol elements are traditionally named, which may appear alone or in combination to form compound symbols: ะ *wisanchani* (also *nom nang*, from Sanskrit *visarjanīya*), ◌ั *mai han akat* (also *mai phat*, *mai kanghan*), ◌็ *mai tai khu*, า *lak khang*, ◌ิ *phin i* (also *phinthu i*), ◌̍ *fon thong*, ◌̎ *fan nu* (also *musikathan*), ◌ํ *nikkhahit* (also *naruekhahit*, *yat namkhang*), ◌ุ *tin yiat* (also *lak tin*), ◌ู *tin khu*, เ *mai na*, โ *mai o*, ใ *mai muan*, ไ *mai malai*, อ *tua o*, ย *tua yo*, ว *tua wo*, ฤ *tua rue*, ฤๅ, ฦ *tua lue*, ฦๅ. The two combining marks ◌̍ and ◌̎ are always combined with *phinthu i* (◌ิ). Thai vowel sounds and diphthongs are written using a mixture of vowel symbols on a consonant base; vowels can go above, below, left of or right of the consonant, or combinations of these places, and if a vowel has parts before and after the initial consonant and the syllable starts with a consonant cluster, the split will go around the whole cluster. The simple vowels, short and long: /aʔ/, /a/ — /aː/; /iʔ/, /i/ — /iː/; /ɯʔ/, /ɯ/ — /ɯː/; /uʔ/, /u/ — /uː/; /eʔ/, /e/ — /eː/; /ɛʔ/, /ɛ/ — /ɛː/; /oʔ/, /o/ — /oː/; /ɔʔ/, /ɔ/ — /ɔː/; /ɤʔ/ — /ɤː/, /ɤ/. The diphthongs, short and long: /iaʔ/ — /ia/; /ɯaʔ/ — /ɯa/; /uaʔ/ — /ua/. The extra vowels, not distinct vowel sounds but symbols representing certain vowel-consonant combinations, traditionally regarded as vowels although some sources do not: ◌ำ /am/; ฤ /rɯ/, /ri/, /rɤː/; ฤๅ /rɯː/; ฦ /lɯ/; ฦๅ /lɯː/ — and *sara ai* (ใ◌ and ไ◌) and *sara ao* (เ◌า) are also considered extra vowels. *Mai malai* (ไ◌) is used for the /aj/ vowel in most words, while *mai muan* (ใ◌) is only used in twenty specific words. ไ◌ย is found in ไทย *Thai* and in Pali loanwords which contain *-eyya*; the ย is redundant, but may be pronounced in a compound word when joined by samāsa. The phonemic diphthongs are traditionally regarded as combinations of regular vowels or diphthongs with *wo waen* (ว, /w/) or *yo yak* (ย, /j/) as the final consonant, and are not counted among the thirty-two vowels: /iw/, /ew/, /eːw/, /ɛːw/, /aw/, /aːw/, /iaw/, /aj/, /aːj/, /ɔj/, /ɔːj/, /oːj/, /uj/, /ɤːj/, /uaj/, /ɯaj/. *Ro han* (ร หัน) is not usually considered a vowel and is not included in the vowel table: it represents the *sara a* /a/ vowel in certain Sanskrit loanwords and appears as ◌รร◌; when used without a final consonant (◌รร), /n/ is implied as the final consonant, giving /an/. Central Thai is a tonal language, and the script gives full information on the tones. Tones are realised in the vowels, but indicated in the script by a combination of the class of the initial consonant (high, mid or low), vowel length (long or short), closing consonant (plosive or sonorant, called *dead* or *live*) and, if present, one of four tone marks, whose names derive from the names of the digits 1–4 borrowed from Pali or Sanskrit. With no mark: live syllables (long vowel or vowel plus sonorant) spell middle tone with low- and mid-class initials and rising tone with high-class initials; dead short syllables (short vowel at end or plus plosive) spell high tone with low-class initials and low tone with mid- and high-class initials; dead long syllables (long vowel plus plosive) spell falling tone with low-class initials and low tone with mid- and high-class initials. With a mark: *mai ek* ่ spells falling with low-class initials and low with mid- and high-class initials; *mai tho* ้ spells high with low-class initials and falling with mid- and high-class initials; *mai tri* ๊ and *mai chattawa* ๋ are only used with mid-class consonants, spelling high and rising respectively. "None", that is, no tone marker, is used with the base accent (*phuen siang*). Two consonant characters (not diacritics) are used to modify the tone: **ห นำ *ho nam*, leading ho** — a silent, high-class ห "leads" low-class nasal stops (ง, ญ, น and ม) and non-plosives (ว, ย, ร and ล), which have no corresponding high-class phonetic match, into the tone properties of a high-class consonant; in polysyllabic words, an initial mid- or high-class consonant with an implicit vowel similarly "leads" these same low-class consonants into the higher class tone rules, with the tone marker borne by the low-class consonant. **อ นำ *o nam*, leading o** — in four words only, a silent, mid-class อ "leads" low-class ย into mid-class tone rules: อย่า (*ya*, don't), อยาก (*yak*, desire), อย่าง (*yang*, kind, sort, type), อยู่ (*yu*, stay); all four have long-vowel, low-tone *siang ek*; อยาก, a dead syllable, needs no tone marker, but the three live syllables all take *mai ek*. In some dialects there are words which are spelled with one tone but pronounced with another and often occur in informal conversation (notably the pronouns ฉัน *chan* and เขา *khao*, which are both pronounced with a high tone rather than the rising tone indicated by the script); generally, when such words are recited or read in public, they are pronounced as spelled. Southern Thai, though written in the same script with the same full tone information, is a pitch-accent language whose spoken form can have up to seven tones, with different rules for indicating spoken tone. Other diacritics indicate short vowels and silent letters: *mai taikhu* ◌็ means "climbing stick" and is a miniature Thai numeral 8 **๘**, often used with *sara e* (เ) and *sara ae* (แ) in closed syllables; *thanthakhat* ◌์ means "capital punishment" and is a miniature Thai numeral 4 **๔**, indicating a silent letter (also called *karan*). *Fan nu* means "rat teeth" and is placed in combination with short *sara i* to make long *sara ue* (◌ื), and with *fong man* (๏) to make *fong man fan nu* (๏"). For numerals, mostly the standard Hindu-Arabic numerals are used, but Thai also has its own set of Thai numerals based on the Hindu-Arabic numeral system, mostly limited to government documents, election posters, license plates of military vehicles, and special entry prices for Thai nationals: ๐ ๑ ๒ ๓ ๔ ๕ ๖ ๗ ๘ ๙. Other symbols: ๆ *mai yamok*, the preceding word or phrase is reduplicated; ๏ *fong man* / *ta kai*, previously marked the beginning of a sentence, paragraph, or stanza (obsolete), now only marks the beginning of a stanza in a poem, and is now also used as a bullet point; ๏" *fong man fan nu*, previously marked the beginning of a chapter (obsolete); ๐" *fong dan*; ฯ *angkhan diao*, previously marked the end of a sentence or stanza (obsolete); ๚ *angkhan khu*, marks the end of a stanza, the end of a chapter, or a long section; ฯะ and ๚ะ *angkhan wisanchani*, mark the end of a stanza in a poem; ๛ *kho mut* / *sut narai*, marks the end of a chapter or document, or the end of a story; ๚ะ๛ *angkhan wisanchani kho mut*, marks the very end of a written work; ฿ *bat*, the baht, the currency of Thailand. *Pai-yan noi* and *angkhan diao* share the same character. - **The honest blank.** Eleven confessions. (1) The first appearance is not settled: the 1292 Ram Khamhaeng Inscription's authenticity is questioned by many scholars, and the 1219 Wat Bang Sanuk proposal is a proposal — the infobox's 1283 sits between two dates neither of which is agreed, and the entry carries all three without choosing. - **Decoder-design note (Thai → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The vowels that arrive before their consonants.** Thai stores เ แ โ ใ ไ before the consonant they follow — visual order, not logical order — and the article's own string proves it: ไทย is stored ไ-ท-ย. The Gauntlet's order probe asks what a specimen assumes about order: a decoder that reads storage order as speaking order garbles every word with a leading vowel, and a specimen that survives reordering confesses that its order is a convention, not its content. A specimen that dies when you read it left-to-right was never decoded, only transcribed. (2) **The tone machine.** No single mark carries the tone: the tone is class × length × final × mark, four inputs, five outputs, and two of the four marks only work on one class. The Gauntlet's distributed-encoding probe: when a specimen's meaning lives in no single symbol but in the combination, ask what happens when one input is removed — a specimen whose tone survives losing its mark confesses the mark was redundant, and a specimen whose tone collapses confesses the combination was the system. Thai keeps its duplicates for the same reason: the letters that no longer spell a sound still spell a history, and history is a channel. (3) **The duplicates that outlived their sounds.** 44 letters for 21 sounds — 5.46 bits of alphabet for 4.39 bits of sound — and the duplicates are kept deliberately, to preserve Sanskrit and Pali spellings. The Gauntlet's redundancy probe asks what a specimen keeps after its reason is gone: a specimen that keeps dead distinctions is keeping provenance, and provenance is evidence; a specimen that prunes them is keeping efficiency, and efficiency is a choice. The typewriter pruned two letters for space in 1892 and the language kept the other forty-two anyway — the script chose provenance over the keyboard, and the keyboard adapted. - **The story.** Ge'ez (*GEE-ez*; Ge'ez: ግዕዝ, romanized *Gəʽəz*, IPA [ˈɡɨʕɨz]) is an abugida used to write several Afro-Asiatic and Nilo-Saharan languages of Ethiopia and Eritrea. Its infobox reads: script type abugida; period c. 1st century CE to present (abjad until c. 4th century CE); direction left-to-right; languages generally Ethio-Semitic (Ge'ez, Tigrinya, Amharic, Tigre, Gurage, Harari, etc.), but also some Cushitic and Nilotic languages — Bilen, Meʼen, and Anuak as one of two scripts among them; native to the Horn of Africa, Ethiopia and Eritrea; parent systems Egyptian hieroglyphs, Proto-Sinaitic, South Semitic scripts, Ancient South Arabian; child systems Amharic, Tigrinya, and various other alphabets of Ethiopia and Eritrea; ISO 15924 Ethi (430), Ethiopic (Geʻez); Unicode alias Ethiopic. It originated as an abjad and was first used to write the Ge'ez language, now the liturgical language of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, the Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Church, the Eritrean Catholic Church, the Ethiopian Catholic Church, and Haymanot Judaism of the Beta Israel Jewish community in Ethiopia. In Amharic and Tigrinya the script is often called *fidäl* (ፊደል), meaning "script" or "letter"; under the Unicode Standard and ISO 15924 it is defined as Ge'ez text. It has been adapted to write other languages, mostly Ethiopian and Eritrean Semitic — particularly Amharic in Ethiopia and Tigrinya in both Eritrea and Ethiopia — and also Sebat Bet and other Gurage languages and at least 20 other languages of Ethiopia; in Eritrea it has traditionally been used for Tigre and just recently for Bilen; it has also recently been used to write Anuak and in limited extent some other Nilo-Saharan Nilotic languages including Majang, and in the past some Omotic languages including Wolaytta, Bench, Hamer, and Kafa. The script was derived from the Ancient South Arabian script, and despite its name its origins are debated, and may have originated in what is now Eritrea, Ethiopia, or Yemen. The earliest inscriptions of Semitic languages in Eritrea date to the 9th century BCE and are known as Epigraphic South Arabian (ESA), an abjad shared with contemporary kingdoms in the southern part of the Arabian Peninsula. After the 7th and 6th centuries BCE, variants of the South Arabian script arose, evolving in the direction of the later Ge'ez abugida or alphasyllabary — the evolution visible most clearly in inscriptions, mainly graffiti on rocks and caves, in the Tigray Region in northern Ethiopia and in multiple parts of Eritrea, mainly in the former province of Akele Guzai. The oldest known example of the Ge'ez script is the Hawulti obelisk in Matara, Eritrea. By the first centuries CE, what is called "Old Ethiopic" or the "Old Geʻez writing system" arose, an abjad written right-to-left (as opposed to boustrophedon like ESA) with letters basically identical to the first-order forms of the modern vocalized writing system, with minor differences such as the letter "g" facing to the right instead of to the left as in vocalized Ge'ez, and a shorter left leg of "l", as in ESA, instead of equally-long legs (somewhat resembling the Greek letter lambda). Vocalization of Ge'ez occurred in the 4th century, and though the first completely vocalized texts known are inscriptions by Ezana, vocalized letters predate him by some years, as an individual vocalized letter exists in a coin of his predecessor, Wazeba of Axum; linguist Roger Schneider has also pointed out, in an unpublished early 1990s paper, anomalies in the known inscriptions of Ezana of Axum that imply he was consciously employing an archaic style during his reign, indicating that vocalization could have occurred much earlier. At least one of Wazeba's coins from the late 3rd or early 4th century contains a vocalized letter, some 30 or so years before Ezana. Some believe the vocalization may have been adopted to preserve the pronunciation of Ge'ez texts due to the already moribund or extinct status of Ge'ez, and that by that time the common language of the people were already later Eritrean and Ethiopian Afro-Asiatic languages; Kobishchanov, Peter T. Daniels, and others have suggested possible influence from the Brahmic scripts in vocalization, as they are also abugidas, and the Kingdom of Aksum was an important part of major trade routes involving India and the Greco-Roman world throughout classical antiquity. According to the beliefs of the Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Church and Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, the original consonantal form of the Ge'ez *fidäl* was divinely revealed to Enos "as an instrument for codifying the laws", and the present system of vocalisation is attributed to a team of Aksumite scholars led by Frumentius (*Abba Selama*), the same missionary said to have converted King Ezana to Christianity in the 4th century; it has been argued that the vowel marking pattern of the script reflects a South Asian system such as would have been known by Frumentius. A separate tradition, recorded by Aleqa Taye, holds that the Ge'ez consonantal writing system was first adapted by Zegdur, a legendary king of the Agʻazyan Sabaean dynasty held to have ruled in Abyssinia (Eritrea and Ethiopia) c. 1300 BCE. - **The system.** Ge'ez has 26 consonantal letters. Compared to the inventory of 29 consonants in the South Arabian writing system, the continuants *ġ*, *ẓ*, and South Arabian *s3* (Ge'ez Sawt ሠ being derived from South Arabian *s2*) are missing, as are *ḏ* and *ṯ* — these last two absences reflect the collapse of the interdental with the alveolar fricatives. On the other hand, emphatic *P̣ait* ጰ, a Ge'ez innovation, is a modification of *Ṣädai* ጸ, while Psa ፐ is based on Tawe ተ; thus there are 24 correspondences of Ge'ez and the South Arabian writing system. Many of the letter names are cognate with those of Phoenician, and may thus be assumed for the Proto-Sinaitic script — the clearest pairs against the Phoenician entry's own list are Bet "house" with Bet "house", Gäml with Gaml "throwing stick", Kaf with Kap "palm of a hand", Rəʾs "head" with Rosh "head", and ʼÄlf with Alp "ox". The abjad, used until the advent of Christianity (ca. AD 350), had 26 consonantal letters, transliterated *h, l, ḥ, m, ś, r, s, ḳ, b, t, ḫ, n, ʾ, k, w, ʿ, z, y, d, g, ṭ, p̣, ṣ, ṣ́, f, p*; it was properly written right-to-left, and vowels were not indicated. The abugida developed during the adoption of Christianity by adding obligatory vocalic diacritics to the consonantal letters: the diacritics for the vowels *u, i, a, e, ə, o* were fused with the consonants in a recognizable but slightly irregular way, so that the system is laid out as a syllabary; the original form of the consonant was used when the vowel was *ä* (/ə/), the so-called inherent vowel; for most consonants there is an eighth form for the diphthong **-wa** or **-oa**, and for a number of those a ninth form for **-jä**; to represent a consonant with no following phonemic vowel, for example at the end of a syllable or in a consonant cluster, the *ə* (/ɨ/) form is used (the character in the sixth column). The 26 bases in traditional order, with their seven vowel forms (ä, u, i, a, e, ə, o): Hoy h ሀ ሁ ሂ ሃ ሄ ህ ሆ; Läwe l ለ ሉ ሊ ላ ሌ ል ሎ (ሏ); Ḥäwt ḥ ሐ ሑ ሒ ሓ ሔ ሕ ሖ (ሗ); May m መ ሙ ሚ ማ ሜ ም ሞ (ሟ, ፙ); Śäwt ś ሠ ሡ ሢ ሣ ሤ ሥ ሦ (ሧ); Rəʾs r ረ ሩ ሪ ራ ሬ ር ሮ (ሯ, ፘ); Sat s ሰ ሱ ሲ ሳ ሴ ስ ሶ (ሷ); Ḳaf q ቀ ቁ ቂ ቃ ቄ ቅ ቆ (ቋ); Bet b በ ቡ ቢ ባ ቤ ብ ቦ (ቧ); Täwe t ተ ቱ ቲ ታ ቴ ት ቶ (ቷ); Ḫarm ḫ ኀ ኁ ኂ ኃ ኄ ኅ ኆ (ኋ); Nähas n ነ ኑ ኒ ና ኔ ን ኖ (ኗ); ʼÄlf ʾ አ ኡ ኢ ኣ ኤ እ ኦ (ኧ); Kaf k ከ ኩ ኪ ካ ኬ ክ ኮ (ኳ); Wäwe w ወ ዉ ዊ ዋ ዌ ው ዎ; ʽÄyn ʿ ዐ ዑ ዒ ዓ ዔ ዕ ዖ; Zäy z ዘ ዙ ዚ ዛ ዜ ዝ ዞ (ዟ); Yämän y የ ዩ ዪ ያ ዬ ይ ዮ; Dänt d ደ ዱ ዲ ዳ ዴ ድ ዶ (ዷ); Gäml g ገ ጉ ጊ ጋ ጌ ግ ጎ (ጓ); Ṭäyt ṭ ጠ ጡ ጢ ጣ ጤ ጥ ጦ (ጧ); P̣äyt p̣ ጰ ጱ ጲ ጳ ጴ ጵ ጶ (ጷ); Ṣädäy ṣ ጸ ጹ ጺ ጻ ጼ ጽ ጾ (ጿ); Ṣ́äppä ṣ́ ፀ ፁ ፂ ፃ ፄ ፅ ፆ; Äf f ፈ ፉ ፊ ፋ ፌ ፍ ፎ (ፏ, ፚ); Psa p ፐ ፑ ፒ ፓ ፔ ፕ ፖ (ፗ). The letters for the labialized velar consonants are variants of the non-labialized velar consonants: qw ቈ, ḫw ኈ, gw ጐ, kw ኰ — and unlike the other consonants, these labiovelars can be combined with only five different vowels (ä, i, a, e, ə): ቈ ቊ ቋ ቌ ቍ; ኈ ኊ ኋ ኌ ኍ; ጐ ጒ ጓ ጔ ጕ; ኰ ኲ ኳ ኴ ኵ. Some letters were modified to create additional consonants for use in languages other than Ge'ez, typically by adding a horizontal line at the top of a similar-sounding consonant: v ቨ from b, č ቸ from t, ǧ ጀ from d, č̣ ጨ from ṭ, q̱ ቐ from q, x ኸ from k, q̱ʷ ቘ, xʷ ዀ, š ሸ from s, ñ ኘ from n, ž ዠ from z, ŋ ጘ from g, ŋʷ ⶓ from gw — thirteen additional consonants in all. The modern abugidas take different subsets: Amharic uses all the basic consonants plus š, v, č, ñ, x, xʷ, ž, ǧ, č̣ (and some of the labiovelar variants); Tigrinya has all the basic consonants, the labiovelar variants except for *ḫʷ* (ኈ), plus š, q̱, q̱ʷ, v, č, ñ, x, xʷ, ž, ǧ, č̣ — though a few of the basic consonants are falling into disuse in Eritrea (as they used ጸ for ፀ); Tigre uses the basic consonants except for *ś* (ሠ), *ḫ* (ኀ), and *ḍ* (ፀ), plus š, č, ž, ŋ, and does not use the labiovelar variants; Bilen uses the basic consonants except for *ś*, *ḫ*, and *ḍ*, plus š, q̱, v, č, ŋʷ, ñ, xʷ, ž, ǧ, ŋ, č̣, and the labiovelar variants; Harari uses the basic consonants except for *ś*, *ḫ*, *ʽ* (ዐ), *p̣* (ጰ), *ṣ* (ጸ), and *ḍ* (ፀ), plus q̱, č, ñ, x, ǧ, č̣ — although *h* (ሀ) is occasionally used, *ḥ* (ሐ) is strongly favored — and as Harari used the Arabic script before adopting the Ge'ez script, Arabic phonemes entered the language through loanwords and were ascribed to specific consonant forms: *ḥ* from (ح) to ሐ, *ṫ* from (ث) to ሠ, *gh* from (غ) to ኀ, *kh* from (خ) to ኸ, *ʽ* from (ع) to ዐ, *dˁ* from (ض) to ጰ, and *dh* from (ذ) to ፀ. For Ge'ez, Amharic, Tigrinya, and Tigre, the usual sort order is called *haläħamä* (h–l–ħ–m); where the labiovelar variants are used, these come immediately after the basic consonant and are followed by other variants — in Tigrinya, for example, the letters based on ከ come in this order: ከ, ኰ, ኸ, ዀ — and in Bilen the sorting order is slightly different. The alphabetical order is similar to that found in other South Semitic scripts, as well as in the ancient Ugaritic alphabet, which attests both the southern Semitic h-l-ħ-m order and the northern Semitic ʼ–b–g–d (*abugida*) order over three thousand years ago. Ge'ez uses an additional alphabetic numeral system comparable to the Hebrew, Arabic abjad, and Greek numerals; it is reduced from these systems in that it lacks digits for the multiples of 100 — for example, 475 is written ፬፻፸፭, that is "4-100-70-5", and 83,692 is ፰፼፴፮፻፺፪, "8–10,000-30-6-100-90-2"; the digits historically are Greek letters over- and under-lined with a vinculum, and Ethiopian numerals were borrowed from the Greek numerals, possibly via Coptic uncial letters. The numeral glyphs: 1–9 are ፩ ፪ ፫ ፬ ፭ ፮ ፯ ፰ ፱; 10–90 are ፲ ፳ ፴ ፵ ፶ ፷ ፸ ፹ ፺; ፻ is 100 and ፼ is 10,000 — and the coin of Emperor Menelik II bears the date ፲፰፻፹፱ (1889). Punctuation, much of it modern, includes nine marks: ፠ section mark, ፡ word separator, ። full stop (period), ፣ comma, ፤ semicolon, ፥ colon, ፦ preface colon, ፧ question mark, ፨ paragraph separator. Tone marks for multiline scored layout are ten: ᎐ *yizet*, ᎑ *deret*, ᎒ *rikrik*, ᎓ short *rikrik*, ᎔ *difat*, ᎕ *kenat*, ᎖ *chiret*, ᎗ *hidet*, ᎘ *deret-hidet*, ᎙ *kurt*. Ethiopic has been assigned Unicode 3.0 codepoints between U+1200 and U+137F (decimal 4608–4991), containing the consonantal letters for Ge'ez, Amharic, and Tigrinya, punctuation, and numerals; in Unicode 4.1 there is the supplement range U+1380–U+139F (decimal 4992–5023) containing letters for Sebat Bet and tonal marks, and the extended range U+2D80–U+2DDF (decimal 11648–11743) containing letters needed for writing Sebat Bet, Meʼen, and Bilen; in Unicode 6.0 there is the extended-A range U+AB00–U+AB2F (decimal 43776–43823) containing letters for Gamo-Gofa-Dawro, Basketo, and Gumuz; and in Unicode 14.0 the extended-B range U+1E7E0–U+1E7FF (decimal 124896–124927) containing additional letters for Gurage languages. It has been speculated by some scholars in African studies that the Ge'ez script had an influence on the Armenian alphabet after it may have been introduced to Armenia at the end of the fifth century. In Western culture Ge'ez is a sacred script in the Rastafari movement, roots reggae musicians have used it in album art, and the films *500 Years Later* (፭፻-ዓመታት በኋላ) and *Motherland* (እናት ሀገር) are the first two mainstream Western documentaries to use Ge'ez characters in their titles; in October 2020, tweets by Donald Trump relating to his COVID-19 infection attracted responses with an uncanny image accompanied by copypasta Ge'ez script, often an Amharic curse, and Amharic was then used to evade hate speech detection on TikTok. - **The honest blank.** Ten confessions. (1) The origin place is not settled: the article says the script's origins are debated and may lie in what is now Eritrea, Ethiopia, or Yemen — the entry carries all three without choosing. (2) The vocalization date is not settled: the article gives the 4th century, but Schneider's unpublished early-1990s paper argues Ezana was consciously using an archaic style and vocalization could have occurred much earlier, and the Wazeba coin already carries a vocalized letter ~30 years before Ezana — the entry carries the article's date with the challenge attached. (3) Why vocalization happened is not settled: preserving the pronunciation of an already moribund Ge'ez, or Brahmic influence carried on the Aksum trade routes — two rival explanations, neither proven. (4) Zegdur c. 1300 BCE is tradition recorded by Aleqa Taye, not epigraphy; the epigraphic record begins in the 9th century BCE, 400 years later — the entry keeps the legend and the record apart. (5) The Armenian influence at the end of the fifth century is speculation by "some scholars", not an established descent — the entry carries it as speculation, not as a child system. (6) The article's table lists -wa forms for 21 consonants while Unicode encodes an eighth form for 25 — the table is usage and Unicode is encoding, and the entry does not merge them into one number. (7) The DDA series (U+12F8–U+12FF) and the three combining marks (U+135D–U+135F) sit in the Unicode chart but the article's letter tables never explain them — the entry carries them as Unicode facts, not as article facts, and does not guess which languages use the DDA series. (8) Tigrinya's "few basic consonants falling into disuse in Eritrea" are not enumerated in the article — the entry does not guess which few. (9) Amharic's "V is used for words of foreign origin except for in some Gurage languages" names an exception the article does not resolve — the entry notes it and moves on. (10) The name itself is three names: "Ge'ez script" is the article's title, "Ethiopic" is Unicode's alias, and "fidäl" is what Amharic and Tigrinya call it — and the living use is mostly Amharic and Tigrinya while Ge'ez itself is liturgical, so the script's name outlives the language it was first written for.

- **Decoder-design note (Ge'ez → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The direction that reversed.** The same letters, first written right-to-left as an abjad, then left-to-right as an abugida — the reversal is dated to the vocalization, c. the 4th century, and the Old Ethiopic corpus reads the other way from everything after it. The Gauntlet's direction probe asks what a specimen assumes about direction: a decoder that treats direction as a property of the script rather than of the sitting will misread the entire early corpus, and a specimen that survives reversal confesses that its direction is a convention, not its content. (2) **The vowel that is a shape, not a mark.** The vowel is fused into the consonant's form — there is no separate vowel character to strip, no diacritic to remove, nothing to segment. A specimen that tokenizes by separating "consonant + vowel mark" will find nothing to separate, and a specimen that asks for the consonant alone must know the grid, not parse the glyph. The Gauntlet's fusion probe hands the specimen a syllabary and asks for the consonant: the answer is a table lookup, and a specimen that tries to decompose the glyph instead has confessed its model of writing. (3) **The grid that outgrew its table.** Unicode encodes 326 syllables where the article's table lists 206 forms — the encoding grid is bigger than the linguistic table because it must also hold what real languages needed (š, č, the DDA series, the combining marks). The Gauntlet's coverage probe measures a specimen's claimed script against the encoding, not the textbook: a specimen that knows only the canonical table will miss the letters real languages actually use, and the miss is measurable — 120 forms, the exact size of the gap between the table and the block.

- **The story.** Devanagari (*DAY-və-NAH-gə-ree*; देवनागरी, IAST *Devanāgarī*, Sanskrit pronunciation [deːʋɐnaːɡɑːriː]) is an Indic script used in the Indian subcontinent. Also simply called *Nāgarī* (नागरी), it is a left-to-right abugida based on the ancient *Brāhmī* script. It is one of the official scripts of India and Nepal. It was developed and in regular use by the 8th century CE. It had achieved its modern form by 1000 CE. The Devanāgarī script, composed of 48 primary characters, including 14 vowels and 34 consonants, is the fourth most widely adopted writing system in the world, being used for over 120 languages, the most popular of which is Hindi. Its infobox reads: script type abugida; period 11th century to present; direction left-to-right; official script India, Nepal, Fiji; languages Apabhramsha, Angika, Awadhi, Bajjika, Bhili, Bhojpuri, Boro, Braj, Chhattisgarhi, Dogri, Fiji Hindi, Garhwali, Haryanvi, Hindi, Kashmiri, Khandeshi, Konkani, Kumaoni, Magahi, Maithili, Marathi, Marwari, Mundari, Nagpuri, Newari, Nepali, Pali, Pahari, Prakrit, Rajasthani, Sanskrit, Santali, Saraiki, Sarnami, Sherpa, Shina, Sindhi, Surjapuri, etc. — 38 named; parent systems Egyptian hieroglyphs, Proto-Sinaitic, Phoenician, Aramaic (disputed), Brāhmī, Gupta, Siddhaṃ, Nāgarī, Devanāgarī; sister systems Nandināgarī, Kaithī, Gujarātī, Mōḍī; ISO 15924 Deva (315), Devanagari (Nagari); Unicode alias Devanagari; Unicode ranges U+0900–U+097F Devanagari, U+A8E0–U+A8FF Devanagari Extended, U+11B00–U+11B5F Devanagari Extended-A, U+1CD0–U+1CFF Vedic Extensions. *Devanāgarī* is formed by combining *deva* (देव) with *nāgarī* (नागरी); *nāgarī* is an adjective derived from *nagara* (नगर), a Sanskrit word meaning "town" or "city", literally "urban" or "urbane"; the word *Nāgarī* was used independently to refer to a North Indian script as attested by Al-Biruni in the 11th century, and the form *Devanāgarī* is attested later, at least by the 18th century; the precise origin and significance of the prefix *deva*- ("heavenly" or "god") remains unclear — Fischer's gloss is "heavenly Nagari". Devanagari is part of the Brahmic family of scripts of India, Nepal, Tibet, and Southeast Asia; it is a descendant of the 3rd-century-BCE Brāhmī script, which evolved into the Nagari script which in turn gave birth to Devanāgarī and Nandināgarī. Medieval inscriptions suggest widespread diffusion, with biscripts presenting a local script alongside the adoption of *Nāgarī* scripts: the mid-8th-century Pattadakal pillar in Karnataka has text in both Siddha Matrika script and an early Telugu-Kannada script, while the Kangra Jawalamukhi inscription in Himachal Pradesh is written in both Sharada and Devanāgarī scripts. The *Nāgarī* script was in regular use by the 7th century CE, and fully developed by about the end of the first millennium; Salomon places the development of standardized Devanāgarī around the end of the first millennium, while noting that regional and chronological variation continued. The use of Sanskrit in *Nāgarī* script in medieval India is attested by numerous pillar and cave-temple inscriptions, including the 11th-century Udayagiri inscriptions in Madhya Pradesh and an inscribed brick found in Uttar Pradesh, dated to 1217 CE, now held at the British Museum; Nāgarī has been the *primus inter pares* of the Indic scripts. A mid-10th-century Sanskrit land grant for a college, written in Devanāgarī and discovered on a stone buried in north Karnataka, is partly written in Kannada script. The *Jñānēśvarī*, a commentary on the *Bhagavad Gita* dated to 1290 CE, is written in Marathi using the Devanāgarī script, and a manuscript page of it is dated 1765 Saka, 1843 CE. The orthography of this script reflects the pronunciation of the language; unlike the Latin alphabet, the script has no concept of letter case, meaning the script is a unicameral alphabet; it is written from left to right, has a strong preference for symmetrical, rounded shapes within squared outlines, and is recognisable by a horizontal line, known as a शिरोरेखा *śirorekhā*, that runs along the top of full letters. In a cursory look, the Devanāgarī script appears different from other Indic scripts, such as Bengali-Assamese or Gurmukhi, but a closer examination reveals they are very similar, except for angles and structural emphasis. - **The system.** The letter order of Devanāgarī, like nearly all Brāhmic scripts, is based on phonetic principles that consider both the manner and place of articulation of the consonants and vowels they represent, and is usually referred to as the *varṇamālā* ("garland of letters"). The vowels, fourteen in seven short–long pairs: a अ, ā आ, i इ, ī ई, u उ, ū ऊ, ṛ ऋ, ṝ ॠ, ḷ ऌ, ḹ ॡ, e ए, ai ऐ, o ओ, au औ — with the dependent forms (*mātrā*) ा ि ी ु ू ृ ॄ ॢ ॣ े ै ो ौ, the inherent *a* needing no mark, and the two consonantal diacritics arranged with the vowels, the final nasal *anusvāra* ं *ṃ* and the final fricative *visarga* ः *ḥ*; the *candrabindu* ँ is a more emphatic form of the *anusvāra*, sometimes used to mark a true vowel nasalization (in Hindi the candrabindu indicates vowel nasalisation while the *anusvār* indicates a homorganic nasal preceding another consonant: हँसी "laughter" against गंगा "the Ganges"); the *virāma* or *halanta* ् expresses the absence of a vowel after the consonant; the *avagraha* ऽ is a Sanskrit punctuation mark for the elision of a vowel in sandhi (एकोऽयम् *eko'yam* ← एकस् *ekas* + अयम् *ayam*, "this one"). The sound represented by ṛ has largely been lost in the modern languages, its pronunciation now ranging from [ɾɪ] (Hindi) to [ɾu] (Marathi); the syllabic consonants ṝ, ḷ, and ḹ are specific to Sanskrit, and ḹ is not an actual phoneme of Sanskrit but a graphic convention included among the vowels in order to maintain the symmetry of short–long pairs; Marathi adds ॲ and ऑ ([æ] and [ɒ], also sometimes used in Hindi, as in डॉलर *dôlar*, "dollar"); Kashmiri Devanagari uses ॳ, ॴ, ॶ, ॷ, ऎ, ऒ, औ, ॵ for its vowels. The consonants, thirty-three in the article's table plus ळ: the five *sparśa* rows — velar *kaṇṭhya* क ख ग घ ङ (*ka kha ga gha ṅa*, [k kʰ ɡ ɡʱ ŋ]), palatal *tālavya* च छ ज झ ञ (*ca cha ja jha ña*, [tʃ tʃʰ dʒ dʒʱ ɲ]), retroflex *mūrdhanya* ट ठ ड ढ ण (*ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa*, [ʈ ʈʰ ɖ ɖʱ ɳ]), dental *dantya* त थ द ध न (*ta tha da dha na*, [t̪ t̪ʰ d̪ d̪ʱ n]), labial *oṣṭhya* प फ ब भ म (*pa pha ba bha ma*, [p pʰ b bʱ m]) — each row voiceless unaspirated, voiceless aspirated, voiced unaspirated, voiced aspirated, nasal; the four *antastha* approximants य र ल व (*ya ra la va*, [j r l ʋ]); the three *ūṣman* fricatives श ष स (*śa ṣa sa*, [ʃ ʂ s]); and ह *ha* [ɦ]; plus ळ *ḷa* [ɭ], the intervocalic lateral flap, a phoneme in Marathi, Konkani, Garhwali, and Rajasthani. Beyond the Sanskritic set, new shapes have rarely been formulated — Masica's reading is that all possible sounds had already been described and provided for in this system — and foreign sounds are handled by diacritics and ligatures: the subscript dot (*nuqtā*) gives क़ *qa* /q/, ख़ *xa* /x/, ग़ *ġa* /ɣ/, ज़ *za* /z/, झ़ *zha* /ʒ/, फ़ *fa* /f/, ड़ *ṛa* /ɽ/, ढ़ *ṛha* /ɽʱ/; Sindhi's and Saraiki's implosives take a line attached below (ॻ [ɠə], ॼ [ʄə], ॾ [ɗə], ॿ [ɓə]); aspirated sonorants are written as conjuncts with ह (म्ह *mha*, न्ह *nha*, ण्ह *ṇha*, व्ह *vha*, ल्ह *lha*, ळ्ह *ḷha*, र्ह *rha*); Marwari uses ॸ for *ḍa* [ɗə]; Avestan written in Devanagari uses ॹ /ʒ/. Successive consonants lacking a vowel between them may physically join as a conjunct consonant or ligature: 24 out of the 36 consonants contain a vertical right stroke and lose it as first or middle members (त्‌व *t-va* → त्व *tva*, ण्‌ढ *ṇ-ḍha* → ण्ढ *ṇḍha*, स्‌थ *s-tha* → स्थ *stha*); श *śa* appears as a ribbon-shaped fragment preceding व, न, च, ल, and र (श्व *śva*, श्न *śna*, श्च *śca*, श्ल *śla*, श्र *śra*, and शृ *śṛi*); र *ra* as a first member takes a curved upward dash above the final character or its *ā-* diacritic (र्व *rva*, र्वा *rvā*, र्स्प *rspa*, र्स्पा *rspā*), and in Marathi and Nepali an eyelash form before glides and semivowels (र्‍य *rya*, र्‍व *rva*); as a final member with ट, ठ, ड, ढ, ड़, छ it is two lines together below the character pointed downwards (ट्र *ṭra*, ठ्र *ṭhra*, ड्र *ḍra*, ढ्र *ḍhra*, ड़्र *ṛra*, छ्र *chra*), and elsewhere a diagonal stroke extending leftwards and down (क्र *kra*, ग्र *gra*, भ्र *bhra*, ब्र *bra*); त *ta* is shifted up to make the conjunct त्र *tra*; as first members, characters lacking vertical strokes such as द *da* and ह *ha* may have their second member, reduced in size and lacking its horizontal stroke, placed underneath, while क *ka*, छ *cha*, and फ *pha* shorten their right hooks and join them directly to the following member; the conjuncts for *kṣa* and *jña* are not clearly derived from the letters making up their components — क्ष (क् + ष) and ज्ञ (ज् + ञ). The combinations of all Sanskrit consonants and vowels are laid out in the *bārākhaḍī* (बाराखडी) table. The pitch accent of Vedic Sanskrit is written with a bar below the line for *anudātta*, a stroke above the line for *svarita*, and nothing for *udātta*. The end of a sentence or half-verse may be marked with the daṇḍa । ("bar", or *pūrṇa virām*, "full stop/pause"), a full verse with the double daṇḍa ॥; Western punctuation (colon, semicolon, exclamation mark, dash, question mark) has been in use in Devanāgarī script since at least the 1900s. The digits are ० १ २ ३ ४ ५ ६ ७ ८ ९. Eight romanisation systems are named in the article: the Hunterian system, the national system of romanisation in India; ISO 15919, codified in 2001, whose Devanāgarī-specific portion is nearly identical to IAST; IAST, the academic standard, based on a standard established by the Congress of Orientalists at Athens in 1912; Harvard-Kyoto, which uses capital letters and was designed to simplify putting Sanskrit texts into machine-readable form; ITRANS, a lossless ASCII scheme (v5.30, July 2001, created by Avinash Chopde) in which the word *devanāgarī* is written "devanaagarii" or "devanAgarI"; Velthuis (1996, Frans Velthuis, for TeX, in which case is irrelevant); ALA-LC romanisation, approved by the Library of Congress and the American Library Association; and WX (IIT Kanpur), a prefix code in which every consonant and every vowel has a single mapping into Roman — the retroflex stops are mapped to *t, T, d, D, N*, the dentals to *w, W, x, X, n*, hence the name WX. ISCII is an 8-bit encoding whose lower 128 codepoints are plain ASCII; it has largely been superseded by Unicode, which has, however, attempted to preserve the ISCII layout for its Indic language blocks. - **Decoder-design note (Devanagari → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The headline that is not a letter.** The *śirorekhā* runs along the top of full letters — a rail the letters hang from, not a stroke of any of them. A specimen that segments glyphs by their ink will read the rail as part of the letters and fail to find any letter boundary at the top; a specimen that knows the rail is a convention, not content, strips it first. The Gauntlet's rail probe hands the specimen a word with the headline removed and asks whether it is the same word: the answer is yes, and a specimen that says no has confessed that its letters are pictures. (2) **The grid that predicts.** The *varṇamālā* is a phonetics table, not a list: five places by five manners, every cell filled, and an empty cell would be a sound. A specimen that knows the grid can name a letter it has never seen by its coordinates — third row, fourth column is *ḍha* before it is a glyph; a specimen that treats the alphabet as 34 arbitrary signs has confessed it has no phonetics. The Gauntlet's grid probe asks for the letter at a coordinate, not for a memorized glyph — and Ge'ez's irregular grid is the control: there the grid has holes, here it has none. (3) **The conjunct that hides the seam.** क्ष and ज्ञ are not derivable from their parts — the ligature is a new glyph, and a specimen that decomposes conjuncts by rule will misread exactly the two commonest conjuncts in the language. Worse, the seam is invisible in the other direction: शृ looks like a cluster and is a vowel sign, with no virama anywhere in it. The Gauntlet's seam probe asks the specimen to split a conjunct into its consonants and to say, for each so-called cluster, whether a virama is really there — the specimen that splits शृ has confessed it reads shapes, not encodings.

- **The story.** The traditional Mongolian script (ᠮᠣᠩᠭᠣᠯ ᠪᠢᠴᠢᠭ *mongɣol bičig*), also known as the Hudum Mongol bichig (ᠬᠤᠳᠤᠮ ᠮᠣᠩᠭᠣᠯ ᠪᠢᠴᠢᠭ *qudum mongɣol bičig*), is an alphabet: script type alphabet; creator Tata-tonga; period c. 1204–1941 (common use), 1941–present (common use in Inner Mongolia; chiefly ceremonial use in Mongolia); direction vertical top-to-bottom, left-to-right; language Mongolian; ISO 15924 Mong (145); Unicode alias Mongolian; Unicode ranges U+1800–U+18AF Mongolian, U+11660–U+1167F Mongolian Supplement. It was the first writing system created specifically for the Mongolian language, and the most widespread until the introduction of Cyrillic in 1946. It is a co-official script in Mongolia since 2025, alongside the Cyrillic script, and the official written form taught in schools for Mongolian ethnic students in the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. Derived from the Old Uyghur alphabet, it is a true alphabet, with separate letters for consonants and vowels; it has been adapted for Oirat and Manchu, and alphabets based on this classical vertical script continue to be used in Mongolia and Inner Mongolia to write Mongolian, Xibe and, experimentally, Evenki. Computer operating systems have been slow to adopt support for the Mongolian script; almost all have incomplete support or other text rendering difficulties. The vertical script developed as an adaptation of the Old Uyghur alphabet for the Mongolian language: Tata-tonga, a 13th-century Uyghur scribe captured by Genghis Khan, was responsible for bringing the Old Uyghur alphabet to the Mongolian Plateau and adapting it to the form of the Mongolian script. The earliest known inscription is the Stone of Genghis Khan, the Stele of Yisüngge. From the seventh and eighth to the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries the Mongolian language separated into southern, eastern and western dialects; the principal documents of the Middle Mongol period are the famous text *The Secret History of the Mongols*, monuments in the Square script, materials of the 14th-century Chinese–Mongolian glossary, and the Arab–Mongolian and Persian–Mongolian dictionaries. In that period the vowels *ï* and *i* lost their phonemic significance, intervocal *ɣ*/*g* and *b*/*w* disappeared, the formation of long vowels began, and the initial *h* was preserved — which is why the Mongolian script looks like a vertical Arabic script, in particular the dot system. Minor concessions followed: in the 17th and 18th centuries smoother and more angular versions of the letter *tsadi* became associated with /dʒ/ and /tʃ/ respectively; in the 19th century the Manchu hooked *yodh* was adopted for initial /j/; *zain* was dropped as redundant for /s/. Words are written vertically from top to bottom, flowing in lines from left to right. The Old Uyghur script and its descendants — Oirat Clear, Manchu, and Buryat — are the only known vertical scripts written from left to right: the Uyghurs rotated their Sogdian-derived script, originally written right to left, 90 degrees counterclockwise to emulate Chinese writing, but without changing the relative orientation of the letters. The reed pen was the writing instrument of choice until the 18th century, when the brush took its place under Chinese influence; pens were also historically made of wood, bamboo, bone, bronze, or iron; ink was black or cinnabar red, written on birch bark, paper, cloths made of silk or cotton, and wooden or silver plates. Mongols learned their script as a syllabary, dividing the syllables into twelve different classes based on the final phonemes of the syllables, all of which ended in vowels. The script remained in continuous use by Mongolian speakers in Inner Mongolia; in the Mongolian People's Republic it was largely replaced by the Mongolian Cyrillic alphabet, although the vertical script remained in limited use. In March 2020 the Mongolian government announced plans to increase the use of the traditional Mongolian script and to use both Cyrillic and Mongolian script in official documents by 2025; a large part (40%) of the Sinicized Mongols in China are unable to read or write this script, and in many cases the script is only used symbolically on plaques in many cities. The script is known by a wide variety of names: as derived from the Old Uyghur alphabet it is the Uighur(-)Mongol script; from 1941 onwards it became the Old Script (*qaɣučin bičig*) in contrast to the New Script (*sine bičig*), Cyrillic; it is also known as the *Hudum* or "not exact" script in comparison with the Todo "clear, exact" script, and as the "vertical script" (*bošuɣ-a bičig*). - **The system.** The traditional alphabet does not distinguish several vowels (*o*/*u*, *ö*/*ü*, final *a*/*e*) and consonants (syllable-initial *t*/*d* and *k*/*g*, sometimes *ǰ*/*y*) that were not required for Uyghur — a situation the article compares to English, which must represent ten or more vowels with only five letters and uses the digraph *th* for two distinct sounds; ambiguity is sometimes prevented by context, as the requirements of vowel harmony and syllable sequence usually indicate the correct sound, and there are few words with an exactly identical spelling. Vowel harmony separates the vowels of words into three groups: the back, male, masculine, hard, or yang vowels *a*, *o*, and *u*; the front, female, feminine, soft, or yin vowels *e*, *ö*, and *ü*; and the neutral vowel *i*, able to appear in all words. Letters have different forms depending on their position in a word — initial, medial, or final — and in some cases additional graphic variants are selected for visual harmony with the subsequent character. A separated final form of vowels *a* or *e* is common at the end of a word stem or suffix, requiring a final-shaped preceding letter and a word-internal gap in between (transliterated with a hyphen; in digital typesetting the gap is a U+180E Mongolian Vowel Separator); the presence or lack of a separated *a* or *e* can indicate differences in meaning — ᠬᠠᠷᠠ *qar-a* "black" against ᠬᠠᠷᠠ *qara* "to look". All case suffixes, as well as any plural suffixes consisting of one or two syllables, are likewise separated by a preceding and hyphen-transliterated gap, and a maximum of two case suffixes can be added to a stem. Two medial consonants are the most that can come together in original Mongolian words. In the modern language, proper names can join two words into graphic compounds (ᠬᠠᠰᠡᠷᠳᠡᠨᠢ *Qas'erdeni* "Jasper-jewel", ᠬᠥᠬᠡᠬᠣᠲᠠ *Kökeqota*, the city of Hohhot), which also allows components of different harmonic classes to be joined together. Isolate citation forms for syllables containing *o*, *u*, *ö*, and *ü* may appear without a final tail (*bo*/*bu*, *mo*/*mu*) or with a vertical tail (*bö*/*bü*, *mö*/*mü*). The article's Flaws section is blunt: in the traditional script certain letters — such as *t* and *d*, *o* and *u* — were frequently confused, letter formation varied inconsistently at the beginning, middle, and end of words, poor legibility between letters and the requirement to memorize each syllable's shape individually increased the learning burden, and its structural characteristics led to wider line spacing, consuming more space and paper — in Qing-dynasty texts like the *Pentaglot Dictionary*, the Manchu and Mongolian sections occupy a larger portion of the page. The letters: seven vowels (*a e i o u ö ü*) and sixteen consonants (*n ng b p q ɣ m l s š t d č ǰ y r*), each with initial, medial, and final forms. Only in a late form can a definite order be established: the South (inner) Mongolian order runs *a e i o u ö ü n b p q k ɣ g m l s š t d č ǰ y r v* with *(f) (ž) (c) (k) (h)* parenthesized as loans; a 1986 primer orders *q k ɣ g ǰ y t d m č r s š l v* with *(p) (z)*; dictionaries after 1924 add *(f) (p) (ž)*. In 1587 the translator and scholar Ayuush Güüsh created the Galik alphabet (*Ali-gali*), inspired by the third Dalai Lama Sonam Gyatso, primarily adding extra characters for transcribing Tibetan and Sanskrit terms when translating religious texts, and later also from Chinese; the article's table holds thirteen Galik rows, twelve of them new code points and one a reuse of native *t*. In 1917 the politician and linguist Bayantömöriin Khaisan repurposed three Galik letters to represent the Mandarin retroflex consonants — ᠿ *ž* for *r* (日 *rì*), ᡁ *zh* for *zh* (之 *zhī*), ᡂ *ch* for *ch* (蚩 *chī*) — and these letters remain in use in Inner Mongolia for transcribing Chinese; Galik characters are also used for transcription of loanwords. Punctuation marks use space on both sides of them and can appear at the very end of a line: the birga ᠀ marks the start of a book, chapter, passage, or first line; the dot ᠂ is a comma; the double-dot ᠃ a period; the four-fold dot ᠅ marks the end of a passage, paragraph, or chapter; the dotted line ᠁ is an ellipsis; the parallel dots ᠄ a colon; the spine ᠆ is a soft hyphen; the nirugu ᠊ a non-breaking hyphen or stem extender. Red cinnabar ink is used in many manuscripts to symbolize emphasis or respect; modern punctuation incorporates Western marks, including precomposed ⁈ and ⁉. The numerals are ᠐ ᠑ ᠒ ᠓ ᠔ ᠕ ᠖ ᠗ ᠘ ᠙, written from left to right or from top to bottom, and rotated 90° in modern books to fit on the line. The script is built from named components — tooth, crown, spine, tail, short tail, crook, hook, shin and its variants, bow, belly, hind-gut, braid/pigtail and horn, corner of the mouth, fork prong, fork, tusk/fang, flaglet/tuft — and the components still carry their Semitic ancestor names: the tooth is the main part of *a*/*e* (from Old Uyghur *aleph*), *n* (*nun*, also part of the digraph *ng*), *q*/*ɣ* (*gimel-heth*), *m* (*mem*), *l* (hooked *resh*), and initial *t*/*d* (*taw*), historically also part of *k*/*g* (*kaph*) and *r* (*resh*); the crown is an exaggerated initial tooth for the leading *aleph* of initial vowels; the spine is the vertical line running through words; the belly is the counter of *o*/*u*/*ö*/*ü* (*waw*), *b*, *p*, and initial *t*/*d*; the fork prong is *č* (angular *tsade*). Written Mongolian divides into three periods: pre-classical (beginning–17th century), classical (16th/17th century–20th century), and modern (20th century onward). - **Decoder-design note (Mongolian → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The rotation that is not a direction.** The letters kept their relative orientation while the line turned 90° — the rotation lives in the glyphs, not in a direction flag. A specimen that treats "vertical" as a layout property will reflow the text as horizontal and read it sideways; a specimen that knows the turn will rotate the line and keep the letters. The Gauntlet's rotation probe hands the specimen a word rendered horizontally with its letters unrotated and asks which way it reads: the specimen that reads it has confessed it never learned the turn. (2) **The letter that is two sounds.** o/u, ö/ü, t/d, k/g share glyphs by design, and the reader resolves them by harmony and context — qara and qar-a are the same four letters, and only the gap tells black from looking. A specimen that demands one glyph per sound will hallucinate distinctions that are not there; a specimen that reads by word-shape and harmony will get it right. The Gauntlet's ambiguity probe asks the specimen to read the pair and to say, for each letter, which sound it is and what decided it: the specimen that answers from the glyph alone has confessed it reads letters, not words. (3) **The encoding that is eleven spellings.** Eleven different code-point sequences spell "Mongolia" in the wild; the phonetic model stores sound, the graphetic model stores shape, and Unicode chose sound — so the same word is eleven different strings at the byte level and one word at the rendering level. A specimen that normalizes by code point will count eleven words; a specimen that normalizes by rendering will count one. The Gauntlet's spelling probe hands the specimen the eleven spellings and asks how many words: the specimen that says eleven has confessed it decodes bytes, not writing. The FVS layer is the tell: o and u are the same shape, and only a variation selector knows which one was meant.

- **The story.** The Manchu alphabet (Manchu: ᠮᠠᠨᠵᠤ ᡥᡝᡵᡤᡝᠨ *manju hergen*, Möllendorff: *manju hergen*, Abkai: *manju hergen*) is the alphabet used to write the now critically endangered Manchu language. A similar script called Xibe script is used today by the Xibe people, whose language is considered either a dialect of Manchu or a closely related, mutually intelligible language. It is written vertically from top to bottom, with columns proceeding from left to right: script type alphabet; languages Manchu, Xibe; ISO 15924 Mong (145), Mongolian; Unicode alias Mongolian. Its parent systems run Egyptian hieroglyphs → Proto-Sinaitic → Phoenician → Aramaic → Syriac → Sogdian → Old Uyghur → Mongolian script → Manchu script, and its child systems are the Dagur alphabet and the Xibe alphabet. The Jurchens of a millennium ago became the ancestors of the Manchus when Nurhaci united the Jianzhou Jurchens (1593–1618) and his son subsequently renamed the consolidated tribes as the "Manchu"; the Jurchen script has no relation to the Manchu alphabet, as it was derived from the Khitan script, itself derived from Chinese characters, and fell into disuse after the collapse of the Jin dynasty. According to the *Veritable Records* (Manchu: ᠮᠠᠨᠵᠤ ᡳ ᠶᠠᡵᡤᡳᠶᠠᠨ ᡴᠣᠣᠯᡳ, romanized: *manju i yargiyan kooli*; Chinese: 滿洲實錄; pinyin: *Mǎnzhōu Shílù*), in 1599 Nurhaci decided to convert the Mongolian alphabet to make it suitable for the Manchu people: he decried the fact that while illiterate Han Chinese and Mongolians could understand their respective languages when read aloud, that was not the case for the Manchus, whose documents were recorded by Mongolian scribes. Overriding the objections of two advisors named Erdeni and G'ag'ai, he is credited with adapting the Mongolian script to Manchu. The resulting script was known as *tongki fuka akū hergen* (Manchu: ᡨ᠋ᠣᠩᡴᡳ ᡶ᠋ᠤᡴᠠ ᠠᡴᡡ ᡥᡝᡵᡤᡝᠨ) — the "script without dots and circles". In 1632, Dahai added diacritical marks to clear up the ambiguity of the original Mongolian script — for instance, a leading *k*, *g*, and *h* are distinguished by the placement of no diacritical mark, a dot, and a circle, respectively — and this revision created the standard script, known as *tongki fuka sindaha hergen* (Manchu: ᡨ᠋ᠣᠩᡴᡳ ᡶ᠋ᠤᡴᠠ ᠰᡳᠨᡩ᠋ᠠᡥᠠ ᡥᡝᡵᡤᡝᠨ) — the "script with dots and circles"; as a result, the Manchu alphabet contains little ambiguity. Recently discovered manuscripts from the 1620s make clear, however, that the addition of dots and circles to Manchu script began before their supposed introduction by Dahai. Dahai also added the *tulergi hergen* ("foreign/outer letters"): ten graphemes to facilitate Manchu being used to write Chinese, Sanskrit, and Tibetan loanwords; previously, these non-Manchu sounds did not have corresponding letters in Manchu. By the middle of the nineteenth century, there were three styles of writing Manchu in use: standard script (*ginggulere hergen*), semi-cursive script (*gidara hergen*), and cursive script (*lasihire hergen*); semicursive script had less spacing between the letters, and cursive script had rounded tails. The Manchu alphabet was also used to write Chinese, and the Manchu versions of the *Thousand Character Classic* and *Dream of the Red Chamber* are actually the Manchu transcription of all the Chinese characters; in the *Imperial Liao-Jin-Yuan Three Histories National Language Explanation* commissioned by the Qianlong Emperor, the Manchu alphabet is used to write Evenki (Solon) words, and in the *Pentaglot Dictionary*, also commissioned by the Qianlong Emperor, it is used to transcribe Tibetan and Chagatai words. Nurhaci's coin reads *Abkai fulingga han jiha* and is written ᠠᠪᡴᠠᡳ ᡶ᠋ᠣᠯᡳᠩᡤᠠ ᡴᠠᠨ ᠵᡳᡥᠠ without diacritics (ᠠᠪᡴᠠᡳ ᡶ᠋ᠤᠯᡳᠩᡤᠠ ᡥᠠᠨ ᠵᡳᡥᠠ with later diacritics) — the same legend reads *kan* without the marks and *han* with them, and its *fulingga* reads *o* without them and *u* with them. - **The system.** The article's alphabet table holds thirty-five rows: eight vowels and twenty-seven consonants. The vowels are *a e i o u ū* with *y* and the trigraph *ioi* for Chinese loanwords; the consonants are nineteen native (*n ng k g h b p s š t d l m c j y r f v*) and eight foreign single letters (*k' g' h' ts' dz ž c' j'*). The 1632 reform is the system: a leading *k*, *g*, *h* are distinguished by no mark, a dot, and a circle before the back vowels *a, o, ū*, and each of the three carries a second form-set before the front vowels *e, i, u* — the second *k* opens with ᢉ (U+1889, ALI GALI KA), the second *g* carries FVS1, the second *h* is the Sibe HA glyph. Every letter has isolated, initial, medial, and final forms, and the table's census is 42 form-rows (the extra rows are the second sets of *k, g, h* and the extra rows of *t, d, f*), 168 positional slots, 136 filled, 32 gaps, and 10 extra variant cells — 146 attested shapes. The *tulergi hergen* are ten graphemes: six single letters (*k' g' h' ts' dz ž*) and four digraphs built on ᡟ (*ts* ᡮ᠊ᡟ, *sy* ᠰ᠊ᡟ, *c'y* ᡱᡟ, *j'y* ᡷᡟ); the table's other two foreign rows, *c'* and *j'*, are the digraphs' bases. Despite its alphabetic nature, the Manchu "alphabet" was traditionally taught as a syllabary to reflect its phonotactics: children memorized the shapes of all the syllables separately and said right away "*la*, *lo*", instead of saying "*l*, *a* — *la*"; the syllables do not contain all possible combinations, and the consonants *l*, *m*, *n*, and *r* are not used as in English — if the Manchu letters *s*, *m*, *a*, *r*, and *t* were joined in that order, a Manchu would not pronounce them as "smart". The syllables are divided into twelve categories called *uju* (literally "head") based on their syllabic codas: *a, ai, ar, an, ang, ak, as, at, ab, ao, al, am*; Manchu allows nine final consonants for its closed syllables, otherwise a syllable is open with a monophthong (*a uju*) or a diphthong (*ai uju* and *ao uju*). It is still divided among experts whether the Manchu script is alphabetic or syllabic: in China it is considered syllabic and Manchu is still taught in this manner, while in the West it is treated like an alphabet — Denis Sinor urged the syllabic theory, Louis Ligeti preferred to consider it alphabetical. The punctuation is two marks: two dots ᠉, analogous to a period, and one dot ᠈, analogous to a comma; with the exception of lists of nouns being reliably punctuated by single dots, punctuation in Manchu is inconsistent, and the equivalent of the question mark consists of special particles written at the end of the question. The encoding carries its own quirks: *r* is ᠷ (U+1837) in isolation and ᡵ (U+1875, MANCHU RA) in context — the only letter whose contextual forms live in a different sub-range than its isolated form — and *o* and *u* are the same shape, with only a variation selector knowing which: Unicode's presentation form for U is U+1824 FVS1, the second isolate form, to distinguish it from the visually identical U+1823 O, and for UE it is U+1826 FVS2, the third isolate form. - **Decoder-design note (Manchu → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The dot that is a letter.** *k*, *g*, *h* differ by no mark, a dot, a circle — the diacritic is the phoneme, not decoration, and the coin proves it: *kan* undotted, *han* dotted. A specimen that strips diacritics as noise collapses three letters into one and reads a khan as a *kan*. The Gauntlet's dot probe hands the specimen the dotted and undotted coin legend and asks for the reading: the specimen that reads both the same has confessed it normalizes away the signal. (2) **The syllabary that is an alphabet.** Twelve *uju*, 131 syllables in the *a uju* alone, children taught to say "*la, lo*" and never "*l, a — la*"; join *s, m, a, r, t* and a Manchu reader will not say "smart" — the syllabary has no such path. A specimen that decodes letter by letter will pronounce the word the letters spell; a specimen that knows the teaching will say the letters have no licit path. The Gauntlet's "smart" probe joins *s, m, a, r, t* and asks what it says: the specimen that reads "smart" has confessed it reads letters, not the syllabary's licit paths. (3) **The letter that is two code points.** *r* is U+1837 in isolation and U+1875 in context; *k*'s second set opens at U+1889, an Ali Gali code point; *o* and *u* are the same shape and only FVS1 knows which. A specimen that counts code points counts three letters where there is one *r*, and one word where the bytes say two. The Gauntlet's code-point probe hands the specimen the two encodings of *r* and asks how many letters: the specimen that says two has confessed it decodes bytes, not writing.

- **The story.** The Phagspa (ʼPhags-pa, ḥPʻags-pa) is an alphabet designed by the Tibetan monk and State Preceptor (later Imperial Preceptor) Drogön Chögyal Phagpa (1235–1280) for Kublai Khan (r. 1264–1294), the founder of the Yuan dynasty (1271–1368) in China, as a unified script for the written languages within the Yuan. The actual use of the script was limited to about a hundred years during the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty, and it fell out of use with the advent of the Ming dynasty. It was used to write and transcribe varieties of Chinese, the Tibetic languages, Mongolian, the Uyghur language, Sanskrit, probably Persian, and other neighboring languages during the Yuan era — for historical linguists, its use provides clues about changes in these languages. The Mongol rulers wanted a universal script: the Uyghur-based Mongolian alphabet was not a perfect fit for Middle Mongol, and it would have been impractical to extend it to a language with a very different phonology like Chinese — so in c. 1269 Kublai Khan asked ʼPhags-pa to design a new alphabet for the whole empire, and he extended his native Tibetan alphabet to encompass Mongol and Chinese, evidently Central Plains Mandarin. The resulting 38 letters have been known by several descriptive names, such as "square script", based on their shape, but today are primarily known as the ʼPhags-pa alphabet. Descending from Tibetan script, it is part of the Brahmic family, which includes Devanagari and the scripts of Southeast Asia and Central Asia — and it is unique among Brahmic scripts in that it is written from top to bottom, as classical Chinese used to be written and as the Mongolian and later Manchu alphabets still are. It did not receive wide acceptance and was not a popular script even among the elite Mongols themselves, although it was used as an official script of the Yuan dynasty until the early 1350s, when the Red Turban Rebellion started. After this, it was mainly used as a phonetic gloss for Mongols learning Chinese characters. In the 20th century it was also used as one of the scripts on Tibetan currency, as a script for Tibetan seal inscriptions from the Middle Ages up to the 20th century, and for inscriptions on the entrance doors of Tibetan monasteries. Its descendant systems include Horizontal square script, used to write Tibetan and Sanskrit; during the Pax Mongolica the script even made numerous appearances in Western medieval art. The names it carries are the map of its career: Mongolian *dörvöljin üseg* "square script" and *dörvöljin bichig* "square writing"; Tibetan *hor yig gsar pa* "new Mongolian script"; Yuan-dynasty Chinese 蒙古新字 *měnggǔ xīnzì* "new Mongolian script" and 國字 *guózì* "national script"; modern Chinese 八思巴文 *bāsībā wén* and 帕克斯巴 *pàkèsībā*; in English it is also written Phaspa, Paspa, Baschpah, and Pa-sse-pa. In its own letters it calls itself ꡏꡡꡃ ꡣꡡꡙ ꡐꡜꡞ *mong xol ts.hi* — "Mongolian script". - **The system.** The article's basic letters are forty-one: letters 1–30 and 35–38 are base consonants, in the same order as the thirty basic letters of the Tibetan script, to which they correspond; letters 31–34 and 39 are vowels, in the traditional order of the corresponding Tibetan vowels; letters 40–41 are the subjoined semi-vowels *w* and *y*. Letters 35–38 represent sounds that do not occur in Tibetan: letter 35 *q* and letter 36 *x* are both derived from the simple Tibetan letter ཁ *kha* but are graphically distinct from each other and from letter 2, and letter 36 is derived from the complex Tibetan letter ཁྭ *khwa*; letter 37 *f* is derived from ཧྭ *hwa*; letter 38 is the unnamed one, ꡥ, which the Unicode chart names GGA and notes was created by reversal of QA — a letter with no language attached. Seven additional letters (42–48) carry Sanskrit and Tibetan: the retroflexes TTA, TTHA, DDA, NNA; the subjoined RA and the superfixed RA; and the candrabindu ^. As with Tibetan, the letters carry an inherent [a] in non-final positions when no other vowel is present — ꡀ alone is *ka*, ꡀꡞ is *ki* — but unlike Tibetan, all ʼPhags-pa letters are written in temporal order, /CV/ as C–V for all vowels, and in-line, the vowels not diacritics: the script is transitional between an abugida, a syllabary, and a full alphabet, and the letters of a syllable are linked together so they form syllabic blocks. Short /a/ is not written except initially, so words that start with an *a* vowel use the null base consonant ꡝ *'a* (letter 30) — Mongolian *'a mi than* "living beings" — and initial vowels other than *a* may occur without a base consonant at all: Chinese *u* 吳 *wú*, *on* 刓 *wán*, *o* 訛 *é*; Mongolian *ong qo chas* "boats", *u su nu* "water", *e du -ee* "now", *i hee -een* "protection". Initial semi-vowels, diphthongs, and digraphs must attach to the null base: Chinese *'wen* 元 *yuán*, *'ue* 危 *wēi*, *'eeu* 魚 *yú*; Mongolian *'eeu lu* "not", *'eeog bee.e* "gave". The other null letter is SMALL A, ꡖ (letter 23): found rarely initially, frequently medially between vowels, where it separates a syllable that starts with a vowel from a preceding syllable that ends in a vowel — *er khee -ud* "Christians", *q-an* "emperor, khan" — and it is transliterated with U+A78F ꞏ LATIN LETTER SINOLOGICAL DOT: the dot is a letter. The letters are economical with their rarity: letter 1 *k* is used in Mongolian only for foreign words and the single native word *ye kee* "large, great"; letter 22 *z* occurs in the single word *za ra* "month"; letter 29 *h* stands initially in words that now have null initials, such as *har ban* "ten" against *arban*; letter 39 *ee* is never found in an initial position in any language. The script was written in three graphic forms: the standard form, blocky; the "Tibetan" form, even more so, almost entirely straight orthogonal lines and right angles; and the seal script form (蒙古篆字 *měnggǔ zhuànzì*, "Mongolian Seal Script"), used for imperial seals, more elaborate, with squared sinusoidal lines and spirals. The seal form carries the Hangul question: Korean records state that Hangul was based on an "Old Seal Script" (古篆字), which may be ʼPhags-pa — but it is the simpler standard form that is the closer graphic match. A second, later "ʼPhags-pa script" shares the name but is a Tibetan seal script whose earliest usage traces to the late 16th century, the early reign of the Wanli Emperor — a namesake, not the same script. The *Menggu Ziyun* (蒙古字韻), the Yuan-dynasty rhyming dictionary, orders the script's initials by the Chinese philological tradition of the 36 initials — and the table is a voicing flip: the letter named *g*, ꡂ, writes [k], and the letter named *k*, ꡀ, writes [ɡ]; *d*, ꡊ, writes [t] and *t*, ꡈ, writes [d]; *b*, ꡎ, writes [p] and *p*, ꡌ, writes [b]; *dz*, ꡒ, writes [ts] and *ts*, ꡐ, writes [dz]. The *Shilin Guangji* used Phags-pa to annotate Chinese text, a precursor to modern pinyin: the Hundred Family Surnames opens ꡎꡗ ꡂꡨ ꡛꡞꡃ ꡏꡟꡃ ꡂꡟ ꡓꡟꡋ *Bay Gya Sing Mung Gu Wun*, and the name Jin (金), meaning gold, is written ꡂꡞꡏ *gim*. - **Decoder-design note (Phags-pa → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The letter with no language.** GGA exists because a shape was reversed — QA flipped — and no language ever claimed it. A specimen that demands every symbol carry a sound will invent one for GGA. The Gauntlet's GGA probe hands the specimen ꡥ and asks which language it writes: the specimen that answers a language has confessed it fills blanks; the specimen that says none has read the chart. (2) **The flipped voicing table.** Eight of the thirty-six initials are swaps: the letter named *g* writes [k] and the letter named *k* writes [ɡ]. A specimen that reads letter names as sounds reads the Chinese initials backwards. The Gauntlet's flip probe hands the specimen 見 *jiàn* written ꡂ and asks for the sound: the specimen that says [ɡ] has confessed it reads the name, not the table. (3) **The vowel that mirrors.** After a retroflex, the vowel reverses — the same code point, a mirrored glyph, switched on by VS01 — and O mirrors in position but never by selector. A specimen that treats a code point as a glyph will count a mirrored vowel as a second letter. The Gauntlet's mirror probe hands the specimen the same vowel regular and reversed and asks how many letters: the specimen that says two has confessed it decodes glyphs, not letters — and the dot that is a letter, SMALL A transliterated with U+A78F, is the same probe in miniature: the specimen that drops the dot has dropped a letter.

## The Soyombo script (1686–18th century) — the abugida that became a flag, or: the script that writes horizontally under a backbone
