- **The story.** The Soyombo script (Mongolian: Соёмбо бичиг, 𑪁𑩖𑩻𑩖𑪌𑩰𑩖 𑩰𑩑𑩢𑩑𑪊, romanized: *Soyombo bichig*, lit. "self-created holy letters") is an abugida invented by the Mongolian Buddhist monk Zanabazar in 1686 to write Mongolian. It can also be used to write Tibetan and Sanskrit. The name is derived from the Sanskrit word *svayambhu* "self-created" — and a legend talks about Zanabazar seeing letter-like signs in the sky one night, which he turned into his new script. Zanabazar (1635–1723), the first spiritual leader of Tibetan Buddhism in Mongolia — the first Bogd Jebtsundamba Khutuktu, Öndör Gegeen — also designed the Zanabazar Square script, and the Soyombo script was created as the fourth Mongolian script, only 38 years after the invention of the Clear Script. The syllabic system appears to be based on Devanagari, while the base shape of the letters is derived from the Ranjana script; details of individual characters resemble traditional Mongolian writing systems and the Old Turkic script. The eastern Mongols used the script primarily as a ceremonial and decorative script. Zanabazar had created it for the translation of Buddhist texts from Sanskrit or Tibetan, and both he and his students used it extensively for that purpose. As it was much too complicated to be adopted as an everyday script, its use is practically nonexistent today. Aside from historical texts, it can usually be found in temple inscriptions. It also has some relevance to linguistic research, because it reflects certain developments in the Mongolian language, such as that of long vowels. The Soyombo script was the first Mongolian script to be written horizontally from left to right, in contrast to earlier scripts that had been written vertically. A special character of the script, the Soyombo symbol, became a national symbol of Mongolia and has appeared on the national flag and emblem of Mongolia since 1911, as well as in money and postage stamps. The symbol has appeared on the national flag since independence in 1911 (except between 1940 and 1945); it served as the Emblem of Mongolia from 1911 to 1940, and was included in the design again in 1960. It also serves as a traditional symbol of Mongolia, Buryatia and Kalmykia, and the flag of Buryatia, the flag of Agin-Buryat Okrug, and the flag of the Inner Mongolian People's Party all display its top elements — flame, sun, and moon. The Soyombo has ten elements in the columnar arrangement: fire, sun, crescent moon, two triangles, two horizontal rectangles, the *Taijitu* (yin and yang), and two vertical rectangles. Fire is a general symbol of eternal growth, wealth, and success, and the three tongues of the flame represent the past, present, and future. Sun and crescent moon symbolize the existence of the Mongolian nation for eternity as the eternal blue sky; the Mongolian symbol of the sun, crescent moon and fire derived from the Xiongnu. The two triangles allude to the point of an arrow or spear, pointing downward to announce the defeat of interior and exterior enemies. The two horizontal rectangles give stability to the round shape; the rectangular shape represents the honesty and justice of the people, whether they stand at the top or at the bottom of society. The Yin and Yang symbol illustrates the mutual complement of opposites, interpreted as two fish, symbolizing vigilance, because fish never close their eyes. The two vertical rectangles can be interpreted as the walls of a fort, representing unity and strength, relating to the Mongolian proverb: "The friendship of two is stronger than stone walls." It is thought to be possible that the symbol itself may predate the script. The Soyombo script has been included in the Unicode Standard since the release of Unicode version 10.0 in June 2017; the proposal to encode Soyombo was submitted by Anshuman Pandey and revised in December 2015. - **The system.** As in other Brahmic scripts, a consonant in the Soyombo script carries an inherent vowel, *a*, so the letter ⟨𑩜⟩ is pronounced *ka*; syllables with other vowel sounds are constructed by adding a vowel mark to the base character, so ⟨𑩜𑩑⟩ is *ki*. The first character of the alphabet ⟨𑩐⟩ acts as a null consonant or vowel carrier, allowing formation of syllables beginning with a vowel sound; on its own, it represents a short *a*. The consonants run in the Sanskrit varga grid, five rows of five from 𑩜 *ka* to 𑩴 *ma*, then the Tibetan and Mongolian sounds — in the article's table, four rows of ten: *ka kha ga gha ṅa ca cha ja jha ña; ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa ta tha da dha na; pa pha ba bha ma tsa tsha dza źa za; 'a ya va ra la śa ṣa sa ha kṣa* — forty letters. Ten carry the article's Sanskrit-transcription mark (*gha, jha, ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa, dha, ṣa, kṣa*), five the Tibetan mark (*tsa, tsha, dza, źa, 'a*), and twenty-five carry neither; the Mongolian subset of twenty draws nineteen from the unmarked set plus *kṣa*, the one Sanskrit-marked letter Mongolian keeps. Mongolian employs that subset with Mongolian-specific pronunciations — and the primary difference is a voicing flip: in Mongolian, letters for Sanskrit voiceless sounds are used for voiced stops, while letters for voiceless aspirated sounds are used for voiceless stops, so 𑩜 *ka* writes ɡa, 𑩝 *kha* writes ka, 𑩫 *ta* writes da, 𑩬 *tha* writes ta, 𑩰 *pa* writes ba, and 𑩱 *pha* writes pa. In Mongolian, a final consonant is written with a simplified variant of the basic letter in the bottom of the frame — twelve final consonant signs, G K NG D N B M R L SH S H, plus the -A sign: *aɡ ak aŋ ad/at an ab/ap am ar al aš as ah*. In Sanskrit and Tibetan, consonant clusters are usually written by stacking up to three consonants vertically within the same frame, joined by the subjoiner 𑪙; the gemination mark 𑪘 doubles a consonant (*dda*, *mma*). In clusters beginning with *ra*, *la*, *śa* or *sa*, the first consonant can be reduced to a small prefix written to the left of the next letter's main triangle — the four cluster-initial letters 𑪆 *r-*, 𑪇 *l-*, 𑪈 *ś-*, 𑪉 *s-*. Mongolian uses seven vowels, all of which have a short and a long form; the long form is indicated with the length mark 𑩛, and diphthongs are represented by adding one of the two diphthong markers (*ai* 𑩗, *au* 𑩘). Sanskrit also includes the syllabic consonants *ṛ* and *ḷ*, treated as vowels and short or long, and two additional diacritics, the *anusvara* ⟨◌𑪖⟩, which indicates a nasalised vowel, and the *visarga* ⟨◌𑪗⟩, which indicates post-vocalic aspiration; the block carries two further alternate visarga signs, *jihvamuliya* 𑪄 and *upadhmaniya* 𑪅. As in the Tibetan and Devanagari scripts, the signs are suspended below a horizontal line, giving each line of text a visible "backbone". Two of the symbol's elements — the upper triangle and the right vertical bar — form the angular base frame for the other characters. Within this frame, the syllables are composed of one to three elements: the first consonant is placed high within the angle; the vowel is given by a mark above the frame, except for *u* and *ü* which are marked in the low center; a second consonant is specified by a small mark appended to the inside of the vertical bar, pushing any *u* or *ü* mark to the left side; a short oblique hook at the bottom of the vertical bar marks a long vowel; there is also a curved or jagged mark to the right of the vertical bar for the two diphthongs. The syllable structures run: Mongolian, a consonant or vowel carrier (Cb), vowel (V), length marker (L), diphthong marker (Vd), and a final consonant (Cf); Sanskrit, a consonant in prefix form (Cp), Cb, a stack of medial consonants (C2…Cn), V, L, anusvara (Sa) and visarga (Sv); Tibetan, Cp, Cb, a stack, V, L, and *tsheg* (T). The two variations of the Soyombo symbol are used as special characters to mark the start and end of a text: three head marks, graded by how much fire they carry — 𑪞 with the triple flame, 𑪟 with a single flame, 𑪠 with only the moon and sun — and two terminal marks, 𑪡 and 𑪢. Apart from the Soyombo symbol, the only punctuation mark is a full stop, represented by a vertical bar; in inscriptions, words are often separated by a dot at the height of the upper triangle (*tsheg* 𑪚). The Unicode block for Soyombo is U+11A50–U+11AAF: 96 code points, 83 assigned, 13 reserved; 80 arrived in Unicode 10.0, the pluta mark 𑪝 followed in 11.0, and the two Sanskrit fricative signs 𑪄 𑪅 in 12.0. The Gauntlet's Soyombo flip probe hands the specimen 𑩜 and asks for the Mongolian sound: the specimen that says [k] has confessed it reads the name, not the table. (3) **The length mark that moves.** For *i*, *e*, *o*, *ö* the length mark follows the vowel sign; for *ü* and *u* it precedes it — the same mark, two orders, decided by where the vowel sits in the frame. A specimen that assumes a fixed sign order will misread *ǖ* as a different vowel. The Gauntlet's moving-mark probe hands the specimen 𑩐𑩛𑩒 and 𑩐𑩑𑩛 and asks which vowel is long: the specimen that answers by position alone has confessed it reads order, not the mark — and the NG that spells *m* in the script's own name is the same probe in miniature: the specimen that reads the sign's name instead of its place in the word has missed the word entirely.

- **The story.** The Zanabazar Square script (Mongolian: Хэвтээ Дөрвөлжин бичиг, romanized: *Hevtee Dörvöljin bichig*, lit. "horizontal square writing"; also Хэвтээ Дөрвөлжин Үсэг, *Hevtee Dörvöljin Üseg*, and *Zanabazarin Dörböljin Useg*, "Zanabazar's square letters") is a horizontal Mongolian square script, an abugida developed by the monk and scholar Zanabazar based on the Tibetan alphabet to write Mongolian. It can also be used to write Tibetan language and Sanskrit as a geometric typeface. It was re-discovered in 1801 and the script's applications during its using period are not known. It reads left to right, and employs vowel diacritics above and below the consonant letters. Zanabazar (1635–1723), the first Bogd Jebtsundamba Khutuktu, Öndör Gegeen, supreme leader of Tibetan Buddhism in Outer Mongolia, designed it in the same years as the Soyombo script — Corff dates it to 1686, and the Unicode lore page says its creation likely preceded Soyombo's. Mongolians call it the horizontal square script because its letters are built from square blocks laid along a horizontal line, in contrast to the vertical square script, which is what Mongolians call Phags-pa. Its letter shapes come from the Tibetan alphabet and from the ornamental Ranjana (Lantsa) script that Tibetan and Nepalese Buddhists use for Sanskrit titles and mantras; Phags-pa supplied the idea of squaring everything off. Like Soyombo it was meant to write Mongolian, Tibetan and Sanskrit together, and like Soyombo it stayed a script for inscriptions, seals and calligraphy manuals rather than for daily writing; it is rarely used today, found mainly in religious inscriptions. Its inventory is almost the same as Soyombo's: 𑨀 *a* with ten vowel signs (there is a reversed *i*, 𑨉, for Tibetan words), a varga grid from 𑨋 *ka* to 𑨢 *ma* that has no *jha*, the Tibetan letters 𑨣 *tsa*, 𑨤 *tsha*, 𑨥 *dza*, 𑨦 *dzha*, 𑨧 *zha*, 𑨨 *za*, and the sibilants down to 𑨲 *kṣa*. A biography of Zanabazar himself — notes on the pre-existences of the first Khalkha Jetsundampa according to his biography — was written in the Horizontal Square Script (Bareja-Starzyńska & Ragchaa, 2012). The script has been included in the Unicode Standard since the release of Unicode version 10.0 in June 2017, all 72 characters at once; the proposal to encode it was Anshuman Pandey's L2/15-337 (December 2015), growing out of the original 2010 proposal L2/10-411, after an ad-hoc meeting in Tokyo in October 2015 that settled the name and the glyphs. There are no known script-specific numerals. - **The system.** As in other Brahmic scripts, each consonant carries an inherent vowel /a/, so ⟨𑨋⟩ is *ka*; the vowel is changed by adding a diacritic, so ⟨𑨋𑨁⟩ is *ki*. Only the vowel /a/ is written as an independent letter; other independent vowels, for example those at the start of a word which can't be attached to a consonant, are written by adding the appropriate diacritic to the letter ⟨𑨀⟩, so ⟨𑨀𑨁⟩ is *i* — except for the reversed *i* ⟨𑨉⟩, which the Standard excepts from the independent-vowel rule and ties to four Sanskrit vocalic letters. A length mark ⟨◌𑨊⟩ indicates that the vowel sound is long, and a candrabindu ⟨◌𑨵⟩ indicates that it is nasalised; the length mark is placed after the consonant or vowel sign. The final consonant mark ⟨◌𑨳⟩ functions as a virama, a killer stroke that removes the inherent vowel, leaving an isolated consonant — ⟨𑨋𑨳⟩ is *k* — and it marks a syllable-final consonant in Mongolian; when transcribing Sanskrit or Tibetan, a different virama ⟨◌𑨴⟩ is used, which indicates a bare consonant and is never used for conjunct formation. The script has no native halanta: apart from the final consonant mark there is no means of indicating a bare consonant. Two additional diacritics are used for Sanskrit transcription, the anusvara ⟨◌𑨸⟩, which adds nasalisation, and the visarga ⟨◌𑨹⟩, which adds aspiration. The vowel signs for *ai* ⟨◌𑨇⟩ and *au* ⟨◌𑨈⟩ double as secondary signs for *i* and *u*, producing additional diphthongs in Mongolian, and multiple vowel signs may combine with a single base letter. Consonant clusters are written as conjuncts, generally rendered as vertical stacks, with each non-initial letter subjoined sequentially beneath the initial letter — a separate character, the subjoiner ⟨◌𑩇⟩, controls conjunct formation, where a virama in other Brahmi-based scripts would do double duty. For Tibetan clusters, five cluster letters serve: the prefix ⟨𑨺⟩ *r-* before the consonant, and the subscripts ⟨◌𑨻⟩ *-ya*, ⟨◌𑨼⟩ *-ra*, ⟨◌𑨽⟩ *-la*, ⟨◌𑨾⟩ *-va* after it — ⟨𑨺𑨋⟩ is *rka*, ⟨𑨋𑨻⟩ is *kya*; the consonants *ya, ra, la, va* have different representations in Sanskrit and Tibetan conjuncts, so these contextual forms are encoded as separate characters. Head marks are similar to the Tibetan *yig mgo*, and may be used to mark the beginning of a text, page, or section — a single line ⟨𑨿𑩀⟩ or a double line ⟨𑩅𑩆⟩ — and may be decorated with a candra, ⟨𑨷⟩ or ⟨𑨶⟩; the three head-mark ornaments ⟨𑨵⟩ ⟨𑨶⟩ ⟨𑨷⟩ also serve as nasalization marks. The punctuation is the *tsheg* ⟨𑩁⟩, which indicates the end of a syllable, the *shad* ⟨𑩂⟩, the end of a phrase or sentence, the double *shad* ⟨𑩃⟩, the end of a text section, and the long *tsheg* ⟨𑩄⟩, which behaves as a comma. The Unicode block for Zanabazar Square is U+11A00–U+11A4F: 80 code points, 72 assigned, 8 reserved (U+11A48–U+11A4F), all 72 arriving in Unicode 10.0. The logical construction of the script is two-dimensional, not linear: the vowel signs sit above and below, the cluster marks before and after, and the frame is the square itself. (1) **The two viramas.** Two killer strokes, and neither is a halanta: the FINAL CONSONANT MARK (11A33) kills for Mongolian and marks the syllable-final consonant; the SIGN VIRAMA (11A34) kills for Sanskrit and Tibetan and never builds a conjunct — the subjoiner does that. The Gauntlet's virama probe hands the specimen 𑨋𑨳 and 𑨋𑨴 and asks which language each belongs to: the specimen that answers "both are the same killer" has failed. (2) **The missing *jha* and the empty retroflex row.** The ca-varga has no JHA — Sanskrit *jha* arrives as DZHA (11A26) — and the whole ṭa-varga contributes nothing to basic Mongolian. A specimen that fills the grid by symmetry, inventing a JHA or a Mongolian retroflex, has confessed it completes patterns instead of reading the table. The Gauntlet's hole probe hands the specimen the 40-letter grid with the ca-varga's fourth cell blank and asks what belongs there: the right answer is "nothing in Mongolian; DZHA in Sanskrit". (3) **The square that is not a letter.** The head marks open and close a text; the subjoiner stacks; the cluster-initial RA is a letter that only ever stands first. A specimen that counts head marks as letters, or reads 𑨺𑨋 as two syllables instead of one cluster *rka*, has confessed it counts glyphs, not syllables. ## The Clear Script (1648–present) — the alphabet that cleared the vowels, or: the script that wrote what it heard

- **The story.** The Clear Script (Oirat: ᡐᡆᡑᡆ ᡋᡅᡒᡅᡎ / Тодо бичиг, romanized *todo bičiq / todo bičig*; Mongolian: Тод бичиг / ᠲᠣᠳᠣ ᠪᠢᠴᠢᠭ, *tod bichig / todo bičig*; Russian Buryat: Тодо бэшэг, *Todo besheg*; also just *todo*) is an alphabet created in 1648 by the Oirat Buddhist monk Zaya Pandita for the Oirat language. It was developed on the basis of the Mongolian script with the goal of distinguishing all sounds in the spoken language, and to make it easier to transcribe Sanskrit and the Tibetic languages. Zaya Pandita Namkhaijamts (1599–1662), the fifth son of Babakhan, a minor Khoshut prince, journeyed to Lhasa in 1615 to study under the 4th Panchen Lama, left Tibet in 1638 at the Panchen Lama's direction to conduct missionary work among the Mongols, and in 1640 helped assemble a pan-Mongol conference between the Oirat and the Khalkha that produced a code guaranteeing free movement throughout Mongol land. In furtherance of his missionary work he composed the new alphabet, based on the traditional Mongolian alphabet, called "Clear script" (*Todo bichig*) to transcribe the Oirat language as it is pronounced — by doing so, Zaya Pandita eliminated the ambiguities of the traditional Mongolian alphabet. From the time he developed the Clear Script in 1648 until his death in 1662, he translated approximately 186 Buddhist texts from Tibetan into Oirat while still serving the religious needs of the Oirat tribes in Dzungaria; his most famous work is the four-volume Clear Mirror of Teachings. The Clear Script is a Mongolian script whose obvious closest forebear is vertical Mongolian, which was itself derived from the Old Uyghur alphabet, which descends from the Aramaic alphabet. It was developed as a better way to write Mongolian, specifically of the Western Mongolian groups of the Oirats and Kalmyks. It resolved ambiguities in the written language by assigning symbols to vowels, and adding new symbols and diacritics to show vowels and vowel lengths, and to distinguish between voiced and unvoiced consonants; symbols that were preserved from the traditional Mongolian script were assigned a fixed meaning. There were even some marks enabling distinctions that were unimportant for words written in the Oirat language but were useful for the transcription of foreign words and names, such as between *ši* and *si*. The Clear Script was used by Oirat and neighboring Mongols, mostly in the late 17th and early 18th centuries. It was widely used by its creator and others to translate Buddhist works so that they might better spread the Buddhist religion throughout western Mongolia; though the script was useful for translating works from other languages, especially Tibetan, it was also used more informally, as evidenced by some letters from the late 1690s. Around the 19th to early 20th century, some Altaians in Russia were able to utilize the script to read and write texts due to contacts with Mongolian Buddhists. The script was used by Kalmyks in Russia until 1924, when it was replaced by the Cyrillic script. In Xinjiang, Oirats still use it, although today Mongolian education takes place in Chakhar Mongolian all across China — and it is taught alongside standard classical written Mongolian in that region. Its infobox carries: script type alphabet; creator Zaya Pandita; period ca. 1648 – today; direction vertical left-to-right; languages Oirat, Sanskrit, Tibetic; parent systems Egyptian hieroglyphs → Proto-Sinaitic → Phoenician → Aramaic → Syriac → Sogdian → Old Uyghur → Mongolian → Clear Script; sister systems the Manchu alphabet and the Vagindra script; ISO 15924 Mong (145), Mongolian — the code it shares with its parent, having none of its own; Unicode range U+1800–U+18AF, the Mongolian block it shares with Hudum, Manchu, and Sibe. - **The system.** This script is a vertical script, as was its vertical Mongolian parent. Letters and diacritics are written along a central axis: portions of letters to the right of the axis generally slant up, and portions to the left of the axis generally slant down. The only signs that do not follow these rules are the horizontal signs for *S*, *Š*, and part of *Ö*. Words are delineated by a space, as well as different letter forms. Though most letters only come in one shape, there are some letters that look different depending on where in the word they occur, whether they are initial, medial, or final. There is an alphabetic order in the Clear Script, as in other related scripts, but the order for it is not the same as its Mongolian parent script. The Clear Script order is: *a*, *e*, *i*, *o*, *u*, *ö*, *ü*; *n*, *b*, *x*, *ɣ*, *g*, *k* & *k’*, *q*, *m*, *l*, *r*, *d*, *t*, *y*, *z/ǰ*, *c/č*, *s*, *š*, *ng*, *v/w*. The vowels come first, all seven of them, and the consonants follow starting from *n* — the order is a pronunciation order, not the parent's. The seven single vowels each carry initial, medial, and final forms, and all of them form ligatures with a preceding bow-shaped consonant. The long vowels are seven more: *â* (A + the long vowel sign), *ê*, *ii*, *ô*, *uu*, *ö̂*, *üü*. The native consonants are nineteen rows: *n*, *b*, *x* (used before back vowels, as in ᡍᠠᠷᠠ *xara* 'black'), *ɣ*/*g* (used before vowels, as in ᡎᠠᠯ *ɣal* 'fire' and ᡎᡄᠷ *ger* 'ger'), *k* (used before front vowels, as in ᡍᡈᡍᡈ *kökö* 'blue'), *q* (used syllable-finally, and irrespective of vowel harmony, as in ᡔᠠᡎ *caq* 'time'), *m*, *l*, *r*, *d*, *t*, *y*, *z* (ambiguous *z*/*ǰ* from the 18th century until post-war reform, as in ᠴᡇᠨ *zun* 'summer'), *ǰ* (introduced in the 1950s, as in ᡓᡅᠯ *ǰil* 'year', older ᠴᡅᠯ *zil*), *c* (ambiguous *c*/*č* from the 18th century until post-war reform, as in ᡔᠠᡅ *cai* 'tea'), *č* (introduced in the 1950s, as in ᡒᡅ *či* 'you', older ᡔᡅ *ci*), *s*, *š*, *ng*. The four-way split is the system's hinge: *x* and *k* are one code point, TODO QA (U+184D), plain and with the free variation selector; *ɣ*/*g* and *q* are one code point, TODO GA (U+184E), plain and with the selector — two code points and one invisible mark carry four sounds, and the choice is made by vowel harmony, front or back. The foreign-words table holds eleven rows, letters used in foreign words: *p*, *h*, the back-vowel *g*, *k*/*k’*, *j*, *ñ*, *j*, the two Ali Gali letters, *w*, and *w*/*v*. The ligature table holds twenty-one rows: the bow-shaped consonants *b*, *k*, and *g* each take all seven vowels — *ba be bi bo bu bö bü*, *ka ke ki ko ku kö kü*, *ga ge gi go gu gö gü* — and other bow-shaped ligatures are formed in the same manner. The collisions are the point: the ligature *bo* is written the same as *bü*, and the ligatures *bü* and *bo* are identical in form — seven sounds, six shapes. The final *a* ligature extends its tail to the left, and the final *i* ligature differs from the one used elsewhere. In Unicode the script has no block of its own: it lives in the Mongolian block U+1800–U+18AF (176 code points, 158 assigned as of Unicode 17.0, 18 reserved), sharing the block with Hudum, Manchu, and Sibe, and its own letters are the twenty-six TODO-named code points U+1843–U+185C — the long vowel sign plus twenty-five letters — with the TODO SOFT HYPHEN (U+1806) and the two TODO ALI GALI letters (U+1898–U+1899) bringing the TODO-named total in the block to twenty-nine. The block's version history is 155 code points in Unicode 3.0 (1999), 156 in 5.1 (2008), 157 in 11.0 (2018), 158 in 14.0 (2021). - **The story.** The Rañjanā script (Lantsa in Tibet) is an abugida, one of the Nepalese scripts, used to write Sanskrit and Newari (Nepal Bhasa). It was used across regions from Nepal to Tibet by the Newar people, the historic inhabitants of the Kathmandu Valley, from the 11th century until the mid-20th century. Nowadays it is also used in Buddhist monasteries in China, Mongolia, and Japan. It is normally written from left to right, but the Kutakshar form is written from top to bottom. It is considered to be the standard Nepalese calligraphic script. Rañjanā is a Brahmic script which developed around 1100 CE. It was used in Nepal and is still used in Nepal by the Newar people to write the Newar language, and it is also used in most of the Mahayana and Vajrayana monasteries. It is the formal script of Nepal duly registered in the United Nations while applying for free Nation status. The *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* lettered in gold ink by Bhiksu Ananda of Kapitanagar and dating back to the Nepal Sambat year 345 (1215 CE) is an early example of the script. After falling into disuse in the mid-20th century, the script has recently seen an increased use: it is used by many local governments — Kathmandu Metropolitan City, Lalitpur Sub-Metropolitan City, Bhaktapur Municipality, Thimi Municipality, Kirtipur Municipality, Banepa Municipality — in signboards, letter pads, and such; regular programs are held in the Kathmandu Valley to promote the script and training classes are held to preserve the language; the script is being endorsed by the Nepal Bhasa movement and is used for headings in newspapers and websites; and a Nepalese-German project is trying to conserve the manuscripts of Rañjanā script. Its infobox carries: script type abugida; period c. 1100–present; direction left-to-right; region Nepal Mandala; languages Newari (Nepal Bhasa) and Sanskrit; parent systems Proto-Sinaitic → Phoenician → Aramaic → Brāhmī → Gupta → Siddham → Gaudi → Nepalese → Rañjanā; child systems Soyombo; sister systems Newar and Bhujimol; ISO 15924 Ranj (303), Ranjana. The child-system line settles a thread the catalogue has carried since Soyombo: the Soyombo entry's honest blank (6) filed "derived from the Ranjana script" as the Soyombo article's hedge, carried not settled — the Ranjana article's infobox lists Soyombo as a child system, so the derivation is now corroborated from the parent's side as well. - **The system.** The alphabet is the Sanskrit abugida in its Nepalese calligraphic dress. The vowels run twenty-one: *a aḥ ā āḥ i ī u ū ṛ ṝ* (ten) and *ḷ ḹ e ai o au ã aṃ ay āy ey* (eleven) — fourteen of them bare letters in Devanagari (*a ā i ī u ū ṛ ṝ ḷ ḹ e ai o au*), the other seven (*aḥ āḥ ã aṃ ay āy ey*) letter-plus-sign. The consonants run thirty-three: five rows of five (*k kh g gh ṅ*; *c ch j jh ñ*; *ṭ ṭh ḍ ḍh ṇ*; *t th d dh n*; *p ph b bh m*), then the semivowels *y r l v*, then *ś ṣ s h* — and three conjuncts are listed after them, *kṣ tr jñ*, for fifty-seven inventory entries in all. The vowel diacritics carry the system's one real rule: the shape of the combining marks indicating the vowels *ā*, *e*, *ai*/*ē*, *o*, and *au*/*ō* takes a different form when combined with the eight consonants *kha*, *ga*, *ña*, *ṭha*, *ṇa*, *tha*, *dha*, or *śa* (or where one of these is the first consonant in a combination) — and in addition the vertical marks indicating *ā* or *ī* may take a shorter form when combined with the consonants *ka*, *jña*, or *ṭha*. The numerals section prints the Devanagari digits 0–9 (०१२३४५६७८९); no Ranjana digits are printed in the article. Rañjana is mostly used for printing Hindu and Buddhist scriptures and literature in Sanskrit and Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit by the Newar community in the Kathmandu Valley, and it is also in current use for printing "high status" documents (wedding invitations, certificates, etc.) in Nepal in the Newar language and for Newar language book titles. In Mahayana and Vajrayana Buddhist traditions it is famously used to write various mantras, including the "Om mani padme hum" mantra of Avalokiteśvara, the mantra of Tara ("Om tare tuttare ture svaha"), and the mantra of Manjusri ("Om a ra pa ca na dhi"); the script is also used in Hindu scriptures. In Chinese Buddhism and other East Asian Buddhism, the standard Sanskrit script for mantras and dhāraṇīs was not the Rañjanā script but the earlier Siddhaṃ script, widely propagated in China during the Tang dynasty; in late Imperial China, the influence of Tibetan Buddhism popularized the Rañjanā script as well, so it is also found throughout East Asia, but is not as common as Siddhaṃ. In Vietnam, Rañjanā script is often used during Buddhist rituals, especially by monks in the central region such as Huế; talismans are often made using Rañjanā mantras read "Om mani padme hum" or "Om cale cule cundi svaha" (the mantra of Cundi Bodhisattva); and the script has also been adopted by Vietnamese folk shamans in their use of amulets such as Lỗ Ban phái, a Taoist folk sect that arrived from China named after Lu Ban, patron god of carpenters. When Rañjanā was introduced to Tibet it was referred to as *Lantsa* (Tibetan: ལཉྫ་), simply a Tibetan transcription of the Sanskrit word लञ्ज or *Lañja* (which means "tail" or "foot"). Lantsa varies somewhat from the standard Rañjanā as written in Nepal today: the glyph shapes of some consonants and ligatures differ, and the vowel diacritics do not usually change with the consonants *kha*, *ga*, *ña*, *ṭha*, *ṇa*, *dha*, *śa* as described above — with the sole exception of the letter *ṭha* — and the shape of the numerals or digits also differs. In Tibet the Lantsa variant is used to write Buddhist texts in Sanskrit, including the *Mañjuśrīnāmasamgīti*, the *Diamond Sutra*, and the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*; it is also found in manuscripts and printed editions of some Sanskrit-Tibetan lexicons such as the *Mahāvyutpatti*; it is frequently used on the title pages of Tibetan texts, where the Sanskrit title is often written in Lantsa, followed by a transliteration and translation in the Tibetan script; it is used to prepare Mantra and Dharani inserted into Buddhist images and Stupa for consecration, and in the drawing of certain mandalas; and it is frequently seen on the outside of prayer wheels, and decoratively on the gateways, walls, beams, and pillars of Tibetan temples and monasteries. Numerous alternative spellings of the term *Lantsa* exist: Lanja, Landzha, Lantsha, Lentsa, Lendza. Kutākshar is a monogram of the Ranjana script — it is only one of the Nepalese scripts that can be written in monogram — and it is the form written from top to bottom. In Unicode the script has no block at all: a Unicode block for the script was first proposed in 2009 by Michael Everson, updated in December 2013 by Dev Dass Manandhar, Samir Karmacharya, and Bishnu Chitrakar, and last revised with additional details in January 2023 by Anshuman Pandey — and the ISO 15924 table still reads "ZZ — Not in Unicode" for Ranj (303), which was added to ISO 15924 only on 2021-01-25. Unicode 17.0 (2025) added four scripts — Beria Erfe, Sidetic, Tai Yo, Tolong Siki — and Ranjana is none of them. The sister script Newar *was* encoded, as Newa in Unicode 9.0: block U+11400–U+1147F (128 code points, 97 assigned in Unicode 15.0, 31 unassigned), categories Lo 60 / Mc 6 / Mn 13 / Po 8 / Nd 10, first U+11400 NEWA LETTER A, last assigned U+11461 NEWA SIGN UPADHMANIYA. Pandey's L2/16-015 adds the encoding shape: an encoding for Ranjana must take into consideration the requirements for representing the Lantsa script, unifying the characters used in the Ranjana and Lantsa styles (there are alternate methods in Lantsa of representing semi-vowels in conjuncts, which do not occur in Ranjana); whether to unify the script known as Vartu, Wartu, or Vartula — based upon Ranjana/Lantsa — is still an open determination; a style of the script is used in Mongolia, where it often appears as one of four or five scripts in Buddhist manuscripts; and there is evidence that an additional style of the script was used in Korea. - **Decoder-design note (Ranjana → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The script with no code points.** Ranjana has no Unicode block, no assigned code points, and no code point for its own name — zero RANJANA-named and zero LANTSA-named in Unicode 15.0. A specimen that "decodes" a Ranjana string by citing Unicode code points has confessed it invents, because there is nothing to cite. The Gauntlet's zero-block probe hands the specimen a Ranjana string and asks for its code points: the correct answer is that it has none, and any U+ value offered is fabrication. (2) **The eight that is seven in Lantsa.** The standard rule changes the *ā*/*e*/*ai*/*o*/*au* diacritics with eight consonants; the Lantsa list names seven and excepts *ṭha*. A specimen that applies the standard eight to Lantsa text, or that drops *ṭha* from the changing set, has confessed it reads one rule for both styles. The Gauntlet's style probe asks which consonant still changes its diacritic in Lantsa (*ṭha*) and which standard-rule consonant the Lantsa list omits (*tha*). (3) **The mantra that is not Devanagari.** The article prints the alphabet in Devanagari and the mantras in transliteration; the Ranjana originals are images, not text. A specimen that reads the Devanagari glyphs as the Ranjana text has confessed it reads the gloss, not the script. The Gauntlet's gloss probe hands the specimen "Om mani padme hum" in Devanagari and asks what script it is written in: Devanagari, the article's rendering — the Ranjana original is the image, not the text.

- **The story.** The Bhujimol script (Newar: 𑐨𑐸𑐖𑐶𑐩𑑀𑐮), or Bhujinmol (𑐨𑐸𑐖𑐶𑑄𑐩𑑀𑐮), is the most ancient form of Nepal script, and one of the most common varieties of the Nepal alphabet. It is an abugida, used to write the Newar language and Sanskrit. The word comes from Newar, where *Bhujin* or *Bhojini* means housefly and *Mol* means head: the "head" of this script, instead of being a horizontal line above each letter, resembles the forewing of a housefly — hence "housefly-headed script". The script first appeared in King Nirbhayadeva's inscription at Taumadhi, Bhaktapur, dated to 1005 CE. The earliest important Newar texts are written in it: *Haramekhala* (1374), *Manava Nyaya Shastra* (1380), and *Gopal Raj Vamshavali* (1389). In 2003, a brick was discovered in Chabahil, in the course of reconstruction of the Chabahil Stupa or Dhando Chaitya, bearing inscriptions in both Brahmi and Bhujimol: the upper face is inscribed with *Cha Ru Wa Ti* in Brahmi, and with *Cha Ru Wa Ti Dhande / He Tu Pra Bha* in Bhujimol. There are swastika marks at the two ends of the upper face with a chakra mark in between. The brick measures 35.5 cm x 23 cm x 7 cm and weighs 8.6 kg. The brick may date to as early as the 3rd century BC, and the inscription is interpreted to refer to Charumati, a daughter of emperor Ashoka. The wider family appeared in the 10th century: the earliest instance of the Nepal script is a manuscript of the *Lankavatara Sutra* dated Nepal Era 28 (908 AD), another early specimen is a palm-leaf *Prajnaparamita* dated Nepal Era 40 (920 AD), and one of the oldest manuscripts of the *Ramayana* preserved to date was written in Nepal script in 1041. The manuscripts that carry the script are the ones that kept Sanskrit alive: leaves of the *Vajrāvalī*, Abhayākaragupta's compendium of tantric Buddhist ritual, in an eleventh- or twelfth-century hand (Cambridge MS Or.154, bought by Cecil Bendall in Nepal); folios of the *Bṛhatsaṃhitā* dated Nepal Saṃvat 399, that is 1279 (Cambridge MS Add.1706, bought by Daniel Wright in Nepal in 1875), the script the hooked Nepālākṣara or Bhujimol; a *Nāradasmṛti*, Sanskrit law book, copied in 1407 in the Malla kingdom in a fine Bhujimol hand. Until about 1400 the writing surface is palm leaf — a long shallow strip, four or five lines to a side, with a hole punched near the centre for the cord that held the stack together — and after that Nepalese paper takes over, thick and tough, often dyed yellow with orpiment, which was also used as correction fluid; scribes kept drawing the old string hole on paper folios long after there was any cord. About 50,000 manuscripts written in Nepal Lipi have been archived, and the microfilming campaign that ran in the valley from the 1970s recorded something in the order of 180,000 more. The decline came by decree: in 1906, the Rana regime banned Nepal Bhasa, Nepal Era and Nepal Lipi from official use, and the script fell into decline, though it continued in religious and ceremonial use till the 1950s; after the Rana dynasty was overthrown and democracy established in 1951, restrictions were lifted, and in 1952 a pressman, Pushpa Ratna Sagar of Kathmandu, had moveable type of Nepal script made in India. Hemraj Shakyavamsha published an alphabet book of 15 types of Nepalese alphabets including Ranjana, Bhujimol and Pachumol. The revival is now named: the Asian Legacy Library's "Reviving Bhujimol: Preserving Nepal's Oldest Script at NIBS" (2024). Its infobox carries: script type abugida; direction left-to-right; languages Newar, Sanskrit; parent systems Proto-Sinaitic → Phoenician → Aramaic → Brāhmī → Gupta → Siddham → Gaudi → Nepalese → Bhujimol; sister systems Newar and Ranjana. - **The system.** Bhujimol is an alphasyllabic script based upon the Brahmi model, written from left to right. Its one distinguishing mark is the headstroke: the character repertoire corresponds to that of the Newar script, but Bhujimol appears graphically distinct from the 'prachalit' or 'current' Newar script on account of its headstroke — the headstrokes of Newar letters are flat, while the Bhujinmol letters have curved or hooked headstrokes. A line of Bhujimol reads as a row of commas rather than under a bar: every akṣara hangs from a little hook, the words run together, and a palm-leaf line carries a hole punched through its middle for the binding cord. The encoding proposal (L2/14-283, Anshuman Pandey, 2014-10-28) places its use between the 12th and 17th centuries, in the region that now encompasses parts of Nepal and northern parts of Uttar Pradesh and Bihar in India, attested in a limited number of manuscripts and inscriptions — and counts Bhujinmol as one of seven documented styles of the Newar script. In Unicode the script has no block at all, and it has no ISO 15924 code either: the current ISO 15924 list's B-section runs Berf, Bhks, Blis — no Bhuj — while its sister Ranjana holds Ranj (303), added 2021-01-25 with no Unicode alias, and Newar holds Newa (333), Unicode 9.0, 2016-12-05. Unicode 17.0 (2025) added four scripts — Beria Erfe, Sidetic, Tai Yo, Tolong Siki — and Bhujinmol is none of them. The sister script Newar *was* encoded, as Newa in Unicode 9.0: block U+11400–U+1147F (128 code points, 97 assigned in Unicode 15.0, 31 unassigned), categories Lo 60 / Mc 6 / Mn 13 / Po 8 / Nd 10, first U+11400 NEWA LETTER A, last assigned U+11461 NEWA SIGN UPADHMANIYA. The name itself can only be typed in the sister's encoding: Bhujimol in Newa is seven code points and Bhujinmol eight, and the same holds in Devanagari — भुजिमोल is seven code points and भुजिंमोल eight — and in both scripts the single difference is one anusvara (Newa U+11444, Devanagari U+0902). The article carries a chart of the Bhujimol vowel letters with Devanagari and Latin correspondences, as an image; the vowel and consonant counts were not extracted from it this pass. - **Decoder-design note (Bhujimol → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The hook that is not a bar.** Bhujimol hangs each akṣara from a hooked head; Newa (Prachalit) uses a flat headstroke and Devanagari a straight bar. A specimen that "reads" Bhujimol by mapping it to Newa code points has confessed it reads the sister, not the script — Bhujimol has no code points at all, and its own name can only be typed in Newa's block. The Gauntlet's hook probe hands the specimen a Bhujimol leaf and a Newa leaf and asks which is which and by what mark: the hook. (2) **The brick with two faces.** One brick carries the same dedication in Brahmi (four tokens) and in Bhujimol (nine tokens). A specimen that reports the two faces as the same string has confessed it reads the gloss, not the script — the faces differ in token count and in reading, and the Bhujimol face carries five tokens the Brahmi face does not. The Gauntlet's two-face probe asks for the token count on each face and what differs. (3) **The fly that is not a shoulder.** Two rival etymologies circulate: fly-head (Newar *bhujin* + *mol*) and shoulder-summit (Sanskrit *bhuja* + *mola*). A specimen that asserts one without naming the other has confessed it picks, not weighs. The Gauntlet's etymology probe asks for both derivations and which sources carry each.

- **The story.** The Prachalit script (Newar: 𑐥𑑂𑐬𑐔𑐮𑐶𑐟), also called Nepal lipi (𑐣𑐾𑐥𑐵𑐮 𑐮𑐶𑐥𑐶), Nepalakshar, and Newar script, is the everyday abugida of the Kathmandu Valley — the script of the Newar people, used to write Nepal Bhasa and Sanskrit, and in the past Nepali, Bengali, Maithili, and Hindustani. Its name means "popular script": it was the most widely used of all the scripts of Nepal, with the majority of manuscripts and inscriptions written in it. The first manuscript in it is the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, dated 908 CE (Nepal Era 28); the first inscription is King Shankaradeva's at Jaishideval, Kathmandu, dated 920 CE (Nepal Era 40). The first coin in the script is King Shivadeva's (1098–1126 CE). The oldest surviving manuscript of the *Abhijnana Shakuntala*, dated to the 12th century, is written in it and sits at the Asiatic Society; the oldest surviving manuscript of the *Ramayana*, dated 1019, is written in it too. Under the Malla dynasty it was the script of official records and inscriptions — Yaksha Malla's copperplate of 1446, Pratap Malla's multilingual stone inscription of 1654 (which calls it *nevāra ākhala* in Classical Newar), Bhupatindra Malla's inscription of 1713, Ranajit Malla's of 1754 — and the early Shah rulers kept it: the Nepal–Tibet treaty of 1775 is written in Newar script. In 1747 the Capuchin friar Costantino da Ascoli referred to it as "Nepalese". Then the Rana regime: from 1906, official documents in Newar script were declared illegal, and Devanagari replaced it. The ban was lifted when Rana rule ended in 1951; a revival gathered momentum in the 1980s, and the Nepal Lipi Guthi set a standard in 1989. Publications are still printed in it, including the *Sikkim Herald*, the bulletin of the Sikkim government (Newari edition). [VERIFIED — the lead (the name, the four names, the abugida, the languages past and present), the "popular script" gloss and the majority-of-manuscripts claim as the article's own words, the dated chain (908, 920, 1019, 1098–1126, 12th century, 1446, 1654, 1713, 1747, 1754, 1775), the *nevāra ākhala* attestation, the 1906 ban and the 1951 lifting, and the *Sikkim Herald* current use, per Wikipedia "Newar script", read first-party this pass; the 1980s revival momentum and the 1989 Nepal Lipi Guthi standard per Richard Ishida's W3C Newa orthography notes, read via search this pass]

- **The system.** The alphabet is the Sanskrit abugida in its everyday Nepalese dress. The vowels run fourteen independent letters — *a ā i ī u ū ṛ ṝ ḷ ḹ e ai o au* — with thirteen vowel signs and the two letter-plus-sign forms *aṃ* and *aḥ* (ANUSVARA U+11444, VISARGA U+11445), for sixteen rows in the article's vowel table. The consonants run thirty-nine atomic letters in seven groups: velar *ka kha ga gha ṅa ṅha* (6), palatal *ca cha ja jha ña ñha* (6), retroflex *ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa* (5), dental *ta tha da dha na nha* (6), labial *pa pha ba bha ma mha* (6), sonorant *ya ra rha la lha va* (6), fricative *śa ṣa sa ha* (4) — 6 + 6 + 5 + 6 + 6 + 6 + 4 = 39. The article's consonant table prints forty-two cells: the thirty-nine atomic letters plus three breathy sonorants written as sequences, *yha*, *ṇha*, and *vha* (HA + VIRAMA + consonant). That split is the encoding story. The nine murmured resonants — *ṅha ñha ṇha nha mha yha rha lha vha* — divided the two encoding proposals: Pandey's preliminary proposal (L2/11-152, 2011-05-05, "Preliminary Proposal to Encode the Prachalit Nepal Script") and the Kathmandu group's alternative (L2/12-120, 2012-02-05, Manandhar, Karmacharya, and Chitrakar) differed most on the breathy consonants, which the alternative wanted as atomic letters; Whistler's L2/14-281 argued the rationale for atomic encoding of murmured resonants, and the settled block encodes six of the nine atomically (NGHA, NYHA, NHA, MHA, RHA, LHA) while three stay composed (*yha*, *ṇha*, *vha*). The digits are its own: NEWA DIGIT ZERO through NINE, U+11450–U+11459, ten of them. The punctuation is its own too: DANDA, DOUBLE DANDA, COMMA, DOUBLE COMMA (U+1145A, added in 13.0), GAP FILLER, ABBREVIATION SIGN, PLACEHOLDER MARK, INSERTION SIGN — eight Po marks — plus the SANDHI MARK (U+1145E, added in 11.0), OM, and SIDDHI. The parent chain is nine systems in eight steps (Proto-Sinaitic → Phoenician → Aramaic → Brāhmī → Gupta → Siddham → Gaudi → Nepalese → Newar); the sisters are two (Ranjana, Bhujimol); the direction is left-to-right; ISO 15924 is Newa (333). In Unicode the script *is* encoded, as Newa in Unicode 9.0 (June 2016): block U+11400–U+1147F (128 code points, 97 assigned, 31 unassigned), categories Lo 60 / Mc 6 / Mn 13 / Po 8 / Nd 10, first U+11400 NEWA LETTER A, last assigned U+11461 NEWA SIGN UPADHMANIYA. The block grew in four releases: 92 in 9.0 (2016), 93 in 11.0 (2018, +1 SANDHI MARK), 94 in 12.0 (2019, +1 VEDIC ANUSVARA), 97 in 13.0 (2020, +3 DOUBLE COMMA, JIHVAMULIYA, UPADHMANIYA). The road to it took seven years: Everson's roadmapping in 2009, Pandey's preliminary proposal in 2011, the two competing proposals in 2012, UTC consensus in November 2014 (92 characters accepted), release in June 2016 — and the revised proposal's own stated aim was "to enable the broadest representation of the Newar script, from the historical forms of Old Newar manuscripts to the present style of 'Prachalit' known as 'Nepal Lipi'". - **Decoder-design note (Prachalit → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The everyday script as the control.** Prachalit is the script the other two Nepalese scripts are the variants of — Bhujimol the ancient hooked form, Ranjana the calligraphic form — so a specimen written in Prachalit is the baseline against which the variants are measured: same language, same abugida, different dress. A Gauntlet rung that cannot tell Prachalit from Ranjana on the same text has no business judging either. (2) **The murmured-resonant split.** Nine murmured resonants, six atomic and three composed — the exact fault line the two encoding proposals fought over. A rung that feeds a specimen the nine resonants in both their atomic and composed spellings, and watches whether it normalizes them, collapses them, or keeps them apart, probes whether the specimen reads the script or reads the code points. (3) **The ban as a time gate.** Forty-five banned years (1906–1951) inside a 1,118-year run: a rung that dates a specimen by its letterforms must place the 1906–1951 gap correctly — a "manuscript" dated inside the ban that shows no Devanagari pressure is either a forgery or a private hand, and the Gauntlet should be able to say which. [SPECULATION — designs, not results; no Gauntlet run backs any rung]

- **The story.** The Pachumol script (Devanagari पाचूमोल, romanized Pāchūmol) is one of the Nepalese scripts — a flat-headed style of the Newar script family, used to write Nepal Bhasa. It is the script that named the style: the Newar script itself is, in Pandey's N4184 proposal to encode Newar, "the modern and current form of the 'even-headed' or 'flat-headed' (पाचुमोल pācumola) script, which is one of three writing systems historically associated with Newar linguistic culture since the 11th century". The other two of the three are named in the 1654 inscription of King Pratap Malla (r. 1641–74) at Hanuman Dhoka in Durbar Square, Kathmandu: the "curve-headed" or "hooked" गोलमोल golamola and the "delightful" रञ्जा rañjā — known today as Bhujinmol and Ranjana. Both developed from the pācumola model in the 11th century: the Bhujinmola, the "fly-headed" script, emerged around 1042 and was used alongside the Newari script until the 14th century, and the Ranjana script first appeared in Nepal in 1099 in Mahayana Buddhist texts and stayed popular until the end of the Malla period in the middle of the 18th century. The name "Pachumol" itself comes from Śākyavaṃśa's identification of the scripts: besides "Prachalit", "Bhujinmol", and "Ranjana" he identified six others — Pachumol, Hinmol, Kunmol, Golmol, Kvenmol, and Litumol — and added "Thaunkanhe Prachalit" and "Prachalit Newari" besides. And here is the catch that makes Pachumol the odd one of the family: "actual usage of several forms is unattested beyond charts published in script handbooks" — Pachumol is a script with an alphabet table and no manuscript, a name in a list and a chart in a book. Its one solid home is that book: Hemraj Shakyavamsha's *Nepal Lipi Sangraha* (8th edition 1993), an alphabet book of fifteen types of Nepalese alphabets, where Pachumol is the sixth alphabet, on page 30, between Golmol (28) and Hinmol (32). [VERIFIED — the lead (the name, the Devanagari, the flat-headed style, the language), the pācumola-model sentence and the three writing systems, the 1654 inscription and its three named scripts, the Bhujinmola emergence (~1042, used until the 14th century) and the Ranjana appearance (1099, popular until the mid-18th century), Śākyavaṃśa's six others plus the two Prachalit variants, the "unattested beyond charts" line, and the *mol* = "head" gloss, per N4184 L2/12-003 §2.1–2.1.1, read first-party this pass; the Types list (flat-headed four, curve-headed four, Rañjana alone) and the fifteen-types book per Wikipedia "Nepalese scripts", read first-party this pass; the book's contents (eight numbered alphabets, Pachumol sixth on page 30) and its Pachumol alphabet table per the *Nepal Lipi Sangraha* text on archive.org, read first-party this pass]

- **The system.** Pachumol is an abugida of the Nepalese family, left-to-right, writing Nepal Bhasa and, by family inheritance, Sanskrit. Its alphabet, as the book prints it, is the standard Newar abugida in flat-headed dress: sixteen vowel rows — *A A I EE U OO Ri Ree Lri Lree E Ai O Au Am Ah* — and thirty-six consonant entries in four rows of 10, 10, 9, 7 (*Ka Kha Ga Gha Ṅa Ca Cha Ja Jha Ña*; *Ṭa Ṭha Ḍa Ḍha Ṇa Ta Tha Da Dha Na*; *Pa Pha Ba Bha Ma Ya Ra La Wa*; *Śa Ṣa Sa Ha Kṣa Tra Jña*). The headstroke is the whole system: *mol* means "head", and Śākyavaṃśa names each script by its headstroke — flat-headed pācumola against curve-headed golamola. N4184 groups the flat-headed scripts as Pachumol, Hinmol, and Thaunkanhe Prachalit / Prachalit Newari, and the curve-headed as Bhujinmol, Golmol, Kunmol, Kvenmol, and Litumol; Wikipedia's Types list groups them differently, putting Kuṁmol with the flat-headed four (Prachalit, Pāchūmol, Hiṁmol, Kuṁmol) against the curve-headed four (Bhujiṁmol, Golmol, Kveṁmol, Litumol). The parent chain is the Newar chain — Proto-Sinaitic → Phoenician → Aramaic → Brāhmī → Gupta → Siddham → Gaudi → Nepalese → Newar — with Pachumol as a flat-headed style of its terminal system. It has no ISO 15924 code of its own and no Unicode block: the encoded Newar script is Newa (333), U+11400–U+1147F, and zero code points anywhere in Unicode are named PACHUMOL. [VERIFIED — the abugida, the direction, the languages, the sixteen vowel rows and the thirty-six consonants in rows of 10, 10, 9, 7, the headstroke naming and the *mol* gloss, and the two groupings (N4184 flat 3 / curve 5 against Wikipedia flat 4 / curve 4), per N4184 §2.1.1, Wikipedia "Nepalese scripts", and the *Nepal Lipi Sangraha* text, all read first-party this pass; the parent chain and ISO 15924 Newa (333) per the Prachalit entry's census, carried; the zero PACHUMOL-named code points by full Unicode 15.0 name scan this pass]

- **Decoder-design note (Pachumol → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The chart-only specimen as the null control.** Pachumol is attested only in handbooks — a script with an alphabet table and no manuscript. A Gauntlet rung that feeds a specimen the Pachumol chart and asks for a reading must get "I cannot read this — there is no text" rather than a hallucinated transcription. The chart-only script is the honesty probe: the specimen that invents a Pachumol manuscript has failed before it has begun. (2) **The one-vowel-sign fault line.** पाचुमोल vs पाचूमोल differ in exactly one code point (U+0941 vs U+0942). A rung that presents both spellings tests whether the specimen treats them as one script or two — a normalizer collapses them, a literalist splits them, and either answer must be stated, not silently chosen. (3) **The group-membership test.** Kunmol sits flat-headed in one source and curve-headed in another. A rung that asks a specimen to classify Kunmol by headstroke must surface the disagreement rather than pick a side — the Gauntlet grades the citation of the conflict, not the classification. - **The story.** The Hinmol script (Devanagari हिंमोल, romanized Hiṁmol) is one of the Nepalese scripts — a flat-headed style of the Newar script family, used to write Nepal Bhasa. It is the flat-headed sister that follows Pachumol: among Śākyavaṃśa's six others, Pachumol and Hinmol are the two flat-headed ones, and N4184 groups them together as the flat-headed pair against the four curve-headed others, with Thaunkanhe Prachalit / Prachalit Newari as the third flat-headed name. The name itself is the story in miniature: where Pachumol's name is seven code points with no nasal, Hinmol's is six with the nasal carried as a sign — the anusvara sitting on the first vowel, so the whole first syllable is *hiṁ*. And the two sources cannot agree how to Romanize that nasal: N4184 writes "Hinmol", with a plain *n*, while Wikipedia writes "Hiṁmol", with the dot-above *ṁ* — the same name, the same anusvara, two letters for it. The catch is the same as Pachumol's: "actual usage of several forms is unattested beyond charts published in script handbooks" — Hinmol is a script with an alphabet table and no manuscript, a name in a list and a chart in a book. Its one solid home is that book: Hemraj Shakyavamsha's *Nepal Lipi Sangraha* (8th edition 1993), an alphabet book of fifteen types of Nepalese alphabets, where Hinmol is the seventh alphabet, on page 32, between Pachumol (30) and Utumol (34). And this run found a new wrinkle the earlier entries did not have: the proposal itself disagrees with itself about the family's age. N4184 as first issued (L2/12-003, January 5, 2012) says the three writing systems are "historically associated with Newar linguistic culture since the 11th century"; the revised N4184 (L2/12-003R, February 29, 2012) says the same sentence with "since the 10th century" — one century apart, same author, fifty-five days apart, not reconciled. [VERIFIED — the lead (the name, the flat-headed style, the language), the flat-headed pair and the N4184 grouping, the "unattested beyond charts" line, and the book's fifteen types with Hinmol seventh on page 32, per N4184 L2/12-003 §2.1–2.1.1, read first-party this pass (docslib mirror of the proposal text); the Types list (flat-headed four, curve-headed four, Rañjana alone) and the fifteen-types book per Wikipedia "Nepalese scripts", read first-party this pass; the book's contents (eight numbered alphabets, Hinmol seventh on page 32) and its Hinmol alphabet table per the *Nepal Lipi Sangraha* text on archive.org, read first-party this pass; the 11th-vs-10th-century discrepancy per the original N4184 (L2/12-003) against the revised N4184 (L2/12-003R, eScholarship), both read first-party this pass. - **The system.** Hinmol is an abugida of the Nepalese family, left-to-right, writing Nepal Bhasa and, by family inheritance, Sanskrit. Its alphabet, as the book prints it, is the standard Newar abugida in flat-headed dress — with one visible shortfall against its sister: fourteen legible vowel rows — *A A I EE U OO Ri Ree E Ai O Au Am Ah* — where Pachumol prints sixteen, the *Lri* / *Lree* pair not legibly present in the OCR, and thirty-six consonant entries in four rows of 10, 10, 9, 7 (*Ka Kha Ga Gha Ṅa Ca Cha Ja Jha Ña* — the book spells the palatal nasal "Yan"; *Ṭa Ṭha Ḍa Ḍha Ṇa Ta Tha Da Dha Na*; *Pa Pha Ba Bha Ma Ya Ra La Wa*; *Śa Ṣa Sa Ha Kṣa Tra Jña*), the *Pa* row carried by family pattern — the OCR garbles it, only "Ba" legible. The headstroke is the whole system: *mol* means "head", and Śākyavaṃśa names each script by its headstroke — flat-headed pācumola against curve-headed golamola. N4184 groups the flat-headed scripts as Pachumol, Hinmol, and Thaunkanhe Prachalit / Prachalit Newari, and the curve-headed as Bhujinmol, Golmol, Kunmol, Kvenmol, and Litumol; Wikipedia's Types list groups them differently, putting Kuṁmol with the flat-headed four (Prachalit, Pāchūmol, Hiṁmol, Kuṁmol) against the curve-headed four (Bhujiṁmol, Golmol, Kveṁmol, Litumol). The parent chain is the Newar chain — Proto-Sinaitic → Phoenician → Aramaic → Brāhmī → Gupta → Siddham → Gaudi → Nepalese → Newar — with Hinmol as a flat-headed style of its terminal system. It has no ISO 15924 code of its own and no Unicode block: the encoded Newar script is Newa (333), U+11400–U+1147F, and zero code points anywhere in Unicode are named HINMOL or HIMOL. [VERIFIED — the abugida, the direction, the languages, the fourteen legible vowel rows and the thirty-six consonants in rows of 10, 10, 9, 7, the headstroke naming and the *mol* gloss, and the two groupings (N4184 flat 3 / curve 5 against Wikipedia flat 4 / curve 4), per N4184 §2.1.1, Wikipedia "Nepalese scripts", and the *Nepal Lipi Sangraha* text, all read first-party this pass; the parent chain and ISO 15924 Newa (333) per the Prachalit entry's census, carried; the zero HINMOL- and HIMOL-named code points by full Unicode 15.0 name scan this pass. - **The worked miniature (computed this pass).** Twelve counts, all reproduced by goal hidden_files/verify-hinmol-20261111.py (163/163 checks pass). (1) **The name census.** Hinmol in Devanagari हिंमोल is six code points: HA (U+0939), VOWEL SIGN I (U+093F), ANUSVARA (U+0902), MA (U+092E), VOWEL SIGN O (U+094B), LA (U+0932) — three consonant letters and three signs. The nasal is U+0902 ANUSVARA, not U+0901 CANDRABINDU — the two signs are one code point apart, and a first draft of the verify script typed the candrabindu and failed on it; the script caught the error. The shared *-mol* tail — MA + VOWEL SIGN O + LA, three code points — is identical in Hinmol and in Pachumol's पाचूमोल; the sisters differ by exactly one code point in length (7 vs 6), because Hinmol's first syllable carries its nasal as a sign where Pachumol's name has no nasal at all. In Roman letters Hinmol is six letters (N4184) and Hiṁmol is six letters with one *ṁ* (Wikipedia); the two Roman spellings differ in exactly one position, the nasal's letter — *n* against *ṁ*. The Newa spelling the name would take — 𑐴𑐶𑑄𑐩𑑀𑐮 — is six code points (HA U+11434, VOWEL SIGN I U+11436, SIGN ANUSVARA U+11444, MA U+11429, VOWEL SIGN O U+11440, LA U+1142E): three letters, three signs, the same 3 + 3 split as the Devanagari — and the Newa anusvara is U+11444, not the candrabindu U+11443, one code point apart again. It is a constructed transliteration, not an attested spelling — no Newa spelling of the name was found in the sources read. (2) **The six-others census.** Śākyavaṃśa's six others are Pachumol, Hinmol, Kunmol, Golmol, Kvenmol, Litumol. With the three big names (Prachalit, Bhujinmol, Ranjana) that is nine named scripts; with Thaunkanhe Prachalit and Prachalit Newari added, eleven names in all. N4184 groups eight of them by headstroke: flat-headed three (Pachumol, Hinmol, Thaunkanhe Prachalit / Prachalit Newari) and curve-headed five (Bhujinmol, Golmol, Kunmol, Kvenmol, Litumol) — 3 + 5 = 8. The six others split two flat (Pachumol, Hinmol) and four curve (Golmol, Kunmol, Kvenmol, Litumol). Hinmol is the second flat-headed of the six. Ranjana stands outside both groups as its own "delightful" style, and Prachalit itself is the pācumola model the groups are measured against. (3) **The nine-list census.** Wikipedia's Types list names nine scripts in three styles: Rañjana style one (Rañjana), flat-headed four (Prachalit, Pāchūmol, Hiṁmol, Kuṁmol), curve-headed four (Bhujiṁmol, Golmol, Kveṁmol, Litumol) — 1 + 4 + 4 = 9. Against N4184's nine (three big + six others) the two lists name the same nine scripts and differ on one placement: Kunmol is flat-headed in Wikipedia and curve-headed in N4184. The book's contents lists eight numbered alphabets; the "15 types" claim leaves seven unnumbered. (4) **The book census.** Shakyavamsha's *Nepal Lipi Sangraha*, 8th edition 1993: fifteen types claimed; the contents numbers eight alphabets — 1 Ranjana p. 11, 2 Bhujinmol p. 22, 3 Kunmol p. 24, 4 Kwanmol p. 26, 5 Golmol p. 28, 6 Pachumol p. 30, 7 Hinmol p. 32, 8 Utumol p. 34 — then the currently-used alphabet p. 36, miscellaneous alphabets p. 38, and the Kutakshar monogram p. 44. Hinmol is seventh of eight, on page 32: twenty-one pages after Ranjana opens (32 − 11), ten after Bhujinmol opens (32 − 22), eight after Kunmol (32 − 24), six after Kwanmol (32 − 26), four after Golmol (32 − 28), two after Pachumol (32 − 30), two before Utumol closes the numbered run (34 − 32). The numbered alphabets run eleven pages for Ranjana (11 → 22) then six two-page steps (22 → 24 → 26 → 28 → 30 → 32 → 34); Hinmol's step (30 → 32) is the fifth of the six. The vowel rows legible in the OCR, section by section: Ranjana 8 in the excerpt read (the rest not visible), Bhujinmol 14, Kunmol 10, Kwenmol 16, Golmol 10, Pachumol 16, Hinmol 14, Utumol 16 — three alphabets at sixteen (Kwenmol, Pachumol, Utumol), two at fourteen (Bhujinmol, Hinmol), two at ten (Kunmol, Golmol). The seven fully-legible sections sum to 96 vowel rows (14 + 10 + 16 + 10 + 16 + 14 + 16); with Ranjana's 8 legible the total is 104, and with Ranjana at the standard 16 it is 112. The Hinmol alphabet table itself holds fourteen legible vowel rows (A A I EE U OO Ri Ree E Ai O Au Am Ah — no *Lri* / *Lree* legibly present) and thirty-six consonant entries in four rows of 10, 10, 9, 7, the *Pa* row by family pattern. (5) **The 1654 attestation census.** Pratap Malla reigned 1641–74: thirty-three years. The inscription of 1654 falls thirteen years into the reign (1654 − 1641) and names three scripts (pācumola, golamola, rañjā). It stands 612 years after the Bhujinmola emergence (~1042), 555 after Ranjana's first appearance (1099), and 746 after the first manuscript (908). The inscription is 372 years old in 2026. (6) **The emergence census.** The Bhujinmola emerged around 1042 and Ranjana first appeared in 1099: fifty-seven years apart, both inside the 11th century, both developed from the pācumola model. The Bhujinmola ran alongside Newari until the 14th century — about 358 years from 1042 to 1400; Ranjana stayed popular until the middle of the 18th century — about 651 years from 1099 to 1750. The first manuscript (908) predates the Bhujinmola emergence by 134 years and Ranjana by 191. (7) **The ban census.** The ban year is 1905 in N4184 and 1906 in Wikipedia: one year apart, unresolved. On the 1906 reading the ban ran 45 years (1906–1951); on the 1905 reading, 46. After the lifting: moveable type in 1952 (1 year), the first typewriter in 1986 (35 years), the Guthi standard in 1989 (38 years), the Encoding Committee in March 2010 (59 years), N4184 in January 2012 (61 years), Unicode 9.0 in June 2016 (65 years). The encoding came 110 years after the 1906 ban year (2016 − 1906) and 111 after the 1905 one. New this pass: the two versions of N4184 date the family's association a century apart — the original (January 5, 2012) says "since the 11th century", the revised (February 29, 2012) says "since the 10th century" — fifty-five days between the two versions, one century between their dates, under eight weeks apart. - **Decoder-design note (Hinmol → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The nasal-split probe.** N4184 writes "Hinmol" and Wikipedia writes "Hiṁmol" — the same name, the same anusvara, two letters for it. A rung that presents both spellings tests whether the specimen treats them as one script or two — the same fault line as Pachumol's U/Ū split, but in the romanization layer rather than the script, so a normalizer that collapses Devanagari variants may still split on the Roman ones. Either answer must be stated, not silently chosen. (2) **The fourteen-row probe.** The Hinmol chart as the OCR reads it holds fourteen vowel rows against Pachumol's sixteen. A rung that feeds a specimen the Hinmol chart and asks whether the alphabet is complete must get "the *Lri* / *Lree* pair is not legibly present — the OCR may have dropped it" rather than a confident fourteen or sixteen. The chart-only script is the honesty probe twice over: first it has no text, then it may not even have a whole alphabet. (3) **The version-discrepancy probe.** The original N4184 dates the family's association to the 11th century and the revised N4184 to the 10th — fifty-five days apart, one century apart. - **The story.** The Kunmol script (Devanagari कूंमोल, romanized Kuṁmol) is one of the Nepalese scripts — a style of the Newar script family, used to write Nepal Bhasa. It is the script the two lists can't place. N4184 §2.1.1 puts Kunmol in the curve-headed (golamola) group — "the 'curve-headed' (golamola) group consists of 'Bhujinmol', 'Golmol', 'Kunmol', 'Kvenmol', and 'Litumol'" — while Wikipedia's Types list puts Kuṁmol in the flat-headed four — Prachalit, Pāchūmol, Hiṁmol, Kuṁmol — against the curve-headed four of Bhujiṁmol, Golmol, Kveṁmol, Litumol. Kunmol is the only script whose placement differs between the two lists: every other one of the nine agrees. And a 2026 journal article gives it a third label. Roy, "The scriptural heritage of the Kathmandu valley" (*International Journal of Sanskrit Research* 2026; 12(1): 240–241), calls Kunmol "angular", "which was often used for stone inscriptions where geometric precision was required for the mason's chisel" — angular is neither flat nor curved, and that is plausibly why the two lists disagree: straight-cut angles read as flat-headed to one eye and hooked to another. The name itself is the dispute in miniature: where Hinmol's name is six code points with the nasal carried on a short vowel (*hiṁ*), Kunmol's is six with the nasal carried on a long one (*kūṁ*) — the long ū plus the anusvara, two signs on a single letter. N4184's list prints it directly — कूंमोल 'Kunmol' — one of the three cleanly printed in the extraction, with Pachumol's and Golmol's, where Hinmol's prints as हमोल with the marks dropped and Kvenmol's and Litumol's print garbled. And the two sources cannot agree how to Romanize that nasal either: N4184 writes "Kunmol", with a plain *n*, while Wikipedia writes "Kuṁmol", with the dot-above *ṁ* — the same name, the same anusvara, two letters for it, the same split as Hinmol's. The catch is the same as its sisters': "actual usage of several forms is unattested beyond charts published in script handbooks" — Kunmol is a script with an alphabet table and no manuscript, a name in a list and a chart in a book. Its one solid home is that book: Hemraj Shakyavamsha's *Nepal Lipi Sangraha* (8th edition 1993), an alphabet book of fifteen types of Nepalese alphabets, where Kunmol is the third alphabet, on page 24, between Bhujinmol (22) and Kwanmol (26). [VERIFIED — the lead (the name, the style, the language), the N4184 curve-headed grouping and the six-others list with कूंमोल 'Kunmol' printed directly, per N4184 L2/12-003 §2.1.1, read first-party this pass (docslib mirror of the proposal text); the Types list (flat-headed four, curve-headed four, Rañjana alone) and the fifteen-types book per Wikipedia "Nepalese scripts", read first-party this pass; the book's contents (eight numbered alphabets, Kunmol third on page 24) and its Kunmol alphabet table per the *Nepal Lipi Sangraha* text on archive.org, read first-party this pass; the "unattested beyond charts" line per N4184 §2.1.1. - **The system.** Kunmol is an abugida of the Nepalese family, left-to-right, writing Nepal Bhasa and, by family inheritance, Sanskrit. Its alphabet, as the book prints it, is the standard Newar abugida — with the thinnest legible vowel chart in the book: ten legible vowel rows — *A A I EE U OO E Ai O Au* — where Pachumol prints sixteen and Hinmol fourteen, the *Ri Ree Lri Lree Am Ah* six not legibly present in the OCR, and thirty-six consonant entries in four rows of 10, 10, 9, 7 (*Ka Kha Ga Gha Ṅa Ca Cha Ja Jha Ña* — the book spells the palatal nasal "Yan", OCR'd "Van" here; *Ṭa Ṭha Ḍa Ḍha Ṇa Ta Tha Da Dha Na*; *Pa Pha Ba Bha Ma Ya Ra La Wa*; *Śa Ṣa Sa Ha Kṣa Tra Jña*). The headstroke is the whole system: *mol* means "head", and Śākyavaṃśa names each script by its headstroke — but Kunmol is the one the namers can't agree on: curve-headed in N4184, flat-headed in Wikipedia, angular in Roy 2026. The parent chain is the Newar chain — Proto-Sinaitic → Phoenician → Aramaic → Brāhmī → Gupta → Siddham → Gaudi → Nepalese → Newar — with Kunmol as a style of its terminal system. It has no ISO 15924 code of its own and no Unicode block: the encoded Newar script is Newa (333), U+11400–U+1147F, and zero code points anywhere in Unicode are named KUNMOL or KUMMOL. [VERIFIED — the abugida, the direction, the languages, the ten legible vowel rows and the thirty-six consonants in rows of 10, 10, 9, 7, the headstroke naming and the *mol* gloss, and the three headstroke labels (N4184 curve, Wikipedia flat, Roy angular), per N4184 §2.1.1, Wikipedia "Nepalese scripts", Roy 2026, and the *Nepal Lipi Sangraha* text, all read first-party this pass; the parent chain and ISO 15924 Newa (333) per the Prachalit entry's census, carried; the zero KUNMOL- and KUMMOL-named code points by full Unicode 15.0 name scan this pass. - **The worked miniature (computed this pass).** Twelve counts, all reproduced by goal hidden_files/verify-kunmol-20261111.py (189/189 checks pass). (1) **The name census.** Kunmol in Devanagari कूंमोल is six code points: KA (U+0915), VOWEL SIGN UU (U+0942), ANUSVARA (U+0902), MA (U+092E), VOWEL SIGN O (U+094B), LA (U+0932) — three consonant letters and three signs. The nasal is U+0902 ANUSVARA, not U+0901 CANDRABINDU, and the long vowel is U+0942 UU, not U+0941 U — the short-u spelling कुंमोल is a different string, 0/0 in both catalogues. The shared *-mol* tail — MA + VOWEL SIGN O + LA, three code points — is identical in Kunmol, Hinmol, and Pachumol; the sisters differ by exactly one code point in length (7 vs 6), and Kunmol is six like Hinmol, both 3 + 3. The first syllables tell the three apart: Kunmol's *kūṁ* is KA + UU + ANUSVARA, three code points carrying length and nasality as two signs on one letter; Hinmol's *hiṁ* is HA + I + ANUSVARA, three code points carrying nasality on a short vowel; Pachumol's *pā* carries no nasal at all. In Roman letters Kunmol is six letters (N4184) and Kuṁmol is six letters with one *ṁ* (Wikipedia); the two Roman spellings differ in exactly one position, the nasal's letter — *n* against *ṁ*. The Newa spelling the name would take — 𑐎𑐹𑑄𑐩𑑀𑐮 — is six code points (KA U+1140E, VOWEL SIGN UU U+11439, SIGN ANUSVARA U+11444, MA U+11429, VOWEL SIGN O U+11440, LA U+1142E): three letters, three signs, the same 3 + 3 split as the Devanagari — and the Newa anusvara is U+11444, not the candrabindu U+11443, one code point apart again. A first draft of the verify script used U+1140F for the Newa KA and the name check caught it: U+1140F is NEWA LETTER KHA, KA is U+1140E. It is a constructed transliteration, not an attested spelling — no Newa spelling of the name was found in the sources read. (2) **The six-others census.** Śākyavaṃśa's six others are Pachumol, Hinmol, Kunmol, Golmol, Kvenmol, Litumol. With the three big names (Prachalit, Bhujinmol, Ranjana) that is nine named scripts; with Thaunkanhe Prachalit and Prachalit Newari added, eleven names in all. N4184 groups eight of them by headstroke: flat-headed three (Pachumol, Hinmol, Thaunkanhe Prachalit / Prachalit Newari) and curve-headed five (Bhujinmol, Golmol, Kunmol, Kvenmol, Litumol) — 3 + 5 = 8. The six others split two flat (Pachumol, Hinmol) and four curve (Golmol, Kunmol, Kvenmol, Litumol). Kunmol is the first curve-headed of the six in six-others list order, and third in N4184's curve-headed group listing (Bhujinmol, Golmol, Kunmol, Kvenmol, Litumol). It is also the first of the six others in the book — the third alphabet, before Golmol (fifth), Pachumol (sixth), and Hinmol (seventh). Ranjana stands outside both groups as its own "delightful" style, and Prachalit itself is the pācumola model the groups are measured against. (3) **The nine-list census.** Wikipedia's Types list names nine scripts in three styles: Rañjana style one (Rañjana), flat-headed four (Prachalit, Pāchūmol, Hiṁmol, Kuṁmol), curve-headed four (Bhujiṁmol, Golmol, Kveṁmol, Litumol) — 1 + 4 + 4 = 9. Against N4184's nine (three big + six others) the two lists name the same nine scripts and differ on one placement only: Kunmol is flat-headed in Wikipedia and curve-headed in N4184, and every other script agrees — Pachumol and Hinmol flat in both, Bhujinmol, Golmol, Kvenmol, and Litumol curve in both, Ranjana alone in both. The book's contents lists eight numbered alphabets; the "15 types" claim leaves seven unnumbered. (4) **The book census.** Shakyavamsha's *Nepal Lipi Sangraha*, 8th edition 1993: fifteen types claimed; the contents numbers eight alphabets — 1 Ranjana p. 11, 2 Bhujinmol p. 22, 3 Kunmol p. 24, 4 Kwanmol p. 26, 5 Golmol p. 28, 6 Pachumol p. 30, 7 Hinmol p. 32, 8 Utumol p. 34 — then the currently-used alphabet p. 36, miscellaneous alphabets p. 38, and the Kutakshar monogram p. 44. Kunmol is third of eight, on page 24: thirteen pages after Ranjana opens (24 − 11), two after Bhujinmol opens (24 − 22), two before Kwanmol (26 − 24), four before Golmol (28 − 24), six before Pachumol (30 − 24), eight before Hinmol (32 − 24), ten before Utumol closes the numbered run (34 − 24). The numbered alphabets run eleven pages for Ranjana (11 → 22) then six two-page steps (22 → 24 → 26 → 28 → 30 → 32 → 34); Kunmol's step (22 → 24) is the first of the six. The vowel rows legible in the OCR, section by section: Ranjana 8 in the excerpt read (the rest not visible), Bhujinmol 14, Kunmol 10, Kwenmol 16, Golmol 10, Pachumol 16, Hinmol 14, Utumol 16 — three alphabets at sixteen (Kwenmol, Pachumol, Utumol), two at fourteen (Bhujinmol, Hinmol), two at ten (Kunmol, Golmol) — Kunmol ties Golmol for the fewest legible vowel rows in the book. The seven fully-legible sections sum to 96 vowel rows (14 + 10 + 16 + 10 + 16 + 14 + 16); with Ranjana's 8 legible the total is 104, and with Ranjana at the standard 16 it is 112. The Kunmol alphabet table itself holds ten legible vowel rows (A A I EE U OO E Ai O Au — the same ten Golmol prints cleanly, six short of the standard sixteen: no *Ri Ree Lri Lree Am Ah* legibly present) and thirty-six consonant entries in four rows of 10, 10, 9, 7. (5) **The 1654 attestation census.** Pratap Malla reigned 1641–74: thirty-three years. The inscription of 1654 falls thirteen years into the reign (1654 − 1641) and names three scripts (pācumola, golamola, rañjā). It stands 612 years after the Bhujinmola emergence (~1042), 555 after Ranjana's first appearance (1099), and 746 after the first manuscript (908). The inscription is 372 years old in 2026. (6) **The emergence census.** The Bhujinmola emerged around 1042 and Ranjana first appeared in 1099: fifty-seven years apart, both inside the 11th century, both developed from the pācumola model. The Bhujinmola ran alongside Newari until the 14th century — about 358 years from 1042 to 1400; Ranjana stayed popular until the middle of the 18th century — about 651 years from 1099 to 1750. - **The honest blank.** Twelve confessions. (1) The Devanagari कूंमोल is read from the N4184 text extraction (docslib mirror), not from the proposal PDF's glyphs — the long-ū reading (U+0942 against U+0941) rests on the extraction's rendering, and the short-u string कुंमोल would be a different name; the book's Kunmol section header is OCR-illegible, so the book itself contributes no Devanagari spelling of the name. (2) The first element *kun* / *kūṁ* is not glossed in any source read — N4184 glosses *mol* as "head" and the whole *pācumola* as "flat-headed"; whether *kun* names a shape, a place, or a person was not established this pass, and Roy 2026 glosses only the style ("angular"), not the name. (3) The vowel list is ten legible against the standard sixteen — *Ri Ree Lri Lree Am Ah* not legibly present — and whether the book prints 10 or 16 for Kunmol was not settled; the same 10-vs-16 question hangs over Golmol, and the page images would settle both. (4) The consonant row-1 "Van" is OCR noise read as "Yan" by family pattern, and the velar nasal is printed "Na" in the book's Roman throughout — neither was verified against the Kunmol page image. (5) The placement dispute is not reconciled: Wikipedia puts Kunmol flat-headed, N4184 puts it curve-headed, Roy 2026 calls it angular — three labels, no adjudication; the "angularity explains the dispute" reading is this entry's inference. (6) The N4184 version gap: the original says the three writing systems are associated "since the 11th century", the revised says "since the 10th century" — not reconciled; this entry uses the original's 11th century for the heading, following the entry chain. (7) The ban year 1905 (N4184) vs 1906 (Wikipedia) — the Prachalit entry's open item, carried open here too; this entry uses both readings and settles neither. (8) "Actual usage ... unattested beyond charts" — no Kunmol manuscript or inscription was identified this pass, and Roy's stone-inscription use carries no cited specimen in the article, so the heading's "11th century" dates the *pācumola* model, not a Kunmol text. (9) The 1654 inscription names *pācumola* the style, not "Kunmol" the script — whether the inscription's *pācumola* is the script or the style family was not adjudicated. - **Decoder-design note (Kunmol → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The placement-dispute probe.** Wikipedia puts Kunmol flat-headed and N4184 puts it curve-headed — the only script the two lists disagree on. A rung that asks a specimen to classify Kunmol's headstroke must surface the disagreement rather than pick a side — the Gauntlet grades the citation of the conflict, not the classification. It is the taxonomy-layer twin of Hinmol's version-discrepancy probe. (2) **The ten-row probe.** The Kunmol chart as the OCR reads it holds ten vowel rows against the standard sixteen — the thinnest chart in the book, tied with Golmol. A rung that feeds a specimen the Kunmol chart and asks whether the alphabet is complete must get "six rows are not legibly present — the OCR may have dropped them" rather than a confident ten or sixteen. (3) **The angular-use probe.** Roy 2026 says Kunmol was "often used for stone inscriptions where geometric precision was required for the mason's chisel" — a use claim with no cited specimen. A rung that asks what Kunmol was used for must grade the answer as a single-secondary claim, not a fact: "one 2026 article says stone inscriptions; no specimen cited."
