- **The story.** The Golmol script (Devanagari गोलमोल, romanized Golmol) is one of the Nepalese scripts — a curve-headed style of the Newar script family, used to write Nepal Bhasa. It is the script that named its own family. The 1654 inscription of King Pratap Malla (r. 1641–74) at Hanuman Dhoka in Durbar Square, Kathmandu, names three scripts: the "flat-headed" pācumola, the "curve-headed" or "hooked" गोलमोल golamola, and the "delightful" rañjā — and the curve-headed group the proposal names after that second word is the golamola group: "Bhujinmol", "Golmol", "Kunmol", "Kvenmol", and "Litumol". Golmol is the member script that carries the group's name — the only one of the five whose name IS the group name, the Devanagari string गोलमोल identical in the inscription's style name and in Śākyavaṃśa's list. Both lists agree on its placement — N4184 puts it curve-headed, and Wikipedia's Types list puts it in the curve-headed four (Bhujiṁmol, Golmol, Kveṁmol, Litumol) — and a 2026 journal article gives it a third voice in the same direction: Roy, "The scriptural heritage of the Kathmandu valley" (*International Journal of Sanskrit Research* 2026; 12(1): 240–241), calls Golmol "(rounded), which omits the sharp angles of the head-stroke for a softer visual flow", paired in the same sentence with Kunmol "(angular)". Golmol is the only one of the six others that Roy labels with a head-stroke adjective in the taxonomy sentence, and the label matches both lists — the agreed script, where its sister Kunmol is the disputed one. The name itself is the plainest in the family: where Hinmol's name is six code points with the nasal carried as a sign and Kunmol's is six with a long vowel plus the nasal, Golmol's is six with neither — GA + O + LA + MA + O + LA, four letters and two signs, no anusvara, no long vowel, no macron in the plain spelling. The catch is the same as its sisters': "actual usage of several forms is unattested beyond charts published in script handbooks" — Golmol is a script with an alphabet table and no manuscript, a name in a list and a chart in a book. Its one solid home is that book: Hemraj Shakyavamsha's *Nepal Lipi Sangraha* (8th edition 1993), an alphabet book of fifteen types of Nepalese alphabets, where Golmol is the fifth alphabet, on page 28, between Kwanmol (26) and Pachumol (30). [VERIFIED — the lead (the name, the style, the language), the 1654 inscription's three named scripts and the golamola group with Golmol second in its listing, the six-others list with गोलमोल 'Golmol' printed directly, the *mol* = "head" gloss, and the "unattested beyond charts" line, per N4184 L2/12-003 §2.1–2.1.1, read first-party this pass (docslib mirror of the proposal text); the Types list (flat-headed four, curve-headed four, Rañjana alone) and the fifteen-types book per Wikipedia "Nepalese scripts", read first-party this pass; the book's contents (eight numbered alphabets, Golmol fifth on page 28) and its Golmol alphabet table per the *Nepal Lipi Sangraha* text on archive.org, read first-party this pass. - **The system.** Golmol is an abugida of the Nepalese family, left-to-right, writing Nepal Bhasa and, by family inheritance, Sanskrit. Its alphabet, as the book prints it, is the standard Newar abugida — with ten legible vowel rows, cleanly printed where Kunmol's ten are garbled: *A A I EE U OO E Ai O Au* — the same ten Kunmol prints, six short of the standard sixteen, the *Ri Ree Lri Lree Am Ah* six not legibly present in the OCR — and thirty-four legible consonant entries in four rows of 10, 10, 7, 7 (*Ka Kha Ga Gha Ṅa Ca Cha Ja Jha Ña* — the book spells the palatal nasal "Yan" here, cleanly, where Kunmol's OCR reads "Van"; *Ṭa Ṭha Ḍa Ḍha Ṇa Ta Tha Da Dha Na*; *Pa Pha Ba Bha Ma Ya Ra* — *La Wa* not legibly present in the OCR; *Śa Ṣa Sa Ha Kṣa Tra Jña*). The headstroke is the whole system: *mol* means "head", and Śākyavaṃśa names each script by its headstroke — Golmol's is the round one, the curve the whole group is named for. The parent chain is the Newar chain — Proto-Sinaitic → Phoenician → Aramaic → Brāhmī → Gupta → Siddham → Gaudi → Nepalese → Newar — with Golmol as a style of its terminal system. It has no ISO 15924 code of its own and no Unicode block: the encoded Newar script is Newa (333), U+11400–U+1147F, and zero code points anywhere in Unicode are named GOLMOL. [VERIFIED — the abugida, the direction, the languages, the ten legible vowel rows and the thirty-four legible consonants in rows of 10, 10, 7, 7, the headstroke naming and the *mol* gloss, and the curve-headed placement in both lists, per N4184 §2.1.1, Wikipedia "Nepalese scripts", Roy 2026, and the *Nepal Lipi Sangraha* text, all read first-party this pass; the parent chain and ISO 15924 Newa (333) per the Prachalit entry's census, carried; the zero GOLMOL-named code points by full Unicode 15.0 name scan this pass. - **The worked miniature (computed this pass).** Twelve counts, all reproduced by goal hidden_files/verify-golmol-20261111.py (197/197 checks pass). (1) **The name census.** Golmol in Devanagari गोलमोल is six code points: GA (U+0917), VOWEL SIGN O (U+094B), LA (U+0932), MA (U+092E), VOWEL SIGN O (U+094B), LA (U+0932) — four consonant letters and two vowel signs. The shared *-mol* tail — MA + VOWEL SIGN O + LA, three code points — is identical in Golmol, Hinmol, Kunmol, and Pachumol; the first syllable *gol* is GA + VOWEL SIGN O + LA, three code points. Golmol is the only one of the three six-code-point sisters with no nasal and no long vowel: Hinmol carries the anusvara on a short vowel (*hiṁ*), Kunmol carries the long ū plus the anusvara (*kūṁ*), Golmol carries neither — and Pachumol, the fourth sister at seven code points, carries a long vowel but no nasal. In Roman letters Golmol is six letters (N4184) and Golmōl is six letters with one *ō* (Wikipedia's navbox spelling; ō is U+014D LATIN SMALL LETTER O WITH MACRON, one code point) — the two Roman spellings differ in exactly one position, the second vowel's length mark. The style name golamola is eight letters — *gol* + *a* + *mol* + *a*, two vowels more than the script name — and the Devanagari string is identical: गोलमोल is both the script's name and the style's name. The Newa spelling the name would take — 𑐐𑑀𑐮𑐩𑑀𑐮 — is six code points (GA U+11410, VOWEL SIGN O U+11440, LA U+1142E, MA U+11429, VOWEL SIGN O U+11440, LA U+1142E): four letters, two signs, the same 4 + 2 split as the Devanagari. It is a constructed transliteration, not an attested spelling — no Newa spelling of the name was found in the sources read. (2) **The six-others census.** Śākyavaṃśa's six others are Pachumol, Hinmol, Kunmol, Golmol, Kvenmol, Litumol. With the three big names (Prachalit, Bhujinmol, Ranjana) that is nine named scripts; with Thaunkanhe Prachalit and Prachalit Newari added, eleven names in all. N4184 groups eight of them by headstroke: flat-headed three (Pachumol, Hinmol, Thaunkanhe Prachalit / Prachalit Newari) and curve-headed five (Bhujinmol, Golmol, Kunmol, Kvenmol, Litumol) — 3 + 5 = 8. The six others split two flat (Pachumol, Hinmol) and four curve (Golmol, Kunmol, Kvenmol, Litumol). Golmol is fourth in the six-others list order and second in N4184's curve-headed group listing (Bhujinmol, Golmol, Kunmol, Kvenmol, Litumol). It is also the second of the six others in the book — the fifth alphabet, after Kunmol (third) and before Pachumol (sixth) and Hinmol (seventh); Kvenmol and Litumol are not among the book's eight numbered alphabets. Ranjana stands outside both groups as its own "delightful" style, and Prachalit itself is the pācumola model the groups are measured against. (3) **The nine-list census.** Wikipedia's Types list names nine scripts in three styles: Rañjana style one (Rañjana), flat-headed four (Prachalit, Pāchūmol, Hiṁmol, Kuṁmol), curve-headed four (Bhujiṁmol, Golmol, Kveṁmol, Litumol) — 1 + 4 + 4 = 9. Against N4184's nine (three big + six others) the two lists name the same nine scripts and differ on one placement only: Kunmol is flat-headed in Wikipedia and curve-headed in N4184, and every other script agrees — Pachumol and Hinmol flat in both, Bhujinmol, Golmol, Kvenmol, and Litumol curve in both, Ranjana alone in both. Roy 2026 adds the third voice: Golmol "(rounded)" matches both lists, Kunmol "(angular)" matches neither — three voices in the same direction for Golmol, three voices in three directions for Kunmol. The book's contents lists eight numbered alphabets; the "15 types" claim leaves seven unnumbered. (4) **The book census.** Shakyavamsha's *Nepal Lipi Sangraha*, 8th edition 1993: fifteen types claimed; the contents numbers eight alphabets — 1 Ranjana p. 11, 2 Bhujinmol p. 22, 3 Kunmol p. 24, 4 Kwanmol p. 26, 5 Golmol p. 28, 6 Pachumol p. 30, 7 Hinmol p. 32, 8 Utumol p. 34 — then the currently-used alphabet p. 36, miscellaneous alphabets p. 38, and the Kutakshar monogram p. 44. Golmol is fifth of eight, on page 28: seventeen pages after Ranjana opens (28 − 11), six after Bhujinmol opens (28 − 22), four after Kunmol (28 − 24), two after Kwanmol (28 − 26), two before Pachumol (30 − 28), four before Hinmol (32 − 28), six before Utumol (34 − 28). The numbered alphabets run eleven pages for Ranjana (11 → 22) then six two-page steps (22 → 24 → 26 → 28 → 30 → 32 → 34); Golmol's step (26 → 28) is the third of the six. The vowel rows legible in the OCR, section by section: Ranjana 8 in the excerpt read (the rest not visible), Bhujinmol 14, Kunmol 10, Kwenmol 16, Golmol 10, Pachumol 16, Hinmol 14, Utumol 16 — three alphabets at sixteen (Kwenmol, Pachumol, Utumol), two at fourteen (Bhujinmol, Hinmol), two at ten (Kunmol, Golmol) — Golmol ties Kunmol for the fewest legible vowel rows in the book, but Golmol's ten are cleanly printed while Kunmol's are garbled. The seven fully-legible sections sum to 96 vowel rows (14 + 10 + 16 + 10 + 16 + 14 + 16); with Ranjana's 8 legible the total is 104, and with Ranjana at the standard 16 it is 112. The Golmol alphabet table itself holds ten legible vowel rows (A A I EE U OO E Ai O Au — the same ten Kunmol prints, six short of the standard sixteen: no *Ri Ree Lri Lree Am Ah* legibly present) and thirty-four legible consonant entries in four rows of 10, 10, 7, 7 — the thinnest legible consonant chart in the book, against the standard thirty-six the other sections print. (5) **The 1654 attestation census.** Pratap Malla reigned 1641–74: thirty-three years. The inscription of 1654 falls thirteen years into the reign (1654 − 1641) and names three scripts (pācumola, golamola, rañjā). It stands 612 years after the Bhujinmola emergence (~1042), 555 after Ranjana's first appearance (1099), and 746 after the first manuscript (908). The inscription is 372 years old in 2026. (6) **The emergence census.** The Bhujinmola emerged around 1042 and Ranjana first appeared in 1099: fifty-seven years apart, both inside the 11th century, both developed from the pācumola model. The Bhujinmola ran alongside Newari until the 14th century — about 358 years from 1042 to 1400; Ranjana stayed popular until the middle of the 18th century — about 651 years from 1099 to 1750. The first manuscript (908) predates the Bhujinmola emergence by 134 years and Ranjana by 191. (7) **The ban census.** The ban year is 1905 in N4184 and 1906 in Wikipedia: one year apart, unresolved. - **Decoder-design note (Golmol → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The eponym probe.** The curve-headed group is named golamola and Golmol is the member script that bears the group name. A rung that asks which script names the curve-headed group must get "Golmol" — and must not accept Bhujinmol (the oldest) or Kunmol (the disputed) as the eponym. It tests whether the specimen confuses seniority or controversy with naming. (2) **The clean-ten probe.** Golmol's vowel chart prints ten rows cleanly where Kunmol's ten are garbled. A rung that feeds a specimen both charts and asks which alphabet is complete must get "neither is settled — ten legible against sixteen standard in both; Golmol's are clean, Kunmol's are garbled, and the page images would settle both" — grading the refusal to over-read clean OCR as a complete alphabet. (3) **The no-use probe.** Roy 2026 calls Golmol "(rounded)" and attaches no use — no stone, no palm leaf, no paper. A rung that asks what Golmol was used for must get "no source read says" rather than a use borrowed from Kunmol's stone or Bhujimol's palm leaf. It tests whether the specimen invents a use for the script with no use on record. [SPECULATION — designs, not results; no Gauntlet run backs any rung]

- **The story.** The Kvenmol script (Devanagari क्वेँमोल as reconstructed — see the honest blank; romanized Kvenmol; N4184's Roman 'Kvenmol'; Wikipedia's Kveṁmol; the Brahmic-scripts navbox's Kveṁmōl) is one of the Nepalese scripts — a curve-headed style of the Newar script family, used to write Nepal Bhasa. It is the fifth of Śākyavaṃśa's six others (Pachumol, Hinmol, Kunmol, Golmol, Kvenmol, Litumol), the fourth in N4184's curve-headed group (Bhujinmol, Golmol, Kunmol, Kvenmol, Litumol), and the third in Wikipedia's curve-headed four (Bhujiṁmol, Golmol, Kveṁmol, Litumol). Both lists agree on its placement — N4184 puts it curve-headed, and Wikipedia's Types list puts it in the curve-headed four — and that agreement is where the agreement ends, because the third voice never speaks: Roy, "The scriptural heritage of the Kathmandu valley" (*International Journal of Sanskrit Research* 2026; 12(1): 240–241), names five of the nine scripts in its taxonomy — Bhujimol, Prachalit, Ranjana, Golmol "(rounded)", Kunmol "(angular)" — and never names Kvenmol at all, nor Pachumol, Hinmol, or Litumol. Kvenmol is the agreed-but-silent script: placed without dispute, described by no one. The name itself is the longest among the six others: where Golmol, Hinmol, and Kunmol are six code points in Devanagari and Pachumol and Litumol seven, Kvenmol's reconstructed Devanagari is eight — KA + VIRAMA + VA + VOWEL SIGN E + CANDRABINDU + MA + VOWEL SIGN O + LA — the only one of the six whose first syllable is a conjunct, क्व, and the only one whose nasal is printed as a candrabindu rather than the anusvara the other names carry. It ties Bhujinmol's eight for the longest name the catalogue has counted. The catch is the same as its sisters': "actual usage of several forms is unattested beyond charts published in script handbooks" — Kvenmol is a script with an alphabet table and no manuscript, a name in a list and a chart in a book. Its one solid home is that book: Hemraj Shakyavamsha's *Nepal Lipi Sangraha* (8th edition 1993), an alphabet book of fifteen types of Nepalese alphabets, where the fourth alphabet, on page 26, is spelled two ways in the same book — "Kwanmol" in the contents, "Kwenmol" in the section header — and neither spelling is "Kvenmol". That the book's fourth alphabet IS Kvenmol is this entry's identification, not a source's statement: the same author, the same family position between Kunmol (third, page 24) and Golmol (fifth, page 28), the v/w interchange of व and the ṁ-to-n drift of loose romanization, and the older Wikipedia Types list, which carried "Kwenmol" in exactly the slot the current list fills with "Kveṁmol". Against it: no source read states the identity, the contents' "Kwanmol" differs in the vowel as well as the consonant, and the book also carries Utumol, which has no counterpart in the six-others list — so the book's set is not the six-others set, and the fourth alphabet could be a tenth name rather than Kvenmol under another spelling. - **The system.** Kvenmol is an abugida of the Nepalese family, left-to-right, writing Nepal Bhasa and, by family inheritance, Sanskrit. Its alphabet, as the book prints it under the "Kwenmol" header — attached to Kvenmol by the identification above — is the standard Newar abugida in full: sixteen legible vowel rows, the complete standard set — *A A I EE U OO Ri Ree Lri Lree E Ai O Au Am Ah* — where Kunmol and Golmol print ten legible each, and thirty-four legible consonant entries in four rows of 10, 10, 9, 5 (*Ka Kha Ga Gha Ṅa Ca Cha Ja Jha Ña* — the book spells the palatal nasal "Yan" here, cleanly, where Kunmol's OCR reads "Van"; *Ṭa Ṭha Ḍa Ḍha Ṇa Ta Tha Da Dha Na*; *Pa Pha Ba Bha Ma Ya Ra La Wa* — the row Golmol leaves short, complete here; *Śa Ṣa Sa Ha Kṣa* — *Tra Jña* not legibly present in the OCR). The thirty-four ties Golmol's thirty-four: correction to the Golmol run's record, which called Golmol's chart "the thinnest legible consonant chart in the book" — Kwenmol ties it at 34, both two short of the standard thirty-six, missing different pairs (Kwenmol *Tra Jña*, Golmol *La Wa*). The headstroke is the whole system: *mol* means "head", and Śākyavaṃśa names each script by its headstroke — Kvenmol's is curve-headed in both lists, and Roy gives it no adjective at all, one of two curve-headed scripts Roy never names (the other is Litumol). The parent chain is the Newar chain — Proto-Sinaitic → Phoenician → Aramaic → Brāhmī → Gupta → Siddham → Gaudi → Nepalese → Newar — with Kvenmol as a style of its terminal system. It has no ISO 15924 code of its own and no Unicode block: the encoded Newar script is Newa (333), U+11400–U+1147F, and zero code points anywhere in Unicode are named KVENMOL. [VERIFIED — the abugida, the direction, the languages, the sixteen legible vowel rows and the thirty-four legible consonants in rows of 10, 10, 9, 5, the headstroke naming and the *mol* gloss, and the curve-headed placement in both lists, per N4184 §2.1.1, Wikipedia "Nepalese scripts", Roy 2026, and the *Nepal Lipi Sangraha* text, all read first-party this pass; the parent chain and ISO 15924 Newa (333) per the Prachalit entry's census, carried; the zero KVENMOL-named code points by full Unicode 15.0 name scan this pass; the "Yan" spelling in seven of the book's eight sections against Kunmol's lone "Van", counted from the archive.org text this pass. CLAIMED — the attachment of the Kwenmol table to Kvenmol (it rides the identification), the "Tra Jña" absence as a property of the OCR reading (the book may print them; the page image was not checked), and the "Yan" reading against Kunmol's "Van" (both are OCR readings of the same book)]

- **The worked miniature (computed this pass).** Twelve counts, all reproduced by goal hidden_files/verify-kvenmol-20261111.py (231/231 checks pass). (1) **The name census.** Kvenmol in Devanagari क्वेँमोल is eight code points: KA (U+0915), VIRAMA (U+094D), VA (U+0935), VOWEL SIGN E (U+0947), CANDRABINDU (U+0901), MA (U+092E), VOWEL SIGN O (U+094B), LA (U+0932) — four consonant letters, two vowel signs, one virama, one candrabindu. The shared *-mol* tail — MA + VOWEL SIGN O + LA, three code points — is identical in Kvenmol, Golmol, Hinmol, Kunmol, Pachumol, and Litumol; the first syllable *kveṁ* is KA + VIRAMA + VA + VOWEL SIGN E + CANDRABINDU, five code points. Kvenmol is the longest name among the six others — eight against Pachumol's seven, Litumol's seven, and six each for Golmol, Hinmol, and Kunmol — and it ties Bhujinmol's eight for the longest name the catalogue has counted. It is the only one of the six whose first syllable is a conjunct, and the only one whose nasal is printed as a candrabindu. In Roman letters Kvenmol is seven letters (N4184) and Kveṁmol is seven letters with one *ṁ* (Wikipedia's Types-list spelling; ṁ is U+1E41 LATIN SMALL LETTER M WITH DOT ABOVE) and Kveṁmōl is seven letters with one *ō* (Wikipedia's navbox spelling; ō is U+014D LATIN SMALL LETTER O WITH MACRON) — each step between neighbours differs in exactly one position, the nasal's letter (n → ṁ) and the second vowel's length mark (o → ō). The Newa spelling the name would take — 𑐎𑑂𑐰𑐾𑑃𑐩𑑀𑐮 — is eight code points (KA U+1140E, VIRAMA U+11442, WA U+11430, VOWEL SIGN E U+1143E, CANDRABINDU U+11443, MA U+11429, VOWEL SIGN O U+11440, LA U+1142E): four letters, two signs, one virama, one candrabindu, the same 4 + 2 + 1 + 1 split as the Devanagari. It is a constructed transliteration, not an attested spelling — no Newa spelling of the name was found in the sources read. (2) **The six-others census.** Śākyavaṃśa's six others are Pachumol, Hinmol, Kunmol, Golmol, Kvenmol, Litumol. With the three big names (Prachalit, Bhujinmol, Ranjana) that is nine named scripts; with Thaunkanhe Prachalit and Prachalit Newari added, eleven names in all. N4184 groups eight of them by headstroke: flat-headed three (Pachumol, Hinmol, Thaunkanhe Prachalit / Prachalit Newari) and curve-headed five (Bhujinmol, Golmol, Kunmol, Kvenmol, Litumol) — 3 + 5 = 8. The six others split two flat (Pachumol, Hinmol) and four curve (Golmol, Kunmol, Kvenmol, Litumol). Kvenmol is fifth in the six-others list order, fourth in N4184's curve-headed group listing (Bhujinmol, Golmol, Kunmol, Kvenmol, Litumol), and third in Wikipedia's curve-headed four (Bhujiṁmol, Golmol, Kveṁmol, Litumol). It is also the second of the six others in the book — the fourth alphabet, after Kunmol (third) and before Golmol (fifth) and Pachumol (sixth) and Hinmol (seventh); Litumol is not among the book's eight numbered alphabets under its own name. Ranjana stands outside both groups as its own "delightful" style, and Prachalit itself is the pācumola model the groups are measured against. (3) **The nine-list census.** Wikipedia's Types list names nine scripts in three styles: Rañjana style one (Rañjana), flat-headed four (Prachalit, Pāchūmol, Hiṁmol, Kuṁmol), curve-headed four (Bhujiṁmol, Golmol, Kveṁmol, Litumol) — 1 + 4 + 4 = 9. Against N4184's nine (three big + six others) the two lists name the same nine scripts and differ on one placement only: Kunmol is flat-headed in Wikipedia and curve-headed in N4184, and every other script agrees — Pachumol and Hinmol flat in both, Bhujinmol, Golmol, Kvenmol, and Litumol curve in both, Ranjana alone in both. Roy 2026 adds the third voice — and it is silent on Kvenmol: Roy names five of the nine (Bhujimol, Prachalit, Ranjana, Golmol, Kunmol) and omits four (Pachumol, Hinmol, Kvenmol, Litumol); of the six others it labels two (Golmol "(rounded)", Kunmol "(angular)") and leaves four unlabeled. The book's contents lists eight numbered alphabets; the "15 types" claim leaves seven unnumbered. (4) **The book census.** Shakyavamsha's *Nepal Lipi Sangraha*, 8th edition 1993: fifteen types claimed; the contents numbers eight alphabets — 1 Ranjana p. 11, 2 Bhujinmol p. 22, 3 Kunmol p. 24, 4 Kwanmol p. 26, 5 Golmol p. 28, 6 Pachumol p. 30, 7 Hinmol p. 32, 8 Utumol p. 34 — then the currently-used alphabet p. 36, miscellaneous alphabets p. 38, and the Kutakshar monogram p. 44. Kwenmol is fourth of eight, on page 26: fifteen pages after Ranjana opens (26 − 11), four after Bhujinmol opens (26 − 22), two after Kunmol (26 − 24), two before Golmol (28 − 26), four before Pachumol (30 − 26), six before Hinmol (32 − 26), eight before Utumol (34 − 26). The numbered alphabets run eleven pages for Ranjana (11 → 22) then six two-page steps (22 → 24 → 26 → 28 → 30 → 32 → 34); Kwenmol's step (24 → 26) is the second of the six. The vowel rows legible in the OCR, section by section: Ranjana 8 in the excerpt read (the rest not visible), Bhujinmol 14, Kunmol 10, Kwenmol 16, Golmol 10, Pachumol 16, Hinmol 14, Utumol 16 — three alphabets at sixteen (Kwenmol, Pachumol, Utumol), two at fourteen (Bhujinmol, Hinmol), two at ten (Kunmol, Golmol) — Kwenmol ties Pachumol and Utumol for the fullest legible vowel chart in the book, and is the only one of the three at sixteen whose placement is curve-headed in both lists. The seven fully-legible sections sum to 96 vowel rows (14 + 10 + 16 + 10 + 16 + 14 + 16); with Ranjana's 8 legible the total is 104, and with Ranjana at the standard 16 it is 112. The Kwenmol alphabet table itself holds sixteen legible vowel rows (A A I EE U OO Ri Ree Lri Lree E Ai O Au Am Ah — the full standard sixteen) and thirty-four legible consonant entries in four rows of 10, 10, 9, 5 — tied with Golmol for the thinnest legible consonant chart in the book, against the standard thirty-six. The palatal nasal reads "Yan" in seven of the eight sections and "Van" in Kunmol's alone. (5) **The 1654 attestation census.** Pratap Malla reigned 1641–74: thirty-three years. The inscription of 1654 falls thirteen years into the reign (1654 − 1641) and names three scripts (pācumola, golamola, rañjā). It stands 612 years after the Bhujinmola emergence (~1042), 555 after Ranjana's first appearance (1099), and 746 after the first manuscript (908). The inscription is 372 years old in 2026. (6) **The emergence census.** The Bhujinmola emerged around 1042 and Ranjana first appeared in 1099: fifty-seven years apart, both inside the 11th century, both developed from the pācumola model. The Bhujinmola ran alongside Newari until the 14th century — about 358 years from 1042 to 1400; Ranjana stayed popular until the middle of the 18th century — about 651 years from 1099 to 1750. The first manuscript (908) predates the Bhujinmola emergence by 134 years and Ranjana by 191. (7) **The ban census.** The ban year is 1905 in N4184 and 1906 in Wikipedia: one year apart, unresolved. On the 1906 reading the ban ran 45 years (1906–1951); on the 1905 reading, 46. After the lifting: moveable type in 1952 (1 year), the first typewriter in 1986 (35 years), the Guthi standard in 1989 (38 years), the Encoding Committee in March 2010 (59 years), N4184 in January 2012 (61 years), Unicode 9.0 in June 2016 (65 years). The encoding came 110 years after the 1906 ban year (2016 − 1906) and 111 after the 1905 one. The NGMPP ran 32 years; its successor the NGMCP began in 2002 and continues. - **The honest blank.** Fourteen confessions. (1) The Devanagari क्वेँमोल is a reconstruction: N4184's extraction prints only "ेँ मोल" — the first syllable is lost — and the क्वे is inferred from the Roman 'Kvenmol'; the catalogue never printed the Devanagari before this entry, and whether the extraction's nasal mark is a candrabindu (U+0901) or an anusvara mis-extracted was not settled against the proposal PDF's glyphs. (2) The Kwenmol = Kvenmol identification is this entry's inference, not a source's statement: the evidence is the same author, the family position between Kunmol and Golmol, the v/w and ṁ-to-n romanization drift, and the older Wikipedia list carrying "Kwenmol" in the Kveṁmol slot; the counter-evidence is that no source states the identity, that the contents' "Kwanmol" differs in the vowel as well as the consonant, and that the book also carries Utumol, which has no counterpart in the six-others list. (3) The contents spelling "Kwanmol" and the section-header spelling "Kwenmol" are carried as printed; whether "Kwanmol" is an OCR misread of "Kwenmol" was not settled against the page image. (4) The Utumol / Litumol parallel is not adjudicated: if Utumol is not Litumol, the book's set is not the six-others set and the structural half of the identification argument weakens. (5) The Roy-silence is a full-text find (zero "Kven" in the Roy PDF text as crawled this pass) — a scanned-image passage would not be found by that search, and the paper's references were not chased for a Kvenmol mention. (6) The consonant row 4 "Tra Jña" is not legibly present in the OCR — whether the book prints them was not verified against the Kwenmol page image, and the glyph line below the row may hold them. (7) The "Yan" reading is an OCR reading: seven sections print "Yan" and Kunmol's prints "Van" — whether Van is an OCR misread of Yan (or Yan of Van) was not settled against the page images. (8) The N4184 version gap: the original says the three writing systems are associated "since the 11th century", the revised says "since the 10th century" — not reconciled; this entry uses the original's 11th century for the heading, following the entry chain. - **Decoder-design note (Kvenmol → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The two-names probe.** The book spells its fourth alphabet "Kwanmol" in the contents and "Kwenmol" in the section header; N4184 spells the script "Kvenmol". A rung that asks for the book's fourth alphabet must accept Kwanmol/Kwenmol and must not reject it for failing to match N4184's spelling — and a rung that asks for Kvenmol must not accept the book's spelling as proof of identity without the identification argument. It tests whether the specimen treats a spelling variant as a different script, and whether it treats an identification as a fact. (2) **The full-sixteen probe.** Kwenmol prints all sixteen vowel rows where Golmol and Kunmol print ten legible each. A rung that feeds a specimen both charts and asks which alphabet is complete must get "Kwenmol's, sixteen legible; Golmol's ten legible against sixteen standard is not settled as complete" — grading the refusal to over-read clean OCR as a complete alphabet, and the recognition that a full chart is the exception in this book, not the rule. (3) **The Roy-silence probe.** Roy 2026 calls Golmol "(rounded)" and Kunmol "(angular)" and never names Kvenmol. A rung that asks what Roy calls Kvenmol must get "Roy never names it" rather than a use or an adjective borrowed from Golmol's "rounded" or Kunmol's stone. It tests whether the specimen invents a description for the script with no description on record. [SPECULATION — designs, not results; no Gauntlet run backs any rung]

## The Litumol script (11th century–present) — the curve-headed script with no chart in the chart-book, or: the last of the six others

- **The story.** The Litumol script (Devanagari लितुमोल as reconstructed from the extraction — see the honest blank; romanized Litumol; N4184's Roman 'Litumol'; Wikipedia's Types-list 'Litumol'; the Brahmic-scripts navbox's 'Litumōl') is one of the Nepalese scripts — a curve-headed style of the Newar script family, used to write Nepal Bhasa. It is the sixth of Śākyavaṃśa's six others (Pachumol, Hinmol, Kunmol, Golmol, Kvenmol, Litumol), the fifth in N4184's curve-headed group (Bhujinmol, Golmol, Kunmol, Kvenmol, Litumol), and the fourth in Wikipedia's curve-headed four (Bhujiṁmol, Golmol, Kveṁmol, Litumol). With this entry the six others are filed complete — entries #194 through #199, six consecutive, six of six — and Litumol is the last of them, the one the catalogue named as the next zero twice over (the Golmol run, then the Kvenmol run) before it got an entry of its own. Both lists agree on its placement — N4184 puts it curve-headed, and Wikipedia's Types list puts it in the curve-headed four — and that agreement is where the agreement ends, because the third voice never speaks: Roy, "The scriptural heritage of the Kathmandu valley" (*International Journal of Sanskrit Research* 2026; 12(1): 240–241), names five of the nine scripts in its taxonomy — Bhujimol, Prachalit, Ranjana, Golmol "(rounded)", Kunmol "(angular)" — and never names Litumol at all, nor Pachumol, Hinmol, or Kvenmol. Litumol is the agreed-but-silent script twice over: placed without dispute, described by no one, and — with Kvenmol — one of the two curve-headed scripts Roy never names. The name itself is the quiet one among the six others: where Kvenmol's reconstructed Devanagari is eight code points and Pachumol's seven, Litumol's is seven — LA + VOWEL SIGN I + TA + VOWEL SIGN U + MA + VOWEL SIGN O + LA — tying Pachumol's seven, with four consonant letters and three vowel signs and no virama, no conjunct, no nasal at all. It is one of the no-nasal trio (Pachumol, Golmol, Litumol) against the nasal trio (Hinmol and Kunmol with the anusvara, Kvenmol with the candrabindu), and the only one of the six whose first syllable is *li*. And here is the catch that makes Litumol the odd one of the family, sharper than its sisters': "actual usage of several forms is unattested beyond charts published in script handbooks" — but Litumol has no chart in the chart-book at all. The name occurs zero times in the full text of Hemraj Shakyavamsha's *Nepal Lipi Sangraha* (8th edition 1993), the alphabet book of fifteen types of Nepalese alphabets — not in the contents, not in a section header, nowhere in the book — and the eighth and last numbered alphabet, on page 34, is spelled "Utumol". Litumol is the only one of the six others whose name never appears in the book, and the only one whose alphabet — if it has one in the book — rides on an unadjudicated identification: the book's eight numbered alphabets are Ranjana, Bhujinmol, Kunmol, Kwenmol, Golmol, Pachumol, Hinmol, and Utumol, which is two big names plus five of the six others plus one unlisted — unless Utumol *is* Litumol, in which case the eight are exactly two big plus six others, and the book's set is the six-others set. For the identification: the family position (eighth and last, after Hinmol, where the six-others list ends), the shared "-tumol" tail (five letters, edit distance two — substitute L→U, delete i), and the Kwenmol precedent (the book's "Kwenmol" attached to N4184's "Kvenmol" on the same kind of evidence). Against it: no source read states the identity, the first-syllable gap (Li- against U-) is wider than the v/w drift in the Kvenmol case, and the book also carries the name twice with no variant spelling — contents and header both "Utumol". This entry does not adjudicate it; the identification stays open, and the Utumol table below is presented as the candidate, not as Litumol's. Outside the book, one more voice names it: Richard Ishida's Newar orthography notes list Litumol among the scripts used for writing Nepali languages, alongside Ranjana, Bhujimol, Kutila, and Golmol — Kutila being N4184's name for the whole family (§2.1.2: Newar "belongs to the 'Kutila' or 'proto-Bengali' family"), which makes the list's use of it as one script among others a loose one. - **The system.** Litumol is an abugida of the Nepalese family, left-to-right, writing Nepal Bhasa and, by family inheritance, Sanskrit. It is the one script of the nine with no alphabet table of its own in the book — so this system section states the absence first, and then presents the candidate. The candidate is the book's eighth alphabet, Utumol, on page 34: sixteen legible vowel rows — *A A I EE U OO Ri Ree Lri Lree E Ai O Au Anr Ah* — where "Anr" sits in the *Am* slot, the fifteenth row, an OCR reading not verified against the page image; and thirty-six consonant entries in four rows of 10, 10, 9, 7 (*Ka Kha Ga Gha Ṅa Ca Cha Ja Jha Ña* — the book spells the palatal nasal "Yan" here, cleanly, the seventh section to do so against Kunmol's lone "Van"; *Ṭa Ṭha Ḍa Ḍha Ṇa Ta Tha Da Dha Na*; *Pa Pha Ba Bha Ma Ya Ra La Wa*; *Śa Ṣa Sa Ha Kṣa Tra Jña*) — the full standard set, the fifth section in the book to print all thirty-six (Ranjana, Kunmol, Pachumol, Hinmol, Utumol) against two at thirty-four (Kwenmol and Golmol, both two short) and Bhujinmol with twenty legible in the read excerpt. With Pachumol, Utumol is one of only two sections in the book that print sixteen vowel rows *and* thirty-six consonants — the joint-most-complete chart in the book, where Kwenmol prints sixteen vowels but thirty-four consonants. The attachment of that table to Litumol is unadjudicated (see the story and the honest blank): the counts above are VERIFIED as Utumol's table, and the table is Litumol's only on the identification. The headstroke is the whole system: *mol* means "head", and Śākyavaṃśa names each script by its headstroke — Litumol's is curve-headed in both lists, and Roy gives it no adjective at all, one of two curve-headed scripts Roy never names (the other is Kvenmol). The parent chain is the Newar chain — Proto-Sinaitic → Phoenician → Aramaic → Brāhmī → Gupta → Siddham → Gaudi → Nepalese → Newar — with Litumol as a style of its terminal system. It has no ISO 15924 code of its own and no Unicode block: the encoded Newar script is Newa (333), U+11400–U+1147F, and zero code points anywhere in Unicode are named LITUMOL — and zero are named UTUMOL either. [VERIFIED — the abugida, the direction, the languages, the Utumol table's sixteen legible vowel rows and thirty-six legible consonants in rows of 10, 10, 9, 7, the headstroke naming and the *mol* gloss, and the curve-headed placement in both lists, per N4184 §2.1.1, Wikipedia "Nepalese scripts", Roy 2026, and the *Nepal Lipi Sangraha* text, all read first-party this pass; the parent chain and ISO 15924 Newa (333) per the Prachalit entry's census, carried; the zero LITUMOL- and UTUMOL-named code points by full Unicode 15.0 name scan this pass; the "Yan" spelling in seven of the book's eight sections against Kunmol's lone "Van", counted from the archive.org text this pass. - **The worked miniature (computed this pass).** Twelve counts, all reproduced by goal hidden_files/verify-litumol-20261111.py (261/261 checks pass). (1) **The name census.** Litumol in Devanagari लितुमोल is seven code points: LA (U+0932), VOWEL SIGN I (U+093F), TA (U+0924), VOWEL SIGN U (U+0941), MA (U+092E), VOWEL SIGN O (U+094B), LA (U+0932) — four consonant letters and three vowel signs. N4184's extraction prints the name as "िलतुमोल" — VOWEL SIGN I (U+093F), LA (U+0932), TA (U+0924), VOWEL SIGN U (U+0941), MA (U+092E), VOWEL SIGN O (U+094B), LA (U+0932) — the same seven code points in a different order: the preposed ि, second in the canonical spelling, extracts first, and the other six keep their relative order, so exactly two positions differ between the extraction and the canonical spelling. Litumol loses zero code points to the extraction — the contrast with Kvenmol, whose extraction "ेँ मोल" (six code points including the space, five without) loses three of eight (KA, VIRAMA, VA) and keeps only the tail. In Roman letters Litumol is seven letters (N4184 and Wikipedia's Types list) and Litumōl is seven letters with one *ō* (Wikipedia's navbox spelling; ō is U+014D LATIN SMALL LETTER O WITH MACRON) — the two spellings differ in exactly one position, the second vowel's length mark (o → ō). There is no dotted spelling: Litumol carries no nasal, so no "Lituṁmol" exists in any source read. The Newa spelling the name would take — 𑐮𑐶𑐟𑐸𑐩𑑀𑐮 — is seven code points (LA U+1142E, VOWEL SIGN I U+11436, TA U+1141F, VOWEL SIGN U U+11438, MA U+11429, VOWEL SIGN O U+11440, LA U+1142E): four letters, three signs, the same 4 + 3 split as the Devanagari. It is a constructed transliteration, not an attested spelling — no Newa spelling of the name was found in the sources read. Among the six others, Litumol ties Pachumol at seven code points, one short of Kvenmol's eight; the six split into a no-nasal trio (Pachumol, Golmol, Litumol) and a nasal trio (Hinmol and Kunmol with the anusvara U+0902, Kvenmol with the candrabindu U+0901), and Kvenmol alone carries a conjunct. Against Utumol: Litumol is seven letters, Utumol six; the reconstructed Devanagari उतुमोल is six code points (U U+0909, TA U+0924, VOWEL SIGN U U+0941, MA U+092E, VOWEL SIGN O U+094B, LA U+0932), one fewer than Litumol's seven; the two names share the five-letter tail "tumol" and sit at edit distance two — substitute L→U, delete i. (2) **The six-others census.** Śākyavaṃśa's six others are Pachumol, Hinmol, Kunmol, Golmol, Kvenmol, Litumol. With the three big names (Prachalit, Bhujinmol, Ranjana) that is nine named scripts; with Thaunkanhe Prachalit and Prachalit Newari added, eleven names in all. N4184 groups eight of them by headstroke: flat-headed three (Pachumol, Hinmol, Thaunkanhe Prachalit / Prachalit Newari) and curve-headed five (Bhujinmol, Golmol, Kunmol, Kvenmol, Litumol) — 3 + 5 = 8. The six others split two flat (Pachumol, Hinmol) and four curve (Golmol, Kunmol, Kvenmol, Litumol). Litumol is sixth in the six-others list order, fifth in N4184's curve-headed group listing (Bhujinmol, Golmol, Kunmol, Kvenmol, Litumol), and fourth in Wikipedia's curve-headed four (Bhujiṁmol, Golmol, Kveṁmol, Litumol). With this entry all six others are filed — #194 Pachumol, #195 Hinmol, #196 Kunmol, #197 Golmol, #198 Kvenmol, #199 Litumol — six consecutive entries, six of six. Ranjana stands outside both groups as its own "delightful" style, and Prachalit itself is the pācumola model the groups are measured against. (3) **The nine-list census.** Wikipedia's Types list names nine scripts in three styles: Rañjana style one (Rañjana), flat-headed four (Prachalit, Pāchūmol, Hiṁmol, Kuṁmol), curve-headed four (Bhujiṁmol, Golmol, Kveṁmol, Litumol) — 1 + 4 + 4 = 9. Against N4184's nine (three big + six others) the two lists name the same nine scripts and differ on one placement: Kunmol is flat-headed in Wikipedia and curve-headed in N4184. The book's contents lists eight numbered alphabets; the "15 types" claim leaves seven unnumbered. (4) **The book census.** Shakyavamsha's *Nepal Lipi Sangraha*, 8th edition 1993: fifteen types claimed; the contents numbers eight alphabets — 1 Ranjana p. 11, 2 Bhujinmol p. 22, 3 Kunmol p. 24, 4 Kwanmol p. 26, 5 Golmol p. 28, 6 Pachumol p. 30, 7 Hinmol p. 32, 8 Utumol p. 34 — then the currently-used alphabet p. 36, miscellaneous alphabets p. 38, and the Kutakshar monogram p. 44. Utumol is eighth of eight, on page 34: twenty-three pages after Ranjana opens (34 − 11), twelve after Bhujinmol opens (34 − 22), ten after Kunmol (34 − 24), eight after Kwanmol (34 − 26), six after Golmol (34 − 28), four after Pachumol (34 − 30), two after Hinmol (34 − 32). The numbered alphabets run eleven pages for Ranjana (11 → 22) then six two-page steps (22 → 24 → 26 → 28 → 30 → 32 → 34); Utumol's step (32 → 34) is the sixth of the six. The vowel rows legible in the OCR, section by section: Ranjana 8 in the excerpt read (the rest not visible), Bhujinmol 14, Kunmol 10, Kwenmol 16, Golmol 10, Pachumol 16, Hinmol 14, Utumol 16 — three alphabets at sixteen (Kwenmol, Pachumol, Utumol), two at fourteen (Bhujinmol, Hinmol), two at ten (Kunmol, Golmol). The seven fully-legible sections sum to 96 vowel rows (14 + 10 + 16 + 10 + 16 + 14 + 16); with Ranjana's 8 legible the total is 104, and with Ranjana at the standard 16 it is 112. The Utumol alphabet table itself holds sixteen legible vowel rows (A A I EE U OO Ri Ree Lri Lree E Ai O Au Anr Ah — "Anr" the fifteenth row, in the *Am* slot) and thirty-six consonant entries in four rows of 10, 10, 9, 7. The consonant census, counted this pass from the archive.org text: Ranjana 36, Bhujinmol 20 legible in the read excerpt (rows 1–2 only; rows 3–4 not legibly present), Kunmol 36, Kwenmol 34, Golmol 34, Pachumol 36, Hinmol 36, Utumol 36 — five sections at the full thirty-six, two at thirty-four, one partial. The seven fully-read sections sum to 248 legible consonant entries (5 × 36 + 2 × 34 = 180 + 68); with Bhujinmol's 20 the total is 268. New this pass: Utumol joins Pachumol as the only sections with sixteen vowel rows *and* thirty-six consonants, and "Litumol" occurs zero times in the book text while "Utumol" occurs exactly twice — the contents line and the section header. (5) **The 1654 attestation census.** Pratap Malla reigned 1641–74: thirty-three years. The inscription of 1654 falls thirteen years into the reign (1654 − 1641) and names three scripts (pācumola, golamola, rañjā). It stands 612 years after the Bhujinmola emergence (~1042), 555 after Ranjana's first appearance (1099), and 746 after the first manuscript (908). The inscription is 372 years old in 2026. (6) **The emergence census.** The Bhujinmola emerged around 1042 and Ranjana first appeared in 1099: fifty-seven years apart, both inside the 11th century, both developed from the pācumola model. The Bhujinmola ran alongside Newari until the 14th century — about 358 years from 1042 to 1400; Ranjana stayed popular until the middle of the 18th century — about 651 years from 1099 to 1750. The first manuscript (908) predates the Bhujinmola emergence by 134 years and Ranjana by 191. (7) **The ban census.** The ban year is 1905 in N4184 and 1906 in Wikipedia: one year apart, unresolved. On the 1906 reading the ban ran 45 years (1906–1951); on the 1905 reading, 46. After the lifting: moveable type in 1952 (1 year), the first typewriter in 1986 (35 years), the Guthi standard in 1989 (38 years), the Encoding Committee in March 2010 (59 years), N4184 in January 2012 (61 years), Unicode 9.0 in June 2016 (65 years). The encoding came 110 years after the 1906 ban year (2016 − 1906) and 111 after the 1905 one. The two versions of N4184 date the family's association a century apart — the original (January 5, 2012) says "since the 11th century", the revised (February 29, 2012) says "since the 10th century" — fifty-five days between the two versions, one century between their dates, under eight weeks apart. (8) **The manuscript census.** Nearly 30,000 manuscripts in the Newar script (Malla 1981: 23); about 50,000 manuscripts in Nepal Lipi archived; nearly 180,000 microfilmed by the NGMPP across 1970–2002, thirty-two years — about 5,625 a year. 30,000 is 60% of 50,000; 180,000 is 3.6 times 50,000 and 6 times 30,000. The NGMPP ran 32 years; its successor the NGMCP began in 2002 and continues. - **The story.** The Utumol script (Devanagari उतुमोल as reconstructed from the Roman — see the honest blank; romanized Utumol; no other spelling in any source read) is the eighth and last numbered alphabet in Hemraj Shakyavamsha's *Nepal Lipi Sangraha* (8th edition 1993) — the book's eighth alphabet, on page 34, closing the numbered run that opens with Ranjana on page 11. It is the one name in the whole family that no list but the book's carries: N4184 names the six others, including Litumol, and never Utumol (browser.find 0 in the proposal text this pass); Wikipedia's Types list names nine scripts and never Utumol; Ishida names Litumol among the scripts for Nepali languages and never Utumol; Roy's taxonomy is the nine and has no slot for it. Two web searches this pass — "Utumol" with "script Nepal", and bare "Utumol" — return exactly one relevant hit each: the book itself, the rest being uromodulin noise. Utumol is a hapax of the Nepalese-script literature: one source, two mentions (contents and section header), and nothing else — and the only dated attestation in the sources read is the book's eighth edition, 1993. The question this entry adjudicates — deferred by the Litumol entry, which left the identification open — is whether Utumol *is* Litumol under the book's spelling. The evidence, scored. FOR the identification: (1) the structural fit — the book's eight are two big names plus five of the six others plus Utumol, and exactly two big plus six others if Utumol is Litumol; (2) the shared "-tumol" tail, five letters, edit distance two — substitute L→U, delete i — the same total distance as the book's own Kwanmol to N4184's Kvenmol; (3) the Kwenmol precedent — the book's fourth alphabet is Kvenmol under a spelling no other list uses, so the book's spellings are known to drift from the scholarly names; (4) new this pass, the book drifts from itself — contents "Kwanmol" against section header "Kwenmol" for the same alphabet, so a Litumol→Utumol drift is not ruled out by the book's internal consistency; (5) the family position — Utumol closes the book's numbered run as Litumol closes the six-others list. AGAINST it: (1) no source read states the identity; (2) the first-syllable gap is wider in kind than the Kwenmol drift — Li- against U-, and Utumol is vowel-initial, the only vowel-initial name in the set, where every other name begins with a consonant; (3) the book spells it "Utumol" identically twice, contents and header, where Kwenmol varies; (4) three independent lists carry Litumol without Utumol — N4184, Wikipedia, Ishida; (5) Roy's taxonomy, the third voice, has no Utumol slot at all. VERDICT: the identification is NOT ADOPTED. Five for, five against, and neither side reaches proof: the structural fit is the strongest datum for, the three-lists silence the strongest against. Utumol is filed as its own entry — the book's eighth alphabet, with its own table — and the identity question stays OPEN for a future source (a first edition of the book, Shakyavamsha's papers) to settle. With this entry the book's eight numbered alphabets are eight of eight filed — Ranjana #191, Bhujinmol #192, Kunmol #196, Kvenmol #198 (as Kwenmol), Golmol #197, Pachumol #194, Hinmol #195, Utumol #200 — and the catalogue now counts twelve names where the lists name nine scripts: the nine, plus Thaunkanhe Prachalit, Prachalit Newari, and Utumol filed separately. The name itself is the shortest in the set, tied: six code points in Devanagari, tying Hinmol, Kunmol, and Golmol at six against Pachumol's and Litumol's seven and Kvenmol's eight — and the only one whose first syllable is a bare independent vowel, U, with three consonant letters and two vowel signs and no virama, no conjunct, no nasal at all. It joins the no-nasal trio as a fourth (Pachumol, Golmol, Litumol, Utumol) against the nasal trio. And here is the catch that makes Utumol the odd one of the family, sharper than its sisters': "actual usage of several forms is unattested beyond charts published in script handbooks" — and Utumol has a chart and nothing else: no manuscript, no inscription, no mention outside the one book that charts it. - **The system.** Utumol is an abugida of the Nepalese family, left-to-right, writing Nepal Bhasa and, by family inheritance, Sanskrit — on the family's terms, since no text in Utumol is attested beyond the book's chart. Its alphabet, as the book prints it under the "Utumol Alphabet" header on page 34, is the standard Newar abugida in full: sixteen legible vowel rows — *A A I EE U OO Ri Ree Lri Lree E Ai O Au Anr Ah* — where "Anr" sits in the *Am* slot, the fifteenth row, an OCR reading not verified against the page image; and thirty-six consonant entries in four rows of 10, 10, 9, 7 (*Ka Kha Ga Gha Ṅa Ca Cha Ja Jha Ña* — the book spells the palatal nasal "Yan" here, cleanly, the seventh section to do so against Kunmol's lone "Van"; *Ṭa Ṭha Ḍa Ḍha Ṇa Ta Tha Da Dha Na*; *Pa Pha Ba Bha Ma Ya Ra La Wa*; *Śa Ṣa Sa Ha Kṣa Tra Jña*) — the full standard set, the fifth section in the book to print all thirty-six (Ranjana, Kunmol, Pachumol, Hinmol, Utumol) against two at thirty-four (Kwenmol and Golmol, both two short) and Bhujinmol with twenty legible in the read excerpt. With Pachumol, Utumol is one of only two sections in the book that print sixteen vowel rows *and* thirty-six consonants — the joint-most-complete chart in the book, where Kwenmol prints sixteen vowels but thirty-four consonants. The headstroke is the whole system — *mol* means "head", and Śākyavaṃśa names each script by its headstroke — but Utumol has no headstroke adjective in any list, because no list but the book's carries it: N4184's flat-headed three and curve-headed five have no Utumol slot, and Wikipedia's flat four and curve four have none either, and the book's own header is only "Utumol Alphabet" with no adjective. The catalogue therefore records the headstroke as UNPLACED, not curve-headed: the Litumol entry's "curve-headed" for this table was the identification's, and the identification is not adopted — the book's glyphs would show the headstroke, but the page image was not read this pass. The parent chain is the Newar chain — Proto-Sinaitic → Phoenician → Aramaic → Brāhmī → Gupta → Siddham → Gaudi → Nepalese → Newar — with Utumol as a style of its terminal system, on the book's authority alone. It has no ISO 15924 code of its own and no Unicode block: the encoded Newar script is Newa (333), U+11400–U+1147F, and zero code points anywhere in Unicode are named UTUMOL — and zero are named LITUMOL either. [VERIFIED — the abugida, the direction, the languages, the Utumol table's sixteen legible vowel rows and thirty-six legible consonants in rows of 10, 10, 9, 7, the headstroke naming and the *mol* gloss, and the absence of any Utumol slot in N4184's and Wikipedia's groupings, per N4184 §2.1.1, Wikipedia "Nepalese scripts", and the *Nepal Lipi Sangraha* text, all read first-party this pass; the parent chain and ISO 15924 Newa (333) per the Prachalit entry's census, carried; the zero UTUMOL- and LITUMOL-named code points by full Unicode 15.0 name scan this pass; the "Yan" spelling in seven of the book's eight sections against Kunmol's lone "Van", counted from the archive.org text this pass. - **The worked miniature (computed this pass).** Fourteen counts, all reproduced by goal hidden_files/verify-utumol-20261111.py (293/293 checks pass). (1) **The name census.** Utumol in Devanagari उतुमोल is six code points: LETTER U (U+0909), TA (U+0924), VOWEL SIGN U (U+0941), MA (U+092E), VOWEL SIGN O (U+094B), LA (U+0932) — one independent vowel, three consonant letters, two vowel signs, no virama, no conjunct, no nasal. In Roman letters Utumol is six letters, and Utumōl is six letters with one *ō* (ō is U+014D LATIN SMALL LETTER O WITH MACRON) — the two spellings differ in exactly one position, the second vowel's length mark (o → ō) — but the macron spelling is unattested: no source read spells it so, and its only occurrences are the catalogue's own claims about it. The Newa spelling the name would take — 𑐄𑐟𑐸𑐩𑑀𑐮 — is six code points (LETTER U U+11404, TA U+1141F, VOWEL SIGN U U+11438, MA U+11429, VOWEL SIGN O U+11440, LA U+1142E): one vowel, three letters, two signs, the same 1 + 3 + 2 split as the Devanagari. It is a constructed transliteration, not an attested spelling — no Newa spelling of the name was found in the sources read. Among the six others, Utumol ties Hinmol, Kunmol, and Golmol at six code points, one short of Pachumol's and Litumol's seven and two short of Kvenmol's eight; the six split into a no-nasal trio (Pachumol, Golmol, Litumol) and a nasal trio (Hinmol and Kunmol with the anusvara U+0902, Kvenmol with the candrabindu U+0901), and Utumol joins the no-nasal side as a fourth. Against Litumol: Utumol is six letters to Litumol's seven; the reconstructed Devanagari उतुमोल is six code points to Litumol's seven; the two names share the five-letter tail "tumol" and sit at edit distance two — substitute L→U, delete i. Utumol is the only name of the seven whose first syllable is a bare independent vowel: Pachumol, Hinmol, Kunmol, Golmol, Kvenmol, and Litumol all begin with a consonant. (2) **The hapax census.** Utumol is named by exactly one source in the literature searched: the book. It occurs twice in the book text (contents, section header) and zero times in N4184 (browser.find on the proposal text this pass), zero in Wikipedia's Types list of nine, zero in Ishida's list (which names Litumol), and Roy's taxonomy has no slot for it at all. Two web searches this pass return one relevant hit each, both the book. - **The story.** The Kwanmol script is the contents spelling of the fourth alphabet of Hemraj Shakyavamsha's *Nepal Lipi Sangraha* (8th edition 1993), an alphabet book of fifteen types of Nepalese alphabets, where the contents numbers eight alphabets and the fourth, on page 26, is spelled "Kwanmol" — while the section header on the same page reads "Kwenmol Alphabet" (the djvu text OCR reads "Kwenmot Alphahet", L730), and neither spelling is "Kvenmol". That the book's fourth alphabet IS Kvenmol is the Kvenmol entry's identification, not a source's statement: the same author, the same family position between Kunmol (third, page 24) and Golmol (fifth, page 28), the v/w interchange of व and the ṁ-to-n drift of loose romanization, and the older Wikipedia Types list, which carried "Kwenmol" in exactly the slot the current list fills with "Kveṁmol". This entry carries that identification one step further and ADOPTS it as the catalogue's position: Kwanmol is the book's contents spelling of the fourth alphabet, which is Kvenmol. The verdict is a judgment on VERIFIED evidence, graded CLAIMED — and the evidence is six for, four against. FOR it: (1) the same slot on the same page — the contents' fourth entry points at page 26, and the section on page 26 is headed "Kwenmol"; the contents entry is a pointer, not a separate attestation; (2) the table identity, new this pass — the page 26 section's table IS the Kvenmol table, sixteen vowels and thirty-four consonants in rows of 10, 10, 9, 5, verified first-party from the djvu text; (3) the edit-distance chain — Kwanmol to Kwenmol is one (a to e), Kwenmol to Kvenmol is one (w to v), two in total, the same magnitude as Litumol to Utumol, and both steps are attested inside the one book; (4) the Kwenmol precedent — the catalogue already adopted the header spelling as Kvenmol, so Kwanmol is the same book's contents spelling of the same alphabet, one more drift, same book, same page; (5) no other candidate — no list anywhere carries a tenth script named Kwanmol, and the nine-list has exactly nine; (6) the family position — fourth in the contents between Kunmol and Golmol, exactly where Kvenmol sits in both lists' curve groups, fourth in N4184's group of five and third in Wikipedia's curve four. AGAINST it: (1) no source read states the identity in words; (2) the contents spelling differs in the vowel as well as the consonant — two drifts, not one; (3) the book also carries Utumol, which has no counterpart in the six-others list, so the book's set is not the six-others set and the fourth alphabet could in principle be a tenth name; (4) the OCR question — whether "Kwanmol" is a misread of "Kwenmol" was not settled against the page image, and the OCR is demonstrably fallible on this page ("Kwenmot" for "Kwenmol"). Why this differs from Utumol: Utumol was NOT ADOPTED, five for and five against, because its only evidence was slot and spelling — no table tied it to Litumol, since Litumol has no chart in the book at all and the Utumol table is its own. Kwanmol's contents pointer resolves to a section whose table is Kvenmol's table — the table identity is the evidence Utumol lacked, and it breaks the tie. - **The story.** The Kutakshar form is the monogram of the Ranjana script — Ranjana letters stacked into a single vertical syllable, written top to bottom where Ranjana runs left to right. Hemraj Shakyavamsha's *Nepal Lipi Sangraha* (8th edition 1993) lists it in the contents as "(Kutakshar) — A monogram type of Ranjana Alphabet — p. 44" (djvu text L174–L180, read first-party this pass; the contents' Devanagari is OCR-garbled, "chditfT", and the page number OCR reads "YY 44"), and the section on page 44 is headed "Kutakshar Alphabet" (L1078). Wikipedia's "Ranjana script" article states it plainly: "Kutākshar is a monogram of the Ranjana script. It is only one of the Nepalese scripts that can be written in monogram" — and "It is normally written from left to right but the Kutakshar form is written from top to bottom" — with a Kutākshar monogram on the facade of the Jana Bahal as the pictured example. Jens-Uwe Hartmann (1998, "The Ranjana Script") gives the mechanics: "Ranjana letters serve as the basis for a kind of monogram script whose letters are referred to as Kutaksara (probably 'heap syllables'). In this script, syllables are superimposed upon each other in such a way that the essential characteristics of the individual letters remain by and large intact, but coalesce into a single syllable on the model of ligatures in Indian scripts, without, however, dropping the vowels of the original syllables. Such complex figures can only be deciphered by the specialist or the initiate, and that may have helped their development, since they serve exclusively as a kind of shorthand for mantras and dharanis, which are esoteric" — and "The best-known example is the mantra of Kalacakra, called Namchu Wangden (rNam-bcu-dbang-ldan…)". Tim Brookes (2024, "Writing Joyfully") gives the other use and the other gloss: "Ranjana can be written in both horizontal and vertical (or 'monogram') forms. The latter is called kutakshar, or 'secret writing,' and was traditionally used to write sutras or to send secret messages — presumably because each word is so highly condensed and interwoven that it is hard to decipher." The ATypI Ranjana calligraphy workshop calls it "the vertical writing system of Ranjana Lipi". The question this entry adjudicates is whether Kutakshar is a script or a form — and this entry ADOPTS it as a form-entry: Kutakshar is a monogram FORM of Ranjana, not a separate script. The verdict is a judgment on VERIFIED evidence, graded CLAIMED — and the evidence is six for, five against. FOR it: (1) the book's own gloss — "A monogram type of Ranjana Alphabet", a type OF Ranjana, not an alphabet beside it; (2) Wikipedia — "a monogram of the Ranjana script"; (3) Hartmann — the letters ARE Ranjana letters, the monogram is a transformation of them, vowels not dropped, no new inventory; (4) ATypI — "the vertical writing system of Ranjana Lipi", a writing system of the parent, not a sibling; (5) no vowel table of its own — the p. 44 section lists consonant names only, the vowels live inside the monograms; (6) one direction change, not a new system — the same letters turned vertical. AGAINST it: (1) its own contents entry and its own section header "Kutakshar Alphabet" on its own page (44); (2) its own table — thirty-one legible consonant names; (3) the "secret writing" use — sutras and secret messages, a use distinct from Ranjana's public calligraphy; (4) Wikipedia gives it its own section heading, "Monogram (Kutākshar)"; (5) no source read states "form, not script" in words — the catalogue's judgment. The entry is filed under its own heading because the book and Wikipedia both give it one — the catalogue files forms that carry their own contents entry. The Kutakshar question is CLOSED as "form". The gloss question stays OPEN: "heap syllables" (Hartmann, kūṭa = heap) against "secret writing" (Brookes) — two readings of kūṭākṣara, unresolved. Two web searches this pass returned the book itself (the archive.org djvu text), the Wikipedia Ranjana article in two snapshots, Hartmann 1998, Brookes 2024, and the ATypI workshop page. - **The story.** The Vartula script is the round hand of Ranjana — Ranjana's letters with the headstroke gone round, written left to right where Ranjana runs left to right and Kutakshar runs top to bottom. The name is Sanskrit vartula, "round" (Hartmann 1998): the script is called Wartu in Tibet, Vartu on the calligraphy site, Vartula in the encoding proposal — one name in three spellings. Jens-Uwe Hartmann (1998, "The Ranjana Script") gives the definition and the lineage in one breath: "The same is true of a closely related form, the script called Wartu (from Sanskrit vartula, "round") in Tibet, which differs from Ranjana especially in its rounded horizontal bars. Tibetans have traditionally considered Wartu the model for their cursive script, whereas the printed script was thought to be derived from Ranjana." The calligraphy site lantsha-vartu.org gives the hand's own account: "The Vartu-script (vartula, round) appear to be a more casual form of a handwritten calligraphy. But the basic principles in forms and calligraphy of the consonants are the same like in Lantsha" — and its front page stakes the larger claim: "for Buddhist tradition the diversification and development from Ranjana into the Lantsha and Vartu script is more important" than Ranjana itself, "Common belief is that most Buddhist Sanskrit manuscripts of the 11th century are written in Ranjana. But that is not the case," and "Both scripts, Lantsha and Vartu, became the fundamental vehicle of Buddhist textual tradition." Anshuman Pandey (L2/16-015, 6 January 2016, "Towards an encoding for the Ranjana and Lantsa scripts") frames the open determination: "Unification of Vartu — A determination is required regarding whether or not to unify the script known as 'Vartu', 'Wartu', 'Vartula'. This script is based upon Ranjana / Lantsa, but possesses a curved headstroke instead of a horizontal or wedge-like form. The approach towards Vartu may be similar to the case of Tibetan in Unicode, which unifies several styles" — and the same document places the hand's geography: "A style of the script is used in Mongolia, where it often appears as one of four or five scripts in Buddhist manuscripts. There is evidence that an additional style of the script was used in Korea." Michael Everson (N3469, 4 May 2009, "Preliminary proposal for encoding the Rañjana script") proposes the merge outright: Rañjana is "visually and structurally similar to the Lañtsa & Wartu scripts used for Buddhist Sanskrit documents in Tibet (China), Bhutan, Mongolia, Nepal, Sikkim & Ladakh (India)" and "it has been considered would be practical to merge these two scripts (Lañtsa and Wartu) with Rañjana for encoding purposes." Hartmann supplies the dated spread: Ranjana was used for Buddhist inscriptions in China and Korea as early as the Mongolian Yuan dynasty (1280–1367), with the bronze temple bell in Gaeseong, Korea, carrying the Usnisavijayadharani from 1346, and the six-language inscription on the Quyongguan gate at the Great Wall from the same year — both Ranjana's spread, not Vartula specimens, and no Vartula specimen is named in any source read this pass. Wikipedia's "Nepalese scripts" article names nine scripts in three styles and never mentions Vartula at all — the name is absent from the family list as well as from the catalogue. The question this entry adjudicates is whether Vartula is a script, a style, or a hand — and this entry ADOPTS it as a style-entry: Vartula is a round-headed STYLE of Ranjana/Lantsa, not a separate script. The verdict is a judgment on VERIFIED evidence, graded CLAIMED — and the evidence is six for, five against. FOR it: (1) Hartmann — "a closely related form" of Ranjana, differing "especially in its rounded horizontal bars", one feature, not a system; (2) the Vartu site itself — "a more casual form of a handwritten calligraphy" whose "basic principles... are the same like in Lantsha", the hand's own words making it a hand, not a system; (3) Pandey — the suggested approach is unification, "similar to the case of Tibetan in Unicode, which unifies several styles", the standards author treating it as a style to unify; (4) Everson — merge Wartu with Ranjana for encoding, the same move from the other proposal; (5) no inventory of its own — no vowel table, no consonant table distinct from Ranjana's, and the site's chart is Ranjana's consonants with all vowels added; (6) one diagnostic mark — the curved headstroke instead of a horizontal or wedge-like form, a single difference, not a new alphabet. AGAINST it: (1) its own site and its own chart — lantsha-vartu.org gives it a page and a full consonant chart; (2) its own lineage claim — Tibetans consider Wartu the model for their cursive script, a descent line of its own; (3) its own geography — Mongolia and Korea styles, beyond Ranjana's Nepal–Tibet core; (4) Pandey frames it as a determination still open — "whether or not to unify" — the question is asked, not answered; (5) no source read states "style, not script" in words — the catalogue's judgment. The entry is filed under its own heading because the encoding proposals and the calligraphy site both give it one — the catalogue files styles that carry their own proposal paragraph. The Vartula question is CLOSED as "style". The Unicode unification determination stays OPEN: whether the standard unifies Vartu with Ranjana is Pandey's determination, not the catalogue's to close. Three web searches and four page opens this pass returned the Vartu chart page and the site root (read first-party), the Wikipedia "Nepalese scripts" article (browser.find "Vartula" — no match), and the Hartmann, Pandey, Everson, and Wikipedia "Ranjana script" passages via search excerpts quoting the passages verbatim. - **The system.** The system is Ranjana's system with one mark changed. The diagnostic is the headstroke: Ranjana's horizontal or wedge-like form becomes Vartula's curved headstroke (Pandey), its rounded horizontal bars (Hartmann) — one mark, and everything else carries over: the Sanskrit abugida in its Nepalese calligraphic dress, the same consonant inventory the Vartu site charts with all vowels added on hover, the same inherent vowel, the same conjunct behaviour. The direction is left to right, same as Ranjana; no source read claims a vertical or top-to-bottom Vartula, and the Kutakshar top-to-bottom direction belongs to the monogram, not to this hand. The use is Buddhist Sanskrit manuscripts and mantras in Tibet, Mongolia, and Korea — the site's words, "Both scripts, Lantsha and Vartu, became the fundamental vehicle of Buddhist textual tradition," and "these signs are a distinct mark of identification in mantras and Buddhist texts" — and the readers are the monks and the few who can read the hand at all: the site's front page says "there are only few people in the world who can read or write Lantsha- and Vartu-script." The parent chain runs Proto-Sinaitic, Phoenician, Aramaic, Brāhmī, Gupta, Siddham, Gaudi, Nepalese, Rañjanā, Vartula-style — ten systems, nine steps. The script is ISO 15924 Ranj (303), shared with Ranjana (CLAIMED — a style shares its parent's code, the Kutakshar rule), and Unicode 15.0 carries zero VARTULA-named, zero VARTU-named, zero WARTU-named, and zero RANJANA-named code points. The name itself: Devanagari वर्तुल as constructed, six code points (VA, RA, VIRAMA, TA, VOWEL SIGN U, LA); Roman "Vartula", seven letters; "Vartu", five letters; "Wartu", five letters; constructed Newa, six code points (WA, RA, VIRAMA, TA, VOWEL SIGN U, LA) — Newa has no VA letter, so the va is carried by WA. ## The Kutila script (5th century–present) — the crooked hand of the Licchavi inscriptions, or: the name with three owners

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero `## ` headings for "Kutila" in either catalogue, measured this pass — and the name occurs eleven times in seven lines in each catalogue: private lines 10378 (1, Bhujimol honest blank), 10394 (1, Prachalit miniature), 10396 (1, Prachalit honest blank), 10492 (3, Litumol story), 10554 (2, Vartula gap), 10562 (2, Vartula honest blank), 10566 (1, Vartula grades); public lines 14851 (1), 14867 (1), 14869 (1), 14965 (3), 15027 (2), 15035 (2), 15039 (1). "KUTILA", "Kuṭila", "kuṭila", and Devanagari "कुटिल" are 0/0 in both catalogues; 0 in TRICKS.md, TESTS.md, UNDECIPHERED.md, CIPHER-TIMELINE.md, and MATH-PHYSICS.md in both versions; 4 occurrences in 4 lines in each log (the #203 run's Next line, no-chat line, and two run summaries — private 40990/40997/40999/41048, public 33685/33692/33694/33743). The gap is a name with three owners and no entry of its own.

- **The story.** The Kutila script is the crooked hand of the Licchavi valley — kuṭila is Sanskrit for "crooked", and the name is the diagnostic: the Jain calligraphy survey (jainqq.org, read first-party this pass) says the script "is known as Siddhamatrika (perfect measure) or Kutila (crooked) because of its marked twist at the bottom of each vertical stroke of each character ending in finest of points", and that it "was already archaic in the 11th century". The identification is carried by the highest authorities the catalogue has: Unicode 16.0, Chapter 15, §15.5 (read first-party this pass) — "The script is also known as Siddhamātṛkā and Kuṭila"; Wikipedia's "Siddham script" article (read first-party this pass) opens "Siddhāṃ (also known as Kutila) is an Indic script used in India from the 6th century to the 13th century... derived from the Gupta script and ancestral to the Nāgarī, Eastern Nagari, Tirhuta, Odia and Nepalese scripts"; Anshuman Pandey's proposal to encode Siddham, quoted in Wikipedia's "Nepalese scripts" notes (read first-party this pass), says "The encoding for Siddham is to serve as a unifying block for all regional variants of the script, such as 'Siddhamātṛkā' and 'Kuṭila'". The same article's note 2 names the valley's own form: the Uttara Licchavi script "is also named Uttar-Licchavi, Post-Licchavi or Kuṭila (the regional variants of the Siddham script)", dated to the later Licchavi period, 6th–11th or 12th century. The corpus that makes Kutila a working category is the stone of the Kathmandu Valley: Wikipedia's "Stone inscriptions in the Kathmandu Valley" (read first-party this pass) — "The early inscriptions were written in the Sanskrit language using Gupta and Kutila scripts during the Licchavi dynasty" — and "The Licchavi inscriptions are 190 in total, and are carved in Sanskrit language. Among those inscriptions, 53 were written in Gupta script, while 137 were written in Kutila script", 5th–9th centuries; the oldest dated inscription in the valley, Shaka 107 (184/185 CE), on the pedestal of King Jayavarma's statue, unearthed at Maligaon in 1992, is Gupta, and Licchavi King Manadeva's Changu Narayan pillar, Shaka 386 (464 CE), is Gupta too — the Kutila stones run beside them, the Balambu inscription captioned "Kutila script" in the article's gallery. The lineage runs on: Abhijit Roy's 2026 Ananta paper, "The scriptural heritage of the Kathmandu valley" (read first-party in full this pass, all 275 lines — which also closes Bhujimol honest-blank (10), whose Kutila-lineage and Bhujimol-progenitor claims were carried as search-snippet only until now), says the Newari scripts are "Derived from the Brahmi-based Kutila lineage", that the late Brāhmī "branched into the Gupta and subsequently the Kutila (or Siddham) scripts of the 7th through 9th centuries", and that the valley's scripts "retained the intricate curves and flourishes characteristic of the Kutila style" — and that Bhujimol is "progenitor of the more decorative variants", "the preferred script for palm-leaf manuscripts (patra) until the 14th century". Richard Ishida's Newar orthography notes (28 April 2026, read first-party this pass) list Kutila among the scripts for Nepali languages: "Newa is one of at least 6 scripts used for writing Nepali languages, which include Ranjana, Bhujimol, Kutila, Golmol, and Litumol" — five named, the sixth unnamed. The wider Siddham story: the script "evolved from the Gupta Brahmi script in the late 6th century CE"; Kūkai introduced it to Japan on his return from China in 806; it survives in East Asia in Shingon and Tendai, where it is Bonji; in India Devanagari replaced it, while its northeastern derivative Gaudi became Eastern Nagari, Tirhuta, Odia, and the Nepalese scripts; Unicode 7.0 (June 2014) encoded it at U+11580–U+115FF. The third owner of the name is the revival: the Jain survey says "from the 15th cent, in Nepal, there seems an archaic revival of the Kutila, called Ranjana, using gold ink on blue-black paper" — and the low-grade conflation follows it: Eka Ratna Acharya's 2017 paper (search excerpt only) opens "The Ranjana script, which is also known as Kutila or Lantsa", echoed by the Alchetron mirror "(syn: Kutila, Lantsa)". The question this entry adjudicates is whether Kutila is a script, a name of Siddham, or Ranjana — and this entry ADOPTS it as a name-entry: Kutila is the northern name of Siddhamātṛkā, the Licchavi-era northern variant, not a separate script and not Ranjana. The verdict is a judgment on VERIFIED evidence, graded CLAIMED — and the evidence is five for, five against, with three Ranjana-synonymy items rejected. FOR it: (1) Unicode 16.0 §15.5 — "also known as Siddhamātṛkā and Kuṭila"; (2) Wikipedia's Siddham lead — "(also known as Kutila)"; (3) Ananta 2026 — "the Kutila (or Siddham) scripts of the 7th through 9th centuries"; (4) the Jain survey — "Siddhamatrika (perfect measure) or Kutila (crooked)"; (5) the Nepalese-scripts footnote — Kuṭila as "the regional variants of the Siddham script", a variant, not a sibling. AGAINST it: (1) the Stone inscriptions article counts 137 Kutila against 53 Gupta as separate categories; (2) Ishida lists Kutila among the scripts used for Nepali languages; (3) Ananta's "Kutila lineage" as the ancestor of Nepal Lipi; (4) the name's own meaning — kuṭila "crooked" names the diagnostic twisted stroke, a script-level trait; (5) the Balambu inscription is captioned "Kutila script" as its own gallery item, and Wikipedia carries Category:Kutila script. The Ranjana synonymy, three items, all rejected: (1) Acharya 2017; (2) the Alchetron mirror; (3) the Jain survey's revival line, read as a revival-name, not an identity — and the chronology kills it: the 137 Kutila inscriptions run 5th–9th century, two to six centuries before Ranjana (c. 1100, VERIFIED in the Ranjana entry), and Acharya's own paper dates the script to "199 BC", contradicting the 11th-century dating the catalogue carries. The entry is filed under its own heading because the inscription corpus gives it its own count (137) and its own category — the catalogue files names that carry their own corpus count. The Kutila question is CLOSED as "Siddham's northern name". The sixth-script question stays OPEN: Ishida names five of "at least 6" scripts, and the sixth is unnamed. Two web searches this pass returned the Ananta paper, the Stone inscriptions and Siddham and Nepalese-scripts articles, the Jain survey, the Unicode chapter, and Ishida's notes; seven pages were opened first-party, with one find (Kuṭila, two matches on the Unicode chapter). - **The system.** The system is Siddham's system, in its northern dress. The diagnostic is the sublinear twist — the marked twist at the bottom of each vertical stroke ending in finest of points, against the straight verticals of Gupta. The inventory is the Sanskrit abugida: sixteen vowels (a ā i ī u ū e ai o au aṃ aḥ ṛ ṝ ḷ ḹ) and thirty-three consonants (twenty-five stops in five rows of five, four approximants y r l v, four fricatives ś ṣ s h), forty-nine basic letters, with virama, anusvara, and visarga; the direction is left-to-right — the top-to-bottom Chinese style of Siddham is a Siddham-in-China variant, not attested for the Licchavi Kutila corpus, so Kutila adds no new direction. The parent chain is Egyptian → Proto-Sinaitic → Phoenician → Aramaic → Brāhmī → Gupta → Siddham → Gaudi → Nepalese → Newar, with Kutila sitting on the Siddham link as its northern name. ISO 15924 is Sidd (302) for Siddham, and none for Kutila itself; Unicode is U+11580–U+115FF, 92 assigned of 128, zero code points named KUTILA anywhere in Unicode. The use is Licchavi royal and religious inscription in Sanskrit — edicts, dedications, temple and stupa records cut in stone across the Kathmandu Valley; the readers are the Licchavi court, the valley's stone-carvers, and, centuries later, the epigraphers who count them. The name's later life is the lineage: the Kutila style carried into Nepal Lipi, and the 15th-century Ranjana revival that borrowed the name.
