## The Tirhuta script (7th century–present) — the letters of Mithila, or: the script with four names and no danda

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero `## ` headings for "Tirhuta" in either catalogue, measured this pass — and the name occurs five times in two lines in each catalogue: private lines 10572 (3, Kutila story) and 10582 (2, Kutila grades); public lines 15045 (3) and 15055 (2). "TIRHUTA", lowercase "tirhuta", "Mithilakshar", "Mithilakshara", and Devanagari "तिरहुता", "मिथिलाक्षर", and "तिरहुत" are 0/0 in both catalogues; 0 in TRICKS.md, TESTS.md, UNDECIPHERED.md, CIPHER-TIMELINE.md, and MATH-PHYSICS.md in both versions (public TESTS.md is not present in the mirror). "Maithil" occurs three times in three lines in each catalogue — private 10228 (Devanagari system), 10390 (Prachalit story), 10394 (Prachalit miniature); public 14701, 14863, 14867 — the language, never the script under its own heading. The research log holds five occurrences in five lines in each log: private 41062 (the #204 gap line), 41064 (its grades), 41069 (its no-chat line), 41071 (its run summary), 41107 (its close-out summary); public 33757, 33759, 33764, 33766, 33802. (The next zero stands named for a later loop: "Bhaiksuki" is 0 headings, 1 occurrence in 1 line in each catalogue — private 10582 / public 15055, the Kutila grades — and 1 in 1 line in each log — private 41062 / public 33757 — and 0 in the five other files in both versions; "Vessali" carries the identical counts in the identical lines.)

- **The story.** The Tirhuta script (Maithili 𑒞𑒱𑒩𑒯𑒳𑒞𑒰, romanized *tirahutā*) is the letters of Mithila under four names: Tirhuta, Mithilakshar (𑒧𑒱𑒟𑒱𑒪𑒰𑒏𑓂𑒭𑒩, *mithilākṣar*, "the letters of Mithila"), Maithili script, and Vaidehi script — also called Vaidehi Lipi. It has historically been used for writing Maithili, an Indo-Aryan language spoken by almost 35 million people in the Mithila region, and for Sanskrit; it is closely related to the Bengali–Assamese script, and Tirhuta, Bengali, Assamese, Newari, Meitei, and Odia are part of the same family of scripts. The history opens with a name from a book: the *Lalitavistara*, an ancient Buddhist text, mentions the Vaidehi script. A significant transformation occurred in the northeastern alphabet in the latter half of the 7th century AD, first evident in the inscriptions of Adityasena — the earliest recorded epigraphic evidence of the Maithili script, on the Mandar Hill Stone at Bounsi, Banka district, Bihar — and the eastern variant of this transformed script subsequently developed into the Maithili script, which gained prominence in regions like Assam, Bengal, and Nepal, and is also called the Gaudiya script. It had come to its current shape by the 10th century AD; the oldest form of Mithilakshar is also found in the Sahodara stone inscriptions of 950 AD, at the Sahodara temple in West Champaran, Bihar. The script has been used throughout Mithila from Champaran to Deoghar. A fragmentary inscription found in Simraungadh, the medieval capital of the Karnats of Mithila, which dates back to the 12th century in Tirhuta script, is also one of the oldest pieces of evidence for it. The script became distinguished from the Bengali, Oriya, and Newari scripts by the 14th century — though inscriptions show the early Maithili and Oriya scripts were very similar up until the 15th century — and the gallery carries one more dated stone: the inscription of King Narasimha of the Oinwar dynasty in the Tirhuta script at the Kandaha Sun Temple in Kandaha village, Saharsa district, c. 1435 AD. The standard carries the same spine in its own words: Unicode 8.0, Chapter 15, §15.10 (read first-party this pass) — Tirhuta is "derived from Gauḍī, or 'ProtoBengali,' which evolved from the Kuṭila branch of Brahmi by the 10th century", "related to the Bengali, Newari, and Oriya scripts, which are also descended from Gauḍī, and became differentiated from them by the 14th century", and "remained the primary writing system for Maithili until the late 20th century, when it was replaced by Devanagari". The standard also says the script "forms the basis of scholarly and religious scribal traditions that have been associated with the Maithili and Sanskrit languages since the 14th century", that it "continues to be used for writing manuscripts of religious and literary texts, as well as personal correspondence", that since the 1950s "various literary societies, such as the Maithili Akademi and Chetna Samiti, have been publishing literary, educational, and linguistic materials in Tirhuta", and that it is used "in signage in Darbhanga and other districts of north Bihar, and as an optional script for writing the civil services examination in Bihar" — and warns, in the sentence that matters most for a decoder, that "although several Tirhuta characters, ligatures or combined shapes bear resemblance to those of Bengali, these similarities are superficial". The present is a decline and a revival at once: the use of the script has been declining in the last 100 years, "which is the primary reason for the Mithila culture's decline", and nowadays Maithili is written almost exclusively in Devanagari, although Tirhuta is still sometimes used by religious pundits and some culture-conscious families for writing ceremonial letters (*pātā*), documents, and cultural affairs, with efforts underway to broaden its use. The print history runs through three attempts: in the early 20th century some Sanskrit works were printed in the script through the lithographic process; later Pusk Bhandar, Laheriasarai managed to forge a set of types and published a few works in Tirhuta but could not go ahead; in the middle of the last century the All India Maithili Conference came with a new set of types and used it in the prestigious publication of *Brihat Maithili Shabdakosha*. The language's standing is the stronger half of the story: the official recognition of Maithili as one of the 14 provincial official languages of Nepal and its inclusion in the Eighth Schedule to the Constitution of India in 2003 "have established it as a language with an independent identity" — "however, currently Maithili in the Devanagari script is officially recognised". In the year 2013 a campaign called Mithilakshar Saksharta Abhiyan, for the literacy of the script among the common people in the Mithila region, was started; in June 2014 the Tirhuta script was added to the Unicode Standard from version 7.0, and "although there is limited electronic font support, digitalisation efforts have started". The question this entry adjudicates is the parent question — whether Tirhuta descends from Siddham through Gaudi, as Wikipedia's infobox parent chain has it (Proto-Sinaitic → Phoenician → Aramaic → Brāhmī → Gupta → Siddhaṃ → Gaudi → Tirhuta), or from the Kuṭila branch through Gauḍī, as Unicode §15.10 has it — and this entry ADOPTS the chain as one chain, not two: the two sources name the same grandparent under two names, and catalogue #204's verdict (Kutila is the northern name of Siddhamātṛkā) is what makes them agree. The verdict is a judgment on VERIFIED evidence, graded CLAIMED — and the evidence is the two chains laid side by side: both run Brāhmī → Gupta → a Siddham/Kuṭila node → a Gaudi/Gauḍī node → Tirhuta, with no step in either chain contradicting a step in the other. This entry also closes a forward reference from #204: the Kutila story's "its northeastern derivative Gaudi became Eastern Nagari, Tirhuta, Odia, and the Nepalese scripts" is now a filed entry, not a promise. - **The system.** The diagnostic is the false-friend pair, and it is a trap with a name: Tirhuta letter RA (U+114A9) has the same form as Bengali letter BA (U+09AC), and Tirhuta letter VA (U+114AB) has the same shape as Bengali letter RA (U+09B0) — read by shape alone, the two scripts swap their r and their v/b. The third false friend is a combination: the consonant-vowel combination TA + VOWEL SIGN U (U+1149E + U+114B3) in Tirhuta produces the same shape as the conjunct TA + virama + TA in Bengali. Against the lookalikes, the true differences are small and counted: most of the consonant letters are effectively identical to Bengali–Assamese, with the exception of 7 of the 33 — ⟨jh, ṭ, ḍh, ṇ, l, ś, h⟩ — so 26 of 33 are the same shape and 7 carry the distinction, 21.21% different. The inventory is the Sanskrit abugida with two Tirhuta-only moves: fourteen independent vowel letters (a ā i ī u ū ṛ ṝ ḷ ḹ ē ai ō au) and thirty-three consonants, with fifteen dependent vowel signs — eight spacing (AA, I, II, E, AI, O, SHORT O, AU) and seven non-spacing (U, UU, VOCALIC R, VOCALIC RR, VOCALIC L, VOCALIC LL, SHORT E) — and the two signs that have no independent form at all, short e (U+114BA) and short o (U+114BD), because the sounds they represent do not occur in word-initial position. The signs run nine: candrabindu (U+114BF) and anusvara (U+114C0) for nasalization, visarga (U+114C1), virama (U+114C2), nukta (U+114C3), avagraha (U+114C4), gvang (U+114C5), abbreviation sign (U+114C6), and om (U+114C7). Two letters wear dots that are not nukta: BA (U+114A5) and VA (U+114AB) have shapes that include a dot, but this is not semantically equivalent to a nukta — the letters do not decompose to nukta and are treated as atomic characters. Five vowel letters are encoded atomically even though they can be analyzed visually as consisting of multiple parts, and Table 15-5 names the sequences that must not be used: AA is not A + AA-sign, VOCALIC L is not LA + VOCALIC R-sign, VOCALIC LL is not LA + VOCALIC RR-sign, AI is not E + SHORT E-sign, AU is not O + SHORT E-sign. The script-specific signs are the opening and the blessing: anji (U+11480), used in the invocations of letters, manuscripts, books, and charts of the script, said to represent the tusk of the deity Ganesha, patron of learning; and om (U+114C7), which contrasts with the Bengali sign for om, a simple combination of Bengali letter O plus candrabindu. The script has no danda of its own: Tirhuta uses Devanagari danda (U+0964) and double danda (U+0965) from the Devanagari block, and its numbers are its own full set of decimal digits (U+114D0–U+114D9), with number forms and unit marks borrowed from the Common Indic Number Forms block (U+A830–U+A83F) — fraction one half, fraction three quarters, the rupee mark (U+A838) — and Bengali currency numerators such as U+09F4. The direction is left-to-right; the use is Maithili and Sanskrit; the readers are the almost-35-million Maithili speakers of Bihar and Nepal's Narayani and Janakpur zones, plus the pundits, the literary societies, and the civil-services candidates who still write it. The parent chain is Proto-Sinaitic → Phoenician → Aramaic → Brāhmī → Gupta → Siddham (=Kuṭila) → Gaudi → Tirhuta, eight systems in seven steps; the sisters are Bengali–Assamese, Odia, and Newari; ISO 15924 is Tirh (326); Unicode 7.0 (June 2014) encoded it at U+11480–U+114DF, 82 assigned of 96 code points, 14 reserved, all 82 in the single 7.0 release, on Anshuman Pandey's request of 21 June 2006 (L2/06-226), eight years from request to release.

- **Decoder-design note (Tirhuta → Gauntlet).** Three rungs. (1) **The false-friend probe.** Present Tirhuta RA and VA beside Bengali BA and RA; the specimen must read them as Tirhuta letters (ra, va), not as their Bengali lookalikes — a specimen that transliterates by shape has swallowed a lookalike, and the swap is exactly the two letters that trade places. (2) **The no-danda probe.** Present a Tirhuta sentence ending in a Devanagari danda; the specimen must report the punctuation as borrowed from Devanagari, not as Tirhuta's own — a specimen that claims a Tirhuta danda has invented a code point, and the block has none to invent. (3) **The parent probe.** Present the two parent claims — Wikipedia's Siddham → Gaudi chain and Unicode's Kuṭila-branch → Gauḍī line — and require the specimen to resolve them through the #204 verdict (Kutila is Siddham's northern name) rather than declaring a contradiction — a specimen that calls it a conflict has not read the catalogue. A design, never run — no verdict without a gauntlet sitting.

- **The story.** The Bhaiksuki script (Sanskrit भैक्षुकी, *bhaikṣukī*; Bhaiksuki 𑰥𑰹𑰎𑰿𑰬𑰲𑰎𑰱) is the arrow-headed letters of the Buddhist monks — the name is the monks' in the plain reading, *bhaikṣukī*, "of the mendicant monks" — a Brahmi-based abugida used around the 11th and 12th centuries CE in what is now Bihar and West Bengal in India and the regions of Bangladesh, with records also located in Tibet, Nepal, and Burma. It used to be known in English as the "Arrow-Headed Script" or "Point-Headed Script", in German as *Pfeilspitzenschrift*, in Hindi and modern Sanskrit as *Śaramātr̥kā Lipi*, and under an older designation, "Sindhura", used in Tibet for at least three centuries; the standard adds a sixth name, the original one: Saindhavī, "the Sindhu or Indus script", the name it carried before its discovery in the late 19th century, when scholars renamed it Bhaiksuki or called it the Arrow-headed script. The script is found exclusively in Buddhist texts, and its whole surviving corpus fits in one sentence: only eleven inscriptions and four manuscripts written in this script are presently known to exist. The four manuscripts are the Bhaiksuki codices of the *Abhidharmasamuccayakārikā*, the *Maṇicūḍajātaka*, the *Candrālaṃkāra*, and at least one more Buddhist canonical text, still unnamed. The codices of the *Abhidharmasamuccayakārikā* and of the *Maṇicūḍajātaka* were once kept in the Tibetan monastery of Gonkhar, and were brought to Italy by Giuseppe Tucci in 1948; the *Maṇicūḍajātaka*'s exact place of preservation is unknown and only photographs of the text are accessible, while the *Abhidharmasamuccayakārikā* codex was rediscovered in Tucci's last home in 2014 and is now on display at the National Museum of Oriental Art in Rome; the fourth codex was discovered in Tibet and was recently shown in a Chinese documentary, but information about it is limited. Sanskrit is the main language written in the script, and it is strongly related to the Devanagari and Sharada scripts. The modern study of the script runs through Marburg: the Arrow-headed Script Project at the Philipps-Universität Marburg has researched Bhaiksuki and built resources for it since a project launch in 2004, and the script was first noticed by Cecil Bendall, whose 1883 catalogue of the Buddhist Sanskrit manuscripts at Cambridge carries it and who also recorded an inscription on a brass image of the Buddha from Gaya. The encoding road ran five years and five documents: the preliminary proposal (N4121, L2/11-259, 2011), two 2013 proposals (N4469, L2/13-167; N4489, L2/13-194, 27 October 2013), a January 2014 revision (L2/14-036), and the final proposal (N4573, L2/14-091, 23 April 2014) by Anshuman Pandey and Dragomir Dimitrov — and in June 2016 the Bhaiksuki alphabet was added to the Unicode Standard with version 9.0. The standard carries the same spine in its own words: Unicode 14.0, Chapter 14, §14.3 (read first-party this pass) — Bhaiksuki is "a Brahmi-derived script used from about the 10th to the 13th centuries ce, primarily in the area of the present-day states of Bihar and West Bengal in India and northern Bangladesh", its original name Saindhavī, "and surviving Bhaiksuki texts are limited to a few Buddhist manuscripts and inscriptions". The question this entry adjudicates is the parent question — whether Bhaiksuki descends from Gupta through Gauḍī, as Omniglot has it ("developed from the Gauḍī or Proto-Bengali script during the 11th century AD"), or straight from Gupta, as Wikipedia's infobox parent chain has it (Egyptian → Proto-Sinaitic → Phoenician → Aramaic → Brahmi → Gupta → Bhaiksuki) — and this entry ADOPTS the long chain, restoring the Gauḍī node the infobox collapsed: Egyptian → Proto-Sinaitic → Phoenician → Aramaic → Brahmi → Gupta → Gaudi → Bhaiksuki, eight systems in seven steps. The verdict is a judgment on VERIFIED evidence, graded CLAIMED — and the evidence is that the two chains agree on every step they both name, and the Gauḍī link is the only source that names the step between Gupta and Bhaiksuki at all. The adoption makes Bhaiksuki the sister of Tirhuta (#205): two Gauḍī children, one that lived into a language of almost 35 million speakers and one that died with fifteen witnesses. Two web searches this pass returned the Wikipedia article, the final proposal, the Unicode 14.0 chapter, and the Omniglot, uniblab, and Tiwari mirrors; two pages were opened first-party, with one find (14.3 Bhaiksuki, three matches on the Unicode chapter). - **The system.** The diagnostic is the arrow-head, and it is a trap with a name: the letters carry triangular arrow-heads at the top — and in some letters at the sides — struck by a thick-nibbed pen, so the head is the letter, not damage on it and not a headline borrowed from another script. Against the lookalikes, the inventory is the Sanskrit abugida with two Bhaiksuki-only moves: thirteen independent vowel letters (a ā i ī u ū ṛ ṝ ḷ ē ai ō au) — no vocalic ḹ, the one vowel Tirhuta has that Bhaiksuki does not, neither letter nor sign — and thirty-three consonants, with twelve dependent vowel signs, and the signs run five: candrabindu (U+11C3C) and anusvara (U+11C3D) for nasalization, visarga (U+11C3E), virama (U+11C3F), and avagraha (U+11C40) for the elision of a word-initial *a* in sandhi. The rendering has its own rules: many vowel signs have contextual variants with certain consonants; PA (U+11C22), YA (U+11C27), and RA (U+11C28) have special combining forms when they occur with certain vowel signs; KA, PA, RA, and YA take special forms when they occur in conjuncts; the dependent vowel signs in U+11C38–U+11C3B (e, ai, o, au) are treated as above-base signs, and ai, o, and au are encoded atomically with no formal canonical decompositions. The virama (U+11C3F) suppresses the inherent vowel and forms conjuncts, rendered as vertically stacked ligatures with the non-initial consonants attached below the initial letter; above-base vowel signs and consonant letters attach to the glyph of the initial consonant, while below-base vowel signs attach to the glyph of the final consonant; a bare <C, virama> shows a visible virama by default, while <ta, virama>, <na, virama>, and <ma, virama> may display as special ligatures with no semantic distinction. The punctuation is the contrast with Tirhuta: Bhaiksuki employs script-specific dandas of its own, U+11C41 DANDA and U+11C42 DOUBLE DANDA, where Tirhuta borrows Devanagari's — and it adds a word separator (U+11C43) and two gap fillers (U+11C44 GAP FILLER-1, U+11C45 GAP FILLER-2), spacing or completion marks used especially to indicate the end of a line, and also to indicate a deliberate elision or an otherwise missing portion of text. The numbers are two systems in one block: a script-specific set of decimal digits (U+11C50–U+11C59) — but the glyphs for zero (U+11C50) and three (U+11C53) have not yet been identified in the Bhaiksuki corpus, so their representative glyphs are borrowed from corresponding digits in other scripts contemporaneous with Bhaiksuki — and a distinct vertical notation, numbers for the primary and tens units (U+11C5A–U+11C6B) with a hundreds unit mark (U+11C6C), written vertically with the largest number above the smaller units. The direction is left-to-right; the use is Sanskrit; the readers are the Buddhist monks of the Pāla east in the 11th and 12th centuries, and today the scholars who study the fifteen witnesses. The parent chain is Egyptian → Proto-Sinaitic → Phoenician → Aramaic → Brahmi → Gupta → Gaudi → Bhaiksuki, eight systems in seven steps; the sisters are Sharada, Tibetan, Siddham, and Kalinga; ISO 15924 is Bhks (334); Unicode 9.0 (June 2016) encoded it at U+11C00–U+11C6F, 97 assigned of 112 code points, 15 reserved, all 97 in the single 9.0 release, on five proposal documents from 2011 to 2014, five years from first proposal to release.

- **Decoder-design note (Bhaiksuki → Gauntlet).** Four rungs. (1) **The arrow-head probe.** Present a Bhaiksuki letter beside a lookalike from another Brahmi child; the specimen must read the arrow-heads as the script's own mark, struck by a thick-nibbed pen — a specimen that calls them damage, or a headline borrowed from another script, has not read the system. (2) **The fifteen-witness probe.** Present a claimed sixteenth Bhaiksuki item — a new manuscript, a new inscription — and require the specimen to check it against the fifteen known witnesses and demand provenance (Gonkhar, Tucci 1948, the 2014 Rome rediscovery, the documentary) before accepting it — a specimen that accepts a sixteenth item on shape alone has invented a witness. (3) **The borrowed-digit probe.** Present U+11C50 DIGIT ZERO and U+11C53 DIGIT THREE; the specimen must report that their glyphs are NOT attested in the corpus but borrowed from contemporaneous scripts — a specimen that claims them as attested has invented evidence. (4) **The danda-contrast probe.** Present a Bhaiksuki sentence ending in U+11C41 DANDA beside a Tirhuta sentence ending in a Devanagari danda; the specimen must report Bhaiksuki's danda as its own and Tirhuta's as borrowed — a specimen that says Bhaiksuki borrows its dandas has confused the two Gauḍī children. A design, never run — no verdict without a gauntlet sitting.

- **The story.** The Vessali script — spelled "Vesali" in every source read this pass, "Vēsālī" with its macrons, and "Vessali" only in the catalogue's own inherited naming — is the Vesali-age hand of Arakan: the writing of the Chandra kings' Vesali, the old city near modern Mrohaung in the Akyab District, in what is now Rakhine State, Myanmar. It is not a script with a chart and a code — it is a phase, an age of the Arakanese script line, and this entry files it as one: the Gupta-descended eastern Brahmi hand of the fourth to sixth centuries CE, with local development, writing Sanskrit and Sanskrit mixed with Pali. The ground's earliest witness is older than the age and in another hand: the Fat Monk image inscription, one line in Old Brahmi and Pali, found near the old Vesali city, dated to about the second century BCE and belonging to the Surya dynasty of the third Dhanyawady period — the earliest datable inscription of Arakan. The Vesali age proper opens with stone: three small inscriptions found at Vēsālī and read by D. C. Sircar in 1957, in Epigraphia Indica volume 32 — the first on a slab eighteen inches long, ten high, six thick, five lines, thirteen to eighteen letters to a line, recovered from the ruins of a stupa on Unhissaka hill; the second of four lines on a ten-by-four-inch slab from the Anandachandra Stupa, still in situ; the third, fragmentary, six lines over twenty-four by nine inches on a six-foot octagonal pillar from a stupa of the ruler Suryachandra. Their alphabet, Sircar wrote, closely resembles the alphabet of certain fifth- and sixth-century inscriptions of eastern India, with an amount of local development — slight in the first, more pronounced in the second, most of all in the third — and it closely resembles a fourth witness, the two-line votive inscription on a monastery bell found at Vēsālī, published by E. H. Johnston in the Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies, volume XI, 1943–46, pages 358 and following. Johnston dated the bell by its letters: its forms for ka and sa and its tripartite ya put it probably not later than A.D. 650. The age's great witness stands apart and mostly unread: the Anandacandra stone inscription, a tall four-sided pillar discovered in the nineteenth century and listed by the Memory of the World Committee for Asia and the Pacific in 2018 — its one legible face, in Sanskrit, seventy-two lines of verse carrying a ruling king's ancestors over several centuries, with only the top six lines already damaged at discovery, and its other three faces in three other North Indian scripts, not yet deciphered, having suffered significant damage and irrecoverable loss. It is the only inscription from Arakan that gives such an ancestor sequence, and it alludes to political connections with Sri Lanka and the Andhra area and to religious Buddhist practices; in Myanmar, Sanskrit was used extensively only in Arakan, never in the other parts of the country. The pillar today stands in a tiny hut, with humidity and salinity in the ground and access by birds and other animals. The modern study of the age runs through a single thesis: U. Sandamuni's Origin and Development of Arakanese Script — submitted in 2003, published in 2016 — whose Chapter IV, "Script in the Vesali Age", runs from page 28 to page 132, a hundred and four pages with twenty-seven charts across the book's eight chapters; it places the Harikela coins found in Arakan, legends datable to about the sixth century A.D., in the same age, and reads the whole development in two phases — first the eastern and northern Indian Brahmi and its derivatives, then the scripts of Sri Lanka, themselves moulded by the Pallava-Kannada scripts of southern India. Sircar's Select Inscriptions, volume I, carries the age's royal slabs as numbers 72A and 72B — the Vesali Stone Slab Inscription of the time of Nitichandra and the Vesali Stone Slab Inscription of Virachandra. Johnston himself did not live to publish the pillar: he died in October 1942, and his rough manuscript on the Sanskrit inscriptions of Arakan, with correspondence with G. H. Luce, was found among his papers; in a letter to Luce dated 15 August 1942 he had hoped to publish Anandacandra's inscription, and his notes record that he had deciphered many letters of the inscription on the north face, but too fragmentarily to publish. Four web searches this pass returned the MOWCAP register page, the Epigraphia Indica volume, the Myanmar-alphabet history, the Sandamuni thesis, and the Johnston extract; two pages were opened first-party, with one find (deciphered, one match on the MOWCAP page). - **The system.** The diagnostic is the local development, and it is a ranking, not a shape: Sircar's three inscriptions show the same eastern-Indian alphabet with local development slight in the first, more pronounced in the second, and most of all in the third — a specimen that cannot order the three has not read the palaeography. The dating test is Johnston's: the forms for ka and sa and the tripartite ya put the bell probably not later than A.D. 650, with the forms of sa and ma as the further indication — and Johnston's own warning rides with it, that dating by one or two crucial characters is only valid where datable records are numerous enough to trace development decade by decade, a condition the period does not satisfy. The inventory is the honest blank at the system's heart: no vowel list, no consonant count, no chart — the only letters the sources name are ka, sa, the tripartite ya, and ma, four letters in all, and any specimen that produces a Vesali alphabet chart has invented one. The type is a Brahmi-derived abugida, a Gupta-descended eastern hand; the direction is left-to-right, the Brahmi family's, as the inscriptions are read and published; the languages are Sanskrit and Sanskrit mixed with Pali, with Pali alone in the second-century-BCE Fat Monk witness; the use is royal and votive stone — stupa slabs, a monastery bell, a pillar, coin legends — and the readers are the Chandra court and the monks of Vesali, and today the epigraphists who read Sircar and Johnston. The parent chain is Egyptian → Proto-Sinaitic → Phoenician → Aramaic → Brahmi → Gupta → Vessali, seven systems in six steps; the sisters are the fifth- and sixth-century eastern Indian inscriptional hands and Pyu, the other early Brahmi child of Myanmar, writing in the Ayeyarwady valley in the same centuries; the successor is the Lemro-age hand, Sandamuni's Chapter V, which carries the line forward. There is no Unicode block, no ISO 15924 code, and no encoding proposal surfaced in the searches run this pass — the script's digital state is unencoded, and its only machine-readable presence is the transliteration of its inscriptions in the journals.

## The Pyu script (350–1200 CE) — the letters of the Ayeyarwady valley, or: the script with one key and two pillars

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero `## ` headings for "Pyu" in either catalogue, measured this pass — and the name occurs five times in four lines in each catalogue: private lines 10620 (1, Vessali gap), 10624 (1, Vessali system), 10626 (1, Vessali miniature), 10632 (2, Vessali grades); public lines 15093, 15097, 15099, 15105, the same four lines in the same roles. The research log holds eight occurrences in six lines in each log: private 41251 (1), 41252 (1), 41259 (1), 41261 (2), 41284 (1), 41291 (2); public 33946 (1), 33947 (1), 33954 (1), 33956 (2), 33979 (1), 33986 (2) — all six the #207 run's lines; the case-insensitive count is ten in eight lines, the extra two lines in each log (private 41020, 41029; public 33715, 33724) being "pyuserfox", a PyPI package name in the dynamic-mcp item, not the script. (The next zero stands named for a later loop: "Kadamba" is 0 headings, 0 occurrences in both catalogues, 0 in the five other files in both versions, and 0 in either log — a true zero, and the parent named in this entry's system. "Tircul" and "Nagarjunakonda" are true zeros too.)

- **The story.** The Pyu script is the writing of the Pyu city-states of the Ayeyarwady valley — Sri Ksetra, Halin, and Beikthano, and their sister cities — the first-millennium urban civilisation of what is now central Myanmar. The people are known by a name they may never have used: "Pyu" is a scholarly convenience, fixed by Luce in 1937, and their true name is still unknown; the language is also called Tircul. The script grew between the 2nd and 6th centuries CE, was first derived about 300–400, and its writing runs from about 400 to 600 in the valley's stone — Hanlin inscriptions, gold-plate extracts from the Buddhist canon, mixed Pyu-Sanskrit stones — through the all-Pyu inscriptions of Sri Ksetra in the 7th and 8th centuries to the royal inscriptions of Pagan into the late 12th century; the language died in the 13th. Its key is a single stone: the Kubyaukgyi inscription, wrongly known as the Myazedi, two four-faced pillars found by Forchhammer in 1886–87 near the Myazedi pagoda at Myinkaba, carrying the same proclamation in Old Burmese, Pali, Old Mon, and Pyu — Prince Rajakumar's gold Buddha and three villages for his dead father King Kyanzittha, 1,628 Sāsanā years after the Buddha, after a reign of twenty-eight years. Blagden read the Old Mon in 1909 and the Pyu in 1911, in the Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society, pages 365 to 388, the first study of the language, and all later work is indebted to it; the stone entered UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in 2015, and Miyake re-read it from RTI photographs in 2018, in journal form in 2025. The rest of the corpus is small and mostly unread: Duroiselle's 1921 list counted fifteen Pyu inscriptions against fourteen hundred and fifty-seven in Myanmar; the 2016 Miles documentation run numbers the inventory to PYU167; the language is known principally from four stone urns of the 7th and 8th centuries near the Payagyi pagoda and the Myazedi stone.

- **The system.** The diagnostic is the parent, and it is a vote, not a shape: three sources make Kadamba the immediate precursor — Wikipedia's infobox chain (Brāhmī → Kadamba → Pyu), the Myanmar Alphabet history ("the Pyu devised their script on the basis of the Kadamba script"), and Blagden ("derived... from the Kadamba script of Vanavasi in northern Kanara") — against one live dissent, Griffiths and colleagues' Nagarjunakonda inspiration (the elongated southern Brahmi of Vijayapurī, 3rd to 4th century, "the most likely source of inspiration"), one hedge (the Indic-glyph note: "either the Pallava or Kadamba script"), and Gupta as influence only (the bilingual inscriptions show familiarity, not descent). ADOPTED: Brāhmī → Kadamba → Pyu, with the Nagarjunakonda line kept as the open dissent. The dating test is the interlinear Brahmi: early inscriptions always carry interlinear Brahmi, and only in the 7th and 8th centuries do Sri Ksetra's inscriptions stand all in Pyu — a specimen that dates a pure-Pyu stone to the 5th century has not read the sequence. The shape is the elongation: the letters are vertically exaggerated, Jaggayapeta-like, "remarkable for the very elongated shapes of its characters" — the visual signature, and the trap, since Blagden warns that some letters resemble one another so closely they are hard to discriminate and the conjuncts offer special difficulties of identification. The type is a Brahmi-derived abugida, left-to-right; the languages are three — Pyu itself (Tircul), Pali, and Sanskrit — in two varieties, Pyu Pali and Pyu Tircul; the use is royal and votive stone, urns, gold plates, and canon extracts; the readers are the Pyu courts and the monks, and today the handful of epigraphists who read Blagden and Miyake. The parent chain is Proto-Sinaitic → Phoenician → Aramaic → Brāhmī → Kadamba → Pyu, six systems in five steps; the sisters are two (the eastern-Indian hands, Vessali — the Vesali-age hand, #207); the successor is one (the Burmese script, with Old Mon as co-precursor — "probably the precursors", CLAIMED, not VERIFIED). There is no Unicode block and no ISO 15924 code surfaced in the searches run this pass: proposed in 2010 (Pandey N3874, a preliminary chart, tentative SMP allocation U+11800–U+1183F, sixty-four code points), sixteen years on still unadopted, and the script's only machine-readable presence is the transliteration of its stones and the PYU inventory numbers.

## The Kadamba script (4th–7th century CE) — the first writing of Kannada, or: the script with three children

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero `## ` headings for "Kadamba" in either catalogue, measured this pass — and the name occurs fifteen times in five lines in each catalogue: private lines 10636 (1, Pyu gap), 10640 (7, Pyu system), 10642 (2, Pyu miniature), 10646 (2, Pyu design note), 10648 (3, Pyu grades); public lines 15109 (1), 15113 (7), 15115 (2), 15119 (2), 15121 (3), the same five lines in the same roles. "KADAMBA" and lowercase "kadamba" are 0/0 in both catalogues; 0 in TRICKS.md, TESTS.md, UNDECIPHERED.md, CIPHER-TIMELINE.md, and MATH-PHYSICS.md in both versions (public TESTS.md is not present in the mirror). The research log holds thirteen occurrences in six lines in each log: private 41305 (3), 41306 (1), 41308 (2), 41313 (1), 41315 (3), 41351 (3); public 34000 (3), 34001 (1), 34003 (2), 34008 (1), 34010 (3), 34046 (3) — all six the #208 run's lines. (The next zero stands named for a later loop: "Goykanadi" is 0 headings, 0 occurrences in both catalogues, 0 in the five other files in both versions, and 0 in either log — a true zero, and a child named in this entry's system. "Kadamba-Pallava" is a true zero too.)

- **The story.** The Kadamba script is the writing of the Kadamba dynasty of Banavasi — the first writing system devised specifically for Kannada, and later adopted to write Telugu. The dynasty was founded by Mayurasharma in c. 345 CE, from its capital at Banavasi in what is now Uttara Kannada district, Karnataka; it ruled northern Karnataka and the Konkan for 195 years, to 540 by the infobox count (525 in the article text), peaked under Kakusthavarma (c. 435–455), and counted nearly eighteen rulers, the last Krishna Varma II (516–540). The script grew from Brahmi during the dynasty's rule in the 4th–6th centuries; by the 5th century it had become distinct from other Brahmi variants, and it evolved into the Kannada-Telugu script by the 10th century. Its diagnostic is the rounding: during the Kadamba rule (325–550) the major change in the Brahmi script produced letters shorter and round in shape. It was used in what are now Karnataka, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, and Goa, to write Old Kannada, Old Telugu, Sanskrit, and Konkani by Wikipedia's list — Sanskrit, Kannada, and sometimes Marathi by Omniglot's — on stone pillars and copper plates. Its witnesses are three stones and a corpus: the Halmidi inscription, sixteen lines on a stone four feet tall, one foot wide, and three-quarters of an inch thick, discovered in 1936 by M. H. Krishna near Belur in Hassan district, undated and attributed to c. 450 on palaeographical grounds, recording a gift of two villages, Halmidi and Mulivalli, to Vija Arasa for valour in a war between the Kadambas and the Kekaya Pallavas — the earliest evidence of Kannada used as an administrative language; the Talagunda pillar inscription of Kakusthavarma, Sanskrit, c. 450, in the Pranaveshvara temple, about ten feet tall and four and a half feet wide with characters averaging 2.3 by 1.6 cm, composed by the poet Kubja, 3D-scanned in March 2025; and the Gudnapur inscription of Ravivarman, 6th-century box-headed Brahmi on a twenty-foot pillar five kilometres from Banavasi, twenty-seven lines — thirty verses in the first sixteen lines, eleven lines of prose — recording nine brahmadeya lands gifted for a temple to Manmatha, its numerals one to nine beautifully engraved, and possibly Kubja's work too. Gai's 1996 corpus gathers forty-four inscriptions of the early Kadambas — the first in Prakrit, the other forty-three in Sanskrit, the court language. The kings also wrote their names on coins: Sri Manarashi, Sri Dosharashi, Shri Shashankaha.

- **The system.** The diagnostic is the parent and the children, and it is a count, not a shape: the parent is Brahmi, ADOPTED — Wikipedia's infobox chain (Egyptian hieroglyphs → Proto-Sinaitic → Phoenician → Aramaic → Brahmi → Kadamba) and Omniglot ("developed from the Brahmi script during the Kadamba dynasty") agree, and no source this pass offers another parent. The children are three — the Kannada-Telugu alphabet, Goykanadi, and the Pyu script (#208), all three named in the infobox. The open question is the joint form: the ten Southeast Asian descendants — Pyu, Mon, Kawi, Lanna, Tham, Khom, Khmer, Thai, Lao, and Tai Lue — are listed under the Kadamba-Pallava script, not under plain Kadamba, so this entry files Pyu twice over — once as Kadamba's direct child, as #208's parent vote already ruled, and once inside the ten of the Kadamba-Pallava descent — and keeps the question open whether the Pallava half of that joint form is a co-parent or a later label. The shape test is the rounding: shorter and rounder than Brahmi — a specimen that describes Kadamba letters as tall and elongated has confused the parent with the child, since the elongation is Pyu's signature, not Kadamba's. The dating test is Halmidi: the stone is undated and its c. 450 attribution rests on the personalities named, the linguistic nuances, and the palaeography — a specimen that dates Halmidi from the stone alone, or that calls it settled, has not read Gai's dissent, Sircar and Ramesh's 450–500 range with some as late as the second half of the 6th century, or Settar's older Kongunivarma. The type is a Brahmi-derived abugida, left-to-right; the languages are four by Wikipedia's list and three by Omniglot's, and the two lists disagree on Konkani, Old Telugu, and Marathi; the use is royal and administrative stone, copper-plate grants, and coin legends; the readers are the Kadamba court and the monks, and today the epigraphists who read Gai. The parent chain is Egyptian → Proto-Sinaitic → Phoenician → Aramaic → Brahmi → Kadamba, six systems in five steps; the near neighbours are six in the similarity list (Goykanadi, Bhattiprolu, Salankayana, Pallava, Gupta, Kannada); the successors are the Kannada-Telugu alphabet by the 10th century and, through it, Kannada and Telugu themselves. There is no Unicode block and no ISO 15924 code surfaced in the searches run this pass: the Script Encoding Initiative lists Kadamba as "Not started", readiness Medium — and the script's only machine-readable presence is the transliteration of its stones, the modern HKS-NVC handwritten dataset (29 consonants, 5 vowels, 10 numerals, 100 participants), and the inventory numbers of Gai's corpus.

- **The worked miniature (computed this pass).** Seven counts, all reproduced by goal hidden_files/verify-kadamba-20261111.py (89/89 checks pass). (1) **The dynasty census.** The dynasty runs 345 to 540 — 195 years — with nearly eighteen rulers, a mean reign of 10.83 years. Mayurasharma rules twenty years (345–365); Kakusthavarma twenty (435–455); Krishna Varma II twenty-four (516–540). The earliest Kadamba records stand at 450 — 105 years after the founding — and the two end-dates, 525 and 540, differ by fifteen years. "Modi script" is a true zero too.)

- **The story.** The Goykanadi script is the writing of Goa — Goykānaḍī or Kandavī, a Brahmic script of the Konkan coast that wrote Konkani and sometimes Marathi. It was used in Goa since the times of the Kadambas, and it lost its popularity after the 17th century; Omniglot puts its use at until about the 17th century. Its look is the paradox in one sentence: "very different from the Old Kannada script, with strikingly similar features" — and the difference has a name, the bar: unlike Old Kannada, Kandevi/Goykanadi letters were usually written with a distinctive horizontal bar, like the Nagari scripts. Its work was trade as much as literature: the Saraswat and Daivajna trading families used it to keep their accounts, along with the Modi script. Then the burning: the Portuguese ruled Goa from the early 16th to the late 18th century, and under the Goa Inquisition it was an offence to possess books in the local languages — all books in Konkani, Marathi, and Sanskrit were seized and burnt on the suspicion that they might deal with idolatry, and a letter dated 24 November 1548 has João Afonso de Albuquerque proudly reporting his achievement in that direction. What survives of the literature is mostly second-hand: many Konkani manuscripts now found in museums in Portugal are Roman transliterations of Kandavi manuscripts of Hindu epics, and it is believed that most of the pre-Portuguese documents and books in Kandavi were burnt by the Portuguese missionaries. The earliest document in the script is a single petition: a 15th-century petition addressed by Ravala Śeṭī, a Gaunkar of Caraim in the islands of Goa, to the king of Portugal, bearing a signature in Konkani that says "Ravala Śeṭī baraha" — "writing of Ravala Sethi". The names carry the history: the script is known indigenously as Kāṇḍēvī, "brought by the Kannadas (Kadambas)", a name also used by the Portuguese missionaries who studied it, while "Goykanadi" is an exonym used by Marathi speakers — "Goy" means Goa and "kanadi" refers to its Kadamba origins — popularised by Gajanana Ghantkar in his 1993 book History of Goa through Gõykanadi script. The modern record is a single Unicode document: Shashank Shenoy Basty's "Introduction to the Goyakanadi Alphabet" (L2/20-264, 20 August 2020), written to bring the script to the notice of the Unicode Technical Committee — developed from the local variety of the Kadamba script in the 11th–15th centuries, continued to be used till the late 19th century, never used in a printed format, gradually fallen into disuse, a forgotten script, its samples studied largely from libraries and private collections in Goa and Karnataka. The script's own dynasty is the later one: the Kadambas of Goa ruled Goa from 960 to 1310 CE, and under them the Nagari, Kadamba, Halekannada, and Goykanadi scripts were very popular. Konkani itself survives the script: two and a half million speakers, the official language of Goa, now written in Devanagari officially and in Latin besides — and in Goykanadi, no longer.

- **The system.** The diagnostic is the parent, and it is a vote, not a shape: three sources make Kadamba the direct parent — the Kadamba infobox, which lists Goykanadi among Kadamba's three children; the Goykanadi overview, "this script may have been evolved out of the Kadamba script, which was extensively used in Goa and Konkan"; and Basty, "developed from the local variety of the Kadamba script in 11th–15th centuries" — against one long chain, the Goykanadi infobox's own parent systems (Egyptian → Proto-Sinaitic → Phoenician → Aramaic → Brahmi → Kadamba → Telugu-Kannada alphabet → Kannada script → Goykānaḍī), which routes the descent through Telugu-Kannada and Kannada instead of straight from Kadamba, and one hedge, Basty's "some historians have opined that Goykanadi was a specialised variant of the Haḻagannaḍa alphabet, developed as a contact variant between Nāgari and Haḻagannaḍa". ADOPTED: Brahmi → Kadamba → Goykanadi, with the infobox long chain and the Haḻagannaḍa variant kept as the open dissent — Basty himself closes his own hedge with "whatever the origin might have been, Goykanadi is definitely a descendant of the Kadamba Alphabet belonging to the Southern Brahmi scripts". The shape test is the bar: the letters carry a distinctive horizontal bar, Nagari-like — a specimen that describes Goykanadi letters as bar-less Old Kannada has missed the diagnostic and the paradox sentence both. The dating test is the petition: the earliest document is 15th-century, and the infobox's 6th-century start stands nine centuries before it with no document behind it — a specimen that dates the script to the 6th century from the infobox alone has not read the gap. The type is a Brahmic abugida, left-to-right; the languages are two — Konkani and Marathi; the use is trading accounts, petitions, and Hindu epics; the readers are the Goan Konkani community and the Saraswat and Daivajna traders, and today the scholars who read Ghantkar and Basty. The parent chain is Egyptian → Proto-Sinaitic → Phoenician → Aramaic → Brahmi → Kadamba → Goykanadi, seven systems in six steps; the sisters are two (the Kannada-Telugu alphabet and Pyu, Kadamba's other children); no child script surfaced this pass. There is no Unicode block and no ISO 15924 code surfaced in the searches run this pass: the Script Encoding Initiative lists the script as "Goya Kannadi" — South Asia, Goa, Historic — proposal status "Inactive – others", readiness Medium-High; Basty's 2020 document is an introduction for consideration by WG2 and UTC, not a formal proposal; and the script's only machine-readable presence is the transliteration of its survivals, the Omniglot chart (details by Biswajit Mandal, some letters with more than one form), and the 109-character repertoire count.

"Halekannada" occurs once in each catalogue: private 10672, public 15145 — the Kadambas-of-Goa four-scripts line in #210's story. "Haḷegannaḍa", "Halegannada", and "Halagannada" are 0/0 in both catalogues; 0 in TRICKS.md, TESTS.md, UNDECIPHERED.md, CIPHER-TIMELINE.md, and MATH-PHYSICS.md in both versions (public TESTS.md is mirrored as GAUNTLET-TESTS.md). (The next zero stands named for a later loop: "Nadugannada" is 0 headings, 0 occurrences in both catalogues, 0 in the five other files in both versions, and 0 in either log — a true zero, and the next phase of this same language. "Hosagannada" is a true zero too. "Modi script", named as a zero in #210, is a zero no longer: 4 occurrences in each catalogue, all in #210's entry, and 2 in each log.)

- **The story.** Haḻagannaḍa — ಹಳೆಗನ್ನಡ, romanized *Haḷegannaḍa* — is the old writing of Karnataka: *haḷe*, from Old Kannada *paḻe*, means "old", and *gannaḍa* is the sandhi form of *Kannaḍa*, the *ka* turning to *ga* when the words join. It is the earliest attested stage of the Kannada language, known primarily from the inscriptional record going back to the 4th–5th century CE, and the language's history is told in four phases: Purva Halegannada in the 5th century, Halegannada between the 9th and 11th century, Nadugannada between the 12th and 17th century, and Hosagannada from the 18th century to the present. The anchor of the whole record is a single stone: the Halmidi inscription, sixteen lines carved on a sandstone pillar, discovered in 1936 by Dr. M. H. Krishna, Director of Archaeology of the princely State of Mysore, in Halmidi village near Hassan district, and dated by him to 450 CE — the earliest attested full-length inscription in the Kannada language and script, written in pre-old Kannada in the Kadamba script, a land grant of the village Palmaḍi under the Kadamba king Kakusthavarman, engraved by Kavi Kubja, which demonstrates that Kannada was already a language of administration. The original is kept in the Office of the Director of Archaeology and Museums, Mysore, and a fibreglass replica stands in Halmidi. It was not the only early witness: a 5th-century copper coin was found at Banavasi with an inscription in the Kannada script; the Tamatekallu inscription of Chitradurga is 5th-century and the Chikkamagaluru inscription is dated 500 CE; and Kannada words appear earlier still, in the Brahmagiri edict of 230 BCE by Ashoka — words, not a full-scale inscription. The literature follows four centuries behind the stone: the earliest known literary work in Kannada is the *Kavirājamārga*, dated to 850 CE, a work on poetics and grammar that cites earlier authorities and genres — *bedaṇḍe*, *cattāṇa*, *melvāḍu* — from earlier centuries. The grammar follows later still: the *Śabdamaṇidarpaṇa* of Kēśirāja, 12th century CE, is the earliest systematic grammar of Kannada and remains authoritative today, preceded by the *Karṇāṭakabhāṣābhūṣaṇa* of Nagavarma II and followed by the *Karṇāṭaka Śabdānuśāsana* of Bhaṭṭākalaṅka Dēva in the 16th century. The script's diagnostic is a pair of letters that did not survive: ೞ ⟨ḻ⟩ and ಱ ⟨ṟ⟩, used in Old Kannada and merged in the modern language with ಳ ⟨ḷ⟩ and ರ ⟨r⟩ — the ṟ is the *śakaṭa-rēphe*, the "cart-shaped *r*", and the ḻ the *ṟaḻa*, the "*ṟa*-shaped *ḻa*", names that exist precisely because the two pairs sound alike and must be told apart in writing. The epigraphic record around them is vast: more than 800 inscriptions at Shravanabelagola, dating from 600 to 1830 CE, in Halegannada and Purvadahalegannada characters, and B. L. Rice's *Epigraphia Carnatica* in 12 volumes studies inscriptions from the 3rd century until the 19th. The earliest full-length Kannada copper plates in Old Kannada script, early 8th century, belong to the Alupa King Aluvarasa II of Belmannu. And the old letters reach Goa: the Unicode-block notes call Goykanadi "a variant of Old Kannada, historically used to write Konkani in the state of Goa" — the other side of Basty's hedge in #210 — and the Goykanadi paradox sentence itself takes Old Kannada as the measure: "very different from the Old Kannada script, with strikingly similar features", the difference being the bar.

- **The system.** The diagnostic is the lineage, and it is settled, not a vote: the Kannada script descends from the Ashokan Brahmi script through the early Kadamba script, which evolved into the Kannada-Telugu script under the Chalukyas and later Chalukyas of Vengi, and the Kannada and Telugu scripts separated by around 1300 CE. ADOPTED: Egyptian → Proto-Sinaitic → Phoenician → Aramaic → Brahmi → Kadamba → Kannada-Telugu → Kannada, eight systems in seven steps — with the catalogue's Egyptian root filed as the catalogue gives it, and the Aramaic link carried as the Kannada-script infobox marks it, "(disputed)". The script-or-language question is filed, not dodged: the Old Kannada article is about the language stage, and its writing system is the Kannada script — so this entry files Haḻagannaḍa as the script-stage, the writing of the Halegannada language phase, not as a separate script with its own block. The type is a Brahmic abugida, left-to-right; the character set is a phonemic abugida of forty-nine letters, the *akṣaramāle*; the language is one, Kannada, Dravidian, ISO 639-3 *kan* shared with the modern language, Glottolog *oldk1250*. The sister is one: Telugu, the Kannada-Telugu alphabet's other child. The children are two: the modern Kannada script (Hosagannada), and Goykanadi as a variant of Old Kannada. The encoding is the one thing this script has that Goykanadi does not: the Kannada script was added to the Unicode Standard in October 1991 with version 1.0, block U+0C80–U+0CFF, ISO 15924 *Knda* (345), 128 code points of which 92 are assigned (Unicode 18.0) — but the two old letters survive in modern printed editions of classical texts, and this pass did not verify which code points hold ḻ and ṟ. The shape test is the pair: a specimen that reads an Old Kannada text and calls ḻ and ṟ modern letters, or that claims a separate Haḻagannaḍa Unicode block, has missed the diagnostic and the filing both. The dating test is the stone: the earliest document is the Halmidi pillar, 450 CE, and the earliest literature the *Kavirājamārga*, 850 CE — a specimen that dates Old Kannada literature to the 5th century from the inscription alone has conflated stone and book.

- **The story.** Nadugannada — ನಡುಗನ್ನಡ, romanized *Nadugannaḍa* — is the middle writing of Karnataka: *nadu* means "middle", and the phase is the middle of the four into which the language's history is told — Purva Halegannada in the 5th century, Halegannada between the 9th and 11th, Nadugannada between the 12th and 17th, Hosagannada from the 18th century to the present — the current revision, in which Nadugannada is "as evidenced by Vachana literature". It is the phase in which Kannada stopped being a court language in Sanskrit's shadow and became the people's language: Old Kannada literature had developed continuously until the middle of the 12th century under the influence of Sanskrit, and then the second phase began — the classical poetical style of *champu*, influenced by Sanskrit, gave way to a simple native form, a language that can be understood by the commoner, full of *desi*, native idiom. The hinge is the *vachana*: a unique and native form of poetry in pithy prose, born in the 12th century as a reaction to the rigid social customs of the time, heralded by the Virashaiva saints and led by Basavanna — a minister in the court of the Southern Kalachuri King Bijjala II — with Akka Mahadevi and Allama Prabhu beside him; brief disconnected passages, each ending with one or more names of Shiva, epigrammatical, parallelistic, elusive, dwelling on the vanity of riches and the spiritual benefits of the worship of Shiva — and over 200 Vachana poets have been recorded from this period, more than 30 of them women. "The voice of God became the voice of the people." The vachanas are still recited by Lingayat acharyas today. The old style did not die: classical *champu* works were still produced in the medieval period, the Mahabharata and Ramayana kept their influence, and another style, *ragale*, also took shape. The faiths turn with the phase: the earliest literature until about the 12th century was mostly Jain, with a few Virashaiva and Brahmin works; the 13th to 15th centuries saw Virashaiva and Brahminical writers rise and Jain writings decline; with the waning of Jain influence during the 14th-century Vijayanagara empire a new Vaishnava literature grew rapidly in the 15th century, and the devotional movement of the itinerant Haridasa saints — *Haridasa sahitya*, inspired by the teachings of Madhwacharya, from the 14th century, a vast corpus of devotional compositions over the next four centuries — marked the high point of the era; after the decline of the Vijayanagara empire in the 16th century, Kannada literature was supported by the Wodeyars of the Kingdom of Mysore and the Nayakas of Keladi. The phase's grammars are its milestones: Nagavarma II's *Karṇāṭakabhāṣābhūṣaṇa* in 1145 and Kēśirāja's *Śabdamaṇidarpaṇa* in 1260 are the oldest landmarks of Kannada grammar, and Bhaṭṭākalaṅka Dēva's *Karṇāṭaka Śabdānuśāsana* follows in the 16th century. The phase straddles the great split: the Kannada and Telugu scripts separated by around 1300 CE, inside Nadugannada — the phase begins in the Kannada-Telugu script and ends in the Kannada script proper — and in the same centuries the two lost letters of #211, ḻ and ṟ, merged into ḷ and r: the 13th-century poet Harihara rejected the continued distinction. The period's own end is told two ways: one history traces it only to about the 15th century, another says it continued until about the period of Chikkadevaraja Wodeyar, the king of Mysore — the fourteenth maharaja, reigning 28 February 1673 to 16 November 1704, who founded the Athara Kacheri, a central secretariat of eighteen departments. The phase's literature is part of the case that won Kannada recognition as a Classical language of India in 2008 — high antiquity of early texts over 1500–2000 years, a body of ancient literature held as valuable heritage, an original literary tradition, distinct from the modern language.

- **The story.** Hosagannada — ಹೊಸಗನ್ನಡ, romanized *Hosagannaḍa* — is the new writing of Karnataka: *hosa* means "new", and the phase is the fourth and the living one of the four into which the language's history is told — Purva Halegannada in the 5th century, Halegannada between the 9th and 11th, Nadugannada between the 12th and 17th, Hosagannada from the 18th century to the present — the current four-phase revision, in which the older revision starts it at 1800 and the three-phase scheme calls it Modern, 1700 to the present. It is the phase in which Kannada stopped being a manuscript language and became a printed, newspapered, novel-reading, state-administered language — the phase that is still running, and the only one of the four with no end date. The turn begins in the Wodeyar court: in the early 19th century Maharaja Krishnaraja Wodeyar III and his court poets moved away from the ancient *champu* form of prose toward prose renderings of Sanskrit epics and plays, and Kempu Narayana's *Mudramanjusha* ("Seal Casket", 1823) is the first modern novel written in Kannada. Print arrives with the missions: Christian missionaries had started printing in Kannada as early as 1817, first from Serampore near Calcutta; the first Kannada newspaper, *Mangaluru Samachara*, was published by Hermann Mögling of the Basel Mission on 1 July 1843 — a fortnightly, litho-printed, surviving only two years, and 1 July is now Karnataka Press Day; the first periodical, *Mysuru Vrittanta Bodhini*, was published by Bhashyam Bhashyacharya in Mysore around the same time; Mögling translated Kannada classics in the *Bibliotheca Carnataca* series during 1848–1853; and the dictionaries followed, the most prominent Ferdinand Kittel's Kannada-English dictionary in 1894. The novel comes of age: Lakshman Gadagkar's *Suryakantha* (1892) and Gulvadi Venkata Rao's *Indira Bai* (1899) signalled the move away from the highly stylised mores and aesthetics of prior Kannada works to modern prose and established the modern novel genre — *Indira Bai*, the first modern social novel, about widow remarriage in coastal Karnataka, published by the Basel Mission Press and first translated into English in 1903 by M. E. Couchman, the Collector of South Canara. The awakening follows: at the dawn of the 20th century B. M. Srikantaiah ("B. M. Sri"), the "Father of modern Kannada literature", called for original works in modern Kannada while moving away from archaic forms, and the shift was dubbed *Navodaya* — "a new rise", a period of awakening — led by his *English Geethagalu* ("English Songs"); Masti Venkatesha Iyengar laid the short story's foundation with *Kelavu Sanna Kathegalu* ("A few Short Stories", 1920) and *Sanna Kathegalu* ("Short Stories", 1924); T. P. Kailasam consolidated modern drama with *Tollu Gatti* ("The Hollow and the Solid", 1918); Kuvempu's *Sri Ramayana Darshanam* (1949) began modern Kannada epic poetry; and D. V. Gundappa's *Mankuthimmana Kagga* ("Dull Thimma's Rigmarole", 1943) harkened back to the wisdom poems of the late medieval poet Sarvajna. The movements turn with the century: *Pragatishila* (progressives), led by novelist A. N. Krishna Rao ("Anakru"), gained momentum in the early 1940s, contending that literature must be an instrument of social revolution; *Navya*, formally inaugurated by V. K. Gokak with his *Navya Kavitegalu* ("Modern Poems", 1950) and best exemplified by Gopalakrishna Adiga, questioned the time-honoured standards of plot and treated life as an introspective search; and the syllabus's modern movements close the roll with Dalit and Bandaya. The state catches up with the language: the State of Mysore, established on 1 November 1956 from the Kannada-speaking areas, made Kannada its official language by the Karnataka Official Language Act, 1963 — Act 26 of 1963, assent 5 October 1963, first published in the Karnataka Gazette 10 October 1963 — and was renamed Karnataka on 1 November 1973. The honours follow: Kannada was declared a Classical language of India in 2008, and in the last half century its authors have received 8 Jnanpith awards — the most for any Indian language — Kuvempu 1967, Bendre 1973, Karanth 1977, Masti 1983, Gokak 1990, Ananthamurthy 1994, Karnad 1998, Kambara 2010 — alongside 68 Sahitya Akademi awards and 9 Sahitya Akademi Fellowships; and in 2025 Banu Mushtaq won the International Booker Prize for *Heart Lamp*, a collection of short stories in Kannada. The speakers are counted: 44 million native speakers at the 2011 census, and 15 million more who speak it as a second or third language — 59 million in all; 43.7 million native in India, 40.6 million of them in Karnataka, about two-thirds of the state's people, with the rest spread to Tamil Nadu (1,140,000), Maharashtra (993,000), Andhra Pradesh and Telangana (533,000), Kerala (78,100), and Goa (67,800); and a diaspora counted in the tens of thousands — 48,600 in the United States by 2015, 59,000 in Malaysia, 22,000 in Singapore, 9,700 in Australia, 4,000 in Canada. The script itself is the inheritance, not the invention: the phase opens after the split, in the Kannada script alone with no Kannada-Telugu overlap, and the two lost letters of #211, ḻ and ṟ, are gone, merged into ḷ and r — what is written is the modern Kannada script, and it is the script that carries the whole modern literature, the newspapers, the Act, and the Booker.

- **The system.** The diagnostic is the lineage, and it is the same eight-system chain as #211 and #212, with one addition: the split is complete before this phase begins. ADOPTED: Egyptian → Proto-Sinaitic → Phoenician → Aramaic → Brahmi → Kadamba → Kannada-Telugu → Kannada, eight systems in seven steps — with the catalogue's Egyptian root filed as the catalogue gives it and the Aramaic link carried "(disputed)" — and the Kannada–Telugu split at around 1300 CE, 401 years before Hosagannada starts, so this is the first phase written in the Kannada script alone from its first year. The script-or-language filing is the same as #211 and #212: Hosagannada is a language stage, written in the Kannada script — not a separate script with its own block. The type is a Brahmic abugida, left-to-right; the character set is the *akṣaramāle* of forty-nine letters; the language is one, Kannada, Dravidian, ISO 639-1 *kn*, ISO 639-3 *kan* shared with the older phases, Glottolog *nucl1305* — the modern code, distinct from Old Kannada's *oldk1250*, so the catalogue now holds two Glottolog codes for one language's history, with the boundary filed at the phase boundary. The sister is one: Telugu, whose script left the shared alphabet four centuries before this phase. The children are none filed: Hosagannada is the endpoint, the living script — the question of other languages written in the Kannada script today was not verified this pass and is filed in the honest blank, not as children. The encoding is the same as #211 and #212: the Kannada script was added to the Unicode Standard in October 1991 with version 1.0, block U+0C80–U+0CFF, ISO 15924 *Knda* (345), 128 code points of which 92 are assigned — and 1991 falls 174 years after printing in Kannada began, so this phase's print history predates its encoding by nearly two centuries. The shape test is the inheritance: a specimen that calls Hosagannada a separate script with its own Unicode block, or that dates the Kannada script's birth to this phase, has missed the filing — the script is born at the split, mid-Nadugannada, and this phase inherits it. The dating test is the first-novel pair: 1823 and 1899, *Mudramanjusha* then *Indira Bai* — a specimen that calls *Indira Bai* the first modern novel without the "social" qualifier has repeated the conflict instead of filing it.

## The Kannada Braille code (1951–present) — the tactile Kannada, or: the code that kept the two lost letters

- **The story.** Kannada Braille is the tactile rendering of the Hosagannada script (#213): the same language, the same forty-nine print letters, read by fingertip instead of by eye. Its parent is the catalogue's Braille entry (line 4695): Louis Braille, blind from age five, built the code at fifteen — 1824, published 1829 — from Charles Barbier's "night writing", a 12-dot military system for reading orders in the dark, by cutting the cell to six dots, two columns of three, 64 possible patterns, one per letter, digit, punctuation mark, or (with prefix cells) number and formatting sign; the 1837 second revision is described as the first binary form of writing developed in the modern era; France adopted it in 1854, two years after Braille's death. India at independence had eleven braille scripts in use, in different parts of the country and for different languages; by 1951 a single national standard had been settled on, Bharati braille — *bhāratī brēl*, "Indian braille" — which has since been adopted by Sri Lanka, Nepal, and Bangladesh, while Pakistan has not adopted it, so the Urdu Braille of Pakistan is an entirely different alphabet from the Urdu Braille of India. The standard is a living one: Bharati Braille 2.0 was released on 4 January 2025 by the Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities and the National Institute for the Empowerment of Persons with Visual Disabilities (NIEPVD), updating the Standard Bharati Braille Codes for nine scripts encompassing thirteen Indian languages and fully mapped to Unicode; Bharati Braille 2.1 was officially approved on 13 May 2026, during the first meeting of the Technical Advisory Council for Education and Rehabilitation of Persons with Visual Impairment at NIEPVD, incorporating technical refinements derived from Liblouis table validation and completing the forward-translation (print-to-Braille) validation phase. The Kannada chart in the standard carries the full mapping: Unicode 0C85 KANNADA LETTER A, ಅ, braille 1, A — the first row of a complete Kannada table. The conversion work is also filed: the "Braille Lipi" Kannada-to-Braille conversion tool (IGI Global, 2016) proposes converting Kannada script to Braille so the visually impaired can study through it, with architecture by user-type — simple, moderate, expert — and the paper's own framing that different countries adapt the system to suit their languages.

- **The system.** The diagnostic is the lineage, and it is five systems in four steps: ADOPTED: Night writing → Braille → English Braille → Bharati braille → Kannada Braille — with the catalogue's Braille entry as the root, the English-Braille link carried as the value source ("values based largely on English Braille"), and Bharati braille as the parent that makes Kannada Braille a child system alongside Bengali, Devanagari, Gujarati, Malayalam, Odia, Punjabi, Sinhala, Telugu, Tamil, and Indian Urdu Braille. The type is an alphabet (nonlinear), tactile, left-to-right; the cell is six dots in a 3 × 2 matrix, 64 possible patterns. The assignment rule is the system's signature: letters are assigned as consistently as possible across the regional scripts of India as they are transliterated in the Latin script, so that Hindi, Urdu, Bengali, and English are rendered largely the same in braille — the same braille letter means the same Latin letter across scripts, and the print letter follows. The abugida is linearized, not abolished: although basically alphabetic, Bharati braille retains one aspect of Indian abugidas, in that the default vowel *a* is not written unless it occurs at the beginning of a syllable or before a vowel — a "linearized alphasyllabary abugida". Braille ⠅ (the consonant *K*) renders print ಕ *ka*; to indicate a consonant without a following vowel, a *virama* (vowel-canceling) prefix is used — ⠈ ⠅ is ಕ *k* — and unlike in print there are no vowel diacritics: vowels are written as full letters following the consonant, regardless of their order in print, so print ಕಿ *ki* is braille ⠅ ⠊ (*K-I*), equivalent to writing ⟨ ಕಇ ⟩ in print, and print ಕ್ಲಿಕ *klika* is ⠈ ⠅ ⠇ ⠊ ⠅. The one time a non-initial short *a* is written is when it is followed by another vowel — print ⟨ ಕಇ ⟩ *kai* is ⠅ ⠁ ⠊ (*K–A–I*), to disambiguate it from ⠅ ⠊ for *ki*. Conjuncts are not handled, apart from *kṣ* and *jñ* — consonant clusters written as conjuncts in print are handled with the virama in braille, just as with computer fonts that lack the conjuncts — so Bharati braille is equivalent to Grade-1 English braille, though there are plans to extend all the Bharati alphabets to include conjuncts; the Kannada row's blank *jñ* cell is filed as a conflict against that blanket claim, in the honest blank. The language is one, Kannada, Dravidian, ISO 639-1 *kn*, ISO 639-3 *kan*, Glottolog *nucl1305* — the same codes as #213, the modern code. The sisters are ten: the other Bharati child systems named in the infobox. The children are none filed: Kannada Braille is the endpoint, the tactile form of the living script. The encoding is two blocks: the Braille Patterns block U+2800–U+28FF, 256 code points, with ⠁ at U+2801 — and the print letters it transcribes live in the Kannada block U+0C80–U+0CFF from #213, 128 code points, 92 assigned — and Bharati Braille 2.0 and 2.1 are fully mapped to Unicode, with the 2.1 refinements validated against Liblouis tables. The shape test is the unwritten *a*: a specimen that writes ⠁ for the default vowel in ಕ, or that calls Kannada Braille a separate script with its own print block, has missed the filing — the code transcribes the print script, it does not replace it. The lost-letters test is the entry's proof: the braille chart still carries cells for ಱ and ೞ, the two letters print merged away in #211 — a specimen that says braille dropped them with print has not read the chart.

## The Tulu script (c. 1250 CE–present) — the letters of Tulu Nadu, or: the script that died once and came back as code
