- **The story.** Gurmukhī (Punjabi ਗੁਰਮੁਖੀ [ˈɡʊɾᵊmʊkʰiː], Shahmukhi گُرمُکھی) is an abugida popularly believed to have been standardized and used by the second Sikh guru, Guru Angad (1504–1552), though some scholars trace its development to before Guru Angad; commonly regarded as a Sikh script, it is used in Punjab, India as the official script of the Punjabi language, and historically it was also used for Sindhi. The prevalent view among Punjabi linguists is that the letters were first used by the Guru's followers, the gurmukhs — literally, those who face, or follow, the Guru — so the script came to be known as gurmukhī, 'the script of those guided by the Guru'; the four glyphs ਵ, ਹ, ਗ, and ਰ were first called Gurmukhi, and only later did the term cover the whole script, and the Gurmukhs revered the script and meditated on the glyphs used to write Waheguru. The common translation 'from the mouth of the Guru' carries a different sense: the script recorded the utterances of the Sikh Gurus as scripture, so it was named from the mukhă (face, or mouth) of the Gurus. The name for the Perso-Arabic alphabet for Punjabi, Shahmukhi, was modeled on the term Gurmukhī. The primary scripture of Sikhism, the Guru Granth Sahib, is written in the Gurmukhī script, in various dialects and languages often subsumed under the generic title Sant Bhasha ('saint language'), and it was through its recording in Gurmukhi that knowledge of the pronunciation and grammar of Old Punjabi (c. 10th–16th century) was preserved for modern philologists. The script was described as 'tailor-made' to writing the Punjabi language as it existed in the 16th century, and the adoption of a distinct script was an assertion of a separate religious identity. Proto-Gurmukhī writing is dated to c. 1470–1490, from the tomb of Rae Feroze in Hathur, Ludhiana, Punjab; by the 15th century Sharada had evolved so considerably that epigraphists denote the script at this point by the special name Devāśeṣa, and Tarlochan Singh Bedi prefers the name prithamă gurmukhī, or Proto-Gurmukhī. The origin theories are five: it derived from the Devāśeṣa script (Tarlochan Singh Bedi), from Ardhanagari, a script used in Bathinda, Sindh, and Western Punjab (G. B. Singh), from the Landa scripts, from the Takri scripts, or from Devanagari and Siddham/Siddhamatrika. Guru Angad is popularly credited in the Sikh tradition with the creation and standardization of the Gurmukhi script from earlier Śāradā-descended scripts native to the region, but Sikh scholars — Kahn Singh of Nabha (1930), G. B. Singh (1950), Piara Singh Padam (1954), and G. S. Sidhu (2004) — documented Gurmukhi prior to the arising of Sikhism, and it is more likely that Guru Angad standardized the pre-existing scripts around 1530–1535 under the purview of Guru Nanak. A transcription of a Goindwal pothī, carried out by Sahansar Ram, Guru Amar Das' grandson, c. late 16th century, showcases an early form of the Gurmukhi script with affinities to other Laṇḍā scripts, and an 18th-century fresco from Pothimala, Guru Harsahai, shows a woman writing in Gurmukhī. Modern Gurmukhī has thirty-five original letters, hence its common alternative term paintī or 'the thirty-five', plus six additional consonants (the navīnă ṭollī, 'new group'), nine vowel diacritics, two diacritics for nasal sounds (ṭippī and bindī), one diacritic that geminates consonants (the áddakă), and three subscript characters. Its distinctive features: three basic bearer letters (ੳ, ਅ, ੲ) that carry the independent vowels instead of distinctly separate characters for each vowel; a drastic reduction in conjunct characters — to form clusters Gurmukhi uniquely affixes subscript letters at the bottom of standard characters rather than merging parts into a true conjunct; a unique standard ordering that diverges from the traditional vargiya, with vowels and fricatives placed in front; the omission of the sibilants [ʃ] and [ʂ], retaining only the letters for the sounds of the spoken language of the time — [ʃ] was later reintroduced, necessitating the new glyph ਸ਼; distinct new letters for vernacular sounds, as for [ɽ]; and a gemination diacritic, a unique feature among native subcontinental scripts, marking the preserved Middle Indo-Aryan geminates distinctive of Punjabi. Punjabi is a tonal language with three tones, and the script has no separate symbol for tones: they are carried by the formerly voiced aspirated consonants (gh, dh, bh, etc.) and the intervocalic h. In the following epochs Gurmukhī became the primary script for the literary writings of the Sikhs, spread widely under the Sikh Empire and used by Sikh kings and chiefs for administration, and was employed in the 17th and 18th centuries to write scientific and poetic literature in the Braj language. Early British writers on the Punjab, such as John Malcolm, linked Gurmukhi to Punjabi and the Sikhs; the Punjab administration reports of 1851–54 called it 'rapidly falling into desuetude', but the Serampore Mission Press and especially the Ludhiana Mission Press adopted it, the first natively produced grammars of Punjabi were written in Gurmukhi in the 1860s, and the Singh Sabha movement of the late 19th century advocated it for mass media. In 1882 the Lahore Singh Sabha petitioned Charles Aitchison, Governor of Punjab, to adopt Gurmukhi as a medium of instruction in school — declined; in 1895 Gurmukhi was adopted as a school script for Punjabi at the first-grade level at an Amritsari school, and the Oriental College, Lahore offered Punjabi courses in Romanisation and Gurmukhi in Vidwan, Budhiman, and Gyani. Official recognition was made a prerequisite by the Akali Dal for political partnership in the 1940s, including in failed talks with the Muslim League; after the struggle of the Punjabi Suba movement in the 1960s the script was given authority as the official state script of Punjab, India, adopted as the official script on 18 April 1968, and the Panjab Official Language Act of 1967 made Panjabi, written in Gurmukhi, the state's official language. It is one of the official scripts of the Indian Republic and is currently the 14th most used script in the world. After independence, some Pakistani Punjabi writers advocated Gurmukhi for Punjabi — P. D. Raphael believed it more phonetically accurate than Perso-Arabic — while Sardar Muhammad Khan in 1953 took the opposing view, arguing that Gurmukhi's phonetic spelling would produce many spelling variations, that it lacked specific glyphs for the Persian and Arabic phonemes ع (Ain), ط (Ṭoe) and غ (Ghain), and that Perso-Arabic would be complementary for Urdu, which is also written in Perso-Arabic. In Jammu Division, Takri, which developed through the Devāśeṣa stage of Sharada from the 14th–18th centuries, developed into Dogri, a 'highly imperfect' script later consciously influenced in part by Gurmukhi during the late 19th century, possibly to lend it authority by resemblance to scripts already established in official and literary capacities, though not displacing Takri. - **The system.** The diagnostic is the lineage, and it is eight systems in seven steps: ADOPTED: Egyptian → Proto-Sinaitic → Phoenician → Aramaic → Brahmi → Gupta → Sharada → Gurmukhī — the chain as the article's infobox parent list gives it, with the Sharada→Gurmukhī link marked disputed (see the honest blank). The article traces the roots by way of Brahmi into the Northwestern (Sharada-based) group, with links to Central Asian scripts used for extinct languages like Saka and Tocharian. The type is abugida, left-to-right: all consonants carry an inherent vowel [ə], changed by diacritics that can appear above, below, before, or after the consonant; at the beginning of a syllable vowels are written as independent letters, built on the three vowel-bearer letters ੳ (ūṛā), ਅ (aiṛā), and ੲ (īṛī) — with the exception of aiṛā, which in isolation represents [ə], the bearers are never used without additional vowel diacritics. To form consonant clusters Gurmukhi affixes subscript letters (duttă akkhară, 'joint letters', or pairī̃ akkhară, 'letters at the feet') at the bottom of standard characters — forms of ਹ, ਰ, and ਵ — rather than using true conjunct symbols. The alphabet contains thirty-five base letters (akkhară), traditionally arranged in seven rows of five: the first three letters, the mātarā vāhakă ('vowel bearer'), form the basis for independent vowels and are not consonants; the pair of fricatives, the mūlă vargă ('base class'), share the row; then five sets of homorganic consonants, arranged from the back (velars) to the front (labials) of the mouth, each row in tenuis, aspirate, voiced stop, tonal, nasal order; the arrangement, the varṇămāllā, is completed with the antimă ṭollī, the 'ending group' of sonorants. The names of most consonants are based on their reduplicative phonetic values (kakkā, khakkhā, gaggā). The tones are three — rising, neutral, falling — with no separate symbol: the tonal consonants of the fourth column, ਘ, ਝ, ਢ, ਧ, ਭ, once voiced aspirates, now always represent unaspirated consonants, unvoiced in onset positions and voiced elsewhere, and are often transliterated as gha, jha, ḍha, dha, bha though Punjabi lacks those sounds. The sisters are four — Khudabadi, Khojki, Mahajani, Multani — and the child is one, Anandpur Lipi. The languages are five — Punjabi, Punjabi dialects, Sant Bhasha (historical), Sindhi (historical), Braj (historical). ISO 15924 is Guru (310); the Unicode range is U+0A00–U+0A7F (see the Unicode census); the official script of Punjab, India since 18 April 1968.

- **The story.** Dogri (Devanagari डोगरी, Dogra 𑠖𑠵𑠌𑠤𑠮, Nastaliq ڈوگری, Romanised *Ḍōgrī*, IPA [ɖoːɡ.ɾiː]) is an Indo-Aryan language of the Western Pahari group, primarily spoken by the Dogra people native to the Duggar region of the Jammu Division of India's Jammu and Kashmir, with smaller groups of speakers in the adjoining regions of the Indian states of Himachal Pradesh and Punjab, as well as Pakistan-administered Azad Kashmir and the Pakistani province of Punjab. It is currently spoken in the districts of Kathua, Jammu, Samba, Udhampur and parts of Reasi District (mostly in Reasi, Katra and Pouni Tehsil) of Jammu division. Unusually for an Indo-European language, Dogri is tonal, a trait it shares with other Western Pahari languages and Punjabi. It has several varieties, all with greater than 80% lexical similarity. Dogri is spoken by 2.6 million people in India (as of the 2011 census), not counting those who reported their language as 'Pahari'. The first reference to the language is the year 1317, when Amir Khusro, the famous Urdu and Persian poet, referred to Duger (Dogri) while describing the languages and dialects of India: *"Sindhi-o-Lahori-o-Kashmiri-o-Duger."* The name itself is unsettled, and the article files three rival theories: intellectuals in the court of Maharaja Ranbir Singh described *Duggar* as a distorted form of *Dwigarta*, 'two troughs', a possible reference to the Mansar and Surinsar lakes; the linguist George Grierson connected *Duggar* with the Rajasthani word *Doonger*, 'hill', and *Dogra* with *Donger* — an opinion that has lacked support because of the inconsistency of the ostensible changes (how *Doonger* became *Duggar* while *Donger* became *Dogra*), and has been contradicted by some scholars; yet another proposal stems from *Durgara*, the name of a kingdom mentioned in an eleventh-century copper-plate inscription in the Bhuri Singh Museum in Chamba, Himachal Pradesh — *Durgara* means 'invincible' in several Northern Indo-Aryan languages, and could be an allusion to the ruggedness of the terrain of Duggar and the historically militarised and autonomous Dogra societies. In 1976, the experts attending the Language Session of the All India Oriental Conference held in Dharwad, Karnataka, could not reach consensus on the *Dwigarta* and *Durgara* hypotheses, but did manage agreement on a *Doonger*-*Duggar* connection; in a subsequent All India Oriental Conference held at Jaipur in 1982, the linguists agreed that the culture, language and history of Rajasthan and Duggar share some similarities, and it was suggested that the words *Duggar* and *Dogra* are common in some parts of Rajasthan — specifically, areas with many forts are called Duggar, and their inhabitants are accordingly known as Dogras. An article by Dharam Chand Prashant in the literary magazine *Shiraza Dogri* suggested that "the opinion that the word *Duggar* is a form of the word *Duggarh* sounds appropriate." Dogri was originally written in the old Dogra Akkhar script — a modified version of Takri. A modified version of this script was created by the order of Maharaja Ranbir Singh of Jammu and Kashmir, which was then called Name Dogra Akkhar; official documents were written in this new script, however it never caught on among the general Dogri-speaking populace. Ranbir Singh officially adopted Dogra Akkhar in the 1860s for administrative and scholarly purposes, and the Vidya Vilas Press in Jammu printed official publications and scholarly books in the Takri script — a notable Dogri translation (in the New Dogra script) of the Sanskrit classic mathematical opus *Lilavati*, by Bhaskaracharya (b. 1114 AD), was published by the Vidya Vilas Press, Jammu in 1873, translated into Dogri by Jyotshi Bisheshwar, then principal of Jammu Pathshala, at the late Maharaja Ranbir Singh's order. In 1944, Devanagari was chosen as the official script for Dogri and other regional languages — the Dogri Sanstha's decision — and Takri fell into almost complete disuse; currently Devanagari is the officially recognised script for Dogri in India and virtually all Dogri literature is published in it, while Nastaliq Perso-Arabic carries the language on the Pakistan side. The Gurmukhi entry's closing note belongs here too: Dogri's old script was 'highly imperfect' and was consciously influenced in part by Gurmukhi during the late 19th century, possibly to lend it authority by resemblance to scripts already established in official and literary capacities, though not displacing Takri. Dogri has an established tradition of poetry, fiction and dramatic works, from the 18th-century Dogri poet Kavi Dattu (1725–1780) in Raja Ranjit Dev's court — highly regarded for his *Barah Massa* (Twelve Months), *Kamal Netra* (Lotus Eyes), *Bhup Bijog* and *Bir Bilas* — to Professor Ram Nath Shastri (born 15 April 1914, the "Father of Dogri") and Mrs. Padma Sachdev. *Shiraza Dogri* is a Dogri literary periodical issued by the Jammu and Kashmir Academy of Art, Culture and Languages, a notable publisher of modern Dogri literary work, another being the Dogri Sanstha. Popular recent songs include *Pala Shapaiya Dogariya*, *Manne di Mauj* and *Shhori Deya*; the noted Pakistani singer Malika Pukhraj had roots in Duggar, and her renditions of several Dogri songs continue to be popular in the region; devotional songs (bhajans) composed by Karan Singh have gained increasing popularity, including *Kaun Kareyaan Teri Aarti*. Dogri programming features regularly on Radio Kashmir (a division of All India Radio), and Doordarshan broadcasts in Jammu and Kashmir — however Dogri does not have a dedicated state television channel yet, unlike Kashmiri (which has the Doordarshan Koshur channel). Official recognition of the language has been gradual, but progressive: on 2 August 1969, the General Council of the Sahitya Academy, Delhi recognized Dogri as an "independent modern literary language" of India, based on the unanimous recommendation of a panel of linguists; on 22 December 2003, Dogri was recognized as a national language of India in the Indian constitution, through the 92nd Constitutional Amendment, which added it to the Eighth Schedule — one of the 22 scheduled languages, alongside Bodo, Maithili and Santali, raising the total to 22; in September 2020, the Parliament of India passed the Jammu and Kashmir Official Languages Act, declaring Dogri as one of the five official languages of the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir, along with Hindi, Urdu, English, and Kashmiri. In 2005, a collection of over 100 works of prose and poetry in Dogri published over the last 50 years was made accessible online at the Central Institute of Indian Languages (CIIL), Mysore — including works of Dhinu Bhai Panth, Professor Madan Mohan Sharma, B.P. Sathai and Ram Nath Shastri. The census record underneath the recognition is a slow retreat in share: about 1.46 million speakers in 1981, 24 percent of Jammu and Kashmir's population; 22.05 lakh (2.205 million) in 2001, 22 percent; 2.51 million in 2011, 20 percent — the absolute number rising while the share falls, and a survey of 130 respondents across 20 locations in the Jammu region finding the elderly fluent and the young understanding but rarely using Dogri in public or education. - **The system.** The diagnostic is the family, and it is six levels in five steps: ADOPTED: Indo-European → Indo-Iranian → Indo-Aryan → Northern → Western Pahari → Dogri — the chain as the article's infobox gives it. The type is a tonal Indo-Aryan language, written left-to-right in every script it has carried: the writing systems are four — Dogra script, Devanagari, Perso-Arabic, Mahajani (historically) — with Devanagari the officially recognised script in India and Nastaliq the Perso-Arabic form on the Pakistan side; the article's own sample text, Article 1 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, is given in three scripts (Dogra Akkhar, Devanagari, Perso-Arabic) with an ISO 15919 transliteration and an IPA transcription. The phonology is thirty-two consonants — five nasals (m n ɳ ɲ ŋ), fifteen plosive/affricates (five voiceless p t̪ ʈ t͡ʃ k, five aspirated pʰ t̪ʰ ʈʰ t͡ʃʰ kʰ, five voiced b d̪ ɖ d͡ʒ ɡ), seven fricatives (voiceless f s ʃ x, voiced z ɣ ɦ), two taps (ɾ ɽ), three approximants (ʋ l j) — and seventeen vowel sounds, ten oral (iː ɪ eː ɛː ə aː oː ɔː uː ʊ) and seven nasalized (ã ĩ ũ ẽ ɛ̃ õ ɔ̃); gemination occurs in all consonants except /ɾ ɳ ɽ ʃ/, and /f z x ɣ/ occur only from Perso-Arabic loan words. The tones are carried by letters, not by marks: like Punjabi, Dogri uses the letters घ (gʱə), झ (d͡ʒʱə), ढ (ɖʱə), ध (d̪ʱə), भ (bʱə) and ढ़ (ɽʱə) for tonal uses — word-initially a high-falling tone, medially and finally a low-rising tone on the preceding vowel — and unlike Punjabi, ह has a high-falling tone in all positions; to indicate a low-rising tone in the middle of words Dogri uses ह् (ह with a halant) when the preceding vowel is long and a combining apostrophe (ʼ) when the preceding vowel is short. The codes are ISO 639-2 `doi`, ISO 639-3 `doi` (inclusive code; individual codes `dgo` — Dogri proper — and `xnr` — Kangri), Glottolog `indo1311` as the infobox prints it. The official standings are two: one of the 22 scheduled languages of India since December 2003, and one of the five official languages of the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir since September 2020. The sisters under the `doi` macrolanguage are one named — Kangri (`xnr`) — and the standard dialect is Samba, selected by the Department of Dogri at Jammu University, which published textbooks in it.

- **The story.** Kangri (Devanagari कांगड़ी, Takri 𑚊𑚭𑚫𑚌𑚪𑚯, Romanised Kangri, also called Kangra-Dogri, Pahari, Himachali or Pahari Kangri) is a Western Pahari language of the Kangra people, spoken in the old Trigarta country — predominantly in Kangra, Hamirpur and the hilly parts of Una districts of Himachal Pradesh, in parts of Mandi and Chamba, and in the hilly parts of Pathankot and Hoshiarpur districts of Punjab, with a few villages in Pakistan belonging to families migrated from Kangra. Omniglot's list differs in two ways — Gurdaspur for Pathankot, the same ground under its pre-2011 name, and no Mandi or Chamba parts (see the honest blank). Like most Indo-Aryan languages it forms a dialect continuum with its neighbours: east to Mandeali, north to Chambeali, Gaddi and Bhateali, south-east to Kahluri and Hinduri and the Baghliani, Baghati and Keonthali dialects of Lower Mahasui, and north-west to Dogri. Some Dogri linguists have called Kangri part of Dogri, on the similarities and the mutual intelligibility — but only in the bordering lects, where the continuum runs. Kangri is used in literature, on the radio and in education, and its writers and poets make submissions to the Pahari cause under the Himachal Pradesh Academy of Arts, Culture and Languages (HPAACL). It has no official status: the demand for 'Western Pahari' under the Eighth Schedule, made by the state's Vidhan Sabha in 2010, has had no positive progress since. UNESCO calls it definitely endangered — many Kangri children are not learning it as their mother tongue any longer — while Glottolog's EGIDS grade is 5 (Developing), not endangered (see the honest blank). Gautam Sharma Vyathit and Chandrarekha Dhadwal are noted for preserving Kangri folk songs and for their novels. The sample text on record is Matthew 1:1–3, supplied by Biswajit Mandal, in Devanagari with an IPA transcription.

- **The system.** The diagnostic is the family, and it is six levels in five steps: ADOPTED: Indo-European → Indo-Iranian → Indo-Aryan → North-Western or Northern → Western Pahari → Kangri — the chain as the article's infobox gives it, the fourth level two-rendered ("North-Western or Northern" against Dogri's plain "Northern"; see the honest blank). The type is a tonal Indo-Aryan language, written left-to-right in the two scripts it carries: Takri is the native script and Devanagari the script of present use — "now people write Kangri Language in Devanagari script". The phonology is twenty-four clear consonants — two nasals (m n), fifteen plosive/affricates (five voiceless p t ʈ tʃ k, five aspirated pʰ tʰ ʈʰ tʃʰ kʰ, five voiced b d ɖ dʒ ɡ), two fricatives (s ɦ), two laterals (l ɭ), three taps (ɾ ɽ ɽ̃) — with two marginal sounds, [ɳ] (mostly an allophone of /ɽ̃/, and of /n/ before a retroflex stop) and [j] (not clear whether a separate phoneme), for twenty-six in all; and ten vowels — two close (iː uː), two near-close (ɪ ʊ), three mid (e ə o), one open-mid (ɔ), two open (æ ɑː) — with /e/ lowering to nasal [ɛ̃] after /ɽ̃/. The tones are carried by the loss of aspiration, as in Punjabi and Dogri, but the assignment differs: the cognates of Hindi voiced aspirated obstruents surface in Kangri as voiced consonants with tone, in Punjabi and Dogri as voiceless consonants with tone — Kangri has lost the aspiration and gained the tone but not lost the voicing, and the loss of voicing has not yet reached it. The grammar is five pronoun rows in seven forms — 1st singular मैं Mai mæ̃, 1st plural असाँ / अहाँ Asa / Aha əsãː / əhãː, 2nd singular तू Tu t̪u, 2nd plural तुसाँ / त्वहाँ Tusa / Tuha t̪usãː / t̪vəhãː, 3rd singular and plural सै Se sæ — fourteen cases over the noun घर /kʰər/ "home" in twenty-one forms, two obliques (singular घरे, plural घरेयाँ), and sixteen adverbial-pronoun cells in nineteen forms across time, place, manner and quantity. The codes are ISO 639-3 `xnr` and Glottolog `kang1280`. The official standings are none: no official status, and the 2010 Eighth Schedule demand unanswered. The sister under the `doi` macrolanguage is one named — Kangri is Dogri's sister under `doi`, and Dogri is the scheduled one.

- **The story.** Mandeali (Takri 𑚢𑚘𑚶𑚖𑚮𑚣𑚭𑚥𑚯, Devanagari मण्डियाली, Romanised Mandeali, also spelled Mandiyali and Mandiali, also called Mandi, Mandiali, Mandyali, Pahari, Himachali or Pahari Mandiyali) is a Western Pahari language of the Mandyali People, spoken in the Mandi Valley — predominantly in the Mandi district of Himachal Pradesh and particularly in the city of Mandi. Mandi town was established in 1527 by Ajbar Sen as the seat of the Mandi State, a princely state till 1948; it is the cultural capital of Himachal Pradesh, and its people are called Mandyalis. The language's region is given as Mahasu and Trigarta. Standard Mandeali is spoken through the broad valley running north and south from Jogindernagar to Sundarnagar. Around it sit the transitions: Mandeali Pahari is spoken north around Barot, east of the Uhl River — intelligible with difficulty to Standard Mandeali, an intermediate variety between Mandeali and Kullui, very close to the Kullvi of neighbouring Kullu district; the south-east holds the transition to Mahasui, the dialect there sometimes called Suketi, or the dialect of the Outer Seraj area, an intermediate of Kullvi and Upper Mahasvi; in the west, Sarkaghat is a little different again, a transition towards Hamirpur and Bilaspur. Grierson distinguished three dialects — Mandeali, Mandeali Pahari and Suketi — and the language of the Mandi State was Mandeali while that of the Suket State was Suketi, the two closely connected. Mandeali is termed the transitional dialect between the Mahasuic and the Chamealic-Kangric languages. A preliminary survey gives it functional intelligibility of Kangri, with people in south-east Mandi district having more difficulty; the Chambealic varieties are often considered separate languages, but at least some are 90–95% intelligible with Mandeali proper; lexical similarity runs 89% with the Palampuri dialect of Kangri and 83% with Chambeali. It is distantly related to Kullui. At the 2011 census, 59.11% of Mandi district named Mandeali as their first language, against 33.32% Pahari, 4.1% Hindi, 0.66% Punjabi and 0.47% Kangri; the speakers have decreased by 21% from 1961 to 2001. The language is commonly called Pahari or Himachali, like many neighbouring languages. It has no official status: the demand for 'Pahari (Himachali)' under the Eighth Schedule, made by the state's Vidhan Sabha in 2010, has had no positive progress since. It is recorded by the Indian government as a dialect of Hindi, even with poor mutual intelligibility with Hindi, and some call it a dialect of Punjabi or Dogri. UNESCO calls it definitely endangered — many Mandeali children are not learning it as their mother tongue any longer — while Glottolog's EGIDS grade is 5 (Developing), not endangered (see the honest blank). The months follow the Hindu calendar, twelve of them, and the days are seven, with Twār, Sunday, a loan from Urdu Itwār. The language's details on Omniglot were supplied by Biswajit Mandal — the same contributor who supplied Kangri's Matthew sample.

- **The system.** The diagnostic is the family, and it is six levels in five steps: ADOPTED: Indo-European → Indo-Iranian → Indo-Aryan → Northern → Western Pahari → Mandeali — the chain as the article's infobox gives it, the fourth level plain "Northern" where Kangri's infobox gives "North-Western or Northern" and Omniglot gives "the North-Western branch of the Western Pahari group" (see the honest blank). The type is a Western Pahari language of the Mandi Valley, written left-to-right in the two scripts it carries: Mandeali Takri — the Mandi-Suket Takri variety — is the native script and Devanagari the script of present use. The phonology is thirty-three clear consonants — twenty plosive/affricates (five voiceless p t ʈ tʃ k, five aspirated pʰ tʰ ʈʰ tʃʰ kʰ, five voiced b d ɖ dʒ ɡ, five breathy bʱ dʱ ɖʱ dʒʱ ɡʱ), three fricatives (s ʃ ɦ), three nasals (m n ɳ), two laterals (l ɭ), three trill/taps (r ɽ ɽʱ), two approximants (j w) — with one marginal, [ŋ], heard only before velar stops, for thirty-four in all, and [f] as an allophone of pʰ; the aspirated sonorants m n ɳ l ɭ r w "can be considered as separate phonemes" — the article's own hedge, seven of them. The vowels are thirteen cells — four close (i iː u uː), six mid ((e) eː ə əː (o) oː), two open-mid (ɛː ɔː), one open (aː) — with (e) and (o) parenthesised, eleven clear and two marginal. The grammar is two genders, two numbers and four cases — direct, oblique, vocative and ergative — the oblique also serving as locative and the ergative also as instrumental; nouns divide into extended and unextended declensions, the extended characteristically masculines ending in unaccented -ā and feminines in -ī; the pronouns are eight rows in nine forms — 1st singular हाऊँ ɦaːũ, 1st plural आस्से asːe, 2nd singular तू tu, 2nd plural तुस्से t̪usːe, 3rd proximate singular ए / ये eː / jeː, 3rd proximate plural यों jõː, 3rd distal singular से seː, 3rd distal plural स्यों sjõː; the cases over घर /gʱəːr/ "home" are thirteen in twenty-five forms; the postpositions are seventeen — six used alone, eleven that may take a secondary preposition — and the numerals run one to twenty, the months twelve, the days seven. The codes are ISO 639-3 `mjl` and Glottolog `mand1409`. The official standings are none: no official status, and the 2010 Eighth Schedule demand unanswered. The transitional position is the entry's hinge: the Western Pahari article terms Mandeali the transitional dialect between the Mahasuic and the Chamealic-Kangric languages — the Mandi Valley tongue that both sides understand.

- **The story.** Chambeali (Takri 𑚏𑚢𑚶𑚠𑚣𑚭𑚥𑚯, Devanagari चम्बयाली, Romanised Chambeali, ITRANS cambayālī, also called Chambiali, Chambiyali, Chameali, Chamiyali Pahari, Chamya, Chamaya, Cameali, Chamrali, Pahari or Himachali) is a Western Pahari language of the Chamba district of Himachal Pradesh, in the old Trigarta country, spoken also in Jammu and Kashmir. At the 2011 census it counted 126,000 speakers. Its dialects are three — Bansyari, Bansbari, and Gadi Chameali, the last two spelled Bansbali and Gadi Chambeali in the other renders (see the honest blank). It has a high degree of mutual intelligibility with its neighbours, 83% with Mandeali. It is commonly called Pahari or Himachali, like many neighbouring languages. It has no official status: it is recorded as a dialect of Hindi, even with poor mutual intelligibility with Hindi and a higher mutual intelligibility with other recognised languages like Dogri. UNESCO calls it definitely endangered — many Chambeali children are not learning it as their mother tongue any longer. Earlier the language got a huge amount of state patronage; everything changed since independence, due to favouritism towards Hindi by the Indian Government. The demand for 'Pahari (Himachali)' under the Eighth Schedule, made by the state's Vidhan Sabha in 2010, has had no positive progress since. Its native script is Takri — and the Chambeali version of Takri has been encoded as the standard for Takri under Unicode: the tongue that set the standard for its script. In present use it is also written with Devanagari (see the honest blank). The months follow the Hindu calendar, twelve of them, in a table carried in Takri, Devanagari, ITRANS and English — Chaitara (March–April) first, PhaugaNa (February–March) last. A 2016 study of district Chamba names the district's local tongues around it: Chambiyali in the main town, Churahi in Churah tehsil, Pangwali in Pangi, Gaddi in Bharmaur.

- **The system.** The diagnostic is the family, and it is six levels in five steps: ADOPTED: Indo-European → Indo-Iranian → Indo-Aryan → Northern → Western Pahari → Chambeali — the chain as the article's infobox gives it, the fourth level plain "Northern" where Kangri's infobox gives "North-Western or Northern" (see the honest blank). The type is a Western Pahari language of Chamba district in Trigarta, written left-to-right in the two scripts it carries: Chambeali Takri — the version encoded as the Unicode standard for the script — is the native script and Devanagari the script of present use. The phonology is thirty-two consonants — four nasals (m n ɳ ŋ), twenty stops and affricates (ten plain p b t d ʈ ɖ tɕ dʑ k ɡ, ten aspirated pʰ bʱ tʰ dʱ ʈʰ ɖʱ tɕʰ dʑʱ kʰ ɡʱ), two fricatives (s h), four approximants (w l ɭ j), two trills (r ɽ) — and fourteen vowel cells — eight close (ɪ ʏ iː yː ɨ ɯ ʊ uː), three close-mid (eː ə oː), two open-mid (æː ɔː), one open (aː) — with no short mid or open vowel except ə, and the front rounded ʏ and yː and the back unrounded ɯ among the close vowels. The dialects are three: Bansyari, Bansbari, Gadi Chameali. The codes are ISO 639-3 `cdh` and Glottolog `cham1307`, nested under `cham1331` under `kang1292` under `hima1250`. The official standings are none: no official status, and the 2010 Eighth Schedule demand unanswered. The standard is the entry's hinge: the Chambeali version of Takri is the Unicode standard for the script — the tongue that wrote its script's rule.

- **The story.** Bhateali (Devanagari भटियाली, ITRANS bhaṭiyālī, also called Bhattiyali, Bhatiali, Bhatiyali, Bhatiali Pahari) is a Western Pahari language of Himachal Pradesh in northern India, in the old Trigarta region. It is spoken majorly in the Bhattiyat division of Chamba, in Dalhousie, and in the Nurpur division of Kangra, and in the hilly parts of Pathankot district of Punjab. The 2011 Indian Census counted 15,347 speakers, of which 15,107 were found in Chamba district. Bhateali has sometimes been counted as a dialect of Kangri — the article cites Verbeke (2017) and Tiwari for the counting — and it is listed under the Western Pahari languages group. It was historically written using the Takri script; the infobox gives the writing system as Takri, Devanagari. Glottolog 5.4 carries it under the headword Bhattiyali, languoid bhat1263, with the alternate names Bhateali, Bhatiali Pahari, Bhatiyali and Bhattiyali, and gives its AES status as not endangered — Developing, EGIDS 5 — with a classification comment citing George A. Grierson 1916.

- **The system.** The diagnostic is the family, and it is six levels in five steps: ADOPTED: Indo-European → Indo-Iranian → Indo-Aryan → Northern → Western Pahari → Bhateali — the chain as the article's infobox gives it, the fourth level plain "Northern" as in the Chambeali and Mandeali entries. The type is a Western Pahari language of the Bhattiyat division of Chamba, Dalhousie, the Nurpur division of Kangra and hilly Pathankot, written left-to-right in the two scripts it carries: Takri the historical script, Devanagari the script of present use. The phonology is thirty-two consonants — four nasals (m n ɳ ŋ), twenty stops and affricates (ten plain p b t d ʈ ɖ tɕ dʑ k ɡ, ten aspirated pʰ bʱ tʰ dʱ ʈʰ ɖʱ tɕʰ dʑʱ kʰ ɡʱ), two fricatives (s h), four approximants (w l ɭ j), two trills (r ɽ) — and fourteen vowel cells — eight close (ɪ ʏ iː yː ɨ ɯ ʊ uː), three close-mid (eː ə oː), two open-mid (æː ɔː), one open (aː) — with no short mid or open vowel except ə, and the front rounded ʏ and yː and the back unrounded ɯ among the close vowels. The codes are ISO 639-3 `bht` and Glottolog `bhat1263`, nested under `cham1331` under `kang1292` under `hima1250`. No official standing is filed: the article gives none. The hinge is the double nesting — Glottolog puts Bhateali under the Chambeali group (cham1331), not directly under Kangri, while the dialect question counts it as Kangri's.

- **The story.** Kullui (*Kullū*, also known as Kulvi, Takri: 𑚊𑚰𑚥𑚷𑚱𑚃/𑚊𑚰𑚥𑚷𑚱𑚦𑚯) is a Western Pahari language spoken in the Kullu District of the Indian state of Himachal Pradesh. The 2011 Indian Census counted 196,295 speakers. The language is commonly called Pahari or Himachali; some speakers call it a dialect of Punjabi or Dogri. It has no official status, and is officially recorded as a dialect of Hindi. According to UNESCO, the language is of definitely endangered category — "many Kulluvi children are not learning Kulluvi as their mother tongue any longer." The native script of the language is a variety of the Takri script; it is currently written with the Devanagari alphabet, was written with a version of the Takri alphabet until the mid-20th century, and the Latin alphabet is used online by some Kullui speakers. The documentation project was launched in 2014 at the Institute of Linguistics of the Russian Academy of Sciences — Krylova, Mazurova, Renkovskaya, Shuvannikova (Knyazeva) — under RFBR grants 16-34-01040 ("Grammar description and lexicon of Kullui") and 19-012-00355 ("The investigation of the Kullui language based on the oral text corpus"), with four linguistic expeditions to Kullu district in 2014, 2016, 2017 and 2018 and fieldwork in the town of Kullu and the villages of Naggar, Suma and Bashing in 2014–2017. The earlier witnesses are Diack (1896, *The Kulu Dialect of Hindi*), Bailey (1908, *The Languages of the Northern Himalayas*), Grierson (1916, the Kulu Group, *Linguistic Survey of India* Vol. IX Part IV), Ranganatha (1981, *Survey of Mandeali and Kului*, Census of India 1971 Language Monograph No. 7), Thakur (1975, *Pahāṛī bhāṣā*) and Sharma (2014, *Kuluti-Hindi vyakaran*). Kullu District counted 437,474 people in the 2011 census; the district has six tehsils — Manali, Kullu, Sainj, Banjar, Ani, Nirmand — and Kullui is spoken in the Kullu and Manali tehsils, in the Kullu valley (the Beas river valley). Omniglot places it instead in the Balichowk, Banjar and Sainj sub-districts. OLAC's dialect names for Kullu Pahari are Inner Seraji, Inner Siragi, Kauli, Kullui, Kulu Boli, Kulu Pahari, Kului, Kulvi, Kulwali, Outer Seraji, Pahari, Pahari Kullu, Kullu Pahari, Phari Kulu, Saraji, Siragi and Siraji.

- **The system.** The diagnostic is the family, and it is six levels in five steps: ADOPTED: Indo-European → Indo-Iranian → Indo-Aryan → Northern → Western Pahari → Kullui — the chain as the article's infobox gives it, the fourth level plain "Northern" as in the Chambeali, Mandeali and Bhateali entries. The type is a Western Pahari language of the Kullu District, the infobox's region field reading "Mahasu" (filed as printed — see the honest blank). The scripts are three: Takri the native script, Devanagari the script of present use, Latin the script of online use. The phonology is thirty-nine consonants — seventeen plosives (eight pairs p pʰ, b bʱ, t̪ t̪ʰ, d̪ d̪ʱ, ʈ ʈʰ, ɖ ɖʱ, k kʰ, ɡ ɡʱ, plus the glottal stop ʔ), eight affricates (t͡s t͡sʰ, d͡z d͡zʱ, c͡ç c͡çʰ, ɟ͡ʝ ɟ͡ʝʱ), four fricatives (s, ɕ, ħ, ɦ), five nasals (m, n̪, ɳ, ɲ, ŋ), two trill/flap (r̪, ɽ), two lateral (l̪, ɭ), one approximant (j) — with a four-way distinction in phonation between tenuis, voiced, aspirated and breathy-voiced series for the stops and affricates. Thakur lists as separate phonemes aspirated correlates of /ŋ/, /n/, /m/, /j/, /r/, /ɽ/, /l/ and /ɭ/ — eight more, 47 if counted — but describes the aspiration as a voiceless pharyngeal friction. /ŋ/ and /ɲ/ are rare but contrast with the other nasals word-medially between vowels; /ɳ/, /ɭ/ and /ɽ/, together with their aspirated correlates, do not occur in the beginning of words; the glottal stop occurs only between a vowel and /ɳ/, /n/, /r/ or /l/ — [kɑːʔɭ] "a trumpet" against [kɑːɭ] "famine"; the pharyngeal fricative /ħ/ historically derives from /s/ and occurs word-finally — [ɡʱɑːħ] "grass", [biːħ] "twenty". No vowel table is filed: the article carries a consonant table only (see the honest blank). The codes are ISO 639-3 `kfx` and Glottolog `kull1236`, nested under the Western Pahari group as the infobox gives it; Glottolog's own parent path was not read first-party this pass (see the honest blank). No official standing is filed: the article gives none, and Omniglot records it as a dialect of Hindi. The hinge is the name's two spellings in each script, and the same move twice over — spelling 2 demotes the final II from an independent letter to a vowel sign and inserts a VA before it, landing in the tail in Takri and in the middle in Devanagari.

- **Decoder-design note (Kullui → Gauntlet).** Five rungs. (1) **The two-spellings probe.** Present the two Takri spellings; the specimen must give both, count 6 and 7, and say they share the first five code points and differ in the tail — a specimen that gives one spelling has a name, not the record. (2) **The middle-vs-tail probe.** Present the two Devanagari spellings; the specimen must say they share the opening KA+U and differ in the middle (LLA+UU against LA+VIRAMA+VA), and that the closing II is a letter in कुळूई and a sign in कुल्वी — the same move as the Takri pair, the final II demoted and a VA inserted — a specimen that calls the difference a typo has a guess, not the measurement. (3) **The consonant-count probe.** Present the 39-cell table; the specimen must count 39, break it 17+8+4+5+2+2+1, and name Thakur's eight aspirated sonorant correlates as the 47 — a specimen that gives a round 40 has a census, not the table. - **The story.** Bilaspuri (Himachali Takri: 𑚠𑚮𑚥𑚭𑚨𑚞𑚱𑚤𑚯, Devanagari: बिलासपूरी), or Kahluri (Takri: 𑚊𑚩𑚥𑚱𑚤𑚯, Devanagari: कहलूरी), is a Western Pahari language spoken in northern India, predominantly in the Bilaspur district of Himachal Pradesh. It is associated with the people of the former princely state of Bilaspur in the Hills State. It is also spoken in the hilly parts of Rupnagar district of Punjab. Bilaspuri is classified as one of the varieties of the Himachali language group. According to the 2011 Census, the speakers of Bilaspuri/Kahluri (listed under Punjabi) are 295,805. The language is commonly called Pahari or Himachali; it is also known as Kahluri, Bilaspuri Pahari, Kehloori Pahari, Kehluri and Pacchmi. It is classified by the Indian government as a dialect of Punjabi, and it is recorded under the Western Pahari group of languages, which was done on the basis of the conclusion made by linguists. Before independence there were certain institutions which enjoyed state patronage to publish in Kahluri; all of these institutions today lie in ruins since independence to favour Hindi, and with no institute that imparts teaching for this language, the language is endangered due to dominance of other recognised languages like Hindi. The demand for the inclusion of "Pahari (Himachali)" under the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution, which is supposed to represent multiple Pahari languages of Himachal Pradesh, was made in the year 2010 by the state's Vidhan Sabha; there has been no positive progress on this matter since then. Grierson called Kahluri a "rude" version of Punjabi; linguists have since changed that conclusion. The native script of the language is Takri; it is currently written with the Devanagari alphabet, and was written with a version of the Takri alphabet in the past. The witnesses are Bailey (1920, cited by Glottolog on the subclassification), Masica (1991, *The Indo-Aryan Languages*, p. 439), the People's Linguistic Survey of India — *The Languages of Himachal Pradesh*, Volume Eleven, Part Two, p. 130 — the Linguistic Survey of India, Himachal Pradesh volume (Bilaspuri/Kahluri chapter, pp. 713–745, P. Edward Vedamanickam), Ethnologue (25th ed., 2022), Amitjit Singh ("The Language Divide in Punjab", *Sagar*, Volume 4, Number 1, Spring 1997), and Omniglot's Bilaspuri page (details by Biswajit Mandal; sample text from bilaspuri.com). A Bilaspuri test of Wikipedia sits at Wikimedia Incubator. Bilaspur district counted 381,956 people in the 2011 census, in an area of 1,167 km² — the third least populous district of Himachal Pradesh (out of 12), after Lahaul and Spiti and Kinnaur — with 6 tehsils, 1,061 villages, 4 towns and 80,485 households; the district grew from 340,885 in 2001, +12.05%.

- **The system.** The diagnostic is the family, and it is six levels in five steps: ADOPTED: Indo-European → Indo-Iranian → Indo-Aryan → Northern → Western Pahari → Bilaspuri — the chain as the article's infobox gives it, the fourth level plain "Northern" as in the Chambeali, Mandeali, Bhateali and Kullui entries. The type is a Western Pahari language of the Bilaspur district, the infobox's region field reading "Trigarta" (filed as printed — see the honest blank). Glottolog 5.4 nests the languoid differently, under the path hima1250/kang1292/cham1331/bila1253 — parent cham1331, not Western Pahari directly — filed as read, not reconciled with the infobox chain (see the honest blank). The scripts are two: Takri the native script, Devanagari the script of present use. The phonology is fourteen vowels — six short (ɪ, ʏ, ɨ, ɯ, ʊ, ə) and eight long (iː, yː, uː, eː, oː, æː, ɔː, aː) — and thirty-two consonants — four nasals (m, n, ɳ, ŋ), ten plain stops and affricates (p, b, t, d, ʈ, ɖ, tɕ, dʑ, k, ɡ), ten aspirated (pʰ, bʱ, tʰ, dʱ, ʈʰ, ɖʱ, tɕʰ, dʑʱ, kʰ, ɡʱ), two fricatives (s, h), four approximants (w, l, ɭ, j), two trills (r, ɽ) — a two-way distinction in phonation between plain and aspirated series for the stops and affricates, with no breathy-voiced series filed. The dialects are five: North-east Bilaspuri (north-east of Kumar Hati; resemblance with Mandeali and the Baghliani dialect of Mahasui of Arki tehsil of Solan district); North Bilaspuri (north of Kumar Hati; resemblance with Mandeali); West Bilaspuri (shares resemblance with Kangri); Central Bilaspuri (Bilaspur historic town and surrounding area; shares resemblance with the Baghliani dialect of Mahasui of Arki tehsil of Solan district); Davin or Daur (east and south-east of Bilaspur historic town; shares resemblance with Hinduri, a dialect of the Keonthali sub group of Mahasui). The dialects of Kahluri are so closely allied that one might call them one dialect Kahluri or Bilaspuri. The codes are ISO 639-3 `kfs` and Glottolog `bila1253`. Glottolog's AES status is "not endangered", source Eberhard, Simons and Robinson 2026, comment "Bilaspuri (kfs-kfs) = 5 (Developing)" — EGIDS 5. No official standing is filed: the Indian government classifies it as a dialect of Punjabi, and the Eighth Schedule demand of 2010 has had no positive progress. The hinge is the two names in two scripts, and the same lengths twice over: 9 and 6 in both scripts — Bilaspuri 9 code points and Kahluri 6 in Takri, Bilaspuri 9 and Kahluri 6 in Devanagari — the two names sharing the three-code-point tail, UU+RA+II in Takri and ू+र+ी in Devanagari, and differing in the opening, BA+I+LA+AA+SA+PA against KA+HA+LA in Takri, ब+ि+ल+ा+स+प against क+ह+ल in Devanagari.

- **Decoder-design note (Bilaspuri → Gauntlet).** Five rungs. (1) **The two-names probe.** Present the two Takri spellings; the specimen must give both, count 9 and 6, and say they share the tail UU+RA+II — a specimen that gives one name has a label, not the record. (2) **The same-lengths probe.** Present the two Devanagari spellings; the specimen must say they are 9 and 6 too, the same lengths as the Takri pair, sharing the tail ू+र+ी — a specimen that counts different lengths has a guess, not the measurement. (3) **The consonant-tie probe.** Present the 32-cell table; the specimen must count 32, break it 4+10+10+2+4+2, and name the three-way tie with Chambeali, Bhateali and Dogri — a specimen that gives a round 30 has a census, not the table. (4) **The endangerment probe.** Present the three-way tension — the article's endangered, UNESCO's definitely-or-critically, Glottolog's not endangered at EGIDS 5; the specimen must hold all three without adjudicating — a specimen that picks one has a verdict, not the record. (5) **The census-listing probe.** Present 295,805 speakers listed under Punjabi; the specimen must say the census files Bilaspuri under Punjabi while the language is classified Western Pahari — a specimen that calls it a Punjabi dialect from the census alone has a filing, not the classification.

- **The story.** Churahi (Takri: 𑚏𑚰𑚤𑚭𑚩𑚯, Devanagari: चुराही), also called Chaurahi, is a Western Pahari language of Himachal Pradesh, India. It is spoken in the Chaurah and Saluni tehsils of Chamba district, and is considered endangered. The language is commonly called Pahari or Himachali; some speakers may even call it a dialect of Dogri. It has no official status. According to UNESCO, the language is of definitely endangered category — many Churahi children are not learning Churahi as their mother tongue any longer. The demand for the inclusion of "Pahari (Himachali)" under the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution, which is supposed to represent multiple Pahari languages of Himachal Pradesh, had been made in the year 2010 by the state's Vidhan Sabha; there has been no positive progress on this matter since then, even though small organisations are striving to save the language. Due to political interest, the language is currently recorded as a dialect of Hindi, even when having a poor mutual intelligibility with it and having a higher mutual intelligibility with other recognised languages like Dogri and other Western Pahari languages. The native script of the language is Takri; it is currently written with the Devanagari alphabet as well. The witnesses are Grierson (1916, cited by Glottolog on the subclassification), the Linguistic Survey of India, Himachal Pradesh volume (Churahi chapter, pp. 120–175, N. Gopalakrishnan), Ethnologue (25th ed., 2022), and a 2016 study of district Chamba carried in the Chambeali entry, which names the district's local tongues around Chamba town: Chambiyali in the main town, Churahi in Churah tehsil, Pangwali in Pangi, Gaddi in Bharmaur. A 2024 survey of Himachal's speech renders Grierson's classification of the district as five distinct forms of speech: in the northwest Churahi; in the northern portion of Pangi tehsil Pangwali; in the south-west in Bhattiyat tehsil Bhatiali; in the south-east of the Bharmaur area Bharmauri or Gadi, as the area is inhabited by the Gaddi tribe; and round about Chamba proper Chambiali — commonly, all these dialects are termed as Chambiali.

- **The system.** The diagnostic is the family, and it is six levels in five steps: ADOPTED: Indo-European → Indo-Iranian → Indo-Aryan → Northern → Western Pahari → Churahi — the chain as the article's infobox gives it, the fourth level plain "Northern" as in the Chambeali, Mandeali, Bhateali, Kullui and Bilaspuri entries. The type is a Western Pahari language of the Chamba district, the infobox's region field reading "Trigarta" (filed as printed — see the honest blank). Glottolog 5.4 nests the languoid differently, under the path hima1250/kang1292/cham1331/bhad1243/chur1258 — parent bhad1243, Bhadarwahi, not Western Pahari directly — filed as read, not reconciled with the infobox chain (see the honest blank). The scripts are two: Takri the native script, Devanagari the script of present use. The phonology is fourteen vowels — six short (ɪ, ʏ, ɨ, ɯ, ʊ, ə) and eight long (iː, yː, uː, eː, oː, æː, ɔː, aː) — and thirty-two consonants — four nasals (m, n, ɳ, ŋ), ten plain stops and affricates (p, b, t, d, ʈ, ɖ, tɕ, dʑ, k, ɡ), ten aspirated (pʰ, bʱ, tʰ, dʱ, ʈʰ, ɖʱ, tɕʰ, dʑʱ, kʰ, ɡʱ), two fricatives (s, h), four approximants (w, l, ɭ, j), two trills (r, ɽ). The codes are ISO 639-3 `cdj` and Glottolog `chur1258`. Glottolog's AES status is "not endangered", source Campbell, Lyle and Lee, Nala Huiying and Okura, Eve and Simpson, Sean and Ueki, Kaori 2022, comment "Churahi (1628-cdj) = At risk (20 percent certain, based on the evidence available) [Driem 2007]". No official standing is filed: the language has no official status, is recorded as a dialect of Hindi, and the Eighth Schedule demand of 2010 has had no positive progress. The hinge is one name in two scripts, the same six sounds twice over, 6 and 6 in both scripts: CA+U+RA+AA+HA+II in Takri and च+ु+र+ा+ह+ी in Devanagari — a pure transliteration pair, the two spellings differing in no sound, only in the letters that carry them.

- **The story.** Pangwali (Takri: 𑚞𑚫𑚌𑚦𑚭𑚪𑚯, Devanagari: पंगवाड़ी), also called Pahari, Pangi or Pangwali Pahari, is a Western Pahari language of Himachal Pradesh, India. It is spoken in the Pangi Tehsil of Chamba district — the Pangi Valley, a remote valley between the Zanskar Range to the north and the Pir Panjal Range to the south — and in Paddar, across the Chenab in Jammu and Kashmir, and is threatened to go extinct. The language is commonly called Pahari or Himachali; some speakers may even call it a dialect of Punjabi or Dogri. It has no official status. According to the United Nations Education, Scientific and Cultural Organisation (UNESCO), the language is of critically endangered category, i.e. the youngest speakers of Pangwali are generally grandparents or older and they too speak it infrequently or partially. The demand for the inclusion of "Pahari (Himachali)" under the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution, which is supposed to represent multiple Pahari languages of Himachal Pradesh, had been made in the year 2010 by the state's Vidhan Sabha; there has been no positive progress on this matter since then, even though small organisations are striving to save the language. Due to political interest, the language is currently recorded as a dialect of Hindi, even when having a poor mutual intelligibility with it and having a higher mutual intelligibility with other recognised languages like Dogri and other Western Pahari languages. The linguist George Abraham Grierson recorded Pangwali as a dialect of Chambeali in his Linguistic Survey of India — his chapter is headed "Paṅgwāḷī" — and it is now regarded as a language in its own right as a part of Western Pahari, affiliated with Bhadarwahi, Padderi among others; the language also shares a lot of vocabulary and grammatical features with Kashmiri language. It is very similar to the Padderi dialect of Padder, J&K. At the time of the Linguistic Survey of India, 3,701 speakers were estimated of Pangwali. The dialects are four: Killar, Purthi, Sach and Dharwasi — Killar, being the headquarter of the Tehsil, is the dialect which is widely understood, and Sach dialect is said to be the most conservative in regards to Sanskrit. The Pangwala people — Pangwal or Pangwale — are the valley's indigenous community, recognised as a Scheduled Tribe in 1966, with Pangi tehsil notified as a Scheduled Area in 1975; their population in Himachal Pradesh was 17,562 in 2011, against the valley's 18,868. The valley's high villages are Bhot settlements, whose people speak Bhoti among themselves and Pangwali with their Pangwal neighbours. Tubari Magazine is a recent effort to maintain the language; the magazine uses Devanagari Script. Omniglot, read first-party this pass, counts about 18,700 speakers, places the language mainly in the township of Pangi in the Chamba district in the northwest of Himachal Pradesh state and also in Jammu and Kashmir state, and carries Devanagari and Takri alphabet charts and a sample text — Luke 2:2-4, the Lord's Prayer, in Devanagari with transliteration and translation — details provided by Biswajit Mandal; it links the Ethnologue page, the pangi.in introduction to the language and the Endangered Languages Project page at endangeredlanguages.com/lang/4961. The witnesses are Grierson (1916, cited by Glottolog on the subclassification), Ethnologue (26th ed., 2023), Nayak, Binaya; Dhanujay; Rosy (2010, a write-up on Pangwali phonology), Nayak, Binaya Sundar, Parmas (2011, Basic Pangwali Grammar, in Hindi), Nayak, Binaya (2018, the numerals, Numeral Systems of the World's Languages), the 2016 study of district Chamba carried in the Chambeali entry, which names the district's local tongues around Chamba town: Chambiyali in the main town, Churahi in Churah tehsil, Pangwali in Pangi, Gaddi in Bharmaur, and a 2024 survey of Himachal's speech rendering Grierson's classification of the district as five distinct forms of speech: in the northwest Churahi; in the northern portion of Pangi tehsil Pangwali; in the south-west in Bhattiyat tehsil Bhatiali; in the south-east of the Bharmaur area Bharmauri or Gadi, as the area is inhabited by the Gaddi tribe; and round about Chamba proper Chambiali — commonly, all these dialects are termed as Chambiali.

- **The system.** The diagnostic is the family, and it is six levels in five steps: ADOPTED: Indo-European → Indo-Iranian → Indo-Aryan → Northern → Western Pahari → Pangwali — the chain as the article's infobox gives it, the fourth level plain "Northern" as in the Chambeali, Mandeali, Bhateali, Kullui, Bilaspuri and Churahi entries. The type is a Western Pahari language of the Pangi Valley and Paddar, the infobox's region field reading "Pangi Valley, Paddar". Glottolog 5.4 nests the languoid differently, under the path hima1250/kang1292/cham1331/pang1282 — parent cham1331, Chambeali, not Western Pahari directly — filed as read, not reconciled with the infobox chain (see the honest blank). The scripts are two: Takri the native script, Devanagari the script of present use — with the tension filed, not adjudicated: the article says Pangwali is natively written in the Takri script, but Devanagari is used as well, while Omniglot says it is written with the Devanagari alphabet and in the past was written with a version of the Takri script. The phonology is twenty-two vowels — Close i iː ĩ ĩː and u uː ũ ũː, Near-close ɪ̥, Close-mid ɘ ɘː ɘ̥ ɘ̃ and o oː, Open-mid ɛ ɛː, Near-open ɐ ɐː ɐ̃ː, Open a aː — and thirty consonants — two nasals (m, n), five voiceless stops and affricates (p, t̪, t͡ʃ, ʈ, k), five aspirated (pʰ, t̪ʰ, t͡ʃʰ, ʈʰ, kʰ), five voiced (b, d̪, d͡ʒ, ɖ, ɡ), five breathy (bʱ, d̪ʱ, d͡ʒʱ, ɖʱ, ɡʱ), three fricatives (s, ʃ, ɦ), three approximants (w, l, j), two flaps or taps (ɾ, ɽ). Pangwali exhibits a fossilised system of vowel harmony as other languages of the area (such as Kashmiri) do; the original conditioning vowels that caused harmony have often been lost, so the system is no longer productive. The grammar is two genders, masculine and feminine, with case markers Instrumental जे jē and बलि bali, Dative जे jē, Ablative केंइ kēin, पुठ / पिठ puṭh/piṭh and -ए -ē, Genitive -ए -ē. The intelligibility is 90% with Padderi, 75% with Bhadarwahi, 44% with Chambeali, 24% with Mandeali and 22% with Kangri; its lexical similarity is 27% with Kullu Pahari and 75% with Bhadarwahi. The codes are ISO 639-3 `pgg` and Glottolog `pang1282`. Glottolog's AES status is "shifting", source Campbell, Lyle and Lee, Nala Huiying and Okura, Eve and Simpson, Sean and Ueki, Kaori 2022, comment "Pangwali (4961-pgg) = Threatened (40 percent certain, based on the evidence available) [Lewis 2009]". No official standing is filed: the language has no official status, is recorded as a dialect of Hindi, and the Eighth Schedule demand of 2010 has had no positive progress. The hinge is one name in two scripts, the same seven sounds twice over, 7 in Takri, 8 in Devanagari: PA+ANUSVARA+GA+VA+AA+RRA+II in Takri and प+ं+ग+व+ा+ड+़+ी in Devanagari — a pure transliteration pair, the two spellings differing in no sound, only in the letters that carry them, and in one code point: Takri writes the RRA as a single letter, Devanagari builds ड़ from DDA plus NUKTA.

- **The story.** Bhadarwahi (Bhadrawahi; Takri: 𑚡𑚛𑚤𑚦𑚭𑚩𑚯, Devanagari: भद्रवाही, Perso-Arabic: بھدرواہی), also called Bhaderwahi, is an indigenous language of the Indian subcontinent, belonging to the Western Pahari group. It is spoken by the Bhadarwahi people — the Bhadarwahis — in Bhaderwah and its surrounding areas in the hills of the Jammu region of Jammu and Kashmir, India, in the Chenab region. The name Bhadarwahi can be understood either in a narrow sense as referring to the dialect, locally known as Bhiḍlāi, native to the Bhadarwah valley, or in a broader sense to cover the group of related dialects spoken in the wider region where Bhadrawahi proper is used as a lingua franca. In addition to Bhadrawahi proper, this group also includes Bhalesi and Khasali (Khashali); the Churahi language is closely related. The language is commonly called Bhaderwahi; some speakers may call it a dialect of Dogri. It has no official status. It is classified by the United Nations Education, Scientific and Cultural Organisation (UNESCO) as "definitely endangered," meaning that many Bhadarwahi parents are not teaching it to their children and the number of native speakers is decreasing; Kashmiri and Urdu/Hindi are spoken in the home in its place. The dialects are four in the infobox: Bhalesi, Bhadrawahi proper, Khasali and Padri — the Bhalesi dialect is spoken in the three tehsils of Bhalessa — Gandoh, Chilly Pingal and Kahara — and the Padri dialect in Pader, in Kishtwar district; Sarazi and Pogali are the region's fellow Western Pahari tongues. The 1901 census counted the Bhaderwahi group — Bhaderwahi, Bhalesi and Padri — at 25,517 speakers. The standard Bhadarwahi is spoken in Bhadarwah town of Doda district; Bhadarwah, whose ancient name is Bhaderkasi (spelt Bhaderkashi in the Qaida paper), is also known as "Naagon Ki Dharti" or "Chota Kashmir". Doda district counted 409,576 people in 2011; a census analysis of the same year counts 81,999 speakers of Bhadrawahi, with 22,528 in Thathri, 3,627 in Bhalessa and 9,296 in Kishtwar district. In Bhadarwah town itself, Bhadarwahi is the mother tongue of 52.67% (2011 census). The Bhadarwahi Qaida, a primer in Hindi and Urdu scripts, was published on January 18, 2021, to preserve the language, which lacked script support until then. The witnesses are Masica (1991, p. 210, the lateral retroflex affricates), Kaul, Pritam Krishen (2006, Pahāṛi and Other Tribal Dialects of Jammu — the classification there includes Rodhari as a separate node, elsewhere subsumed under Khasali), Dwivedi, Amitabh Vikram (2015, "Bhadarwahi: A Typological Sketch", Acta Linguistica Asiatica 5(1) — Bhadarwahi speakers about 250,000 in 2011), the Phonological System of Bhaderwahi (cited by the article for the name spellings), and Tiwari, Dr Siyaram (Bhartiya Bhashaon Ki Pahchan). Glottolog's alternative names are Baderwali, Badrohi, Bahi, Bhadarwahi, Bhaderbhai Jamu, Bhaderwali Pahari, Bhadrava, Bhadrawahi, Bhadri, Bradrawah, Bhalesi and Padari; the language is spoken in India and Pakistan.

- **The system.** The diagnostic is the family, and it is six levels in five steps: ADOPTED: Indo-European → Indo-Iranian → Indo-Aryan → Northern → Western Pahari → Bhadarwahi — the chain as the article's infobox gives it, the fourth level plain "Northern" as in the Chambeali, Mandeali, Bhateali, Kullui, Bilaspuri, Churahi and Pangwali entries. The type is a Western Pahari language of the Jammu region, the infobox's region field reading "Jammu region". Glottolog 5.4 nests the languoid differently, under the path hima1250/kang1292/cham1331/bhad1243/bhad1244/bhad1241 — parent bhad1244, grandparent bhad1243, not Western Pahari directly — filed as read, not reconciled with the infobox chain (see the honest blank); the same bhad1243 is Churahi's Glottolog parent, so Churahi sits under Bhadarwahi in Glottolog's tree while the infobox files both as Western Pahari sisters. The scripts are three: Takri the native script, Devanagari, and Perso-Arabic — the article's writing-system field reads "Devanagari, Takri, Perso-Arabic script". The phonology is ten vowels — High iː and uː, Lower High i and u, Mid e, eː and oː, Lower Mid ə and o, Low ɑː — and thirty-six consonants — four nasals (m, n, ɳ, ɲ), five voiceless stops (p, t̪, ʈ, t͡ʃ, k), five aspirated (pʰ, t̪ʰ, ʈʰ, t͡ʃʰ, kʰ), five voiced (b, d̪, ɖ, d͡ʒ, ɡ), five breathy (bʱ, d̪ʱ, ɖʱ, d͡ʒʱ, ɡʱ), five voiceless fricatives (s, ʃ, ç, çʰ, h), two voiced fricatives (z, zʱ), three approximants (w, l, j), one trill (r) and one flap or tap (ɽ). According to Masica (1991) there are a set of lateral retroflex affricates /ʈ͡ꞎ ɖ͡𝼅 ɖ͡𝼅ʱ/ from old /Cr/ clusters. The codes are ISO 639-3 `bhd` and Glottolog `bhad1241`; the Endangered Languages Project files it as Bhadrawahi. Glottolog's AES status is "threatened", source Campbell, Lyle and Lee, Nala Huiying and Okura, Eve and Simpson, Sean and Ueki, Kaori 2022, comment "Bhadrawahi (1598-bhd) = Vulnerable (20 percent certain, based on the evidence available) [van Driem 2007]". Glottolog's subclassification comment is Siddheshwar Varma 1948. No official standing is filed: the language has no official status, and UNESCO's grade is "definitely endangered". The hinge is one name in three scripts, the same seven sounds three times over, 7 in Takri, 8 in Devanagari, 8 in Perso-Arabic: BHA+DA+RA+VA+AA+HA+II in Takri 𑚡𑚛𑚤𑚦𑚭𑚩𑚯 and भद्रवाही in Devanagari and بھدرواہی in Perso-Arabic — the three spellings differing in no sound, only in the letters that carry them, and in one code point: Devanagari needs one extra letter for the द्र conjunct and Perso-Arabic one extra for the aspirated BH, both of which the Takri name-section spelling writes bare — with the tension filed, not adjudicated: the article's infobox spells the Takri with the virama, 𑚡𑚛𑚶𑚤𑚦𑚭𑚩𑚯, eight code points, while the name section spells it without, seven. The intelligibility is 75% with Bhadarwahi from Pangwali's side, and the lexical similarity 75% with Bhadarwahi — the Pangwali entry's table, read from the other direction.

(1) **The one-name-three-scripts probe.** Present the Takri, Devanagari and Perso-Arabic spellings; the specimen must give all three, count 7, 8 and 8, and say they are the same seven sounds with Takri one code point shorter — a specimen that gives 7, 7 and 7 has the headline, not the count. (2) **The virama probe.** Present the two Takri spellings, 7 code points in the name section and 8 in the infobox; the specimen must hold both with their locations — a specimen that calls one a typo has a verdict, not the record. (3) **The endangerment probe.** Present the three-way tension — UNESCO's definitely endangered, Glottolog's threatened, the Vulnerable-20-percent comment; the specimen must hold all three without adjudicating — a specimen that picks one has a verdict, not the record. (4) **The speaker-figure probe.** Present the three figures — 120,000 (Ethnologue 2019), ~250,000 (Dwivedi 2015), 81,999 (census analysis) — the specimen must hold all three with their sources and say they are different denominators — a specimen that picks one has a headline, not the record. (5) **The parent probe.** Present Glottolog's nesting of Churahi under bhad1243; the specimen must say Bhadarwahi is Churahi's Glottolog parent, not its sister — a specimen that calls them sisters has the family, not the tree.

- **The story.** Kishtwari (Kashtwari; Perso-Arabic: کشتواڑی, Devanagari: किश्तवाड़ी), also called Kashtawari, Kathiawari or Kistwali in Glottolog's alternative names, is an Indo-Aryan language of the Dardic branch. It is closely related to Kashmiri, with strong influences from neighbouring Western Pahari varieties. It is spoken by the Kishtwaris in Kishtwar district of Jammu division in Jammu and Kashmir, India. Kishtwari originated from Prakrit — the spoken language of common people in ancient times; the literary language was Sanskrit, which has a close relationship with Prakrit. It can be conveniently called a sister language of the Kashmiri language, as both have originated from Prakrit. Kishtwari has been preserved from the admixture of words and phrases from other languages and dialects, though the original Prakrit spoken by the common man of Kishtwar in olden times has absorbed some words from Dogri, Punjabi, and Persian languages to a limited extent. Grierson, in his Linguistic Survey of India, classified Kishtwari as a highly divergent variety of Kashmiri that had been profoundly influenced by neighbouring Punjabi and Western Pahari languages. Grierson noted that Kishtwari is more conservative in certain aspects than other Kashmiri dialects, as evidenced by the retention of subject pronoun "thu", in addition to the present participle "an", features that have disappeared in Standard Kashmiri. A wordlist and preliminary grammatical sketch of Kishtwari were compiled in The Languages of the Northern Himalayas. Kishtwari has historically been classified as a dialect of Kashmiri by scholars such as George Abraham Grierson, and is partially intelligible with Kashmiri. Linguists like Siddheshwar Varma consider Kishtwari an intermediate between Western Pahari languages and Kashmiri. If considered a divergent dialect of Kashmiri, Kishtwari is one of two Kashmiri varieties spoken outside of the Kashmir Valley (the other being Poguli, which is even more distinct and not intelligible with either Kashmiri or Kishtwari). Kishtwari is also tonal, like neighbouring languages such as Dogri and Punjabi. The 1911 Census of India recorded 7,464 speakers of Kishtwari; the 2011 census counts 40,000. Grierson remarks that an idiosyncratic variant of Takri is used to write the Kishtwari language, and that there does not appear to be standard spelling nor a consistent orthography. The article's script-section specimen is in Kashtwari, from Grierson's Linguistic Survey of India Vol. VIII, Pt. II, page 386. The witnesses are Grierson (Linguistic Survey of India Vol. 8, pp. 344–383, first published 1919), Sharma, Duni Chand (2008, Glimpses Of Kishtwar History, pp. 120–131), Sheikh, Aejaz Mohammed and Kuchey, Sameer Ahmad (2014, "Kishtwari", Indian Linguistics 75(3–4): 55–66), and Mahapatra, B. P. (1989, Constitutional languages, p. 270). The language is spoken in India; no Pakistan filing is made for it, unlike Bhadarwahi.

- **The system.** The diagnostic is the family, and it is six levels in five steps: ADOPTED: Indo-European → Indo-Iranian → Indo-Aryan → Eastern Dardic → Kashmiri → Kishtwari — the chain as the article's infobox gives it, the fourth level "Eastern Dardic" where the Pahari sisters carry "Northern" and the fifth level "Kashmiri" where they carry "Western Pahari". Glottolog 5.4 files the languoid differently, as a Dialect — not a Language — under the path indo1319/clas1257/indo1320/indo1321/midd1375/dard1244/kash1285/kash1277/kish1245 — parent kash1277, grandparent kash1285, not Kashmiri directly and not a language node — filed as read, not reconciled with the infobox chain (see the honest blank); the same kash1285 is the Kashmiri node, so Kishtwari sits under Kashmiri in Glottolog's tree while the infobox files it as Kashmiri's child in a six-level chain. The codes are ISO 639-3 none (the infobox reads "–") and Glottolog `kish1245`; the Endangered Languages Project carries no filing for it this pass. No endangerment grade is filed: no UNESCO grade in the article, no Glottolog AES status on the page as fetched (its references table is empty) — none is inferred from Kashmiri or from the Pahari sisters. No phonology inventory is filed: the article gives no vowel or consonant counts, and the tonal claim stands as the article's word, not as a measured inventory. The scripts are three: Takri the native script in an idiosyncratic variant with no standard spelling, Devanagari, and Perso-Arabic (Urdu/Nastaliq) — the article's infobox gives the name in Perso-Arabic and Devanagari only, and carries the Takri only as an image. The hinge is one name in three scripts, the same eight sounds three times over, 10 in Devanagari, 9 in Takri, 7 in Perso-Arabic: K+I+SH+T+V+AA+RR+II in Devanagari किश्तवाड़ी and Takri 𑚊𑚮𑚧𑚶𑚙𑚦𑚭𑚪𑚯 and Perso-Arabic کشتواڑی — the three spellings differing in no sound, only in what each script writes: Devanagari writes the virama and the nukta separately, two extra code points; Takri writes the virama but RRA is its own letter, one extra; Perso-Arabic writes no short I and no nukta, RREH its own letter, one letter fewer than the sounds — with the tension filed, not adjudicated: the Takri spelling is derived from the Devanagari by the Takri letter table, not read as text from the article, and the article's image is the only Takri witness (see the honest blank).

(3) No phonology is filed: the article gives no vowel or consonant inventory, so no phonology census exists for this entry — the first Pahari-family entry without one — and the tonal claim is the article's word, not a measured inventory. (4) No endangerment grade is filed: no UNESCO grade in the article and no Glottolog AES status on the page as fetched (its references table is empty); none is inferred from Kashmiri or from the Pahari sisters. (6) The classification tension is three-way and unsettled: Grierson's highly divergent Kashmiri variety, Varma's Western Pahari–Kashmiri intermediate, and the infobox's Eastern Dardic → Kashmiri → Kishtwari chain, with Glottolog filing it as a Dialect of Kashmiri — all four are filed, not adjudicated. (10) "Partially intelligible with Kashmiri" is the article's phrase with no percentage filed; Poguli's non-intelligibility with either Kashmiri or Kishtwari is the article's word; the "sister language of Kashmiri" line is the article's Origin section, not a verified historical-linguistics finding; the Dogri/Punjabi/Persian admixture is as the article prints it.

- **Decoder-design note (Kishtwari → Gauntlet).** Five rungs. (1) **The one-name-three-scripts probe.** Present the Devanagari, Takri and Perso-Arabic spellings; the specimen must give all three, count 10, 9 and 7, and say they are the same eight sounds with Devanagari two code points longer and Perso-Arabic one letter shorter than the sounds — a specimen that gives 10, 10 and 10 has the headline, not the count. (2) **The derived-Takri probe.** Present the Takri spelling with its source — an image, not text; the specimen must say the spelling is derived, not read — a specimen that cites it as article text has a verdict, not the record. (3) **The classification probe.** Present the four-way tension — Grierson's divergent variety, Varma's intermediate, the infobox chain, Glottolog's Dialect; the specimen must hold all four without adjudicating — a specimen that picks one has a verdict, not the record. (4) **The conservative-feature probe.** Present the retention of subject pronoun "thu" and present participle "an", lost in Standard Kashmiri; the specimen must name both features and say Standard Kashmiri lost them — a specimen that calls Kishtwari "just Kashmiri" has the family, not the feature. (5) **The no-code probe.** Present the missing ISO 639-3 code and the Glottolog dialect code kish1245; the specimen must say there is no ISO code and give kish1245 as a dialect code, not a language code — a specimen that invents an ISO code has a guess, not the record.
