- **The story.** Sirmauri (Devanagari: सिरमौरी) is a Western Pahari language spoken in the Sirmaur district in the northern Indian state of Himachal Pradesh and in the Kalesar area of Yamunanagar district of Haryana and in border areas of Uttarakhand. Its two main varieties are Dharthi (also called Giriwari) and Giripari. The infobox files the region as Mahasu, the ethnicity as the Sirmauri people, and the native speakers as 107,401 (2011 census). The language family is Indo-European → Indo-Iranian → Indo-Aryan → Northern → Western Pahari → Sirmauri; the dialects are Dharthi and Giripari; the writing system is the Sirmauri script. The native script of the language is called the Sirmauri script — the Sirmauri Takri Varnamala chart heads the article's script section — and the script is under proposal to be encoded in Unicode: "Proposal to encode Sirmauri in Unicode" (L2/25-038, 2024-10-25), replacing the preliminary L2/18-085 (Pandey, 2018), which relied solely on Grierson's charts and specimens. The proposal's background: Sirmauri is a Brahmi-based script written left to right; it was the official script of Sirmaur — also spelled "Sirmour" and "Sirmur" in English sources — a former princely state in pre-independence India, used as the official script in royal gazettes for recording land records, revenue records and accounts; the script of Jaunsar, identified by Grierson as "Jaunsari", is considered a variant of Sirmauri and should be unified in Unicode with "Sirmauri"; Grierson published specimens in the Linguistic Survey of India, Vol. IX, Part IV (1916), Specimens of the Pahari Languages and Gujuri — the Sirmauri form of Takri chart at p. 459 and specimen at p. 468, the Jaunsari form chart at p. 384 and specimen at p. 401; the Jaunsari letters also appear in a chart in Die Schrift (1969) by Hans Jensen, based on Grierson. Pabuchi was a script used by a class of astrologers. The grammar gives three postpositions across three genders — genitive /ra/ /ree/ /roo/, locative /da/ /dee/ /doo/, ablative /sa/ /see/ /soo/ (Language in India). The Sirmauri language is commonly called Pahari or Himachali. The language has no official status and is recorded as a dialect of Hindi. According to UNESCO, the language is in the critically endangered category — the youngest speakers of Sirmauri are generally grandparents or older and they too speak it infrequently or partially. Earlier the language enjoyed some state patronage, but this ended after independence due to the government favoring Hindi more. The demand for the inclusion of "Pahari (Himachali)" under the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution was made in 2010 by the state's Vidhan Sabha; no positive progress has been made since. Some small organisations are attempting to save the language (The Statesman). The witnesses are the Census of India 2011 Statement 1 (Office of the Registrar General & Census Commissioner, India); Grierson, Linguistic Survey of India, Volume 9.4, pp. 458–459 and pp. 383–84, 458–59 (1916); Language in India (postpositions); the Sirmauri Unicode proposal (L2/25-038); "Endangered Language" (15 April 2011); "Pahari Inclusion" (The Statesman); and the external links, Pradeep speaking Sirmauri and Kirnish speaking the Giripari dialect of Sirmauri.

- **The system.** The diagnostic is the family, and it is six levels in five steps: ADOPTED: Indo-European → Indo-Iranian → Indo-Aryan → Northern → Western Pahari → Sirmauri — the chain as the article's infobox gives it, the fourth level "Northern" where Kishtwari carries "Eastern Dardic" and the fifth level "Western Pahari" where Kishtwari carries "Kashmiri". Glottolog 5.4 files the languoid as a Spoken L1 Language — not a Dialect — under the path indo1319/clas1257/indo1320/indo1321/midd1375/dard1244/hima1250/nucl1728/sirm1239 — the nine nodes in eight steps: Indo-European, Classical Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Middle-Modern Indo-Aryan, Eastern Dardic, Himachali, Nuclear Himachali, Sirmauri — filed as read, not reconciled with the infobox chain (see the honest blank); Glottolog's fourth-from-top node is Eastern Dardic where the infobox carries Northern, and its Pahari node is Himachali → Nuclear Himachali where the infobox carries a single Western Pahari. The codes are ISO 639-3 srx (the infobox and Glottolog's hid agree) and Glottolog sirm1239; the Endangered Languages Project carries it as ELP 5415 (Sirmauri); Wikidata Q7530505; Glottolog places it at latitude 31.1, longitude 77.17. The children are two dialects, not languages: Dharthi [dhar1245] and Giripari [giri1243] — the newick reads ('Dharthi [dhar1245]':1,'Giripari [giri1243]':1)'Sirmauri [sirm1239][srx]-l-':1. The meds are two: Hendriksen 1986, a grammar, and Grierson 1916, phonology_or_text; the subclassification comments cite Hans Hendriksen 1987 and Hans Hendriksen 1976, 1979, 1986. The endangerment filing is three-way and unresolved: UNESCO critically endangered (the article, citing "Endangered Language", 15 April 2011); Glottolog AES status: not endangered (source: the Lyle Campbell team — Campbell, Lyle and Lee, Nala Huiying and Okura, Eve and Simpson, Sean and Ueki, Kaori 2022); and Glottolog's own comment: Sirmauri (5415-srx) = At risk (20 percent certain, based on the evidence available) [Lewis 2009] — all three filed, none adjudicated (see the honest blank). The scripts are three: the Sirmauri script, the native script, unencoded and under proposal (L2/25-038); Devanagari, which writes the name सिरमौरी; and Takri, in its Sirmauri form — Grierson's chart (1916b: 459) is captioned "Chart of the Sirmauri form of Takri". The hinge is one name in three spellings, the same seven sounds three times over, 8 in Roman, 7 in Devanagari, 7 in the Sirmauri script: S+I+R+M+AU+R+I in Roman "Sirmauri" and Devanagari सिरमौरी and the Sirmauri script 𑡺𑡾𑡵𑡳𑢄𑡵𑡾 — the three spellings differing in no sound, only in what each spelling writes: Roman writes the AU diphthong as two letters, one extra; Devanagari writes it as the single vowel sign ौ; the Sirmauri script writes seven glyphs where Roman writes eight letters — which glyph carries the AU diphthong is not filed, and no letter-by-letter mapping of the Sirmauri-script glyphs is claimed (see the honest blank).

- **The story.** Mahasu Pahari (Takri: 𑚢𑚩𑚭𑚨𑚱 𑚞𑚩𑚭𑚪𑚯; Devanagari: महासुई) is a Western Pahari language spoken in Himachal Pradesh. It is also known as Mahasui or Mahasuvi. The speaking population is about 1,000,000 (2001, per the article's lead; 2002 per the infobox, citing Ethnologue 18th ed., 2015). Omniglot's page, titled "Mahasu Pahari language", dates the 1,000,000 figure to 2002. Global Recordings Network files it as "Pahari, Mahasu" (ISO bfz, GRN 3105). It is more commonly spoken in Himachal Pradesh's Shimla and Solan districts, in western parts of Uttarkashi district in Uttarakhand and in Kalka and Pinjore of Panchkula district in Haryana. Shimla and Solan were parts of the old Mahasu district. Himachal Pradesh State on 1 September 1972 reorganised the districts dissolving Mahasu district; the Solan district was carved out of Solan and Arki tehsils of the then Mahasu district and tehsils of Kandaghat and Nalagarh of the then Shimla District of Punjab. The Shimla Hill States had been integrated in 1948 into one administrative unit called Mahasu district, and the Keonthali dialect and its subdialects conjointly came to be termed Mahasui. The infobox files the region as Mahasu, the ethnicity as the Mahasui people, and the native speakers as 1 million (2002). The language family is Indo-European → Indo-Iranian → Indo-Aryan → Northern → Western Pahari (Himachali) → Mahasu Pahari; the writing system is Tankri script, Devanagari. According to different locations, the language has developed several dialects. Lower Mahasu Pahari (Baghati, Baghliani, Keonthali), Upper Mahasu Pahari (Rampuri, Rohruri, Shimla Siraji, Sodochi). The Kiunthali variety appears to be understood by others, and their attitude toward it is favorable. Rampuri is also called Kochi; Rohruri is also called Soracholi; and Sodochi is also known as Kumharsaini or Kotgarhi after the Kumarsain and Kotgarh areas of Shimla District respectively. Intelligibility among dialects is above 85%. Lexical similarity is 74%–82% with upper dialects, and 74%–95% with lower dialects. The language is used in home and for religious purposes. It is understood and spoken from people of vital age group. It is considered to be highly endangered as the number of people speaking it is constantly going down. It is closely related to Sirmauri, Jaunsari, Bangani and Kullui. The detailed dialect list gives nine Upper varieties — Bishashau (Chaupal), Barari (Kotkhai), Kochi Rampuri (Rampur Bushahr), Kochi Rohruri (Rohru), Kuari (Dodra Kwar), Shimla Saraji (Theog and Narkanda), Shodochi (Jubbal), Shoracholi (Kumarsain), Tharochi (Kuppar and nearby areas of Jubbal and Kotkhai) — and three Lower — Baghati (eastern Solan district and Kalka, Pinjore, etc. areas of Panchkula district in Haryana), Baghliani (western Solan district: Arki, Darlaghat, Ramshahar and Nalagarh tehsils), Keonthali (south-western Shimla district: Shimla city, Junga and other nearby areas, named after the former Keonthal state) — with Hinduri (eastern Nalagarh) also included in the Keonthali group. The native script of the language is a variety of Takri Script — Omniglot names the variety Kōchi. There are some written records of the language in Takri script and Nastaliq script but nowadays Devanagari script is usually used. The infobox caption reads "Mahasui written in Tankri script and Bushahri script". The language is commonly called Pahari or Himachali. The language has no official status and is recorded as a dialect of Hindi. According to UNESCO, the language is of definitely endangered category, i.e. many Mahasui children are not learning Mahasui as their mother tongue any longer. Earlier, the language had state patronage. Everything changed since independence, due to favoritism towards Hindi by the Indian Government. The demand for the inclusion of "Pahari (Himachali)" under the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution, which is supposed to represent multiple Pahari languages of Himachal Pradesh, had been made in the year 2010 by the state's Vidhan Sabha. There has been no positive progress on this matter since then even when small organisations strive to save the language and demand it. Due to political interest, the language is currently recorded as a dialect of Hindi, even when having a poor mutual intelligibility with it. The witnesses are Grierson, Linguistic Survey of India, Volume 9.4, pp. 613–14 and pp. 383–84 (1916); Mahasu Pahari at Ethnologue (18th ed., 2015); Mallikarjun, B. (2002), "Mother tongues of India according to the 1961 census", Language in India; T. Grahame Bailey 1908, Bailey 1915, and Bailey 1920; Hans Hendriksen (1976); Verma (1978), Pahari Language: A Linguistic Analysis; Jouanne, Thomas (2014), A preliminary analysis of the phonological system of the Western Pahārī language of Kvār, University of Oslo; "Endangered Language (Mahasui)"; "Vanishing voices of the mountains: The struggle to preserve Pahari languages", The Indian Express (2025-05-08); "Pahari Inclusion", Zee News and The Statesman; and the external links, a Mahasuvi Pahari sample in the Rohruri dialect and interviews in Rohruri and Shodochi.

- **The system.** The diagnostic is the family, and it is six levels in five steps: ADOPTED: Indo-European → Indo-Iranian → Indo-Aryan → Northern → Western Pahari → Mahasu Pahari — the chain as the article's infobox gives it, the fourth level "Northern" where Kishtwari carries "Eastern Dardic" and the fifth level "Western Pahari" where Kishtwari carries "Kashmiri". The codes are ISO 639-3 bfz (the infobox and Glottolog's hid agree) and Glottolog maha1287; the Endangered Languages Project carries it as ELP 5660 (Mahasu Pahari); Wikidata Q6733460; Glottolog places it at latitude 31.0088, longitude 77.5317. - **The story.** Jaunsari (Devanagari: जौनसारी) is a Western Pahari language of northern India spoken by the Jaunsari people in the Kalsi, Chakrata and Tyuni sub-districts of Dehradun district, in the Garhwal region of Uttarakhand state. It is closely related to Sirmauri and Mahasu Pahari — the two sisters this catalogue filed as #238 and #239 — and it is the third tongue of the same hill corridor, the one that stayed on the Uttarakhand side of the line while its sisters were filed under Himachal. The census counts 136,779 native speakers (2011). The Jaunsari are a Scheduled Tribe in Uttarakhand, and the people number about 92,000, about 130,000 counting those of ancestral descent (search-result read only — see the honest blank). The dialects of Jaunsari share about 60% of their basic vocabulary with each of the neighbouring varieties of Bangani, Jaunpuri, Nagpuriya and Sirmauri — Matthews 2008, a 210-item wordlist, the average figures running 58% to 61% with significant variation between the Jaunsari dialects themselves. The home is Jaunsar-Bawar, a hilly region in the Garhwal division: Jaunsar the lower half, Bawar the snow-clad upper region up to the Kharamba peak (3,084 m), 1,002 km² and 398 villages; incorporated in Chakrata tehsil in 1829, before that part of the Punjab state of Sirmur until the British defeated it with Dehradun after the 1814 war with the Gurkhas, a British Indian Army cantonment from 1866. The script hinge: Jaunsari was historically written in Jaunsari Script, also known as Dhankri Script, and the Devanagari script is being used these days in certain works — the same two-script shape as its sisters, but with its own twist: an older crawl of the same article names the historical script "Sirmauri script", not Dhankri, so the historical name itself is a two-way tension, filed not adjudicated. The status hinge: the language has no official status; UNESCO files it as definitely endangered — many Jaunsari children are not learning Jaunsari as their mother tongue any longer — while the Ethnologue reports otherwise, and Glottolog files AES threatened with a comment of Vulnerable (80 percent certain) — three verdicts that do not agree, and this catalogue holds all three rather than picking one. The one piece of state action on the record: in 2016 the State Council of Educational Research and Training (SCERT) announced that Garhwali, Kumaoni, Jaunsari and Rang would be introduced on a pilot basis for students in standards one to ten in government schools under the 'Know Your Uttarakhand' project.
- **The system.** Six-level family chain, Indo-European → Classical Indo-European → Indo-Iranian → Indo-Aryan → Middle-Modern Indo-Aryan → Eastern Dardic → Himachali → Jaunsari; Glottolog 5.4 files it as a Spoken L1 Language under the path indo1319/clas1257/indo1320/indo1321/midd1375/dard1244/hima1250/jaun1243 — the parent path identical to Sirmauri's and Mahasui's through hima1250, diverging only at the leaf jaun1243. ISO 639-3 jns, Glottolog jaun1243, ELP Jaunsari, Wikidata Q6164857, latitude 30.5587, longitude 77.9084. Child dialect count 0 in Glottolog — no child varieties filed, against the article's unnamed dialects that vary enough to move the similarity figures. Meds: Satish, Umadatt Sharma 1972 grammar_sketch (358 pp); George A. Grierson 1916 phonology_or_text (8 pp — the Linguistic Survey of India, Volume 9.4, pp. 383–84, the same survey that anchors the sisters). Subclassification comments cite Hendriksen 1987 and Hendriksen 1976, 1979, 1986 — the same citations as Sirmauri's and Mahasui's, the third tongue standing on the same three Hendriksen legs.

- **The story.** Gaddi (also called Gaddki, Gaddiyali or Bharmauri; Takri: 𑚌𑚛𑚯, 𑚌𑚛𑚊𑚯, 𑚌𑚛𑚮𑚣𑚭𑚥𑚯, 𑚡𑚤𑚢𑚵𑚪𑚯; Devanagari: गदी, गदकी, गदियाली, भरमौड़ी) is a Western Pahari language of northern India spoken by the Gaddi people primarily in the Bharmour region of Chamba district and the upper reaches of Kangra district in Himachal Pradesh, with Gaddi villages also in Udhampur, Kathua and Doda districts of Jammu. The census counts 181,000 native speakers (2011) — the exact mother-tongue figure is 181,069 in the LDC-IL parallel corpus (2026), against an older 110,000 (2007). The language has traditionally been written in Takri; Devanagari is the script of present use. The four dialects are unnamed, given by region: the first across Bharmaur, Chhatrari and Bhatyat tehsils of Chamba and the Gaddi-speaking regions of Kangra; the second across Piyuhar, Belaj, Guun, Bakani, the upper part of Mehla and Kaded; the third in Basu and adjoining areas; the fourth in Lilh and Paho. The language is commonly called Pahari or Himachali, and some speakers call it a dialect of Dogri. The status hinge: the language has no official status; UNESCO files it as definitely endangered — many Gaddi children are no longer learning Gaddi as their mother tongue — while Glottolog files AES not endangered (Campbell et al. 2022) with the comment "Gaddi (4193-gbk) = At risk (20 percent certain, based on the evidence available)" [van Driem 2007] — three verdicts that do not agree, and this catalogue holds all three rather than picking one. The one piece of state action on the record: the demand for the inclusion of 'Pahari (Himachali)' under the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution, made in 2010 by the state's Vidhan Sabha, with no positive progress since — the same demand filed in the Kangri, Chambeali, Bilaspuri and sister entries. The Gaddi people live by sheep-herding and cultivation (search-result read only — see the honest blank). New scholarship on the record: Kumari et al., *A Grammar of Gaddi*, UCL Press, 2026; and the LDC-IL Bharmauri/Gaddi Parallel Text Corpus, 2026 — 5,332 sentences, 159 grammatical categories, 32,351 words, 150,257 characters.
- **The system.** Six-level family chain, Indo-European → Indo-Iranian → Indo-Aryan → Northern → Western Pahari → Gaddi — the chain as the article's infobox gives it, the fourth level plain "Northern" as in the Chambeali, Mandeali, Bhateali and Kullui entries. Glottolog 5.4 files it as a Spoken L1 Language under the path indo1319/clas1257/indo1320/indo1321/midd1375/dard1244/hima1250/kang1292/cham1331/gadd1242 — parent cham1331 (Chamealic), the same nesting as Bilaspuri's, filed as read, not reconciled with the infobox chain (see the honest blank) — and the Glottolog path runs through Eastern Dardic (dard1244) while the infobox chain has no Dardic level at all. ISO 639-3 gbk, Glottolog gadd1242, ELP Gaddi, Wikidata Q17455500, latitude 32.36, longitude 76.5713. Child dialect count 2 in Glottolog — Bharmauri (bhar1240) and Macleod Ganj (macl1238) — against the article's four unnamed regional dialects; the Macleod Ganj child is the Dharamshala exile-community variety the article's four do not name. Meds: Hilal Ahmad Dar 2022 grammar_sketch (142 pp); T. Grahame Bailey 1908 grammar_sketch (8 pp). Subclassification comment cites George A. Grierson 1916 — the same survey that anchors the sisters. Alternative names (Glottolog/ELCat): Bharmauri Bhadi, Gaddi, Gaddyali, Gadi, Gadiali, Pahari Bharmauri, Panchi Brahmauri Rajput; Bharmauri. The infobox region field reads "Trigarta" (filed as printed — see the honest blank), the same field Bilaspuri's infobox carries. The phonology is fourteen vowels — six short (ɪ, ʏ, ɨ, ɯ, ʊ, ə) and eight long (iː, yː, uː, eː, oː, æː, ɔː, aː) — and thirty-two consonants — four nasals (m, n, ɳ, ŋ), ten plain stops and affricates (p, b, t, d, ʈ, ɖ, tɕ, dʑ, k, ɡ), ten aspirated (pʰ, bʱ, tʰ, dʱ, ʈʰ, ɖʱ, tɕʰ, dʑʱ, kʰ, ɡʱ), two fricatives (s, h), four approximants (w, l, ɭ, j), two trills (r, ɽ) — the inventory is Bilaspuri's twin, the same 14/32 counts cell for cell.

- **Decoder-design note (Gaddi → Gauntlet).** Five rungs. (1) **The 14/32 census.** Present the article's vowel and consonant tables; the specimen must reproduce 14 vowels (6 short, 8 long) and 32 consonants with the manner breakdown 4/10/10/2/4/2, and must note the inventory is Bilaspuri's twin — a specimen that reports Jaunsari's 34/13 has read the wrong sister. (2) **The four-vs-two dialect tension.** Present the article's four unnamed regional dialects and Glottolog's two child dialects; the specimen must name Bharmauri and Macleod Ganj as Glottolog's children and say the Macleod Ganj variety is the Dharamshala exile-community variety the article's four do not name — a specimen that merges the two lists has lost the tension. (3) **The script hinge.** Present the four names in Takri and Devanagari; the specimen must give the code-point counts 3/4/7/6 against 3/4/7/7, name the nukta as the one-code-point difference on Bharmauri, and say the Roman "dd" is a single DA in both scripts — a specimen that counts Bharmauri the same in both scripts has not counted. (4) **The three-verdict reconciliation.** Present the three endangerment verdicts and ask which is right; the correct answer is that the catalogue holds all three — a specimen that picks UNESCO and discards the Glottolog AES has mistaken a verdict for a fact. (5) **The family-chain walk.** Present the infobox chain (six levels, "Northern" fourth) and the Glottolog path (nine levels through Eastern Dardic and Chamealic); the specimen must answer that the infobox chain has no Dardic level while Glottolog runs through dard1244, and that Gaddi diverges from Bilaspuri only at the leaf (gadd1242 against bila1253, both under cham1331) — a specimen that puts the divergence higher has not walked the chain.

- **The story.** Baghati (Devanagari बघाटी; Takri 𑚊𑚂𑚍𑚝𑚦; pronounced /bə.ɡʱaː.ʈiː/) is a dialect of Lower Mahasu Pahari belonging to the Western Pahari group of languages (as per Grierson) — the first dialect-level heading in this catalogue; every prior Western Pahari heading was filed as a language. It got its name from the former princely Baghat State. It is spoken mainly in eastern Solan district of Himachal Pradesh — district headquarters Solan, Kandaghat, Waknaghat, eastern parts of Kunihar, Chail, Dharampur, Kuthar, Subathu, Kasauli, Parwanoo — and in Kalka and Pinjore in Panchkula district of Haryana. In Kalka, eastern Baddi, Barotiwala and Pinjore its sub-dialect Pinjore Baghati, also known as Patiala Baghati (got its name from the hilly parts of the former princely Patiala State), is spoken. The neighbour chain runs east to west: Sirmauri immediately east (Baghati is Sirmauri's immediate western neighbour); in Kunihar and Arki the speech is known as Baghliani, after Baghal state; west of that is the Nalagarh area, and the speech of its people is called the Hinduri dialect, after Hindur state. No speaker figure exists anywhere on the record — the article gives none, and no census figure is filed. The earliest dated record on file is the Revd. T. Grahame Bailey's "Dialects of the Simla Hills" (read January 30, 1905): Baghati-speaking people seem to avoid using the letter h nearly as much as Italians — "afnd" for Hindi "hatna" (return), "aul" for "hal" (plough) — and in Baghati the h is separated from the g by a vowel, as in "gbhra" (horse); Keonthali (Bailey's "Kitthali") has most of the grammatical features of Baghati. The newest dated scholarship on the record is the March 2024 Journal of Language Survey Reports finding, from the SIL Sociolinguistic Survey of Haryanvi: Baghati is one of the closest dialects related to Haryanvi — lexical similarity 66% with Rohtak Haryanvi, 67% with Jind, 72% with Naraingarh, 66% with Loharu, 69% with Taoru, 69% with Fatehabad, 64% with Braj Bhasha (Palwal), 67% with Hindi, 65% with Punjabi.

Glottolog 5.4 files it as a Dialect (not a Language) under the path indo1319/clas1257/indo1320/indo1321/midd1375/dard1244/hima1250/nucl1728/maha1287/lowe1245/bagh1249 — eleven levels, parent lowe1245 (Lower Mahasu Pahari), child dialect count 0, child language count 0 — and the Glottolog path runs through Eastern Dardic (dard1244) and Nuclear Himachali (nucl1728) while the infobox chain carries neither, and carries no "Western Pahari" level at all. ISO 639-3: none (–). Glottolog bagh1249, ELP Baghati (1584), Wikidata Q30557234. The Mahasui entry's filing stands: Lower Mahasu Pahari [lowe1245] holds three dialects — Baghati [bagh1249], Baghliani [bagh1250] and Kiunthali [kiun1241] — spelled Keonthali in the Baghati article; the two spellings are filed, not reconciled. - **The story.** Hinduri (or Handuri; Devanagari हिंडूरी, hiṁḍūrī, and हंडूरी, haṁḍūrī) is a Western Pahari language of northern India. It is spoken in southern Solan district, in southern parts of Ramshehar Tehsil, and in eastern Nalagarh. It was classified as a dialect under the Mahasui Keonthali Group (as per Grierson). It got its name from the former princely Hindur state — Nalagarh. Verma's "Pahari Language: A Linguistic Analysis" (1978) spells it Handuri and says the word means literally the language of the state of Hindur or Nalagarh, lying immediately to the south-west of the rest of the Simla Hill States — but it is not the language of the whole of the state, and it is also spoken in other states adjoining: in Nalagarh itself two languages are spoken, Powadhi Panjabi of the plains to the west and Handuri to the east, which is also spoken in the state of Mailog, lying to the east of Nalagarh; to the north-east of Nalagarh and to the north of Mailog lie the states of Baghal and Kunhiar, where the language is Baghali. The 2001 census counts 47,800 native speakers, with the census results conflating some speakers with Hindi — the only speaker figure anywhere on the record. The language is commonly called Pahari or Himachali; some speakers may even call it a dialect of Punjabi or Dogri. It has no official status. According to UNESCO it is of critically endangered category — the youngest speakers of Handuri are generally grandparents or older, and they too speak it infrequently or partially. The demand for the inclusion of "Pahari (Himachali)" under the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution, supposed to represent multiple Pahari languages of Himachal Pradesh, was made in 2010 by the state's Vidhan Sabha, with no positive progress since. The language is currently recorded as a dialect of Hindi, even when having a poor mutual intelligibility with it.

Glottolog 5.4 files it as a Language (not a Dialect) under the path indo1319/clas1257/indo1320/indo1321/midd1375/dard1244/hima1250/nucl1728/hind1267 — nine levels including Hinduri itself, parent nucl1728 (Nuclear Himachali) directly, child dialect count 0, child language count 0 — and the Glottolog path runs through Eastern Dardic (dard1244) and Nuclear Himachali (nucl1728) while the infobox chain carries neither, and carries no "Western Pahari" level at all; unlike Baghati, no maha1287 or lowe1245 level intervenes between Nuclear Himachali and the entry. **The correction this entry carries.** The article's infobox files Glottolog `maha1287` beside Baghliani — but maha1287 is the PARENT, Mahasu Pahari (level Language, ISO bfz), not Baghliani's own code. Baghliani's own Glottolog code is bagh1250, level Dialect under Lower Mahasu Pahari — and it was already on file, unnamed, in the Mahasui entry's newick, which quotes Lower Mahasu holding Baghati [bagh1249], Baghliani [bagh1250] and Kiunthali [kiun1241]. The code was filed; this entry names it as Baghliani's own. And unlike Hinduri, the authorities agree here: the article calls Baghliani "a dialect of Lower Mahasu Pahari" and Glottolog files it at level Dialect — the clean case, no language-vs-dialect split to hold. - **The story.** Baghliani (Devanagari बघल्याणी, Takri 𑚊𑚂𑚍𑚥𑚣𑚞𑚦, pronounced [bə.ɡəl.jaː.ɳiː]) is a dialect of Lower Mahasu Pahari belonging to the Western Pahari group of languages. It is spoken in the western Solan district of Himachal Pradesh, the area which was part of the former princely state of Baghal — the dialect takes its name from the state. It is also spoken in bordering villages of Bilaspur district, where it grades into a mix of Baghliani and Bilaspuri before core Bilaspuri takes over. The notable areas are Arki Tehsil (capital of the former Baghal state), Darlaghat, Ramshehar, Badi Dhar, western parts of Kunihar, and northern parts of Nalagarh, where it makes a gradual transition with Hinduri — in proper Nalagarh, Hinduri replaces Baghliani. Sharma (2024) spells it Baghlani and places it precisely: in Kunihar and Arki the dialect is known as Baghlani, perhaps after Baghal state, and to the west of it is the Nalagarh area, whose speech is called Hinduri after Hindur state. Verma (1978) spells it Baghali and puts it in Baghal and Kunhiar, north-east of Nalagarh and north of Mailog. The article's own specimen states the kinship in the tongue's own words: "Himācalō ré Arkī-Dārlāghāṭ tehsilō dé Bāghlī-Baghlyāṇī glāoēṅ. É buili Māhāsui dé paṛoīṅ hor Baghāṭī hor Hindurī sāthī miloīṅ." — "Baghli–Baghliani is spoken in the Arki and Darlaghat tehsils of Himachal. It belongs to the Mahasui group and is similar to Baghati and Hinduri." The specimen itself names its two neighbours. No speaker figure exists anywhere on the record; no official status is stated; no endangerment grade of its own is given.
- **The system.** The infobox family chain is seven levels in six steps: Indo-European → Indo-Iranian → Indo-Aryan → North-Western or Northern → Western Pahari → Mahasu Pahari → Baghliani. Glottolog 5.4 files it as a Dialect, not a Language: bagh1250, level Dialect, category Dialect, hid null (no ISO 639-3 code), child family count 0, child language count 0, child dialect count 0, latitude null, longitude null, links [] — and the Glottolog path runs indo1319/clas1257/indo1320/indo1321/midd1375/dard1244/hima1250/nucl1728/maha1287/lowe1245/bagh1250, eleven levels including Baghliani itself, parent lowe1245 (Lower Mahasu Pahari), siblings Baghati [bagh1249] and Kiunthali [kiun1241] under the same parent. The infobox's Glottolog code maha1287 is the parent: Mahasu Pahari, level Language, ISO bfz, coordinates 31.0088°N, 77.5317°E, AES status "not endangered" with the comment "Mahasu Pahari (5660-bfz) = At risk (20 percent certain, based on the evidence available) [van Driem 2007]" (Campbell et al. 2022) — two filings on the parent, neither of them Baghliani's own. Parent meds: three — "45662", grammar, 1976, Hans Hendriksen 1976, 1979, 1986; "44562", grammar_sketch, 1920, Bailey, Thomas Grahame 1920; "127531", grammar_sketch, 1908, T. Grahame Bailey 1908. (44/42, 26/22). **The correction this entry carries.** Three authorities, three positions on whether Sanskrit has speakers — and the catalogue files all three without settling them. The article's infobox Revival row says "There are no known native speakers of Sanskrit", and its lead says there are no first-language speakers of Sanskrit in India — while the same article's census footnote records 24,821 Indians reporting Sanskrit as their mother tongue in 2011, and Glottolog files sans1269 under the category "Spoken L1 Language". The article itself glosses the census figures as a wish to be aligned with the prestige of the language, and its quoted sources doubt the Sanskrit villages outright — McCartney finds it very difficult to believe Jhiri is a village where everyone speaks fluent Sanskrit at mother-tongue level, and Devy says "Sanskrit has influence without presence". The catalogue's position: the census series is a prestige signal, not a speaker count; the Glottolog category is a filing, not a field observation; the article's "no native speakers" is the position the catalogue carries as the working fact. Second correction: Glottolog files Classical Sanskrit (clas1258) and Vedic Sanskrit (vedi1234) as the two child DIALECTS of the Sanskrit languoid, while the article treats them as historical varieties — Vedic the most archaic, Classical the refined and standardised form codified by Pāṇini. The catalogue keeps Glottolog's filing and the article's staging side by side; it does not promote the children to languages. Third: the Glottolog coordinates (20.0, 77.0) are round numbers — a centroid, not a surveyed point — and the article's infobox gives no coordinates at all. The next zero stands named for a later loop: "Classical Sanskrit" is 0 headings, 0 occurrences in each catalogue and each log — to be re-measured, not assumed. "Vedic Sanskrit" stands at 1 in each catalogue (the Devanagari span) and 1 in each log (the Yajnadevam Indus claim, 2026-10-12).
- **The story.** Sanskrit (Devanagari संस्कृत, stem Saṃskṛta, nominal singular संस्कृतम्, Saṃskṛtam) is a classical language of the Indo-Aryan branch of Indo-European. Its name is a compound: sám ('together, good, well, perfected') + kṛta- ('made, formed, work') — sáṃskṛta-, "well prepared, pure and perfect, polished, sacred". The most archaic variety is Vedic Sanskrit, found in the Rigveda — 1,028 hymns composed between 1500 and 1200 BCE — orally transmitted by methods of memorisation of exceptional complexity, rigour and fidelity, as a single text without variant readings. Classical Sanskrit is the refined and standardised form that emerged in the mid-1st millennium BCE and was codified in the most comprehensive of ancient grammars, the Aṣṭādhyāyī ('Eight chapters') of Pāṇini. The two great epics, the Mahābhārata and the Rāmāyaṇa, were composed in Epic Sanskrit, used in northern India between 400 BCE and 300 CE. Kālidāsa, the greatest dramatist in Sanskrit, wrote in Classical Sanskrit. The language was a link language in ancient and medieval South Asia, became a language of religion and high culture across Southeast Asia, East Asia and Central Asia, and remains a ceremonial and ritual language in Hindu and Buddhist hymns and chants. It has no attested native script: originally orally transmitted, not attested in writing until the 1st century BCE in Brahmi, and written since in many scripts — today most commonly Devanagari. The oldest surviving Sanskrit inscription in the Kathmandu valley is dated 464 CE; the early-1st-century BCE Hathibada Brahmi inscription is one of the oldest Hindu Sanskrit inscriptions. The oldest Sanskrit college, Benares Sanskrit College, was founded in 1791. Sanskrit is one of 22 Eighth Schedule languages; it is a state-additional official language in Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand (Uttarakhand's second official language since 2010) and a recognised minority language — a "Protected Language" — in South Africa. The revival villages are doubted on the record: even in Mattur, often called India's Sanskrit village, hardly a handful indicated Sanskrit as their mother tongue.
- **The system.** The infobox family chain is four levels in three steps: Indo-European → Indo-Iranian → Indo-Aryan → Sanskrit; early form Vedic Sanskrit. Glottolog 5.4 files it as a Language: sans1269, level language, category "Spoken L1 Language", hid san, pk 6182, father_pk 4079, family_pk 143, bookkeeping false — and the Glottolog classification runs four levels (Indo-European indo1319, Classical Indo-European clas1257, Indo-Iranian indo1320, Indo-Aryan indo1321) with Sanskrit itself as the fifth; the Glottolog path runs indo1319/clas1257/indo1320/indo1321/sans1269. Its newick holds two children, both filed as dialects: 'Classical Sanskrit [clas1258][cls]' and 'Vedic Sanskrit [vedi1234][vsn]'. ISO codes: 639-1 sa, 639-2 san, 639-3 san — inclusive code, with individual codes cls (Classical Sanskrit) and vsn (Vedic Sanskrit). The Glottolog record carries latitude 20.0, longitude 77.0; macroareas {}; child_family_count 0, child_language_count 0, child_dialect_count 2; links: Wikipedia Sanskrit, phoible.org/languages/sans1269, Wikidata Q11059 — no ELP link. Its meds are six: four long_grammar (Thomas Oberlies 2003, 688 pages; Whitney 1997, 576 pages; William Dwight Whitney 1994 [1924], 576 pages; Whitney 1879, 514 pages), one grammar (Bopp 1854, no page count), one grammar_sketch (Toon Van Hal and Christophe Viell 2013 [1732], 291 pages). Era: c. 1500–600 BCE (Vedic Sanskrit); 700 BCE – 1350 CE (Classical Sanskrit). Region: South Asia (ancient and medieval), parts of Southeast Asia (medieval). Writing system: Devanagari (present day); originally orally transmitted; Brahmi from the 1st century BCE; later various Brahmic scripts. The article's writing-system section counts the ancient lists, not a single inventory: the Buddhist Lalitavistara Sūtra lists sixty-four lipi the Buddha knew as a child, Brahmi topping the list; the Jain Pannavana Sutta lists eighteen writing systems, Brahmi topping the list and Kharoshthi fourth; the Jain text elsewhere says Brahmi is written in 18 different forms, details lacking; Salomon questions the historical value of the Buddhist list and the reliability of the Jain lists, and no Sanskrit or Prakrit inscription dated before the 3rd century BCE has been found. The Nagari script used for Classical Sanskrit holds fourteen vowels and thirty-three consonants; Vedic Sanskrit adds two allophonic consonantal characters (the intervocalic ḷa and ḷha). The Aṣṭādhyāyī's apparatus includes the Śivasūtras and the Dhatupatha, a list of 2,000 verbal roots. The Mitanni treaty — generally dated to the 16th century BCE, date and significance debated — carries Vedic Sanskrit names and technical terms beyond ancient India, the language recognised outside India before any written record of it survives at home.

- **Decoder-design note (Sanskrit → Gauntlet).** Five rungs. (1) **The native-speaker probe.** Present the infobox "no known native speakers", the 2011 census figure 24,821, and the Glottolog category "Spoken L1 Language"; the specimen must hold all three without collapsing them — a specimen that reports 24,821 native speakers has mistaken a prestige claim for a speaker count, and one that reports zero has erased the census. (2) **The child-dialect probe.** Present the Glottolog newick (Classical clas1258, Vedic vedi1234 as child dialects) against the article's staging (Vedic the most archaic variety, Classical the codified form); the specimen must say Glottolog files them as dialects while the article stages them as historical varieties — a specimen that calls them separate languages has mistaken the filing for a split. (3) **The coordinate probe.** Present Glottolog (20.0, 77.0) and the infobox's absence of coordinates; the specimen must say the pair is a round-number centroid, not a surveyed point — a specimen that treats (20.0, 77.0) as a field location has mistaken a centroid for a place. (4) **The code probe.** Present ISO 639-3 san (inclusive) with cls and vsn as individual codes; the specimen must name all three and say san is the inclusive code — a specimen that gives only san has dropped the two individual codes. (5) **The script probe.** Present "Devanagari (present day)" with Brahmi from the 1st century BCE and "written in many scripts"; the specimen must say Sanskrit has no attested native script and was orally transmitted first — a specimen that names Devanagari as Sanskrit's script has mistaken the present-day habit for the language's own script.

- **The story.** Classical Sanskrit is the refined and standardised grammatical form of Sanskrit that emerged in the mid-1st millennium BCE and was codified in the most comprehensive of ancient grammars, the Aṣṭādhyāyī ('Eight-Chapter Grammar') of Pāṇini — the foundation of Vyākaraṇa, a Vedāṅga. Pāṇini's comprehensive and scientific theory of grammar is conventionally taken to mark the start of Classical Sanskrit; his systematic treatise made Sanskrit the preeminent Indian language of learning and literature for two millennia. It is unclear whether Pāṇini himself wrote his treatise or orally created it and transmitted it through his students; modern scholarship generally accepts that he knew of a form of writing, based on references to words such as lipi ('script') and lipikara ('scribe') in section 3.2 of the Aṣṭādhyāyī. The Aṣṭādhyāyī was not the first description of Sanskrit grammar, but it is the earliest that has survived in full, and the culmination of a long grammatical tradition that Fortson calls "one of the intellectual wonders of the ancient world". Pāṇini cites ten scholars on the phonological and grammatical aspects of the Sanskrit language before him, as well as the variants in usage in different regions of India: Āpiśali, Kaśyapa, Gārgya, Gālava, Cakravarmaṇa, Bhāradvāja, Śākaṭāyana, Śākalya, Senaka and Sphoṭāyana. The formalisation of the language is credited to Pāṇini, along with Patañjali's Mahābhāṣya and Kātyāyana's commentary, which preceded Patañjali's work. The Classical Sanskrit language formalised by Pāṇini, states Renou, is "not an impoverished language", rather it is "a controlled and a restrained language from which archaisms and unnecessary formal alternatives were excluded": the Classical form simplified the sandhi rules but retained various aspects of the Vedic language, while adding rigor and flexibilities, and Pāṇini included numerous "optional rules" beyond the Vedic Sanskrit's bahulam framework, to respect liberty and creativity so that individual writers separated by geography or time would have the choice to express facts and their views in their own way. The phonetic differences between Vedic Sanskrit and Classical Sanskrit, as discerned from the current state of the surviving literature, are negligible when compared to the intense change that must have occurred in the pre-Vedic period between the Proto-Indo-Aryan language and Vedic Sanskrit; the noticeable differences in Vedic include more grammatical categories as well as the differences in accent, semantics, syntax, declension, and internal and external sandhi rules. According to Richard Gombrich, the archaic Vedic Sanskrit found in the Rigveda had already evolved in the Vedic period, as evidenced in the later Vedic literature: the language in the early Upanishads of Hinduism and the late Vedic literature approaches Classical Sanskrit, while the archaic Vedic Sanskrit had by the Buddha's time become unintelligible to all except ancient Indian sages. Kālidāsa, the greatest dramatist in Sanskrit, wrote in Classical Sanskrit, and the foundations of modern arithmetic were first described in Classical Sanskrit. The era is 700 BCE – 1350 CE. Classical Sanskrit is the standard register as laid out in the grammar of Pāṇini, around the fourth century BCE, and its position in the cultures of Greater India is akin to that of Latin and Ancient Greek in Europe. A section of European scholars state that Sanskrit was never a spoken language — but the textual evidence in the works of Yāska, Pāṇini, and Patañjali affirms that Classical Sanskrit in their era was a spoken language (bhāṣā) used by the cultured and educated, with some sūtras expounding upon the variant forms of spoken Sanskrit versus written Sanskrit; the Chinese Buddhist pilgrim Xuanzang mentioned in his memoir that official philosophical debates in India were held in Sanskrit, not in the vernacular language of that region; and according to Madhav Deshpande, Sanskrit was a spoken language in a colloquial form by the mid-1st millennium BCE which coexisted with a more formal, grammatically correct form of literary Sanskrit — with the cities of Varanasi, Paithan, Pune and Kanchipuram as centres of Sanskrit learning and debate until the arrival of the colonial era. Nāgārjuna (c. 200 CE), one of the early and influential Buddhist philosophers, used Classical Sanskrit as the language for his texts. Pollock's "Sanskrit Cosmopolis" — the region over which Sanskrit's influence grew, all of South Asia and much of southeast Asia — thrived between 300 and 1300 CE. A 17th-century birch bark manuscript of Pāṇini's grammar treatise from Kashmir survives as the section's image.

- **The story.** Vedic Sanskrit, also simply the Vedic language, is the earliest attested form of the Sanskrit and Prakrit languages, members of the Indo-Aryan subgroup of the Indo-European family. It is attested in the Vedas and related literature compiled over the period of the mid-2nd to mid-1st millennium BCE, and it was orally preserved, predating the local advent of writing by several centuries. The extensive ancient literature in Vedic Sanskrit that has survived into the modern era is a major source for reconstructing Proto-Indo-European and Proto-Indo-Iranian history. The separation of Proto-Indo-Iranian into Proto-Iranian and Proto-Indo-Aryan is estimated, on linguistic grounds, to have occurred around or before 1800 BCE. The date of composition of the oldest hymns of the Rigveda is vague at best, generally estimated to roughly 1500 BCE; both Asko Parpola (1988) and J. P. Mallory (1998) place the locus of the division of Indo-Aryan from Iranian in the Bronze Age culture of the Bactria–Margiana Archaeological Complex (BMAC), and Parpola (1999) has "Proto-Rigvedic" Indo-Aryans intrude the BMAC around 1700 BCE, assuming early Indo-Aryan presence in the Late Harappan horizon from about 1900 BCE and a "Proto-Rigvedic" (Proto-Dardic) intrusion to Punjab corresponding to the Gandhara grave culture from about 1700 BCE — on this model Rigvedic within the larger Indo-Aryan group is the direct ancestor of the Dardic languages. The early Vedic Sanskrit language was far less homogeneous than the language described by Pāṇini, that is, Classical Sanskrit; the language in the early Upanishads and the late Vedic literature approaches Classical Sanskrit, and the formalisation of the late form of Vedic Sanskrit into the Classical form is credited to Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī, along with Patañjali's Mahābhāṣya and Kātyāyana's commentary that preceded Patañjali's work. Five chronologically distinct strata can be identified within the Vedic language: Ṛg-vedic, Mantra, Saṃhitā prose, Brāhmaṇa prose, and Sūtras. The first three are commonly grouped together as the Saṃhitās, comprising the four Vedas — ṛg, atharvan, yajus, sāman — the oldest texts in Sanskrit and the canonical foundation both of the Vedic religion and of the later religion known as Hinduism. Many words in the Vedic Sanskrit of the Ṛg·veda have cognates or direct correspondences with the ancient Avestan language, but these do not appear in post-Rigvedic Indian texts; the text of the Ṛg·veda must have been essentially complete by around the 12th century BCE. The Mantra period includes the mantra and prose language of the Atharvaveda (Paippalāda and Śaunakīya), the Ṛg·veda Khilāni, the Sāmaveda Saṃhitā, and the mantras of the Yajurveda — texts largely derived from the Ṛg·veda but changed by linguistic change and reinterpretation, in which the more ancient injunctive verb system is no longer in use. In the Saṃhitā period the injunctive, subjunctive, optative and imperative (the aorist) disappear, and new innovations appear such as periphrastic aorist forms — before the time of Pāṇini, because Pāṇini lists those from the northwestern region who knew these older rules of Vedic Sanskrit. In Brāhmaṇa prose the archaic verb system has been abandoned and a prototype of pre-Pāṇini structure emerges; the Yajñagāthās provide a probable link between Vedic Sanskrit, Classical Sanskrit and the languages of the Epics, and complex metres such as Anuṣṭubh and the rules of Sanskrit prosody were being innovated. The Sūtra language, the last stratum, comprises the bulk of the Śrautasūtras and Gṛhyasūtras and some Upaniṣads such as the Kaṭha and Maitrāyaṇīya — texts that elucidate the state of the language which formed the basis of Pāṇini's codification into Classical Sanskrit. Vedic differs from Classical Sanskrit to an extent comparable to the difference between Homeric Greek and Classical Greek. In phonology: Vedic had a voiced retroflex lateral approximant [ɭ] as well as its breathy-voiced counterpart [ɭʱ], intervocalic allophones of ḍ and ḍh; the vowels e and o were realised in Vedic as diphthongs ai and au, but became monophthongs in later Sanskrit (daivá- > devá-, áika- > ekā-), though the diphthongal quality still resurfaces in sandhi; the vowels ai and au were realised in Vedic as long diphthongs āi and āu, but became correspondingly short in Classical Sanskrit (dyā́us > dyáus); the Prātiśākhyas claim the "dental" consonants were articulated from the teeth ridge (dantamūlīya, alveolar), but became dentals later, whereas most other authorities including Pāṇini designate them as dentals; the pluti (trimoraic) vowels were on the verge of becoming phonemicised during middle Vedic, but disappeared again; and Vedic often allowed two like vowels to come together in hiatus without merger during sandhi, reconstructed as the influence of an old laryngeal still present in the Proto-Indo-Iranian stage (PIE *h₂weh₁·nt- → va·ata-). Early Vedic had a tonal system inherited from the Proto-Indo-European accent, distinguishing only tone height: the contraction of two syllables, the first carrying an udātta (high pitch) and the second a so-called "dependent svarita" (high falling pitch), gave rise to a small number of words with the "independent svarita" on a short vowel in a late pronunciation of Vedic. The tonal system persisted for some time after the Vedic period; Pāṇini marked the position of the accent, giving accent rules for both the spoken language of his time and the differences of Vedic accent, but no extant post-Vedic text with accents is found. Pluti, or prolation — overlong vowels noted with a numeral "3" indicating three morae — is recorded 3 times in the Rigveda and 15 times in the Atharvaveda, typically in cases of questioning and where two options are compared ("Was it above? Was it below?", Rigveda 10.129.5d; "Is this larger? Or this?", Atharvaveda 9.6.18); the pluti attained the peak of their popularity in the Brāhmaṇa period of late Vedic Sanskrit (roughly the 8th century BCE), with some 40 instances in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa alone. The era is c. 1500–600 BCE; the region, the northwestern Indian subcontinent.

- **The story.** Epic Sanskrit is the language of the two great Sanskrit epics, the Mahābhārata and the Rāmāyaṇa — a range of oral storytelling registers, used in northern India between 400 BCE and 300 CE, and roughly contemporary with classical Sanskrit. The term, as John J. Lowe puts it (2017, p. 58, quoted in the Sanskrit article's note 33), "refers to the language of the two great Sanskrit epics, the Mahābhārata and the Rāmāyaṇa" — and, Lowe continues, "it is likely, therefore, that the epic-like elements found in Vedic sources and the two epics that we have are not directly related, but that both drew on the same source, an oral tradition of storytelling that existed before, throughout, and after the Vedic period." The Indian epic poetry article stages it one step further: "The language of these texts, termed Epic Sanskrit, constitutes the earliest phase of Classical Sanskrit, following the latest stage of Vedic Sanskrit found in the Shrauta Sutras." The two epics together comprise the Itihāsa (lit. "writer has himself witnessed the story") or Mahākāvya ("Great Compositions"), a canon of Hindu scripture; Itihāsa and the Puranas are mentioned in the Atharva Veda and referred to as the fifth Veda. The Suparṇākhyāna, a late Vedic poem considered to be among the "earliest traces of epic poetry in India," is an older, shorter precursor to the expanded legend of Garuda that is included within the Mahābhārata. The Mahābhārata itself is one of the longest epic poems known: its longest version consists of over 100,000 shlokas (verses) or over 200,000 individual lines (each shloka a couplet), and long prose passages — at about 1.8 million words in total, roughly ten times the length of the Iliad and the Odyssey combined, or about four times the length of the Rāmāyaṇa, albeit more than 2.5 times shorter than the world's longest poem, the Epic of Manas; within the Indian tradition it is sometimes called the fifth Veda. The Rāmāyaṇa runs 24,000 couplets (48,000 lines). The bulk of the Mahābhārata was probably compiled between the 3rd century BCE and the 3rd century CE, with the oldest preserved parts not much older than around 400 BCE, and the text probably reached its final form by the early Gupta period (c. 4th century CE). The Mahābhārata itself (1.1.61) distinguishes a core portion of 24,000 verses — the Bhārata proper — as opposed to additional secondary material; at least three redactions are commonly recognised: Jaya (Victory) with 8,800 verses attributed to Vyasa, the Bharata with 24,000 verses as recited by Vaisampayana, and finally the Mahābhārata as recited by Ugrashrava Sauti with over 100,000 verses — though John Brockington argues that Jaya and Bharata refer to the same text, and ascribes the Jaya-with-8,800-verses theory to a misreading of a verse in the Adi Parva (1.1.81). The epic started as an orally-transmitted tale of the charioteer bards, and — unlike the Vedas, which have to be preserved letter-perfect — it was a popular work whose reciters would inevitably conform to changes in language and style. The earliest known references to bhārata and the compound mahābhārata date to Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī (sutra 6.2.38) and the Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra (3.4.4); the Mahābhārata was not recited in Vedic accent. The Greek writer Dio Chrysostom (c. 40–c. 120 CE) reported that Homer's poetry was being sung even in India. The copper-plate inscription of the Maharaja Sharvanatha (533–534 CE) describes the Mahābhārata as a "collection of 100,000 verses" (śata-sahasri saṃhitā). The deviations from Pāṇini in the epics are generally considered to be on account of interference from Prakrits, or innovations, and not because they are pre-Paninian; traditional Sanskrit scholars call such deviations ārṣa (आर्ष), meaning "of the ṛṣis", and in some contexts there are also more "prakritisms" (borrowings from common speech) than in Classical Sanskrit proper. The Handbook of Comparative and Historical Indo-European Linguistics ("Other Sanskrits") gives the deeper characterisation: "Epic Sanskrit must have developed out of a courtly or bardic lingua franca spanning Uttar Pradesh, eventually to buckle under the social pressure of Classical Sanskrit. It has many features, including its use of case, which suggest a kind of semantic syncretism seen in older Middle Indic (Oberlies, this handbook) but already underway in the Pancala dialect of Vedic. It makes use of the imperfect narrative past, as Western Vedic would, but it also employs the perfect as a narrative past, just as Eastern Vedic would. Unlike Classical Sanskrit, which from its inception was codified by Panini and preserved by a dedicated community of grammarians (the antecedents of the vyakarana tradition), there is no evidence that Epic Sanskrit had such institutional policemen. As such it exhibits a great degree of internal diversity. This is far more true of the Mahabharata than the Ramayana" — the Mahabharata being much larger, its older parts clearly predating a standardized sloka, with more independence from the prosodic norms of Classical Sanskrit, while the Ramayana has already come under the influence of Classical Sanskrit, is referred to as adikavya ("the first kavya [poetry]"), and its aetiology of the sloka is a charter myth of Classical Sanskrit poetry and drama; the Mahabharata, on the other hand, is classified as itihasa ("history") rather than poetry. Deviation from Classical Sanskrit is even greater in Buddhist Sanskrit and Aisa, a Saiva Sanskrit. The later classical epics are NOT Epic Sanskrit: the Buddhist kavi Aśvaghoṣa (1st–2nd century) wrote Buddhacarita and Saundarananda, and Kālidāsa wrote Raghuvamsha and Kumarasambhava in later Classical Sanskrit rather than Epic Sanskrit, as did Māgha (Śiśupālavadha), Bhāravi (Kirātārjunīya), Śrīharṣa (Naiṣadhacarita) and Bhaṭṭi (Bhaṭṭikāvya). The grammar of record is Thomas Oberlies, A Grammar of Epic Sanskrit (De Gruyter, 2003) — 631 pages, volume 5 of Indian Philology and South Asian Studies. The era is 400 BCE–300 CE; the region, northern India.

- **The story.** Old Indo-Aryan (OIA) is the earliest stage of the Indo-Aryan branch of Indo-Iranian — the stage from which all known languages of the later stages, Middle and New Indo-Aryan, are derived. Its main representative is Vedic Sanskrit, attested from the second millennium BCE onwards; the oldest layer is the language of the Rigveda, dated to the second half of the second millennium BCE. The article's history list stages it as: Proto-Indo-Aryan (before 1500 BCE, reconstructed); Old Indo-Aryan (c. 1500–500 BCE) — early Old Indo-Aryan including Vedic Sanskrit (c. 1500 to 500 BCE), late Old Indo-Aryan including Epic Sanskrit and Classical Sanskrit (c. 200 CE to 1300 CE), and Mitanni Indo-Aryan (c. 1400 BCE); then Middle Indo-Aryan or Prakrits (c. 600 BCE to 1400 CE). The Proto-Indo-Aryan section gives a second dating — Old Indo-Aryan (1500–300 BCE), directly attested as Vedic and Mitanni-Aryan — and the Sanskrit article's three-stage division, carried in the Epic entry's miniature, gives a third: Old Indo-Aryan (1500–600 BCE), Middle Indo-Aryan (600 BCE–1000 CE), New Indo-Aryan (1000 CE–present). Vedic Sanskrit is the earliest evidence of the group, in the Vedas, the foundational canon of the Hindu synthesis; the Indo-Aryan superstrate in Mitanni is of similar age to the language of the Rigveda, but its only evidence is a few proper names and specialised loanwords. The Mitanni evidence is a superstrate, not a text: the kingdom's records are in Hurrian and Akkadian, and the Indo-Aryan shows through in names and terms. In a treaty between the Hittites and the Mitanni, the deities Mitra, Varuna, Indra, and the Ashvins (Nasatya) are invoked. Kikkuli's horse training text carries the technical terms aika (eka, "one"), tera (tri, "three"), panza (panca, "five"), satta (sapta, "seven"), na (nava, "nine") and vartana ("turn", a round in the horse race) — and the numeral aika, "one", is of particular importance because it places the superstrate in the vicinity of Indo-Aryan proper, as opposed to Indo-Iranian in general or early Iranian (which has aiva). Another text has babru (babhru, "brown"), parita (palita, "grey") and pinkara (pingala, "red"). The Mitanni warriors were called marya, the term for "warrior" in Sanskrit. The Sanskritic readings of the royal names, after Mayrhofer, render Artashumara as Ṛtasmara, "who thinks of Ṛta"; Biridashva as Prītāśva, "whose horse is dear"; Priyamazda as Priyamedha, "whose wisdom is dear"; Citrarata as Citraratha, "whose chariot is shining"; Indaruda as Indrota, "helped by Indra"; Shativaza as Sātivāja, "winning the race price"; Šubandhu as Subandhu, "having good relatives"; Tushratta as Tvaṣṭar, "whose chariot is vehement". From Vedic Sanskrit, "Sanskrit" — literally "put together, perfected, elaborated" — developed as the prestige language of culture, science and religion, as well as the court and theatre. Sanskrit of the later Vedic texts is comparable to Classical Sanskrit, but is largely considered mutually unintelligible with Vedic Sanskrit. Broadly, Classical Sanskrit is seen as the Eastern dialect spoken by Rigvedic tribes and later polities of the Heartlands, while sister dialects in the east were more influenced by non-Indo-Aryanic groups and were not preserved like the Kuru-Pancala-Gandhara dialect (Classical Sanskrit), gradually evolving into Pali and other prakrits. Two sound changes mark the split: Pali retains the retroflex ḷ and ḷh (ळ, ळ्ह) of the Vedic language, while Sanskrit replaces them with ḍ and ḍh; and the instrumental plural भिस् (bhis) in the masculine, which Classical Sanskrit replaces with ऐस् (ais). Apabhraṃśa is the conventional cover term for the transitional dialects connecting late Middle Indo-Aryan with early modern Indo-Aryan, spanning roughly the 6th to 13th centuries. Kulikov's chapter in Kapović (2017) sets the chronology: the early Vedic period cannot be dated earlier than 1500 BC and hardly begins much later than 1200 BC; the middle Vedic period probably starts after 800 BC; the post-Vedic period must have started somewhere in the second half of the first millennium BC, hardly much earlier than 300 BC; the Middle Indo-Aryan époque lasts approximately from 600 BC. The Inner–Outer hypothesis argues for a core and periphery: Outer Indo-Aryan, generally including Eastern and Southern Indo-Aryan and sometimes Northwestern Indo-Aryan, Dardic and Pahari, represents an older stratum of Old Indo-Aryan mixed to varying degrees with the newer stratum that is Inner Indo-Aryan — a contentious proposal since Hoernlé in 1880, refined by Grierson, most recently iterated by Southworth and Zoller on the evidence of an Outer past tense in -l-, with Chatterji and Masica among the sceptics.

- **The story.** Proto-Indo-Aryan (PIA), sometimes Proto-Indic, is the reconstructed proto-language of the Indo-Aryan languages — the reconstructed ancestor of every Indo-Aryan language, including Old Indo-Aryan, and by definition not Sanskrit itself: contrary to popular opinion, Sanskrit was not the ancestor of the Indo-Aryan languages, though Vedic Sanskrit is very close to PIA in form, especially Vedic Sanskrit, so the distinction is often moot. It is intended to reconstruct the language of the Indo-Aryans who had migrated into the Indian subcontinent. Being descended from Proto-Indo-Iranian — which in turn is descended from Proto-Indo-European — it has the characteristics of a satem language. The history list stages it as Proto-Indo-Aryan (before 1500 BCE, reconstructed), the predecessor of Old Indo-Aryan (1500–300 BCE on this article's dating), which is directly attested as Vedic and Classical Sanskrit, as well as by the Indo-Aryan superstrate in Mitanni. Vedic Sanskrit is very close to Proto-Indo-Aryan, and the Indo-Aryan languages article says the same from the other direction; some Prakrits display a few minor features derived from Proto-Indo-Aryan that had already disappeared in Vedic Sanskrit — the other Indo-Aryan languages preserve a small number of conservative features lost in Vedic, showing they had a separate descent from Proto-Indo-Aryan. This language is usually associated with the Fedorovo Culture, in the Andronovo Horizon; its parent Proto-Indo-Iranian is, by the companion article, often connected with the Sintashta culture of the Eurasian Steppe and the early Andronovo horizon — two cultures, one horizon, the parent a step earlier, its speakers assumed to have lived in the late 3rd millennium BCE, removed less than a millennium from Proto-Indo-European on one side and less than a millennium from Vedic Sanskrit and Old Avestan on the other. PIA is one of the three known descendants of Proto-Indo-Iranian, alongside Proto-Iranian and Proto-Nuristani. The differences from Vedic are few but diagnostic. First, the representation of Proto-Indo-European *l and *r: Vedic, as also most Iranic languages, merges both as /r/, but later some instances of Indo-European /l/ again surface in Classical Sanskrit, indicating the contrast survived in an early Indo-Aryan dialect parallel to Vedic — a dialect with only /l/ is additionally posited to underlie Magadhi Prakrit — though the article itself says it is not clear the contrast actually survived anywhere in Indo-Iranian, not even in Proto-Indo-Iranian, as /l/ is also found in place of original *r in Indo-Iranian languages. Second, the common consonant cluster kṣ /kʂ/ of Vedic and later Sanskrit has a particularly wide range of Proto-Indo-European and Proto-Indo-Iranian sources, which partly remain distinct in later Indo-Aryan languages: PIE *ks, *kʷs, *gs, *gʷs > PII *kš > Middle Indo-Aryan kh-, -kkh-; PIE *dʰgʷʰ, *gʰs, *gʷʰs > PII *gʱžʱ > Middle Indo-Aryan gh-, -ggh-; PIE *tḱ, *ǵs, *ḱs > PII *tć, *ćš > Middle Indo-Aryan ch-, -cch-; PIE *dʰǵʰ, *ǵʰs > PII *ȷ́ʱžʱ > Middle Indo-Aryan jh-, -jh-. Third, the pronouns and numerals: most personal pronouns are identical between Proto-Indo-Iranian and Proto-Indo-Aryan and show modest differences between Proto-Indo-Aryan and Sanskrit — I *aȷ́ʰám > Sanskrit aham, You *tuHám > tvam, He *sá, She *sáH > sā, It *tád > tad, We *wayám, You (all) *yúH > yūyám, They (m.) *táy > te, They (f.) *tā́s (or *táHas?) > tāḥ, They (n.) *tá > tāni — and most numerals are identical between Proto-Indo-Iranian and Proto-Indo-Aryan, with minimal differences between Proto-Indo-Aryan and Sanskrit, e.g. the loss of the fricative *H — One *Háykas > eka, Two *dwáH > dvá, Three *tráyas > tráyaḥ, Four *čatwā́ras > catvā́raḥ, Five *pánča, Six *šwáćš > PIA *ṣwáṭṣ > ṣáṭ, Seven *saptá, Eight *Haštā́ > PIA *Haṣṭā́ > aṣṭá, Nine *Hnáwa > náva, Ten *dáća > PIA *dáśa. The notation is its own system, filed by Wiktionary's entry guidelines: the IAST transcription of Sanskrit as a base, with the vowels *e and *o written as *ay and *aw, reflecting the diphthongal character still present in PIA (and Vedic), Classical Sanskrit *ai and *au written as long diphthongs *āy and *āw; the dot underneath consonants used strictly to indicate retroflexion and the dot above not used at all, so *l̥ and *r̥ rather than *ḷ and *ṛ; anusvara *ṃ not used, write the actual sound it represents; visarga *ḥ not used, write *s, or if the RUKI sound law applies, *ṣ; *ṅ and *ñ written as plain *n before a homorganic obstruent; the thorn clusters in Proto-Indo-European all realised in Sanskrit as kṣ, but in PIA written as *ṭṣ < *tḱ, *ḍẓʰ/*gẓʰ < *dʰgʷʰ, and *źʰ < *dʰǵʰ, partly continued in some Middle Indo-Aryan languages such as Pali; the sound *v not used in PIA as it is in IAST, use *w instead; voiced sibilants probably existed in PIA, later discarded in Sanskrit but possibly part of early Vedic, as evidenced by the treatment of *ḍ and *ḷ as clusters (< PIA *ẓḍ); PIA possessed a laryngeal *H which probably represented a glottal stop, although it may be present in early Vedic based on metrical evidence and hiatus. The article's references run Cardona and Jain (2007) The Indo-Aryan Languages, the Encyclopedia Iranica "ARYANS" entry, Wheeler on the Indo-European family, Radhakrishnan and Moore (1957) p. 3, Witzel on the Vedas and Upaniṣads in Flood (2003) p. 68, MacDonell (2004) pp. 29–39, Masica (1991) pp. 156 and 97, Kobayashi (2004) Historical Phonology of Old Indo-Aryan Consonants pp. 60–65, with Morgenstierne (1974) "Early Iranic Influence upon Indo-Aryan" as further reading; its note 1 warns that "Indic" in modern and colloquial context refers more generally to the languages of the Indian subcontinent, thus also including non-Aryan families like Dravidian and Munda (Reynolds and Verma 2007).

- **Decoder-design note (Proto-Indo-Aryan → Gauntlet).** Five rungs. (1) **The no-node probe.** Present the indo1321 and indo1320 records; the specimen must say Glottolog files no Proto-Indo-Aryan node and no "proto" string in either record — a specimen that cites a Glottolog id for PIA has invented one. (2) **The *l/*r probe.** Present Vedic merging *l and *r as /r/; the specimen must say the contrast's survival is attested only by later /l/ resurfacing in Classical Sanskrit and the Magadhi /l/-only dialect hypothesis, and that the article itself says it is not clear the contrast survived anywhere in Indo-Iranian — a specimen that asserts the contrast survived has overstated the article. (3) **The kṣ probe.** Present the 12 Proto-Indo-European sources; the specimen must give all four Middle Indo-Aryan outcomes (kh-, gh-, ch-, jh-) and not collapse them — a specimen that gives one outcome has collapsed four distinct mergers. (4) **The second-carrier probe.** Present Old Indo-Aryan (1500–300 BCE) from the Proto-Indo-Aryan article; the specimen must say 300 BCE now has two carriers and the 600- and 500-BCE end dates still have one each — a specimen that calls 300 BCE settled has mistaken a second carrier for a consensus. (5) **The notation probe.** Present IAST-based PIA notation; the specimen must write *e/*o as *ay/*aw, use *w not *v, write *l̥/*r̥ not *ḷ/*ṛ, and never write *ṃ or *ḥ — a specimen that writes PIA with anusvara or visarga has used Classical Sanskrit notation, not PIA notation.

- **The story.** Proto-Nuristani (PNur) is the reconstructed proto-language of the Nuristani languages — the reconstructed ancestor of every Nuristani language, and the latest common form of all modern-day Nuristani languages. It is descended from Proto-Indo-Iranian, which in turn is descended from Proto-Indo-European, and it is one of the three known descendants of Proto-Indo-Iranian, alongside Proto-Indo-Aryan and Proto-Iranian — the triad the catalogue now holds complete as siblings, with Proto-Nuristani the last of the three to get its own entry. The article files it as "around 800 BC" with its region the Fergana Region, modern-day Uzbekistan, and its break-off into distinct languages from around the 8th century BCE — the era and the break-off sharing one boundary, as the Proto-Indo-Aryan split and the Rigveda shared 1500 BCE. The Nuristani languages, known earlier as the Kafiri languages, are one of the three groups within the Indo-Iranian language family, alongside the Indo-Aryan and Iranian languages, and they were not described in literature until the 19th century — no direct attestation until the 1800s, so the reconstruction rests on extensive internal comparison between the modern languages and external comparison with earlier attested Indo-Iranian forms. Since diverging, the Nuristani-speaking peoples kept social contact with other Indo-Iranian peoples, and the article's history is a braid, not a split: some sound changes shared with Indo-Aryan and Iranian at different stages, some specific to Nuristani; early on Nuristani has more in common with Iranian, before Indo-Aryan loanwords arrived starting from the Middle Indo-Aryan period and the subsequent convergence. The diagnostics are three. First, the Ruki sound law does not apply after *u — the earliest divergence may be marked by exactly that: Northeastern Katë musë /muˈsɘ/ "mouse" < *mūs-a-ka-* keeps its *s where RUKI would have turned it; Halfmann posits a merger of *s and *š as *s, subsequently palatalized near *i. Second, the shared Iranian traits: the merger of the tenuis and breathy-voiced consonants, the preservation of the distinction between the two sets of Indo-Iranian voiced palatals (which merged in Indo-Aryan), and the fronting of the Proto-Indo-Iranian primary palatal consonants — retained as dental affricates in Proto-Nuristani, against simplification to sibilants in most Iranian languages. Third, the distinguishing trait: no debuccalizing of /s/ to /h/ as in Indo-Aryan. Later, Proto-Nuristani *ǰ /*d͡z/ shifted to /z/ in all Nuristani varieties other than Southeastern Katë and Tregami, while Proto-Nuristani *ċ /*t͡s/ shifted to /s/ only in Ashkun — though sometimes retained as /t͡s/, with the evidence suggesting that reflex comes instead from Proto-Nuristani *ċċ*. The article's ten reconstructions, "very tentative" by its own word: *ačāni "eyes" (Halfmann 2023), *āp-pešáni "water mill" (Halfmann 2023), *dáca "ten" (Kreidl 2021), *dúǰitā "daughter" (Kreidl 2021), *dū́ "two" (Kreidl 2021), *dvára- "door" (Halfmann 2023), *dvāráka- "doorjambs" (Halfmann 2023), *Kānta-ka- "Katë" (Halfmann 2024), *páda- "footprint" (Kreidl 2021), *pra-dā- "to give" (Kreidl 2021). Wiktionary already files Reconstruction:Proto-Nuristani/dū́ "two", from PII *dwáH — the same *dwáH the Proto-Indo-Aryan entry files as PIA *dwáH > dvá. The references run Hegedűs (2022), Halfmann (2025, Reichert Verlag), Hegedűs (2012) on the RUKI-rule in Nuristani, and Strand (2023) on the Kâmboǰâs and Sakas in the Holly-Oak Mountains, in Cacopardo's Roots of Peristan; further reading adds Kreidl (2021) on lambdacism and Old Iranian *t in Pashto, Halfmann (2023) on a Bactrian loanword, Halfmann (2024) on Katë, Kreidl (2024) on Prasun, and Kümmel (2022). Jakob Halfmann is currently working on the reconstruction through systematic analysis of the sound developments found in the modern languages — a live reconstruction, still being written.

- **The decoder-design note (Gauntlet mappings — SPECULATION, designs until run).** A gauntlet probe for a PNur-class specimen: feed it the RUKI-after-*u* test — a specimen that applies RUKI after *u, turning *mūs-a-ka-* toward a *ṣ form, betrays an Indo-Aryan-shaped rule, not a Nuristani one; the *ǰ → /z/ and *ċ → /s/ reflexes are the extraction-only re-interrogation keys — ask the specimen to derive Northeastern Katë musë and the Ashkun reflex separately, then compare the two derivations; a specimen that gives one rule for both has failed the probe. The 2,600-year silence is the time-dilation scenario: a language with no attestation until the 19th century must be interrogated from its daughters only, so the container holds the daughters apart (Katë, Prasun, Ashkun, Nuristani Kalasha, Tregami, Dameli in separate cells) and the extraction asks each for the same proto-form before any comparison. No verdict without a gauntlet run.

- **The story.** Proto-Iranian (PIr), or Proto-Iranic, is the reconstructed proto-language of the Iranian languages — the reconstructed ancestor of every Iranian language, including Persian, Pashto, Sogdian, Zazaki, Ossetian, Mazandarani, Kurdish and Talysh. Its speakers, the hypothetical Proto-Iranians, are assumed to have lived in the 2nd millennium BC and are usually connected with the Andronovo archaeological horizon — the same horizon the Proto-Indo-Aryan entry files for the Fedorovo Culture, so the two siblings share one horizon and the parent Proto-Indo-Iranian sits a step earlier at Sintashta. Proto-Iranian was a satem language descended from Proto-Indo-Iranian, which in turn came from Proto-Indo-European; it was likely removed less than a millennium from the Avestan language, and less than two millennia from Proto-Indo-European — the closest a reconstruction in this catalogue has yet come to an attested tongue, which is why the heading calls it the reconstruction Avestan almost is. The article files its era as 1900 BC – 1600 BC, with reconstructed ancestors Proto-Indo-European then Proto-Indo-Iranian. Skjærvø postulates at least four dialects that initially developed out of Proto-Iranian, two of which are attested by texts: Old Northwest Iranian (unattested, ancestor of Ossetian), Old Northeast Iranian (unattested, ancestor of Middle Iranian Khotanese and modern Wakhi), Old Central Iranian (attested, includes Avestan and Median, ancestor of most modern Iranian languages), Old Southwest Iranian (attested, includes Old Persian, ancestor of modern Persian). The terminology traps the unwary: Ossetian has often been classified as a "Northeast Iranian" language in modern terms, while "Northwest Iranian" usually refers to languages to the northwest of Persian, such as Zaza or the Caspian languages — the old dialect names and the modern group names point in opposite directions, a terminology inversion. The descriptive phonology is a full inventory: 24 consonant segments — 6 plosives, 4 affricates, 9 fricatives, 2 nasals, 1 liquid, 2 semivowels — with the laryngeal series *h and *H, and 3 vowel qualities with a length contrast, *H and *r̥ able to function as the syllabic core. The article's correspondence table runs 13 Proto-Indo-European forms to their Avestan reflexes, and its lexicon table twelve Proto-Iranian reconstructions — *pHtā́ "father", *máHtā "mother", *Hácwah "horse", *bagáh "portion, part", *bráHtā "brother", *búHmiš "earth, land", *mártyah "mortal, man", *mā́Hah "moon", *wáhr̥ "spring", *Hr̥táh "truth", *drúxš "falsehood", *háwmah "pressed juice" / "ephedra" — each carried across Avestan, Old Persian, Persian, Zaza, Kurdish, Pashto and Vedic Sanskrit, with *háwmah's Avestan *haoma* against Vedic *sóma* the clearest pair in the table. The development into Old Iranian is seven named changes with one relative chronology, the ordering proof: the syllabic laryngeal deleted in non-initial syllables; *l > *r, found widely across the Iranian languages and in Vedic Sanskrit, though /l/ survives unsystematically in New Persian, Kurdish and Zazaki (Persian *lab* "lip", Zazaki *lü* "fox"); *s > *h, debuccalization in all Iranian languages except when preceded by *k, *n, *p or *t, or followed by *t — five blockers; the Proto-Indo-Iranian aspirated stops *pʰ, *tʰ and *kʰ spirantized into *f, *θ and *x, reverted to aspirates in Parachi, varieties of Kurdish and the Saka languages (Khotanese and Tumshuqese, but not Wakhi, which retains the fricatives), and merged with the voiceless aspirated stops in Balochi; *c and *dz > *s and *z, with Old Persian showing /θ/ and /d/ instead — and the ordering proof, that *c > *s must be newer than *s > *h since the new *s was not affected by the earlier change; *cw > *sp, failing in Old Persian (showing /s/), possibly likewise Kurdish and Balochi, with the Saka languages showing /š/ and Ossetian /fs/; *θr > *c, typical for Old Persian and its descendants. The Old Iranian stage itself — Avestan and Old Persian — is a dialect continuum, not a pair of parents: many Old Iranian features may not have occurred yet in Proto-Iranian, and most Iranian languages cannot be derived from either attested Old Iranian language, so numerous unwritten Old Iranian dialects must have existed. The references run Liverani (2013), Mallory & Adams (2006, 1997), Skjærvø (2009, 2003), Cathcart (2015), Korn (2003) and Schwarz (2008), with Windfuhr's The Iranian Languages as the volume; further reading adds Cathcart's dissertation, Kontovas on Proto-Iranic *w- reflexes, and Kümmel on prothetic h- in Khotanese.

- **The decoder-design note (Gauntlet mappings — SPECULATION, designs until run).** A gauntlet probe for a PIr-class specimen: feed it the *s > *h test with its five blockers — a specimen that turns *s to *h after *k, *n, *p or *t, or before *t, betrays a rule without its conditions; the *c > *s ordering test is the extraction-only re-interrogation key — ask the specimen to derive Avestan *dasa* and then ask whether the new *s should have become *h, and a specimen that applies *s > *h to it has failed the chronology; the four-dialect split is the time-dilation scenario — hold the four dialects in separate cells (Old Northwest, Old Northeast, Old Central, Old Southwest) and ask each for the same proto-form before any comparison, so no dialect can borrow another's answer; the *cw > *sp divergence is the control — Ossetian /fs/ against the rest's /sp/ separates a specimen that knows the exception from one that smooths it. The short gap is the point: Proto-Iranian sits less than a millennium from Avestan, the shortest attested reach of the three siblings, so the container's job here is not bridging silence but holding the attested daughters apart long enough to check the reconstruction against them. No verdict without a gauntlet run.
