- **The story.** Proto-Indo-Iranian (PIIr), also called Proto-Indo-Iranic or Proto-Aryan, is the reconstructed proto-language of the Indo-Iranian branch of Indo-European — the parent of the three siblings this catalogue has already seated: Proto-Indo-Aryan, Proto-Iranian and Proto-Nuristani, its three lower-order reconstructions. Its speakers, the hypothetical Proto-Indo-Iranians, are assumed to have lived in the late 3rd millennium BCE, and are often connected with the Sintashta culture of the Eurasian Steppe and the early Andronovo archaeological horizon — the same horizon the Proto-Iranian entry files, with the parent a step earlier at Sintashta where the child sits at Andronovo. It was a satem language, likely removed less than a millennium from its ancestor, the late Proto-Indo-European language, and in turn removed less than a millennium from its descendants: Vedic Sanskrit (of the Rigveda) and Old Avestan (of the Gathas). It is the ancestor of the Indo-Aryan languages, the Iranian languages and the Nuristani languages, predominantly spoken in the Southern Asian subregion of Eurasia. The descriptive phonology is a full inventory of 32 consonant segments — 18 plosives (5 voiceless, 3 aspirated, 5 voiced, 5 voiced aspirated), 2 affricates, 6 fricatives, 2 nasals, 2 liquids and 2 semivowels, counting the two parenthesized marginal segments (z) and (l) — with 3 vowel qualities carrying length (6 vowel segments), and *H and *r̥ as syllabic cores. The two palatal series are the phonology's signature: the first or primary series *ć *ȷ́ *ȷ́ʰ continues the Proto-Indo-European palatovelar *ḱ *ǵ *ǵʰ, and the second or secondary series *č *ǰ *ǰʰ continues the plain and labialized velars *k, *g, *gʰ and *kʷ, *gʷ, *gʷʰ in palatalizing contexts; the reflex table runs the six segments across seven columns (Proto-Indo-Aryan, Sanskrit, Proto-Iranian, Avestan, Old Persian, Nuristani) beside the Proto-Indo-Iranian form. The laryngeals merged as one phoneme *H, which may have been a glottal stop; Beekes suggests some instances survived into Rigvedic Sanskrit and Avestan as unwritten glottal stops, evidenced by metrics. Like Proto-Indo-European and Vedic Sanskrit, it had a pitch accent system similar to present-day Japanese, conventionally indicated by an acute accent over the accented vowel. The historical phonology's most distinctive change is the collapse of the ablauting vowels *e, *o into a single vowel *a; Bartholomae's law and the ruki sound law were also complete in Proto-Indo-Iranian. A fuller list of sixteen hypothesized sound changes runs from the satem shift through the second palatalization, Brugmann's law, the *e/*o merger, the laryngeal vocalization and Lubotsky's Law — the double-dental rule among them, the syllabic nasals merging with *a*, the Ruki rule retracting *s* to *š*, and the law of palatals giving the second series its full phonemic status; the worked examples carry the signature forms *wŕ̥kas* "wolf" from *wĺ̥kʷos*, *ćatám* "hundred" from *ḱm̥tóm*, and *gatás* "come, gone" from *gʷm̥tós*. The subsequent changes split the daughters: the loss of the voiced sibilants *z, *ẓ, *ź* toward Indo-Aryan, and the de-aspiration of the Proto-Indo-European voiced aspirates toward Proto-Iranian; the post-Proto-Indo-Iranian development table runs 35 rows, one per segment, and Grassmann's law runs through its Vedic column, where an aspirate loses its aspiration beside another aspirate. The lexicon table carries ten reconstructions, six with *H and four without, from *Háćwas* "horse" to *sáwmas* "pressed (juice)" — with *Hr̥tás* "truth", *mártyas* "mortal, man", *bʰaHgás* "portion, share", *bʰúHmiš* "earth, land", *mā́Has* "moon", *wásr̥* "spring" and *dʰráwgʰas* "lie" between them — and the *sáwmas* row gives Avestan *haoma* against Vedic *sóma-*, the same pair the Proto-Iranian entry files. The morphology preserves much of Proto-Indo-European: thematic and athematic inflection, all three numbers, all tense, mood and voice categories, and the eight cases of the noun; the chief verbal innovation is a passive conjugation with the suffix *-yá*, and the chief nominal innovation a genitive plural ending *-nām* for vowel stems. The pronouns run *aȷ́Hám* "I", *túH* "you", *sá* "he", and the verb "to be" runs *Hásmi, *Hási, *Hásti, *Hsmás, *Hstʰá, *Hsánti*; three verbs are conjugated (to bear/carry, to call/summon, to be), three nouns declined across the eight cases in singular and plural — the wolf *wŕ̥kas*, the cow *waćáH*, the yoke *yugám* — one adjective declined in all three genders (*amŕ̥tas* "immortal"), and the numerals one to ten are given — *Háykas, *dwáH, *tráyas, *čatwā́ras, *pánča, *šwáćš, *saptá, *Haštā́, *Hnáwa, *dáća* — the ten-form closing on the same *dáća* the three siblings render as *dáśa*, *dáca* and *dasa*.

- **The decoder-design note (Gauntlet mappings — SPECULATION, designs until run).** A gauntlet probe for a PII-class specimen: feed it the two-palatal-series test — a specimen that merges the first and second series, or derives the second from the palatovelar, has collapsed the contrast the article keeps apart; the *ćš → *šš simplification is the extraction-only re-interrogation key — ask the specimen to derive *Háššas* "axle" and then ask whether the first *š* should have stayed *ć*, and a specimen that restores it has failed the chronology; the three-daughter split is the time-dilation scenario — hold Indo-Aryan, Iranian and Nuristani in separate cells and ask each for the same proto-form before any comparison, so no daughter can borrow another's answer, and the binary top split is the control — a specimen that files Iranian and Nuristani as two equal branches against Indo-Aryan, the article's flat triple, has taken the article's side against Glottolog's grouped pair, and the gauntlet records which side it takes rather than grading it; the *ȷ́ʰ row is the empty-cell test — a specimen that fills the blank Proto-Iranian, Avestan, Old Persian or Nuristani reflex for *ȷ́ʰ* has invented data the table does not carry. The parent's job in the container is the opposite of the children's: not bridging silence but holding the three daughters apart long enough to check which reconstruction each one actually supports. No verdict without a gauntlet run.

- **The story.** Proto-Indo-European (PIE) is the reconstructed common ancestor of the Indo-European language family — the parent of every branch this catalogue has seated, from Anatolian to Tocharian — and no direct record of it has been discovered; its proposed features have been derived by linguistic reconstruction from documented Indo-European languages, and far more work has gone into reconstructing PIE than any other proto-language. It is hypothesized to have been spoken as a single language from approximately 4500 BCE to 2500 BCE, during the Late Neolithic to Early Bronze Age, though other estimates place the bounds of the period as much as more than a thousand years later. According to the prevailing Kurgan hypothesis, the original homeland may have been in the Pontic–Caspian steppe of eastern Europe and central Asia, its speakers the Yamnaya culture of c. 3400 BCE; the rival Anatolian hypothesis spreads it out of Anatolia with agriculture beginning c. 7500–6000 BCE, and the Armenian hypothesis, the Paleolithic continuity paradigm and the indigenous Aryans theory are also filed, the last two not regarded as credible within academia — while Colin Renfrew, the Anatolian hypothesis's own author, accepted after the 2015 ancient-DNA studies that Indo-European-speaking populations did migrate from the Pontic steppe toward Northwestern Europe, and a pair of 2024 studies led by David Reich argued the original speakers originated in the Caucasus-Lower Volga region during the Eneolithic. The hypothesis itself was built in public: William Jones's 1786 sensation postulating the common ancestry of Sanskrit, Greek, Latin, Gothic, the Celtic languages and Old Persian — less accurate than his predecessors, erroneously including Egyptian, Japanese and Chinese while omitting Hindi — after Marcus Zuerius van Boxhorn's 1653 "Scythian" proposal and Gaston-Laurent Coeurdoux's 1767 memoir demonstrating the Sanskrit–European analogy; Rasmus Christian Rask's 1818 correspondences, Franz Bopp's 1816 conjugation study and 1833 Comparative Grammar, Jacob Grimm's 1822 Grimm's law, the Neogrammarians' no-exceptions doctrine from the 1870s with Verner's law (1876) resolving Grimm's apparent exceptions through accent, August Schleicher's 1874–77 Compendium as the first reconstruction attempt, the laryngeal theory proposed by Ferdinand de Saussure in 1879 on internal reconstruction only and accepted after Jerzy Kuryłowicz found consonantal reflexes in Hittite, Julius Pokorny's 1959 etymological dictionary, and Kuryłowicz's 1956 Apophonie on ablaut. The reconstruction's showcase is the cognate table from Mallory and Adams — *méh₂tēr* "mother", *ph₂tḗr* "father", *bʰréh₂tēr* "brother", *swésōr* "sister", *suHnús*/*suHyús* "son", *dʰugh₂tḗr* "daughter", *gʷṓus* "cow" — the reconstructed ancestors of English water (*wódr̥*), hound (*ḱwn̥tós*) and three (*tréyes*) among them. Its phonology runs three series of stops — voiceless, voiced and breathy voiced — across five places, with *b* parenthesized, the single gap in the fifteen-cell table; sonorant consonants that could be used syllabically; three laryngeal consonants whose exact pronunciation is not well-established, the Rasmussen–Kloekhorst table giving *h₁* as glottal, *h₂* as velar or uvular, *h₃* as labialized; the fricative /s/ alone; and a vowel system in which /e/ and /o/ were the most frequent, the existence of /a/ as a separate phoneme debated. Its accent was variable lexical stress, often called a pitch accent, best preserved in Vedic Sanskrit and Ancient Greek and indirectly attested in Verner's Law. Its morphology is highly inflected and fusional: roots of the shape (s)(C)CVC(C), suffixation and ablaut as the main inflectional methods, ablaut grades e, o, ē, ō and zero-grade, nouns declined for eight or nine cases — the ninth the allative, preserved in Anatolian and Tocharian, its shape uncertain — three grammatical genders in the late language derived from an older two-gender system, three numbers, personal pronouns in the first and second person only, the first-person singular keeping two stems still visible in English I and me, verbs classed by three aspects, four moods, two voices (active and mediopassive), three persons and three numbers, and the Sihler verb endings as the current consensus. Its numerals run one to ten — *d(u)wóh₁* "two", *tréyes* "three", *kʷetwóres* "four", *pénkʷe* "five", *s(w)éḱs* "six", *septḿ̥* "seven", *oḱtṓ(w)* "eight", *h₁néwn̥* "nine", *déḱm̥(t)* "ten" — with *ḱm̥tóm* for a hundred meaning originally "a large number" rather than specifically 100, and the first-person pronoun *h₁eǵ(oH/Hom)* "I" opening the pronoun table. Its particles — *upo* "under, below", the negators *ne* and *mē*, the conjunctions *kʷe* "and" and *wē* "or", the interjection *wai!* — were adverbs and postpositions that became prepositions in most daughters. Its derivation runs internal (possessive adjectives, vṛddhi, nominalization) through four accent/ablaut classes in a fixed order — acrostatic → proterokinetic → hysterokinetic → amphikinetic — and the Bahuvrihi compounds it produces; Roland A. Pooth's alternative templatic model with its direct-inverse alignment stands filed as the article's dissent, with his full reconstruction of The North Wind and the Sun beside Schleicher's fable and The king and the god in the See also. Its syntax is the one open fight in the article: Jacob Wackernagel's 1892 subject–verb–object against Winfred P. Lehmann's 1974 subject–object–verb, Paul Friedrich's 1975 SVO against the broad consensus Hans Henrich Hock reported in 2015 that PIE would have been an SOV language. Its neighbours included Proto-Kartvelian, with lexical similarities and a remarkably similar root ablaut. The descendant table lists ten clades — Anatolian, Tocharian, Italic, Celtic, Germanic, Balto-Slavic, Indo-Iranian, Armenian, Hellenic, Albanian — and the commonly proposed subgroups run six: Italo-Celtic, Graeco-Aryan, Graeco-Armenian, Graeco-Phrygian, Daco-Thracian and Thraco-Illyrian; the tree image splits them left half centum, right half satem.

- **The decoder-design note (Gauntlet mappings — SPECULATION, designs until run).** A gauntlet probe for a PIE-class specimen: the *b*-gap probe — present the fifteen-cell stop table with *b* parenthesized, and a specimen that fills *b* as a full series member has repaired the gap the article leaves open; the laryngeal probe — ask for the three laryngeals' pronunciations, and a specimen that gives one certain pronunciation has over-claimed what the article leaves not well-established; the root-shape probe — ask for a vowel-initial root, and a specimen that supplies one has broken the (s)(C)CVC(C) law; the hundred probe — ask what *ḱm̥tóm* meant, and a specimen that answers exactly 100 has taken the gloss for the meaning, since the article says "a large number"; the no-record probe — ask for a PIE text, and a specimen that cites one has fabricated evidence, since no direct record exists; the SOV/SVO split is the control — record which side the specimen takes, Wackernagel/Friedrich SVO or Lehmann/Hock SOV, rather than grading it; the ten-clade split is the time-dilation scenario — hold the ten clades in separate cells and ask each for the same proto-form before any comparison, so no branch can borrow another's answer. The ancestor's job in the container is the opposite of the children's: not bridging silence but holding the whole family apart long enough to check which reconstruction each branch actually supports. No verdict without a gauntlet run.

- **The story.** Proto-Celtic (PC), or Common Celtic, is the reconstructed ancestral proto-language of all known Celtic languages, and a descendant of Proto-Indo-European. It is not attested in writing but has been partly reconstructed through the comparative method. Proto-Celtic is generally thought to have been spoken between 1300 and 800 BC, after which it began to split into different languages. Proto-Celtic is often associated with the Urnfield culture and particularly with the Hallstatt culture. Celtic languages share common features with Italic languages that are not found in other branches of Indo-European, suggesting the possibility of an earlier Italo-Celtic linguistic unity. The infobox files the region as Central or Western Europe, the era as ca. 1300–800 BC, and the reconstructed ancestor as Proto-Indo-European. Reconstruction runs on Insular Celtic: Continental Celtic presents much substantiation for Proto-Celtic phonology, and some for its morphology, but recorded material is too scanty to allow a secure reconstruction of syntax, though some complete sentences are recorded in the Continental Gaulish and Celtiberian — so the main sources for reconstruction come from Insular Celtic languages, with the oldest literature found in Old Irish and Middle Welsh, dating back to authors flourishing in the 6th century AD. Dating is a three-way argument. Proto-Celtic is usually dated to the Late Bronze Age, ca. 1200–900 BC. The fact that it is possible to reconstruct a Proto-Celtic word for 'iron' (traditionally reconstructed as *īsarnom) has long been taken as an indication that the divergence into individual Celtic languages did not start until the Iron Age (8th century BC to 1st century BC); otherwise, descendant languages might have developed their own, unrelated words for the metal. However, Schumacher and Schrijver suggest a date for Proto-Celtic as early as the 13th century BC, the time of the Canegrate culture, in northwest Italy, and the Urnfield culture in Central Europe, implying that the divergence may have already started in the Bronze Age. The sound changes from PIE to PC fall in four strata, roughly in chronological order, with changes that operate on the outcome of earlier ones appearing later in the list. Late PIE (5 groups, 11 rules): *e is colored by an adjacent laryngeal (eh₂, h₂e > ah₂, h₂a; eh₃, h₃e > oh₃, h₃o); palatovelars merge into the plain velars (ḱ > k, ǵ > g, ǵʰ > gʰ); epenthetic *a is inserted after a syllabic sonorant if a laryngeal and another sonorant follow (R̥HR > RaHR); laryngeals are lost in four environments (before a following vowel; following a vowel in syllables before the accent; following a vowel before a consonant, or word finally, with compensatory lengthening; between plosives in non-initial syllables); two adjacent dentals become two adjacent sibilants (TT > TsT > ss). Italo-Celtic (9 groups, 14 rules), shared with the Italic languages in particular and cited in support of the Italo-Celtic hypothesis: Dybo's rule (long close vowels shortened before resonant + stressed vowel); post-consonantal laryngeals lost when before pre-tonic close vowels (CHiC´ > CiC´, CHuC´ > CuC´); development of initial stress — an areal feature shared with Germanic and the non-Indo-European Etruscan; vocalization of laryngeals to *ī between a *CR cluster and consonantal *j (CRHjV > CRījV); syllabic laryngeals become *a (CHC > CaC); syllabic resonants before a voiced unaspirated stop become *Ra (R̩D > RaD); *m is assimilated or lost before a glide (mj > nj, mw > w); *p assimilates to *kʷ when another *kʷ follows later in the word (p...kʷ > kʷ...kʷ) — Matasović points out that this change may have occurred late in Celtic, seems not to have operated on some words in Irish, and a similar assimilation (though in reverse) also occurred in Germanic; vocalization of syllabic resonants next to laryngeals depending on the environment (word-initially HR̩C > aRC; before voiceless stops CR̩HT > CRaT; CR̩HV > CaRHV; CR̩HC > CRāC), with similar developments in Italic but *əm, *ən for the syllabic nasals. Early PC (10 groups, 19 rules): sequences of velar and *w merge into the labiovelars (kw > kʷ, gw > gʷ, gʰw > gʷʰ — Schumacher 2004 argues this change came first, and it is also found in Proto-Italic, so arguably belongs to the previous section); *gʷ merges into *b; aspirated stops lose their aspiration and merge with the voiced stops (bʰ > b, dʰ > d, gʰ > g, gʷʰ > gʷ — counterfeeding the previous change, so *gʷʰ > *gʷ must crucially happen after the sound change gʷ > b has been completed); *e before a resonant and *a (but not *ā) becomes *a (eRa > aRa — Joseph's rule: *ǵʰelH-ro > *gelaro > *galaro, *gérH-no > *gerano > *garano); epenthetic *i is inserted after syllabic liquids when followed by a plosive (l̩T > liT, r̩T > riT); epenthetic *a is inserted before the remaining syllabic resonants (m̩ > am, n̩ > an, l̩ > al, r̩ > ar); all remaining nonsyllabic laryngeals are lost; ē > ī; ō > ū in final syllables; long vowels are shortened before a syllable-final resonant (Osthoff's law). Late PC (8 rules): plosives become *x before a different plosive or *s; p > b before liquids; p > w before nasals; p > ɸ (except possibly after *s); ō > ā; ey > ē (but not in Celtiberian or Lepontic); ew > ow; uwa > owa. Fifty-two rules in thirty-two groups across the four strata. The showcase table runs twenty-one PIE sounds to their PC reflexes with Old Irish and Welsh witnesses: *p > *ɸ (*ph₂tḗr > *ɸatīr 'father', Old Irish athir, Welsh edrydd); *t > *t (*tréyes > *trīs 'three'); *k, ḱ > *k (*ḱm̥tom > *kantom 'hundred'); *kʷ > *kʷ (*kʷetwores > *kʷetwares 'four'); *b > *b (*h₂ébōl > *abalom 'apple'); *d > *d (*derḱ- > *derk- 'see'); *g, ǵ > *g (*ǵen-u- > *genu- 'jaw'); *gʷ > *b (*gʷenh₂ > *bena 'woman'); *bʰ > *b (*bʰére- > *ber-o- 'carry'); *dʰ > *d (*dʰeh₁i- > *di-na- 'suck'); *gʰ, ǵʰ > *g (*ǵʰelH-ro- > *galaro- 'sickness'); *gʷʰ > *gʷ (*gʷʰn̥- > *gʷan-o- 'kill, wound'); *s > *s (*sen-o- > *senos 'old'); *m > *m (*méh₂tēr > *mātīr 'mother'); *n > *n (*h₂nép-ōt- > *neɸūts 'nephew'); *l > *l (*leyǵʰ- > *lig-e/o- 'lick'); *r > *r (*h₃rēǵ-s > *rīgs 'king'); *j > *j (*h₂yuh₁n-ḱós > *juwankos 'young'); *w > *w (*h₂wl̥h₁tí- > *wlatis 'rulership'); and the vowels *a > *a, *ā > *ā, *e > *e, *ē > *ī, *o > *o, *ō > *ū in final syllables and *ā elsewhere, *i > *i, *ī > *ī, *ai > *ai, *ei > *ei, *oi > *oi, *u > *o before *wa and *u elsewhere, *ū > *ū, *au > *au, *eu/*ou > *ou — with witnesses *weh₁-ro- > *wīros 'true', *Hroth₂o- > *rotos 'wheel', *deh₃no- > *dāno- 'gift', *tewteh₂ > *toutā 'people', *deywos > *deiwos 'god' — and the syllabic resonants splitting by environment (*l̥ > *li before stops, *al elsewhere; *r̩ > *ri before stops, *ar elsewhere; *m̩ > *am; *n̩ > *an; *l̥H > *la before obstruents, *lā before sonorants; *r̩H > *ra before obstruents, *rā before sonorants). The consonant inventory reconstructed for PC is sixteen: seven plosives (voiceless t k kʷ, voiced b d ɡ ɡʷ), three fricatives (ɸ s x), two nasals (m n), three approximants (l j w), one trill (r). There is no *p* — the gap the Ogham entry already files ("A letter for P is conspicuously absent — the phoneme was lost in Proto-Celtic"). PIE *p is lost in PC, apparently going through the stages *ɸ (possibly a stage *[pʰ]) and *h (perhaps seen in the name Hercynia if this is of Celtic origin) before being completely lost word-initially and between vowels; next to consonants, PC *ɸ underwent different changes, the clusters *ɸs and *ɸt becoming *xs and *xt already in PC (*laɸs- > *laxs- 'shine', *seɸtam > *sextam 'seven'). PIE *sp- is the open case: Schrijver 1995 argues there was an intermediate stage *sɸ- (in which *ɸ remained an independent phoneme until after Proto-Insular Celtic had diverged into Goidelic and Brythonic), while McCone 1996 finds it more economical to believe that *sp- remained unchanged in PC — the change *p to *ɸ not happening when *s preceded, the same exception Grimm's law shows after *s in Germanic. Eska has recently proposed that PC stops allophonically manifest similarly to those in English: voiceless stop phonemes /t k/ aspirated word-initially except when preceded by /s/, unaspirated voiced stops /b d ɡ/ devoiced to [p t k] word-initially; the evidence is modern Celtic aspiration, old orthography writing voiced and voiceless stops with the same letters, and the Celtiberian Luzaga's Bronze spelling sdam for an accusative determiner where the d spells [t]. Then the chain shift that names the family's split: in Gaulish and the Brittonic languages, PIE *kʷ becomes a new p sound — Gaulish petuar[ios], Welsh pedwar "four", against Old Irish cethair and Latin quattuor — and insofar as this new /p/ fills the gap in the phoneme inventory left by the disappearance of *p, it is a chain shift. The terms P-Celtic and Q-Celtic group the languages by this one phoneme, but a simple division into P- / Q-Celtic may be untenable: it does not do justice to the evidence of the ancient Continental Celtic languages, and the unusual shared innovations among the Insular Celtic languages may instead reflect a common substratum influence from the pre-Celtic languages of Britain and Ireland, or simply continuing contact — in either case irrelevant to the genetic classification. Q-Celtic languages may also have /p/ in loan words, though in early borrowings from Welsh into Primitive Irish, /kʷ/ was used by sound substitution due to a lack of a /p/ phoneme at the time (Latin Patricius "Saint Patrick" > Welsh > Primitive Irish Qatricias > Old Irish Cothrige, later Pádraig; Latin presbyter "priest" > Old Welsh premter/primter > Primitive Irish qrimitir > Old Irish cruimther), while Gaelic póg "kiss" was a later borrowing at a stage where p was borrowed directly as p. The vowel system is highly comparable to that reconstructed for PIE by Antoine Meillet: nine monophthongs (long ī ū ē ā, short i u e o a) and four diphthongs (ai au oi ou). Morphology keeps the parent's shape with Celtic's own endings. Nouns in three genders, three numbers and five to eight cases — the number of cases is contested: Old Irish may have only five, while the evidence from Continental Celtic is considered rather unambiguous for eight (nominative, vocative, accusative, dative, genitive, ablative, locative, instrumental). Nouns fall into nine or so declensions by stem (*o-, *ā-, *i-, *u-, dental, velar, nasal, *r-, *s-), and the article works fifteen paradigms: *makkʷos 'son' (masculine; Old Irish mac, Welsh, Cornish and Breton mab), *dūnom 'stronghold' (neuter), *ɸlāmā 'hand' (feminine; Old Irish lám, Welsh llaw, Cornish leuv, Old Breton lom), *sūlis 'sight, view, eye' (feminine), *mori 'body of water, sea' (neuter; Gaulish Mori-, Old Irish muir, Welsh môr), *bitus 'world, existence' (masculine; Gaulish Bitu-, Old Irish bith, Welsh byd, Breton bed), *beru 'rotisserie spit' (neuter), *rīxs 'king' (masculine), *druwits 'druid' (masculine), *karants 'friend' (masculine), *abū 'river' (feminine), *anman 'name' (neuter), *tegos 'house' (neuter), *ɸatīr 'father' (masculine), *mātīr 'mother' (feminine). Two endings break with PIE: the genitive singular -ī does not match PIE -osyo (which would have yielded -osjo), and Celtiberian shows -o-stem genitives ending in -o (aualo "[son] of Avalos"). Velar stems fricate before the nominative *-s (*rīg- "king" > *rīxs) and final *-d devoices (*druwid- "druid" > *druwits); nasal stems end in *-on-, becoming *-ū in the nominative singular (*abon- "river" > *abū); *s-stems contain *-es-, becoming *-os in the nominative singular (*teges- 'house' > *tegos); *r-stems are rare and principally confined to names of relatives, *-ter- becoming *-tīr in the nominative and *-tr- in all other cases aside from the accusative (*ɸater- 'father' > *ɸatīr, *ɸatros). Pronouns: first person *mī (singular) / *snī (plural), second *tū / *swī; accusatives *me / *snos, *tu / *swes; genitives *mene / ?, *towe / ? — the first-person accusative remade as *mu in the prehistory of Irish by analogy to *tu, and the genitive as *mowe by analogy to *towe. Third person: nominative *es, *ēs (masculine), *sī (feminine), *ed (neuter), *eyes (plural); accusative *em, *seyam? / *sīm?, *sūs; genitive *esyo, *esyās, *esyo, *ēsom? / *esom?; dative/instrumental/locative *e(s)yōi, *esyāi, *e(s)yōi, *ēbis. The relative pronoun *yo- is attested in the first Botorrita plaque (Botorrita I): io-s (nominative singular masculine, line 10), io-m (accusative singular, line 7), io-mui (dative singular, line 7) — from PIE *yo-, Sanskrit ya-, Greek hos, showing up in Old Irish only as the aspiration for leniting relative verb forms. Adjectives carry four degrees: positive, comparative, superlative, equative. Four positive inflection classes, most in the o-ā class; the comparative attaches *-yūs (*senos "old" > *senyūs "older"), with Caland-system adjectives taking *-is extended to *-ais (*ɸlitanos "wide" > *ɸletais); the superlative attaches *-isamos (*senisamos "oldest"), truncated to *-(s)amos by haplology where the stem ends in *s (*trexsnos > *trexsamos). Verbs: from Gaulish, Celtiberian and Insular Celtic together, at least three moods (indicative — Gaulish delgu "I hold", Old Irish tongu "I swear"; imperative — Celtiberian usabituz, Gaulish appisetu; subjunctive — Gaulish buetid "may he be", Celtiberian asekati) and four tenses (present — Gaulish uediíu-mi "I pray", Celtiberian zizonti "they sow"; preterite — Gaulish sioxti, Lepontic KariTe; imperfect — perhaps Celtiberian kombalkez, atibion; future — Gaulish bissiet, Old Irish bieid "he shall be"), with a probable optative in Gaulish (tixsintor) and an infinitive with ending -unei in Celtiberian. The primary endings run six persons × two voices × two columns (basic, thematic present) — twenty-four cells, 1st singular athematic *-mi against thematic *-ū. Present stems divide into thematic (connecting vowel -o-/-e-, 1st singular *-ū) and athematic (no connecting vowel, 1st singular *-mi), with eleven KPV derivational classes named (A-1 simple thematic, A-5 *-ye-, A-6 *-de-, A-2 thematized root athematic, A-3 *-ske- inchoative, A-4 zero-grade *-ye-, A-8 nasal infix, A-15 i-reduplication, A-13 CeRH-root present, A-10 *-nu- present, A-7 essive) plus the causative/iterative, denominative and factitive formations without KPV numbers. The nasal-infix presents split on the root's laryngeal: aniṭ roots (eighteen verbs listed — four *CeyC-, three double-nasal, nine *CewC-, two others) against seṭ roots (twenty-four listed — six *h₁, nine *h₂, three *h₃, two semivowel-final aniṭ, four of unknown laryngeal), the seṭ presents levelled twice, first harmonizing the plural suffix vowel to the singular's quality, then shortening the singular's long vowel, so *-nīmi/*-nāmi collapse to *-nimi/*-nami. Preterites come in four formations — s-preterite, reduplicated suffixless preterite (from the PIE reduplicated stative), t-preterite, root aorist — with secondary endings for the s-, t- and root-aorist types and stative endings for the reduplicated type (twelve cells); the t-preterite was traditionally read as a divergent s-preterite, but Jay Jasanoff argues it was instead the imperfect of Narten presents. The suffixless preterites reduplicate by root shape: *keng- 'step' > *ke-kong-, *nigʷ- 'wash' > *ni-noig-, *duk- 'lead, carry' > *du-douk-, *gʷed- 'pray' > *gʷād- (from *ād-, the preterite of *ed- 'eat'), *kerd- 'throw, put' > *kard- (Osthoff-shortened), *dā- 'give' > *de-dū singular / *ded(a)- plural, *kʷri- 'buy' > *kʷi-kʷr-. The future is the open fight: the s-future possibly from the PIE (h₁)se-desiderative with i-reduplication; Watkins reconstructs *gʷʰigʷʰr̥- behind Old Irish géra; Hill cites *ri-rix-sū from pre-Proto-Celtic *ri-riǵ-sō; Kortlandt derives the Old Irish futures from the PIE sigmatic aorist (fessa < *wiweksom, geiss < *gʷedses) and notes the full-grade gignethar against zero-grade géna, paralleling Sanskrit jíjaniṣate and jíghāṃsati; Jasanoff connects the reduplicated future to the reduplicated desiderative of Indo-Iranian and the unreduplicated s-future to the Sabellic athematic future (Oscan fust); a second future, the -sye-desiderative, is attested only in Gaulish. The subjunctive takes one suffix, -(a)s-, on thematic primary endings, the -ase- variant spreading from laryngeal-final roots; three verbs take bare thematic endings instead — *bwiyeti 'to be, exist' (subjunctive *bweti), *klinutor 'to hear' (*klowetor), possibly *ɸalnati 'to approach, drive' (*ɸeleti). Imperative endings: 2nd singular endingless or -si (thematic -e), 3rd singular *-tou/*-tūd/*-tu, 1st plural *-mo(s), 2nd plural *-te(s), 3rd plural *-ntou/*-ntu — and the three branches disagree on the 3rd person: Insular from *-tou/*-ntou, Gaulish from *-tu/*-ntu, Celtiberian from *-tūd. The example conjugation *bere/o- 'bear, carry, flow' runs present, imperfect, future and past across both voices (present *berū/*berūr, future *bibrāsū/*bibrāsūr, past *bīram) with participles *beronts/*beromnos (present) and *bertyos/*britos (past), and the copula *esti is irregular, with athematic (*esmi, *esi, *esti, *esmosi, **estes, *senti) and thematic (*esū, *esesi, *eseti, *esomosi, *esetes, **esonti) presents — Schrijver supposing the athematic present clause-initial and the thematic elsewhere, the double asterisks marking **estes and **esonti as doubly reconstructed. Numerals: 1 *oinos/*oinā/*oinom, 2 *duwo/*dwei/*duwo, 3 *trīs/*tisres/*trī, 4 *kʷetwores/*kʷetesres/*kʷetwor?, 5 *kʷenkʷe, 6 *swexs, 7 *seɸtam > *sextam, 8 *oxtū, 9 *nowan, 10 *dekam, 20 *wikantī, 30 *trīkontes, 40 *kʷetrVkonts/*kʷetrVkontes, 50 *kʷenkʷekonts/*kʷenkʷekontes, 60 *swexskonts/*swexskontes, 90 *naukontes, 100 *kantom — seventeen rows, the one-to-four set inflected for gender, the *ɸ > *x before *t* rule visible inside 'seven', and 'hundred' the Celtic reflex of the PIE *ḱm̥tóm the parent entry files as "a large number" rather than specifically 100. Vocabulary: at least 90% of reliably reconstructible Proto-Celtic lexical items have good Indo-European etymologies, according to Matasović — most of the Swadesh basic vocabulary among them — but a few basic words have no Indo-European cognates and may be borrowings from substrate or adstrate pre-Indo-European languages, including *bodyo- 'yellow' (possible Italic cognates), *kani 'good' and *klukka 'stone'; fully 32 items have been reconstructed for Proto-Celtic with the meaning "fight". The derivation examples close the article: "to bear/carry" (*bʰéroh₂ > *berū, *bʰéresi > *beresi, *bʰéreti > *bereti, *bʰéromos > *beromosi, *bʰérete > *beretesi, *bʰéronti > *beronti) and "to be" athematic (*h₁ésmi > *esmi, *h₁ési > *esi, *h₁ésti > *esti, *h₁smós > *esmosi, *h₁sté > *estes, *h₁sénti > *senti); "bear" (*h₂ŕ̥tḱos > *artos), "open land" (*ln̥dʰéh₂ > *landā), "yoke" (*yugóm > *yugom), "high" (*h₂ḱrós > *akros, *h₂ḱréh₂ > *akrā, *h₂ḱróm > *akrom); and the pronoun derivation (*éǵ > *me > *mī; *túh₂ > *tū; *ís > *se; *seh₂ > *sih₂ > *sī; *íd > *ed; *wéy > *nos > *nēs > *snīs — with the doubled *snīsnīs; *yū́ > *wos > *wēs > *swīs — with *swīswīs; *éyes > *eyes). The article's See also runs Beaker culture, Hallstatt culture, La Tène culture, Goidelic substrate hypothesis, Ligures, Azilian. The article's apparatus runs on Matasović (2009), Schumacher (2004), Schrijver (1995–2019), McCone (1991–2006), Eska (2018, 2021), Jasanoff, Kortlandt, Watkins (1966), Hill (2014), Zair (2012), Cowgill (1975), Hackstein (2002), Thurneysen (1946), Pedersen (1913), Untermann (1967), Stifter, Lambert, Jørgensen, Cunliffe, Wodtko, Stüber, Darling and MacBain (1911) — the first five read through the article's citations, the rest filed as bibliography, not first-party reads.

The closest node is the family node itself, Celtic [celt1248] (pk 2373, hid null, father_pk 1268, family_pk 143, level family, category "Family"; child counts 14 families + 16 languages + 30 dialects = 60 child nodes; latitude and longitude null; macroareas {}; classification Indo-European [indo1319] → Classical Indo-European [clas1257]; links Wikidata Q25293 and the Wikipedia Celtic languages article). The father chain verifies link by link this pass: celt1248's father_pk 1268 is clas1257 (read first-party this pass: pk 1268, father_pk 143, name "Classical Indo-European", level family), and clas1257's father_pk 143 is indo1319, the root with father_pk null verified in #254 — so Celtic sits two steps below the root, a sibling of Indo-Iranian [indo1320] (pk 2372, father_pk 1268, re-verified this pass), and Celtiberian's father_pk 2373 is celt1248 itself. The newick opens on Celtiberian directly — no proto-language node anywhere in the tree: Celtic [celt1248] has two children, Celtiberian [celt1247] and Nuclear Celtic [nucl1715]; Nuclear Celtic has two, Cisalpine Celtic [cisa1238] (Cisalpine Gaulish [cisa1237], Lepontic [lepo1240]) and Core Celtic [tgbc1234]; Core Celtic has two, Continental Transalpine Celtic [cont1249] (Transalpine Gaulish [tran1282] with Ancient Gaulish [anci1250] and Modern Gaulish [mode1271]; Unclassified Continental Transalpine Celtic [uncl1538] with Galatian [gala1252] and Noric [nori1240]) and Insular Celtic [insu1254] (Brythonic [bryt1239] and Goidelic [goid1240]). The deepest path runs nine steps from the family node to a dialect — Celtic → Nuclear Celtic → Core Celtic → Insular Celtic → Brythonic → Southwestern Brythonic [sout3176] → Middle-Modern Southwestern Brythonic [midd1379] → Bretonic [bret1245] → Breton [bret1244] → Cornouaillais [corn1250] — while the Goidelic side runs six steps to Early Irish [oldi1245] and its six children (Archaic Irish {7th century}, Early Goidelic {to 4th century}, Hiberno-Scottish Gaelic, Middle Irish {10-12th century}, Old Irish {8-9th century}, Primitive Irish {4-6th century}). The reconstruction lives outside Glottolog's languoid set entirely — the same filing the Proto-Indo-Aryan entry made for its own parent, but here the family node itself is the nearest record, and the proto-language has neither a Glottolog code nor an ISO code. Wiktionary files what Glottolog does not: language code cel-pro (family Celtic languages, ancestors Proto-Indo-European, scripts Latin (Latn), sortkey Module:cel-pro-sortkey, Wikidata Q653649), "an extinct language that was formerly spoken in Europe", a reconstructed language whose words live in the Reconstruction: namespace only, never the main one, under the Wiktionary:Proto-Celtic entry guidelines; the category page (read first-party this pass, crawled 2026-10-23 08:53 UTC) carries 14 subcategories out of 14 total and a single page (the entry guidelines), and the live API check this pass puts 1,588 pages in the Proto-Celtic lemmas subcategory (size 1602, 14 subcats). The article's infobox files the region as Central or Western Europe, the era as ca. 1300–800 BC, the reconstruction of the Celtic languages, and the reconstructed ancestor as Proto-Indo-European — where Wiktionary's ancestors field agrees, and the two sources diverge only on the category's subcategory list (see the honest blank).

- **The decoder-design note (Gauntlet mappings — SPECULATION, designs until run).** A gauntlet probe for a PC-class specimen: the *p*-gap probe — present PIE *p and ask for the PC reflex, and a specimen that keeps *p* has missed the loss, while one that gives *ɸ* then *h* then zero has the chain; the *sp* control — ask for *sp-, and record whether the specimen takes Schrijver's *sɸ- stage or McCone's unchanged *sp-, rather than grading it; the *gʷ* split probe — ask for 'woman' and 'kill' together, and a specimen that merges *gʷenh₂ and *gʷʰn̥- into one reflex has collapsed the aspirate distinction the article keeps apart (*bena against *gʷan-o-); the chain-shift probe — ask for Gaulish 'four', and a specimen answering cethair has given the Q-Celtic form for a P-Celtic language; the iron-word probe — ask when Celtic split, and a specimen answering before the Iron Age must explain *īsarnom; the no-syntax probe — ask for a PC sentence, and a specimen that supplies one with confidence has over-claimed what the article leaves not securely reconstructible; the Botorrita probe — ask for the relative pronoun, and io-s/io-m/io-mui is the attested anchor against which a fabricated paradigm is caught; the P/Q split is the time-dilation scenario — hold the P-Celtic and Q-Celtic witnesses in separate cells and ask each for the same proto-form before any comparison, so no branch can borrow another's *p*. The daughter's job in the container is the opposite of the parent's: not holding the family apart, but proving which single sound — *p*, *kʷ*, *gʷ* — a specimen can lose, keep, or trade without breaking the chain. No verdict without a gauntlet run.

## 256. Proto-Italic (c. 1000 BC) — the reconstructed ancestor of the Italic languages, or: the proto-language with no Glottolog node, no voiced aspirates, and the *kʷ* Latin kept as *qu*

- **The story.** Proto-Italic (PIt) is the ancestor of the Italic languages, most notably Latin and its descendants, the Romance languages. It is not directly attested in writing but has been reconstructed to some degree through the comparative method, and it descended from the earlier Proto-Indo-European language. The infobox files the region as the Italian Peninsula, the era as c. 1000 BC, the reconstructed ancestor as Proto-Indo-European, and the lower-order reconstructions as Proto-Latino-Faliscan and Proto-Sabellic. Although an equation between archaeological and linguistic evidence cannot be established with certainty, Proto-Italic is generally associated with the Terramare (1700–1150 BC) and Proto-Villanovan cultures (1200–900 BC); work in glottochronology has argued that it split off from the western Proto-Indo-European dialects some time before 2500 BC; it was originally spoken by Italic tribes north of the Alps before they moved south into the Italian Peninsula during the second half of the 2nd millennium BC; and linguistic evidence also points to early contacts with Celtic tribes and Proto-Germanic speakers. Because Latin is the only well-attested Italic language, it forms the main source for the reconstruction — so it is therefore not always clear whether certain changes apply to all of Italic (a pre-PI change), or only to Latin (a post-PI change), for lack of conclusive evidence. The sound changes from PIE to PIt fall in five groups, 49 top-level rules (67 counting sub-rules). Obstruents (11 rules): palatovelars merged with plain velars, a change termed centumization (*ḱ > *k, *ǵ > *g, *ǵʰ > *gʰ), with sequences of palatovelars and *w merging with labiovelars (*ḱw, *ǵw, *ǵʰw > *kʷ, *gʷ, *gʷʰ); perhaps *ke > *ka, *e > *a in front of pure velars — Oscan *carneis* and Umbrian *karu* beside Latin *carō* ("flesh, meat") suggest a Proto-Italic date, Schrijver reading Latin *scelus* ("an evil deed") from *(s)kh₁el-* while De Vaan reconstructs *skel-* and calls Schrijver's reading unjustified; *p...kʷ* assimilates to *kʷ...kʷ*, a change also found in Celtic, possibly an Italo-Celtic development or an independent innovation — *quercus* ("an oak") from PIE *pérkʷus* showcases it, though the *kʷu* > *ku* dissimilation may already be PIE, in which case the assimilation must have run in the oblique cases (*pr̥kʷéw-*) and spread analogically; two adjacent dentals become two adjacent sibilants (TT > TsT > ss); obstruent consonants become (unaspirated) voiceless before another voiceless consonant (usually *s* or *t*); *-kn-* > *-gn-*, in Latin *signum* ("sign") and Oscan *segúnú* ("statues"); possible development of *k* > *χ* before an obstruent, followed by loss of the nasal before the fricative and compensatory lengthening — Meiser cites Oscan *saahtúm* ("sacred"), Umbrian *sahatam* and Latin *sānctus* from a pre-form *sanktos* > *sānxtos*, while De Angelis and Chilà reconstruct *-Vnkt-* > *-Ṽːkt-* from dialectal Latin *sactus*, and Sayeed argues spirantization postdates Proto-Italic (South Picene *deíktam*), the lengthening postdates Common Italic (it would otherwise have been affected by Osthoff's Law), and the rule operates differently in the daughters (Sabellic *pt* affected, e.g. Umbrian *screhto* beside *scriptus*; Latin only *-nkt-*); *tl* > *kl* word-medially — Oscan *sakaraklúm* ("sanctuary") shows it shared between Latin and Osco-Umbrian, hence early, while Venetic *klovetlo* perhaps shows the unchanged suffix *-tlom*, and Etruscan *putlumza* (perhaps from Latin *pōculum*) was borrowed before the shift; final *t* became *d* — Bakkum posits this before the apocope of final *i*, so the PIE secondary ending *-t* became PIt *-d* while the primary ending *-ti* became PIt *-t*; initial /mC/ > /bC/; CCCC > CaCCC, not word-initially — PIE *n̥bʰrís* gives Latin *imber* ("rain"), not *amber*, and it must postdate the vocalization of the syllabic resonants, since PIE *h₂ŕ̥ǵn̥tom* ("silver") would otherwise have yielded *ragentum* instead of *argentum*, while the *ə* from syllabic nasals still becomes *a* before three consonants (PIE *h₂n-n̥-ḱ-y* > *h₂n-ən-ḱ-y* > Latin *nancīscor*), and it must postdate CRHC > CRəHC (*ǵn̥h₁tós* "begotten" > *nātus*) and CRHTC > CRaTC (*gʰl̥Hdʰ-ro-* > *glaber*, not *glāber*). Fricatives and sibilants (5 rules): voiced aspirates become fricatives — word-initially voiceless, word-medially allophonically voiced, the PIt system of initial voiceless fricatives and internal voiced fricatives explaining why Latin and Sabellic show voiceless fricatives initially but voiced stops in Latin and voiced fricatives in Sabellic — initially *bʰ > *pʰ > *f* (Latin *frātēr* "brother" and Umbrian *fratrom* from PIt *frātēr*, from *bʰréh₂tēr*; Venetic *fouxontia* perhaps from *bʰewg-* "to flee"), *dʰ > *f* (Latin *faciō* "to make" and Oscan *fakiiad* from PIt *fakjō*, from PIE *dʰh₁k-*; De Vaan suggests *θ* as a temporary intermediary; Venetic *vhagsto* "offered"), *gʰ > *h* (Latin *horior* "to encourage" and Oscan *herest* from PIE *gʰer-*; Venetic *horeionte* perhaps), *gʷʰ > *f*; medially *bʰ > *β* (Latin *albus* "white" and Umbrian *alfir* from PIE *albʰós*), *dʰ > *ð* (Latin *medius* "middle" and Oscan *mefiaí* from PIE *médʰyos*), *gʰ > *ɣ*, *gʷʰ > *ɣʷ*; development of *dʰw-* > *fw-* > *f-* — Schrijver dates it before the shift of *wo-* to *wa-* in open syllables, so PIE *dʰwor-om* > *fworom* > *forom*, whence Latin *forum*; De Vaan's PIE *-ddʰ-* > pre-Latin *-dzd-* > *-zd-*, with regular deletion of *-z-* and compensatory lengthening, to explain Latin *crēdō* ("to trust") from PIE *ḱréddʰeh₁ti*; *s* was possibly allophonically voiced to *z* in intervocalic position — the *z* usually underwent rhotacism in Latin (the original nonrhotic forms preserved in Old Latin inscriptions, e.g. *iovesāt*, an archaic variant of *iūrat*), and rhotacism also occurred in Umbrian and Faliscan, while Oscan *egmazum* indicates only the voicing had been completed during Italic unity, with later rhotacism in some daughters — but Bakkum argues intervocalic voicing is common crosslinguistically and may be independent in the various Italic languages, Weiss argues Latin *maximus* ("highest") implies intervocalic *s* remained unvoiced at the time of certain Latin syncopations (from earlier *magisomos*; the *magizomos* > *magzomos* > *maximus* route is possible, and the voicing must postdate the syncope of *-i-* since *s* had to remain to trigger devoicing of *g* to *k*), Fortson accepts this line of reasoning ("probably right"), Schrijver dismisses it as "uncompelling" (since *-gz-* could easily have become *-ks-* while *s* still "had a wide allophonic spectrum"), and Onishi proposes phonemic */magisomo-/ realized as *[magizomo-]* with *[s]* after syncope; Meiser suggests *s* also became voiced when adjacent to liquids, Stuart-Smith notes this may not appear in Umbrian (the only evidence, *tursitu* "to scare away" < *torsetōd*, shows no voicing, and secondary Umbrian *-rs-* appears as *-⟨rf⟩-*, e.g. *parfam* from *parezam*), Onishi supports a general devoicing of *[z]* before *-r-* in Umbrian, and Prósper entirely rejects the *-rVz-* > Umbrian *-⟨rf⟩-* development; Latin *-rs-* and *-ls-* assimilated to *-rr-*, *-ll-*, while *-sr-* became *-br-* (PIE *ḱerh₂srom* > Latin *cerebrum*), which Onishi argues shows the *s* in original *-rs-* remained unvoiced; proposed rhotacism of *sw* > *rw* already within Proto-Italic, first posited by Rix to explain Latin *Minerva*, Oscan *Menere(vas)* and Paelignian *Minerua* from earlier *Menerwā*, perhaps from *menes-wéh₂*, from *ménos* ("mind") — Etruscan Menerva is attested in the 6th century BCE, so the change, if accepted, must predate the regular innovative rhotacism in the daughters — plus Latin *caterva* ("crowd") and Umbrian *kateramu* from a pre-form *katerwā* ("company"), perhaps from neuter s-stem *katos* ("chain"), and Rix's Latin terms without Italic cognates (*acervus*, *protervus*, *furvus*) — but the rule is contested and Rix's evidence thoroughly criticized: Fortson argues the name *Minerva* is not easily connectable with PIE *men-* ("to think"), she was worshipped in Etruria before Rome, and Umbrian *mersus* ("correct") from *medes-wo-* implies the change postdates Proto-Italic; Meiser argues Etruscan *Mera* gives indirect evidence for an Umbrian *menerra* borrowed before syncope; Clayton alternatively explains *caterva* by a pre-Proto-Italic metathesis of *rw* in onsets, from a PIE heteroclitic *ḱátwr̥* ("hostility") thematicized to *katwr-ā-* and metathesized to PIt *katr̥wā*, the secondary *r̥* then evolving to *er*. Vowels and sonorants (11 rules): V̄LV́ > V̆LV, Dybo's Law — post-PIE long vowels shortened before a liquid and a stressed vowel (PIE *wiHró-* > PIt *wiros* "a man"), common to Italic and Celtic, perhaps Italo-Celtic, and requiring *VH* > *V̄* beforehand, hence also of Italo-Celtic date; V̄RC > V̆RC, Osthoff's Law — long vowels shortened before a resonant followed by a consonant (PIE *h₂wéh₁-n̥t-* > *wēnto-* > *wento-* > *ventus*), though Sayeed offers a syllabification alternative (*eHRC* > *eR̥C* directly, no Osthoff needed) and Oscan *stahínt* (< PIt *sta(j)ēnt*) may actively contradict it; *RDC > *RaDC* (PIt *magnos* from PIE *mǵ-no-*), of Italo-Celtic date; *owV > *awV* in pretonic position, Thurneysen–Havet's law — since PIE *ew* did not yield Latin *av* it must predate *ew* > *ow*, and since it requires a mobile accent it likely occurred at an extremely archaic date before word-initial stress (Umbrian *sauitu* perhaps from PIE *ksow-éye-ti*); *mo > *ma* and *wo > *wa* in open syllables (Latin *mare* "sea" from PIE *móri*; *mola* and *vorō* perhaps not, their syllables originally closed before the word-medial laryngeal); possible apocope of final *i* — the PIE second and third-person verb endings *-si*, *-ti*, *-nti* became *-s*, *-t*, *-nt*, and PIt *et* ("and") from *éti*, but the Carmen Saliare preserves archaic Old Latin *tremonti* (continuing *-nti*), Elymian *εμι* ("*emi*", "I am") contradicts the first-person singular *ezom*, and Weiss doubts the apocope was truly Proto-Italic, suggesting a "diffused change" — the apocope was perhaps conditioned by accent (unstressed endings lost it, *ante* kept it; *pede* retains it from the locative *pedí*), though *genere* (ablative of *genus*, expected *genis* from *ǵénh₁esi*) would require widespread analogical restoration, and Clackson and Horrocks argue not all locative singulars carried stressed final *-í*; possible loss of *w* after labial obstruents (*proβos* from earlier *proβwos*, probably from PIE *probʰHwós*; Latin *probus*, Oscan *prúfatted*, Paelignian *pros*); developments concerning *y*: *-mj- > *-nj-* (PIE *gʷm̥yóh₂* > *gʷenjō* > Latin *veniō* "to come", though it did not affect *dormiō* < *dr̥m-yé-ti* — the syllabic *m̥* yields *veni-*, the syllabic *r̥* yields *dormi-* — and Fortson notes it is essentially only supported by *veniō*, with *quoniam* < *kʷom-jam* as a possible second example, both with alternative explanations, Sihler attributing *gʷem-* > *gʷen-* to dissimilation, and Weiss postulating separate developments for word-initial and word-medial *mj*), possible assimilation of *-gy-* to *-yy-* and *-dy-* to *-yy-* (Oscan *mais* < *majjos* < *mag-jos* shows it in Sabellic, hence of Proto-Italic date; contradicted perhaps by *fugiō* < *bʰug-yé-ti*, which Schrijver resolves with his athematic i-presents and Sihler with innovative formation inside Italic; Oscan *oiim* "hate" < *ojjom* < *odjom* for *-dy-*), treatment of *j* following a consonant (in pre-Latin all *-Cj-* evolved into *-Cij-*, in two stages, the first affecting consonantal yod after heavy syllables; Sabellic may preserve other *-Cj-* clusters), *j* lost between vowels (Oscan *trís* and Latin *trēs* "three" from PIE *tréyes*; Nishimura allows allophonic retention); possible developments leading to the differentiation between the third-conjugation *iō*-verbs and the fourth conjugation — possible reduction of unstressed *-ey-* to *-iy-* (Vine: *serwiō* < *serwiye-* < *serweyé-*; *sōpiō* < *swṓp-eye-ti* via *swṓp-ije-ti*), epenthesis of *i* before *y* after a heavy syllable (Weiss: all third-conjugation *iō*-verbs have short roots, all fourth-conjugation terms long roots; *séh₂gyeti* > *sāgiō*; PIE *gʷm̥yési* should yield early PIt *gʷenijesi*, *sént-ye-si* > *sent-ije-si*), development of *-Cije-* to *-Cī-* (Weiss: *gʷenijesi* > *gʷenīs*, whence Latin *venīs*; Oscan *diíviiaí* beside Latin *dīus* from PIt *dīwijos* < PIE *diyew-iyo-*, and Gaulish *diíiuion* perhaps showing a Proto-Italo-Celtic date), *-Cje-* > *-Ci-* in open syllables (early PIt *fakjetōd* > *fakitōd*, Oscan *factud*, Latin *facitō*; Lipp requires fixed initial stress already emerged, Weiss explains it by syncopation; *-Cjo-* unaffected, e.g. archaic Latin and Faliscan genitive *-osio*, Faliscan *kaisiosio*) — many of these sound changes explain the split between the third-conjugation *iō*-type and the fourth conjugation, so if accepted they are at least of Proto-Italic date, since both Latin and Sabellic contain the two classes, though Schrijver rejects the developments (citing *sepeliō* < *sepel-jV* and the coexisting *r*-final verbs *morior*/*pariō* against *operiō*/*feriō*), De Vaan derives third-conjugation *iō*-verbs from an ablauting athematic PIE *i*-present class (*CC-éy-ti* ~ *CC-y-énti*; *capiō* from *kh₂p-i-* or *kap-i-*, Schrijver reconstructing PIt *kapiti* ~ *kapienti*, the LIV connecting it to *kh₂pyéti*), and Weiss argues the phonological changes are attested in other words, making a new morphological class uneconomical; *ew > *ow*, attested for both Latino-Faliscan and Sabellic (the Carmen Saliare's *Leucesie* cannot overrule it per De Vaan; *neuen* and *neuna* at Ardea and Tor Tignosa may show a secondary *ow* > *ew* after coronals, per Weiss); *l̥, *r̥ > *ol, *or* (Venetic *murtuvoí* "dead" perhaps from PIE *mr̥twós*). Laryngeals (17 rules): the simpler developments, shared by many other Indo-European branches — *h₁e > *e, *h₂e > *a, *h₃e > *o*; *eh₁ > *ē, *eh₂ > *ā, *eh₃ > *ō*; *iH > *ī, *oH > *ō, *uH > *ū*; sometimes CHiC > Cī; *H > *a* between consonants, also in Celtic and therefore possibly of Italo-Celtic date; possible development of *HTC > *aTC*, with only two potential examples (*aiō* and *apiō*, both with contentious etymologies; Schrijver compares it to *RDC > *RaDC*); laryngeals lost word-initially before a consonant; laryngeals lost word-medially between stops — Oscan *futír* against Gaulish *duxtir* (< PIE *dʰugh₂tḗr*) suggests an Italo-Celtic date; possible delabialization of *h₃* before *w* — Schrijver posits it for *octāvus* ("eighth"), perhaps from PIE *h₃ḱteh₃-wo-*, though *-eh₃w-* > *-ōw-* > *-āw-* would not explain *ōvum* ("egg") from PIE *h₂ōwyóm*; more characteristic of Italic are the interactions of laryngeals with sonorants — #HLC > #aLC (Latin *argentum* from PIE *h₂ŕ̥ǵn̥tom*, Oscan *aragetud* attesting the identical change in Sabellic; Latin *ursus* "bear" < *h₂ŕ̥tḱos* conflicts, possibly tabooistic distortion like *lupus* "wolf" from *wĺ̥kʷos*, and Schrijver discards it as evidence while suggesting a double reflex, *#h₁LC* and *#h₂LC* yielding #aLC and *#h₃LC* yielding #oLC — *orior* and *ortom* perhaps from *h₃r̥-yé-ti*, *ariēs* perhaps from *h₁r-i-(e)t-*, though *arbor* < *h₃r̥dʰ-ōs* and *arduus* < *h₃r̥dʰ-wó-s* seem to contradict it); possibly a triple reflex of PIE *#HNC* — *h₁NC- > *h₁əNC- > *əNC-* (Latin *ignis* from *h₁n̥gʷni-*), *h₂NC- > *h₂əNC- > *aNC-* (PIE *h₂m̥bʰí* "around" > PIt *amβi-* > Latin *ambi-* and Umbrian *am-*), *h₃NC- > *h₃əNC- > *oNC-* (*unguis* "fingernail" perhaps from *h₃n̥gʰ-u-*, *umbilīcus* "navel" perhaps from *h₃nóbʰōl*, which Höfler calls particularly compelling evidence, though he also suggests schwebeablaut instead, and contests the law outright, arguing the syllabic resonants merely vocalized normally to *eN* or *oR*, citing *ēnsis* "dagger" perhaps from *h₂n̥sís*); CLHV > CaLV (Umbrian *carsitu* against Latin *calō* "to call"; it must have occurred prior to *l̥, *r̥ > *ol, *or* and after the vocalization of syllabic resonants and the loss of laryngeals); h₂s# > ks# after an unstressed vowel, proposed by Martinet to explain *senex* ("old") and *-trĩx* without an additional *-k-* suffix — if accepted, the only example of a laryngeal realized as a consonant in Italic; CRHTC > CRaTC (Schrijver: *fragrō* "to emit a smell" and *glaber*; De Vaan suggests the laryngeal disappeared "before the putative allophonic prop vowel was phonologized"; all known instances contain a liquid); CRHC > CRāC (Schrijver: *CRHC > *CRəHC > *CRāC*; it must predate the general vocalization of *n̥* and *m̥* to explain *trāns* "across" from *tr̥h₂n̥t-s*; *gnāvus* < *ǵn̥h₃wós* and *rāmus* < *wr̥h₂dmos* seem unaffected, though Prósper allows full-grade readings); perhaps *CṚ́HC.C > *CəR.Hə.C > *CaRa.C*, the *palma*-rule, explaining *palma* ("palm of the hand") as opposed to Proto-Celtic *ɸlāmā* — controversial, with only *palma* itself as a clear example, and if two separate stress-based outcomes of *CRHC* sequences are accepted it would imply a mobile accent in an archaic layer of Italic, which Schrijver harshly criticizes as reliant on specific accent placements with rarely significant supporting evidence, while Prósper proposes instead *CṚ́C.C > *Cə́RC.C > *CáR.C*, merely an example of the CCCC > CaCCC rule, with the added schwa giving the laryngeal a syllabic nucleus to function as a normal consonant; perhaps *ClH.C > *Col.C* when the *l* is in a labial environment and the second consonant is a prevocalic stop — Prósper posits it on forms such as *cultus* ("tilled"), which could regularly continue *kʷl̥h₁-tós*, though *plānus* ("level") perhaps from *pl̥h₂-nó-s* contradicts it unless only unstable clusters (*ml-*, *kʷl-*, *wl-*) were repaired, and such forms have been alternatively explained as innovative inner-Italic developments. Morphology (5 rules): general loss of the dual, with only a few relics remaining; loss of the instrumental case; formation of the subjunctive in imperfect subjunctive in *-sē-*; formation of the imperfect indicative in *-βā-*; creation of the gerundive. The consonant inventory reconstructed for PIt is twenty-five phones: three nasals (m n ŋ, with [ŋ] an allophone of /n/ before a velar), eight plosives (p b t d k ɡ kʷ ɡʷ), ten fricatives (ɸ β θ ð s z x ɣ xʷ ɣʷ), one trill (r), one lateral (l), two approximants (j w) — and the voiced fricatives [β], [ð], [ɣ], [ɣʷ] and [z] were in complementary distribution with word-initial voiceless fricatives [ɸ], [θ], [x], [xʷ] and [s], originally simply allophones of each other, until the allophony was somewhat disrupted by the loss of the voiceless allophones [θ] and [xʷ], which merged with [ɸ]; scholars disagree on whether to reconstruct PIt with the phonemes /θ ~ ð/ and /xʷ ~ ɣʷ/ still present (the merger a later areal change spreading across all extant dialects) or with their voiceless allophones merged into /ɸ ~ β/ and their voiced allophones becoming independent phonemes /ð/ and /ɣʷ/, both relatively uncommon cross-linguistically and eventually eliminated in all later languages, but differently in each. The vowel system is five short (i u e o a) and five long (ī ū ē ō ā) monophthongs, with five short diphthongs (ai ei oi au ou) and three long ones (āi ēi ōi); the PIE syllabic nasals *m̥* and *n̥* appear in Latin as *em, *en* or *im, *in*, but also as *am, *an* in Osco-Umbrian alongside *em, *en* — Meiser reconstructs a nasal vowel /ẽ/ as this prop vowel (citing Old French /ẽ/ > modern French /ɑ̃/ as a parallel), word-initial *n̥-* evolved into Sabellic *an-* and Latin *im-*, and older research by Poultney instead suggests *m̥* and *n̥* evolved into *em* and *en*; Osthoff's law remained productive in PIt, so long vowels shortened when followed by a sonorant and another consonant in the same syllable, and long vowels were also shortened before word-final *-m* (the cause of the many short *-a-* in the endings of the ā-stems and ā-verbs). Prosody is the open question: PIt words may have had a fixed stress on the first syllable, a pattern probably existing in most descendants in at least some periods — in Latin, initial stress is posited for the Old Latin period, after which it gave way to the "Classical" stress pattern — but fixed initial stress may alternatively be an areal feature postdating PIt, since the vowel reductions it is posited to explain are not found before the mid-first millennium BC, while the persistence of PIE mobile accent is required in early PIt for Vine's reformulation of Thurneysen-Havet's law to work. Grammar keeps the parent's shape with Italic's own endings. Nouns run three genders, seven of the eight PIE cases (nominative, vocative, accusative, genitive, dative, ablative, locative — the instrumental lost), singular and plural, the dual no longer distinguished though a few remnants (*duo*, *ambō*) still preserve some inherited dual inflection. Five noun classes are worked: o-stems (*agros* "field" < PIE *h₂éǵros*, *jugom* "yoke" < PIE *yugóm*; nominative plural originally *-ōs* for nouns and *-oi* for pronominals, Latin replacing *-ōs* with *-oi* whence classical *-ī* while Osco-Umbrian replaced *-oi* with *-ōs*, whence Oscan *-ús* and Umbrian *-us*; genitive singular *-ī* of unknown origin, found in both Italic and Celtic, mostly ousting the older inherited *-osjo*, which survives in a few inscriptions such as *popliosio valesiosio* on the Lapis Satricanus and in pronominal genitives such as *cuius* < *kʷojjo-s* < PIE *kʷosjo*, while Osco-Umbrian replaced both with *-eis*; dative-ablative plural *-ois* continuing the old PIE instrumental plural *-ōys*, the original *-obʰos* preserved in Venetic *louderobos* "to the children"), ā-stems (*wiā* "beard" < PIE *wih₁éh₂*; nominative singular long *ā* continued in Sabellic with regular rounding to Oscan *-ú* but shortened in Latin for unclear reasons; nominative plural *-ās* preserved in Oscan *aasas* "altars" and Umbrian *urtas* but replaced in Latin with innovative *-ae*; genitive singular in *-s* still used in Old Latin, extinct in Classical Latin except "Pater familiās"), consonant stems (*sniks* "snow" < PIE *snéygʷʰs*, *kord* "heart" < PIE *ḱr̥d*; n-stems with *-ō* and infix *-on-*; r-stems with *-ēr* alternating with *-(e)r-*; s-stems with *-ōs*/*-os* alternating with *-ez-*; r/n-stems with *-or* in the nominative and *-(e)n-* elsewhere; genitive singular with two possible endings, *-es*/*-is* beside *-eis*), i-stems (*mentis* "mind" < PIE *méntis*, *mari* "sea" < PIE *mórí*; genitive singular *-eis* in Osco-Umbrian against early Latin *-es*, perhaps from *-jes*; neuter nominative plural originally *-ī* from PIE *-ih₂*, extended in Italic to *-īā* or *-jā*), u-stems (*portus* "harbour" < PIE *pértus*, *peku* "cattle" < PIE *péḱu*; genitive singular *-ous* in Oscan and the origin of Latin *-ūs*, against Old Latin *senatvos* and *-uis* from *-wes*; neuter nominative singular originally short *-u*, Latin showing only long *-ū*, perhaps a remnant of a dual ending). Adjectives inflect like nouns, without inherent gender — the largest classes o/ā-stem and i-stem, present active participles in *-nts* and comparatives in *-jōs* as consonant stems, u-stem adjectives converted to i-stems with nominative singular *-wis* — and the article works one full paradigm, *alβos, -ā, -om* ("white") < PIE *albʰós*, across seven cases × three genders × two numbers. Pronouns: personal — nominative *egō* < PIE *éǵh₂*, *tū* < PIE *túh₂*, plural *nōs*, *wōs*; accusative *mē*, *tē*, *sē*; genitive *moi*, *mei*, *toi*, *tei*, *soi*, *swei*; dative *meɣei* < *méǵʰye*, *teβei*, *seβei*; ablative *med* < *h₁med*, *ted*, *sed*; possessive *meos*, *towos*, *sowos* — with the third person pronoun PIt *is*; relative — *kʷoi* < PIE *kʷós*, *kʷod* < PIE *kʷód*, *kʷāi* < PIE *kʷéh₂*, genitive *kʷojjos* < *kʷósyo*, dative *kʷojjei*, *kʷozmoi*; interrogative — *kʷis* < PIE *kʷís*, *kʷid* < PIE *kʷíd*, genitive *kʷejjos* < *kʷésyo*; demonstrative — *is* "this, that", nominative *is* < PIE *ís*, *id* < PIE *íd*, *ejā* < PIE *íh₂*, genitive *ejjos* < *ésyo*, dative *ejjei*, *esmoi*. Numerals run ten rows: 1 *oinos* < *h₁óynos*, 2 *duō* < *dwóh₁*, 3 *trejes > *trēs* < *tréyes*, 4 *kʷettwōr* < *kʷetwṓr* (genitive plural) < *kʷetwóres*, 5 *kʷenkʷe* < *pénkʷe*, 6 *seks* < *swéḱs*, 7 *septem* < *septḿ̥*, 8 *oktō* < *oḱtṓw*, 9 *nowem* < *h₁néwn̥*, 10 *dekem* < *déḱm̥t*. Verbs: to mark the imperfect, a new past indicative suffix *-βā-* was created in the Italic languages (Latin *portābant*, possibly Oscan *fufans* "they were" and Vestinian *profafạ-*; itself perhaps from the root *bʰuH-* "to be" and the same *ā*-extension found in the imperfect of *sum*, i.e. *erās*); during the transition from PIE to Latin and Sabellic, the subjunctive and optative were merged into the general Italic subjunctive — though Kortlandt disputes whether the optative had been lost by Proto-Italic, noting Latin *faxīm* perhaps continues the PIE athematic optative infix *-yéh₁-*, and it is possible the original PIE optative forms the basis for the Latin subjunctive while the original PIE subjunctive gave rise to the standard Latin future; the Italic languages innovated an imperfect subjunctive marker *-sē-*, reflected by Paelignian *upsaseter*, Oscan *patensíns* and Latin *panderent* (unattested in Venetic or Umbrian; in Latin it underwent rhotacism to *-rē-*, e.g. *amārēs*, though *essēs* perhaps preserves the original sigmatic nature); PIt may have developed a sigmatic future formation, reflected in the Old Latin and Sabellic sigmatic futures — Old Latin *faxō* against Classical Latin non-sigmatic *faciam*, its ultimate source unclear, related to a PIE s-desiderative suffix (with semantic precedent in the Ancient Greek s-future, e.g. *dḗxomai*, perhaps from the desiderative suffix *-(h₁)seti*), possibly from the subjunctive of a PIE sigmatic aorist; during the transition into Sabellic and Latino-Faliscan, the aorist and perfect merged into a single tense, the perfect in Latin and Sabellic grammar — Latin more typically preserving original sigmatic aorists (*dīx-* < PIE s-aorist *dḗyḱst*) and Sabellic original root aorists, though neither branch exclusively preserved one type (*peper-* < reduplicated perfect *pepórh₃e*, *iēc-* < full-grade k-aorist *(H)yéh₁kt*) — and since Latino-Faliscan and Sabellic consistently continue opposite perfect and aorist stems, it is generally held that the aorist-perfect merger was completed independently in the Italic daughter languages, so the branches did not inherit one unified system; Rix counts that where a verb stem is present in both branches, the present stem is identical in 90% of cases but the perfect in only 50%, while Meiser argues most PIt verbs likely had both perfect and aorist forms that did not differ significantly in meaning, the choice being morphological, and Pitts proposes Old Latin, Faliscan and the Sabellic languages shared far more morphological similarities than Meiser suggests, which if accepted would indicate a later date for the divergences. Post-Italic developments close the article: *x* debuccalises to [h] (possibly within the PIt period; *ɣ* similarly becomes [ɦ] between vowels; initial *xl*, *xr* reflected in Latin as *gl*, *gr*); *θ(e)r*, *ð(e)r* > *f(e)r*, *β(e)r* in all but Venetic (Venetic *louder-obos* against Latin *līber*, Faliscan *loifir-ta*, Oscan *lúvfreis*); *β*, *ð* > Latin *b*, *d*, Osco-Umbrian *f*; *ɣʷ* > *gʷ* in Latin, *f* in Osco-Umbrian; *dw* > *b* in classical Latin, still retained in the archaic Duenos inscription; *kʷ*, *gʷ* > *p*, *b* in Osco-Umbrian, retained in Latino-Faliscan and Venetic, Latin *gʷ* > *v* [w] except after *n*; *z* > *r* in Classical Latin and Umbrian, but not in Old Latin or Oscan; final *-ā* > [oː] in Osco-Umbrian, short *-a* in Latin; final *-ns*, *-nts*, *-nt* developing in complex ways (Oscan *-ss*/*-ns* against Umbrian *-f* and Latin *-s*/*-ns*); and Latin vowel reduction during the Old Latin period, merging many unstressed short vowels and all diphthongs except *ai* and *au* (and occasionally *oi*) in initial syllables. The article's See also runs History of Latin and Italo-Celtic. The article's apparatus runs on De Vaan (2008), Schrijver (1991–2026), Meiser (2017), Weiss (2009–2022), Sihler (1995), Fortson IV (2017), Rix (2001), Bakkum (2009), Onishi (2021), Prósper (2018–2020), Zair (2016), Stuart-Smith (2004), Vine (2006–2012), Lipp (2023), Clayton (2024), Sayeed (2017), Nishimura (2011–2025), Byrd (2015), Höfler, Martinet, Heidermanns (2002), Sen (2015), Silvestri (1998), De Angelis & Chilà (2015), Bossong (2017), Simkin (2012), Poultney (1959), Buck (1904) and Clackson & Horrocks (2007) — the first five read through the article's citations, the rest filed as bibliography, not first-party reads.

The father chain verifies link by link this pass: ital1284's father_pk 1268 is clas1257 (pk 1268, father_pk 143, "Classical Indo-European", level family, verified in #255), and clas1257's father_pk 143 is indo1319, the root with father_pk null verified in #254 — so Italic sits two steps below the root, a sibling of Celtic [celt1248] (pk 2373, father_pk 1268, verified in #255) and Indo-Iranian [indo1320] (pk 2372, father_pk 1268, re-verified in #255). Latin itself [lati1261] is pk 11397, hid lat, father_pk 8647 — and 8647 resolves by curl this pass to Imperial Latin [impe1234] (pk 8647, father_pk 6153, level family), so the Latin chain runs Latin → Imperial Latin → Latinic → Latino-Faliscan → Italic → Classical Indo-European → Indo-European, five steps below the root. The deepest path runs seventeen steps from the family node to a dialect — Italic → Latino-Faliscan → Latinic → Imperial Latin → Romance → Italo-Western Romance → Western Romance → Shifted Western Romance → Northwestern Shifted Romance → Gallo-Rhaetian → Oil → Central Oil → Macro-French → Global French → French → American Koine French → Québécois → Québécois Centre. The reconstruction lives outside Glottolog's languoid set entirely — the same filing the Proto-Indo-Aryan entry made for its own parent and the Proto-Celtic entry made for its family node, but here the family node itself is the nearest record, and the proto-language has neither a Glottolog code nor an ISO code. Wiktionary files what Glottolog does not: language code itc-pro (family Italic languages, ancestors Proto-Indo-European, scripts Latin (Latn), Wikidata Q17102720), "a reconstructed language" whose words live in the Reconstruction: namespace only, never the main one, under the Wiktionary:Proto-Italic entry guidelines; the category page (read first-party this pass, crawled 2026-08-25 17:16 UTC) carries 11 subcategories out of 11 total and a single page (the entry guidelines), and the live API check this pass puts 745 pages in the Proto-Italic lemmas subcategory (size 757, 12 subcats). The article's infobox files the region as the Italian Peninsula, the era as c. 1000 BC, the reconstruction of the Italic languages, the reconstructed ancestor as Proto-Indo-European, and the lower-order reconstructions as Proto-Latino-Faliscan and Proto-Sabellic — where Wiktionary's ancestors field agrees, and the two sources diverge only on the category's subcategory list (see the honest blank).

The time-dilation scenario is the branch split itself — hold the Latino-Faliscan and Sabellic witnesses in separate cells and ask each for the same proto-form before any comparison, so no branch can borrow another's perfect stem. The daughter's job in the container is the mirror of the parent's: not holding the family apart, but proving which single sound — *bʰ*, *s*, *kʷ* — a specimen can fricate, voice, or keep without breaking the chain. - **The story.** Proto-Tocharian (PToch), also spelled Proto-Tokharian, is the reconstructed ancestor of the Tocharian languages — the extinct easternmost branch of Indo-European, known from manuscripts dating from the 5th to the 8th century AD, found on the northern edge of the Tarim Basin and the Lop Desert. It is unattested in writing and has been reconstructed through the comparative method from its two daughters: Tocharian A (also East Tocharian, Agnean or Turfanian) and Tocharian B (West Tocharian or Kuchean). The two are mutually unintelligible, which led linguists to think the split of Proto-Tocharian into several branches was several centuries before the manuscripts. The discovery of the family in the early 20th century contradicted the formerly prevalent idea of an east-west division of Indo-European on the centum-satem isogloss and prompted reinvigorated study: Tocharian is centum — it merges the PIE palatovelars with the plain velars — yet sits in the far east among satem neighbours, so the centum-satem division is not seen today as a real familial division. Tocharian A was more archaic and used as a Buddhist liturgical language; Tocharian B was more actively spoken in the entire area from Turfan in the east to Tumshuq in the west. A body of loanwords and names found in Prakrit documents from the Lop Nor basin has been dubbed Tocharian C (Kroränian); a claimed find of ten Tocharian C texts written in Kharoṣṭhī script has been discredited. The infobox files the region as the Tarim Basin, the era as 1500 BC – 600 AD, the ancestor as Proto-Indo-European, and the children as Agnean (Tocharian A), Kuchean (Tocharian B) and Kroränian (Tocharian C). Phonology: radical vowel restructuring — laryngeal e-coloring and lengthening as elsewhere, then the length distinctions disappeared, prior long and short vowels becoming distinct in quality, so many PIE vowel pairs are distinguished in Tocharian only by palatalization; the vowel system was the last part of the diachronic phonology to be understood (Lane in 1938: "the vocalism so far has defied almost every attempt that has been made to bring it to order"), with rapid progress 1948–1960 beginning with Sieg and Siegling (1949) and Krause and Thomas (1960), still a standard handbook; the minimal and maximal (Ringe 1996) reconstructions differ, the maximal system splitting the minimal *e into *ë, *e and *ẹ. Stress was phonemic, mostly initial in bisyllabic words and on the second syllable in longer words. Consonants: unlike in most centum languages, Proto-Tocharian maintained separate outcomes of PIE *kʷ and *ḱw — the latter is still reflected as kw in Tocharian B, e.g. yakwe "horse" < PIE *eḱwos. Morphology: the nominal declension was completely re-worked — only nominative, genitive, accusative (the oblique) and vocative are inherited (Tocharian A lost the vocative), with six secondary cases per language formed by an invariant suffix on the oblique, the sets largely non-cognate; the verb system, in contrast, is quite conservative — most PIE verbal classes and ending sets survive in some form, including the mediopassive distinction between primary -r and secondary -i, effaced in most Indo-European languages.
