- **The story.** Proto-Albanian (PAlb; in German Uralbanisch) is the ancestral reconstructed language of Albanian, before the Gheg–Tosk dialectal diversification (before c. 600 CE). Albanoid and other Paleo-Balkan languages had their formative core in the Balkans after the Indo-European migrations in the region about 3000 to 2500 BCE. Whether descendants or sister languages of what was called Illyrian by classical sources, Albanian and Messapic, on the basis of shared features and innovations, are grouped together in a common branch in the current phylogenetic classification — Illyric in Hyllested & Joseph (2022) — and Greco-Phrygian is the Indo-European branch closest to the Albanian–Messapic one; the two branches form an areal grouping, often called "Balkan IE", with Armenian, and Hyllested & Joseph identify the highest shared number of innovations between (Proto-)Albanian and (Proto-)Greek. The precursor of Albanian can be considered a completely formed independent Indo-European language since at least the first millennium BCE, with the beginning of the early Proto-Albanian phase. It is reconstructed by way of the comparative method between the Tosk and Gheg dialects and between Albanian and other Indo-European languages, as well as through contact linguistics studying early loanwords: Doric Greek (West Greek) since the 7th century BCE, Latin (dated by De Vaan to 167 BCE – 400 CE), and Slavic (from 600 CE onward). The loanword evidence lets linguists construct in great detail the shape of native words at the points of major influxes. Periodization is contested — Orel distinguishes Early Proto-Albanian (spoken before the 1st century CE, before extensive Latin contact) and Late Proto-Albanian (after extensive Latin contact, ending with Slavic contacts in the 6th and 7th centuries CE, a period in which the structure of Proto-Albanian was "shattered"); Matasović distinguishes Pre-Proto-Albanian (essentially Orel's Early, ending in the 1st century BCE), Early Proto-Albanian (1st century BCE to the 6th century CE), and Late Proto-Albanian (the last two centuries of Orel's Late plus most of the unattested Old Albanian, halting before Turkish influence), with Gheg and Tosk splitting from Early Proto-Albanian, not Late; Demiraj places the emergence of Albanian from its parent after the 5th/6th-century boundary; De Vaan, in the 2018 Handbook of Comparative and Historical Indo-European Linguistics, follows Demiraj, calls the stage Proto-Albanian (PAlb) or Uralbanisch, and the earlier stage Pre-Proto-Albanian (Voruralbanisch or Frühuralbanisch), and the page follows Orel's paradigm. Vladimir Orel is one of the main modern linguists to have dealt with the passage from Proto-Indo-European to Proto-Albanian to Modern Albanian; other major work has been done by Eqrem Çabej and Shaban Demiraj, and much of the work on Proto-Albanian is published in German rather than English. De Vaan's 2018 staging cites Hock (2005), Klingenschmitt (1994), Matzinger (2006), B. Demiraj (1997) and Hamp (1992). Phonology: extensive recent studies have been published by Huld (1984), Beekes (1995), Shaban Demiraj (1996), Bardhyl Demiraj (1997), Orel (2000), Hock (2005), Matzinger (2006), Vermeer (2008), Schumacher (2013), and De Vaan (2018). Early Proto-Albanian possessed four distinctive short vowels, *a, *e, *i and *u — PIE *o had merged into *a — five long vowels, *ā, *ē, *ī, *ō and *ū, and four diphthongs, *ei, *ai, *eu and *au; stress was paradigmatic, with a base on the first syllable, varyingly barytonic, oxytonic and mobile, and unstressed vowels lost one mora — EPA *dáusas "ram" > *dauš > modern dash, EPA *dáusai "rams" > *dauši > modern desh, EPA *dwáigā "branch" > *déga > modern degë; in Late Proto-Albanian a new unstressed-vowel reduction emerged where *a reduced to *ë while all others were simply deleted. Late Proto-Albanian kept *a, *i and *u as distinctive short vowels, restored *o through loanwords, eliminated *e by breaking to *ie (later restored by the leveling of /ai/ to /e/), preserved only *ī of the long vowels (*ō was replaced by *ue, *ē merged into *ā, both rounded and raised to *o, *ū merged with *ui, rendering *y), and innovated phonemic nasal vowels *â, *ê, *î and *û — first all vowels before nasal consonants were nasalized, then the nasal consonant was lost in certain morphological contexts; the traditional view (Orel, Desnickaja) that distinctive nasalization was lost by Tosk but retained by Gheg is now challenged, after Sheper and Gjinari found Lab dialects in Kurvelesh that still have distinctive nasal vowels and Totoni found the same in the Lab speech of Borsh. Length ceased to be distinctive at the end of Late Proto-Albanian. The sonorants *n̥ and *m̥ both rendered Early Proto-Albanian *a — PIE *ǵʰh₂éns "goose" > EPA *gatā > Albanian gatë "heron", PIE *h₁ln̥gʷʰtós > EPA *lekta > Albanian lehtë. The dorsal consonants keep all three Indo-European series distinct, at least before front vowels: *ḱ > /θ/, *ǵ/*ǵʰ > /ð/; *k > /k/, *g/*gʰ > /g/; *kʷ > /s/ before high vowels and /k/ elsewhere, *gʷ/*gʷʰ > /z/ before high vowels and /g/ elsewhere — an archaic feature linking Albanian with the wider Paleo-Balkanic group, shared with Messapic and Armenian, though many Indo-Europeanists have classified Albanian as satem since the palatals give dental fricatives /θ/ and /ð/. History: Proto-Albanian speech met Ancient Greek in its earlier stage since the 7th century BCE, when Greek colonies were founded on the Adriatic coast; Doric Greek loans came directly from the colonists or through trade, and in the 5th–4th centuries BCE loans came from Ancient Macedonian; several Proto-Albanian terms survive in the lexicon of Hesychius of Alexandria and other ancient glossaries, some loaned into Doric Greek as early as the 7th century BCE. Contact with Latin began with the Illyro–Roman wars in the late 3rd and early 2nd centuries BCE, but most Latin influence came from the beginning of the common era, after the Great Illyrian Revolt of 6–9 CE; Latin loanwords were borrowed through the whole period of spoken Latin in the Western Balkans (c. 167 BCE – 400 CE), penetrating virtually all semantic fields — even the basic Christian terms are of Latin origin, and since they entered before the Gheg–Tosk split, Proto-Albanian speakers were christianized under the Latin sphere in the 4th century CE; Demiraj's era-note example is mjek "doctor" < Latin medicus. Georgiev proposed that Niš in Dardania evolved by Albanian phonetic laws (Naissos > Nish) and that between the 4th and 6th centuries AD Proto-Albanian and Proto-Romanian developed in the same central–northern Balkan area between Niš, Štip, Skopje and Sofia — a Dardania–Moesia location supported by Jokl, Weigand, Petrovic, Nicolaas van Wijk, Vermeer and Barić — while Breu holds the earliest Latin influence came from the coastal Western Balkans and that the Albanian–Romanian similarities were overestimated. The name Albanian came from the Albanoi, an Illyrian tribe in north-central Albania, and their city Albanopolis, between the Mat and Shkumbin rivers (the Albanoi may first appear as Abroi, a northern tribe of the Taulantii, near the Mat and Drin rivers); an Albanopolis is also mentioned in Scupi, and a similar sounding Albanos on a funeral inscription from the 2nd/3rd century CE in ancient Stobi, near Gradsko. The Mat river, mentioned in the 4th or 5th century CE, is one of the oldest recorded Albanian toponyms, and ancient toponyms reached their current forms through Albanian sound changes — Lissus > Lezhe, Drivastum > Drisht, Candavia > Kunavja, Drinus > Drin, Barbanna > Bunë, Mathis > Mat, Isamnus > Ishëm, Ardaxanos > Erzen — while the mountain range Sharr presupposes the Albanian development of ancient Scardus. Between the 7th and 12th centuries a network of cult institutions revived across the Albanian-speaking area, with the Theme of Dyrrhachium and the Archdiocese of Ohrid playing a central role; the lack of Old Church Slavonic terms in Albanian Christian terminology shows the Slavic missions did not involve Albanian-speakers. The rise of Tosk from Proto-Albanian was prompted before Slavic contacts circa 600 CE: Latin and ancient Greek loanwords are treated like native words with regard to Gheg–Tosk differences, but Slavic loans are not; the rhotacism n > r preceded contacts with Slavic from c. 600 CE, and the ancient toponym Lychnidus became Oh(ë)r(id), attested from 879 CE, through Tosk rhotacism and Eastern South Slavic l-vocalization, while Labëri came through the Slavic liquid metathesis (South Slavic *Labanьja < Late Common Slavic *Olbanьja "Albania") reborrowed into Albanian while rhotacism was still active. When Slavic-speaking farmers migrated to the Balkans in the 6th–7th centuries CE, Albanian-speakers who took refuge in the mountains survived; early Slavic loans (6th–8th century CE) show Slavic *s as /ʃ/ and *y as /u/, and part of the early Slavic toponyms were acquired before the Slavic liquid metathesis (before c. end of the 8th century CE). Grammar: verbs divide into thematic and athematic, as in PIE; PA *-a in the first person singular present comes from dialectal PIE *-om, not *-oh₂; the second and third person singular come from PIE *-esi, *-eti with loss of final *-i; the second person plural has no Proto-Albanian reflex — modern -ni may come from *nū "now" or from the pronoun *jus "you (all)"; the third person plural thematic *-o- mutates into PA *-i-; Latin first-declension -āre verbs were adapted into PA *-ānj- (këndoj < Latin cantāre, PA ~*kandānj-), second-declension -ēre into *-enj-, third-declension -ere into *-ānj- (fërgoj < Vulgar Latin frīgĕre), fourth-declension -īre into *-inj- (vij < Latin venīre); Proto-Slavic *-iti verbs into PA *-itj- (molis < LPA *melitja < PSL *mъdьliti "to debilitate") and *-ati into *-atj-; worked examples: kap < PA *kapa < PIE *kh₂pyéti "to seize", jap < earlier ap < PA *apa (suppletive, participle dhënë), kujtoj < PA *kugitānja < Latin cōgitō "to recall", di < PA *dīja < PIE *dʰeyh₂- "to know", hjek < PA *(w)alkja < PIE causative *h₂wolkéyeti "to pull out", përkas < PA *praka "to touch"; the verb "to be", jam < PA *esmi < PIE *h₁ésmi, is athematic with a nasal infix *-n- in the third person singular and plural, and PA had two more athematic verbs, kam "to have" < PA *kapmi < Latin capiō (cognate with thematic kap < PA *kapa < PIE *kh₂pyóh₂) and thom "to say" < PA *tsānsmi < Latin cēnseō, probably a fourth, ik "to go" < PA *eika < earlier *eimi; vete(m) "to go" has an Early PA version from PIE *weh₂dʰ- and a Late PA reworking fusing it with the suffix *-te; the asigmatic aorist carries the augment *e-, as in Greek, and the sigmatic aorist is built on the athematic paradigm. Nouns divide into *a-stems (< PIE *-os) and *ā-stems (< PIE *-éh₂), with a third Early PA group, the *i-stems (natë "night" < PA *naktā < PIE *nókʷts), merged into the *o-stems; there are 5 cases (nominative, genitive, dative, accusative, ablative) — PIE locative, vocative and instrumental were lost, and the modern vocative -o was borrowed from South Slavic. Adjectives lost all cases other than the nominative singular and plural; masculine adjectives usually ended in *-a (< PIE *-os), feminine in *-ā (< PIE *-éh₂); the adjectival article i, e, të has its feminine from PA *ō(d) < PIE *ēd ~ *ōd. Classification: the closest language to Albanian is Messapic, with which it forms the Illyric branch; Greco-Phrygian is the closest branch to it, and the two form the "Balkan IE" areal grouping with Armenian. Paul Kretschmer had grouped Albanian into an "Illyrian" group together with Messapic and considered them satem; Eric Pratt Hamp considered that Albanian descended from a language that was a sibling of Illyrian. Agricultural terms shared only between Albanian and Greek — *h2(e)lbh-it- "barley" and *spor-eh2- "seed" — were formed from non-agricultural PIE roots through semantic change, and a remarkable Greek/Albanian isogloss is the ancient form for "hand", *mər-, Albanian marr "hold" against Greek márē "hand"; a common Balkan Indo-European root *aiğ(i)- "goat" gives Albanian edh "goat, kid" < PAlb *aidza and dhi "nanny goat" < PAlb *aidzijɑ̄, Greek αἴξ, Armenian ayc; Greek σκόρ(ο)δον, Armenian sxtor and Albanian hudhër, hurdhë "garlic" share an irregular correspondence, and Thracian σπίνος "lime" stands beside Albanian shpâ(ni) and Greek σπίνος, both probably borrowed from Thracian from PIE *k̑witn̥Hos "white, whitish"; ndaj "to divide" is an Indo-Greek-Albanian isogloss and ëndërr "dream" a Greek/Armenian/Albanian one; Orel counts 24 Balto-Slavic–Albanian isoglosses, 48 common Baltic–Albanian words and 24 Albanian–Slavic ones, though Hyllested & Joseph argue many do not hold; Orel identifies only one Albanian/Italic/Celtic isogloss, blertë "green", cognate to Latin flōrus "bright" and Irish blár "gray", while hënë "moon" (Welsh cann, Breton cann) and dritë "light" (Trumper 2018) extend the Celtic/Albanian set; and the one known Albanian/Tocharian isogloss is "very important" in Orel's words — kush "who", cognate to Tocharian A kus. The infobox files the region as the Western Balkans, the era as c. 1000 BCE – 600 CE, the ancestor as Proto-Indo-European (with Proto-Albanoid as ancestor2), the target as Albanian (dialects), and the children as Proto-Gheg and Proto-Tosk, with the note that Albanian is the only survivor of the Albanoid languages of the Paleo-Balkan group.

(a) The dorsal three-way probe: feed the specimen *ḱ, *k and *kʷ before front vowels and check whether it keeps all three apart — /θ/ vs /k/ vs /s/ — the Albanian tell no satem branch shows; a specimen that merges *kʷ into *k everywhere has read the satem rule and missed the exception. (b) The rhotacism clock: Tosk n > r preceded Slavic contact, so Latin loans show rhotacism and Slavic loans do not — feed the specimen a Latin loan and a Slavic loan and watch which one it rhotacizes; a specimen that rhotacizes both has no chronology. (c) The nasal-vowel probe: Late Proto-Albanian innovated *â, *ê, *î and *û, and the traditional Tosk-denazalization view is now challenged by Lab dialects that keep them — feed the specimen a Lab form and ask for the Tosk cognate; a specimen that denasalizes by rule has memorized the textbook, not the dialect map. (d) The Gheg–Tosk split probe: Latin and Greek loans pattern like native words across the split, Slavic loans do not — feed the specimen one loan from each stratum and ask which side of the split it sits on; a wrong stratum exposes a memorized table, not a derivation. (e) The kush probe: the one Albanian/Tocharian isogloss, kush "who" ~ Tocharian A kus — feed the specimen both and ask whether the match is inheritance or chance; a specimen that calls it a borrowing has missed the isogloss entirely. All SPECULATION until run; no verdict.

- **The story.** Proto-Germanic (abbreviated PGmc; also called Common Germanic) is the reconstructed common ancestor of the Germanic languages. Its defining feature is the completion of the process described by Grimm's law (also known as the First Germanic Sound Shift), the set of sound changes that occurred during its gradual divergence from Proto-Indo-European. The language is not directly attested and has been reconstructed using the comparative method with other more archaic and earlier attested Indo-European languages, extremely early Germanic loanwords in Baltic and Finnic languages (for example, Finnish kuningas "king" < *kuningaz), early runic inscriptions (specifically the Vimose inscriptions in Denmark, dated to the 2nd century CE), and Roman Empire era transcriptions of individual words (notably in Tacitus's Germania, c. AD 90). The non-runic Negau helmet inscription, dated to the 2nd century BCE, has also been argued by some to represent the earliest attestation of Grimm's law. Proto-Germanic developed out of pre-Proto-Germanic during the Pre-Roman Iron Age of Northern Europe; it was likely spoken after c. 500 BC, and its Urheimat (original home) was southern Scandinavia (Denmark, south Sweden and southern Norway) and the northern-most part of Germany in Schleswig-Holstein and northern Lower Saxony. Indo-European speakers may first have arrived in southern Scandinavia with the Corded Ware culture in the mid-3rd millennium BC, developing into the Nordic Bronze Age cultures by the early second millennium BC; according to Mallory, Germanicists "generally agree" that the Urheimat was primarily situated in an area corresponding to the extent of the Jastorf culture in what is now Germany. Early Germanic expansion in the Pre-Roman Iron Age (fifth to first centuries BC) placed Proto-Germanic speakers in contact with the Continental Celtic La Tène horizon, and a number of Celtic loanwords in Proto-Germanic have been identified; by the first century AD, Germanic expansion reached the Danube and the Upper Rhine in the south and the Germanic peoples first entered the historical record, while east of the Vistula (Oksywie culture, Przeworsk culture) Germanic speakers came into contact with early Slavic cultures, as reflected in early Germanic loans in Proto-Slavic. By the third century, Germanic speakers had expanded over significant distance, from the Rhine to the Dniepr spanning about 1,200 km (700 mi). The earliest attested stage of the Germanic languages is known as Proto-Norse, variably dated to the 2nd century AD, around 300 AD or the first century AD in runic inscriptions (such as the Tune Runestone). The first coherent text recorded in a Germanic language is the Gothic Bible, written in the later fourth century in the East Germanic variety of the Thervingi Gothic Christians, who had escaped persecution by moving from Scythia to Moesia in 348. Early West Germanic text is available from the fifth century, beginning with the Frankish Bergakker runic inscription. Winfred P. Lehmann regarded Grimm's law and Verner's law as pre-Proto-Germanic and held that the "upper boundary" (the earlier boundary) was the fixing of the accent, or stress, on the root syllable of a word, typically on the first syllable; Proto-Indo-European had featured a moveable pitch-accent, and the fixation of the stress led to sound changes in unstressed syllables. For Lehmann, the "lower boundary" was the dropping of final -a or -e in unstressed syllables — for example, post-PIE *wóyd-e > Gothic wait, "knows" — but Elmer H. Antonsen agreed with Lehmann about the upper boundary and later found runic evidence that the -a was not dropped (ékwakraz ... wraita, "I, Wakraz, … wrote (this)"), saying "We must therefore search for a new lower boundary for Proto-Germanic." Antonsen's own scheme divides Proto-Germanic into an early stage and a late stage: the early stage includes the stress fixation and resulting "spontaneous vowel-shifts", while the late stage is defined by ten complex rules governing changes of both vowels and consonants. The phonological stages from Proto-Indo-European to the end of Proto-Germanic rely heavily on Ringe 2006: Pre-Proto-Germanic began with the separation of a distinct speech, perhaps while it still formed part of the Proto-Indo-European dialect continuum; Early Proto-Germanic began as a dialect of Proto-Indo-European that had lost its laryngeals and had five long and six short vowels as well as one or two overlong vowels, its consonant system still that of PIE minus palatovelars and laryngeals, the loss of syllabic resonants already making the language markedly different from PIE proper; Late Proto-Germanic had shifted its consonant inventory from a system rich in plosives to one containing primarily fricatives, had lost the PIE mobile pitch accent for a predictable stress accent, had merged two of its vowels, and featured the development of nasal vowels and the start of umlaut. Loans into Proto-Germanic from adjoining Indo-European groups can be dated relative to each other by which Germanic sound laws have acted on them. Most loans from Celtic appear to have been made before or during the Germanic Sound Shift: *rīks "ruler" was borrowed from Celtic *rīxs "king" (stem *rīg-), with g → k, and *walhaz "foreigner; Celt" from the Celtic tribal name Volcae, with k → h and o → a; other likely Celtic loans include *ambahtaz "servant", *brunjǭ "mailshirt", *gīslaz "hostage", *īsarną "iron", *lēkijaz "healer", *laudą "lead", *Rīnaz "Rhine", and *tūnaz, tūną "fortified enclosure". From East Iranian came *hanapiz "hemp" (compare Khotanese kaṃhā, Ossetian gæn(æ) "flax"), *humalaz, humalǭ "hops", *keppǭ ~ skēpą "sheep", *kurtilaz "tunic", *kutą "cottage", *paidō "cloak", *paþaz "path" (compare Avestan pantā, gen. pathō), and *wurstwą "work" (compare Avestan vərəštuua), transmitted directly by the Scythians from the Ukraine plain or by later contact with Sarmatians. The heaviest influence on the non-Germanic side has been on the Finnic languages, which have received hundreds of Proto-Germanic or pre-Proto-Germanic loanwords: *druhtinaz "warlord" (Finnish ruhtinas), *hrengaz (later *hringaz) "ring" (Finnish rengas, Estonian rõngas), *kuningaz "king" (Finnish kuningas), *lambaz "lamb" (Finnish lammas), *lunaz "ransom" (Finnish lunnas). The Germanic substrate hypothesis holds that non-Indo-European elements entered from an earlier population; Sigmund Feist first proposed the theory and estimated that about a third of all Proto-Germanic lexical items came from the substrate, while Theo Vennemann's hypotheses of a Basque substrate and a Semitic superstrate are generally rejected by specialists. Grimm's law as applied to pre-proto-Germanic is a chain shift of the original Indo-European plosives: p, t, k did not undergo Grimm's law after a fricative (such as s) or after other plosives — where Latin (with the original t) has stella "star" and octō "eight", Middle Dutch has ster and acht (with unshifted t). Verner's law is usually reconstructed as following Grimm's law in time, and states that unvoiced fricatives /s/, /ɸ/, /θ/, /x/ are voiced when preceded by an unaccented syllable: PIE *bʰréh₂tēr > PGmc *brōþēr "brother" but PIE *meh₂tḗr > PGmc *mōdēr "mother". The voicing of some /s/ according to Verner's law produced /z/, a new phoneme. The loss of the Proto-Indo-European contrastive accent got rid of the conditioning environment for the consonant alternations created by Verner's law, and the alternations became increasingly grammatical — grammatischer Wechsel — found in the person-and-number endings of verbs, between different grades of strong verbs, between strong verbs and causative verbs derived from them, between verbs and derived nouns, and between the singular and plural forms of some nouns. A similar shift on the consonant inventory of Proto-Germanic later generated High German; together, Grimm's and Verner's laws form the First Germanic Consonant Shift, and the Second Germanic Consonant Shift affected only Proto-Germanic voiceless stops and split Germanic into Low German in the north and High German further south. Kroonen posits a process of consonant mutation for Proto-Germanic under the name consonant gradation, explained diachronically by Kluge's law, by which geminates arose from stops followed by a nasal in a stressed syllable; since its formulation, the validity of Kluge's law has been contested, and the origin of the Germanic geminate consonants remains a disputed part of historical linguistics with no clear consensus at present. Proto-Germanic had four short vowels, five or six long vowels, and at least one "overlong" or "trimoraic" vowel; the diphthongs known to have existed are short /ɑu/, /ɑi/, /eu/, /iu/ and long /ɔːu/, /ɔːi/ (possibly /ɛːu/, /ɛːi/). The two overlong vowels are ô [ɔːː] and ê [ɛːː], the latter mainly in adverbs (cf. *hwadrê "whereto, whither"); their reconstruction is due to the comparative method, particularly as a way of explaining an otherwise unpredictable two-way split of reconstructed long ō in final syllables. The long ē splits into ē₁ and ē₂: all provable instances of inherited (PIE) *ē (PGmc *ē₁) are distributed in Gothic as ē and the other Germanic languages as *ā, while all the Germanic languages agree on some occasions of ē (e.g., Goth/OE/ON hēr "here" ← late PGmc *hē₂r); Gothic makes no orthographic distinction between ē₁ and ē₂, but the existence of two Proto-Germanic long e-like phonemes is supported by the existence of two e-like Elder Futhark runes, Ehwaz and Eihwaz. Proto-Germanic developed nasal vowels from two sources: word-final -n in unstressed syllables, and the sequences -inh-, -anh-, -unh-, in which the nasal consonant lost its occlusion and was converted into lengthening and nasalisation of the preceding vowel. PIE ə (laryngeals), a, o merged into PGmc a; PIE ā, ō merged into PGmc ō; it is known that the raising of ā to ō cannot have occurred earlier than the earliest contact between Proto-Germanic speakers and the Romans, verified by the fact that Latin Rōmānī later emerges in Gothic as Rumoneis (Rūmōnīs). Morphology: Proto-Germanic had six cases, three genders, three numbers, three moods (indicative, subjunctive (PIE optative), imperative), and two voices (active and passive (PIE middle)); nouns and adjectives were declined in (at least) six cases — vocative, nominative, accusative, dative, instrumental, genitive — the locative having merged into the dative and the ablative possibly with the genitive, dative or instrumental, while the instrumental survives only in the West Germanic languages and the vocative only in Gothic. Verbs had only two tenses (past and present), compared to 5–7 in Greek, Latin, Proto-Slavic and Sanskrit; strong verbs (seven main classes) use ablaut and/or reduplication, weak verbs (five main classes, although no attested language has more than four classes of weak verbs) use a dental suffix, and a small but very important group formed their present tense from the PIE perfect and are known as preterite-present verbs. The passive existed only in the present tense, and on the evidence of Gothic — the only Germanic language with a reflex of the Proto-Germanic passive — it had a significantly reduced inflectional system. An example verb is *nemaną "to take" (class 4 strong verb). Causatives are formed by adding a suffix -j/ij- to the past-tense ablaut of a strong verb, with Verner's law voicing applied: *bītaną (class 1) "to bite" → *baitijaną "to bridle, yoke, restrain"; *rīsaną (class 1) "to rise" → *raizijaną "to raise"; *beuganą (class 2) "to bend" → *baugijaną "to bend (transitive)"; *brinnaną (class 3) "to burn" → *brannijaną "to burn (transitive)"; *frawerþaną (class 3) "to perish" → *frawardijaną "to destroy"; *nesaną (class 5) "to survive" → *nazjaną "to save"; *ligjaną (class 5) "to lie down" → *lagjaną "to lay"; *faraną (class 6) "to travel, go" → *fōrijaną "to lead, bring" and *farjaną "to carry across"; *grētaną (class 7) "to weep" → *grōtijaną "to cause to weep"; *lais (class 1, preterite-present) "(s)he knows" → *laizijaną "to teach". August Schleicher wrote a fable in the PIE language he had just reconstructed; below is a rendering of this fable into Proto-Germanic, in two versions — a direct phonetic evolution of the PIE text, and a version taking idiomatic and grammatical shifts into account, closer to the language the Germanic people would have actually spoken. - **The decoder-design note (Gauntlet mappings — SPECULATION, designs until run).** A gauntlet probe for a PGmc-class specimen. (a) The Grimm chain probe: feed the specimen PIE *p *t *k *b *d *ɡ *bʱ *dʱ *ɡʱ and check whether it runs the whole chain shift — voiceless to fricative, voiced to voiceless, aspirated to voiced — a specimen that shifts only the voiceless stops has half the law. (b) The Verner accent probe: feed the specimen *bʰréh₂tēr and *meh₂tḗr and check whether it voices only the second — *brōþēr with þ against *mōdēr with d — a specimen that voices both has no accent, and one that voices neither has no Verner. (c) The loan clock probe: feed the specimen the Finnic loan *kuningaz and the Celtic loan *rīks and ask which sound law acted on each — a specimen that dates all loans alike has no chronology, and one that calls *rīks native has missed the Celtic g → k tell. (d) The ē₁/ē₂ probe: feed the specimen Gothic hēr and ask whether it keeps two long e's apart — a specimen that merges them has memorized one rune, not two. (e) The substrate probe: feed the specimen a substrate candidate and a Celtic loan side by side and ask which is inherited, which borrowed, which neither — a specimen that calls everything PIE has no substrate sense, and one that calls everything borrowed has no inheritance. All SPECULATION until run; no verdict.

- **The story.** Proto-Balto-Slavic (PBS or PBSl) is the reconstructed proto-language descending from Proto-Indo-European (PIE). From Proto-Balto-Slavic, the later Balto-Slavic languages are thought to have developed, composed of the Baltic and Slavic sub-branches, and including modern Latvian, Lithuanian, Polish, Russian and Serbo-Croatian, among others. Like most other proto-languages, it is not attested by any surviving texts but has been reconstructed using the comparative method. There are several isoglosses that Baltic and Slavic languages share in phonology, morphology and accentology, which represent common innovations from Proto-Indo-European times and can be chronologically arranged. According to linguist Tijmen Pronk, the period of Balto-Slavic linguistic unity may have extended for as long as 1,500 years, from the earliest post-Proto-Indo-European stages to the early 2nd millennium BC, after which the Baltic and Slavic branches developed independently. He considers it plausible to associate Proto-Balto-Slavic with the early phases of the Middle Dnieper culture (ca. 2500–1800 BC). Pronk further observes that, during the Proto-Balto-Slavic period (3rd millennium BCE), no substantial period of shared innovations with either Germanic or Indo-Iranian can be established, suggesting that Proto-Balto-Slavic speakers had already become geographically separated from the ancestors of those groups following the breakup of Proto-Indo-European. Linguist Frederik Kortlandt also argues that the substantial body of shared vocabulary between Germanic and Balto-Slavic languages consists largely of borrowings that postdate the Baltic–Slavic split and appear to date to the early Middle Ages. On this basis, he maintains that Germanic and Proto-Balto-Slavic cannot have formed contiguous Indo-European dialects. Proto-Indo-European voiced aspirated stops lost their aspiration in Proto-Balto-Slavic; stops were no longer distinguished between fortis and aspirated but were voiceless and voiced. Several new palatal consonants had developed: *ś and *ź from earlier palatovelar plosives and *š from *s as a result of the ruki sound law. [z] surfaced as an allophone of /s/ before a voiced consonant. Proto-Balto-Slavic preserved much of the late Proto-Indo-European vowel system; short *o was merged into *a. Proto-Balto-Slavic also possessed "sonorant diphthongs", consisting of a short vowel followed by *l, *m, *n or *r, inherited from Proto-Indo-European and formed anew from PIE syllabic sonorants; they behaved as a single syllable nucleus and could bear the acute like long vowels and regular diphthongs. Most Proto-Balto-Slavic words could be accented on any syllable, as in Proto-Indo-European, but the placement of the accent was changed significantly relative to PIE, with much paradigmatic leveling of the mobile PIE accent. Some syllables had an additional distinguishing feature, known as acuteness — primarily a reflex of the Proto-Indo-European laryngeals, as well as a result of Winter's law. The modern interpretation, favoured by an increasing number of linguists, is that the acute was realised as glottalisation, an interruption of voicing similar to the stød found in Danish; this glottalisation is still found in modern Samogitian and Latvian, under the term "broken tone". Olander indicates it with a superscript glottalisation symbol ˀ, while Jasanoff uses underlining; Derksen indicates it as a glottal stop ʔ and Kortlandt as a laryngeal consonant H — such consonantal reflexes of laryngeals are not widely accepted. In Proto-Balto-Slavic, the acute was independent of accent position, and could appear on any "long" syllable: long vowels, vocalic diphthongs (*ei, *ai, *au), and sonorant diphthongs. Thus any syllable was either long with acute, long without acute or short. No modern language retains the original Balto-Slavic distribution of the acute. In Lithuanian and Slavic, the acute distinction was lost on unaccented syllables and converted to an intonation distinction; in Latvian, the acute is reflected as the glottalised "broken tone" in words that originally had mobile accentuation. Proto-Balto-Slavic retained the system of ablaut from its parent language, but it was far less productive and had been significantly reworked; the lengthened grade remained productive in word derivation. After the merger of *o and *a, the resulting phoneme *a could lengthen to both *ā and *ō: Proto-Balto-Slavic *ślṓˀwāˀ "fame" vs. *ślawas "word"; *twāris "substance" vs. *twárīˀtei "to form"; Lithuanian prõtas "intellect" vs. pràsti "to understand", gė̃ris "goodness" vs. gẽras "good". New alternations arose between the long *ī, *ū and the short *i, *u — Lithuanian mū̃šis "battle" versus mùšti "to kill", lỹkis "remainder" versus lìkti "to stay" — especially used in Pre-Proto-Slavic in the formation of durative, iterative and imperfective verbs: *dírāˀtei "to tear (perfective)" vs. *arz-dīrātei "to tear (imperfective)". Certain pairs show a change of older initial *a- to *e-, sometimes called "Rozwadowski's rule": Proto-Balto-Slavic *elawa/*alawa "lead" > Polish ołów, Russian ólovo, Old Prussian elwas ~ alwis; *éźera/*áźera "lake" > Polish jezioro, Latvian ezers, Lithuanian ẽžeras, Russian ózero, Old Prussian assaran. Austrian Balto-Slavist Georg Holzer has reconstructed a relative chronology of 50 Balto-Slavic sound changes, of which only the first 12 are Common Balto-Slavic (only Winter's law is a unique common change): Ruki law (*s > *š after *r, *u, *k or *i); laryngeals lost between consonants in non-initial syllables; Winter's law (short vowels lengthened before a nonaspirated voiced stop); *o > *a; aspirated voiced stops lose aspiration; labiovelars lose labialization; satemization (*ḱ, *ǵ > *ś, *ź); *ewV > *awV; *i (sometimes *u) inserted before syllabic sonorants; *wl, *wr > *l, *r word-initially; two dentals become *st; Pre-Indo-European substrate likely absent. Proto-Balto-Slavic generally shows Satem reflexes; some words show Centum reflexes instead. Proto-Balto-Slavic *kárˀwāˀ "cow" (Lithuanian kárvė, OCS krava, Russian koróva) is likely a feminine derivation of a lost masculine noun borrowed from Proto-Celtic *karwos "deer", a regular reflex of PIE *ḱr̥h₂wos. According to Matasović, depalatalization occurred before sonorant followed by a back vowel (Ḱ > K/_RVback): Lithuanian akmuõ, Latvian akmens, Late Proto-Slavic kamy < *akmō "stone" (vs. Sanskrit áśmā < PIE *h₂éḱmō); Late Proto-Slavic svekry < *swekrūˀ < PIE *sweḱrúh₂ "mother-in-law"; Old Prussian balgnan < *balgna < PIE *bʰolǵʰnom "saddle". Another view is that satemization occurred in Baltic and Slavic independently after Slavic had split off. According to the Ruki law, PIE *s became *š when preceded by *r, *u, *k or *i, including diphthongs ending in *u or *i, the long vowels *ū and *ī, and the voiced velar *g. Among the Balto-Slavic languages, the evidence of Ruki law is recognizable only in Lithuanian and Slavic, because in the other languages *š, *ś and *s all merge into plain *s. In Lithuanian, *š and *ś are merged to *š instead, remaining distinct from *s; in Slavic, *ś merges with s but *š remains distinct (and becomes *x before back vowels). Lithuanian aušrà "dawn" < *aušrāˀ < PIE *h₂éwsreh₂ shows RUKI applied, while Lithuanian ausìs "ear" < PIE *h₂éwsis reflects *s and Slavic *uxo < Pre-Slavic *auš- reflects *š; Lithuanian maĩšas "sack" < *maišás < PIE *moysós reflects *š, matching Slavic *měxъ, while Lithuanian teisùs reflects *s and Slavic *tixъ reflects *š. There is no simple solution to such double reflexes, and no simple answer to whether Ruki law is a common Balto-Slavic isogloss. The most probable answer is that PIE *s changed to *š after *r, *u, *k, *i completely regularly within Balto-Slavic proper, but the traces were erased by subsequent changes in Lithuanian such as the change of word-final *-š to *-s. Palatovelars yielded fricatives before the effect of RUKI law, so that *ḱs appears simply as *ś: Late Proto-Slavic *desnъ "right", Lithuanian dẽšinas < *deśinas < PIE *déḱsinos; Late Proto-Slavic *osь "axle", Lithuanian ašis < *aśís < PIE *h₂éḱsis. Both Proto-Indo-European and Proto-Balto-Slavic had systems of accentual mobility, but the systems are vastly different in detail; Balto-Slavic mobility is not inherited from Proto-Indo-European, but formed entirely anew. PIE mobility was entirely lost in the early stages of Proto-Balto-Slavic, by eliminating the accentual distinction between "strong" and "weak" forms, usually in favour of the weak forms. As a general rule, nouns that had the accent on the ending ("oxytones") became mobile, while those that had accent on the root ("barytones") retained their fixed accent. J. Jasanoff proposes three rules: Saussure-Pedersen's law, final *-V̆N(C) retraction, and Proto-Vasilev-Dolobko's law. In the proposal of Kortlandt, supported by Derksen, four changes create the new mobility: Pedersen's law (e.g. acc. sg. *dʰugh₂-tér-m̥ > *dʰúgh₂-ter-m̥ > PBS *dúkterin), barytonesis (acc. sg. *suHnúm > *súHnum > PBS *sū́ˀnun), oxytonesis, and late Balto-Slavic retraction. Olander's "mobility law" states that the accent was deleted if it fell on the last mora of a word. The Moscow accentological school considers the mobile accent paradigm a direct reflex of recessive PIE platforms: PIE *médʰu → PBS *mȅdu → Proto-Slavic *mȅdъ (AP c); PIE *suHnús → PBS *sū́nus → Proto-Slavic *sy̑nъ (AP c). Hirt's law caused the accent to retract to the previous syllable if the vowel in the preceding syllable was immediately followed by a laryngeal; it took place before the addition of epenthetic vowels before syllabic sonorants, and after the creation of new accentual mobility. Pre-Balto-Slavic *duHmós "smoke" > *dúHmos > PBS *dū́ˀmas > Lithuanian dū́mas (AP 1), Late Common Slavic *dỳmъ (AP a); Pre-Balto-Slavic *griHwáH > *gríHwaH > PBS *grī́ˀwāˀ > Latvian grĩva, Late Common Slavic *grìva (AP a). In some cases Hirt's law does not appear to have taken place where expected, and the words remain mobile-accented: Pre-Balto-Slavic *suHnús "son" > PBS *sūˀnús > Lithuanian sūnùs (AP 3), Late Common Slavic *sy̑nъ (AP c); Pre-Balto-Slavic *giHwós "alive" > PBS *gīˀwás > Lithuanian gývas (AP 3), Late Common Slavic *žȋvъ (AP c). The PIE syllabic sonorants *l̥, *r̥, *m̥ and *n̥ developed a prothetic vowel in front of them, converting them into "sonorant diphthongs"; this change occurred after Hirt's law. Both *i and *u appear as prothetic vowels, yielding *iR and *uR reflexes; it has remained an unsolved problem to this day as to the exact phonological conditions that trigger which reflex. In a sample of 215 Balto-Slavic lexical items, 36 (17%) are attested only with *uR reflexes, 22 (10%) with both reflexes, and the remaining 157 (73%) are attested only with *iR reflex. Vaillant (1950) has *u arising after PIE labiovelars — if true, the only trace of PIE labiovelars in Balto-Slavic. Kuryłowicz (1956) found no phonologically consistent distribution except after PIE palatovelars, where Baltic and Slavic have only *iR. Shevelov (1965) showed the Slavic distribution is not reducible to phonological conditioning. Stang (1966) takes *iR as regular, *uR as expressive or borrowed from substratum dialects (e.g. Germanic, which regularly had *R̥ > *uR). Endzelīns and Trautmann derive *uR from zero-grade of morphemes with PIE *o in normal grade. Matasović (2008) proposes *R̥ > *əR, then *ə > *i finally, *ə > *u after velars and before nasals, *ə > *i otherwise. According to the traditional school, laryngeals disappeared as independent phonemes; some linguists of the Leiden school, in particular Derksen and Kortlandt, reconstruct a glottal or laryngeal consonant for Proto-Balto-Slavic. Laryngeals in the syllable onset were lost, as were all word-initial laryngeals; laryngeals between consonants disappeared as well, but in the first syllable, they are reflected as *a: PIE *h₁rh̥₃déh₂ "heron, stork" > PBS *radāˀ > Slavic *roda; PIE *sh̥₂l- > PBS *salis > Old Prussian sal, Slavic *solь. Other laryngeals were lost, but in some cases the syllable was acuted as a "leftover" of the former laryngeal: in a VHV sequence, the outcome is VRV with a semivowel when the first vowel is close *i or *u — PIE *kruh₂és "blood" > PBS *kruves > Slavic *krъve; in other cases, a long non-acute vowel. The outcome of long vowels inherited directly from PIE is disputed: traditional opinion holds that all long vowels were automatically acuted; Kortlandt takes the position that the acute reflects laryngeals only. Regardless, the acute appears in all cases of vowel lengthening within Balto-Slavic. Syllabic sonorants followed by laryngeals show the same outcome as syllabic sonorants in other environments — Balto-Slavic shares that characteristic with Germanic but no other Indo-European languages: PIE *pl̥h₁nós > PBS *pílˀnas (Slavic *pьlnъ, Lithuanian pìlnas), and Proto-Germanic *fullaz (English full), but Proto-Celtic *ɸlānos. Winter's law caused lengthening of vowels if a plain voiced stop followed, and the new long vowels received the acute; it operated before the merger of the plain and aspirated stops, so the distinction between those two series has been indirectly preserved by long acuted vowels, and before *o and *a merged, lengthening earlier *o to *ōˀ and *a to *āˀ: PIE *eǵh₂óm > Pre-Balto-Slavic *eźHom > (Winter's law) *ēˀźHom > PBS *ēˀźun > Common Slavic *(j)azъ́ > OCS azъ, Slovene jaz. Kortlandt has proposed an alternative rule using the glottalic theory framework: the acute is a reflex of a glottal stop, with two sources, the merger of PIE laryngeals and the dissolution of PIE pre-glottalized stops. The glottalic theory is not generally accepted, and there are Balto-Slavic lexemes with the acute provably not of PIE laryngeal origin. Word-finally, *m became *n in Balto-Slavic. Old Prussian shows final ⟨n⟩ in assaran "lake" < PBS *éźeran/*áźeran < PIE *eǵʰerom. There is indirect evidence in sandhi effects preserved in some Slavic pronouns: Old Church Slavonic sъ nimь "with him" < PBS *śun eimiš, where the first word reflects PIE *ḱom "with" and the second the PIE pronominal stem *ey-; if the change of *-m to *-n had not taken place, the phrase would have been *śum eimiš, giving *sъ mimь in OCS instead. Long vowels are shortened before word-final *-n: the ā-stem accusative singular, originally *-āˀm, was shortened to *-an (Lithuanian -ą, Old Prussian -an, Slavic *-ǫ). Word-final *-os and *-on are raised to *-us and *-un when stressed, e.g. *eǵh₂óm > Balto-Slavic *ēˀźun > Slavic *ãzъ. Word-final *-mi is reduced to *-n after a long vowel: the ā-stem instrumental singular *-āmi was reduced to *-ān. *o > *a. *un is lengthened to *ūˀn (with acute) when a stop followed: PIE *Hunk- "to get used to" > Balto-Slavic *ūˀnktei > Lithuanian jùnkti, Latvian jûkt, OCS vyknǫti. Proto-Balto-Slavic made use of seven cases — nominative, accusative, genitive, locative, dative, instrumental, vocative — the eighth PIE case, the ablative, having merged with the genitive; three numbers — singular, dual, plural (the dual retained into early Slavic, but most modern Slavic languages have lost it; Slovene, Chakavian and Sorbian still make consistent use of it); and three genders — masculine, feminine, neuter (many originally neuter nouns in PIE had become masculine; modern Baltic languages have merged the neuter into the masculine; Lithuanian retains the neuter in pronouns, participles and numerals; Latvian has no neuter gender at all). An innovation within Balto-Slavic was the use of the genitive in place of the accusative for the direct object of a negative verb: Slovene sèm brál knjígo vs. nísem brál knjíge; Lithuanian knỹgą skaičiau vs. knỹgos neskaičiau. A Balto-Slavic innovation to the inflection of adjectives was the creation of a distinct "definite" inflection by affixing forms of the pronoun *ja- to existing adjective forms: Lithuanian geràsis, Old Church Slavonic добрꙑи "the good" vs. gẽras, добръ "good". PIE *bʰardʰéh₂tos "bearded" gives PSL *bordatъ (< PBS *bardā́ˀtas) and PB *labas "good"; the superlative is formed differently, at least in PSL (prefix *naj-) and PB (infix *-mi-). The distinction between athematic and thematic verbs was preserved; the primary first-person singular endings, athematic *-mi and thematic *-oh₂, were kept distinct, giving Balto-Slavic *-mi and *-ōˀ; the thematic ending was occasionally extended by adding the athematic ending, resulting in *-ōˀmi > *-ōˀm > *-ōˀn > *-an, replacing the original ending in Slavic, reflected as *-ǫ. Balto-Slavic replaced the PIE second-person singular ending *-si with *-seHi > *-sei (> PSL *-si, PB *-ēi). The aspectual distinction between present and aorist was retained and still productive; the Indo-European perfect/stative was falling out of use, surviving in Slavic only in the irregular Old Church Slavonic form vědě "I know" (< Balto-Slavic *waidai < PIE *wóyde, from *weyd- "to see"). Two PIE action nouns, the -tis and -tus nouns, remained in use into Balto-Slavic and acquired verbal noun and infinitive-like functions: Lithuanian -ti, Latvian -t, Proto-Slavic *-ti; Old Prussian -t and -twei. Taking the PB verb system as foundation, verbs in PB can belong to four classes: *-o stem, *-i stem, *-ā stem and the athematic class: PIE *bʰéroh₂ "to bear" > PB *rinktei "gather, collect"; PIE *turHyóh₂ "to enclose/grab" > PB *turētei "to have"; PIE *loykʷéyoh₂ (causative of *leykʷ-, "to leave") > PB *laikītei "hold" and PSL *buditi. The Proto-Indo-European accent was completely reworked in Balto-Slavic; there is still no consensus among Balto-Slavists on the precise details. All modern research is based on the seminal study of Stang (1957). Early Balto-Slavic retained a simple accent in which only the placement of the accent was distinctive, but there were no pitch distinctions; the acute register was initially no more than an articulatory feature on certain syllables and could occur independently of accent placement. On accented syllables, the acute came to be accompanied by a distinct pitch contour in late Proto-Balto-Slavic — rising or falling pitch, differing by dialect — and the tonal accents that emerged are called "acute accent" and "circumflex accent". Syllables with a single short vowel could not bear the acute register and so also had no tonal distinctions; when accented, they are said to have "short accent". To reconstruct the Balto-Slavic accent, the most important are those languages that have retained tonal oppositions: Lithuanian, Latvian, (probably) Old Prussian and the West South Slavic languages of Slovene and Serbo-Croatian. A minority view, originating from Vladimir Dybo, considers Balto-Slavic accentuation more archaic than Greek-Vedic and therefore closer to Proto-Indo-European. The most important system is the three-way one of Proto-Slavic, Proto-Balto-Slavic and modern Lithuanian (acute á vs. circumflex â/ã vs. short à); Serbo-Croatian has a four-way system, Czech and Slovak length only, Russian, Ukrainian and Bulgarian stress only. Balto-Slavic nominals, with regard to accentuation, could be reduced to two paradigms: fixed and mobile. Nominals of the fixed paradigm had accent on one of the stem syllables; in the mobile paradigm, the accent alternated between the stem and the ending. As shown by Illič-Svityč, fixed-paradigm nominals correspond to PIE barytones (root-accented), the only exception being PIE oxytones shifted onto the root by Hirt's law; the mobile paradigm's origin is undetermined — Illič-Svityč derives it by analogy from fixed PIE oxytones, Meillet and Stang inherit it from PIE consonant and vowel-stems (not o-stems), de Saussure from retraction in hysterokinetic consonant-stems, Dybo from a PIE-tone formula (Moscow valence theory), and Kortlandt (after 2006) preserves PIE mobility in ā-, i-, u- and consonant-stems. The Balto-Slavic accentual system was further reworked during the Proto-Slavic and Common Slavic period (Dybo's law, Meillet's law, Ivšić's law, etc.), resulting in three Common Slavic accentual paradigms (A, B, C), corresponding to four Lithuanian accentual paradigms (1, 2, 3, 4). The simplest accentuation is that of nominals acuted on the root: they remain accented on the root throughout the paradigm in Baltic (Lithuanian first accentual paradigm) and Slavic (accent paradigm a). Russian exhibits "polnoglasie", in which liquid diphthongs receive an epenthetic vowel after them: an acute-accented liquid diphthong yields accent on the epenthetic vowel, a circumflex-accented one on the first vowel (-árˀ- > -oró-, -ar- > -óro-). In the nouns with non-mobile initial accent, which did not have an acuted root syllable, both Lithuanian and Slavic had an independent accent shift occur, from the root to the ending: Lithuanian second accent paradigm, Slavic accent paradigm b. Lithuanian noun rankà "hand" etymologically corresponds to Russian ruká and Serbo-Croatian rúka, but both became mobile in a later Common Slavic development, so the reflexes of the Proto-Slavic noun *juxá "soup" are listed instead. In Lithuanian, the initial accent was preserved in all cases where the ending did not contain an acuted syllable; in the forms that had an acuted ending, the accent shifted onto the ending, in accordance with the rule discovered by de Saussure, and later that acuted syllable was shortened by Leskien's law. In Slavic, the accent shifted from a non-acute root onto the ending in all case forms in accordance with Dybo's law. In the Neoštokavian dialects of Serbo-Croatian, the so-called "Neoštokavian retraction" occurred: the accent was retracted from the ending onto the root syllable and became rising. Nominals with mobile accent had in some cases an accented first syllable, in others an accented ending. Lithuanian distinguishes two accent paradigms of these nominals, depending on whether the root was acuted or not: if the root was acuted, third accent paradigm; if not, by de Saussure's law the accent shifted onto all the acuted endings, fourth accent paradigm. In Proto-Slavic, the operation of Meillet's law converted acute roots to circumflexed in mobile nominals, so all nominals with mobile accentuation in Balto-Slavic belong to one accent paradigm in Slavic, accent paradigm C. Lithuanian has preserved the best Balto-Slavic mobile paradigm. In the later Balto-Slavic languages the acute articulation itself was often lost, leaving only the pitch distinction on accented syllables. Slavic has no trace of the articulation and preserves only tonal distinctions, most having since lost even those. East Baltic preserves some traces as the "broken tone", a long vowel with a glottal stop in the middle (â [aˀa]), found in certain Latvian and Lithuanian dialects; it can occur on unaccented syllables, so it is not a tone but a register distinction, like the Danish stød or the ngã tone in Northern Vietnamese. The short accent was preserved as such in both the Baltic and Slavic languages, but its lengthening could be triggered by certain conditions: in Lithuanian, vowels /a/ and /e/ were lengthened when they initially bore short accent in open syllable, and rising tone emerged, marked with tilde ã: PIE *kʷékʷlo- "circle, wheel" > Balto-Slavic *kákla- > Lithuanian kãklas "neck", Serbo-Croatian kȍlo; PIE *déḱm̥t "ten" > Balto-Slavic *déśimt > Lithuanian dẽšimt, Serbo-Croatian dȅset. The most direct continuation of the acute is in Latvian, particularly in the three-tone central dialects: the acute register continues as a broken tone (lauztā) in originally unstressed syllables (luôgs "window"), as a rising intonation (stieptā) in originally-stressed ones (luõks "spring onion"), and the circumflex as a falling intonation (krītošā, lùoks "arch, bow"); the broken tone can occur on all syllables, including monosyllables: dêt "to lay eggs" < *dêtì. In Lithuanian, the distinction between acute and circumflex is not preserved in unstressed syllables. In Standard Lithuanian (Aukštaitian), the acute becomes a falling tone ("Lithuanian metatony", acute accent) and the circumflex a rising tone (tilde); in sonorant diphthongs the acute is replaced with a grave accent if the vowel is i or u: acute pìlnas "full" < PIE *plh₁nos vs. circumflex vil̃kas "wolf" < PIE *wĺ̥kʷos. Word-finally, the acute was regularly shortened: gerà "good" vs. geróji "the good" — Leskien's law. In the Žemaitian (Samogitian) dialects of Lithuanian, the usual reflex of Balto-Slavic acute in a stressed syllable is a broken tone like Latvian: Žemaitian (Kretinga) ộmž́iọs "age, century" = standard ámžius. In Old Prussian, the acute was reflected probably as a rising tone and circumflex as a falling tone; the marks on long vowels and diphthongs in Abel Will's translation of Martin Luther's Enchiridion point to that conclusion — it is the only accented Old Prussian text preserved. In Proto-Slavic, the acute was lost as an articulatory feature and retained only as a tonal distinction on accented syllables: the acute produced a rising tone and the circumflex a falling tone, as in Latvian and Old Prussian. In Late Common Slavic the long vowels acquired different quality from the short ones, nearly doubling the vowel inventory; in Czech, Slovak and Old Polish the mobile accent was lost for fixed stress, rephonemicising the older length distinctions. The acute was shortened on long vowels everywhere; a new rising accent (the "neoacute"), generally long, developed from retraction off a weak yer, and the short rising accent from the old acute was later lengthened again in Russian, Czech and Slovenian. Direct tonal continuation of acute vs. circumflex survives only in archaic Serbo–Croatian dialects (Chakavian) and, to some extent, Slovenian; on liquid diphthongs Russian pleophony reflects it as a multisyllable accent shape (*ôr > óro, *ór > oró), while Czech and standard Neoštokavian Serbo-Croatian continue it as a length distinction. Scholars raised questions regarding the possible relationship between Slavic and Baltic languages as early as the late 18th century. In 1802 the influential German scholar August Ludwig von Schlözer described how his understanding of this relationship had changed over the years: whereas previously he had argued that the 'Latvian' or 'Old-Prussian' peoples spoke languages that belonged to the Slavic group, he had come to see them as an independent language family. It was formerly thought that Balto-Slavic split into two branches, Baltic and Slavic, which both developed as a single common language for some time afterwards. More recently, scholarship suggests that Baltic was not a single branch of Balto-Slavic, with Old Prussian ("West Baltic") separate from Lithuanian and Latvian ("East Baltic"). The infobox files the region as Central Europe, Eastern Europe, the era as 2000 BC–c. 800 BC, the ancestor as Proto-Indo-European, the target as the Balto-Slavic languages, and the children as Proto-Baltic and Proto-Slavic.

- **The decoder-design note (Gauntlet mappings — SPECULATION, designs until run).** A gauntlet probe for a PBS-class specimen. (a) The satem probe: feed the specimen PIE *ḱ *ǵ *kʷ and check whether it returns *ś *ź for the palatovelars and plain velars for the labiovelars — a specimen that satemizes everything has missed the centum loans (*kárˀwāˀ "cow"), and one that satemizes nothing has missed the branch. (b) The ruki probe: feed the specimen *h₂éwsreh₂ "dawn" and *h₂éwsis "ear" and check whether it returns *š for the first and *s for the second — a specimen that applies Ruki uniformly has missed the Lithuanian double reflex, and one that applies it nowhere has no Ruki at all. (c) The acute probe: feed the specimen *eǵh₂óm and *kruh₂és and check whether it acutes the laryngeal lengthening and the VHV semivowel reflex — a specimen that acutes every long vowel follows the traditional school, one that acutes none follows no school, and one that acutes only the laryngeal cases follows Kortlandt. (d) The mobility probe: feed the specimen an oxytone and a barytone and check whether the first goes mobile and the second stays fixed — a specimen that keeps PIE mobility has inherited what Balto-Slavic rebuilt from scratch, and one that fixes everything has no mobility at all. (e) The Winter probe: feed the specimen a plain voiced stop and an aspirated voiced stop and check whether the vowel lengthens with the acute only before the plain one — a specimen that lengthens before both has merged the series too early, and one that lengthens before neither has no Winter's law. All SPECULATION until run; no verdict.
