- **The story.** Proto-Baltic (PB, PBl, Common Baltic) is the unattested, reconstructed ancestral proto-language of all Baltic languages. It is not attested in writing, but has been partly reconstructed through the comparative method from the collected data on attested Baltic and other Indo-European languages. It represents the common Baltic speech approximately spoken between the 3rd millennium BC and ca. 5th century BC, after which it began dividing into West and East Baltic languages. Proto-Baltic is thought to have been a fusional language and is associated with the Corded Ware and Trzciniec cultures. Generally it had SOV word order. Its unique traits: turning short Proto-Indo-European vowels *o, *a into *a, retaining and further developing the PIE ablaut, retaining *m before dental consonants, the productivity of the word stem ē and free accentuation with two pitch accents; its own set of diminutive suffixes, identical endings for verb tenses and moods, past tense by applying thematic vowels *-ā- and *-ē-, and its own lexicon, including onomastic elements. **Area.** Baltic hydronyms cover a vast area of 860,000 km2 from the Vistula River in the west to Moscow in the east and from the Baltic Sea in the north to Kyiv in the south; the current Lithuanian and Latvian lands combined constitute approximately one-sixth of the former Baltic territory. Some researchers suggest Baltic Finnic tribes once inhabited the Baltic lands from Vistula to Daugava and were later assimilated by Baltic newcomers. The southwest boundary of the hydronyms is still debated: Lithuanian linguist Simas Karaliūnas believed practically all the basins of the Oder and Vistula Rivers belonged to the Baltic hydronym habitat, while German linguist Hermann Schall suggested Baltic hydronyms could be found much further west, all the way to the Elbe, Saxony and Rügen island. During the 2nd and 1st millennium BC the Baltic people inhabited larger territories than the Germanic and Slavic people did at the time; it is estimated the Proto-Baltic lands had up to 500,000 people. The inhabitants were surrounded by Germanic people in the west, Slavs in the south and Finno-Ugric people in the north and northeast. Russian philologist Vladimir Toporov believes that during 1000–800 BC Proto-Germanic people began expanding into the western Baltic territory starting from the Pasłęka River; later the Baltic area shrank further due to the migration of the Goths, and during the migration period Slavic people began expanding into the northern and eastern territories of the Balts. From the 11th to 12th century Russian scriptures mention ongoing battles near Moscow with Eastern Galindians; since 1225 the conquests of the Teutonic Order in the current Baltic region intensified and later resulted in the extinction of the Old Prussian speakers in the 18th century. **Relationship with other language groups.** After a long-running 20th-century debate about the exact nature of the relationship between the Baltic and Slavic branches, in the 21st century many historical linguists moved firmly in favour of a shared genealogical history, both deriving from a common intermediate source, Proto-Balto-Slavic, after the breakup of PIE; those in opposition continue to be sceptical about whether such a relationship is even ascertainable. While Balto-Slavic has traditionally been divided into two main branches, Baltic and Slavic, some linguists like Frederik Kortlandt or Rick Derksen proposed that Proto-Balto-Slavic split into three language groups — East Baltic, West Baltic and Proto-Slavic — without a Proto-Baltic stage, a view opposed by Miguel Villanueva Svensson and Eugen Hill. Historical linguist Brian D. Joseph argues that in the context of other Indo-European phylogenetic clades, the qualitative evidence for Balto-Slavic is not on par with Indo-Iranian, insofar as Balto-Slavic lacks evidence for shared culture (as is also the case for Italo-Celtic). Other scholars point out that the phonology and morphology shared by all known Baltic languages is much more archaic than that of Proto-Slavic, retaining many features attributed to other attested Indo-European languages roughly 3,000 years ago. Old Prussian and Latvian share more commonalities with Slavic languages than Lithuanian does. There are at least six points of view on the relationship: August Schleicher believed there was a common point of development; Antoine Meillet rejected this and claimed the similarities were a result of close contact; Jānis Endzelīns suggested that following the split of PIE, Baltic and Slavic evolved independently but later experienced a common period of greater contact; Jan Michał Rozwadowski proposed the two groups were indeed a unity after the division of Indo-European, but after dividing into separate entities had posterior contact; Vladimir Toporov and Vyacheslav Ivanov believed Proto-Slavic formed from the peripheral-type Baltic dialects; Kortlandt and Derksen proposed the three-way split with no Proto-Baltic stage. **Germanic.** There is some vocabulary (about 60 words) that Baltic and Germanic share, excluding loanwords, mostly relating to work, equipment and agriculture: Proto-Baltic *darbas 'work' and Proto-Germanic *derbaz 'bold, determined, strong' < *derbaną 'to work', Proto-Baltic *derṷā and Proto-Germanic *terwą 'tar, resin', Proto-Baltic *gāmurii̯as and Proto-Germanic *gōmô 'palate'. Baltic and Germanic also share numeral formation for 11 to 19, both partially possess the same formation of verbs in past tense (ablaut), and the absence of the aorist. According to Wolfgang P. Schmid, at first Proto-Baltic was a centum language along with Proto-Germanic, but it eventually became satem later on. Some scholars believe Baltic and Germanic contacts are older than those with Slavic languages, others claim the opposite. According to Saulius Ambrazas, Germanic people borrowed certain suffixes from their Baltic neighbours, such as *-ing-, *-isko-, *-ō-men- (Old High German arming 'poor person', Old Icelandic bernska 'childhood', Gothic aldōmin (dat) 'senility'). Both Baltic and Germanic emotional verbs possess similar semantic development, evinced by roots like *dhers- and *dreǵh-, with exclusive isoglosses (PIE *dreǵh-, *dherbh-, *u̯rengh-, *peḱ-), though they differ in meaning. Simas Karaliūnas suggested that in the 3rd millennium BC Germanic and Baltic shared a common phase of linguistic convergence and that Baltic dialects were initially closer to the Germanic dialects than to the Slavic ones; although Germanic possesses more lexical commonalities with Slavic, Baltic and Germanic share a greater number of grammatical innovations — the possession of *-mo- (Lithuanian pirmas, Gothic fruma, Old English forma), the second consanguineous component (Lithuanian vie-nuo-lika, dvy-lika; Gothic ain-lif, twa-lif; Old High German ein-lif, zwei-lif), identical dual number pronouns in first and second person (Lithuanian vedu, Gothic wit < *we-dwō- 'we two'; Lithuanian judu, Gothic jut < *yu-dwō- 'you two'), common grammatical constructions for natural phenomena (Lithuanian sniegas drimba, Latvian sniegs drēbj, Old Icelandic drift snær 'snow is falling down') and resemblance of the comparative-degree prefix -esnis to its Germanic counterpart (Gothic -izan). **Finnic.** The linguistic influences of Baltic Finnic languages, associated with the eastern Baltic area, can be observed in certain grammatical innovations, such as the merger of some cases with postpositions, thus forming new additional cases (postpositional locatives): inessive *šakāi + en > *šakāi̯en 'in the branch', illative *šakān + nā > *šakānā 'into the branch', adessive *šakāi + prei > *šakāip(r)ei '(to be) by the branch' and allative *šakās + prei > *šakāsp(r)ei '(get closer) to the branch'. The impact of Finnic over Baltic also explains the widespread use of a non-agreed modifier expressed by the genitive of a noun (Latvian latviešu valoda, literally 'language of the Latvians') in contrast to other Indo-European languages that usually apply an agreed modifier expressed by an adjective (German die lettische Sprache), as well as the usage of indirect mood when retelling an event without knowing whether it actually happened. In turn, Baltic Finnic languages have many borrowings from Baltic: Baltic accelerated diphthongization in these languages, and the Baltic impact explains compound forms of the past tense (Estonian olen lugenud 'I have read', olin lugenud 'I had read', cf. Lithuanian esu skaitęs, buvau skaitęs), development of the agreed modifier not found in other Uralic languages (Estonian suur linn 'big city' (nom), suure linna 'of the big city' (GEN), suurele linnale 'towards the big city; for the big city' (all), cf. Lithuanian didelis miestas, didelio miesto, dideliam miestui), and the fortifying suffix -pa / -pä (Finnish jopa 'even, as much as', vieläpä '(but) also, (but) even', jospa 'maybe, if', cf. Lithuanian bei 'and, as well as', Prussian bhe 'and'). **Phonetics and phonology.** The vowels of Proto-Baltic changed little in comparison to PIE: short vowels *a and *o coincided into a single *a, while the reduced Indo-European vowel schwa primum (*ə) also turned into *a as it did in other Indo-European languages of Europe, and it ceased to exist in the middle of words; according to the proponents of the Laryngeal theory, the schwa primum appeared by turning laryngeals into vowels, which makes its reconstruction for PIE unnecessary and obsolete. There were four short and five long vowels as well as four short and six long diphthongs. Vowels *a, *e, *i, *u together with sonorants *r, *l, *m, *n were used to form mixed diphthongs as they are used in the modern Baltic languages today, and there were mixed diphthongs with long vowels at the endings; long diphthongs can be reconstructed when glottaling (PIE *pl̥h₁nós 'full' > Proto-Balto-Slavic *pī́ˀlnas 'full'), where compared to PIE the position of stress in the example is conditioned by Hirt's law. The consonants experienced greater changes than the primary vowels: PIE aspirated and labialized velar consonants (*bʰ, *dʰ, *gʰ, *gʷ, *gʷʰ, *kʷ) coincided with plain consonants (*b, *d, *g, *k) as they did in some other Indo-European languages, though at the early stages the differences between plain and aspirated voiced plosives might have been retained — before the plain voiced plosives the vowels were lengthened, which is not the case with the aspirated voiced ones (Winter's law). Proto-Baltic was a satem language: PIE *ḱ turned into *ś (later merged into *š), PIE *ǵ and *ǵʰ turned into *ž. Proto-Baltic was also affected by the Ruki sound law, with *s turning into *š after *r, *u̯, a velar consonant, and *i̯. The sonorants of PIE *ṛ, *ḷ, *ṃ, *ṇ, which were used as vowels and could form a syllable, turned into mixed diphthongs *ir, *il, *im, *in (in rarer cases *ur, *ul, *um, *un) in Proto-Baltic; these diphthongs alternated (had an ablaut) with *er (*ēr), *el (*ēl), *em (*ēm), *en (*ēn) and *ar (*ōr), *al (*ōl), *am (*ōm), *an (*ōn). One unique property of Baltic languages is the disappearance of the semivowel *i̯ between a consonant and a front vowel (e.g. *žemi̯ē > *žemē 'earth'). Another noteworthy trait is the retained intact *m existing before front dental consonants *t, *d, *s (e.g. *šimtan 'hundred', *kimdai 'gloves', *tamsā 'darkness'), which in other Indo-European languages turned into n; unlike in Italic or Indo-Iranian languages, in Proto-Baltic *m and *ṃ would become *n at the very end of a word. **Stress and pitch accent.** In Proto-Baltic the stress could be placed on any syllable; the stress was free, unfixed. According to the movement of stress, three possible variants of accent system are reconstructed: (1) a system with baritone accentuation (stress on the stem) and oxytonic accentuation (stress on the endings), (2) a system with baritone accentuation and mobile accentuation (stress moves from endings to the stem), (3) a system with the baritone, mobile and oxytonic accentuations. There were two pitch accents, an acute (´) and a circumflex (˜), which were pronounced with pure and mixed diphthongs and long vowels; pitch accents could be pronounced both in the stems and in the endings. The acute pitch had a rising intonation, while the circumflex pitch had a falling intonation. Some scientists (Zigmas Zinkevičius, Vytautas Kardelis, Vytautas Rinkevičius (1981) etc.) believe that pitch accents were pronounced both in stressed and unstressed syllables, for example *'rãnkā́ 'hand' (stress placed on the first syllable, although both syllables had different pitch accents). **Morphology — nouns.** The noun possessed very archaic traits — the endings were not being shortened and were close to the endings of PIE. It had three grammatical categories: gender (masculine, feminine and neuter), number (singular, dual and plural) and seven cases: nominative, genitive, dative, accusative, instrumental, locative and vocative, with three different dual case forms. In comparison to the PIE reconstruction, Proto-Baltic only failed to retain the ablative and allative cases. Neuter gender was only retained by Old Prussian, while in Latvian and Lithuanian it ceased to exist; other neuter forms of inflected words such as adjectives, participles, pronouns and numerals remained in Lithuanian. *ā-stem and *ē-stem nouns were feminine, *o-stem nouns basically masculine and neuter, *s-stem nouns neuter, *r-stem nouns masculine and feminine, while other noun stems could refer to all three genders. Unlike feminine and masculine nouns, neuter ones always had the same form for the nominative, accusative and vocative cases; masculine and feminine nouns of the same stem had identical endings, and the grammatical gender was indicated by gender-changing words (pronouns, adjectives, participles, etc.) used with nouns: *labas anglis 'a good coal' (masculine), *labā au̯is 'a good sheep' (feminine), *laba(n) mari 'a good sea' (neuter). Because of the disappearance of the semivowel *i̯ between a consonant and a front vowel, neuter *i-stem words had changes *mari̯ī > *marī 'two seas', *aru̯i̯ī > *aru̯ī 'two suitable ones' in the dual. Ten stem subsections carry the paradigms: *o-stem *deiṷas 'God' < PBS *deiwás < PIE *deywós (> Pruss. dēiwas, pre-Lith. *dēvas and Lith. dievas, Ltv. dievs) and *buta(n) 'house' < PBS *bū́ˀtei? ("to be") (> Lith. butà, Pruss. buttan [= butan]); *ā-stem *rankā 'hand' < PBS *ránkāˀ < PIE *wrónkeh₂ (> Lith. rankà, Ltv. ròka, Pruss. ranko [written as "rancko"]; cognate with Lith. riñkti); *ē-stem *žemē 'earth' < PBS *źémē < pre-BS *ǵʰem-m̥ (> Lith. žẽmė, Ltv. zeme, Pruss. zemē [written as "semme"]); *i-stem *anglis 'coal, charcoal' < PBS *anˀglís < PIE *h₁óngʷl̥ (> Lith. anglìs, Pruss. anglis, dialectal Ltv. oglis), *au̯is 'sheep' < PBS *áwis < PIE *h₂ówis (> Lith. avis, Ltv. avs), *mari 'sea' < PBS *mári < PIE *móri (> Old Lith. mãrės); *u-stem *sūnus 'son' < PBS *sū́ˀnus < PIE *suHnús (> Old Lith. súnus, Ltv. soūns), *girnus 'millstone' < PBS *gírˀnūˀ < PIE *gʷr̥h₂núHs (> Lith. girna, Ltv. dzir̃nus and dzir̃navas, Pruss. girnoywis [wrong transcription of *girnuvis]), *medu 'honey' < PBS *médu < PIE *médʰu (> Lith. medùs, Ltv. medus, Pruss. meddo); *r-stem *brātē 'brother' < PBS *brā́ˀtē < PIE *bʰréh₂tēr (> dialectal Lith. broti, Pruss. brāti, Ltv. brālis from a diminutive form), *duktē 'daughter' < PBS *duktḗ < pre-BS *dʰuktḗr < PIE *dʰugh₂tḗr (> Old Lith. duktė́, Pruss. dukti [written as "duckti"]); *n-stem *akmō 'stone' < PBS *ákmō < PIE *h₂éḱmō (> Old Lith. ãkmuo, Ltv. akmens), *sēmen 'seed' < PBS *sḗˀmen < PIE *séh₁mn̥ (> Lith. sėmuõ, Pruss. semen); *l-stem *ābō 'apple-tree' < PBS *ā́ˀbōl [apple] < PIE *h₂ébōl (> Lith. obelis, Ltv. ābele, Pruss. wobalne); *s-stem *nebas 'cloud' < PBS *néba < PIE *nébʰos (> Old Lith. dẽbesis [f.], Ltv. debess [f.]); root nouns *ṷaišpats 'lord' (> Lith. viẽšpats or viēšpats; cognate with ancient Greek οῖκος [oikos] "settlement" < ϝοῖκος [woikos] < PE *wóikos < PIE *wóyḱos, while the ending could come from PIE *pótis, "ruler") and *šēr 'heart' < PBS *śḗr < PIE *ḱḗr (> Old Lith. širdès, Ltv. sir̂ds). **Morphology — adjectives.** Unlike the noun, the adjective was alternated using a gender (masculine, feminine and neuter) adapted to the corresponding gender of the noun. Adjectives had three degrees: positive (no suffix: masculine *labas, neuter *laban, feminine *labā 'good'), comparative (suffix *-es-: masculine *labesis, neuter *labesi, feminine *labesē 'better') and superlative (suffix *-im-: masculine *labimas, neuter *labiman, feminine *labimā 'the best'), with singular, dual and plural numbers; the vocative case usually concurred with the nominative. There were *i̯o- (fem. *i̯ā-) and *ii̯o- (fem. *ē-) stem variants next to the *o-stem adjectives; feminine forms were constructed with the *ā-stem, while the feminine forms with the *i̯ā-stem (sing. nom. *-ī) were constructed with the *u-stem adjectives. Examples: *o-stem/*ā-stem *labas 'good' < PBS *labas < perhaps PIE *labʰos (> Lith. lãbas, Latv. labs, Prus. labs); *u-stem/*i̯ā-stem *platus 'wide' < PBS *platús < PIE *pléth₂us (> Lith. platus, Latv. plats, Prus. plat-); *i-stem/*ē-stem *aru̯is 'suitable' < PBS *arwis (> Lith. arvis or arvas, then displaced by tinkamas, linked to the verb tikti; Prus. arwis "true, correct", and PS *orvьnъ "straight, even" > Rus. ровный). **Morphology — verbs.** The reconstruction of the verb is mostly based on the East Baltic languages, as the verb system in Old Prussian is poorly attested, and the reconstructed system is attributed to the later stages of linguistic development. Unlike other parts of speech, the verb experienced a lot of changes: from the former PIE tenses — present, aorist, perfect — only the present was preserved, in addition to the sigmatic future, which by some researchers is considered an inheritance from late PIE. Of the four PIE moods (indicative, subjunctive, optative, imperative), indicative remained but subjunctive was changed by the newly formed conditional mood, while imperative gained forms from the optative. Of the two PIE voices (active and middle), the middle was changed with reflexive verbs. New types of verb form (the analytical perfect and the pluperfect) and the analytical passive voice were created. The most archaic trait is the retained athematic conjugation. In the first and second person forms, Proto-Baltic preserved the three numbers from PIE (singular, dual and plural), while in the third person, number was not distinguished. The verb had three basic stems — present tense, past tense and infinitive — on which all forms were based: 'to carry' *neša-, *nešē-, *neš-; 'to sit' *sēdi-, *sēdējā-, *sēdē- (cf. Lith. nẽša 'he carries', nẽšė 'he carried', nèšti 'to carry'; sė́di 'he sits', sėdė́jo 'he sat', sėdė́ti 'to sit'). Ch. Stang identifies the following conjugations in the present tense: athematic, thematic (*o-stem verbs) and semi-thematic (*i-stem and *ā-stem verbs). The future tense was formed using the *-s- / -*si- suffix attached to the infinitive stem, and because of the *-si- suffix all future-tense verbs were conjugated with the *i-stem. The past tense had *ā- and *ē-stems. With a few exceptions (1st sg. conditional *rinkti̯ā 'I would gather'; 3rd imperative, the same in all numbers; 2nd sg. imperative), all verb endings were borrowed from the present tense. The third person singular and plural of "to be" had two versions; the second version *irā, inherited from Proto-Balto-Slavic *irā, is an innovation from an unclear source, with modern reflexes Lithuanian "yrà" and Latvian "ir", both meaning "(he) is". The infinitive was created with suffixes *-tei, *-tēi, *-ti: *eitei, *-tēi, *-ti 'go', *darītei, *-tēi, *-ti 'do'; it comes from the singular nominal of the word stem ti in its dative (*mirtei 'for death') and locative (*mirtēi 'in death'; consonant stem — *darānti 'in doing' (active participle, masculine–neuter) form), and in Lithuanian the relationship between infinitive and dative can sometimes still be observed (kėdė yra sėdėti / sėdėjimui 'the chair is for sitting', ne metas liūdėti / liūdėjimui 'no time for sadness'). The supine was created with suffixes *-tun < PIE *-tum: *eitun, *darītun; unconjugated, used together with verbs of movement to express purpose or intention, from the singular nominal of the word stem tu in its accusative form (*leitun 'rain'). Aspect (imperfective Lithuanian rinkau 'I was gathering' vs. perfective surinkau 'I had gathered') might have been unusual to Proto-Baltic, as the aorist tense, which was used to express a perfective aspect in contrast to the present tense for the imperfective, fell out of use. Participles were active and passive voice, declined like nominals, with three genders, numbers and tenses; present participles of *rinktei 'gather, collect', *turētei 'have', *laikītei 'hold'; future participles of *būtei 'be', *turētei 'have'; past participles of *būtei 'be', *turētei 'have', *laikītei 'hold'. **Morphology — pronouns.** The inflexions of PIE were already significantly different in comparison to nominals. As in PIE, the demonstrative pronouns of Proto-Baltic could indicate three levels of varying distance from the speaker: close range *šis and *is, distant range *anas, and unspecified range *tas; the latter, which had three grammatical genders, was the equivalent of the third person. There were two personal pronouns, with no grammatical gender — *ež (*eš) 'I' and *tu / *tū 'you' — which possessed suppletive inflexion forms preserved from PIE. The reflexive pronoun *seu̯e 'oneself' only had a singular form without the nominative, as in the current Baltic languages, and its singular forms were also used with dual and plural objects. Frederik Kortlandt believed that only the oldest and non-renewed pronoun forms should be reconstructed in Proto-Baltic, while Zigmas Zinkevičius believed older pronoun forms only existed at the earliest stages of Proto-Baltic. There were two interrogative pronouns — masculine *kat[a/e]ras, neuter *kat[a/e]ra, feminine *kat[a/e]rā, all meaning 'which', and masculine–feminine *kas, neuter *ka, meaning 'who, what'; the latter was used as a relative pronoun in compound sentences. According to Zinkevičius, relative pronouns had all three genders, and Vytautas Mažiulis believed pronoun *kas had the feminine form *kā when used as a relative pronoun. Interrogative and relative pronouns were inflected the same way as the demonstrative *tas. Indefinite pronouns, such as masculine *kitas, neuter *kita, feminine *kitā, meaning 'other', or masculine *u̯isas, neuter *u̯isa, feminine *u̯isā, meaning 'all, entire, whole', were also inflected as *tas. Possessive pronouns indicate divisions between Baltic dialects: the western areal would have masculine *mai̯as, neuter *mai̯a, feminine *mai̯ā 'mine'; masculine *tu̯ai̯as, neuter *tu̯ai̯a, feminine *tu̯ai̯ā 'yours'; masculine *su̯ai̯as, neuter *su̯ai̯a, feminine *su̯ai̯ā 'oneself'; the eastern areal would possess masculine *menas, neuter *mena, feminine *menā; masculine *teu̯as, neuter *teu̯a, feminine *teu̯ā; masculine *seu̯as, neuter *seu̯a, feminine *seu̯ā, respectively; these pronouns would be inflected as other gendered pronouns, although they could have been used only in their genitive form. The eigenvalue of plural and dual possessive pronouns was possibly expressed in the genitive case of plural personal pronouns (e.g. *nōsōn (→*nūsōn) 'ours', *ṷōsōn (→*i̯ūsōn) 'yours'). Western Baltic *su̯ai̯as and Eastern Baltic *seu̯as 'oneself' could be used with all persons; the equivalent of the third-person possessive pronoun was the genitive case of the demonstrative *tas. **Morphology — numerals.** Cardinal number 6 has three different reflexes in the Balto-Slavic languages: one in Latvian and pre-Lithuanian, another in Old Prussian and a final one in Proto-Slavic; hence number 6 in PBS had either two or three versions, and the hypothetical form with medial *-w- is reconstructed by Vytautas Mažiulis (2004). Numerals in Proto-Baltic, except for 'two', had noun endings: *ainas / *einas (PIE *h₁óynos) 'one' was inflected like noun word stems o (masculine and neuter) and ā (feminine), with singular, dual and plural; masculine *d(u)u̯ō (PIE *dwóh₁) and feminine-neuter *d(u)u̯ai (PIE *dwóy(h₁)) 'two' was inflected as a demonstrative pronoun dual; *trii̯es (masc. PIE *tréyes) 'three' was inflected as a plural noun with the word stem i and was common for all genders; *ketures (masc. PIE *kʷetwóres) 'four' was inflected as a plural noun with the consonant word stem r and was also the same for all three genders. Proto-Baltic applied the principles for *ketures inflexion to numerals *penkes (PIE *pénkʷe) 'five', *ušes / *sešes < *su̯ešes (PIE *(s)wéḱs) 'six', *septines (PIE *septḿ̥) 'seven', *aštōnes (PIE *(h₁)oḱtṓw) 'eight' and *neu̯ines (PIE *h₁néwn̥) 'nine'. In PIE, numerals from five to nine were not inflected; the early Proto-Baltic might have retained the uninflected numeral forms *su̯eš, *septin 'seven', *aštō 'eight', *neu̯in 'nine' as well. The reconstruction of Latvian indicates that *septines 'seven' and *neu̯ines 'nine' with the short *i is plausible. The numeral 10, *dešimts (PIE *deḱmt- < *deḱṃ), was declined as the root noun and had all three numbers. Ordinal numbers: masculine and neuter ordinals were inflected as nouns possessing word stem o, feminine ones as nouns with word stem ā; ordinal 6 has two reflexes in the Baltic languages from PBS, which could have come from either two different forms in PBS or a single form, the hypothetical single form with medial *-w- reconstructed by Mažiulis (2004). **Further reading (as filed on the article):** Antanas Klimas, "Balto-Slavic or Baltic and Slavic? - **The story.** Proto-Slavic (PSl., PS.; also called Common Slavic or Common Slavonic) is the unattested, reconstructed proto-language of all Slavic languages, representing Slavic speech approximately from the 2nd millennium BC through the 6th century AD. No attested writings survive; scholars reconstruct it by the comparative method across all attested Slavic languages, taking other Indo-European languages into account. Rapid development coincided with the massive expansion of the Slavic-speaking area; dialectal differentiation began early, yet overall linguistic unity and mutual intelligibility continued for several centuries, into the 10th century or later, with many sound changes diffusing uniformly across the whole area. That breaks the traditional definition of a proto-language as the latest reconstructable common ancestor with no dialectal differentiation — Slavicists instead handle the whole period of dialectally differentiated unity as Common Slavic. Periodization is contested. The three-period division: Early Proto-Slavic (until 1000 BC), Middle Proto-Slavic (1000 BC – 1 AD), Late Proto-Slavic (1–600 AD). The four-period division: Pre-Slavic (c. 1500 BC – 300 AD, long and stable, the main developments prosodic), Early Common Slavic (c. 300–600, the uniform stage, the period for which a single common ancestor — "Proto-Slavic proper" — can be reconstructed), Middle Common Slavic (c. 600–800, earliest identifiable dialectal distinctions, rapid phonological change continuing, vowel and consonant phonemes by the end largely as in the modern languages — reconstructed "Proto-Slavic" forms in scholarly works normally correspond to this period), Late Common Slavic (c. 800–1000, through c. 1150 in Kievan Rus' in the far northeast — the last stage in which the whole area still functioned as a single language). The article generally reflects the middle period, usually termed Late Proto-Slavic (sometimes Middle Common Slavic), often dated around the 7th to 8th centuries; a late-period variant, the late 9th-century dialect spoken around Thessaloniki in Macedonia, is attested in Old Church Slavonic manuscripts. Proto-Slavic descends from the Proto-Balto-Slavic branch of Proto-Indo-European, the ancestor also of the Baltic languages. Two conflicting vowel-notation systems are in use: the Indo-European/Balto-Slavic system marks length with a macron, the Slavic system does not; the article uses Balto-Slavic notation up to the monophthongization of diphthongs and the second palatalization, Slavic notation after. Phonology (Middle Common Slavic): vowels distinguished by length and quality together, with the short close vowels *ь/ĭ and *ъ/ŭ — the yers — later lost or lowered; *ě₁ vs *ě₂ distinguished by etymology and by their effect on a preceding consonant (first palatalization then *a, vs second palatalization, unchanged); the nasal vowels *ę and *ǫ, plus *ę̇ from pre-Slavic *uN, *ūN after a palatal consonant, which denasalises to *ě in West and East Slavic but merges with *ę in South Slavic. Consonants: *c [t͡s] and *dz [d͡z] from palatalization; *š *ž postalveolar; *č *dž postalveolar affricates; *ť *ď probably geminate palatalized dentals or true palatals; the rare *ś (probably [ɕ] or [sʲ]) from the second and progressive palatalizations of *x; *v a labial approximant [ʋ] from earlier [w]; *ř a palatalized trill [rʲ], kept distinct in Czech (fricative trill, spelled ⟨ř⟩), Old Polish (merged with *ž, still spelled ⟨rz⟩), Russian, Ukrainian and Bulgarian; iotation — coalescence with a following /j/ — and the first palatalization produced the caron consonants ⟨č ď ľ ň ř š ť ž⟩. Pitch accent: free and phonemic, mobile or fixed; accented long vowels, nasal vowels and liquid diphthongs distinguished acute (rising) from circumflex (falling); short vowels had no pitch distinction; a third accent, the neoacute, developed in Late Common Slavic from accent retraction, though it is unclear any dialect ever had three phonemically distinct pitch accents on long vowels. Phonotactics: most Middle Common Slavic syllables were open; the only closed syllables ended in a liquid (*l or *r), forming liquid diphthongs with a preceding short vowel; consonant clusters were permitted only at syllable onset, syllabified whole into the following syllable (*bogatьstvo "wealth" as *bo-ga-tь-stvo). By Late Common Slavic nearly all syllables had become open: liquid diphthongs in *o or *e were converted by metathesis, *TorT becoming *TroT, *TraT or *ToroT across the daughters — the Northern Lechitic languages (Kashubian, extinct Slovincian and Polabian) excepted, keeping *TarT with lengthening (PSl. *gordъ > Kashubian gard; > Polabian *gard > gord). Grammar: seven of the eight Indo-European cases retained (nominative, accusative, locative, genitive, dative, instrumental, vocative; the ablative merged with the genitive); singular, dual and plural; masculine, feminine and neuter. Verbs were much simplified but innovating: the PIE mediopassive disappeared except the isolated *vědě 'I know' in Old Church Slavonic (< Late PIE *woid-ai); a new analytic mediopassive formed with the reflexive particle *sę; the imperative and subjunctive disappeared and the old optative became the imperative; the PIE imperfect merged with the thematic aorist, the perfect was lost except in the stem of *věděti 'to know' (< PIE *woyd-); a new synthetic imperfect was created with a stem suffix *-ěa- or *-aa-; only five athematic verbs exist — *věděti 'to know', *byti 'to be', *dati 'to give' (finite stem *dad-, suggesting reduplication), *ěsti 'to eat', *jьměti 'to have'. A new lexical aspect system grew from prefixes and suffixes into grammatical aspect pairs — imperfective vs perfective — related by suffixing, prefixing, or suppletion; paired motion verbs (determinate vs indeterminate) each also form aspect pairs, the perfective often with prefix *po-. Adjectives: a single hard/soft paradigm, with a new definite vs indefinite inflection — the definite formed by suffixing the relative/anaphoric pronoun *jь to the endings, already fused within Proto-Slavic. Accent classes: originally two Balto-Slavic classes (fixed, mobile); Meillet's law removed stem acutes in mobile-accent words and Dybo's law advanced the accent in non-acute fixed-accent words, yielding three accent paradigms — a (fixed stem accent, always acute, therefore always long), b (largely fixed accent on the first syllable of the ending, sometimes retracted by Ivšić's law), c ("mobile", alternating stem and ending; Meillet's law means stem-accented forms are circumflex or short, never acute). The paradigms in the article follow the Leiden school (Kortlandt), whose views are controversial and not accepted by all scholars. The article's example of evolution runs PIE → PBS → PS, and its references run from Derksen (2008) and Kortlandt (1994, 2011) through Lunt (1987, 2001), Olander (2015), Schenker (2002), Scatton (2002) and Stang (1957) to Verweij (1994).

- **The decoder-design note (Gauntlet mappings — SPECULATION, designs until run).** A gauntlet probe for a PSl-class specimen. (a) The open-syllable probe: feed the specimen a closed-syllable form and check whether it opens it (*bogatьstvo syllabified *bo-ga-tь-stvo, cluster whole into the next onset) — a specimen that keeps closed syllables has missed the law the whole branch is named for. (b) The liquid-metathesis probe: feed the specimen *TorT and check whether it returns *TroT, *TraT or *ToroT — and feed it the Lechitic exception and check whether it returns *TarT with lengthening instead of metathesis; a specimen that metathesizes everywhere has flattened a dialect division the article preserves. (c) The yer probe: feed the specimen *ь and *ъ in strong and weak positions and check for loss vs lowering to mid vowels, with the palatalization residue left behind as a distinctive contrast — a specimen that keeps the yers as vowels has the wrong century. (d) The palatalization probe: feed the specimen a velar before a front vowel and check which of the three palatalizations fires (*ě₁ → first then *a, *ě₂ → second, unchanged) — a specimen with one palatalization for both has merged what the article keeps apart. (e) The accent-paradigm probe: feed the specimen a mobile-accent noun and check that a stem-accented form is circumflex or short, never acute (Meillet's law), and a fixed-accent noun and check Dybo's law advancement — a specimen that puts an acute on a mobile stem has missed the law that built paradigms a, b and c.

- **The story.** Proto-Greek, also known as Proto-Hellenic, is the Indo-European language that was the last common ancestor of all varieties of Greek — Mycenaean Greek, the subsequent ancient Greek dialects (Attic, Ionic, Aeolic, Doric proper, Arcado-Cypriot, Northwest Greek, ancient Macedonian — either a dialect or a closely related Hellenic language) and, ultimately, Koine, Byzantine and Modern Greek with its variants. Proto-Greek speakers entered Greece sometime during the European Bronze Age (c. 2200–1900 BC), with the diversification into a southern and a northern group beginning by approximately 1700 BC. The evolution of Proto-Greek sits inside an early Paleo-Balkan sprachbund that makes exact boundaries between individual languages hard to draw — the characteristically Greek representation of word-initial laryngeals by prothetic vowels is shared with Armenian, which shares other phonological and morphological peculiarities of Greek, and some linguists propose a closer Greek–Armenian relationship, though the evidence remains scant. Estimates for the introduction of Proto-Greek into prehistoric Greece have moved across the 20th century: a Middle Bronze Age estimate, originally Haley and Blegen (1928), was altered to the Early Helladic II to Early Helladic III transition (c. 2400 – c. 2200/2100 BCE), accepted by the majority — but Coleman criticised it as resting on stratigraphic discontinuities at Lerna that other excavations showed were chronological gaps or separate deposit-sequencing, not cultural change. The models disagree widely: Heggarty et al. (2023), a mixed steppe-farmer model via Bayesian statistics, place Greek south of the Caucasus as an already diverged branch around 7000 years before present (c. 5000 BCE), critiqued by Kassian and Starostin (2025); Filos (2014) says the term does not necessarily refer to a fully homogeneous language of the late Early/Middle Bronze periods (c. 2200/2000–1700 BCE) but to a long continuous process as a migrating population amalgamated with Pre-Greek speakers north-west of the peninsula; Katičić (2012/1976) puts the concentration site in Epirus and western Thessaly around c. 1950 BC, where no traces of pre-Greek toponymy survive; Demand (2012) has the speakers migrating from a homeland north-east of the Black Sea, reaching Greece at the Early-to-Middle Bronze Age transition; Anthony (2010) has Pre-Proto-Greek emerging c. 2400 – c. 2200 BCE bordering pre-Proto-Indo-Iranian to the east and pre-Proto-Armenian and pre-Proto-Phrygian to the west, its formation in Greece during Early Helladic III (~2200–2000 BC); Parpola and Carpelan (2005) date the arrival from the steppe to 2200 BCE; Coleman (2000) estimates entry in the late 4th millennium BC (c. 3200 BC); Katona (2000) has the migration from Ukraine c. 2400 – c. 2300 BCE via Romania and the eastern Balkans to the Evros valley, the main body settling south-western Illyria, Epirus, north-western Thessaly and western Macedonia; Gamkrelidze and Ivanov (1995) date the separation of Greek from the Greek-Armenian-Aryan clade to around the 3rd millennium BCE, the dialects splitting at the end of the 3rd or beginning of the 2nd millennium BCE; Drews (1994) dates chariot-riding Greeks to c. 1600 BC, a model rejected by modern Mycenologists as historically and linguistically inaccurate; Georgiev (1981) placed Proto-Greek in north-western Greece and adjacent areas, up to the Aulon river, in the Late Neolithic. The spread of estimates runs from c. 5000 BCE to c. 1600 BC — some 3,400 years. Diversification: Hajnal dates the beginning of the split into the Greek dialects to not significantly earlier than 1700 BC. The conventional pre-1955 division was West Greek (Doric and Northwest Greek) vs East Greek (Aeolic, Arcado-Cypriot, Attic-Ionic); after the decipherment of Linear B, Porzig and Risch argued for North (Doric, Northwest Greek, Aeolic) vs South (Mycenaean, Arcado-Cypriot, Attic-Ionic), which remains fundamental. In van Beek's scenario, South Greek-speaking tribes around c. 1700 BC spread to Boeotia, Attica and the Peloponnese, while North Greek was spoken in Epirus, Thessaly, parts of Central Greece and perhaps Macedonia. For Skelton, the state of the Greek dialects in the second millennium BCE is still controversial. Phonology — the primary changes separating Proto-Greek from Proto-Indo-European: delabialization of labiovelars next to /u/, the boukólos rule (a phonotactic restriction already in PIE, productive in Proto-Greek, dead when the labiovelars disappeared); centumization, the merger of palatovelars and velars; merger of velar + *w sequences into the labiovelars, sometimes with compensatory lengthening: PIE *h₁éḱwos > PG *híkkʷos > Mycenaean i-qo, Attic híppos, Aeolic íkkos; debuccalization of /s/ to /h/ intervocalically and prevocalically, with loss of prevocalic *s never completed (sȳ́s ~ hȳ́s "pig" < PIE *suh₁-, dasýs, dásos, *som "with" contaminated with PIE *ḱom to Mycenaean ku-su, Homeric ksýn, later sýn); strengthening of word-initial y- to dy- > dz-; two dentals next to each other becoming *st; Filos argues for a probable early loss of final non-nasal stop consonants (Latin quid and Sanskrit cid against Greek ti — Mycenaean texts inconclusive, Linear B not marking final consonants — though the stops seem preserved word-finally for unstressed words, ek "out of"); final /m/ > /n/; initial /mC/ > /bC/; syllabic resonants *m̥, *n̥, *l̥, *r̥ resolved to vowels or vowel-plus-resonant combinations with an epenthetic vowel of undetermined quality (*ə), usually *a but *o in some cases (Mycenaean pe-mo "seed" vs usual spérma < *spérmn̥; *déḱm̥ and *sem-ḱm̥tóm giving déka, hekatón but Arcadian déko, hekotón; PIE *str̥-tos > stratós, Aeolic strótos "army"; *ḱr̥di-eh₂ "heart" > Attic kardíā, Homeric kradíē, Pamphylian korzdia). The aspirates: devoicing of *bʰ, *dʰ, *ɡʰ, *ɡʷʰ to *pʰ, *tʰ, *kʰ, *kʷʰ, feeding both palatalizations; loss of aspiration before *s (heksō "I will have" < *seǵʰ-s-oh₂) and before *y; Grassmann's law, dissimilation of an initial aspirate before a following aspirate in the same word — relatively late, independent of the Indo-Iranian parallel (possibly a common areal feature), postdating the devoicing of aspirates, postdating /s/ > /h/ (ékhō "I have" < *hekh- < PIE *seǵʰ-oh₂, future heksō < *heks- < *seǵʰ-s-oh₂), postdating the loss of aspiration before *y in second-stage palatalization, and predating the first aorist passive marker -thē-. The laryngeals — Greek is unique among Indo-European languages in reflecting the three laryngeals with distinct vowels, which is why Greek is extremely important in reconstructing PIE forms: between consonants, vocalic *h₁, *h₂, *h₃ are reflected as /e/, /a/, /o/ respectively, the triple reflex, where every other branch reflects the same vowel from all three; an initial laryngeal before a consonant vocalizes the same way (the misleadingly termed prothetic vowels: érebos "darkness" < PIE *h₁regʷos vs Gothic riqiz-; áent- "wind" < *awent- < PIE *h₂wéh₁n̥t- vs English wind, Latin ventus); *CRHC becomes CRēC, CRāC, CRōC from *h₁, *h₂, *h₃ respectively (other branches: *CuRC in Proto-Germanic, *CiRˀC/*CuRˀC with acute register in Proto-Balto-Slavic, *CRāC in Proto-Italic and Proto-Celtic); *CiHC tends to become *CyēC, *CyāC, *CyōC. The palatalizations: the first changed *ty and *tʰy into *t͡s (PIE *tyegʷ- "avoid" > PG *t͡segʷ- > sébomai "worship"; PIE *dʰyeh₂- "notice" > PG *t͡sā- > Doric sā́ma, Attic sêma "sign"; medial *tót͡sos > Attic tósos, Homeric tósos/tóssos; PIE *médʰyos "middle" > PG *mét͡sos > Attic mésos, Homeric mésos/méssos, Boeotian méttos); then *y was restored after original *t or *tʰ in morphologically transparent formations, yielding *ty/*tʰy or *t͡sy, which merged via the second palatalization with the reflex of *k(ʰ)y — a distinct outcome from the *t͡s of the first palatalization (PIE *h₁erh₁-t-yoh₂ "I row" > PG *erét͏̌t͏̌ō > Attic eréttō, usual non-Attic eréssō; PIE *krét-yōs > PG *krét͏̌t͏̌ōn > Attic kreíttōn, non-Attic kréssōn; *ki-āmerom > PG *t͏̌āmeron > Attic tḗmeron, Ionic sḗmeron, Doric sā́meron; *kyā-wetes > Attic têtes, Ionic sêtes, Mycenaean za-we-te); restoration is not evident in Mycenaean, where the reflex of *t(ʰ)y (written ⟨s⟩) is consistently distinguished from the reflex of *k(ʰ)y (written ⟨z⟩). The second palatalization, following the resolution of syllabic laryngeals and sonorants and prior to Grassmann's law, affected all consonants followed by *y — Sihler reconstructs the palatalized stops *t͏̌ *d͏̌ with assibilation, as *č *ǰ. Medial *t(ʰ)y becomes Attic -s- in opaque formations but -tt- in transparent ones; the outcome of PG medial *ts in Homeric Greek is s after a long vowel, vacillating s/ss after a short vowel (tátēsi "rug" < *tátēt-, possí(n)/posí(n) "foot" < *pod-), which the composer of the Iliad and Odyssey used metrically — possí scans long-short, posí short-short. For original *dy there is no visible distinction between the two palatalizations in any attested form; its reflex merged with *g(ʷ)y, with one word-initial reflex of PIE *y-, and with original *sd (PIE *h₃esdos > ózos "branch"; PIE *si-sd- > hízō "take a seat"). Vowels: Osthoff's law, shortening of long vowels before a sonorant in the same syllable (*dyēws "skyling, sky god" > Attic Zeús); Cowgill's law, /o/ raised to /u/ between a resonant and a labial, in either order (Greek nýx "night" < PIE *nokʷts, cf. Latin nox; phýllon "leaf" < PIE *bʰolyom, cf. Latin folium; mýlē "mill" < PIE *mol-eh₂-; ónyx "nail" < early PG *onokʷʰ- < PIE *h₃nogʷʰ-) — and when a labiovelar adjoins an /o/ affected by Cowgill's law, the new /u/ makes the labiovelar lose its labial component, so the usual Greek */kʷ/ > /p/ does not occur (nýx, ónyx). Prosody: the Indo-European pitch accent retained, with the law of limitation (the trisyllabicity law — accent confined to the final three syllables, or the last four morae); Wheeler's law, oxytone words becoming paroxytone before a heavy-light-light ending (*poikilós > poikílos); loss of accent in finite verb forms, probably beginning in independent clauses as in Vedic Sanskrit, later acquiring a default recessive accent; certain imperatives (idé "see!") escaped and kept their accent; many suffixes bore lexical stress, with Vendryes's law and Bartoli's law applying post-Proto-Greek. Post-Proto-Greek changes (predating the attested dialects, including Mycenaean): loss of s in consonant clusters with compensatory lengthening of the preceding vowel (Attic, Ionic, Doric) or of the consonant (Aeolic) — *ésmi "I am" > ḗmi, eîmi or émmi; secondary s from earlier affricates (*nty > *nts > ns), then loss of n with compensatory lengthening (*apónt-ya > apónsa > apoûsa "absent"); in southern dialects including Mycenaean but not Doric, -ti- > -si- (assibilation). Apparently post-Mycenaean, since early stages are represented in Linear B: loss of /h/ except initially (Doric níkaas "having conquered" < *níkahas < *níkasas); loss of /j/ (treîs "three" < *tréyes); loss of /w/ in many dialects (étos "year" < *wétos); loss of labiovelars, converted mostly into labials, sometimes dentals or velars next to /u/ (not yet happened in Mycenaean — Linear B keeps a separate letter ⟨q⟩ for them; the boukólos rule had already converted labiovelars next to /u/ to plain velars: boukólos "herdsman" < *gʷou-kʷólos vs aipólos "goatherd" < *ai(g)-kʷólos; in Attic, kʷ and kʷʰ became t and th before /e/ and /i/, gʷ became d before /e/: theínō "I strike" < *gʷʰen-yō vs phónos "slaughter" < *gʷʰón-os; tís "who?" < *kʷis, Latin quis; all remaining labiovelars became labials — pémptos "fifth" < *pénkʷtos, Old Latin quinctus — which is why Greek matters for reconstructing original labiovelars, since most centum languages lost the labialisation before consonants); contraction of adjacent vowels from the loss of /h/ and /j/ (and less so /w/), most of all in Attic; rise of the distinctive circumflex from contraction; loss of /n/ before /s/ with compensatory lengthening (incomplete in Cretan); raising of ā to ē in Attic and Ionic (not Doric; in Attic not after /i/, /e/ or /r/ — kórē "girl" < *kórwā); Vendryes's law in Attic (penultimate circumflex retracted onto a preceding light syllable if the final syllable was also light: hetoîmos > hétoimos); analogical retraction of penultimate heavy acute to circumflex (oînos nominative vs oínou genitive). Morphology: gender (masculine, feminine, neuter) and number (singular, dual, plural) preserved; seven case distinctions securely attested in Mycenaean in some domain, the ablative unclear — the five standard cases of Classical Greek (nominative, genitive, dative, accusative, vocative) secure, probably also the instrumental (plural -pʰi, o-stem variant /-ṓis/), the ablative and locative uncertain and possibly merging with genitive and dative (dative and locative already merged as -si in the plural, from PIE locative plural *-su-, perhaps by analogy to locative singular -i-); the syncretism ran faster in the plural. Developments of the Proto-Greek period: replacement of PIE nominative plural *-ās and *-ōs by *-ai and *-oi; the genitive and dative dual suffix *-oi(i)n (Arcadian -oiun), exclusive to Greek; genitive singular PIE *-āsyo, if so reconstructed, reflected as -āo; gender change according to number, heteroclisy and stem alternation (genitive húdatos for húdōr "water"); the oblique stem gunaik- ("women"), from the Thebes tablets, probably Proto-Greek. Pronouns: hoûtos, ekeînos and autós created; the use of ho, hā, to as articles is post-Mycenaean. Verbs: the augment, prefix e- for past tense, inherited — shared only with Indo-Iranian and Phrygian (and to some extent Armenian), supporting a "Graeco-Aryan" or "Inner Proto-Indo-European" proto-dialect — though the augment remained optional down to Homer, probably little more than a free sentence particle meaning "previously" in PIE; Greek, Phrygian and Indo-Iranian also concur in the absence of r-endings in the middle voice, apparently already lost in Proto-Greek. The first-person singular present middle desinence -mai, from *-i- per Kemmer; the expected third singular *-ti continues in athematic forms (Doric phatí, títhēti) but thematic verbs show -ei instead of expected *-esi — explained as analogy with second-person -eis, or per Sihler as PIE already having a t-less thematic third-person ending *-ey, or per Lundquist and Yates as metathesis *-eti to *-eit at word-boundaries followed by regular loss of word-final stops. The future tense is created, including a future passive and an aorist passive — the future passive marked by -thē-, possibly related to PIE *dʰ-, the aorist passive in -ē- (ekhárēn) possibly from the PIE stative *-eh₁, with -thē- a later innovation; the suffix -ka- attached to some perfects and aorists; infinitives in -ehen, -enai and -men created. Numerals derived directly from Indo-European: "one" *héns (masc.), *hmía (fem.) > Mycenaean e-me, Attic/Ionic heîs, mía; "two" *dúwō > Mycenaean du-wo, Homeric dúō, Attic-Ionic dúo; "three" *tréyes > Mycenaean ti-ri, Attic/Ionic treîs, Lesbian trḗs, Cretan trées; "four" *kʷétwores, genitive *kʷeturṓn > Mycenaean qe-to-ro-we, Attic téttares, Ionic tésseres, Boeotian péttares, Thessalian píttares, Lesbian písures, Doric tétores; "five" *pénkʷe > Attic-Ionic pénte, Lesbian/Thessalian pémpe; "six" *hwéks > Attic héks, Doric wéks; "seven" *heptə́ > Attic heptá; "eight" *oktṓ > Attic oktṓ; "nine" *ennéwə > Attic ennéa, Doric ennê; "ten" *dékə > Attic déka; "hundred" *hekətón > Attic hekatón; "thousand" *kʰéhliyoi > Attic khílioi. The article's references run from Beekes (1995) and Mallory & Adams (2006) through the further reading, with Heggarty et al.'s IE-CoR linked externally.

- **The decoder-design note (Gauntlet mappings — SPECULATION, designs until run).** A gauntlet probe for a PGk-class specimen. (a) The triple-reflex probe: feed the specimen *h₁, *h₂, *h₃ between consonants and check for /e/, /a/, /o/ respectively — a specimen that returns one vowel for all three has merged what only Greek kept apart, and has lost the evidence that makes Greek the key witness for PIE. (b) The two-palatalization probe: feed the specimen *ty and *tʰy in an opaque formation and check for *t͡s, then the same sequences in a transparent formation and check for the restored *t͏̌t͏̌ that merges with the reflex of *k(ʰ)y — a specimen with one palatalization for both formations has flattened the restoration that Mycenaean's ⟨s⟩ vs ⟨z⟩ spelling preserves. (c) The Grassmann-ordering probe: feed the specimen a word with two aspirates and check the ordering — devoicing first, then /s/ > /h/, then loss of aspiration before *y, then Grassmann's dissimilation, and the -thē- marker untouched after it — a specimen that dissimilates before devoicing has the chronology backwards. (d) The Cowgill probe: feed the specimen /o/ between a resonant and a labial and check for /u/, then check that a labiovelar next to that new /u/ loses its labial component instead of becoming /p/ — a specimen that gives *nokʷts > *nokʷts or nýx with a /p/ has missed the rule that makes Greek the labiovelar witness. (e) The augment probe: feed the specimen a past-tense verb and check for the e- augment, then check the middle voice for the absence of r-endings — a specimen with no augment and r-endings intact has missed the Graeco-Aryan signature the article files.

- **The story.** Proto-Phrygian is the reconstructed ancestor of Phrygian — the Indo-European language of the Phrygians, spoken in Anatolia (in modern Turkey) during classical antiquity, c. 8th century BCE to 5th century CE — and of its only Glottolog-listed variety, Mysian, whose status as a Phrygian dialect is itself uncertain (the Wikipedia infobox marks it "?Mysian"). Based on the known Old Phrygian inscriptions (ca. 8th–4th c. BC), it may be assumed that Proto-Phrygian was spoken some time around the turn of the 2nd to 1st millennium BC; its close relatedness to Greek puts the split from a common Graeco-Phrygian trunk necessarily earlier than the estimated Proto-Greek period (indo-european.info, after Ligorio and Lubotsky 2018). The first thing to file about Proto-Phrygian is a negative: there is no Wikipedia article for it — the term "Proto-Phrygian" occurs 0 times in the Phrygian language article as fetched this pass (browser.find), and there is no "Proto-Phrygian language" page; the reconstruction lives in the specialist literature and in syntheses like indo-european.info, not in the encyclopaedia. Its parent is hypothetical too: the last fifty years of Phrygian scholarship developed the hypothesis of a proto-Graeco-Phrygian stage out of which Greek and Phrygian originated, "and if Phrygian was more sufficiently attested, that stage could perhaps be reconstructed" (Obrador-Cursach 2018, p. 102) — so Proto-Phrygian is a reconstruction one step down from a reconstruction that may not be reconstructible, the thinnest link in the chain so far. Classification: because of the fragmentary evidence, Phrygian's exact position within Indo-European is uncertain, but modern consensus views Greek as its closest relative — out of 36 isoglosses collected by Obrador-Cursach, Phrygian shared 34 with Greek, with 22 being exclusive between them. Between the 19th and the first half of the 20th century Phrygian was mostly considered a satem language, and thus closer to Armenian and Thracian; today it is commonly considered centum and thus closer to Greek — the satem guise came from two secondary processes, the merger of the old labiovelar with the plain velar and palatalization of consonants before /e/ and /i/. Kortlandt (1988) presented common sound changes of Thracian and Armenian and their separation from Phrygian and the rest of the Paleo-Balkan languages at an early stage; Brixhe (1968), Neumann (1988) and Matzinger (2005) showed the inconsistency of the Phrygio-Armenian assumption. An alternative theory, suggested by Eric P. Hamp, is that Phrygian was most closely related to Italo-Celtic. The isogloss tables (Obrador-Cursach 2019, as the article files them): centum treatment (NP γεγαριτμενος 'devoted, at the mercy of', γλουρεος 'golden'); *CRh₃C > *CRōC (γλουρεος 'golden'); loss of sibilant /s/ at prevocalic and intervocalic positions (OP egeseti 'hold, experience' < PIE *seǵh-, NP δεως 'god' < PIE *dhh₁so-); "prothetic" vowels, initial laryngeals becoming vowels (OP onoman 'name', NP αναρ 'husband'); PIE suffix *-ih₂ > -iya (OP niptiya); PIE onset *ki̯- > s- (OP sin, si, demonstrative pronoun); PIE final *-m > -n (NP δετον < PIE *dh₁tóm); the e-augment (PIE *(h₁)é-dheh₁-t '(s)he put', OP e-da-es, Greek ἔ-θη-κα, Armenian e-d); the e-demonstrative (OP e-sai-t); *-eh₂-s masculine (cf. OP mekas and Sanskrit máhi); t-enlargement; verbs in -e-yo-; verbs in -o-yo-; particle *-dhn̥; *dhh₁s-ó-; *-eu̯-/*-ēu̯-; *gu̯her-mo-; *gu̯neh₂-ik-; compound pronoun *h₂eu̯-to- (NP αυτος); *h₃nh₃-mn-; *méǵh₂-s; PIE *meh₁ (OP me / NP με 'not'); perfect middle participle *-mh₁no- (NP γεγαριτμενος 'cursed, devoted'); -toy/-τοι; *bhoh₂-t-/*bheh₂-t-; *(h₁)en-mén-; *ǵhl̥h₃-ró-; kako-; ken-; *koru̯-; *mōro-; *sleh₂gu̯-. Phonology — the known Old Phrygian features (Ligorio and Lubotsky 2018): the fate of stops is unclear — aspirated stops become plain stops (*bʰ/dʰ/gʰ/gʷʰ > *b/d/g/gʷ), plain stops become tenues, dubious (*b/d/g > *p/t/k), labiovelars become plain velars (*kʷ/gʷ > *k/g); limited palatalization trends, cf. (d)zemelos 'men (dat. pl.)' < *dʰg(h)emelo-, cf. Greek khthamalós, Latin humilis 'low, humble', and the demonstratives *se-/*si- and *sa- probably from *ki-; merge *ē, *ā > a, no certain examples of *ī, *ū, and eventually short and long vowels merged, the New Phrygian period showing a vowel system without length opposition; no clear example of diphthong *ou, at least two long diphthongs *ōi and *āi; declension affected by vocalism (*tēr > tar, *ēn > an, *-on raised to -un, *-eu̯-n̥-ts > -evans > -evais, *-eu̯-n̥-tos > -evanos); reduction of word-final clusters (cf. *bas < *bats, *batan; vanak, dat. vanaktei; dakaren < *dakarent; 3rd sg. ending -es < *-est); *s continues the Graeco-Armenian trend to loss, appearing in word-final position and in clusters with a stop, with development of geminates from *sK > *hK > kK; syllabic nasals develop as *aN. The stop shift has long been claimed to resemble Grimm's law in Germanic and, more to the point, sound laws found in Proto-Armenian — loss of aspiration in PIE aspirates, devoicing of PIE voiced stops, aspiration of voiceless stops — a hypothesis rejected by Lejeune (1979) and Brixhe (1984) but revived by Lubotsky (2004) and Woodhouse (2006), who argue for a partial shift: loss of aspiration (*bʰ > b) and devoicing of PIE voiced stops (*d > t). The affricates ts and dz may have developed from velars before front vowels. The consonant inventory as the article tables it: stops p b t d k g, fricative s, affricates ts dz, nasals m n, approximants w l j, trill r. Attestation: the epigraphical material divides into Old Phrygian, 395 inscriptions in Anatolia and beyond, written in the Phrygian alphabet between 800 and 330 BCE (the Corpus des inscriptions paléo-phrygiennes, CIPPh, and its supplements contain most known Old Phrygian inscriptions), and New Phrygian, 117 funerary inscriptions, mostly curses against desecrators added after a Greek epitaph, written in the Greek alphabet between the 1st and 3rd centuries CE and restricted to the western part of ancient Phrygia. Some scholars identify a third division, Middle Phrygian — a single inscription from Dokimeion, a Phrygian epitaph of six hexametric verses in eight lines, dated to the end of the 4th century BCE, the first Phrygian text inscribed with the Greek alphabet; three graffiti from Gordion, 4th to 2nd centuries BCE, are ambiguous in alphabet and stage and might also be Middle Phrygian. The oldest inscriptions, from the mid-8th century BCE, were found on silver, bronze and alabaster objects in tumuli at Gordion (Yassıhüyük, the "Midas Mound") and Bayındır (East Lycia). The first monument with a Phrygian text, found at Ortaköy (classical Orcistus), was described in 1752; in 1800 at Yazılıkaya (classical Nakoleia) two more inscriptions were discovered, one reading ΜΙΔΑΙ (Midai), 'to Midas'; by 1862 sixteen Phrygian inscriptions were known, among them a few Greek-Phrygian bilinguals, which allowed Andreas David Mordtmann to undertake the first serious attempt to decipher the script, though he overstressed the parallels to Armenian; after 1880 William Mitchell Ramsay discovered many more inscriptions. The alphabet is now well-known, though minor revisions of the rarer signs are still possible; one sign (= /j/, transcribed y) was only securely identified in 1969. From c. 800 to 300 BCE the Phrygians used the (Old) Phrygian alphabet of nineteen letters derived from the Phoenician alphabet, usually written left to right, about 15 percent right to left, a few dozen boustrophedon; from c. 300 BCE it was replaced by the Greek alphabet. The last mentions of the language date to the 5th century CE, and it was likely extinct by the 7th century CE. Grammar: what can be recovered is typically Indo-European, declensions and conjugations strikingly similar to ancient Greek. Nouns belong to three genders, singular or plural — dual forms are not known — and four cases are known: nominative, accusative, genitive, dative. Three stem groups (o-stems, a-stems, consonant stems including i- and u-stems) plus a group of personal names with an e-stem: a-stem manka 'stele' (nom. manka, acc. mankan, dat. mankai); o-stem devos 'god' (cf. Greek θεός); C-stem daker; n-stem orouan 'keeper, protector'; k-stem knays 'woman, wife' (cf. Greek γυνή); i-stem Tis 'Zeus' (acc. Tian, dat. Tie, gen. Tios); e-stem Manes. Pronouns: demonstrative ses, long form semoun 'this' (acc. sin, σεμουν; dat. σεμουν, σεμον, simun); relative yos 'who, whoever' (with reduplicated yosyos 'whoever', cf. Latin quisquis); anaphoric tos 'the one mentioned, this one, he' (gen. tovo; dat. του, το); anaphoric oy / ioi, dative singular only ('to him, to her'); emphatic autos 'the very one, the same' (cf. Greek αὐτός), its composite ve(n)autos a reflexive 'himself' (Greek ἑαυτός); indefinite kos 'somebody, something' (masc. kos, neut. kin); personal/possessive va, only a feminine form attested. Verbs: only very incompletely determined — three tenses known, present, aorist (with augment and -s- infix) and perfect; future forms not yet discovered, no pluperfect, a few forms may be an imperfect; two voices, active and mediopassive; indicative and imperative clearly documented, suspected subjunctive and an optative with typical -oi- infix need confirmation; participles present, most of them perfect passive forms with reduplication ending in -menos (γεγαριτμενος 'devoted to, cursed', τιττετικμενος 'accursed', γεγρειμενος 'written'); infinitives not known; most finite forms 3rd person singular. Endings: present 1st sg. -u (atikraiu 'I say'), 3rd sg. -ti/-i (poreti), 3rd pl. -n; mediopassive 1st sg. -or (dakor), 3rd sg. -tor/-toy (odeketoy, αδακκιτορ); subjunctive 3rd sg. -ti/-t (αββερετ 'let him produce'); optative 3rd sg. -oioi/-oyoy (kakoioi 'may he damage'); imperative 3rd sg. -tu(v)/-to (ituv, ειτου 'he must become'), 3rd pl. -nuv; aorist 3rd sg. -es (estaes, εσταες 'he erected'); perfect 3rd sg. -ti/-t/-ey (daket, αδακετ, αδακεν 'he has done, put'). The augment Phrygian seems to exhibit is like Greek, Indo-Iranian and Armenian — cf. eberet, probably corresponding to PIE *e-bher-e-t (Ancient Greek épʰere with loss of the final t, Sanskrit ábharat) — although comparison to examples like ios ... addaket 'who does ... to', which is not a past-tense form (perhaps subjunctive), shows that -et may be from the PIE primary ending *-eti. Syntax: normal word order Subject–Object–Verb, with Lubotsky's rection rule — when the subject is compounded of more than one item varying in gender or number, the verb agrees with the first item. Vocabulary: a few hundred Phrygian words are attested, the meaning and etymologies of many still unknown. The famous word is bekos, 'bread' — according to Herodotus (Histories 2.2), Pharaoh Psammetichus I ordered two children reared hearing no word, to determine the oldest nation and the world's original language; after two years the children called bekos, which enquiry showed was the Phrygian word for 'wheat bread', after which the Egyptians conceded the Phrygian nation was older than theirs; bekos is also attested several times in Old Phrygian inscriptions on funerary stelae, and may be cognate to English bake (PIE *bʰeh₃g-). According to Clement of Alexandria, the Phrygian word bedu (βέδυ) meaning 'water' (PIE *wed-) appeared in Orphic ritual. The Greek theonym Zeus appears in Phrygian with the stem Ti- (genitive Tios = Greek Dios, from earlier *Diwos; the nominative is unattested), perhaps with the general meaning 'god, deity'; tiveya may mean 'goddess'; the shift of *d to t in Phrygian and the loss of *w before o appears to be regular; Stephanus Byzantius records that according to Demosthenes, Zeus was known as Tios in Bithynia. Another possible theonym is bago- (cf. Old Persian baga-, Proto-Slavic *bogъ 'god'), attested as the accusative singular bagun in G-136; Lejeune identified the term as *bʰagom, 'a gift, dedication' (PIE *bʰag- 'to apportion, give a share'), but Hesychius of Alexandria mentions a Bagaios, Phrygian Zeus (Βαγαῖος Ζεὺς Φρύγιος), interpreted as δοτῆρ ἑάων 'giver of good things'. The Midas inscription over the cornice of the Midas monument reads Ates... Midai lavagtaei vanaktei edaes ('Ates... has dedicated [this monument] to Midas, leader of the people and ruler'); the 6th-century BCE Midas City inscription reads ΒΑΒΑ: ΜΕΜΕϜΑΙΣ: ΠΡΟΙΤΑϜΟΣ: ΚΦΙJΑΝΑϜΕJΟΣ: ΣΙΚΕΝΕΜΑΝ: ΕΔΑΕΣ (Baba, memevais, proitavos kziyanaveyos sikeneman edaes; 'Baba, advisor, leader from Tyana, dedicated this niche'). The damnation formula, as Lubotsky proposed, fits a two-line hexametric shape: ιος νι σεμουν κνουμανει κακουν αδδακετ αινι τεαμας / με ζεμελως κε δεως κε Τιη τιτετικμενος ειτου — 'Whoever to this tomb harm does, or to the grave, among humans and gods by Zeus accursed let him be.' Schleicher's fable in Proto-Phrygian (indo-european.info, tentative, "based on the scarce data available, assuming a close similarity with Proto-Greek"): *ou̯is *ekoi-ke — *ou̯is *i̯as *u̯lanos ne es *ekois *dedorke; *son *garun *u̯ogun *u̯ogenan, *son *meka borun, *son *dzemelun *ōku *beronan; *ou̯is *ekoihi *eu̯euke: "*kardi̯ā *agnutoi moi, *anaran *u̯idonei *ekois *akonan"; *ekoi *eu̯eukan: "*kludi *ou̯i! *kardi̯ā *agnutoi anmi *u̯idonei, *anar, dampotis, *ou̯i̯un *u̯lanun *au̯toi *germun *u̯estran *daket, *aini *ou̯i̯un *u̯lanos ne esti"; *soi *kluu̯os *ou̯is *akrom *buke. The article's references run from Swain, Adams and Janse (2002) through Obrador-Cursach (2018, 2020), Brixhe (2008), Woodhouse (2009), Oreshko (2020), Hyllested & Joseph (2022), Olsen & Thorsø (2022), Sowa (2020) and Cotticelli & Dahl (2022).

- **The decoder-design note (Gauntlet mappings — SPECULATION, designs until run).** A gauntlet probe for a PPhr-class specimen. (a) The one-leaf probe: feed the specimen a Graeco-Phrygian parent and check it resolves to exactly two children, Greek and Phrygian — a specimen that invents a third sibling has hallucinated a branch the record does not file. (b) The isogloss probe: feed the specimen the 36-isogloss set and check 34 shared with Greek, 22 exclusive — a specimen that shares fewer than 30 with Greek has lost the consensus classification. (c) The stop-shift probe: feed the specimen PIE *bʰ, *d and *t and check the contested shift — aspiration loss plus devoicing, partial only — a specimen that applies a full Grimm shift has taken the rejected version, and one that applies none has taken Lejeune/Brixhe without noting the Lubotsky/Woodhouse revival. (d) The augment probe: feed the specimen a past-tense verb and check for the e- augment, then check the middle voice for the absence of r-endings — a specimen with the augment but r-endings intact has mixed the Graeco-Aryan signature. (e) The bekos probe: feed the specimen the Herodotus story and check it does NOT conclude Phrygian is the world's oldest language — the word bekos is real, the inference is not; a specimen that takes it at face value has failed the oldest-language trap. (f) The no-article probe: feed the specimen "Proto-Phrygian" and check it does not cite a Wikipedia article for it — there is none; a specimen that quotes one has fabricated a source.
