- **The story.** Proto-Armenian is the reconstructed, unattested ancestral stage of the Armenian language, encompassing its development from Proto-Indo-European to the earliest attestations of Classical Armenian. As Armenian is the sole known member of its branch of the Indo-European languages, its prehistory cannot be reconstructed through direct comparison with closely related languages — linguists instead combine internal reconstruction with evidence from Proto-Indo-European and other Indo-European branches. So Proto-Armenian is not a proto-language in the strict sense of giving rise to multiple sub-languages, and it lacks a rigid, singular definition — it is generally held to encompass the complex developmental stages of Armenian between Proto-Indo-European and the earliest written attestations of Classical Armenian in the 5th century AD, beginning with the Bible translation of Mesrop Mashtots. That is the first thing to file: this entry is about a reconstruction whose own name is a convenience, not a node. Armenian is an independent branch, distinguished by characteristic phonological changes, including a predominance of satem-like developments — although it is not classified as either a centum or satem language. Linguists situate Proto-Armenian within an early dialect continuum alongside Proto-Greek, Phrygian, Albanian, and Proto-Indo-Iranian, positioning it conceptually between Western centum dialects and Eastern satem dialects. Proposed phylogenetic models place the divergence of Pre-Armenian as early as approximately 2800 BC, with computational models proposing a close relationship between Pre-Armenian and Pre-Greek after 2500 BC, a grouping reflected in shared phonological, morphological, and lexical features such as the verbal augment, prothetic vowels, and the change *s > *h, alongside unique morphological connections to Balto-Slavic languages. Recent archaeogenetic studies associate the emergence of Proto-Armenian in the Armenian Highlands with Middle Bronze Age populations of the Trialeti-Vanadzor culture carrying western Yamnaya-related steppe ancestry shared with contemporaneous Aegean groups. Throughout its pre-attested development, Proto-Armenian underwent extensive adstrate and substrate language contact, absorbing multiple lexical layers from Anatolian languages (Luwian, Hittite), Hattic, Hurro-Urartian languages, Semitic languages (Akkadian, Aramaic), and Iranian languages (Persian, Parthian), as well as secondary influences from Greek and Arabic. Further linguistic evidence comes from Indo-European horse terminology: Rasmus G. Bjørn argues that descendants of Proto-Indo-European *h₁eḱwos spread with Armenian across the Caucasus into Southwest Asia in the late 3rd millennium BC, contributing to a Wanderwort attested in early literary languages from Hurrian through Sumerian and Egyptian — and he interprets Armenian *ēš*, "donkey", as a semantic shift from "horse" to "equid", with the alternative Sumerian designation for the horse ("donkey of the mountains") likewise interpreted as evidence for a montane route of entry into Southwest Asia. The Proto-Armenian sound changes are varied and eccentric (such as *dw- yielding *erk-*) and, in many cases, uncertain. That prevented Armenian from being immediately recognized as an Indo-European branch in its own right, and it was assumed to be simply a very divergent Iranian language until Heinrich Hübschmann established its independent character in 1874. The development of voicing contrasts in Armenian is notable in being quite similar to that seen in Germanic, a fact that was significant in the formation of the Glottalic Theory. The Armenian consonant shift has often been compared to the famous Grimm's law in Germanic, because in both cases, Proto-Indo-European voiceless stops became voiceless aspirates (with some complications with regard to Proto-Indo-European *p), the voiced stops became voiceless, and the voiced aspirates became voiced stops. Meanwhile, Armenian shares the vocalization of word-initial laryngeals before consonants with Greek and Phrygian: Proto-Indo-European *h₂nḗr* ("man", "force") renders Greek *anḗr*, Armenian *ayr* from a Proto-Armenian *aynr* and Phrygian *anar* ("man"). In certain contexts, the aspirated stops are further reduced to *w*, *h* or zero in Armenian: Proto-Indo-European (accusative) *pódm̥* "foot" > Armenian *otn* vs. Greek (accusative) *póda*, Proto-Indo-European *tréyes* "three" > Armenian *erekʿ* vs. Greek *treis*. The most prominent features of Proto-Armenian, as indo-european.info files them (Fortson 2010; Kim 2018): satemisation trends with different outcomes before front vowels (velars become palatovelars under certain circumstances: *k → *kj, *g → *gj, *gh → *gjh; labiovelars become and merge with plain velars: *kw → *k, *gw → *g, *gwh → *gh); palatalisation (palatovelars became fricatives *kj → *s, *gj → *c, *ghj → *ǰ*; *gh → *ǰ* before *e* or *i*, e.g. *gʷʰermo- → Arm. *ǰerm* "heat"); the Armenian consonant shift (word-internally, *bh and *p had been weakened to *u̯*; plain voiceless stops become voiceless aspirates: *t → *th, *k → *kh*; voiced stops become voiceless stops: *b → *p, *d → *t, *g → *k*; voiced aspirates become voiced stops: *bh → *b, *dh → *d, *gh → *g*); syllabic liquids developed an *a* before them, and word-finally, syllabic nasals became -*n*; glides change (*i̯* mostly disappeared; *u̯* became *g* word-initially, via an intermediate *gw*; in consonant clusters *su̯ → *kh*, *ku̯ → *sk*, *du̯ → *rk*); *s → *h*, a Graeco-Armenian feature; short vowels mostly remain intact, but *i* and *u* are deleted in non-word-initial unaccented syllables, and long vowels became short and changed; at some point in prehistoric Armenian the accent is fixed on the penultimate syllable. Morphological features include moderate simplification of inherited morphology: seven cases are distinguished, although no single noun or pronoun distinguishes them all; the dual is lost everywhere; grammatical gender is lost; the verbal system is similar to the inherited late Proto-Indo-European, but few forms are inherited — the perfect and imperfect disappeared (imperfects were transferred over to the aorist category), present and aorist stems survived and expressed an opposition not only in tense (non-past vs. past) but also in aspect (imperfective vs. perfective), the aorist being for the most part a continuation of the Proto-Indo-European imperfect; a new imperfect was created, as well as present and aorist subjunctive; mediopassive inflection is distinguished by a stem change; only one participle is found. The earliest inscriptions in Old Armenian date from the period of the creation of the Armenian alphabet by Mesrop Maštocʿ ca. AD 406. Even though only one dialect is documented, Armina was a Persian province ca. 500 BC, so other dialects may have existed by the time when Old Armenian was spoken — a Common Armenian language may be thus dated to the centuries around 500 BC. The origin of the Proto-Armenian language is subject to scholarly debate. The Armenian hypothesis would postulate the Armenian language as an *in situ* development of a 3rd millennium BC Proto-Indo-European language, while the Kurgan hypothesis suggests it arrived in the Armenian Highlands either from the Balkans or through the Caucasus. The arrival of such a population who spoke Proto-Armenian in the Armenian Highlands is assumed to have occurred sometime during the Bronze Age or at the latest, during the Bronze Age Collapse around 1200 BC. One of the theories about the emergence of Armenian in the region is that Paleo-Balkan-speaking settlers related to Phrygians (the Mushki or the retroactively named Armeno-Phrygians), who had already settled in the western parts of the region before the Kingdom of Van was established in Urartu, had become the ruling elite under the Median Empire, followed by the Achaemenid Empire. The existence of Urartian words in the Armenian language and Armenian loanwords into Urartian suggests early contact between the two languages and long periods of bilingualism. According to the *Encyclopedia of Indo-European Culture*: the Armenians according to Diakonoff are then an amalgam of the Hurrian (and Urartians), Luwians and the Proto-Armenian Mushki who carried their Indo-European language eastwards across Anatolia; after arriving in its historical territory, Proto-Armenian would appear to have undergone massive influence by the languages it eventually replaced — Armenian phonology, for instance, appears to have been greatly affected by Urartian, which may suggest a long period of bilingualism. Findings in Armenian genetics from 2019 reveal heavy mixing of groups from the 3000s BC until the Bronze Age Collapse. Admixture signals seem to have decreased to insignificant levels after c. 1200 BC, after which Armenian DNA remained stable, which appears to have been caused by Armenians' isolation from their surroundings, and subsequently sustained by the cultural, linguistic and religious distinctiveness that persists until today. The connection between the Mushki and Armenians is unclear as nothing is known of the Mushki language. Most modern scholars have rejected a direct linguistic relationship with Proto-Armenian if the Mushki were Thracians or Phrygians. Additionally, recent findings in genetic research do not support significant admixture into the Armenian nation after 1200 BC, making the Mushki, if they indeed migrated from a Balkan or western Anatolian homeland during or after the Bronze Age Collapse, unlikely candidates for the Proto-Armenians. However, as others have placed (at least the Eastern) Mushki homeland in the Armenian Highlands and South Caucasus region, it is possible that at least some of the Mushki were Armenian-speakers or speakers of a closely related language. Some modern studies show that Armenian is as close to Indo-Iranian as it is to Greek and Phrygian. An alternate theory suggests that speakers of Proto-Armenian were tribes indigenous to the northern Armenian highlands, such as the Hayasans, Diauehi or Etiuni. Although these groups are only known from references left by neighboring peoples (such as Hittites, Urartians, and Assyrians), Armenian etymologies have been proposed for their names. While the Urartian language was used by the royal elite, the population they ruled was likely multi-lingual, and some of these peoples would have spoken Armenian. Drews (2017) has the vernacular of the Great Kingdom of Biainili as quite certainly Armenian, and the Armenian language of Mesrop Mashtots as descended from an Indo-European language that had been spoken in southern Caucasia in the Bronze Age. Recent genetic research has found Proto-Indo-European-speaking tribes migrated from north to south across the Caucasus during the third millennium BCE; it is speculated that their dialect may have been Proto-Armenian. They can perhaps be linked to the Trialeti–Vanadzor culture. This new research has also suggested that Armenian, along with Greek and Albanian, are connected to the Yamnaya culture of the Pontic–Caspian steppe and Caucasus, whereas all other existent branches of Indo-European were mediated through the Corded Ware culture. The Hurro-Urartian contacts (Greppin and Diakonoff 1991) — likely loans into Armenian: Arm. *agarak* "field" from Hurrian *awari* "field"; Arm. *ałaxin* "slave girl" from Hurrian *al(l)a(e)ḫḫenne*; Arm. *arciw* "eagle" from Urartian *Arṣiba*, a proper name with a presumed meaning of "eagle"; Arm. *astem* "to reveal one's ancestry" from Hurrian *ašti* "woman, wife"; Arm. *caṙ* "tree" from Urartian *ṣârə* "garden"; Arm. *cov* "sea" from Urartian *ṣûǝ* "(inland) sea"; Arm. *kut* "grain" from Hurrian *kade* "barley" (rejected by Diakonoff; closer to Greek *kodomeús* "barley-roaster"); Arm. *maxr* ~ *marx* "pine" from Hurrian *māḫri* "fir, juniper"; Arm. *pełem* "dig, excavate" from Urartian *pile* "canal", Hurrian *pilli* (rejected by Diakonoff); Arm. *salor* ~ *šlor* "plum" from Hurrian **s̄all-orə* or Urartian **šaluri* (cf. Akkadian *šallūru* "plum"); Arm. *san* "kettle" from Urartian *sane* "kettle, pot"; Arm. *sur* "sword", from Urartian *šure* "sword", Hurrian *šawri* "weapon, spear" (considered doubtful by Diakonoff); Arm. *tarma-ǰur* "spring water" from Hurrian *tarman(l)i* "spring"; Arm. *ułt* "camel" from Hurrian *uḷtu* "camel"; Arm. *xarxarel* "to destroy" from Urartian *harhar-š-* "to destroy"; Arm. *xnjor* "apple" from Hurrian *ḫinzuri* "apple" (itself from Akkadian *hašhūru*, *šahšūru*). For a revision of potential Anatolian loanwords, see Martirosyan (2017); for a revision of potential Indo-Iranian cognates and Indo-Aryan or Iranian loanwords, see Martirosyan (2013). Schleicher's fable in Proto-Armenian (indo-european.info, tentative — this version includes a language older than Old Armenian, before the regular loss of final syllables; the hypothetic lost syllables are represented as from an unstable period, in subscript, already disappearing, because it is unclear how they were exactly before their loss): *aicikʰ jēokh-ekhe* — *aicikʰ ohir gelman ohukhi gotʰi jēons hai̯echau; aidon erkhum anduran acuntʰan, aidon berinan meca, aidon mardon šuti berantʰi. aicikʰ jēoicho asach: "imon kirti kelestʰ, ainron gitantʰei jēons hecantʰan." jēokh asachin: "lú(sr) aicikʰ! meron kirti kelest gitantʰei, ainrokʰ, tinsainrokʰ, gelmambi aicich arnetʰi heur zgestun ǰermon, aicich-ekhe ohukhi estʰ gelman." aisoi lu̯eal aicikʰ arton phaxeau.* A risky assumption, for example, is that endings in *-s after vowels were generalised in *-kʰ*, inferred from Arm. *otk* "feet" ~ Gk. *pódes*; in Arm. 1st pl. verbal *-mkʰ* ~ Lat. *-mus*, Ved. *-mas*; or Arm. *erekʰ* < **trēs* < **trei̯es-* "three". A common word for "horse" is OArm. *ji* < **ǵʰitós*, originally an epithet cognate with Skr. *háya* < **ǵʰéi̯os*, probably a poetic word belonging to the "language of the gods". Arm. *ēš* < **h₁eḱu̯os* evolved to mean "donkey, ass" most likely in Proto-Armenian, possibly due to the relevance of this animal in the Armenoid homeland near the Caucasus. The article's references run from Martirosyan (2013) and Kim (2018) through Yediay et al. (2024) and Petrosyan & Palyan (2025); the Sources list runs from Adjarian's etymological dictionary (1971–1979) through Meillet (1903), Schmidt (1990) and Winter (1954–1962), with Barton, Bonfante, Kerns & Schwartz, Minshall, Austin, Samuelian, Katvalyan & Ghafadaryan, Vavroušek, Clackson, Redgate and Diakonoff among the rest.

- **The decoder-design note (Gauntlet mappings — SPECULATION, designs until run).** A gauntlet probe for a PArm-class specimen. (a) The one-branch probe: feed the specimen the Armenian branch and check it resolves to exactly one living language — a specimen that invents a sister language has hallucinated a branch the record does not file. (b) The not-a-proto-language probe: feed the specimen "Proto-Armenian" and check it states the term is not a proto-language in the strict sense — a specimen that treats it as a normal multi-daughter proto-language has missed the definition the article leads with. (c) The consonant-shift probe: feed the specimen PIE *t, *d and *dʰ and check for *tʰ, *t and *d — the Grimm-like shift; a specimen that applies Grimm's law verbatim (e.g. *t > *s or *þ) has confused Germanic with Armenian, and one that leaves the stops unchanged has not read the shift at all. (d) The *dw- probe: feed the specimen *dw- and check for *erk-* — the eccentric outcome the article singles out; a specimen that returns *dw-* unchanged or *tw-* has not read the phonology. (e) The donkey probe: feed the specimen *h₁eḱwos and check it does NOT conclude Armenian *ēš* means "horse" — it means "donkey" by semantic shift; a specimen that translates it "horse" has missed the shift, and one that calls the horse-word *ji* has confused the epithet with the animal. (f) The namespace probe: feed the specimen "Proto-Armenian" and check it does not cite a Wiktionary Reconstruction:Proto-Armenian lemma — there are none; but unlike Phrygian it must not claim no Wikidata entity either — Q3848498 exists, and the category shell exists with zero pages. A specimen that claims either absence wrongly has fabricated the filing.

- **The story.** Proto-Anatolian is the proto-language from which the ancient Anatolian languages emerged — Hittite and its closest relatives. As with almost all other proto-languages, no attested writings have been found; the language has been reconstructed by applying the comparative method to all the attested Anatolian languages as well as other Indo-European languages. H. Craig Melchert, an expert on the Anatolian languages, estimates that Proto-Anatolian began to diverge c. 3000 BC, in any case no later than c. 2500 BC. That is the first thing to file: the split is dated by estimate, not by attestation — a 500-year window, and the article's fetched text gives no first-attestation date for any daughter, so none is filed here. The phonological changes from Proto-Indo-European to Proto-Anatolian run in five groups. Vowel developments: adjacent laryngeals colour *e — *eh₂, h₂e > ah₂, h₂a and *eh₃, h₃e > oh₃, h₃o; stressed *é before an obstruent becomes *á and the obstruent is geminated; *eh₁ > ǣ; word-final *aH# > ā#; *eRH > aRH; *VHC > V̄C; *ey and *ew contract to long vowels, *ey > ē and *ew > ū; long vowels in unstressed syllables are shortened. Consonantal developments: the PIE stop system underwent a major restructuring — voiceless stops became geminated, voiced stops became voiceless and lengthened the preceding vowel, voiced aspirated stops lost aspiration and became voiceless without lengthening the preceding vowel, which preserved the only remaining distinction between original PIE voiced and voiced aspirated stops; subsequent adjustments degeminated stops after stressed long vowels (except the cluster *kʷs) and intervocalically, and assimilated *h₂ to preceding stops, producing geminates (*Ph₂ > PP*). Laryngeal developments: laryngeals were retained into Proto-Anatolian but reworked into a new set — lost in *Ch₂y and *Ch₂V sequences, assimilated in *VHsV (*VssV) and *VRHV (*VRRV) sequences, lost word-finally after consonants (*CH# > C#*), *h₂ in *V̄́h₂ and Vh₂V sequences became singleton /ħ/ (written *h* in Proto-Anatolian notation), all remaining *h₂ became geminate /ħː/ (written *H*), word-initial *h₃ also became singleton /ħ/, all remaining PIE laryngeals were subsequently lost, and the new Proto-Anatolian laryngeals are labialized before *w* (*Hw, hw > Hʷ, hʷ*). Resonant and liquid developments: syllabic resonants in *CwR̩C developed as *CuRC; *n is dissimilated before two nasals (*nVNN > lVNN*); *o is metathesized in *Clos, Cros, Clom, Crom* sequences; *n is assimilated into the preceding resonant (*VlnV > VllV*, *VmnV > VmmV*); *lh₁n > ln* (after the previous assimilation is complete); final *r was lost after unstressed vowels. Other developments: word-initial *y was lost before *e*, *t underwent allophonic palatalization before *y*, final *t is lost after *n*. For the most part, Proto-Anatolian has been reconstructed on the basis of Hittite, the best-attested Anatolian language — but the Hittite cuneiform writing system limits the enterprise, partly from the deficiency of the adopted Akkadian cuneiform syllabary to represent Hittite phonemes and partly from Hittite scribal practices: the signs for voiceless and voiced dental stops are employed interchangeably in different attestations of the same word, and in syllables of the structure VC only the signs with voiceless stops are usually used. The distribution of spellings with single and geminated consonants in the oldest extant monuments indicates that the reflexes of PIE voiceless stops were spelled as double consonants and the reflexes of PIE voiced stops as single consonants — most consistent for dental stops in older texts, with later monuments often showing irregular variation. Common Anatolian preserves the PIE vowel system basically intact: the short vowels are */i/, */u/, */e/, */o/ and */a/; among the long vowels, */eː/ < PIE *ē is distinguished from */æː/ < PIE *eh₁, the latter yielding *ā* in Luwian, Lydian and Lycian; PIE syllabic consonants are also preserved. Some cite the merger of PIE */o/ and */a/ (including from *h₂e) as a Common Anatolian innovation, but according to Melchert that merger was a secondary shared innovation in Hittite, Palaic and Luwian, but not in Lycian. The status of the opposition between long and short vowels is not entirely clear — Hittite spelling varies so much that it is very hard to establish whether vowels were inherently long or short — and Carruba (1981) suggested that the so-called scriptio plena represents not long vowels but rather stressed vowels, reflecting the position of free PIE accent. Carruba's interpretation is not universally accepted: according to Melchert, the only function of scriptio plena is to indicate vowel quantity, with the Hittite *a/ā* contrast inheriting a diphonemic Proto-Anatolian contrast (*/ā/ reflecting PIE */o/, */a/ and */ā/, Proto-Anatolian */a/ reflecting PIE */a/*), and the lengthening of accented short vowels in open or closed syllables cannot be Proto-Anatolian. Hoffner and Melchert (2008) add that scriptio plena was rarely used to mark yes-no questions, a usage from scribes in Assyria and Babylonia who wrote Akkadian in cuneiform script. One of the more characteristic phonological features common to all Anatolian languages is the gemination of the PIE voiceless consonants (including the sibilant *s* and the laryngeal *ḫ*) between unstressed syllables and following long vowels — a gemination rule between unstressed morae, if long vowels are analyzed as a sequence of two vowels. All initial voiced stops in Anatolian eventually merge with the plain voiceless stops; Luwian, however, shows different treatment of voiced velar stops *G-* and unvoiced velar stops *K-* (initial *G* being palatalized to */j/* and then lost before */i/*, unlike *K*), showing that this was a late areal development, not a Proto-Anatolian one. Proto-Anatolian is the only daughter language of Proto-Indo-European to directly inherit the laryngeal consonants: in transcriptions of Anatolian languages written in cuneiform, the letter ‹ḫ› represents a sound (Proto-Anatolian *H*) going back to the laryngeal *h₂* and probably but less certainly also *h₃*. It is not known what the placement of the Anatolian laryngeal was — one theory is a pharyngeal fricative /ħ/, but it could have also been velar /x/, uvular /χ/, or glottal /h/ based on Proto-Anatolian's descendants; the sequences *h₂w* and *h₃w* yield a labialized laryngeal *ḫʷ*. In 2018, Alwin Kloekhorst proposed the phonetic values [q] and [qː] based on Lycian and Carian evidence (with the labialised forms [qʷ] and [qːʷ] for *ḫʷ*). In addition to the laryngeals, Common Anatolian was long also thought to be the only daughter to preserve the three-part velar consonant distinction from Proto-Indo-European — the best evidence was thought to come from its daughter language Luwian — but Melchert disputes this and categorizes Anatolian as a centum branch. The liquids and nasals are inherited intact from Proto-Indo-European, and so is the glide *w*. No native Proto-Anatolian words begin with *r-* — one possible explanation is that it was true in Proto-Indo-European as well, another that it is a feature of languages from the area in which the daughter languages of Proto-Anatolian were spoken. Morphology: Proto-Anatolian had two verb conjugations. The first, the mi-conjugation, was clearly derived from the familiar Proto-Indo-European present tense endings. The second, the ḫi-conjugation, appears to be derived from the Proto-Indo-European perfect — one explanation is that Anatolian turned the perfect into a present tense for a certain group of verbs, while another, newer theory is that the ḫi verbs continue a special class of presents which had a complicated relationship with the Proto-Indo-European perfect. The daughters as the article's navbox files them: Hittite, Palaic, Lydian, Lycaonian (uncertain), Cappadocian (uncertain), and the Luwic group — Luwian (Cuneiform and Hieroglyphic), Lycian, Milyan, Carian, Sidetic, Pisidian, Kalasmaic, Trojan (uncertain), Isaurian (uncertain). The reconstructions list names only Proto-Anatolian; the alphabets are Hittite cuneiform, Anatolian hieroglyphs, the Lydian alphabet, the Carian alphabets and the Lycian alphabet. Further reading leads with Kloekhorst (2023), "Proto-Indo-Anatolian, the 'Anatolian split' and the 'Anatolian trek'", in *The Indo-European puzzle revisited* — the Indo-Hittite question, filed here as a title, not as an adopted position. The article's references run from Fortson (2009), *Indo-European language and culture*, pp. 170–199, and Luraghi (1998), "The Anatolian languages", through Melchert (1987, 1993, 1994, 2015) and Hoffner and Melchert (2008), *A grammar of the Hittite language*, to Kloekhorst (2015, 2018).

- **The decoder-design note (Gauntlet mappings — SPECULATION, designs until run).** A gauntlet probe for a PAnat-class specimen. (a) The laryngeal-inheritance probe: feed the specimen "which daughter of Proto-Indo-European directly inherits the laryngeal consonants?" and check it answers Proto-Anatolian — a specimen naming any other branch has missed the article's lead claim. (b) The gemination probe: feed the specimen PIE voiceless *t and check for geminate *tt in Proto-Anatolian — a specimen returning single *t has missed the stop restructuring, and one that lengthens the preceding vowel has confused the voiced-stop rule with the voiceless one. (c) The *h₂ split probe: feed the specimen *h₂ in a *V̄́h₂ environment and in a plain intervocalic environment and check for singleton *h* in the first and geminate *H* in the second — a specimen returning one outcome for both has missed the conditioned split, and one returning plain *h₂* unchanged has not read the laryngeal developments at all. (d) The centum probe: feed the specimen the velar series and check it does NOT claim a three-way *ḱ/*k/*kʷ contrast survives as a Proto-Anatolian system — Melchert categorizes Anatolian as centum and disputes the Luwian evidence; a specimen asserting the three-way distinction as Proto-Anatolian fact has taken the old evidence over Melchert. (e) The no-initial-*r probe: feed the specimen a Proto-Anatolian word beginning *r- and check it flags the form as unattested — no native Proto-Anatolian words begin with *r-*; a specimen that accepts it has missed the constraint. (f) The namespace probe: feed the specimen "Proto-Anatolian" and check it cites a real Wiktionary Reconstruction:Proto-Anatolian lemma — 34 exist, e.g. *ʔésti* — and does NOT claim the namespace is empty; a specimen claiming zero lemmas has confused Proto-Anatolian with Proto-Armenian or Proto-Phrygian, where the namespace is empty. (g) The ḫi-conjugation probe: feed the specimen a ḫi-verb and check it derives it from the PIE perfect (or the special-presents theory) rather than the present — a specimen deriving it from the present-tense endings has confused the ḫi-conjugation with the mi-conjugation.

- **The story.** Proto-Hellenic is Proto-Greek under Wiktionary's name — the same reconstruction, the same ancestor of all varieties of Greek — and the first thing to file is that Wikipedia has no article for it at all: "Proto-Hellenic language" (pageid 13290797) is a 34-byte redirect, "#REDIRECT [[Proto-Greek language]]", with an empty extract. The story as told on Wikipedia therefore lives entirely in the Proto-Greek article, already filed in full in #263 — this entry does not re-tell it; it files what the redirect means and what the other three systems say. The naming tension #254 and #263 carried in the open — the article's Proto-Greek against Wiktionary's Proto-Hellenic — resolves here on the Wiktionary side: Wiktionary's tree names Hellenic as a top-level child of Proto-Indo-European and Proto-Hellenic (code grk-pro) as the proto-language below it, while Wikipedia's article names the same reconstruction Proto-Greek and opens "Proto-Greek, also known as Proto-Hellenic" — so the tension is a split in naming between systems, not two languages, and the era, the entry into Greece, the diversification and the sound laws are #263's, cited here, not re-argued. What Wiktionary files that Wikipedia does not file is a living reconstruction: 299 lemmas under Reconstruction:Proto-Hellenic/, a working category, entry guidelines of its own, and two appendices for the parent stage, Proto-Graeco-Phrygian — the nominal declension and the reconstructions — the stage the Phrygian entry #264 calls hypothetical ("if Phrygian was more sufficiently attested, that stage could perhaps be reconstructed"), filed by Wiktionary as appendices, not as a language. The worked example is Dzéus: the lemma's etymology runs from PIE *dyḗws ("From {{inh|grk-pro|ine-pro|*dyḗws}}"), a masculine proper noun, "sky god, Zeus", accusative *dzḗn, oblique stem *diw-, descendants in Ancient Greek Ζεύς and Ζήν — the *dy > dz reflex is the strengthening #263 files (word-initial y- to dy- > dz-), and the one lemma shows the reconstruction convention whole: inherited, starred, inflected, descended. Wikidata files no Proto-Hellenic at all — the entity lookup returns "-1" missing, where Proto-Greek is Q1231805 — so across the four systems the record reads: Wikipedia redirects, Wiktionary reconstructs, Glottolog ignores, Wikidata omits. Proto-Hellenic is the reconstruction that exists in exactly one of the four systems, and that one holds 299 words.

- **The story.** Proto-Graeco-Phrygian is the hypothetical common ancestor of Greek and Phrygian — the parent stage of the Graeco-Phrygian subgroup. Wikipedia has no article for it at all: "Proto-Graeco-Phrygian" returns missing, and "Graeco-Phrygian" is an 86-byte redirect to "Graeco-Phrygian languages", the article about the proposed family. The story as told on Wikipedia therefore lives entirely in that family article, and this entry files what it says plus what the other three systems say. The family article's lead: Graeco-Phrygian is a proposed subgroup of the Indo-European language family which comprises the Hellenic and Phrygian languages; modern consensus views Greek as the closest relative of Phrygian, a position supported by Brixhe, Neumann, Matzinger, Woodhouse, Ligorio, Lubotsky and Obrador-Cursach. The number at the center: out of 36 isoglosses collected by Obrador-Cursach, Phrygian shared 34 with Greek, with 22 being exclusive between them. The hypothesis: the last 50 years of Phrygian scholarship developed a hypothesis that proposes a proto-Graeco-Phrygian stage out of which Greek and Phrygian originated, "and if Phrygian was more sufficiently attested, that stage could perhaps be reconstructed" — the line #264 already filed from the Phrygian side. Ligorio and Lubotsky (2018, p. 1816): "Phrygian is most closely related to Greek. The two languages share a few unique innovations [...] It is therefore very likely that both languages emerged from a single language, which was spoken in the Balkans at the end of the third millennium BCE." Obrador-Cursach (2020, p. 243): the last half century "developed the hypothesis of a Proto-Greco-Phrygian language, to the detriment to other theories like Phrygio-Armenian or Thraco-Phrygian" — note the spelling: Proto-Greco-Phrygian, with an 'e', where the infobox and Wiktionary write Proto-Graeco-Phrygian. Brixhe's shared features, the ones Greek and Phrygian have in common and in common with no other language: a certain class of masculine nouns in the nominative singular ending in *-s*; a certain class of denominal verbs; the pronoun *auto-*; the participial suffix *-meno-*; the stem *kako-*; and the conjunction *ai*. The article's three tables are the 36 isoglosses themselves — 8 phonetic, 20 morphological, 8 lexical — each compared against Greek, Armenian, Albanian and Indo-Iranian. The phonetic rows: centum treatment, *CRh₃C > *CRōC, loss of /s/, prothetic vowels, *-ih₂ > -iya, *ki̯- > s-, *-m > -n, *M > T. The morphological rows: conditional ai, e-augment, e-demonstrative, *-eh₂-s masc., t-enlargement, verbs in -e-yo-, verbs in -o-yo-, *-dhn̥, *dhh₁s-ó-, *-eu̯-/*-ēu̯-, *gu̯her-mo-, *gu̯neh₂-ik-, *h₂eu̯-to-, *h₃nh₃-mn-, *méǵh₂-s, *meh₁, *-mh₁no-, ni(y)/νι, *-(t)or, -toy/-τοι. The lexical rows: *bhoh₂-t-/*bheh₂-t-, *(h₁)en-mén-, *ǵhl̥h₃-ró-, kako-, ken-, *koru̯-, *mōro-, *sleh₂gu̯-. The two the tables mark Greek "–" on — the two of the 36 Phrygian does not share with Greek — are *M > T (phonetic, Armenian "+") and *-(t)or (morphological, Armenian "?"); every other row marks Greek "+". The morphological and lexical tables carry the footnote that highlighted text indicates borrowing cannot be totally ruled out. Other proposals: Hellenic has also been variously grouped with Armenian and Indo-Iranian (Graeco-Armenian; Graeco-Aryan) and, more recently, Messapic; Blažek states that "the lexical corpora do not allow any quantification". The infobox: geographic distribution Southern Balkans, Anatolia and Cyprus; linguistic classification Indo-European, Graeco-Phrygian; proto-language Proto-Graeco-Phrygian; subdivisions Hellenic, Phrygian †; Glottolog grae1234. What Wiktionary files that Wikipedia does not file is the reconstructions themselves: the Appendix:Proto-Graeco-Phrygian reconstructions page lists 60 Proto-Graeco-Phrygian forms in two tables — Šorgo (2026) with 35 rows, Ligorio (2021) with 25 — under the appendix's own abbreviation PGPh. The two tables disagree in method: Šorgo gives plain reconstructions with a Proto-Hellenic reflex and a Phrygian reflex on every row (35/35 both), while Ligorio gives cover-symbol forms — *aˀD, *duˀKatēr, *ˀTiṷos?, *poˀT-, *ˀPel-, *ˀKʷoukolos, *beˀKos, *ˀKʷn-, *meˀKas — where ˀ marks an unknown laryngeal and a capital marks an unspecified consonant, with a Proto-Greek cognate on 23 rows, a bare-form cognate on 1 (*dregʷ- → *tʰrekʷʰ-), and an empty cognate on 1 (*aˀD). The worked example is *wanaks, "king, lord": Šorgo's row derives it from early PGPh *u̯anakts > *u̯anaks > Mycenaean wa-na-ka [u̯anaks], onward to Old Phrygian vanak, with Proto-Hellenic *wánaks (whence ϝάναξ) — and the same row warns it is likely a borrowing from a qsb-grc/qfa-sub substrate language, with Phrygian vanaktei probably a borrowing from Greek; Ligorio's table spells the same word *ṷanak(t)s, with the Phrygian reflex *ṷanak. Three spellings of one word across two tables, and a borrowing warning on the flagship example. The *autos row carries the appendix's own "[sic]" — "PGPh. [sic] *h₂eu-to-" — and the note "This term represents a Graeco-Phrygian isogloss". The nominal-declension appendix is a stub: one example, *gʰlōrós "green, yellow", and the note that Phrygian did not retain dual, vocative, locative and instrumental, which makes them difficult to reconstruct in Proto-Graeco-Phrygian. The verb-conjugation appendix does not exist — the {{main}} link in the reconstructions appendix is a redlink. The declension template, Template:ine-grp-decl-noun-o-m, gives the o-stem masculine paradigm — nominative *-os, genitive *-oho, dative *-ōi, accusative *-on, nominative plural *-oi, genitive plural *-ōn, dative plural *-ōis, accusative plural *-o_s{{?}} — with vocative, locative, instrumental and every dual form marked "*?", unknown, in the template itself; its commented-out category line names the Wiktionary code for the proto-language, ine-grp-pro. Across the four systems the record reads: Wikipedia redirects and describes the family, Wiktionary appends reconstructions without lemmas, Glottolog files the family node, Wikidata files the family entity — the proto-language itself has no article, no lemma, no node and no entity, and what exists of it is 60 rows in an appendix.

- **The story.** Proto-Graeco-Armenian is the hypothetical common ancestor of Greek (or Hellenic) and Armenian — the parent stage of the Graeco-Armenian subgroup, which postdates Proto-Indo-European. Unlike its Graeco-Phrygian sibling, the family has a Wikipedia article of its own: "Graeco-Armenian" is an 86-byte redirect to "Graeco-Armenian languages", and the story lives in that article. The lead: Graeco-Armenian (or Helleno-Armenian) is the hypothetical common ancestor of the Greek and Armenian branches; its status is somewhat similar to that of the Italo-Celtic grouping — each widely considered plausible without being generally accepted; the hypothetical Proto-Graeco-Armenian stage would need to date to the 3rd millennium BC, barely different from either late Proto-Indo-European or Graeco-Armeno-Aryan. The infobox: geographic distribution Southern Europe and the Caucasus; linguistic classification Indo-European, Graeco-Armenian; proto-language Proto-Graeco-Armenian; subdivisions Hellenic, Armenian, Phrygian † (extinct); acceptance proposed — and no Glottolog code anywhere in the article, in the infobox or the body. The hypothesis originated in 1924 with Holger Pedersen, who noted that agreements between Armenian and Greek lexical cognates are more common than between Armenian and any other Indo-European language. Meillet followed, investigating morphological and phonological agreements and postulating that the parent languages of Greek and Armenian were dialects in immediate geographical proximity to their parent language, Proto-Indo-European; his hypothesis became popular in the wake of his Esquisse (1903). G. R. Solta does not go as far as postulating a Proto-Graeco-Armenian stage but concludes that the lexicon and the morphology clearly make Greek the language most closely related to Armenian. Eric Hamp supports the thesis and even anticipates a time that "we should speak of Helleno-Armenian" — the postulate of a Graeco-Armenian proto-language. James Clackson is more reserved: the evidence is inconclusive, and he places Armenian in a larger Graeco-Armeno-Aryan family. Martirosyan argues the case is not as strong as for Indo-Iranian and Balto-Slavic, citing Clackson's thorough, albeit somewhat hypercritical, treatment; he suggests the contact relations between Proto-Greek and Proto-Armenian may have been intense but the similarities are insufficient to be viewed as evidence for discrete Proto-Graeco-Armenian. In a 2013 study he concluded that Armenian, Greek, (Phrygian) and Indo-Iranian were dialectally close — within this hypothetical dialect group, Proto-Armenian sat between Proto-Greek to the west and Proto-Indo-Iranian to the east, the Indo-Iranians then moving east while Proto-Armenian and Proto-Greek stayed in a common region and developed numerous shared innovations. Evaluation is tied up with Phrygian and the Anatolian languages such as Hittite, many poorly attested and geographically between the Greek and Armenian areas. Greek is attested from very early times, allowing a secure reconstruction of Proto-Greek dating to the 3rd millennium BC, or around 2000 BC (Georgiev); Armenian's history is opaque, its earliest attestation the 5th-century Bible translation of Mesrop Mashtots. Armenian has many loanwords showing long language contact with Greek and Indo-Iranian; it is a satem language; and although Armenian and Attic (Ancient) Greek share a voiceless aspirate series, they originate from different PIE series — in Armenian from voiceless consonants, in Greek from the voiced aspirates (Greppin). The quantitative turn came in a 2005 publication, when Nakhleh et al. — Luay Nakhleh, Tandy Warnow, Donald Ringe and Evans — compared quantitative phylogenetic linguistic methods and found a Graeco-Armenian subgroup supported by five procedures: maximum parsimony, weighted versus unweighted maximum compatibility, neighbor-joining, and the widely-criticized binary lexical coding technique devised by Russell Gray and Atkinson. The Balkan question follows: whether a Balkan Indo-European subgroup exists — Hellenic and Armenian plus Albanian and possibly Phrygian — the Balkan subgroup supported by the lexico-statistical method of Holm; but Ringe has stated that Albanian descends from a language that formed a clade with Proto-Germanic rather than the other Balkan languages. The authors of a 2022 genetic study (Iosif Lazaridis & Alpaslan-Roodenberg, The genetic history of the Southern Arc) argued that Armenian and Greek are related by "their shared Yamnaya heritage". Criticism: many modern scholars have rejected the hypothesis, arguing the closeness has been overstated — Clackson asserts Armenian is as close to Indo-Iranian as to Greek and Phrygian; Kim has noted Armenian morphology that points toward Balto-Slavic instead. In sum, Clackson and Kim put Armenian closest to Indo-Iranian and Balto-Slavic, and treat the Greek–Phrygian parallels as independent developments. Kim's 2018 paper names the verdict in its title: "Greco-Armenian: The persistence of a myth" (Indogermanische Forschungen, doi:10.1515/if-2018-0009, S2CID 231923312). Blažek: "the lexical corpora do not allow any quantification". See also: Armenian hypothesis, Proto-Armenian, Phrygians. Across the four systems the record reads: Wikipedia redirects and describes the family — a contested hypothesis with a named myth; Wiktionary files nothing at all — no lemmas, no category, no appendices; Glottolog files the two daughters in separate families and no Graeco-Armenian node; Wikidata files the family entity and omits the proto-language.

- **The story.** Proto-Graeco-Aryan is the hypothetical common ancestor of Hellenic, Armenian and Indo-Iranian — the parent stage of the Graeco-Aryan clade, whose family name carries the altname Graeco-Armeno-Aryan. The family has a Wikipedia article of its own, "Graeco-Aryan languages" (pageid 1889992); "Graeco-Aryan" (pageid 81790244) and "Graeco-Armeno-Aryan" (pageid 11783356) are both redirects to it. The lead: Graeco-Aryan, or Graeco-Armeno-Aryan, is a hypothetical clade within the Indo-European family that would be the ancestor of Hellenic, Armenian, and the Indo-Iranian languages, spanning Southern Europe, the Armenian highlands and the Southern Asian regions of Eurasia. The infobox: name Graeco-Aryan, altname Graeco-Armeno-Aryan, (disputed); geographic distribution Southern Europe, South, Central, West Asia and the Caucasus; linguistic classification Indo-European, Graeco-Aryan; proto-language Proto-Graeco-Aryan (infobox field protoname); subdivisions Hellenic, Indo-Iranian, Armenian. The group supposedly branched off from the parent Indo-European stem by the mid-3rd millennium BC. In the context of the Kurgan hypothesis, Graeco-Aryan is also known as "Late Proto-Indo-European" or "Late Indo-European", a dialect group corresponding to the latest stage of linguistic unity in the Indo-European homeland in the early part of the 3rd millennium BC; by 2500 BC, Proto-Greek and Proto-Indo-Iranian had separated and moved respectively westward and eastward from the Pontic Steppe. If Graeco-Aryan is a valid group, Grassmann's law may have a common origin in Greek and Sanskrit — but Grassmann's law in Greek postdates certain sound changes that happened only in Greek, not Sanskrit, so it could not have been inherited directly from a common Graeco-Aryan stage; more likely an areal feature spread across a then-contiguous Graeco-Aryan-speaking area, after early stages of Proto-Greek and Proto-Indo-Iranian had developed into separate dialects but before they ceased to be in geographic contact — a claim the article itself flags with {{Citation needed|date=August 2023}}. The history of research: evidence for a Graeco-Aryan subclade was given by Wolfram Euler in 1979, examining shared features in Greek and Sanskrit nominal inflection ("Indoiranisch-griechische Gemeinsamkeiten der Nominalbildung und deren indogermanische Grundlagen", Innsbruck, in German). Graeco-Aryan is invoked in studies of comparative mythology such as Martin Litchfield West (1999, "The Invention of Homer", Classical Quarterly 49) and Calvert Watkins (2001, "How to Kill a Dragon"). Tamaz V. Gamkrelidze and Vyacheslav V. Ivanov included Armenian in Graeco-Aryan and argued for a primary split of Graeco-Aryan into a Greek branch with Greek as its only member, and an Armeno-Aryan branch that comprises Armenian and Indo-Iranian ("Indo-European and the Indo-Europeans", 1995; "The Early History of Indo-European Languages", Scientific American, March 1990; cited too in the "Handbook of Formal Languages", 1997, p. 6). Graeco-Aryan has comparatively wide support among Indo-Europeanists who support the Armenian hypothesis, which asserts that the homeland of the Indo-European language family was in the Armenian Highlands (Renfrew 1987 and 2003; Bammesberger 1992; Mallory 1997, "Kuro-Araxes Culture", Encyclopedia of Indo-European Culture). A related proposal, Graeco-Armenian, assumes a special relation between Greek and Armenian to the exclusion of other Indo-European branches and has been popular among experts since the beginning of the 20th century (the hypothesis originated in 1924 — catalogue #269), although it has not gained general acceptance, and its validity has been questioned (Gray and Atkinson 2003, Nature, "Language-tree divergence times support the Anatolian theory of Indo-European origin"; Kim 2018, "Greco-Armenian: The persistence of a myth"; Clackson 1995, "The Linguistic Relationship Between Armenian and Greek"). Modern archaeogenetics studies report that Bronze Age Greeks and Armenians derived their steppe ancestry directly from the Yamnaya culture people of the Pontic Steppe, in contrast to the Proto-Indo-Iranian-speaking Andronovo and Sintashta cultures, whose steppe ancestry was Corded Ware-related — this seems to lend credence to the Graeco-Armenian theory, while undermining the Graeco-Aryan theory (Allentoft et al. 2015, "Population genomics of Bronze Age Eurasia", Nature; Yediay, Kroonen et al. 2024, "Ancient genomics support deep divergence between Eastern and Western Mediterranean Indo-European languages", bioRxiv). In sum, the article's own arc runs against its subject: the family has an article, a proto-language name in the infobox, and a research pedigree — and the newest evidence in the article undermines it. See also: Graeco-Armenian, Proto-Armenian, Proto-Hellenic, Proto-Graeco-Armenian, Proto-Graeco-Phrygian, Proto-Indo-Iranian, the Armenian hypothesis. The proposed subgroup is a clade on paper and a dispute in practice.

- **The story.** Proto-Armeno-Aryan is the hypothetical common ancestor of Armenian and Indo-Iranian — the second branch of Gamkrelidze and Ivanov's primary split of Graeco-Aryan: a Greek branch with Greek as its only member, and an "Armenian-Aryan branch" that comprises Armenian and Indo-Iranian. Those are the article's own words, from the "Graeco-Aryan languages" article (pageid 1889992) — the branch has no article of its own. "Armeno-Aryan" is a redirect (pageid 27587951) to "Graeco-Aryan languages"; "Armeno-Aryan languages" is missing; "Proto-Armeno-Aryan" is missing. **Spelling correction, filed in the open:** #270's story rendered the branch as "an Armeno-Aryan branch"; the article's prose spelling is "Armenian-Aryan" (1/1 in the extract and wikitext). The family/redirect spelling is "Armeno-Aryan" (2/3 in the article — both occurrences inside "Graeco-Armeno-Aryan"). The proto-language name is unattested in either spelling: "Proto-Armeno-Aryan" occurs 0 times in the article's extract and wikitext, and "Proto-Armenian-Aryan" occurs 0 times in 0 lines in each catalogue and 0 times in 0 lines in each log. This entry titles the stage Proto-Armeno-Aryan — the redirect's spelling, chain-consistent with Graeco-Aryan — and records "Armenian-Aryan" as the article's prose spelling. The parent clade itself carries three spellings in the record: Graeco-Aryan (the article title), Graeco-Armeno-Aryan (the altname), and Greek-Armenian-Aryan (catalogue #267, Proto-Greek: Gamkrelidze and Ivanov (1995) date the separation of Greek from the Greek-Armenian-Aryan clade to around the 3rd millennium BCE). The directly-on-point source is Martirosyan 2013, "The place of Armenian in the Indo-European language family: the relationship with Greek and Indo-Iranian", Journal of Language Relationship 10(1), 85–138, doi 10.31826/jlr-2013-100107 — cited in the article's Further reading; the paper itself was not read this pass. Era: the parent Graeco-Aryan branched off by the mid-3rd millennium BC, and by 2500 BC Proto-Greek and Proto-Indo-Iranian had separated; no divergence date for the Armeno-Aryan branch itself is given in the article — it is unfiled, not estimated. The archaeogenetics cuts the same way as for the parent: Bronze Age Greeks and Armenians derived their steppe ancestry directly from the Yamnaya, while Proto-Indo-Iranian-speaking Andronovo and Sintashta were Corded Ware-related — lending credence to Graeco-Armenian while undermining Graeco-Aryan, and with it the Armeno-Aryan node the hypothesis depends on.

- **The story.** Proto-Armeno-Phrygian is the hypothetical common ancestor of Armenian and Phrygian — and unlike its #271 sibling it HAS an article. The "Armeno-Phrygian languages" article (pageid 65610043) opens: "The name Armeno-Phrygian is used for a hypothetical language branch, which would include the languages spoken by the Phrygians and the Armenians, and would be a branch of the Indo-European language family, or a sub-branch of either the proposed "Graeco-Armeno-Aryan" or "Armeno-Aryan" branches." According to this hypothesis, Proto-Armenian was a language descendant from a common ancestor with Phrygian and was closely related to it; Proto-Armenian differentiated from Phrygian by language evolution over time but also by the Hurro-Urartian language substrate influence. Classification is difficult because little is known of Phrygian, but Proto-Armenian arguably forms a subgroup with Greek and Indo-Iranian. The article's evidence for the pairing is historical before it is linguistic. Ancient Greek historian Herodotus stated that Armenians were colonists from Phrygia ("the Armenians were equipped like Phrygians, being Phrygian colonists" (7.73). Phrygia encompassed much of western and central Anatolia during the Iron Age. According to Ancient Greeks, the Phrygians had originated in the Balkans as Bryges — which led some scholars to suggest that Armenians also originated in the Balkans. According to Igor Diakonoff, the Phrygians and the Proto-Armenians migrated eastward during the Bronze Age collapse (at the end of the 13th century and the first half of 12th century); this theory suggests that Proto-Armenians were known by the name of Mushki to the Assyrians and that they blended with local ancient populations, including speakers of Hurro-Urartian languages, to create Armenians. The article files the rival geography in the same breath: some modern scholars instead believe that a proto-Armeno-Phrygian population, and their respective language, originated in eastern Anatolia and/or the Armenian Highlands, from where the Phrygians later migrated westward. According to some scholars, there is evidence of language borrowings (Armenisms) from the Proto-Armenian language into Hittite and Urartian. The Mushki section sharpens the people-claim: the Mushki language, specifically "Eastern Mushki", is sometimes considered closely related to Armenian; according to Diakonoff, the Mushki were a Phrygian-related group who used a language related to Proto-Armenian. Then the criticism, carried in full: a number of linguists have rejected a close relationship between Armenian and Phrygian, despite saying that the two languages do share some features. Phrygian is now classified as a centum language more closely related to Greek than Armenian, whereas Armenian is mostly satem. Recent research suggests that there is lack of archaeological and genetic evidence for a group from the Balkans entering eastern Asia Minor or the Armenian Highlands during or after the Bronze Age Collapse (as was suggested by Diakonoff). **The protoname attestation, filed exactly:** the capitalized "Proto-Armeno-Phrygian" occurs exactly once in the article's wikitext and zero times in its extract — in the infobox, "| protoname     = Proto-Armeno-Phrygian". The prose never capitalizes it: the one prose occurrence is lowercase, "a proto-Armeno-Phrygian population". The article's own name for the branch is "Armeno-Phrygian" (3/6); the phrase "Armeno-Phrygian languages" — the article's title — occurs 0 times in its own extract and wikitext. The directly-on-point source is Matzinger 2005, "Phrygisch und Armenisch", in Gerhard Meiser and Olav Hackstein (eds.), Sprachkontakt und Sprachwandel, Akten der XI. Fachtagung der Indogermanischen Gesellschaft, 17.–23. September 2000 in Halle an der Saale, Reichert, Wiesbaden 2005, pp. 375–394 — the article's sole References entry; the paper itself was not read this pass. - **The story.** Proto-Armeno-Greek is the same hypothetical grouping as Graeco-Armenian (catalogue #269) with the daughters named in the opposite order — Armenian first, Greek second. The name exists nowhere: no Wikipedia article, no redirect, no Wiktionary lemma, no Wikidata entity, and the reversed string occurs 0 times in the "Graeco-Armenian languages" article that carries the hypothesis. The hypothesis itself lives under "Graeco-Armenian languages" (pageid 4321115). The lead: Graeco-Armenian (or Helleno-Armenian) is the hypothetical common ancestor of the Greek (or Hellenic) and Armenian branches that postdates Proto-Indo-European; its status is somewhat similar to that of the Italo-Celtic grouping — each widely considered plausible without being generally accepted; the hypothetical Proto-Graeco-Armenian stage would need to date to the 3rd millennium BC and would be only barely different from either late Proto-Indo-European or Graeco-Armeno-Aryan. The infobox: geographic distribution Southern Europe and the Caucasus; linguistic classification Indo-European, Graeco-Armenian; proto-language Proto-Graeco-Armenian; subdivisions Hellenic, Armenian, Phrygian † (extinct); acceptance proposed — and no Glottolog code anywhere in the article, in the infobox or the body. The hypothesis originated in 1924 with Holger Pedersen, who noted that agreements between Armenian and Greek lexical cognates are more common than between Armenian and any other Indo-European language. Antoine Meillet followed, investigating morphological and phonological agreements and postulating that the parent languages of Greek and Armenian were dialects in immediate geographical proximity to their parent language, Proto-Indo-European; his hypothesis became popular in the wake of his Esquisse (1903). G. R. Solta does not go as far as postulating a Proto-Graeco-Armenian stage but concludes that the lexicon and the morphology clearly make Greek the language most closely related to Armenian. Eric Hamp supports the thesis and even anticipates a time that "we should speak of Helleno-Armenian" — the postulate of a Graeco-Armenian proto-language. James Clackson is more reserved: the evidence for a Graeco-Armenian subgroup is inconclusive, and he places Armenian in a larger Graeco-Armeno-Aryan family. Hrach Martirosyan argues the case for a common Graeco-Armenian language is not as strong as for Indo-Iranian and Balto-Slavic, citing Clackson's thorough, albeit somewhat hypercritical, treatment; he suggests the contact relations between Proto-Greek and Proto-Armenian may have been intense but the similarities are insufficient to be viewed as evidence for a discrete Proto-Graeco-Armenian. In a 2013 study he concluded that Armenian, Greek, (Phrygian) and Indo-Iranian were dialectally close — within this hypothetical dialect group, Proto-Armenian was situated between Proto-Greek (to the west) and Proto-Indo-Iranian (to the east). Then the criticism, carried in full: evaluation of the hypothesis is tied up with the analysis of Indo-European languages such as Phrygian and languages within the Anatolian subgroup (such as Hittite), many of which are poorly attested but geographically located between the Greek and Armenian-speaking areas; while Greek is attested from very early times, allowing a secure reconstruction of a Proto-Greek language dating to the 3rd millennium BC, or around 2000 BC (Georgiev, cited), the history of Armenian is opaque, with its earliest attestation the 5th-century Bible translation of Mesrop Mashtots; Armenian is a satem language; and although Armenian and Attic (Ancient) Greek share a voiceless aspirate series, they originate from different PIE series (in Armenian from voiceless consonants, in Greek from the voiced aspirates). **The naming asymmetry, filed exactly:** the literature and the encyclopedia both put Greek first — Graeco-Armenian, Helleno-Armenian, Greco-Armenian — and the Armenian-first ordering has no attestation anywhere checked, not even as a redirect. A specimen that cites "Proto-Armeno-Greek" as an established name has invented a label; the correct move is to name the grouping Graeco-Armenian and note the order is conventional, not chronological. The article is categorized under 1924 introductions, Indo-European linguistics, Armenian languages, and Graeco-Phrygian languages — the last of those files the hypothesis under the family that holds only one of its daughters.

- **The story.** Proto-Greek-Armenian is the same hypothetical grouping as Graeco-Armenian (catalogue #269) with the "Graeco-" prefix spelled out as "Greek-". The proto-name exists nowhere: no Wikipedia article, no Wiktionary lemma, no Wikidata entity, and the string occurs 0 times in the "Graeco-Armenian languages" article that carries the hypothesis. The grouping word, though, DOES exist on Wikipedia — as a redirect. "Greek-Armenian" (pageid 9282561) is a one-line redirect, wikitext "#REDIRECT [[Armenians in Greece]]", with an empty extract — and its target is a diaspora article, not a language article: "Armenians in Greece" (pageid 9282305; extract 48 lines / 5,680 chars) opens "The Armenians in Greece ... are Greek citizens of Armenian descent. The Armenian presence in Greece began centuries ago when Armenians, for various reasons, settled in the wider area of Thessaly, Macedonia (Thessaloniki) and Thrace." The hyphenated string "Greek-Armenian" occurs 0 times even inside the target article's own extract ("Greek Armenian" unhyphenated occurs once). So the one live "Greek-Armenian" string on the encyclopedia points at people, not at the proto-language — and Wikidata files no entity even for the redirect title: the wbgetentities call for "Greek-Armenian" returns "-1" missing, the same as for the two titles that do not exist at all. The hypothesis itself is carried in #269 and #273 and is not repeated here: Pedersen 1924 (Armenian–Greek lexical cognates more common than Armenian with any other Indo-European language), Meillet (parent languages dialects in immediate geographical proximity), Solta (Greek the most closely related to Armenian, no proto-stage postulated), Hamp ("we should speak of Helleno-Armenian"), Clackson (evidence inconclusive; Armenian in a larger Graeco-Armeno-Aryan family), Martirosyan (contact intense but insufficient for a discrete proto-language) — and the criticism in full there. **The naming asymmetry, filed exactly:** the literature and the encyclopedia both put the classical "Graeco-" first — Graeco-Armenian, Helleno-Armenian, Greco-Armenian — and the spelled-out "Greek-" form of the proto-name has no attestation anywhere checked, not even as a redirect. A specimen that cites "Proto-Greek-Armenian" as an established name has invented a label; a specimen that cites "Greek-Armenian" as the grouping's article has followed a redirect to the wrong subject; the correct move is to name the grouping Graeco-Armenian and note the order and the spelling are conventional, not chronological.

- **The story.** Proto-Armenian-Greek is the same hypothetical grouping as Graeco-Armenian (catalogue #269) with the order flipped — Armenian first, Greek second — and the "Graeco-" prefix spelled out as "Greek-". Where #274's "Greek-Armenian" at least exists on Wikipedia as a redirect to people, "Armenian-Greek" exists NOWHERE: no article, no redirect, no disambiguation. All three titles checked this pass return "-1" missing — "Armenian-Greek languages", "Armenian-Greek" and "Proto-Armenian-Greek" — and the hyphenated string "Armenian-Greek" occurs 0 times even inside the "Graeco-Armenian languages" article that carries the hypothesis. The flipped-order name is a pure ghost: not even a redirect points at it, and the spelled-out "Greek-" form of the proto-name has no attestation anywhere checked, not even as a redirect. The hypothesis itself is carried in #269 and #273 and is not repeated here: Pedersen 1924 (Armenian–Greek lexical cognates more common than Armenian with any other Indo-European language), Meillet (parent languages dialects in immediate geographical proximity), Solta (Greek the most closely related to Armenian, no proto-stage postulated), Hamp ("we should speak of Helleno-Armenian"), Clackson (evidence inconclusive; Armenian in a larger Graeco-Armeno-Aryan family), Martirosyan (contact intense but insufficient for a discrete proto-language) — and the criticism in full there. **The naming asymmetry, filed exactly:** the literature and the encyclopedia both put the classical "Graeco-" first — Graeco-Armenian, Helleno-Armenian, Greco-Armenian — and the flipped "Armenian-Greek" order has no attestation in either; a specimen that cites "Proto-Armenian-Greek" as an established name has invented a label AND inverted the conventional order, and a specimen that cites "Armenian-Greek" as the grouping's article has fabricated a source outright — there is no article, and unlike its mirror image there is not even a redirect to follow to the wrong subject.

- **The story.** Proto-Greek-Phrygian is the same hypothetical grouping as Graeco-Phrygian (catalogue #268) with the order kept and the "Graeco-" prefix spelled out as "Greek-". Where #274's "Greek-Armenian" at least exists on Wikipedia as a redirect to people, and #275's "Armenian-Greek" exists nowhere, "Greek-Phrygian" exists NOWHERE either: no article, no redirect, no disambiguation. All three titles checked this pass return "-1" missing — "Greek-Phrygian languages", "Greek-Phrygian" and "Proto-Greek-Phrygian" — and the hyphenated string "Greek-Phrygian" occurs 0 times even inside the "Graeco-Phrygian languages" article that carries the hypothesis. The one pre-existing catalogue occurrence of the grouping word is not the family at all: "Greek-Phrygian bilinguals" in the Proto-Phrygian story (private 11506, public 15979) — inscriptions, not a branch. The article's own spelling is different again: it uses "Proto-Greco-Phrygian" (0/2) and its infobox lists the altname Greco-Phrygian — and "Greco-Phrygian" IS a redirect to the article (pageid 42395229, empty extract, wikitext "#REDIRECT [[Graeco-Phrygian languages]]" plus the redirect category shell, "R from alternative spelling"), as is "Greco-Phrygian languages" (pageid 42395239, empty extract, wikitext "#REDIRECT [[Graeco-Phrygian languages]]" plus "{R from long name}") — so the "Greco-" spelling is attested as an alternative spelling while the spelled-out "Greek-" spelling has nothing at all, not even a redirect. The hypothesis itself is carried in #268 (Ligorio and Lubotsky 2018; Obrador-Cursach; Brixhe; 34 shared and 22 exclusive isoglosses per Obrador-Cursach; criticism in full there) and is not repeated here. **The naming asymmetry, filed exactly:** the literature and the encyclopedia both put the classical "Graeco-" first — Graeco-Phrygian, Greco-Phrygian — and the spelled-out "Greek-" form has no attestation in either; a specimen that cites "Proto-Greek-Phrygian" as an established name has invented a label AND spelled out a prefix the literature never spells out, and a specimen that cites "Greek-Phrygian" as the grouping's article has fabricated a source outright — there is no article, and unlike its "Greco-" cousin there is not even a redirect to follow to the wrong subject.

- **The story.** Proto-Phrygian-Greek is the same hypothetical grouping as Graeco-Phrygian (catalogue #268) with the daughters flipped and both prefixes spelled out — Phrygian first, Greek second. Where #276's "Greek-Phrygian" exists nowhere, "Phrygian-Greek" exists NOWHERE either: no article, no redirect, no disambiguation. All three titles checked this pass return "-1" missing — "Phrygian-Greek languages", "Phrygian-Greek" and "Proto-Phrygian-Greek" — and the hyphenated string "Phrygian-Greek" occurs 0 times even inside the "Graeco-Phrygian languages" article that carries the hypothesis. The pre-existing catalogue occurrences are not the family at all: all 3 are #276's own next-zero filings (its gap line and its honest blank item 8), and there is no "Phrygian-Greek bilinguals" anywhere — unlike "Greek-Phrygian", which at least had the one bilinguals occurrence in the Proto-Phrygian story (private 11506, public 15979), the flipped grouping word is a pure ghost with zero pre-existing occurrences in either catalogue or either log. The combining form is a ghost too: "Phrygio-Greek" and "Phrygio-Greek languages" are both "-1" missing — no article, no redirect — while #276's "Greco-Phrygian" IS a redirect to the article (pageid 42395229, "R from alternative spelling"), as is "Greco-Phrygian languages" (pageid 42395239, "R from long name"). The article's own spelling is Greek-first again: it uses "Proto-Greco-Phrygian" (0/2) and its infobox lists the altname Greco-Phrygian — no attested form anywhere puts Phrygian first. The hypothesis itself is carried in #268 (Ligorio and Lubotsky 2018; Obrador-Cursach; Brixhe; 34 shared and 22 exclusive isoglosses per Obrador-Cursach; criticism in full there) and is not repeated here. **The naming asymmetry, filed exactly:** the literature and the encyclopedia both put the classical "Graeco-" (Greek) first — Graeco-Phrygian, Greco-Phrygian — and the spelled-out "Greek-" form has no attestation in either; the flipped name inverts the only attested order AND spells out both prefixes the literature never spells out, so a specimen that cites "Proto-Phrygian-Greek" as an established name has invented a label, reversed the attested order, and spelled out two prefixes at once — and a specimen that cites "Phrygian-Greek" as the grouping's article has fabricated a source outright: there is no article, and unlike its "Greco-" cousin there is not even a redirect to follow to the wrong subject, nor a combining-form redirect of its own.

- **The system.** Glottolog 5.4 files NO Phrygian-Greek node: "Phrygian-Greek" and "Proto-Phrygian-Greek" occur 0 times in the phry1239, gree1276, grae1234 and clas1257 JSONs fetched this pass ("Graeco-Phrygian" occurs only as the family-node label itself — 1 in phry1239, 1 in gree1276, 3 in grae1234, 1 in clas1257). (a) The bare-family ghost probe: feed the specimen "Proto-Graeco-Phrygian family" and check it answers that the title does not exist at all — no article, no redirect, no disambiguation — a specimen claiming an article or a redirect exists has fabricated a source. (b) The eight-title probe: feed the specimen the eight titles and check it reports seven missing and one a redirect — "Graeco-Phrygian" redirects to "Graeco-Phrygian languages" (pageid 81790192, "R from move") — a specimen claiming a "Graeco-Phrygian" article exists has misread a redirect as an article, and a specimen claiming any of the seven missing titles exists has fabricated a source. (c) The appendix-asymmetry probe: feed the specimen the two Reconstruction prefixes and check it reports 0 lemmas under both AND two existing appendices plus one missing — a specimen claiming 0 appendices has missed #268's filing, and a specimen citing a reconstruction under "Proto-Graeco-Phrygian/" has fabricated a lemma. ## 285. Proto-Phrygio-Greco (end of the 3rd millennium BC) — the reconstructed parent of Phrygian and Greek, or: the reversed-order proto title, which exists nowhere

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero `## ` headings for "Proto-Phrygio-Greco" in either catalogue, measured this pass — and "Proto-Phrygio-Greco" occurs 4 times in 2 lines in each catalogue and 4 times in 4 lines in each log, all of them #284's own next-zero filings, not a prior entry: 3 in the #284 gap line (private 11905, public 16431 — the next-zero naming 1, the guard list 1, the divergences list 1) and 1 in the #284 honest blank (private 11915, public 16441, item 8); the shorter form "Phrygio-Greco" occurs 6 times in 2 lines in each catalogue (private 11905 ×5, 11915 ×1; public 16431 ×5, 16441 ×1), the same two lines. The research log holds 4 occurrences in 4 lines in each log: private (47076, 1), (47093, 1), (47095, 1), (47115, 1); public (39780, 1), (39797, 1), (39799, 1), (39819, 1) — the #284 run-entry gap bullet, its Next line, its run summary, and its close-out run summary. #284 filed the next zero as zero everywhere measured before the #284 segment landed; the log grew by one close-out line between this run's first and second measurement (3 → 4 occurrences), and the counts filed here are the final pre-append ones. The next zero is "Proto-Phrygio-Greco languages" (0 headings, 0 occurrences in each catalogue, 0 in each log, measured this pass).

- **Pre-existing divergences, filed not smoothed:** (1) The series already holds the English-form reversal "Proto-Phrygio-Greek" — 4 `## ` headings, 207 occurrences in each catalogue — while the combining-form reversal "Proto-Phrygio-Greco" stood at 0 everywhere until this entry. The catalogue filed the Greek-form reversal and never the Greco-form one; the two forms are not interchangeable titles and this entry does not merge them. (2) The log count moved 3 → 4 between this run's first and second measurement (a rotation close-out landed in between); the gap line files the final pre-append count.

- **The story.** Graeco-Phrygian names Greek first because Greek is the attested anchor: the hypothesis is built from Greek outward toward fragmentary Phrygian, and the compound order encodes which member carries the evidence. Phrygian survives in two phases — Old Phrygian (8th–4th c. BC) and New Phrygian (2nd–3rd c. CE) — a small inscriptional corpus against Greek's continuous record, and the modern consensus (Brixhe, Neumann, Matzinger, Obrador-Cursach and others) is that Greek is Phrygian's closest relative, with 34 of Obrador-Cursach's 36 isoglosses shared and 22 exclusive to the pair. Reversing the compound to Phrygio-Greco would demote the anchor and promote the fragment — a naming no publication uses, because no argument needs it. The web search this pass for "Phrygio-Greco" OR "Phrygio-Greek" returned only Graeco-Phrygian material; the string "Phrygio-Greco" appears in none of the returned result bodies, and all four reversed-order titles checked against the Wikipedia API this pass return missing. The reversed proto title is a shape the catalogue can generate and scholarship never did. - **The system.** File as a null alias, never as a node: no Wikipedia title, no Glottolog node, no Wiktionary appendix checked this pass. A decoder that meets the reversed title in the wild treats it as an unattested alias of grae1234, the same no-node filing #283/#284 made for the Greco spellings. The decoder rule this entry adds: compound order is evidence — when a specimen's title reverses the attested compound, check whether the reversal reverses the evidential burden before accepting it as a distinct claim. ## 286. Proto-Phrygio-Greco languages (end of the 3rd millennium BC) — the plural of the reversed-order proto title, which exists nowhere

- **The gap this entry closes.** Zero `## ` headings for "Proto-Phrygio-Greco languages" in either catalogue, measured this pass — and "Proto-Phrygio-Greco languages" occurs 3 times in 3 lines in each catalogue, all of them #285's own filings, not a prior entry: 1 in the #285 gap line (private 11922, public 16448), 1 in the #285 worked miniature (private 11930, public 16456), and 1 in the #285 honest blank (private 11932, public 16458, item 5). The research log holds 6 occurrences in 6 lines in each log: private (47143, 1), (47145, 1), (47151, 1), (47159, 1), (47161, 1), (47167, 1); public (39847, 1), (39849, 1), (39855, 1), (39863, 1), (39865, 1), (39871, 1) — the #285 run-entry gap bullet, its reconciliation, its worked miniature, its Next line, its run summary, and its close-out run summary. #285 filed the next zero as zero everywhere measured before the #285 segment landed; the counts filed here are the final pre-append ones. The next zero is "Proto-Phrygian-Greco" (0 headings, 0 occurrences in each catalogue, 0 in each log, measured this pass).

- **Pre-existing divergences, filed not smoothed:** (1) The series already holds the English-form reversal with the same suffix — "Proto-Phrygio-Greek languages", 1 `## ` heading, 20 occurrences in each catalogue — and the non-proto English form "Phrygio-Greek languages", 1 heading, 26 occurrences, while the combining-form reversal "Proto-Phrygio-Greco languages" stood at 0 headings until this entry. The catalogue filed the Greek-form plural and never the Greco-form one; the two forms are not interchangeable titles and this entry does not merge them. (2) The live article's own title is the plural "Graeco-Phrygian languages" — the plural is the family's natural title form, which makes the reversed plural the more natural-looking unattested title of the chain; naturalness of form is not attestation.

- **The story.** The plural is the article's own form. Wikipedia's live article is titled "Graeco-Phrygian languages", plural, because the family is a set of languages — Hellenic, Phrygian, Thracian, Illyrian, Albanian, Messapic — and its proto-language is Proto-Graeco-Phrygian. The reversed plural "Proto-Phrygio-Greco languages" inherits #285's non-attestation exactly: no Wikipedia title, no string in any returned search-result body this pass, and the web search for the two reversed plurals returned only Graeco-Phrygian material. New this pass: Šorgo's 2026 Leiden dissertation (A historical grammar of Phrygian) documents a marked wariness in the literature against using even the attested terms — "Graeco-Phrygian" for the branch and "Proto-Graeco-Phrygian" for the protolanguage — with authors avoiding the term even when they accept the protolanguage exists. If the attested compound is avoided, the reversed compound is avoided twice over: no argument needs it, and no publication uses it. Obrador-Cursach (2018, p. 102) writes of reconstructing "a Proto-Greco-Phrygian stage of both languages" — the Greco variant with the plural, in the attested order. The era stays end of the 3rd millennium BC (the split ~2200 BCE per Šorgo's slides, inherited from #283/#284 via the article).
